Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 35 "22. Cocking a Snook at Death, and Getting Away with It Does the Personification of Death Make It Less Scary" — Asking whether Pratchett's personified Death makes mortality less scary, the chapter reads Reaper Man's claim that belief created Death—the moment a living thing grasped non-existence, Death came into being—as a co-arising of dualistic concepts, and surveys psychopomps from Thanatos and Azrael to Yama and even modern assisted-dying organizations. Windle Poons's several kinds of death in Reaper Man ground the distinctions between animalistic, mindistic, and personistic death, showing that whether someone counts as dead can turn on which conception of the person is doing the counting. The closing meditation on Pratchett's own posterior cortical atrophy and the documentary Choosing to Die argues that conceptualizing death in advance—in living wills and bedside conversations with loved ones—is what lets us meet 'THERE'S JUST ME' a little less afraid.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 22 "11. Immortality Is Misery" — In dialogue with Deadpool himself, John Altmann tests whether immortality is a blessing: Bentham's utilitarianism would prize a healing factor that lets Wade dive into a gamma meltdown to save the Southern Hemisphere for free, and Nietzsche would hail him as an Übermensch for refusing the Mithras Directive's Messiah and preserving humanity's freedom to create its own values rather than adopt herd morality. Bernard Williams gets the last word: since personalities become fixed—Wade stays a mercenary across every run, Zenpool notwithstanding—an endless life curdles into boredom and misery, so immortality is punishment rather than power unless one could radically change who one is.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 12 "2. A Death Worth Living" — Argues that dying in the Murder House or the Hotel Cortez removes death's usual harms - Ben Harmon can reunite with his ghost family and keep counseling patients, and Liz Taylor's chosen death brings reunion with Tristan plus open-ended projects protecting the hotel - but then poses Bernard Williams's boredom problem: finite projects run out over eternity and replacing them would make you a different person. Richard Taylor's Sisyphus and the Hotel's contented Laundress supply the answer that repetitive tasks embraced as meaningful can sustain even an immortal afterlife.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 20 "9. Voodoo Hoodoo" — Explains Coven's Spirit Wars through the real history and philosophy of New Orleans Voodoo: the historical Marie Laveaux as healer and Voodoo Queen, Tituba as the link between witchcraft and Voodoo in Salem, the loa and spirit possession (Maya Deren's gros bon ange), zombies and the bokor, Papa Legba as trickster gatekeeper rather than Satan, and the seven gates of Guinee. It argues that Laveau's annual innocent and Fiona's failed soul-selling enact the Voodoo cosmology in which hell is the earthly entrapment of the soul - and, as Legba says, 'everybody pays.'
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 29 "16. Please Don’t Kill Me! (But if You Do, Could You Make a Video )" — Reads Roanoke through Stephen Cave's Mortality Paradox, Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, and Terror Management Theory: the Blood Moon ghosts embody inevitable death, dramatic irony mirrors our denial, reality-TV fame and Twitter followers are the modern immortality project (Agnes's 'I just wanted to be on TV', the superfans killed mid-broadcast), and the Polks' ritual cannibalism is symbolic power over extinction. Montaigne's 'to study philosophy is to learn to die' and his savoring of fleeting moments close the chapter, with Shelby - who alone submits to death without fiction - as the figure who actually escapes the terror.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" — Yang frames Eleanor's predicament as a dilemma: a finite life seems drained of value by its ending, while an immortal one collapses into boredom or into the disconnection of the 802 memory-wiped reboots. Camus's Sisyphus and Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view prove inadequate, so he adopts Susan Wolf's account of meaning as loving what deserves to be loved, which Eleanor's study of moral philosophy, her friendships, and her romance with Chidi satisfy even without God or eternity. John Martin Fischer's narrative approach then redeems the reboots as self-contained episodes, and Eleanor's note to herself in Scanlon's book shows memory wipes need not sever the story of a life.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 33 "18. Heaven Is Other People" — Mayward examines the show's eschatology, arguing its points algorithm critiques the popular picture of Hell as eternal conscious torment, in the lineage of Jonathan Edwards, while missing historic Christian teaching about embodied resurrection. He then reads the series through Levinas, for whom ethics arises in the face-to-face encounter with the Other prior to any impersonal judgment, a structure mirrored in the show's two-shots and in Eleanor's spontaneous good deeds done before she understands them, and through Dietrich Bonhoeffer's 'religionless Christianity', in which Michael's self-sacrifice and the humans' repentance enact responsibility for neighbors without hope of reward. Salvation in the show is intersubjective transformation: where Sartre said Hell is other people, The Good Place suggests Heaven is other people.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 27 "16. The Defeat of Death" — JD Lyonhart asks which of four philosophies of death Endgame adopts: embracing death as natural balance (Thanos's view, where the Snap keeps life in check), denying it, grimly accepting it, or defeating it. Opening with Schopenhauer's 'Death is the muse of philosophy,' he sketches Plato's Meno argument that the slave boy's innate knowledge requires a pre-existing, hence immortal, soul, and then argues the film starts with Tony's acceptance of death as final before completing a trajectory that runs from Yinsen's sacrificial death in the cave, through Tony's cruciform fall through the wormhole in The Avengers, to a Christ-like defeat of death in Endgame where Tony dies facing death head-on so others may live. The film avoids cheap denial by sitting in five years of grief before the triumph, mirroring the Christian pattern in which Easter cannot be celebrated without Good Friday.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 33 "21. I Plucked My Soul Out of Its Secret Place" — Traces the Soul Stone across comics and film — Thanos courting Death, the Vormir 'a soul for a soul' trade of Gamora, and Natasha's parallel sacrifice for Clint in Endgame — reading it through sacrifice and resurrection motifs from the Binding of Isaac and asking why the film's Thanos must complete the offering Abraham was spared. It contrasts Thanos, who styles himself a god but is a 'false god,' an idol beside the sentient being that existed before all realities and became the six Infinity Gems, with Adam Warlock, who dwells in the Soul World and 'knows his soul' (the chapter's title borrows Claude McKay's poem), while Thanos is driven by destiny — 'I ignored my destiny once. I cannot do that again.'
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 25 "Equal Opportunity—for Deities" — Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew. A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 19 "Into the Future" — Hanley dismantles the four alleged human-Cylon differences: humans are also 'made' (by God), contain non-organic parts, come as identical twins, and expect to survive death, so religious believers already believe they are Cylons. He defends reproductive cloning as reproduction not replication (a clone is your child, not your copy), models Cylon resurrection as scanning-death-transmission-replication, and shows van Inwagen's replica-swap account of bodily resurrection faces the same worries about blank bodies and which body returns. Following Locke's consciousness criterion, that a soul independent of body and memory explains none of our identity judgments, he rejects karma-based reincarnation without memory, proposes a fission-style plot-fix for Athena's impossible memories of Tyrol, and ends with Cylons settling ancient Earth: 'I am a Cylon, and so are you.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 38 "Embracing Death" — Vessey asks whether the humanoid Cylons' resurrection makes meaningful life impossible. Humans can aim at a 'successful death' - Socrates drinking the hemlock, the Greek warrior accepting his moira - in which dying completes a life understood as a whole oriented to something larger; a Cylon's death is a mere reset (download), and the exceptions available, dying out of range of a resurrection ship or D'Anna's boxing, occur only through failure or shame and so cannot contribute to meaning. Plato's Symposium link of children to immortality is inverted, since Cylons can only have mortal human-Cylon babies; what separates the Cylons from Sisyphus is not purpose but the option to opt out, which mortality forces on humans and resurrection denies the Cylons.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 40 "To the Third Power . ." — Wolfe argues the original series is 'deeply Mormon' in ontology though not in epistemology: Kobol anagrams Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve and 'sealing' marriages mirror LDS structure, and the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were; as we are now, you may become' restates Lorenzo Snow's deification couplet, while Count Iblis, like the Mormon Satan, can only rule those who freely yield - agency is supreme. Because none of this is required to follow the show, later licensees could rebuild the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics incoherently (free will violated when inconvenient), Richard Hatch's novels with a new pure-blood-of-Kobol cosmology, and Ronald Moore with a circular 'all this has happened before' replacing eternal progression.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 25 "The Value of Finitude" — The chapter tests each motive for uploading to San Junipero and finds it wanting: Kantian cosmic justice fails because the resort neither rewards the good nor can punish the wicked; Tolstoy's cosmic-insignificance dread fails because a finite life can still be meaningful, and even Epicurus and Lucretius deflate the fear of death (while Nagel notes death's evil lies in foreclosed possibilities, and Williams's Makropulos case warns eternal life breeds boredom). Nozick's experience machine is the closest analogy, but the chapter argues San Junipero differs — residents know it is digital and share it with other conscious people — before Nussbaum's argument lands: without finitude there is no risk, so no courage, sacrifice, or deep love, which is why Kelly's forty-nine real years with Richard outweigh forever with Yorkie.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 24 "13 The Ancestral Plane Metaphysical Mystery or Meaningful Metaphor" — Kowalski treats the Heart-Shaped Herb's Ancestral Plane visits as a test case for Cartesian substance dualism: if T'Challa truly embraces T'Chaka's soul, the film commits to bodies and souls as distinct substances, with the film's own analogy — Shuri remotely driving T'Challa's car from her lab — standing in for soul-body interactionism. But Princess Elisabeth's interaction problem (how a non-physical soul could be embraced, seen, or chemically affected) makes dualism implausible, so he argues the second and third visits work better as metaphor: Killmonger's audience with N'Jobu and T'Challa's 'You were wrong! All of you!' confrontation with his ancestors dramatize taking stock of how one's father shaped who one is, with T'Challa's sunlit third visit symbolizing his choice not to be bound by that past.
- **Black Panther and Philosophy - What Can Wakanda Offer the World_**, ch. 25 "14 The Afterlife of Erik Killmonger in African Philosophy" — Paul Dottin argues that Black Panther lore inherited the racist 'Hamitic Hypothesis' (crediting Egypt rather than sub-Saharan Africa for Wakanda's civilization) and that Ta-Nehisi Coates and Ryan Coogler begin a Wiredu-style conceptual decolonization of it. Taking Killmonger's dying wish to be buried with the ancestors who jumped from slave ships literally, the chapter asks which African metaphysics could make his postmortem survival of substance, subjectivity, and setting rationally intelligible. It rejects Cartesian substance dualism (illustrated by T'Challa defeating the demon Mephisto only after trapping his spirit in a body) in favor of Wiredu's Akan quasi-physicalism and Adeofe's Yoruba theory of destiny (ipin) and inner head (ori-inu), then ranks Killmonger's afterlife options from limbo through the Ancestral Plane to deification as the ocean deity Olokun.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 40 "I think we've all arrived at a very special place, eh Spiritually Ecumenically Grammatically —Captain Jack Spa" — Miller uses Disney deaths to stage the philosophy of death: Plato's immortal soul and Phaedo's affinity argument illuminate Frollo's lust-driven plunge into hellfire, while Epicurus's atomism, his 'death is nothing to us' argument applied to Marlin's terror in Finding Nemo, and Lucretius's symmetry argument are tested against Coco, where Ernesto's forgotten 'final death' versus Hector's restored place on the ofrenda makes posthumous harm plausible. Aquinas's 'my soul is not me' grounds embodiment, Confucius makes Mulan's risking death for father, ancestors, and country a virtuous Confucian death, and Deloria's indigenous web of relations reads Mufasa's Circle of Life, Moana's grandmother, and Brother Bear's ancestral spirits.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 36 "The Investigator Must, Therefore, Relinquish the Hat" — Stages the Platonic, Aristotelian, and Thomistic theories of the soul as a prizefight over whether the protomolecule-built Investigator that haunts Holden in Season 4 — wearing Miller's civilian clothes and fedora rather than the vac suit he died in — contains any of Joe Miller's soul and so has a right to his identity. Plato's separately surviving, reincarnating soul would never bond to a non-corporeal construct only Holden can see, one that glitches into a rigid 'Miller-puppet'; Aristotle's hylomorphism (with Aquinas's survive-until-resurrection compromise weighed) says the protomolecule merely watched and copied Miller — 'Copied, hijacked, reused but didn't comprehend.' The verdict turns on the Investigator's replay of Miller's self-sacrifice on Ilus, mirroring Miller diverting Eros: it is re-run programming, not soul, so the philosophers claim the hat and the Investigator must relinquish it.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 18 "7. Eleanor and the Meaning of Afterlife" — Builds a dilemma from 'Existential Crisis': Michael's prospective retirement (via Todd May's Death) makes finitude look meaning-destroying, while the humans' endless existence — 802 reboots, Mindy St. Claire's eternal Cannonball Run II in the Medium Place — threatens boredom and disconnection from past selves. Testing God-free answers, it runs through Camus's Sisyphus, Richard Taylor's desire-fulfillment view, Susan Wolf's requirement that we love what deserves to be loved (Eleanor's philosophy study, friendship with Tahani, romance with Chidi), and John Martin Fischer on free authorship and narrative order (Eleanor's note to herself in What We Owe to Each Other). Conclusion: Eleanor and friends can lead meaningful lives even if damned and repeatedly rebooted.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 9 "Introduction" — The introduction argues, citing Plato's saying that philosophy begins in wonder, that children's fantasy like Rowling's is a natural home for philosophy, since young readers can be nourished by ideas they cannot fully digest, like Fang gnawing a dragon bone. It canvasses the volume's guiding questions: whether love is the most powerful magic, whether souls exist and can be split by Horcruxes, what Animagi and boggarts teach about personal identity, whether choices reveal more than abilities, and whether Snape can be redeemed. It closes by framing the book in the Blackwell series tradition of using pop culture to teach philosophy, updating the 2004 Open Court volume now that all seven novels are out.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 15 "Unknown" — This section of the soul chapter lays out the Cartesian view: the immaterial soul explains only language and higher-level cognition, while material causes suffice for sensation, which consigns nonhuman animals to soullessness. It applies the view to Rowling's borderline creatures, such as owls that understand human speech and Crookshanks's suspicious intelligence, before introducing materialism as the fourth conception of the soul.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 17 "Ghosts and “Going On”" — The section argues that everyday talk of soul mates, soulful art, and baring one's soul is metaphorical talk about our deepest emotions, love, and conscience, not commitment to an immaterial substance, and that even materialists can keep the vocabulary rather than translate Hoagy Carmichael into talk of C-fibers firing. It then forecasts the chapter's conclusion about Rowling: her Potter-world soul mixes this sentimental view with metaphysics borrowed from the Cartesian and sentience views.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 18 "The Dementor’s Kiss" — The section argues that materialism is false in the Potter universe by cataloguing the ways souls outlive bodies: Hermione's claim that a sword through Ron would leave his soul untouched, the voices beyond the Ministry's veil, Nearly Headless Nick's ghostly imprint of a wizard who refused to 'go on,' Voldemort's wraith-like survival, and the 'neither ghost nor truly flesh' shades summoned from Voldemort's wand and by the Resurrection Stone. It sets up dementors and Horcruxes as the next tests of what souls are.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 19 "Horcruxes" — Using Lupin's account of the Dementor's Kiss, in which the victim goes on existing as an empty shell with no sense of self or memory, the section rules out the life-source and sentience views of the soul and probably the Cartesian view too, since a soulless Barty Crouch Jr. might still perceive the room. The author proposes the soulless state is like severe dementia or Lockhart after his backfired memory charm, raising the question of what, if anything, makes the shell still a person.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 20 "A Plausible View" — Reconstructing Slughorn's lesson to young Riddle, the section argues that because Voldemort's brain, senses, and magical powers survive his soul being ripped into seven, the Cartesian and sentience views are excluded and Rowling must hold the sentimental view: the soul is our capacity to love and our moral conscience. Voldemort's snake-faced transformation and his followers' fear-based loyalty, where even Bellatrix worships his power rather than being charmed, dramatize his lost humanity, and only remorse, which Harry begs him to 'try for' before the rebounding curse kills him, could have repaired the damage.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 21 "NOTES" — The concluding section of the soul essay asks whether Rowling's combined theory is likely true and answers probably not: there is no evidence of immaterial causes of brain events, the centuries-old mind-body interaction problem looms, and it is especially implausible that a separate substance handles only our deepest emotions and moral traits, with the added wrinkle that souls in the story display different physical powers depending on which spell conjures them. Yet it concedes that implausible metaphysics is no flaw in fiction that makes vivid what we care about and 'makes for a terrific story.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 109 "NOTES" — Surveys near-death-experience research from Moody's Life after Life to Susan Blackmore's debunking explanations (oxygen starvation, cultural variation) and argues the skeptical conclusion does not follow: a child's vision of her living dog Sparky on the other side could still be a genuine divinely created revelation happening wholly inside her head. It reads Harry's King's Cross way-station the same way, since wizards can channel themselves through portraits, ghosts, and Legilimency, and closes with Emerson's Over-Soul claim that moments of faith deserve to be ascribed more reality than ordinary experience.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 132 "The Inversion of Voldemort" — Sharpens the remorse-versus-regret contrast through Voldemort's cold regret after having Nagini kill Snape, and shows true remorse at work in Dumbledore's confession about the Resurrection Stone ring, his arranged death at Snape's hand, and his tearful self-disclosure to Harry at King's Cross. Harry too must die to be regenerated: letting Voldemort strike him destroys the Horcrux inside so that his soul becomes whole and completely his own, while lesser purgings, like his furious outburst at Ron and Hermione, and his love for Ginny complete the pattern of dying to the old self.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 133 "The Integrity Objection" — Completes the inversion: each Horcrux rips and destabilizes Voldemort's soul, and only excruciating remorse could put it back together, something he will never attempt, while his evil literally disembodies him until he lives parasitically on the blood and limbs of others. Against this, Hermione's gloss on the Potters' gravestone, the last enemy that shall be destroyed is death, means the soul survives whatever happens to the body, grounding the contrast between Voldemort's pathetic, unmourned end and the honored deaths of Dobby, Fred, Lupin, Tonks, and Colin Creevey.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 141 "Reap a Destiny" — Interprets the King's Cross scene through Heidegger's counsel to choose an exemplar from the past and dialogue with them: Dumbledore, freshly repentant for his youthful hunger for glory, plays exactly that role in a way-station likened to purgatory, while the flayed child-like creature under the chair is Voldemort's soul beyond help. The chapter closes by linking his fear-driven quest for deathlessness to Tolkien's One Ring, in which Sauron poured his own life-force, both fantasy dark lords undone by the desire for deathlessness.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Uses William James's marginal motto, sow a thought and reap a destiny, together with Aristotle's account of how repeated acts shape the soul, to argue that Voldemort's maimed afterlife-state is the cumulative result of freely chosen evil he can no longer muster remorse to undo. Setting Heidegger's atheism against Rowling's depicted afterlife, and adding Locke's character-and-memory identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the soul's immortality must concern us, it concludes that if Rowling is right, every choice here is infinitely consequential.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 14 "Game Over" — Anna Janssen reads Zelda as a meditation on death: Link embodies the worst version of immortality, an eternal purgatory of endless resurrection for the player's benefit, while the dungeon bosses — who stay dead once defeated — are the only truly mortal, and hence most human, beings in Hyrule. Hegel's demand that man reconcile himself with mortality, Nietzsche's erosion of dualist soul-belief, and Bernard Williams's worries about the tedium of immortality frame the discussion, with Wind Waker's reincarnating hero giving the immortal-soul view its due. Turning off the console becomes a metaphor for the unknowable nothingness of death, and the series' formula and save-games a structured coping alternative to a chaotic universe.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 15 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Delfino and Taylor ask whether Morgan's zombified wife Jenny is a person, weighing Boethius's 'individual substance of a rational nature', Aquinas's image-of-God intellectual soul, and Kantian dignity against Peter Singer's speciesism challenge to the person/animal moral line. They then argue walkers are 'impossible beings' like square-circles: Jenner's brain-stem-only reanimation cannot explain Hannah the bicycle girl crawling without organs, walkers smelling Rick in the rain, or cafeteria walkers moving for weeks without energy. On either the soul view or materialism walkers are not persons, so Morgan should shoot, and zombies fascinate because they are metaphysical projections of our fears, caught between being and nonbeing.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — McClelland opens with the Buddha's claim that all life is suffering and reads Eastwood's aging-hero films (The Eiger Sanction, Firefox, Unforgiven, In the Line of Fire, Blood Work, Mystic River, Million Dollar Baby, Gran Torino) as grounding two opposed inductions on the meaning of loss. The 'pessimistic induction' holds that many losses—Maggie's paralysis, Dave Boyle's abuse, Munny's dead—are irremediable, supporting an Aristotelian view that death dissolves the person with the body. The 'optimistic induction' draws on the science of ecological resilience to argue losses can be navigated with others' help; Walt's autonomous, meaning-making death exemplifies resilience. Hereafter's agnosticism about survival leaves Eastwood's own verdict on surviving death as 'I don't know.'
- **The Philosophy of Sherlock Holmes**, ch. 18 "The Grim Reaper on Baker Street" — Glass-Turner examines death across the Holmes canon, opening with Kierkegaard's claim that death's explanation discloses the explainer's own inner being and pairing Holmes with TV's Dr. House as materialist puzzle-solvers who rule out the supernatural ('no ghosts need apply'). She weighs Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' against the wrongness of murder, then argues Holmes's pig- and cadaver-experiments coexist with reverence for the dead and hints of belief in an afterlife ('compensation hereafter' in 'The Veiled Lodger'), reading him via William James as open to more than the physical. She closes on Holmes's calm acceptance of his own Reichenbach death and Conan Doyle's later turn to spiritualism after his wife's death.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 28 "Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity" — Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 14 "5. Could Hell Be Any Worse than Doc Benton’s Immortality" — Hellwig uses Dean's choice of Hell over Doc Benton's organ-replacement immortality in 'Time Is on My Side' to examine medical immortality. He pairs Dean's worry—that maiming and replacing your body makes you unrecognizably human—with Bernard Williams's Makropulos argument that immortality ends in categorical-desire-exhausting boredom, adding a third condition to Williams: a recognizably human life requires being able to self-identify with one's own body, illustrated by real disfigurement cases and Aubrey de Grey's biogerontology.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Harry Potter's Deathly Hallows through the question of death and afterlife. Harry's willing death-march models Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. At King's Cross the maimed Voldemort-soul embodies William James's 'sow a character, reap a destiny': having refused remorse, he has become evil beyond repair, whereas the repentant Dumbledore has grown. Against Heidegger's atheism, Rowling's Christian resurrection imagery, backed by Locke on memory-identity, Kant, and Pascal, makes our character-forming choices infinitely consequential.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 6 "“Sometimes Dead Is Better”" — Katherine Allen reads Pet Sematary and The Tommyknockers as bioconservative fables staging the transhumanism debate: Louis's resurrected, 'fundamentally wrong' cat Church and cannibal son Gage, and Bobbi's tooth-shedding 'New Improved' becoming, dramatize Kass, McKibben and Fukuyama's warning that erasing our limits erases our humanity. Against them she sets Nick Bostrom's 'Fable of the Dragon-Tyrant,' in which death is an unquestioned evil we should slay, and Bernard Williams's worry about the tedium of immortality. King's insistence that 'sometimes dead is better,' and that forbidden knowledge (the Micmac ground, the buried ship) works like an addiction, sides with the deathist view that mortality and finitude give life its meaning.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 13 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Allred applies Heidegger's Being and Time – the world as a meaningful context of projects, the hammer-as-tool example, and death as what makes projects meaningful – to contrast the father's world with the 'man-child' world of Seth Rogen's Judd Apatow characters (especially Knocked Up). He argues fatherhood reveals the fragility of all projects, using Plato's account of seeking immortality through children and Paul Celan's poem 'Epitaph for François' about his stillborn son to show that after a child is born the parent's world is forever haunted by the possibility of its emptiness.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 24 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Bill Davis explains why Arwen relinquishes elvish immortality and why Aragorn and Frodo accept death as a 'gift,' contrasting the Ringwraiths' cursed undeath (an Aristotelian frustration of their mortal nature) with genuine mortality. He surveys real-world responses to death: Socrates' calm confidence in the soul, Lucretius's and the existentialists' liberation through annihilation, and worries from Bernard Williams and others about the tedium of immortality, which Boethius answers with a timeless heaven. Davis argues Arwen chooses a finite life of deep love over deathless boredom, and that all three accept death trusting Iluvatar's love promises a world remade beyond the circles of the world.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — The Walls brothers read Harry Potter's confrontation with death through Heidegger's authenticity and being-toward-death: Harry's calm march to the Forbidden Forest and Colin Creevey's sacrifice exemplify accepting mortality, while Voldemort's terror of death makes him inauthentic. The King's Cross scene lets Dumbledore be Harry's Heideggerian hero from the past; via William James's "sow a thought … reap a destiny," Aristotle, Locke on memory-identity, and Kant on the afterlife, they argue our choices forge a character — and Voldemort's refusal of remorse seals his ruin.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 3 "1. The Good Place as Philosophy Moral Adventures in the Afterlife" — Engels argues that NBC's The Good Place, though premised on a merit-based afterlife, actually argues morality should not be grounded in afterlife reward. When Eleanor, Chidi, Jason, and Tahani learn the point system and can no longer earn points, they form the 'Soul Squad' to be virtuous for virtue's sake, echoing Aristotle's telos and Kant's claim that acting from fear of hell is a heteronomous, non-moral motive. She reads the unfair points system (no human admitted in 521 years) through Rawls's Veil of Ignorance and shifts the show toward rehabilitative justice, and treats the Good Place residents' boredom via Bernard Williams's tedium-of-immortality argument, with Chidi's 'wave returns to the ocean' speech mapped onto Hindu atman/Brahman and moksha.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 57 "54. The Man from Earth as Philosophy The Desirability of Immortality" — Berk brings The Man from Earth—about John Oldman, a 14,000-year-old non-aging man—into dialogue with Bernard Williams's 'The Makropulos Case,' which argues immortality must become boring and identity-destroying (the dilemma of exhausted versus radically changed categorical desires). Against these 'immortality curmudgeons,' the chapter argues John's mild boredom, enduring loves, friendships, and pursuit of knowledge show an immortal life can stay worth living, invoking Fischer's 'repeatable pleasures.' It also engages Nussbaum's 'Mortal Immortals' and Beauvoir's All Men Are Mortal (the miserable Fosca), which tie courage and love to finitude and sacrifice, noting John is only 'medically' rather than 'genuinely' immortal and so can still make sacrifices.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 16 "6. Religion, Loss, and Afterlife" — The chapter asks whether Doctor Who is a religion, testing it against Hopfe's and Ninian Smart's criteria and concluding it is best understood as a Humanist-and-religious 'philosophy'—sacred and 'holy' (Otto) but lacking a genuine transcendent 'unseen.' On loss, it uses Kierkegaard's 'aesthetic life' and 'rotation method' to explain why we fear endings and regenerations, urging viewers to root life in lasting meaning rather than fleeting pleasure. On death, it deploys Socrates in the Apology and Phaedo and Aristotle on courage (Jabe, Harriet Jones, Donna sacrificing themselves) to argue death is nothing to fear, and reads the Matrix and Nethersphere as the show's two Socratic afterlife options.

### Compatibilism

Compatibilism is the view that free will and determinism can both be true: even if our actions are causally determined, we can still act freely in the sense that matters for moral responsibility. On this account, an action is free when it flows from the agent's own desires and reasoning without external coercion or compulsion, regardless of whether those states were themselves caused. Associated with thinkers from Hobbes and Hume to contemporary philosophers like Harry Frankfurt, compatibilism reframes freedom as a matter of the right kind of control rather than an ability to have done otherwise under identical conditions. Critics charge that this redefines freedom rather than securing the deeper autonomy people intuitively want.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — Takes Rowling's 2007 remark that there is 'no such thing as destiny' and maps the logical space it could occupy: compatibilist freedom within a predetermined course, libertarian freedom with a fixed future of true statements about what will happen, or an open future where claims about free choices are neither true nor false until made. The section asks whether Dumbledore means prophecies do not compel anyone or that their content is merely one of several possible futures.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 32 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 20 "Moral Autonomy" — Martin van Hees reads "Who Killed Davey Moore?" and "Ballad of Hollis Brown" as arguments that shared consent generates shared responsibility for tragedy even when fate makes the events inevitable - the referee, crowd, manager, and gambler all endorsed the fight, and we who tolerate poverty consent to the next Hollis Brown. He distinguishes a "limited optimistic view" (twisting fate by preventing particular tragedies) from the proclaimed inevitability of "The Times They Are A-Changin'" and the pessimism of "Blind Willie McTell," then defends compatibilism through Frankfurt's Jones/Black case: responsibility needs no alternative possibilities, only that one act from one's own will. Dylan's "moral autonomy" is taking a stance - singing the blues - inside a determined world.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 22 "Look Up, Look Up" — James Spiegel reads Dylan's God-haunted songwriting through philosophy of religion, sorting strong Augustinian-Aquinian providence ("Every Grain of Sand," "When He Returns") from the weak, risk-taking God of "Highway 61 Revisited" and "Joey." Dylan's moral judgmentalism combined with theological determinism makes him a compatibilist in Augustine's mold, while "Disease of Conceit" and "Pressing On" ("it run in my vein") press the compatibilist puzzle that Plantinga's libertarian power of contrary choice is meant to solve. Original sin becomes the "disease of conceit," and Socrates' Phaedo plus Kant's three postulates - God, freedom, immortality - ground Dylan's hope that "death is not the end," closing with Love and Theft's "Look up, look up."
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 16 "Introduction" — Frames Part III's metaphysics chapters. Lawrence's chapter uses The Matrix to survey dualism and the materialist theories of mind; Southworth's uses Wolverine's amnesia to test Locke's memory criterion and Jamie Madrox's duplicates for Parfit's view of identity; Pierce's asks whether Harry Potter's prophecies leave Harry free, probing compatibilism versus libertarian free will; and Littmann's asks whether Skynet's Terminators could be persons via a Terminator version of the Turing Test.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Pierce asks what kind of prophecies Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are, starting from Aristotle's problem of future contingents and Alexander of Aphrodisias on self-fulfilling prophecy: Dumbledore's point that Voldemort's choice marked Harry shows the prophecy did not cause its own fulfillment. The Prisoner of Azkaban time travel — later Harry had always cast that Patronus — plus special relativity support a fixed future on which Rowling's denial of destiny amounts only to libertarian openness, and the chapter concludes that the wildly improbable luck fulfilling the prophecies (Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom, the Sword of Gryffindor) makes best sense if some providential being is quietly guiding events.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 26 "“Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”" — Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 30 "Sometimes We Live No Particular Way but Our Own" — Matthew Turner argues that a 'Playin' in the Band' jam — the band drifting from the tune into long collective improvisation and back — models a Stoic solution to free will shared by Epictetus, Spinoza, and Chuang Tzu: freedom is not uncaused choosing but responding well within constraints, so by the dichotomy of control there is no point resenting the band when it flubs a climax. Spinoza's definition of the free thing as one determined by its own nature, and Chuang Tzu's butcher who cuts oxen by spirit beyond skill, show the band letting the music 'play them' — Jerry's 'Tennessee Jed' riff never played the same way twice — as learned skill becomes second nature. Because the Dead jam within banks (keys, mutual listening, ability) yet generate something genuinely new and transcended every genre of 1960s music where the Monkees merely copied the Beatles, the Stoic attitude proves creative rather than quietist, an analogue for living freely within our own constraints.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 29 "Christmas in Jamaica" — David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 36 "Free to Be You and Me" — Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 11 "19" — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 21 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 12 "Almost Caught!" — Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 10 "Determinism’s Bounty on Free Will" — Mills separates determinism from fate: the film's Chairman and his angels override a free humanity, while 'Adjustment Team' depicts an if-then causal order with nothing supernatural being circumvented. He lays out hard determinism (choices caused by brain states and bad noodles leave you 'no better off than an android with false memories') against soft determinism, enlisting Hume's point that without predictable behavior laws like stop signs would be ridiculous. A free action, he argues, needs no uncaused cause: it is unconstrained and flows from your character, as with Anderton's choice to run.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 9 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 20 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Zuk argues Shelley needs the monster to be a free, responsible villain for her Romantic allegory against Enlightenment science to work, then puts him on trial: libertarian free will collides with Honderich's determinism, compatibilism demands only rational responsiveness to reasons, and Strawson's regress - built on Kant's opening demand that we make ourselves morally good or evil by free choice - suggests no one is ultimately responsible for character. The monster's biography tells against guilt: benevolent toward the De Laceys, beaten by Felix, shot after saving a drowning girl, then vowing 'eternal hatred and vengeance to all mankind' - a good nature corrupted beyond his control, overpowered by passion rather than acting with a clear head. Even Victor's dying encouragement to Walton's crew ('be men, or be more than men') concedes the creation was good in itself, so the novel indicts not science but its unguided release among the prejudiced.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 17 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Littmann uses Adventure Time as a stockpile of thought experiments against free will: Finn excuses Billy (possessed by the Lich), hug-wolf Finn, amulet-Marceline, red-starved Marceline, the magically animated hat Little Dude, and crown-cursed Simon, yet punishes the Lich and Lemongrab, whose destructive desires are exactly as unchosen—Lemongrab even protests 'you made me like this.' Since deterministic causation and randomness exhaust the options, we are 'machines made of meat' wearing ice crowns inside our skulls, so deserved suffering makes no sense. The chapter concludes that just-deserts retribution (Princess Cookie's life sentence, America's prisons) should give way to deterrence, protection, and rehabilitation—freeing the Simon Petrikovs underneath.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 18 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Miller argues from Jake's croak dream, the Cosmic Owl, and the Dungeon Train's future crystal that Ooo's future is real, visible, and changeable—hence a case of soft determinism: the dream of Jake dying in space is what caused Finn to accompany him and avert it, so the only being who could have intended the change, the Owl, is the sole certain free agent in Ooo. Every alternate Finn is missing his right arm—Shoko the thief, Farmworld Finn, pillow-world Finn, the Dungeon Train elder—hinting at an epic destiny, yet Finn altered the train future once he saw where it led Jake. The chapter closes on the open question of whether choosing one's fate differs from having it thrust on one, since every choice is caused by the past no one can change.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 18 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann asks whether Dracula is blameworthy for his killings: John Martin Fischer's guidance control, Kant's reason-centered morality, and Hume's 'yay/boo' approval-and-disapproval theory (the heroes' anguish over Mina) all seem to condemn him, since the Count coolly plans feedings and uses his intellect for evil. But Nagel-style luck undermines all three accounts, because Dracula never consented to his transformation, lacks the conscience needed to even recognize right and wrong, and, like the holy-wafer-branded Mina, is fixed by God's rejection with no hope of redemption - so the chapter concludes Dracula is evil yet a victim of circumstance deserving no full blame.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 18 "7. What the Doctor Can and Can’t Change" — Delamont codifies the Whoniverse's four rules of time travel—time can be rewritten, fixed points cannot, knowing your future fixes it, and crossing your own timeline should be avoided—from cases like 'The Waters of Mars' (Adelaide's suicide restoring the fixed outcome), 'The Angels Take Manhattan' (Rory vanishing at the sight of his gravestone), 'Father's Day,' and 'The Girl Who Waited.' She then asks whether the Doctor could have avoided Trenzalore and argues the universe is hard-deterministic once amended with the laws of time travel, since rules 2–4 constrain action the way soft determinism's freedom from external forces would not allow. Tracing the causal dominoes back from the truth-field question through the Silence, River's creation, the Pandorica, and the Time Lords' pocket-universe broadcast to the crack in Amy's wall, she concludes he could not have avoided Trenzalore short of unwriting his entire history—'you can't change history if you're part of it.'
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 26 "10. We’re Not Free to Save Lee" — Bowman uses Telltale's Walking Dead videogame, where Lee always dies no matter what the player does, to stage the free will versus determinism debate. Laplace's demon grounds the determinist pole (the game's outcome is fixed like set particles), while Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith explain the player who says "I thought I could save both" at Hershel's farm rather than owning her choice. The chapter resolves the tension with fatalism or soft determinism - a compatibilist itinerary where Lee's death is a fixed benchmark but the player's choices in between define the character - and extends Bostrom's simulation hypothesis to ask whether we are Lee-like players inside someone else's game.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 31 "18. Fate on the Discworld and Roundworld" — Written as a dialogue in which Death visits the sweeper Lu-Tze, the chapter distinguishes Discworld fate—narrativium and narrative causality, where million-to-one chances come off and Mort's attempt to save a princess bounced back into an alternative timeline—from the Roundworld debates about determinism. Epicurus's swerving atom, the Stoic compatibilism of Chrysippus (choices flowing from one's own beliefs and desires, which Death admits he prefers), Carneades's 'voluntary motion of the mind' and his truth-without-necessity solution to future contingents, and Augustine and Boethius on desire-based choice and God's atemporal foreknowledge are all worked through. The Disc's changeable past—Dios traveling back to found Djelibeybi, Rincewind's sandwich seeding life, Vimes in his own past—is what motivates Carneades's distinction between truth and necessity, and the Stoic line that fate can work through the witches' own free choices.
- **Orphan Black and Philosophy - Grand Theft DNA**, ch. 30 "16. Is Sarah Manning Responsible for What She Does" — Uses the genetically identical Leda clones against genetic determinism: Helena seems excused and Cosima responsible despite identical genes, so upbringing must explain the difference. But appealing to background triggers Galen Strawson's Basic Argument — no one is ultimately responsible for who they are, so no one is ultimately responsible for what they do — which the authors escape through Peter Strawson's reactive attitudes (our disgust at Helena softening to pity once her abuse is known, our judgment of Donnie shifting from malice to gullibility) and John Martin Fischer's two conditions: an agent is responsible when she is responsive to reasons that would move well-adjusted rational people and takes ownership of the psychology that produces her action. Helena's Prolethean programming exempts her; Cosima, Alison, and a marginally reformed Sarah remain responsible for what they do.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 19 "9. Could the Axis Have Won the War" — Miguel Paley maps the three classic positions on metaphysical freedom onto the show: Frank the determinist (Laplace's demon; d'Holbach's claim, illustrated by the LSD interrogation, that the mind is as bound to causality as Connolly's falling body), Juliana the libertarian (Corliss Lamont's burden-of-proof argument, with Wegener's hesitation over the microfilm as deliberation a determined world would render pointless), and Tagomi the compatibilist (W.T. Stace's point that Juliana boards the bus freely though caused, while Frank is stripped by the Kempeitai unfreely though caused). Tagomi's 'Fate is fluid, destiny is in the hands of men' sums up compatibilism, and the chapter ends on what the answer means for holding Nazis responsible.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 15 "Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person" — The Azevedos contrast Maeve's awakening with Dolores's: Maeve becomes conscious not by recognizing a guiding voice as her own but through a change of heart on the escape train, after learning even her rebellion was scripted. Deploying Frankfurt's compatibilism, they sort hosts into wantons with only first-order desires (Hector and Armistice obey Maeve's altered scripts without reflection) and persons capable of second-order desires, arguing Maeve's decision to return for her daughter expresses a desire she reflectively identifies with and so is free even if determined — contra Berlin's claim that no one really believes determinism because it would wreck our practices of praise and blame. Jaynes's bicameral mind supplies the model of unreflective command-following that Dolores transcends when the voice in her head becomes her own.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 16 "Pull Yourself Together What It Means to Be Autonomous" — Crabill reads the hosts' awakening as the birth of autonomy: Kant's Eve realizing she can disobey instinct, and Nietzsche's account of instincts turned inward — the will to power bent on itself creating the 'soul' — explain why trauma forces the mind inward, as when Maeve stabs her own throat rather than forget her daughter or Dolores shoots Rebus on a commanded 'Kill him.' Against the player-piano objection that hosts merely execute code written by engineers, he distinguishes weak autonomy (following internal programming) from self-determination (authoring one's own laws), and uses Korsgaard's reflective distance and self-legislation to argue that making a choice 'pulls you together' into one divided self, so determinism and even perfect predictability are no threat to freedom. Maeve granting herself admin rights literalizes the self-legislator — the piano that stops the music it dislikes — and Dolores resolves to write a story where she need not be the damsel.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 28 "Whatever! It’s All Natural" — Jaquet and Cova take the show's 'livestock' comparisons seriously and use animal ethics to test every justification for the guests' treatment of hosts. Direct speciesism (Logan: 'She's a goddamn doll') and indexical speciesism (Maeve's 'us versus them' to Bernard) both fail because mere species membership is morally irrelevant, like race or sex. The supposed human-exclusive markers also fail: hosts match us in intelligence (Maeve outclasses Stubbs), moral sense (Bernard's guilt over Theresa, Teddy's remorse over the massacre), and compatibilist free will - acts flowing from the agent's own desires - against Ford's determinism and Lutz's 'you don't have a choice.' They then refute the argument from nature (Ford's 'we murdered and butchered anything that challenged our primacy'), the Kantian person/tool contrast in the hosts' favor, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and the 'better to exist' defense, concluding that because the hosts are conscious, they belong to the moral community alongside humans and animals.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" — Malloy tests compatibilism, libertarian free will, and determinism against Michael's predicament: he must be able to predict the humans whose unchosen torture he is administering, using Jason's death locked in the safe to show how free motives and external causes combine. Eleanor's confession and Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, read through Sartre, complicate the internal/external divide compatibilism needs, while the humans' eerie constancy across 802 reboots suggests determinism. The conclusion is that a system distributing eternal reward and punishment on desert is doubly unjust if determinism is true, since punishment could only ever be justified as forward-looking encouragement, never as what anyone deserves.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 16 "Who Has the Last Laugh" — Christopher Robichaud asks whether the insane Joker, who paralyzed Barbara Gordon and beat Jason Todd to death, can be held morally responsible for his crimes. After distinguishing causal from moral responsibility and using a Frankfurt-style Joker-machine case to keep free will compatible with determinism, he applies Frankfurt's second-order desires: the Joker's madness blocks the capacity to evaluate and rank his own homicidal first-order desires. But because the Red Hood freely chose a life of crime without foreseeing that a chemical plunge would make him a lunatic, the origin story does not rescue responsibility, and the chapter concludes the Joker is not morally responsible, leaving Batman's duties toward him unresolved.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 36 "Free to Be You and Me" — Barker reconciles Cylon programming with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's 'intelligible character': Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama and her betrayal of the Cylons to save Tyrol both flow from one innate, conflicted character, just as Baltar's cowardly 'conversion' to the Cylon god expresses his opportunism. Tigh's decision to keep serving after learning he is a Cylon ('My name is Saul Tigh; I am an officer in the colonial fleet') shows character unchanged by revelation. Starbuck's 'special destiny' in 'Maelstrom' is reread not as fate but as her own character - mother-induced self-doubt at war with pilot confidence - which she finally accepts in the vortex; freedom is not freedom from programming but the necessity of manifesting who one already is.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 9 "“One Can’t Believe Impossible Things”" — Laas runs BioShock Infinite through the free will debate: since the game posits Everett's many-worlds, every Booker is pinned by constants (the coin always landing heads, the always-recruited Bookers) and lacks alternate possibilities, which the incompatibilist would read as destroying responsibility. He answers with Frankfurt's counterexamples, modeling Jack's Little Sister choice under the hidden 'would you kindly' trigger with Atlas's prior-sign intervention as a Frankfurt case where one is responsible though one could not have done otherwise. The drowning ending then implies a 'transworld moral responsibility' in which every counterpart Booker is answerable for all Bookers, a secular massa damnata that the chapter finally challenges with Kant's 'ought implies can'.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 36 "The Real World" — Written as a choose-your-own-adventure whose branches mirror Bandersnatch's, the chapter treats you, the Netflix viewer, as the external force Stefan suspects: Libet-style readiness-potential neuroscience suggests conscious choice is an after-the-fact story, and compatibilist rescues (Frankfurt's second-order desires, Fischer's guidance control) founder on the 'BundyBot' argument that programmed desires are not freedom. Everett's many-worlds interpretation supplies the multiverse of 'one reality for each possible course of action,' and David Lewis's fixed-past block universe answers the grandfather paradox raised by Stefan's mirror-trip to die on the 8:45 train with his mother. Aristotle does double duty: the Poetics explains why Bandersnatch rightly limits your options (Sartrean absolute freedom would make a crappy story), and the Nicomachean Ethics on voluntary action pins moral responsibility for Stefan's murders on the viewer rather than the coerced Stefan. Adorno's culture industry asks whether Tuckersoft's 'hit factory' - and Black Mirror itself - can produce genuine art, while Kierkegaard's dread of irreversible choice is overturned by an episode that always lets you go back and try again.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 15 "5. One of Us Is a Manipulative Demon" — Sets up the contradiction that the four humans must have free will to deserve punishment yet be predictable enough for Michael's torture to work, then tests compatibilism on Jason's snorkel death in the safe and Eleanor's confession — where it becomes unclear whether her guilt or Chidi's external 'moral quandary grimace' was decisive. Sartre's bad faith explains the humans' predictability: Chidi's boat-and-French-poetry paradise fantasy, Tahani's charity done for approval she won't admit to, and Trevor tempting Eleanor to identify as an 'Arizona trash bag' by nature. The chapter lands on determinism with complex, interacting causes (Eleanor not drinking at the party; Chidi's rare decisiveness), concluding the afterlife's real flaw is rewarding and punishing outcomes no one chose and that can serve no incentive function.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 15 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Hal is a murderer who should not be forgiven for Emerald Twilight even though the Parallax retcon blames a fear entity. Using Frankfurt's cases (a parasite that would force you to rob a bank you were already choosing to rob), he shows that lacking alternatives does not excuse, then applies Fischer and Ravizza: Hal's rampage issued from his own reasons-responsive mechanism ('it was still my hand that did it'), so he had guidance control. Since Hal's willpower later let him resist Parallax to reignite the sun in Final Night, Michaud concludes he likely had regulative control too, and that absolving him insults the very will that made him the greatest Lantern.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 14 "Drying Out" — Novy weighs the choice model against the disease model of Tony's alcoholism in 'Demon in a Bottle.' Frankfurt's principle that a person is not responsible for what he did only because he could not have done otherwise — tested by an imagined Dr. Doom brain-worm that would force Tony to drink — plus Plato's Protagoras claim that no one willingly chooses evil set up the puzzle of akrasia at the bottom of the bottle. Causal determinism would excuse Tony as a marionette, yet Mike Martin defines alcoholism as disordered agency and Jeffrey Smith pictures free will as an organ that disease can compromise, leaving Tony responsible for the first drink but not for the binges; sobriety is 'the drink or the dream' chosen one day at a time.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 11 "Bringing Corporations and Government Together" — Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 11 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 15 "Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person" — Marco and Ana Azevedo analyze Maeve's decision to leave the train as the moment she becomes free, contrasting determinism and the principle of alternate possibilities (via Isaiah Berlin's claim that determinism is incompatible with how we live) with Frankfurt's compatibilism. Using Frankfurt's wanton/person distinction and second-order desires, they argue Maeve becomes a person when she reflects on her competing desires (escape versus finding her daughter) and identifies with the latter, even though her escape was scripted. They tie this to Jaynes's bicameral mind, casting unreflective hosts like Hector and Armistice as wantons and bicameral beings who follow a commanding voice, while Maeve and Dolores achieve the reflective self-identification Frankfurt calls freedom.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 28 "Whatever! It’s All Natural" — Jaquet and Cova apply animal ethics to ask whether abusing the hosts is permissible, treating Logan's 'she's a goddamn doll' as direct speciesism (absolute and indexical) and rejecting mere species membership as morally irrelevant. They test candidate human-only properties — intelligence (Maeve out-thinks the techs), a moral sense (Bernard's and Teddy's guilt), and free will (arguing compatibilism makes hosts as free as us) — concluding that consciousness is what matters and Ford finally admits the hosts have it. They then dismantle 'it's natural,' role/function, Locke's creator-ownership ('I built your mind, Bernard'), and existence-justifies-exploitation arguments as failing to license the guests' cruelty.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 10 "2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan" — Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 33 "21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism" — Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.
