- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 26 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 11 "5. Minority Report" — Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 9 "7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel" — Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 94 "88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will" — Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.

### The Gettier Problem

The Gettier problem, named for Edmund Gettier's brief 1963 paper, challenges the long-standing definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Gettier presented cases in which a person holds a belief that is both true and justified yet intuitively fails to count as knowledge, because the belief is true only by luck—its justification and its truth are connected in the wrong way. The problem prompted decades of work in epistemology attempting to add a fourth condition or reformulate the analysis so as to rule out such accidentally true justified beliefs.

- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 13 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Kevin Kinghorn uses virtue epistemology (Sosa, Code) to solve the puzzle of why Uncle Andrew alone hears only roaring when Aslan sings Narnia into being: he fails all four intellectual virtues. He does not value truth for its own sake (unlike Frank the Cabby), indulges wishful thinking (like Edmund defending the Witch for Turkish Delight, or imagining Jadis fancies him), lets fear dictate belief (terror of the animals he has vivisected), and lacks Socratic self-knowledge, which the dragonized Eustace painfully acquires. A closing reading of Prince Caspian has each character's ability to see Aslan track their earlier trust in Lucy's testimony: sin blinds, and faith produces its own authenticating evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 12 "Introduction" — Frames Part II's epistemology chapters. Jacoby's chapter uses Stan Marsh debunking TV psychic John Edward, holistic healers, and Mormon belief to teach the ethics of belief against Pascal's wager; Lawrence's uses The Matrix to pose the skeptical problem and Descartes' response; Silverman's uses Adama's lie about Earth in Battlestar Galactica to raise the Gettier problem and the Clifford–James dispute over believing without sufficient evidence.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene asks what, if anything, walkers know. Rick's optimistic feeling that Lori and Carl survived turns out true, yet is not knowledge - true belief is necessary but insufficient, the gap Gettier cases exploit - and since walkers can never weigh evidence or think about their thoughts, only externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge can count them as knowers. Walker behavior defeats Jenner's 'mindless instinct' line: Jenny turning the handle of her old house, the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, a walker smashing the department store window with a rock, and the horde seeing through Rick and Glenn's gut disguise once rain washes the scent away. Zombie knowledge is real but limited to simple things recalled from the person's past, the more complex the task the less likely they know it.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 20 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Robert Arp argues that Jeopardy! contestants display only declarative memory - the mere recalling level of Bloom's Taxonomy, which trained apes like Koko and Kanzi can approximate - rather than genuine smarts. Working through the Theaetetus analysis of knowledge as justified true belief, with the correspondence theory of truth and Aristotle's demand for explanation and evidence, he shows that a lucky Final Jeopardy! guess ('What is tree pulp?') is a true belief that falls short of knowledge because it is true only by accident. Real knowledge lives at the analysis, synthesis, and especially evaluation levels - constructing and critiquing arguments - though he concedes many contestants can probably do this off-stage, so it would be a fallacy of hasty conclusion to insist they all ain't smart.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 14 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Senors use Psych to separate true belief from knowledge: Shawn's hunch that Shabby the sea lion was murdered is true but shabbily evidenced, and his justified, true belief that a Clayton family member sabotaged the plane fails to be knowledge when the killer turns out to be a son-in-law he had no reason to think existed - a textbook Gettier case from 'He Dead.' They then weigh the two main theories of justification, evidentialism (with its base rates and prior probabilities) and reliabilism, and both vindicate the careful, methodical work of Lassiter and Juliet while Shawn's trigger-happy belief-forming habit strikes out twice. Shawn is redeemed only as an evidence-generator whose disregard for priors takes 'impossible' suspects like a murdered sea lion seriously, so that pairing his talents with the detectives' rigor yields the complete detective.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 28 "Psych and Philosophy" — Ronda Bowen argues that because Shawn delivers true conclusions under a false justification (psychic power), the SBPD's beliefs are Gettier-style justified true beliefs rather than knowledge, using Plato's Theaetetus (perception and true judgment fail as definitions) as the frame and Gettier's Smith/Jones and Ford/Brown cases to model episodes like 'Spellingg Bee,' where the police infer Miklous's guilt from Shawn's staged psychic demonstration. John Hawthorne's lottery propositions explain why Lassiter's 'Shawn isn't a psychic' certainty can never be fully justified, and the chapter closes on internalism versus externalism and the reliability of testimony, concluding the detectives become internally justified only when they re-derive Shawn's conclusions through their own reasoning.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 30 "Psych and Philosophy" — Courtland Lewis replays Plato's Theaetetus with Shawn and Henry to show that perception and true judgment fail as accounts of knowledge, then recasts both Gettier cases with Psych material: Chief Vick's justified-but-lucky belief about the chief-of-police job, and Juliet's disjunction 'Shawn is a psychic or Gus is in Mazatlan.' Since justified true belief is not knowledge, he argues Shawn's trained senses fit reliabilism - distinguished from lucky predictors like Leonard Koppett and probed through Lehrer's Mr. Truetemp against Gus's super sniffer - and closes by combining reliabilist-foundationalism (Alston's two levels of knowledge), coherence theory, and Klein's infinitism into Shawn's observe-eliminate-conclude method.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 13 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter turns Raylan's claim that shooting Tommy Bucks was 'justified' into a question of epistemic justification, expounding Plato's Meno definition of knowledge as justified true belief, Gettier's 1963 counterexamples (rebuilt with Boyd truly but luckily predicting that a marshal will be arrested), and the repairs of Goldman's no-false-causal-link condition and Harman's inference to the best explanation. It then grades the show's reasoners: Raylan knows the Crowes rather than Boyd killed Wade Messer, Boyd knows Cassie milks the revival snakes' venom, Art Mullen does not yet know Raylan helped Winona return the evidence-room money, and gut-feeling victims like Ellen May do not know what they saw. Against Humean skepticism about cause and effect it defends inductive, detective-style knowledge - Raylan can know who done it without courtroom proof.
- **It's Always Sunny and Philosophy - The Gang Gets Analyzed**, ch. 7 "It’s Always Sunny and Philosophy" — Using 'Flowers for Charlie', where a placebo pill convinces two scientists and even the Waitress that Charlie has become a genius, the chapter asks what actually makes something philosophy. Sounding smart is not philosophy: big words, the Sokal-style hoax paper submitted to a leading journal, and the 'Guru Effect' of credulous admirers all fail, yet Charlie's pronouncements turn out true by sheer luck - which is exactly Edmund Gettier's problem of epistemic luck illustrated with the broken-clock example. Since we can never verify our premises or our reasoning, the chapter sides with Aristotle's response to Plato's theory of forms that we can never determine what a thing is, only what it is not, and concludes the show is philosophical precisely because the Gang is the exact antithesis of reality, truth, and right action.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's belief that Green raped Anna counts as knowledge. His belief is true, and Plato's Theaetetus defines knowledge as justified true belief, but Mrs. Hughes's false testimony, Anna's denials, and mere observed flirting mean Bates's reasons are defective: his belief could be true by coincidence, a Gettier-style failure in which truth is not earned by justification. The chapter also examines testimony - a reliable testifier like Mrs. Hughes would normally confer justification, but she deliberately lies - and concludes with Anna's own verdict that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 28 "16. Getting at the Truth" — The chapter sets out the Platonic justified-true-belief analysis of knowledge with Discworld examples—Archchancellor Ridcully as a fallible authority, the physics of thaum particles as coherentist justification—before constructing a Discworld Gettier case in which a young wizard sees a fake level-seven wizard killed and truly but accidentally reports that 'a level seven wizard was killed.' It then tests the standard repairs, applying Nozick's truth-tracking function and Goldman's causation function to a case where a man blames the notorious Reacher Gilt for a theft actually committed by the dwarf he bumped into, and argues that neither truth-tracking nor specificity makes the problem go away. The upshot is that Discworlders, used to expecting to be wrong, may let go of false 'knowledge' more easily than our confidently wrong Roundworld.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 28 "16. How Close Is That World to Our World" — Brett Coppenger treats the show as a nearby possible world identical to ours until the 1930s, then uses Gettier-style cases — Joe Blake forming justified true beliefs while driving through Alvin Goldman's Barn Façade County — to show such beliefs can still fail to be knowledge. Robert Nozick's truth-tracking conditions, defined via what happens in the closest possible worlds, handle the barns but generate 'abominable conjunctions' (knowing Jones killed the Crown Prince while not knowing the Crown Prince was killed), and the chapter closes on the thought that the large stock of shared knowledge is exactly what makes that dystopia feel only a few big events from our world.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 24 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Builds the justified-true-belief account of knowledge from Bluth cases (Tobias's belief in his own acting lacks justification, Michael's belief that he crashed the car under Lucille's manipulation lacks truth), then shows the writers smuggling Gettier cases into the show: George Sr. 'knows for a fact' the government has no case via Cindi Lightballoon's blind faith, Buster forms the true belief that Oscar is his father from George Sr. disguised as Oscar, and Michael's disbelief of Maggie Lizer is luckily true despite the swapped pregnancy bodysuit. The chapter closes by surveying fixes: demanding certainty, Russell's no-false-premises condition, and Goldman-style causal theories of knowing.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 30 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — In the method of ordinary language philosophy (Wittgenstein, Austin, Ryle), Stern and Wilkinson defend the Dude's retort to Jesus as no misuse of 'opinion': knowledge is justified true belief, undermined by Gettier-style epistemic luck, and opinions are beliefs supported only by subjective justification — like the taste of White Russians, Locke's secondary qualities — rather than public evidence. Jesus's claim that he and Liam will 'fuck you up' is a prediction that could in principle be publicly justified, but with no available evidence it is an unsupported opinion; Donny's gut-feeling Raiders pick shows opinions need not concern 'matters of opinion', and it is stubborn Walter who is truly 'opinionated'.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 21 "10. Does Bates Know Who Raped Anna" — The Nisleys ask whether Bates's conviction that Mr. Green raped Anna counts as knowledge, starting from the Theaetetus's definition of knowledge as justified true belief. Bates's belief is true, but his evidential position is compromised: Mrs. Hughes, though genuinely reliable, gives him false testimony pointing to a stranger, Anna denies it was Green, and his own grounds (Green's flirting and Green's admission that he left the concert) are too weak, so the truth of his belief is largely coincidental, exactly the Gettier predicament that true belief is not sufficient for knowledge. The chapter applies reliabilist reasoning about testimony to conclude that Bates 'might have suspected, but he did not know.'
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 23 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Abraham Schwab turns Ygritte's 'You know nothing, Jon Snow' into a theory of epistemic humility: Jon misreads wildling courtship norms, Sam's dragonglass shatters on wight Small Paul, Lord Mormont assumes Mance fights like a southern king and pays for it at the Fist of First Men, while Arya's accurate self-knowledge keeps her alive. Formalizing with justified true belief - Sam's lucky dagger thrust is not knowledge, and the Watch's warranted belief that the dead Othor was harmless justifies falsity - he uses Lysa's letter, which sent Ned to King's Landing on a lie, to ask what justification is: Descartes's absolute certainty is too strict, reliabilism vindicates testimony ('dark wings, dark words'), so that only Sansa need witness Ned's beheading for the Starks to know it, and between Melisandre's circular dogma about Azor Ahai and total skepticism, moderate skepticism best governs belief - a humility the south lacked about the Horn of Winter.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 14 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Richard Greene surveys zombie types, from the radio-using corpse of Return of the Living Dead to White Zombie's servants, to fix walkers as the standard zombie worth asking what they know. Against Dr. Jenner's 'mindless instinct' verdict he cites the little girl walker retrieving her teddy bear, Jenny working her former home's doorknob, walkers breaking a shop window with a rock, and their sniffing out Rick and Glenn's gut disguise as evidence of genuine beliefs. He argues that zombie knowledge, which cannot involve weighing evidence, supports externalist, reliability-based accounts of knowledge over internalist ones, and that walkers know only simple things recalled from past experience—the more complex the task, the less likely they know it.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 13 "“Freaks of Nature” Extrasensory Perception and the Paranormal in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Keith Allen uses Stereo, Scanners, and The Dead Zone to explore the philosophy of ESP: telepathy and precognition challenge C. D. Broad's 'basic limiting principles' about causation (action at a distance, backward causation, changing the future). He asks whether ESP has the phenomenal 'tang' of genuine perception (Hume on force/vivacity; Nagel's 'what it is like'), and uses BonJour's reliable-clairvoyant Norman case plus Gettier to argue about internalist justification and knowledge, asking whether Johnny Smith needs reasons to trust his precognitive visions.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 61 "58. Tom Sawyer as Philosopher Lying and Deception on the Mississippi" — The chapter treats Mark Twain's Tom Sawyer novels as applied epistemology, arguing lying is far broader and more varied than spoken falsehood. Using Augustine's intent-to-deceive definition it analyzes Tom whitewashing the fence, the blood oath about Injun Joe's murder, Huck's 'sacrifice lie' about smallpox, and disguises as 'showing the false' (mimicking, inventing, decoying) versus 'hiding the truth' (masking, repackaging, dazzling). It invokes Gettier's method of counterexamples as a parallel to Twain showing the traditional definition of lying is too narrow, and links Tom's gaslighting of Aunt Sally and evolutionary/self-deception to modern fake news and deepfakes.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 17 "7. Knowledge, Space, and Time" — The chapter uses the TARDIS to defend a 'block universe' theory of spacetime over Presentism (since the Doctor visits past and future), then turns to epistemology, distinguishing belief from knowledge and 'belief in' the Doctor from 'belief that' he exists. It re-stages Gettier's justified-true-belief counterexample as picking the Doctor's next companion by a blue jean jacket, surveys Descartes's Cogito foundationalism, Hume's induction, and Reid's direct perception, and endorses Alston's reliabilist two-level foundationalism plus Klein's infinitism. It argues the Doctor's benefit-of-the-doubt toward non-rational creatures fits a reliabilist 'lower level' of knowledge and an imaginative, engaged, virtuous (Zagzebski) search for truth.

### Reliabilism

Reliabilism is a family of theories in epistemology, associated especially with Alvin Goldman, that ground the justification or knowledge-status of a belief in the reliability of the process that produced it. On this view a belief counts as justified when it is formed by a process—such as accurate perception or sound reasoning—that tends to yield true beliefs, rather than by any evidence the believer can consciously cite. Reliabilism arose partly as a response to Gettier-style cases and shifts the focus of epistemic evaluation from internal reasons to the truth-conducive workings of belief-forming mechanisms.

- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Adama's 'true lie' about Earth to motivate the Gettier problem: Starbuck's belief that Earth exists is true and justified by Adama's testimony, yet because that testimony is a lie, her justified true belief is not knowledge — just as Helo's true belief that the woman before him is 'Sharon' rests on mistaking Boomer for Athena. Goldman's reliabilism then questions whether sight, memory, and testimony are reliable belief-formers in a world of humanoid Cylons, weighing Hume's suspicion of testimony against Plantinga's defense of it. Finally Clifford's evidentialism is set against James's will to believe: the Colonials' forced, momentous choice to seek Earth shows that in an uncertain world pragmatic belief can be reasonable — 'so say we all.'
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 13 "More than a Feeling" — Rachel Robison-Greene asks whether Dexter's rule to 'be sure' actually gives him knowledge of his victims' guilt. Distinguishing Cartesian certainty - skeptical hypotheses about deceiving senses, dreams and evil demons, echoing The Matrix - from mere felt certainty, she tests the belief-truth-justification analysis of knowledge traced to Plato against the show: LaGuerta's witness theory fails on belief, Deb's conviction that Neil Perry is the Ice Truck Killer fails on truth, and Astor's accusation of Dexter fails on justification. Neither strong internalism (Dexter straps down Jamie Jaworski without knowing how the murder was done), weak internalism, coherence theory (his false but coherent case against Jonathan Farrow), nor reliabilism (his spidey-sense is explicitly not sufficient by his own admission) captures his practice, so his 'certainty' is just a feeling - and the people on his table may include ones he does not know to be guilty.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 8 "Education never ends Watson. It is a series of lessons with the greatest for" — J. Solomon Johnson asks whether Holmes's conclusions are knowledge or luck, walking through justified true belief with a Holmesian Gettier case (Watson rightly believing the killer was a former ship hand for the wrong reason), Moore's proof that knowledge entails belief, and Russell's stopped clock as an unsafe belief. BBC Sherlock's fake Vermeer and the 2009 film's 'resurrected' Lord Blackwood illustrate beliefs that fail safety or sensitivity across nearby possible worlds, while 'The Stock-Broker's Clerk' shows Holmes's observation of the scorched slippers making his belief sensitive. The verdict: Holmes is justified by the track record of his own expert methods, a professional billiards player rather than a beginner's-luck fluke, though real-world imitators could never rule out enough alternatives to match him.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 128 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — This section rebuilds the evidential case for the precogs from their verified early track record, which was free of errors of commission (predicting murders that never happened) and omission (missing murders that did). The still-zero present-murder rate rules out omissions, and cases like Howard Marks, caught mid-attempt, form a random and representative sample of the precogs' predictions showing commissions have not crept in, since arrest-timing delays correlate with nothing systematic about guilt.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 129 "Philip K. Dick and Philosophy" — The section concedes that Precrime techs erred in the Anne Lively case, failing to notice that some previsions showed ripples moving toward the shore and others away. Against Descartes's dream and evil-genius skepticism, updated as Putnam-style brain-in-a-vat scenarios via the Dream Crabs of 'Last Christmas' and the Dream Lord's two-worlds game, she deploys Goldman's three criteria for perceptual knowledge: justification is packed into reliable belief-forming processes, and doubt is warranted only in known abnormal contexts like funhouses or Dream Lord games.

The chapter cautions against confirming vague prophecies like bunny-shaped clouds, concluding Cooper becomes a truly "Special Epistemic Agent."

Strange's photographic memory exemplifies reliabilist epistemic ability, while Montmarquet's responsibilist virtues (impartiality, intellectual courage) are measured against Pangborn's self-serving magic, Kaecilius's courage without impartiality, and Mordo's epistemic rigidity and blind deference to authority ('no more questions'), each a vice of excess or deficiency. The Book of Cagliostro frames Wong's 'no knowledge in Kamar-Taj is forbidden, only certain practices,' and Strange emerges closest to the balanced intellectual character, though Aristotle demands consistency, not a single virtuous act.

Through the Invitation to Love Ouija-board example she shows how a reliable but unrecognized source yields externally justified belief (reliabilism); Cooper then earns internal justification the way one tests a hypothesis—treating the giant's predictions ('man in a smiling bag', 'the owls are not what they seem', 'without chemicals he points') as testable predictions that come true, making him a 'special epistemic agent.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica to explore knowledge as justified true belief. Adama's 'true lie' about knowing Earth's location makes Starbuck's belief in Earth a Gettier case, a justified true belief resting on false justification. He tests Adama's testimony against Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for spotting Cylons; memory deceives Boomer and Tigh) and Hume's skepticism about testimony versus Plantinga's defense of it. Finally, against Clifford's evidentialism he deploys William James's 'will to believe,' arguing that faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice that gives the Colonials purpose.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 14 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Roche's 'Seeing Snakes' attacks the psychedelicist claim (William James on nitrous oxide, Huxley's 'reducing valve,' Leary) that drugs including cannabis reveal reality-as-it-is. He deploys Russell's line that we 'can make no distinction between the man who eats little and sees heaven and the man who drinks much and sees snakes,' and a reliabilist demand that knowledge have a source proven reliable over independently verifiable cases, to argue drug 'revelations' are indistinguishable from delusion. Foucault is cited that drugs have 'nothing to do with truth and falsity,' and Nietzsche's Dionysian veil-of-Maya passage is used as an example of the mystical rhetoric he debunks.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 15 "“You Have to Have Something to Live For. Let it be Earth”" — Eric Silverman uses Battlestar Galactica's Adama, who lies that he knows Earth's location, to run the Gettier problem: Starbuck's true belief that Earth exists rests on a false justification (that Adama knows), so it is justified-true-belief without being knowledge. He tests testimony via Goldman's reliabilism (sight is unreliable for telling Cylons from humans) and the Hume/Locke/Plantinga debate over testimony's epistemic role. He closes with James's 'will to believe': faith in Earth is a forced, momentous choice where agnosticism forfeits meaning, so belief without certainty can be reasonable.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 17 "7. Knowledge, Space, and Time" — The chapter uses the TARDIS to defend a 'block universe' theory of spacetime over Presentism (since the Doctor visits past and future), then turns to epistemology, distinguishing belief from knowledge and 'belief in' the Doctor from 'belief that' he exists. It re-stages Gettier's justified-true-belief counterexample as picking the Doctor's next companion by a blue jean jacket, surveys Descartes's Cogito foundationalism, Hume's induction, and Reid's direct perception, and endorses Alston's reliabilist two-level foundationalism plus Klein's infinitism. It argues the Doctor's benefit-of-the-doubt toward non-rational creatures fits a reliabilist 'lower level' of knowledge and an imaginative, engaged, virtuous (Zagzebski) search for truth.

### Free Will vs Determinism

The free will problem asks whether human beings can act freely and be morally responsible if every event, including our choices, is fixed by prior causes. Determinism holds that the state of the world at any moment, together with the laws of nature, necessitates exactly one future, which seems to leave no room for genuine alternatives. Hard determinists conclude that free will is therefore an illusion, while libertarians insist that we do possess a freedom incompatible with determinism and so deny that determinism is true of our choices. The dispute bears directly on praise, blame, punishment, and desert.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 47 "Fate, Freedom, and Foreknowledge" — Schick opens with the Morpheus-Neo exchange on Fate ('I don't like the idea that I'm not in control of my life') and Cypher's 'You call this free?', arguing that whatever freedom the enslaved enjoy outside the Matrix may be equally illusory: if the Oracle's prophecies are true, the future is fixed, and then no one, not even Neo, is in control of his life. He poses the subversive question of whether Cypher's return to happy slavery was really a betrayal, and sets out to examine the natures of fate and freedom.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 49 "Unknown" — Schick quotes Nozick's experience-machine passage at length and catalogs the parallels with the Matrix: floating in a tank, electrodes stimulating the brain, experiences indistinguishable from reality, the only difference being that Nozick's users unplug every two years. He rehearses Nozick's three reasons not to plug in - we want to do things rather than merely experience doing them, we want to be a certain sort of person rather than an 'indeterminate blob', and we want contact with a deeper reality - then turns the lesson on the Oracle's world: do the freed make real choices either, or are their choices pre-ordained?
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 52 "Unknown" — This section lays out causal determinism through Laplace's demon: an intelligence that knew every force and every position could compute the entire future, leaving no one free or responsible, so people in the Matrix would be no worse off than we are. It notes that both sides of the nature-nurture debate (including B.F. Skinner) agree behavior is caused by forces beyond our control, and turns to Epicurus, who posited random atomic 'swerves' to make room for free will. Modern quantum indeterminacy, it concludes, likewise expels determinism from physics and at least makes free will possible, though randomness alone cannot ground responsibility.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 53 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that the Oracle's predictions come true not because the future is fixed but because they are self-fulfilling: her remark about the vase is what brings about its breaking ('would you still have broken it if I hadn't said anything?'), and Morpheus's 'she told you exactly what you needed to hear' shows she shapes rather than reads the future. On this reading the Oracle needs no real foreknowledge, only believers who trust that she knows the path. Only so can Neo be in control of his life in a world where 'anything, within the bounds of reason, is possible.'
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 75 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that egotism - each individual's spontaneous belief that he is 'the One', the center of the universe for which everything was made - is the fundamental moral error, and that morality demands recognizing our oneness with all intelligent beings. The red pill symbolizes the basic choice between two matrices: the world of separate egos, bodies colliding in space and time under deterministic causality, and the world of human unity and freedom seen from the standpoint of moral consciousness - and the initial choice must then survive a crisis in which its realizability is doubted.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 85 "Unknown" — The chapter reads the film through Dostoevsky's Notes from Underground, a satire of Chernyshevsky's rationalist-utopian What Is to Be Done?: the underground man sees that social science's 'logarithm' of desire reduces us to piano keys governed by natural law, and responds with hyperconscious spite, inertia, and the deliberate choice of the harmful to prove he can will - anticipating Nietzsche's claim that humans would 'rather will nothing than not will'. Shigalyov's 'starting from unlimited freedom, I conclude with unlimited despotism' names the Enlightenment's contradiction, and the underground man's life is the reductio ad nihilum of theories his opponents only dare carry halfway.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 86 "Unknown" — The chapter aligns the Nebuchadnezzar with the underground man's cell: in the 'desert of the real' the rebels begin from Morpheus's felt 'something is wrong' and live the quest ('it's the question that drives us') that The X-Files-style paranoia cannot complete, risking either permanent entrapment or Mark Edmundson's 'facile transcendence'. It contrasts Neo's shallow freedom-as-control ('No... because then I wouldn't be in control') with Morpheus's providential fate, reads Cypher as consciously relinquishing willing for comfort, and likens the Matrix's project of changing 'the human being into a battery' to Diderot's piano-key man and Agent Smith's utopian 'we're the cure'.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 98 "Real Genre and Virtual Philosophy" — Knight and McKnight argue The Matrix must be read as a mixed-genre film: pure genres are 'a theorist's fiction', and the film's genre inheritance supplies the narrative roots of its philosophical thematics - Plato's cave from the Republic, Descartes's Dream Hypothesis from the Meditations, Nietzsche's Ubermensch, Zen Buddhism, and apocalyptic Christianity. Recognizing the genre mix explains both why the film raises questions about justified true belief in a virtual world, free will versus deterministic control, and appearance versus reality, and why it offers no philosophical answers, only genre ones.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 33 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Uses the show to argue the problem of evil is evidential rather than logical, and tests each theodicy against Sopranos cases: evil as natural-law by-product (Junior's and Jackie's cancers), punishment for sin (Carmela's cancer scare, Ralph telling Father Phil his hospitalized son is God's payback in 'Whoever Did This'), God's higher morality (rejected as meaningless as 'a triangle with four sides'), long-run goods (Artie's restaurant fire), and character-building (rejected with Melfi's 'How many people have to die for your personal growth?'). The free-will defense also fails - God could have given us Meadow-like dispositions - and Tony's 'You're born to this shit' versus Melfi's insistence on genuine choice dramatizes the debate. The chapter ends with Tony as the Old Testament Yahweh writ small: a jealous, vengeful, tribal ruler whose appeal is no more mysterious than His.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 35 "NOTES" — Defends a fixed-time theory from the Prisoner of Azkaban time-travel episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and Buckbeak and Sirius are saved without anything changing, while acknowledging Hermione's warnings about wizards killing their past selves complicate the picture, and adds special relativity's absence of an absolute present as further support. The section then argues that the sheer improbability of the luck fulfilling the prophecies, the Myrtle's-bathroom Polyjuice chain, Felix Felicis, the capture that delivers Griphook, and Harry's arrival at the Shrieking Shack, makes better sense with something like divine providence guiding events than with pure chance.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — Argues Merope did not truly love Riddle because the potion robbed him of the freedom to do otherwise, invoking Harry Frankfurt's denial that alternative possibilities are necessary for freedom and noting that even compatibilists deny potion-induced affection is free, since Tom would not have wanted to love her under magical inducement. Real love respects the beloved's true interests and creates a relationship in which both grow, and even self-administered potions wrong the user by forfeiting the moral growth that only uncoerced commitment makes possible.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Contends that Voldemort was not his mother's son: what defines a person is the habitual pattern of choices, as in Aristotle's 'we are what we consistently do', and Merope, who freed Riddle at the cost of her own life and renounced magic entirely, is a genuine though partial redemption, whereas Voldemort followed Marvolo Gaunt and Salazar Slytherin instead. Quoting William Hasker on how love potions trap both parties because love must be freely bestowed, the section argues character is destiny only if forged by free choice, and that Harry, protected by his mother's sacrificial love, shows what Voldemort's rejection of love and vulnerability destroyed.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 142 "NOTES" — Argues via William James's 'sow a thought... reap a destiny' and Aristotle's account of how repeated action incrementally shapes the soul that Voldemort's flayed remnant is a character fully forged by choices, stuck with itself forever - a postmortem fate Heidegger's atheism cannot frame but Rowling's afterlife can. The section weighs Locke's memory-and-character account of identity, Kant's postulate that harmony of virtue and happiness requires an afterlife, and Pascal on why the immortality question must govern how we live, and ends asking whether Voldemort's evil is ignorance, as Plato held, or a cultivated appetite that only vice can satisfy.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 31 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jonathan Sanford distinguishes necessity of the end, of compulsion, and of nature to argue Christ's passion was both necessary and free: justice requires reparation for the harmony Adam and Eve broke, God cannot simply waive it without making a mockery of sin, yet no compulsion operates on Christ — unlike the blind inner drives Nietzsche's will to power or Schopenhauer's will would represent. Using Aristotle, he argues Christ's fully virtuous character (practical wisdom plus courage and temperance become a 'second nature') makes disobedience nearly unimaginable, and his divinity makes it impossible, so his choice 'could not have been different' precisely because it was perfectly free; the Gethsemane agony shows not division in the God-man but the difficulty of holding his human and divine wills in unity.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 9 "“This One a Long Time Have I Watched”" — Eberl argues that Anakin and Luke are radically free despite the Chosen One prophecy and Obi-Wan's 'you cannot escape your destiny.' Borrowing Augustine and Aquinas on God's eternity, he holds that foreknowledge (like the Jedi prophecy fulfilled when Vader destroys the Emperor) does not compel events - Anakin's choice makes the prophecy true, not vice versa - and applies Aristotle's tomorrow's-sea-battle to future-contingents like Obi-Wan's self-surrender on the Death Star. Using Locke's locked-room example and Augustine's account of 'inordinate desire,' he concludes that Anakin's fall stems from his own disordered will to control fate ('learn to stop people from dying'), while Han Solo embodies libertarian alternative possibilities ('No mystical energy field controls my destiny').
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 15 "The Fate of Evil after the Overthrow of the Empire" — Brown treats Luke's 'Is the Dark Side stronger?' as the problem of evil: distinguishing natural evils (the wampa, bigger fish) from moral evils (Tarkin destroying Alderaan), he surveys the Platonic craftsman working recalcitrant matter and the Manichean dualism of two gods - the Emperor as would-be 'evil incarnate' - before giving Augustine's answer. On Augustine's free-will defense, no creature is inherently evil; the origin of each moral evil is the creature's own pride and free choice, so Anakin, not the Emperor's seduction, is responsible for his turn ('I'm a Jedi. I know I'm better than this'). The chapter ends on whether evil can ever be finally defeated, arguing the Jedi prophecies of 'balance' fit a world where evil is a permanent possibility that heroism needs.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 38 "The Vigilante Man of Faith Hero or Tragic Figure" — Morris answers his title question 'both': Daredevil refuses to kill even Doctor Octopus ('Then I'd be no better than you'), saves the cancer-stricken Bullseye, and tells Typhoid Mary 'You are who you are because of the choices you make', denying that accidents or heritage define a person. To Detective Manolis he gives a law-and-society argument against private killing - 'The moment one man takes another man's life in his own hands, he is rejecting the law... I'm not God - I'm not the law - and I'm not a murderer' - yet his repeated sparing of Bullseye makes him feel complicit in later murders, the tragic cost of his faith, which he nonetheless concludes is strength rather than weakness.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 20 "Moral Autonomy" — Martin van Hees reads "Who Killed Davey Moore?" and "Ballad of Hollis Brown" as arguments that shared consent generates shared responsibility for tragedy even when fate makes the events inevitable - the referee, crowd, manager, and gambler all endorsed the fight, and we who tolerate poverty consent to the next Hollis Brown. He distinguishes a "limited optimistic view" (twisting fate by preventing particular tragedies) from the proclaimed inevitability of "The Times They Are A-Changin'" and the pessimism of "Blind Willie McTell," then defends compatibilism through Frankfurt's Jones/Black case: responsibility needs no alternative possibilities, only that one act from one's own will. Dylan's "moral autonomy" is taking a stance - singing the blues - inside a determined world.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 20 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Feldman tests Harley's 'Great American Freedom Machine' slogan against each conception of freedom: metaphysical freedom (universal causation, divine foreknowledge, fate) cannot depend on your vehicle; legal freedom actually shrinks for riders through helmet mandates and extra licensing; and circumstantial freedom is gained equally by any vehicle, a wheelchair being the true freedom machine. Borrowing Socrates' comparison method from the Philebus, he argues the alleged 'feeling of freedom' is really a feeling of happiness or exhilaration combined with the false belief that one is freer than a Camry driver. What really binds him to his 1986 FXRT is fun, the thrill of leaning to the edge, and the sensory and historical pleasures of the air-cooled V-twin line back to the Silent Grey Fellow, which have nothing to do with freedom.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 20 "Poker and Philosophy" — Northcott loses his first casino tournament to a fluky inside straight and mines the bad beat for philosophy of science: objective odds collapse into knowledge-relative probabilities (a card-tracking magician would assign different numbers to the very same draw), Laplacean determinism versus quantum chance bears on whether decision theory presupposes free will, and bad-beat counterfactuals — 'I'd have won the tournament but for that hand' — get David Lewis's possible-worlds closeness analysis and Hume's counterfactual account of causation, with no settled verdict. Even game theory cannot deliver a perfect system: a Nash-equilibrium strategy is only optimal against other optimal players, so the mindless all-in 'Stupidus' beats it. Conclusion: no can't-lose system exists, and poker will never be a game for robots.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 30 "Oh Yes, There Will Be Blood" — Rachel Robison asks why blood, of all substances, carries metaphysical powers in vampire lore - Elizabeth Bathory's youth-giving baths, Dracula's control over Mina once she drinks his blood, Sookie's bond with Bill in True Blood. Her explanation is historical: the ancient cardiocentric view (Aristotle, Empedocles, Chrysippus placing the rational center in the heart and making blood its product) plus Galenic humorism and bloodletting made blood the carrier of the self, so drinking someone's blood plausibly transmits bits of their personal identity, knowledge, and even domination over one's free will. She then tests the show's synthetic 'True Blood': either some essential property of blood (or of the act of drinking it) carries the power, or the legend is parasitic on our lingering habit of locating emotion and character in the heart ('hot blooded') - either way the myth stays credible because our metaphors of blood never died.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" — David Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman's dedication without reducing it to trauma-determined compulsion: Alfred's butler's-world illustrates being-in-the-world and the thrown-project, and Bruce's confrontation with death, culminating in the bleeding alley scene of Miller's Batman: Year One, is Angst, the recognition of finitude that strips ordinary meanings away. Seen this way, "I shall become a bat" is an authentic, responsible choice of a whole life rather than a mechanical effect of childhood trauma. Hart concludes that Heidegger's analysis dissolves the free will versus determinism debate, since Batman neither blindly follows causes nor chooses from nowhere.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 48 "Reap a Destiny" — Jonathan and Jerry Walls read Deathly Hallows philosophically: Harry's willing march into the Forbidden Forest is Heideggerian authenticity, confronting being-toward-death, while Voldemort's horcruxes and the maimed King's Cross stowaway are the inauthentic flight from mortality that ruins the soul. The afterlife scene raises the stakes of this life: by James's "sow a thought... reap a destiny," Aristotle's habituation, and Locke's memory-based identity, Voldemort's lifelong refusal of remorse fixes his character beyond repair, and Kant and Pascal supply reasons why belief in an afterlife transforms morality. Dumbledore's purgatory-like repentance, contrasted with Voldemort's fate, shows that our choices reap a destiny we must live with forever.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 14 "“Your Heavenly Father Feeds Them”" — Calef takes the Tides restaurant scene ('Who are you? What are you?') and Diogenes's plucked rooster versus Plato's 'featherless biped' as a springboard for testing every classic criterion of humanity against the film. Aristotle's rational soul fails because Mrs. Bundy's 'brain pans' reasoning is wrong and some humans cannot reason; Descartes's language test fails because the myna bird can learn to talk while horrified humans go mute; Rousseau's free will fails because the birds behave unpredictably and resist instinct while humans are trapped, caged, and herd-like; Aristotle's political animal and Hobbes's social contract fail because the town's hoods and lawbreakers contrast with birds that flock together across species. Even the appeal to God's favor turns dark, as the drunk quotes scripture while Revelation's birds gather for a supper of human flesh, leaving the film a mirror in which we must examine ourselves.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 26 "“Just Like Mary Shelley, Just Like Frankenstein”" — Chuck Ward uses 'Mama Tried' (the meek family's rebel son doing life without parole) and the mysterious birthmark in 'Mississippi Half-Step Uptown Toodleloo' to ask whether character is fixed from birth, setting the songs' fatalism against Aristotle's account of character as habituated choice and Plato's claim that traits tend to be inherited. He surveys behavioral genetics, twin studies, The Bell Curve, and the supposed 'criminality gene' before arguing that genetic determinism is a mistaken reductionism: like the groovy atmosphere of a Dead show, which shapes the very individuals who produce it, complex systems admit top-down causation, so genes never act alone. The chapter's payoff is that the songs' studied ambiguity — mama tried, yet 'that leaves no one but me to blame' — shows art expressing, rather than resolving, the tension between free will and determinism.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 29 "Christmas in Jamaica" — David Werther frames Jack Cash's saw death—which Cash told Nick Tosches he considered murder—and the 1982 armed robbery at Cinnamon Hill as tests of Epicurus's old questions (quoted via Hume): could a good, powerful God have prevented these evils? Distinguishing the evidential from the logical problem, he answers the logical problem with Plantinga's libertarian free will: not even God could ensure Cash freely 'walked the line' with Vivian, since guaranteeing fidelity would eliminate freedom. He rebuts the compatibilist counterobjection by arguing, with Aquinas, that nothing can be the cause of its own nature, and argues heaven can still fulfill Johnny and June's hope of meeting 'on the far side banks of the Jordan' even if the redeemed can no longer act wrongly.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 36 "Free to Be You and Me" — Bryan Barker reconciles Cylon programming and human 'destiny' with freedom through compatibilism and Schopenhauer's intelligible character: Boomer's sabotage and shooting of Adama under activation, Baltar's cowardly conversion to the Cylon God, Tigh's decision to stay at his post upon learning he is a Cylon, and Starbuck's flight into the storm in 'Maelstrom' all express innate, unchanging character rather than external compulsion. Even destiny, as in Leoben's prophecies to Starbuck, works like determinism unless reframed as character. On this view we are free because everything we do manifests who we immutably are, whether that character is programmed or born.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 40 "To the Third Power . ." — Ivan Wolfe shows that Glen Larson's original series is 'ontologically Mormon': Kobol anagrammatizes Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve mirrors the LDS hierarchy, marriage is a 'sealing' for eternity, the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were' restates Lorenzo Snow's couplet on human deification, and Count Iblis can rule only those who freely submit, since agency is supreme in Mormon theology. Because none of this is epistemologically required viewing knowledge, later licensees could rewrite the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics became an incoherent muddle by abandoning the inviolability of free will, while Hatch's novels and Moore's re-imagining built new ontologies, Moore replacing progressive godhood with the circular 'all this has happened before.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 44 "Human, Machine, or Something In-between" — Heather Rolufs maps Boomer Sharon and Caprica Six onto Eve and Lilith: Boomer's unwitting shooting of Adama parallels Eve eating the fruit before she could understand disobedience, raising whether her free will was ever real, while Baltar repeats Adam's blame-shifting and Six gains the rebuttal Eve never had. The Lilith material from the Alphabet of Ben Sira and the Zohar explains Six's red-dressed seduction of Baltar and her ambivalent violence, snapping a baby's neck as a mercy before the attack yet later risking herself to return Hera. The chapter argues the show lets these demonized first women of myth be reread as neither machines nor demons but human.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 28 "A Link to the Present" — Compagno argues that the word 'I' in Zelda simultaneously names Link, the virtual body, and the player, the invisible will, and builds this into a 'Schopenhauerian Console': as Schopenhauer held, we have freedom of action but not freedom of will, since the decisions of the unknowable will never appear in consciousness (against Descartes' free mind and Dennett's Cartesian theater critique). Kant's transcendental subject, standing at the border of experience, becomes the player's perspective from which Hyrule exists, what Foucault would call an empirical-transcendental doublet. The payoff: Link's quest is fated and scripted, yet the player wills it in a perpetual present, enacting Schopenhauer's lesson that a determined life is still lived as one's own free act.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "Rescuing Princess Zelda" — Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 20 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier tests Pullman's many-worlds premise, setting Asriel's coin-toss explanation and the Barnard-Stokes hypothesis against Book III's claim that unchosen possibilities are 'snuffed out like candles,' then measures the trilogy against David Lewis's causally independent possible worlds, which forbid the subtle knife's transworld travel and leave the chill Lyra feels at the thought of 'another Lyra' in Will's Oxford as an unresolved transworld-identity puzzle. Compiling fourteen kinds of conscious beings from humans and dæmons to specters and the Abyss itself, he argues Pullman's cosmology is panpsychist and aesthetic rather than moral or epistemic, ordered by what the alethiometer, the knife, and the spyglass can and cannot do, with the alethiometer submitting to the knife and love alone able to break it, as Will's love for his mother and for Lyra does twice. Peirce's agapicism, evolution by creative love alongside chance and mechanical necessity, supplies the closest philosophical analogue to Pullman's 'Matter loved Dust.'
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 21 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Michaud asks whether a prophesied savior can be a hero: since Lyra can succeed only in ignorance of the witches' prophecy (Dr. Lanselius's condition), either others keep her ignorant and she saves the world or someone tells her and she fails, so the outcome never depends on her any more than Iorek's eating of Iofur's heart depends on bear choice. Frankfurt's counterexample, recast with the Magisterium's Fra Pavel standing by to force your choice, shows one can be blameworthy despite being unable to do otherwise, and Fischer's guidance control, a reasons-responsive decision-making mechanism that is your own, checked across possible worlds, explains why responsibility survives absent alternatives. But Lyra's case exposes a flaw in that account: her success hinges on things she cannot control, so responsibility is shared among all who kept the prophecy secret, and heroism lies in character and self-sacrifice rather than sole control of the outcome.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 13 "Singing of the Good Things" — Scott Calef asks whether Led Zeppelin's lives of wealth, groupies, and no-questions-asked liberty were genuinely free and therefore enviable. Locke's distinction between weak freedom (doing what you want, with Page happily locked in his suite at the Riot House) and strong freedom (being able to do otherwise, defended via beer-spilling concert excuses) is destabilized by the observation that no one ever does other than what they did. Rousseau then dominates: the state of nature versus LA, freedom as the capacity to resist natural impulse, which explains both Zep's libertine promiscuity and the paradox that heroin and alcohol enslave the very freedom that took them (the post-Physical Graffiti decline, Bonzo's death), while the band's violence—Bonham's assaults, the Oakland beating—shows society's suppression of natural pity, not natural aggression as Hobbes would have it. Socrates gets the last word: doing what we please is not doing what we truly want, so only the temperate person is free.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 14 "True Selves Found or Made" — Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 13 "Which World Am I In" — Juan Ferret tells the story from inside the game: Admetus the Human Mage, chased through Alterac Valley by an Undead Rogue, works through Zeno's paradox of motion, the convergence of infinite series, and whether space and time are discrete, coached by a bodiless voice that turns out to be his player. The voice's revelations — 'You are my creation,' autorun, polymorph, Blink — force the free-will-versus-determinism question from the character's side, since every action is controlled from above. Reference frames, Heisenberg's uncertainty, EPR entanglement, and hidden nods to David Lewis ('Siwel Divad' on possible worlds) and many-worlds theory leave the mage wondering which world, server, or parallel universe he really inhabits.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 34 "One Last Anguished Existential Scream" — Argues Neon Genesis Evangelion and Akira dramatize a justified anxiety about humanity's evolutionary future: SEELE's Human Instrumentality Project — dissolving everyone into the Sea of LCL because separate, mutually harming individuals have 'run the course' of their evolution — is Heideggerian anxiety (the objectless unease that breaks us out of 'the They') curdled, via Mary Midgley's 'fatalism,' into the belief that genes, Moore's Law, or 'the Market' leave no room for human choice. Akira's Numbered Children, who sacrifice themselves to remove Tetsuo and save Kaneda, model the responsible alternative: accepting that the power is coming, screaming about it, and still choosing how humanity faces it rather than abdicating to fate.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 16 "Added Time" — McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run. Hume's empiricist argument against miracles then shows we could never be justified in believing either goal miraculous, since the mundane explanation—Maradona's cheek and skill, lapses of concentration, a missed handball call—always has the whole of past experience on its side.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 39 "Choosing the Scapegoat" — Northcott dissects England's penalty shoot-out misery to ask whether 'bad luck' is objective or a scapegoat: what counts as luck depends on the reasonable standard of preparation, so what was bad luck twenty years ago (no practice) is negligence today, and under Laplace's demon's determinism no sixty-percent chances would exist at all. He rehabilitates objective luck relative to shared standards of reasonableness, concluding that shoot-outs genuinely are more of a lottery than open play — though not a total one. On blame, he uses the deviation-from-default account of causation and Mill's problem of causal selection to argue that singling out a referee over missed open goals or injuries has no objective justification; moral feelings and prejudice pick our scapegoats.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 10 "Intending the Way Out" — Stages the paradox of foreknowledge through Paul's prescient dream of meeting Chani and his futile struggle against the foreseen jihad: since knowledge (on Plato's justified-true-belief account) is factive, a known future seems unalterable. It tests the classic escapes—Boethius's God in ever-present eternity and Aquinas's seeing all time 'under the aspect of eternity,' Laplace's demon, Richard Taylor's fatalism—and finds the Atreides oracles are no gods, only probabilistic predictors whose visions fix the possibilities they see. The way out is Anscombe's Intention: like God knowing creation because He authored it, Paul and Leto know their futures practically, as agents whose intentions help decide which possibilities become actual, so freedom survives as terrific responsibility.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 26 "In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . ." — Continues the earlier defense of oracular freedom ('Curse of the Golden Path'): because an oracle's gaze from a present moment fixes the very set of future possibilities, Paul and Leto are free precisely where they are blind—above all in their 'vision-battle' in the Tanzerouft, which no oracle can foresee, and which Paul's single whispered 'Don't' concedes to his son's Golden Path. Leto's breeding of Siona, invisible to prescience, is read as his deliberate self-blinding—'the price of freedom is an invigilance of eternity'—and the whole affair vindicates heroism as steering probabilities rather than escaping fate. Paul emerges as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense, whose hamartia is his all-too-human refusal to become a monster to save the future.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 11 "You Can’t Help What Happened to You. But You Can Make the Best of It" — Daniel Haas asks whether we can blame Dexter at all if his Dark Passenger is a compulsion formed by the shipping-container trauma he did not choose, and whether consistency then forces us to excuse the Trinity Killer and Ice Truck Killer too. Distinguishing attributive responsibility from accountability, he argues psychopaths cannot be motivated by moral reasons because they lack the moral emotions, and that it was sheer luck whether a traumatized boy landed in Harry's loving home and Code (Dexter) or a mental institution (Brian). Yet Dexter's critical reflection on and revision of Harry's Code, and his willingness to forgo turning himself in to spare Deb, Rita and the kids, paradoxically make him more accountable than ordinary psychopaths and even praiseworthy for his quest to become 'a little wooden boy' who is more human, even if he still deserves to be locked up.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 12 "Almost Caught!" — Nicolas Michaud deploys Harry Frankfurt's attack on the principle that blame requires alternative possibilities: through a 'Dex kills Deb' case with a counterfactual intervener and a locked-steering-wheel driver, he shows one can be blameworthy despite having no choice, provided one acts because one wants to. Applied to Dexter, the question is which level of compulsion he has - and since he never truly restrains himself, never turns himself in, and his Season 2 relapse reads as empowerment rather than addiction, he seems to want to want to kill, so Frankfurt's verdict is guilt despite inevitability. The chapter closes with a fictional Princeton encounter where Dexter faces a dilemma - either his victims are blameless compulsives, making him a killer of innocents who violates Harry's Code, or wanting to kill makes them and him blameworthy - and Dexter's choice to kill Frankfurt himself proves he acts freely and is guilty.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 28 "A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives" — David Ramsay Steele first calculates that Dexter is a public benefactor - each killed predator saves several net lives a year - and then explains the deeper appeal through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and Adam Smith's invisible hand: like good law, Harry's Code channels an amoral appetite (the thrill of killing) into socially beneficial results without reforming the appetite itself, refuting Christianity's fixation on pure motives. Dexter thus does totally the right thing for totally the wrong reason. Finally Steele doubts Dexter's own story: the spontaneously unlocked door of the Castillos' shed shows real empathy, and it was Harry's deliberate instruction (Nurse Mary), not fate, that made him a killer - 'addiction is always a choice.'
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 37 "Dexter, Hero of Our Time" — David Ramsay Steele compares Dexter with the rational vigilante heroes of earlier popular fiction - Edgar Wallace's Four Just Men, E.W. Hornung's Raffles, Bulldog Drummond, the Saint - who killed bad guys for justice and were read without moral panic, and asks why the Parents Television Council now singles Dexter out. His answer: Dexter is ideologically 'safe' because the modern 'ideology of childhood trauma' works like the folk-tale love potion, presenting the hero as a puppet of irresistible compulsion rather than a responsible agent, so no one can accuse the show of endorsing calculated vigilantism. The chapter is thus a free-will-and-excuse argument: determinism-as-excuse has become the price of admission for unofficial justice on screen.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 20 "Videogame Apocalypses and Secularism" — Rachel Wagner, Tyler DeHaven, and Chris Hendrickson argue Halo satisfies the Society of Biblical Literature definition of apocalypse: revelatory narrative, otherworldly mediators (Cortana, 343 Guilty Spark), predetermined eschatology, with Master Chief as a Davidic messiah whose name John-117 echoes the Gospel of John. The Covenant's Tower-of-Babel hubris versus human secularism, and the Flood read through the Book of Enoch's Watchers, turn the story into a critique of rampant consumption and blind religion. Where traditional apocalypses are quietist—God the programmer's deterministic script, salvation not depending on human action—Halo's procedural rhetoric hands agency to the player as messiah, and the chapter closes asking whether videogame apocalypse offers only temporary, magic-circle comfort for secular angst in a morally relativist age.
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 25 "What You Really Wanted Was Inside You All Along" — Robert Kincaid maps Freud's structural model of the psyche onto Conch Street: Patrick under his rock is the pleasure-principle Id, guilt-administering Squidward the Super-Ego, and mediating SpongeBob the Ego, so 'Mermaid Man and Barnacle Boy IV' becomes the Ego minimizing, rationalizing and literally shrinking its own conscience and desires to dodge guilt over the belt.
