Lewis's tools then dissolve the puzzles: the Hurley-Miles 'we already had this conversation' exchange, baby and adult Miles as one person spread like a time-worm, the Faraday-kills-Eloise grandfather paradox, and the Locke-Richard compass causal loop, whose point of origin the show leaves unresolved.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Pierce argues that Lost's time travel runs on a fixed-time model in which nothing that happened can be undone, so the live question is ethical: Kate insists saving young Ben is still obligatory and Sayid remains responsible for shooting him, while Jack's plan to detonate Jughead at the Swan shows that trying to change the past can cause the very evil it targets, the Incident. Using Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity - future-tense truths made true by our own free choices - he shows that 'whatever happened, happened' does not abolish moral responsibility, applying the point to the Man in Black's causal-loop manipulation of Locke, Richard, and Ben. Desmond's consciousness travel in 'The Constant' is treated as the exception requiring hyper-time or alternate realities, and Pierce concludes that morality in time travel is simply ordinary morality, with Kate offering the most balanced view of the characters' choices.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 11 "Bringing Corporations and Government Together" — Guilfoy stages Galbraith's The Affluent Society against Friedman's Capitalism and Freedom through the Heineken case: Don's end-aisle display made Betty serve the beer at her dinner party, and when she found out she had been the target demographic she accused him ('You embarrassed me'). Galbraith's deep-self compatibilism holds that advertising-created desires are not genuinely ours, so Betty's choice was unfree, and that consumerism produces private wealth amid public squalor (the Cadillac picnic litter scene, the Madison Square Garden account Lane kills for lack of profit); Friedman's libertarian free will answers that Betty simply chose, desires are reasons rather than causes, and Pete's Admiral Negro-market pitch shows the market punishing racist irrationality. Both economists converge on the danger dramatized in 'The Inheritance': when Sterling Cooper sells corporations to congressmen and congressmen to corporations, consumers lose under either theory.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Uses the holodeck as a working model for the ancient claim that everyday reality is appearance: Plato's cave shadows, maya in Hindu and Buddhist thought, and Bostrom's simulation argument (his ancestor simulations mirrored in Data and Geordi's endless Holmes holoprograms) converge with quantum "holographic universe" speculation to suggest our universe may be a cosmic holoprogram with limit conditions like light speed as processing boundaries. Moriarty seizing the Enterprise in "Ship in a Bottle", Vic Fontaine, and the EMH dramatize self-aware programs confronting their code, and the chapter argues our "free will" may be similarly bounded - Data-as-Holmes must stay in character, and Picard "can't transcend the script" any more than his NPCs can. Picard's closing admission that our reality may be "an elaborate simulation running inside a little device" delivers the skeptical upshot, alongside the ethical question of whether self-aware holograms deserve rights.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Michaud puts Jar Jar Binks on trial for proposing the emergency powers that let Palpatine become Emperor and doom the galaxy. He weighs Nagel's resultant moral luck through a two-Lukes landspeeder case, Susan Wolf's virtue-based reply that equal fault can deserve different feelings, Kant's 'ought implies can' and the categorical imperative, and a Frankfurt-style scenario in which Palpatine's hypothetical mind-trick removes Jar Jar's ability to choose otherwise. The verdict: as a deceived, politically limited character trying to do good, Jar Jar is not guilty of the Empire's crimes - only of being obnoxious.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 14 "Moral Autonomy" — Challans reads the clone army as a Foucauldian project of discipline: Kaminoan reconditioning, punishment of 'aberrance,' and the inhibitor chips produce the 'docile bodies' that made Order 66 executable, with Palpatine's propaganda framing the Jedi as traitors to supply its legitimacy. Milgram's obedience experiments explain why most clones became 'agentic' executioners, while the rare independence of Rex, Fives, and Tup in the Umbara arc — 'we are not a bunch of unthinking droids!' — shows how fragile moral autonomy is. He concludes that military competence itself requires independent judgment, as his Delta Force versus Rangers comparison after Mogadishu illustrates, making Rex the exemplar of the moral autonomy the chips were designed to destroy.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 20 "The End" — Berghofer uses the Rebels episode 'A World Between Worlds' to ask whether Ezra changed the past when he pulled Ahsoka out of her duel with Vader, arguing that past-changing time travel breeds contradiction: the grandfather paradox looms over his attempt to save Kanan ('if he is taken out of this moment, you all die'), and on the Lewis-style consistent model Ezra caused but never changed the past. He surveys presentism, eternalism, and the growing block to locate Star Wars' metaphysics of time — Ezra's travel rules out presentism, and the Mortis god's 'the future, by its nature, can be changed' fits a growing block with an open future. Anakin's tragedy of acting to prevent prophesied events and thereby causing them frames the whole analysis.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 27 "16. You Made Me First" — Starting from the Joker's 'You made me' / Batman's 'You made me first' exchange in Tim Burton's Batman, the chapter argues origin stories fix character: Bruce's witnessed trauma destines him to darkness (and we expect his death to match), while Kal-El is sent to Earth as an act of hope that the chapter reads through William James's will-to-believe—belief itself makes success possible, like Bruce's ropeless leap in The Dark Knight Rises. Against 'I can do whatever I want' free will it deploys Schopenhauer's 'we can do what we will, but we cannot will what we will': Bruce cannot will away his vengeance, and Red Son's Soviet-raised Superman shows biology and upbringing determining who Clark becomes. Superman still wins because his origin story permits the hope that Bruce's cannot.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 11 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Ralston and Applegate read the Winchesters' contested destiny through the free will debate: the angels' case for determinism runs from a cupid arranged to couple John and Mary, through Azazel's deal and Mary's death, to Zachariah and Michael's claim that 'free will is an illusion' and the brothers must say yes as vessels. Sartre supplies the response: with no pre-given essence, the Winchesters are radically free and responsible, Dean admirably resisting 'bad faith' while Sam's early rebellions are self-deceptive until he stops blaming family expectations. Hume's point that free choices must still flow from the agent's character and values grounds a two-stage model of free will used to argue that soulless Sam, lacking the moral filter of the soul, has more options but is less free and less responsible.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Leiber develops three themes of the resistance: the time-travel paradoxes (Skynet's own mission proves the T-101 must fail, and future John has no need to send Reese), the moral status of machines, and the inevitability of smart weapons. La Mettrie's Man a Machine and Turing's 1950 test ground the claim that the T-101 who asks to be lowered into the molten steel is a rights-bearing person committing suicide, not a broken appliance - 'human chauvinism' says otherwise. Then, via Laplace's determinism, Einstein's conserved space-time, and his father Fritz Leiber's 'Law of Conservation of Reality,' he argues the continuum resists change, so 'Judgment Day is inevitable' is a scientist's claim about conserved mass-energy-time rather than a prophecy - with Augustine's puzzle about time framing why the future seems to protect the past.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Interrogates the tension in Cohle's 'deny our programming' line: if we are programmed biological puppets, how could we deny the program? It contrasts Sartre's radical free will and its crushing responsibility with Frankfurt cases and second-order desires — Marty as the 'wanton' who never acts on his desire not to desire affairs — and with Schopenhauer's will and Spinoza's causal determinism, both of which locate a kind of freedom in increased consciousness of our causes. The chapter concludes that self-consciousness, Rust's 'tragic misstep,' is in fact the only tool for reprogramming ourselves, imagined through a world of philosophical zombies who could neither suffer nor choose.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 11 "The Maze Is it Consciousness" — Lucía Carrillo González frames the whole park as a Turing Test scenario, noting guests and viewers cannot distinguish hosts like Dolores and Bernard from humans, and aligns Arnold with Turing's view that minds are computers that 'think' by responding to inputs (Abernathy's anomalous reaction to the photograph). Against this she sets Searle's Chinese Room and Ford's eliminativism, which hold the hosts merely simulate understanding. Citing qualia and the hosts' perfect, meaningful memories (Maeve recalling her daughter, technicians needing to erase trauma), she argues the hosts may genuinely experience states, and reads the Maze as the inward journey to consciousness, questioning whether humans' own free will is any less scripted.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 15 "Leaving the Train Maeve’s Choice as a Free Person" — Marco and Ana Azevedo analyze Maeve's decision to leave the train as the moment she becomes free, contrasting determinism and the principle of alternate possibilities (via Isaiah Berlin's claim that determinism is incompatible with how we live) with Frankfurt's compatibilism. Using Frankfurt's wanton/person distinction and second-order desires, they argue Maeve becomes a person when she reflects on her competing desires (escape versus finding her daughter) and identifies with the latter, even though her escape was scripted. They tie this to Jaynes's bicameral mind, casting unreflective hosts like Hector and Armistice as wantons and bicameral beings who follow a commanding voice, while Maeve and Dolores achieve the reflective self-identification Frankfurt calls freedom.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 19 "Part III Endless Forms Most Beautiful" — Muntersbjorn reads Westworld through Annette Baier's claim that persons are 'second persons first,' arguing the hosts' captivity models how selfhood and freedom depend on others who challenge our self-deceptions. She uses Dolores's scripted 'that doesn't look like anything to me' and Walter's milk-pouring glitch to distinguish Baier's harmless 'ignoring' from dangerous self-deception, and invokes Descartes's window automata and Russell's thinking gramophone as versions of the problem of other minds. She concludes via the Golden Rule that if hosts ever become persons, they too will be second persons shaped by how we treat them.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kowalski uses Min Farshaw's visions in the Amazon series to explore whether foreknowledge is compatible with free action, tracing the problem from Aristotle and Cicero through Augustine. He lays out the argument that if Min truly foreknows Tam raising Rand, it must come true and thus seems unfree, then surveys reconciliation projects: Boethius and Aquinas make God timeless so he does not literally foreknow, while Augustine (in the dialogue with Evodius) argues foreknowledge does not cause what is foreknown, so choices explain foreknowledge rather than vice versa. He notes Min is not timeless and her visions are fallible (Mat spears rather than stabs Rand), concluding WoT keeps its characters both free and fated for dramatic tension while offering only 'a semblance of choice.'
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Held reads Rand's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a recapitulation of the free-will defense to the problem of evil, opening with Hume's statement of Epicurus's questions and Camus's refusal to love a world that tortures children. Drawing on Augustine (evil as privation, our limited perspective, the corruptible will) and Alvin Plantinga's claim that a world with significantly free creatures is more valuable, he argues Rand's competing visions teach that a world without Shai'tan removes choice: Elayne 'simpering,' Aviendha vapid, people reduced to complacent automatons who cannot choose to be good. He concludes with Camus that the struggle itself justifies existence and that heroism is impossible without the possibility of cowardice.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 16 "The Breaks of the Game" — Davison analyzes luck and fairness in basketball, using Dennett's claim that the more skill (control) a player has, the less luck is involved, so luckiness is relative to persons and times (a fan's half-court shot versus Meadowlark Lemon's). Distinguishing fairness as equality from fairness as desert, and invoking Bernard Williams's 'constitutive luck,' he argues that the game's mechanisms (spherical ball, jump ball, many possessions, referees) minimize luck, and that famous lucky plays like Robert Horry's shot, NC State over Houston, and the phantom foul on Scottie Pippen do not make outcomes unfair, since fallible human refs are a necessary part of the game.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 27 "Touchdowns, Time, and Truth" — Campbell applies the truthmaker theory and correspondence theory of truth to 'touchdown truths,' using plays like Devin Hester's opening kickoff return in Super Bowl XLI. He distinguishes truthbearers (propositions) from truthmakers (events), separates an agent's 'making it the case' from a truthmaker's 'necessitating,' and uses a tenseless view of semantics plus Perry's being-true/being-made-true distinction to defuse fatalism. He then argues that since only the final score fixes 'real' touchdowns, their truthmakers are events involving referees' beliefs, endorsing a Modest Touchdown Antirealism while retaining bivalence and semantic realism.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 14 "Deception and Disorder Unraveling Cronenberg's Divided Minds" — Simon Riches traces Cronenberg's shift from bodily 'body horror' madness to psychological unraveling, focusing on Tom Stall's oscillation between Tom and Joey in A History of Violence. He treats self-deception via Davidson's 'divided minds' and Dennett's narrative-self view of multiple personality, situates hallucination (Spider, Videodrome) between Cartesian deception and psychosis, and uses Foucault, Kuhn, Szasz, and social constructionism to argue the category of mental disorder is socially contingent, so the line between self-deception and delusion (and mental order and disorder) is unclear.
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 15 "Psychological Determinism in the Films of David Cronenberg" — Daniel Shaw argues Cronenberg's oeuvre embodies psychological determinism (in Skinner's and Freudian terms), reading Dead Ringers as his masterpiece: Beverly Mantle's drug-fueled disintegration and murder of Elliot flow from an ambivalence and symbiotic bond he cannot escape, analyzed through Freud's Little Hans conflict of ambivalence and dream-as-wish. Surveying Shivers, The Brood, The Fly, and Crash as portraits of characters helplessly driven by parasites, disease, instinct, or trauma, he holds Eastern Promises (with its in-control hero Nikolai) is the pointed exception that proves Cronenberg's pessimistic determinist rule.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 25 "Nihilism and Freedom in the Films of Stanley Kubrick Daniel Shaw" — Shaw surveys Kubrick's oeuvre to argue that, contrary to his nihilistic reputation, Kubrick affirms human free will. Centering on A Clockwork Orange, he reads the 'Ode to Joy' ending as celebrating Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice against the Ludovico technique's deterministic conditioning, invoking Burgess's 'clockwork orange' and the chaplain's warning. Using Kevin Stoehr's Nietzschean distinction between active and passive nihilism, and reading Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's account of love and radical freedom, Shaw contends Kubrick's protagonists (Dax, Bowman, Joker, Bill Harford) exercise real choice, making dehumanization the loss of that choice.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — R. Barton Palmer situates Scorsese as a 'saint of cinema' whose Emersonian transcendentalism—the 'influx of light and power' breaking through the material everyday—pervades even his commercial films, focusing on Bringing Out the Dead against Casino and Taxi Driver. He traces the Bressonian 'decisive moment' and Schrader's Calvinist-Jansenist reading of predestination and grace (Ace Rothstein's inexplicable survival in Casino, the elect/damned divide of Taxi Driver and Hardcore), where Travis Bickle remains 'God's lonely man' beyond redemption. Palmer argues Scorsese departs from Schrader's bleak limited atonement: Frank Pierce earns communal grace through willed effort, releasing Mary's father, asking forgiveness, and ending in a Pieta embrace that affirms redemption is attainable within the material world.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 24 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Shaw asks whether Kubrick's worldview is nihilistic by tracking the free-will-versus-determinism question across his films, arguing (against Vincent Canby) that A Clockwork Orange celebrates rather than condemns Alex's recovered capacity for moral choice: the state's Ludovico conditioning, which makes him retch at sex and violence, is more monstrous than Alex because it destroys the free will that grounds human meaning. Invoking Kevin Stoehr's distinction between Nietzsche's passive and active nihilism, Shaw claims Kubrick highlights the negative to point beyond it. He surveys the oeuvre—Dax, Bowman, Barry, Wendy, Joker, Bill Harford as choosing agents—and reads Eyes Wide Shut through Sartre's Being and Nothingness on the contradiction of wanting the beloved's freely-given yet secure love.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 23 "Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime" — Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I's chapters, arguing the Whedonverse embodies serious philosophy. It reads Angel, Buffy, Simon Tam, Echo, and the Avengers through Heidegger's inauthenticity/angst and Sartre's existentialism (Dr. Horrible and the Operative as inauthentic 'monsters'), then adds Rawls and Aristotle to claim some authentic lives are better led, using Gyges's ring (in 'Gone' and 'In the Dark') and Aristotelian friendship (Team Angel, Serenity's crew) as touchstones. It defends an atheistic moral realism via Kant on personhood and Locke's natural rights (Mal insisting Saffron is 'no one's property'), and closes on free will: reading The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse, and The Cabin in the Woods against d'Holbach's hard determinism, Flamson's compatibilism, and Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions (Connor's choice in 'Inside Out').
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' through the Whedonverse, building on Mulhall, Wartenberg and Shaw's hierarchy of filmic philosophizing. It reads Angel's 'Deep Down' and 'Epiphany' speeches as endorsing that kindness is a self-standing good regardless of God, framing sacrifices by Simon (for River), Cordy (for Angel) and Buffy (for Dawn) as a cinematic thought experiment refuting the claim that ethics is incoherent without God. It reads Connor as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will (Darla and faux-Cordelia 'stir up' quantum indeterminacy), Angel/Angelus as a years-long test of memory-continuity personal identity against Parfit's Neo-Lockean view, and 'The Cabin in the Woods' plus Dollhouse's 'Man on the Street' as endorsing a Noddings-style ethics of care and Whedon's religious non-realism, with Angel offered as a Socrates-like moral exemplar.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 14 "Prognosis" — William Eaton reconstructs the Doctor's "Blink" philosophy of time using David Lewis's four-dimensionalism. He shows how Lewis's external/personal-time distinction explains the Doctor meeting his own regenerations and reversed causation (a black eye before the punch), and how "Blink" hinges on a closed causal chain (the DVD Easter-egg transcript that authors itself). He rehearses the Grandfather/Bilking paradox and Lewis's "can" equivocation solution, then places the Doctor alongside Horwich and Ismael, arguing the Doctor goes furthest by holding closed causal chains actually exist.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 10 "2. The Winchesters’ Revolt Against the Divine Plan" — Steele argues the Winchesters' fifteen-season revolt against Chuck's authored 'divine plan' stages the free-will-versus-determinism debate: Chuck writes their lives yet Sam shooting God shows the plan can be surprised, leaving 'free will in the details' as compatibilism. She frames the cosmic contest of angels, demons, and Chuck as Nietzsche's competing wills to power, but concludes Supernatural finally rejects Nietzsche for Rousseau, championing individual free will and a General Will where Sam and Dean rebuild Heaven to match their own choices.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 23 "12. Finally Free" — McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 18 "9. The Prequel versus Free Will" — Frim argues that Better Call Saul, precisely because it is a prequel, illustrates Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason—every event, including Walt's meth empire or Jimmy's burner-phone hustle, has a causal 'because' stretching infinitely back—and thus a deterministic universe. He dismantles the appeal to Heisenberg/quantum indeterminacy (randomness is not free choice) and refutes three myths: that determinism is boring (the causal 'Story One' is far more gripping than the free-will 'Story Two'), amoral (murder is wrong for its effects; we can keep 'suffering' and drop 'guilt'), and mindless (Nacho's ordered mind versus Tuco's drug-addled one shows minds function well or badly). He enlists Socrates' 'no one goes willingly toward the bad' to recast wrongdoing as disordered reasoning.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 30 "19. Can We Blame Jimmy for Being Jimmy" — The chapter runs Thomas Nagel's 'Moral Luck' argument on Jimmy, cataloguing his constitutive, circumstantial, causal-deterministic, and outcome luck (the con-man 'wolves and sheep' encounter, the Chicago sunroof children, the missed 1.6 million) to suggest we cannot fairly blame him. It then rebuts Nagel with a poker-and-wager analogy: since 'wagering on freedom weakly dominates' wagering on fatalism, we should treat character as cultivable through virtue theory's habits. It concludes that because nobody prevented Jimmy from changing and he has the resourcefulness to do so, his moral decline was unnecessary and blameworthy.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 6 "In the Wrong Hands, It’s a Weapon—in the Right Hands, Deliverance" — The editors' introduction frames Foundation's central conceit, psychohistory, as a vehicle for the question of determinism: if the chain of events from the founding of Rome to the reader's own hands was fixed by preceding causes, only a predictor's lack of information stands between us and perfect foresight. It uses Gibbon's Decline and Fall (Asimov's model) to raise whether the fall of empires must happen as it does, and previews the volume's further questions about obligations to future generations, science versus religion, and the ethics of deception and robot programming.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 12 "4. Demons, Game Shows, and Baguettes" — Wenmackers traces psychohistory's scientific lineage from Newtonian determinism through Laplace's demon, arguing Foundation stays within nineteenth-century limits by predicting only probabilities. She uses Newcomb's Paradox to capture the unease of living under a predicted Seldon Plan, Poincare's chaos and the three-body problem to show determinism need not mean predictability, and Poincare's baguette-fraud tale plus Quetelet's social physics and statistical mechanics to explain psychohistory's core assumption that mobs of billions behave lawfully even when individuals do not. She suggests Seldon's science was in some sense historically inevitable.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 33 "21. A Foundation-al Lesson on Free Will and Determinism" — Simpson argues Asimov balances determinism and free will through probabilistic psychohistory and reads the Mule—an unpredictable mutant—as an Epicurean 'swerve' meant to break the plan's apparent determinism, though he shows randomness no more secures freedom than determinism (the free-will dilemma). Turning to compatibilism, he uses Han Pritcher's mental 'Conversion' by the Mule to defeat classical hypothetical analyses and Gary Watson's valuational account, since Pritcher still does what he 'wants.' He builds on Frankfurt's rejection of alternative possibilities and Susan Wolf's requirement of responsiveness to the True and the Good, contrasting the manipulated Lord Stettin with Second-Foundationer Lady Callia, to give an account of free agency that would have let Asimov grant his characters agency in a deterministic universe without needing the Mule.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Richard Davies uses Aristotle's Poetics (the principles of closure, relevance, and the unities of place and time) to defend Lost's tangled narrative as an epic rather than a broken tragedy, arguing that flashbacks, flash-forwards like Jack's 'We have to go back,' and multi-season arcs such as Juliet's remain within Aristotelian bounds. He then imports McTaggart's contrast between eternalism and presentism to explain why a flash-forward is philosophically unsettling, and argues that changing the past (as season 5's time travel invites) generates a logical contradiction from which anything follows, so viewers must 'shield' Hurley's 1977 experiences to keep enjoying the plot.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Jeremy Pierce argues that Lost mostly assumes fixed (eternalist) time and moves from its metaphysics to its ethics: even if 'whatever happened, happened,' ordinary morality still applies, so Sayid's shooting young Ben is wrong regardless of his good intentions and Jack is responsible for detonating Jughead even though he causes the very Incident he meant to prevent. Invoking Carneades' distinction between truth and necessity, Pierce holds that foreknowledge (the Man in Black's manipulation, Desmond's course-corrected saving of Charlie) does not erase free choice, concluding via Kate that morality in time travel is 'simply morality, period.'
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 9 "1. Lost in Time" — Rard uses David Lewis's definition of time travel—a discrepancy between the duration of the journey and the gap between departure and arrival—to show that 'The Rip Van Winkle Caper' suspended-animation heist is NOT time travel, while 'Last Flight' (Terry returning to save Mackaye) is, complete with a self-consistent causal loop. She then applies Lewis's argument that mundane events always thwart attempts to change the past to 'No Time Like the Past,' where Paul Driscoll is repeatedly distracted from killing Hitler and even accidentally causes the schoolhouse fire he meant to prevent, illustrating that the past is unalterable but interactable.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone" — Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Dromm and Salter analyze Persuasion by distinguishing persuasion (rational, argument-based belief change), influence (nonrational, resting on a person's charisma or status, as Lady Russell has over the Elliots), and 'overpersuasion.' Against Captain Wentworth's view that persuadability is a vice and firmness of mind a virtue (his hazelnut analogy, Louisa Musgrove's fatal fall from the Cobb), they adapt Mill's On Liberty: just as free discussion lets a society exchange error for truth and gain confidence in true beliefs, a persuadable person is happier and epistemically better off. They add that Anne broke the engagement from a sense of duty, not fickleness, and it is her own persuasion that finally reunites her with Wentworth.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 21 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza, Gagliardini Graça, and Jáuregui-Olaiz chart sailing's aesthetic facets — sublime, tempestuous, graceful, existential. They deploy Kant's analysis of the sublime as the balance between the imagination's failure before the ocean's immensity/power and the pleasure of meeting it through skill and reason (Ilundáin sailing in thirty-knot gusts on the point of balance between fear and joy). Dewey's notion of 'an experience' anchors sailing's transformative, self-revealing potential, terrifying storms included (Jáuregui's Snowgoose ordeal mistaking a bordello's red light for a harbor). Closing with Rosencrantz and Guildenstern, they argue freedom is 'relative' and earned: we cannot change the wind but adjust the sails, gaining restrained autonomy by cultivating skill within constraint.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Felipe Carvalho frames a friend 'Toby's' worry – tattoos are forever, so should one be impulsive or cautious? – as a problem about bodily freedom versus irreversible change. He rejects the hedonist position (seize the day, regret is just part of freedom) as too simple and the Millian position (drawing on Mill's On Liberty argument that one cannot freely alienate one's freedom, as in selling oneself into slavery) as too precautionary, noting his friend's happy irreversible ear surgery. He proposes a 'middle path' learned from the tattoo community: a complex interplay of motif, the tattooist-as-artist, and the body-as-canvas that lets permanence guide more principled choices – so no 'I Love Becky' tattoos.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Heaps uses the loaded question a stranger asks a tattooed person ('aren't you afraid of being stuck with it?') to raise the freedom-versus-determinism problem, then rejects Kant's Critique of Practical Reason solution of an 'alternate nature' of rational autonomy because it quarantines free choice from the physical act of being inked. He argues instead for an 'embodied freedom' that rests on but is not determined by biology, illustrated by deciding, saving for, sitting through, and healing a tattoo. He closes with Socrates' 'know thyself' and 'the unexamined life is not worth living,' making self-examination the way to develop the effective willingness that real freedom requires.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 28 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Decker reads Ray Bradbury's 'The Illustrated Man' (William Phelps, whose witch-inked tattoo of murdering his wife Lisabeth becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy) and 'The Illustrated Woman' (Emma and Willy Fleet's shared delusion of an invisible masterpiece) to ask whether 'the body is our fate.' He aligns Phelps's predetermined tattoo with Alvin Goldman's 'Book of Life' thought experiment about foreknowledge and lost free will, and with Foucault's claim that power socially constructs docile bodies. Against this fatalism he sets George Herbert Mead's creative social self, 'taking the attitude of the other,' arguing tattooing is a plural renegotiation of identity rather than a fixed inscription.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 16 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Vargas argues that a psychopathic serial killer can be profoundly evil yet not morally responsible. Reviewing the clinical literature (Hare, the moral/conventional rule distinction, the 'mrah'/harm thought experiment), he holds that psychopaths are blind to moral rules and so, since blame requires understanding wrongdoing, cannot be blamed — the appropriate response is quarantine rather than resentment. He then separates evil from responsibility: to be evil is to desire others' harm for its own sake, and such evil, like being a jerk, need not be something one is responsible for, which is why psychopathic killers can be genuinely evil though not blameworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 26 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Deal compares fictional Dexter Morgan with real killer John Wayne Gacy to explore whether serial killers are morally responsible, working through moral agency, free will, determinism, and Dennett's compatibilism (from Freedom Evolves). He argues moral responsibility requires intentional choice and the capacity to know right from wrong, which the delusional self-narratives of Dexter (the 'Dark Passenger') and the denying Gacy call into question. Drawing on experimental philosophy (Knobe and Nichols) and cognitive 'frames,' he shows our verdicts hinge on emotion: the 'abused child' frame makes Dexter sympathetic while the 'murderous psychopath' frame condemns Gacy, so how a killer's story is framed drives our attribution of responsibility.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 19 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 9 "3. Terminator I & II" — Rowlands uses the Terminator cyborg to pose the mind-body problem: how the inside view (consciousness, intentionality) meshes with the outside view (neurons firing). He rejects dualism because it only says what mind is not and cannot explain mind-body interaction (no mass, so no momentum/energy transfer), and because it would make intelligent-machine sci-fi impossible. He argues for materialism, then distinguishes 'nerd' symbol-crunching AI (Schank's restaurant scripts, Deep Blue) from 'jock' neural-network, embodied designs as the route to building an intelligent Terminator that can flexibly respond like Arnie mugging the biker.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 11 "5. Minority Report" — Rowlands uses Minority Report's precogs (a truncated Laplace's demon) to argue the film is about determinism: to certainly foresee a murder the future must be fixed by the past, distinct from predestination. He runs the dilemma of determinism, using Cruise's choice not to shoot Leo Crow: if actions are caused they are inevitable and unfree; if uncaused (indeterminism) they are merely random, citing Libet/Kornhuber experiments and the involuntary-arm-twitch example. He rejects Hume's compatibilism (freedom is doing as you please) because genuine freedom requires 'pleasing as you please,' and rejects agent-causation theory as reviving dualism's problems.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 15 "Who is Who" — The time-travel chapter grounds Doctor Who's paradoxes in Parmenides and Zeno on the impossibility of change and Aristotle on the logical necessity of past and future statements ('You can't rewrite history!' in 'The Aztecs'), then deploys determinism, David Lewis on the paradoxes of time travel, and the consistency/autonomy principles ('Father's Day,' the Reapers). It uses Leibniz's possible worlds and the many-worlds interpretation of quantum mechanics to read 'Inferno' and 'Turn Left,' arguing quantum indeterminacy and entanglement make the Doctor's 'wibbly-wobbly, timey-wimey' theory of fixed points and flux coherent.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 34 "Determinism and the Dark Knight" — Hart uses Heidegger's Being and Time to explain Batman beyond the free-will/determinism binary. Dasein is a "thrown-project" always being-toward-death; Alfred's world of trays and clocks illustrates the interpretive horizon of a chosen life. Witnessing his parents' murder confronts Bruce Wayne with Angst and his own finitude, and — as in Miller's Year One, where a bat crashes through the window and he decides "I shall become a bat" — he authentically chooses his crime-fighting mission rather than being mechanically driven by trauma or vengeance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 9 "7. Doctor Who as Philosophy Four-Dimensionalism and Time Travel" — Decker asks what the universe must be like if Doctor Who's time travel were real, using David Lewis's distinction between personal and external time and the TARDIS as a Wellsian (not Thornian) time machine traversing a 'hypertime' vortex. After surveying the arrows of time and paradoxes like the bootstrap paradox ('Day of the Daleks') and the grandfather paradox (imagined via Tegan's grandfather), and rejecting Deutsch-Lockwood's Many-Worlds and growing-block solutions, he argues the Whoniverse fits 'Four-Dimensional Realism'/eternalism, quoting the Twelfth Doctor that time's passage is an illusion of 'still pictures.' He then confronts 4DR's threat to free will and moral responsibility, finding compatibilism and 'fixed points' inadequate given eternalism's succession-not-production of events.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 13 "11. Futurama as Philosophy Wisdom from the Ignorance of a Delivery Boy" — Lewis surveys how Futurama's satire raises philosophical questions without taking sides. 'Zoidberg's Freedom Lesson' pits Mill's harm principle and free speech against Feinberg's offense principle; the mutants' and robots' oppression is read through Foucault's disciplinary normalcy and Locke's and Rawls's social contracts (state of nature, veil of ignorance). 'The Problem with Popplers' stages Bentham's utilitarianism, a might-makes-right food-chain view, and an intelligence criterion that commits Singer's 'speciesism,' with sentimentality winning. 'The Late Philip J. Fry' and 'Free Will Hunting' dramatize determinism, Nietzsche's eternal recurrence, and Sartre's existentialist free will, while 'Godfellas' and 'A Clockwork Origin' probe the problem of evil, fine-tuning, and Occam's razor.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 51 "48. The Matrix as Philosophy Understanding Knowledge, Belief, Choice, and Reality" — Perez reads the Matrix trilogy as a sustained argument about how choosing what to believe and 'know' shapes the reality we live in. He opens with Descartes' dream problem and cogito, contrasting Descartes' foundationalism with Rorty's anti-foundationalism to explain Cypher's choice to reject reality for the Matrix's certitude, and uses Searle's brute vs. institutional facts (the cookies, the steak, 'there is no spoon') to show social reality is constructed. Against the fatalism of the Oracle, Architect, and Merovingian, he argues nearly every character makes free choices, and resolves the tension via Hume's compatibilism — liberty requires necessity, and choices gain meaning only in response to causality — while noting agent-causation objections (Reid, O'Connor, Rowe) that make Neo's 'Because I choose to' significant. Gettier's justified-true-belief critique and Plato's Cave frame the knowledge and enlightenment themes.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 91 "86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom" — Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 94 "88. Watchmen as Philosophy Illustrating Time and Free Will" — Goldberg and Gavaler argue that Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen operationalizes eternalism (McTaggart's B-series) both through its rigid 3x3 grid and mirror-symmetric layouts and through Doctor Manhattan, who narrates all moments as simultaneously present ('nothing ever ends'). Because eternalism means no one could have done otherwise, libertarian free will is ruled out, and the chapter argues the operative view is compatibilism rather than determinism, using Frankfurt's rejection of the principle of alternative possibilities and Dennett's Luther example to read Doctor Manhattan's hesitant killing of Rorschach as free action he could not have done otherwise.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "2. The Dangers of Being the Doctor" — The chapter weighs the Doctor's ethic of interference against the Time Lords' non-interference, using determinism and the 'butterfly effect' (Martha in 'The Shakespeare Code') to concede when disengaged observation is prudent, while insisting that non-interference fails to protect human dignity. Drawing on Terrence Des Pres's account of dignity as 'inward resistance,' and real-world dissidents Adam Michnik and Václav Havel's 'power of the powerless,' it reads 'Rosa,' 'The Woman Who Fell to Earth,' and the people of Le Chambon as models of dignified, communal resistance to wrongdoing. Citing Iris Young, it argues everyone bears moral responsibility to engage rather than remain a detached, complicit 'objective observer.'

### Properly Basic Belief

A properly basic belief is one a person is rationally entitled to hold without inferring it from other beliefs or supporting it with argument. The idea challenges classical foundationalism, which restricts the legitimately basic to what is self-evident, incorrigible, or evident to the senses; Alvin Plantinga argued that this criterion is both too narrow and self-refuting, since it does not itself meet its own standard. On his reformed epistemology, beliefs such as the existence of other minds, the reality of the past, and belief in God can be properly basic when they arise in the appropriate circumstances from properly functioning cognitive faculties. The account thus aims to show that religious belief need not rest on evidential proofs to be rational.

- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 13 "2. Maybe Jenner Was Right" — Cowan uses Jenner's suicide in the exploding CDC (1.6 'TS-19') to pose Camus's question 'Why should I not commit suicide?', and rejects Jenner's despair the Camusian way: Michonne in 4.9 'After' - slaying her own walker look-alike and then her two pet walkers - is his Sisyphus in revolt, unlike Gareth, whose revolt lacks the respect for human dignity that makes Sisyphus happy. He then objects that Camus never explains why human life has intrinsic dignity in a godless universe, noting that Sartrean authenticity could equally license the Governor's Woodbury experiments or Gareth's cannibalism, and turns to Hershel's providential hope as the religious alternative. Following Plantinga, he argues belief in God can be properly basic through a sensus divinitatis - Hershel seeing God's hand in 2.4 'Cherokee Rose' and the tornado-spared barn of 5.10 'Them' - so if God exists, Jenner was not right.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 16 "4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" — Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.

### The Watchmaker Argument (design)

The watchmaker argument, given its most famous form by the English clergyman William Paley in Natural Theology (1802), reasons that just as finding a watch on a heath would lead one to infer a designer, the intricate order and apparent purpose of living things point to an intelligent designer of nature. It is a version of the teleological, or design, argument for the existence of God. The argument was influentially challenged by David Hume before Paley and later undercut by Darwin's account of how natural selection can produce apparent design without a designer.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 101 "Superheroes, Duty, and the Biggest of Big Pictures" — Argues that non-theistic karma undermines itself: the impersonal moral laws connecting each soul's deeds to its circumstances in the next life would be enormously complex and would serve the moral end of justice, and order that intricate serving a moral end demands an intelligent cause, so reincarnation becomes evidence for God. It closes the chapter by comparing the universe's moral order to a superhero's origin story — it would have to begin with something like a God.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 18 "The Epilogue A Question of Belief" — Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 27 "Lessons to Take Away" — Kinghorn asks what makes Hitchcock's trademark plot twists improbable, distinguishing physical, statistical and evidential probability and illustrating each with the fraying jacket seam in Saboteur, the sea of identical umbrellas in Foreign Correspondent, the porter uniforms in North by Northwest, and Manny Balestrero's uncanny double in The Wrong Man. The core of the chapter is a three-question method for assessing evidence - does the evidence fit the theory, does it fit rival theories too, how likely was the theory beforehand - worked out through Jeff and Doyle's debates over Thorwald's guilt in Rear Window, where Jeff turns out to be a methodologically sound amateur sleuth despite his bias against marriage. A closing lesson defends design-argument-style reasoning about God from a confused objection that demands statistics where only evidential probability is at issue.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 8 "Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New ‘Intelligent Falling’ Theory" — Ruiz uses Onion stories—'Jesus Answers Half The Prayers At Area Roulette Table,' 'God Answers Prayers Of Paralyzed Little Boy,' 'Christianity Celebrates One Billionth Unanswered Prayer'—to argue that belief in God lacks rational justification. Following Hume's empiricism (all ideas trace to sense perception), methodological naturalism, and Ockham's Razor, he shows that feelings of God's presence, scriptural circularity, and answered prayers (riddled with selection bias) all fail as evidence, and the prayer hypothesis is unfalsifiable—a theory that explains any outcome, like the brain tumor thanking God for its surviving surgery, is supported by no evidence. He closes by dismantling Paley's watchmaker design argument through the infinite regress ('who designed God?') and by treating 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' as the reductio of design reasoning.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Smithka tests Berkeley's 'to be is to be perceived' against two monsters: the Vashta Nerada, whose existence is inferred from indirect evidence (counting shadows, the 'ghosting' of Miss Evangelista) much like Neptune was inferred from Uranus's orbit, and the Weeping Angels, which act only when unperceived and so falsify Berkeley's principle. Working through Locke on substance, Hume's skepticism about unperceivable causes like God, Paley's watchmaker design argument, and scientific realism (Sellars, Churchland) versus van Fraassen's empirically adequate anti-realism, she concludes the Doctor is a realist about unobservables — for whom the Angels are real but 'doomed to be perceived'.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 25 "Futurama and Philosophy" — DePoe weighs the multiverse against the fine-tuning argument for God's existence: just as Farnsworth's box in 'The Farnsworth Parabox' spills out universe-1's golden Bender plus togas, pirate, and hippie universes, an infinite multiverse would realize every possibility and make our life-permitting constants certain rather than miraculous, while 'Time Keeps on Slippin''s chronoton-disturbed cosmos illustrates what fine-tuning means. He then asks what is metaphysically primitive, staging the 1948 Copleston-Russell exchange ('I should say that the universe is just there, and that's all') and applying Ockham's razor to weigh one infinitely complex God against infinitely many unobservable universes. The chapter concludes in evidential stalemate, closing with the God Entity's counsel in 'Godfellas': 'When you do things right, people won't be sure you've done anything at all.'
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 13 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Shea stages the Wu-Malcolm dispute through Hume's Dialogues: Jurassic Park is an 'intelligent design' so botched that, like Philo's world of needless suffering, it points to ignorant or malicious designers rather than a perfect God, undercutting Richard Owen-style design arguments. He then explains Hammond's folly with Darwinian natural selection and memetics, treating the dinosaur-theme-park as a meme that infected InGen's investors by exploiting evolved desires for profit, fame, and importance. Hammond's fatal errors were assuming evolution 'wants' humans to survive, that complexity means better adapted, and that he could outsmart selection, which the all-female raptors breeding and life 'finding a way' quickly refute.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Lumpenhouwer takes the Abbey's religious silences - Anna's 'we'll only fall out,' Alfred's baffled 'What?' at transubstantiation, and the Catholic baptism fight over baby Sybbie - and brings in Aquinas to make God-talk possible. Reason alone can know that God exists (the argument from design through final causes like the candle flame, carefully distinguished from Paley's watchmaker), revelation grasped by faith tells us God is personal, and human words reach God only analogically, as when Matthew calls God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave, or by way of negation. Against Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death, the chapter insists that mystery limits rather than excuses reason, ending with Aquinas's 'straw' and the Abbey's three attitudes: confident belief, searching doubt, and keep-it-private spirituality.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 14 "4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk" — Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 20 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning. Her claim that 'all that science stuff comes from Jesus' occasions Plantinga's argument that Darwinian naturalism undermines trust in our cognitive faculties, plus origin-of-life and fine-tuning probability arguments, tempered by Kitcher's caution that such estimates rest on unknown background conditions. Van Inwagen on why Genesis need not teach literal science, and Locke's advice to proportion belief to evidence, frame the mutual education Mary and Sheldon owe each other.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Klumpenhouwer uses the Abbey's awkward silences about religion - Anna refusing to discuss it over dinner, Thomas showing off with 'transubstantiation' - to introduce Aquinas on how God can be known and talked about. Mary's wartime bedside prayer ('I'm not even sure that you're there') shows she wants not just proof of existence but a personal God, so the chapter distinguishes Aquinas's argument from design - carefully separated from Paley's divine-watchmaker version - from knowledge of God through revelation and faith. Aquinas's two indirect ways of speaking, analogy (Matthew calling God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave) and negation, explain why the 'God is good' sign over Charles Grigg's workhouse should trouble us, and why Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death overstates the mystery of God's otherness.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Doomed to Be Perceived" — Paula Smithka uses the Vashta Nerada and Weeping Angels to examine perception and the reality of unobservables. She sets Berkeley's "to be is to be perceived" against Locke's hidden substance and Hume's empiricist skepticism (and Paley's design argument), then distinguishes direct from indirect perceptual evidence, using the shadows, skeletal remains, and Neptune's discovery to frame scientific realism versus van Fraassen's antirealism. The Weeping Angels invert Berkeley, existing only when unperceived and turning to stone when observed, so for them to be is NOT to be perceived.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 36 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Arp frames a dialogue between two ex-seminarians who once got matching cross tattoos: Bill, who added more Christian ink, and Rick, who now regrets his cross as an atheist secular humanist. Bill defends God via Aquinas's combined proof from motion and causation—tracing the tattoo artist and even the Big Bang back to an unmoved mover / uncaused cause—and the 'three Ms' of mind, meaning, and morality, gesturing toward Paley-style design. Rick counters with a self-sustaining infinite series, the interaction problem between a supernatural God and nature, and the charge that God is a comforting fiction, so morality and meaning are humanly made rather than divinely guaranteed.

### Paradigm Shifts

A paradigm shift, a notion made central by Thomas Kuhn in The Structure of Scientific Revolutions (1962), is a fundamental change in the framework of assumptions, methods, and exemplary problems that guides a scientific community. Kuhn argued that science proceeds not by steady accumulation but through long periods of 'normal science' under a reigning paradigm, punctuated by crises when mounting anomalies force a revolutionary switch to a new one. Because rival paradigms can be 'incommensurable,' the transition involves a wholesale reorientation of how practitioners see the world, not merely the addition of new facts.

- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 19 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Steele starts from Orwell's worry that laypeople accept scientific consensus as unreflectively as tribesmen accept witch-doctors — sharpened by Lysenko and Nazi 'racial science' — and answers it with Popper's critical rationalism: since Hume's problem of induction bars proof from instances, we can only provisionally prefer theories that survive severe attempts at falsification, so trusting experts is reasonable exactly when their community tests rather than defends its theories. Kuhn's paradigms explain why dissident alternatives like Atkins talk past the dominant school (Atkins and Agatston are cardiologists, not dieticians), and the 2002–2004 studies showing improved lipids on more fat figure as the kind of surprise that precedes paradigm change. His verdict: neither trusting nor resisting experts is foolish; 'human knowledge is too important to be left to experts.'
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 21 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Womack tests whether Atkins counts as a Kuhnian paradigm shift, using the Ptolemaic-to-Copernican transition as the model: paradigms define which problems matter, normal science accumulates anomalies, and crisis ends in a new paradigm. Measured against the dieting paradigm's own goals, Atkins flunks — its short-term wins fade by twelve months in the JAMA comparison with the Ornish, Zone, and Weight Watchers diets, with 30–50 percent dropout — so the dieting paradigm itself, which treats obesity as an individual plate problem, is the thing in crisis. Her proposed replacement shifts from the individual to the 'toxic food environment': sidewalks, zoning, food advertising rules, and the French Paradox as the existence proof.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 16 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach recounts the failure of the Enlightenment quest for certainty from Descartes and Locke through Kant to the positivists, and argues that Lewis's Narnia instead models knowing as perspectival (the Stable door whose inside is bigger than its outside), value-laden (the Dwarfs' self-chosen dark paradigm that turns Aslan's feast into refuse and violets into stable litter), and personal (Lucy's unarguable knowledge that she has seen Aslan in Prince Caspian, read through Michael Polanyi's tacit knowledge). Kuhn's competing paradigms frame theism versus atheism, James's will to believe opens the chapter, and Plantinga's defeaters keep personal knowledge from collapsing into mere subjectivity.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 101 "Wittgenstein Ultimate Bullshit Detector—or Bullshitter" — Fuller argues that mastering a discipline converts critics into loyal insiders — Thomas Kuhn's 'normal science' enshrines the tendency, cognitive dissonance explains it, and Blaise Pascal's wager is the general model of betting on a way of life that makes you receptive to its confirming signs. Against this he sets the Protestant tradition of Luther's conscience, 'playing it by ear', which like the Sophists concedes that reality rarely yields yes-or-no answers — the gap we fill being bullshit — and he frames the dispute as realism versus antirealism, reading Frankfurt's On Bullshit as an ad hominem attack on antirealists. He then re-examines Frankfurt's star witness: Wittgenstein's rebuke of Fania Pascal for saying she felt 'like a dog that has been run over' now looks like a spectacular lack of imagination, since evolutionary psychology, being forged at that very moment, has been narrowing the human-animal mental gap ever since.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 10 "CHAPTER 3 “LOOKING FOR THE INNER HEAT”" — The chapter reads Dylan's self-becoming as a chain of identity-emulations and overcomings — Hank Williams, Woody Guthrie, Ramblin' Jack Elliott — with Jon Pankake's folk-police critique and the Mike Seeger epiphany acting as Kuhnian anomalies that force a paradigm shift from folksinger to songwriter, each gatekeeper playing the 'Hegelian negative' Dylan needed. It argues Dylan fused folk, beat poetry, and rock and roll into an 'archaic revival' of mythic, enchanted consciousness against modern rationalization, rejecting the Sartrean/beat existentialism of a meaningless world in favor of co-creating meaning, and treating authenticity as the refusal of fixed identity (the Zimmerman-to-Dylan renaming, 'I'm gonna get me a new Bob Dylan'). The Newsweek exposé, Irwin Silber's open letter, and Johnny Cash's guitar-gift blessing stage his passage from 'King of Folk' to electric rock, with the little-known 1962 cut of Presley's 'That's All Right' showing that going electric was a return home — folk having been, in Dylan's words, 'just an interruption.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 18 "Vertigo and Epistemological Vertigo" — Flory reads Vertigo as an epistemological parable: Scottie's 'hardheaded Scot' method, collecting facts and deducing from universal principles, fails three times (the step-stool 'cure' for his acrophobia, explaining away Madeleine's 'possession' with the horse statue, forcing Judy up the bell tower for confirmation), delivering an implicit critique of Vienna Circle positivism in the manner of Carnap and Ayer. Against Scottie, the chapter mobilizes Kuhn's theory-laden facts, Aristotle's point that human conduct resists codification by exceptionless laws, and Hume's 'slave of the passions,' with Descartes's automata and Chalmers's philosophical zombies framing the problem of other minds. Midge, who knows people emotionally as well as factually, models the alternative: philosophers who fear 'epistemological vertigo' should give up epistemological training wheels and accept that minds, especially emotions, escape law-like rules.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 11 "Thematic Synchronicity" — Jones asks what the famous Dark Side of the Rainbow synchronization (album plus The Wizard of Oz, started on the third MGM lion roar) could mean given that the band denies designing it. He catalogs vivid syncs ('Time''s chimes as Miss Gulch bicycles past, 'Money''s cash register entering Munchkinland, 'Us and Them''s 'black and blue' over the Witch and Dorothy), then rejects both the Waters-conspiracy model and Jung's acausal 'synchronicity' as pseudoscience, proposing instead Conrad's apophenia and Kuhn's point that suspecting patterns others miss is the lifeblood of discovery. His resolution is 'thematic synchronicity': both works stage the struggle between security and transcendence, Dorothy's 'Over the Rainbow' against 'Eclipse''s 'all you touch and all you see is all your life will ever be,' so the coincidences feel objective because they are subjectively real to everyone.
