- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 31 "Self-Fulfilling Prophecies" — The section argues that Dumbledore treats even the real prophecy as fallible, telling Harry he is 'quite free to turn your back on the prophecy,' which suggests likelihood rather than guarantee. Yet the involuntary trance source, Trelawney's spade readings that fit the hidden Harry she cannot see, and the lightning-struck tower card point to occasional access to possible or fixed futures beyond mere category-1 guessing.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 32 "Destiny" — Testing whether Trelawney's first prophecy was self-fulfilling, the section deploys Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus story, where a prediction that causes its own fulfillment would be the prophet's deed rather than a revelation of what was going to happen. It concludes the prophecy did not make Voldemort attack: he chose Harry as the half-blood he saw himself in, acting on incomplete information from Snape's interrupted eavesdropping, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish real predictions from Trelawney's usual fare.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 34 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — The section argues the second real prophecy, about the servant rejoining the Dark Lord that night, cannot be merely 'likely but fallible': Wormtail's escape depended on a chain of improbable contingencies such as Lupin forgetting his Wolfsbane potion and the last-minute switch of Secret-Keeper. The first prophecy likewise required Voldemort to mark Harry through events, from Snape's plea to Lily's sacrifice, that flow from the prophecy itself, so genuine prophecy needs a stronger tie to the actual future than probability.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 35 "NOTES" — The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Johnson asks whether Isaac's paintings and Hiro's visions make the future fated, running Aristotle's sea-battle argument: if propositions about the future are already true (by bivalence and the correspondence theory of a 'written timeline'), then Sylar's exploding New York is inevitable and no one is free. He extends the problem to infallible foreknowledge via Future Hiro as a stand-in for God, considers and rejects Boethius's timeless-knowledge solution, and uses open theism plus a probability calculation about Ando's waffles order to show probabilistic foreknowledge is useless. He concludes most of Isaac's 'prophecies' are really self-fulfilling, as when Noah's efforts to dodge the eighth painting cause his shooting, and that the Heroes universe leaves room to deny fate.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 39 "a19.xhtml" — Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 14 "“I Know All of This Because I Have Done Everything I Can to Get to the Truth”" — Daniel Wack reads Veronica Mars as film noir refashioned for teen television: the class-riven town without a middle class supplies the corrupt noir milieu, but the genre's gender roles are reversed, so Logan becomes the homme fatal whose drunken promise of an 'epic' love offers the redemption-through-romance the femme fatale always dangles and never delivers. Following Cavell and Pippin, he argues the characters are trapped by a fatalism they did not choose — inherited zip codes, Aaron Echolls's abuse, Jake Kane's affair with Lianne — and Logan's dream of a private, redeemed world fails because accepting it would cost Veronica the active, truth-generating detective self she built after her rape. Investigating Lilly's murder, her mother's disappearance, and her own assault, she learns the truth restores nothing, but that detective work gives her a new way to order and survive her world.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 9 "H E N R I B E R G S O N" — Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kowalski uses Min Farshaw's visions in the Amazon series to explore whether foreknowledge is compatible with free action, tracing the problem from Aristotle and Cicero through Augustine. He lays out the argument that if Min truly foreknows Tam raising Rand, it must come true and thus seems unfree, then surveys reconciliation projects: Boethius and Aquinas make God timeless so he does not literally foreknow, while Augustine (in the dialogue with Evodius) argues foreknowledge does not cause what is foreknown, so choices explain foreknowledge rather than vice versa. He notes Min is not timeless and her visions are fallible (Mat spears rather than stabs Rand), concluding WoT keeps its characters both free and fated for dramatic tension while offering only 'a semblance of choice.'
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 23 "Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime" — Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 6 "Part Five D Is for Destiny" — This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone" — Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil" — James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 91 "86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom" — Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

### The Best of All Possible Worlds

The doctrine of the best of all possible worlds is Gottfried Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil, holding that a perfectly wise and good God, surveying every possible world, necessarily chose to create the one with the greatest overall balance of goodness. Apparent evils and imperfections are permitted only because they are inseparable from a greater good or a richer, more harmonious whole. Since God could not do less than the best, the actual world, for all its flaws, must be optimal—a claim Voltaire later famously satirized but which Leibniz meant as a serious defense of divine justice.

- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 28 "“A Boy Named Sue” A Cashian Theodicy" — Jamie Carlin Watson reads Cash's Christian worldview as Augustinian: evil is not a positive substance but a privation or corruption of good (contra the monism Leibniz risks and the Manichean dualism Augustine rejected), so humans alone bear blame for moral evil through freely corrupting good things—'Cocaine Blues,' 'The Wall,' the Folsom prisoner who admits he 'had it coming,' and the divided self of 'The Beast in Me' echoing Romans 7. Natural evil, as in 'Guess Things Happen That Way' and the flood of 'Five Feet High and Rising' (Cash's mother's 'blessing' of rich river dirt), serves punishment or greater goods. 'A Boy Named Sue' dramatizes the residual tension: the father's get-tough-or-die theodicy convinces neither Sue nor us that the sheer amount of evil is justified.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 21 "Death on Veridian III" — Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "Rescuing Princess Zelda" — Collins runs the problem of evil in Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem (an all-good, all-powerful God inconsistent with Ganondorf's evil) partially dissolves because nothing in the games says the three goddesses are omnipotent or omniscient, and Plantinga's free will defense, plus the best-of-all-possible-worlds idea, shows the Triforce is itself a free-will device, since a wish-granter that could grant any desire cannot limit evil without undoing itself. A 'game-making theodicy' modeled on Hick's soul-making theodicy explains why evil must be excessive and randomly distributed (else players would never strive to grow), and why the goddesses therefore provided a chosen hero: Link, unlike anyone on Earth, is the divine answer to excessive evil, divinely marked to reclaim the Triforce and rescue Zelda.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 9 "Is Monk’s Certainty Justified" — Rauhut tests Monk's method against two models of discovery: Holmes-style eliminatism, modeled on Popper's falsification via reductio ad absurdum, and CSI-style confirmationism in the mold of Hempel and Carnap (Gil Grissom letting evidence speak). Monk fits neither — in 'Mr. Monk and the Astronaut' he refuses to eliminate the alibi-solid Steve Wagner, and in 'Mr. Monk Falls in Love' he ignores a hatpin, a motive, and a confession pointing at Leyla. Instead Monk is an 'epiphanist': he registers every anomaly (the secretary hired from a Lamaze-class ad in 'Mr. Monk Fights City Hall', Crawford's odd phrasing 'No, she wouldn't be drinking now'), suddenly sees the one theory explaining all of them, and only afterwards manufactures shareable evidence for others. His absolute certainty, the chapter argues, rests on a metaphysical faith that only the true theory can explain every anomaly — a Leibnizian 'best of all possible ordered worlds' — the same obsession with order that makes him notice anomalies at all, though it makes him epistemically irresponsible by ordinary standards that weigh alternative hypotheses and simplicity.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 22 "Herr Leibniz Consoles Mr. Monk" — Kavas distinguishes Monk's method from Holmes's modus ponens, Poirot's elimination, and Goren's profiling: Monk accepts only what completes a coherent total narrative, so 'Here's what happened' re-tells the order of the whole world, as in the chess-game solution of 'Mr. Monk and the Genius'. The chapter uses the Tractatus's world of contingent, logically independent facts to model Monk's picture-completion, then brings in Leibniz: the principle of sufficient reason, the best of all possible worlds, and preestablished harmony justify Monk's faith that even Trudy's death must have a reason. Monk emerges as a pessimistic Leibniz who takes the world to be the worst possible precisely because, since learning the bomb was meant for Trudy in 'Mr. Monk Goes to Jail', he cannot see any sufficient reason for her death ('Why her?').
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 30 "Voltaire Lives" — Douglas Ficek traces The Onion's God stories — 'Lord Under Investigation For Failure To Provide,' God refusing to heal paralyzed little Timmy Yu, and 'God Cites Moving In Mysterious Ways' — back through Voltaire's Candide to Leibniz's theodicy, the 'best of all possible worlds' doctrine that Dr. Pangloss keeps reciting through hanging, slavery, and syphilis until Candide concludes we must cultivate our garden. The chapter's sharpest claim is that theodicy works by victim-blaming: Jerry Falwell's 9/11 rant earned the headline-only 'Jerry Falwell: Is That Guy A Dick Or What?' because he excused God by blaming secular Americans, just as Pastor Ellsworth blames heathen tsunami victims. Following theologian Dorothee Soelle, Ficek names this 'theological sadism,' and offers the Bible-drop missionaries of 'Poverty-Stricken Africans Receive Desperately Needed Bibles' as a modern Pangloss who mistakes moral obliviousness for grace.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 38 "The Odd Thought of Doctor Who" — Maps Leibniz's monadology onto the Whoniverse: the Doctor's individual concept survives each regeneration as a thinking monad while its bodily monads are replaced, parallel Liz Shaws in 'Inferno' show incompossible predicates, and the Time Lords play Leibniz's God permitting minimal evil, which the Doctor accepts in refusing to avert the Daleks' creation in 'Genesis of the Daleks'. The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the principle of indiscernibles, the Matrix becomes a failed pre-established harmony haunted by confused perceptions, and the Master hallucinates against the Doctor like Descartes's evil demon. The Valeyard is modeled as an incompossible world on Leibniz's Sextus Tarquinius pyramid and Borges's forking paths, closing with Leibniz's own 'odd thought' academy of wonders.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 30 "Time Enough to Drink the Poison" — Domino reads 'The Veiled Lodger' as a drama about hope in a world after God: Holmes's 'Your life is not your own; keep your hands off it' revives Plato's Phaedo argument that we are the gods' possessions, but deist-or-atheist Mrs. Ronder is unmoved, so Holmes falls back on the Leibnizian alternative to the Stoic and Cartesian 'patience without hope' — the example of patient suffering as 'the most precious of all lessons,' grounded in Leibniz's hope that the world is no 'cruel jest.' Jefferson Hope's two pill boxes in A Study in Scarlet literalize the Leibnizian link between hope and divine justice by letting God choose who dies, while Trelawney Hope's gullibility makes the surname ironic. Mrs. Ronder's true hope was reunion with Leonardo, which his death destroyed; what saves her is a new hope founded on Watson's text, since only a writer ('I have made a slight change of name and place') can change the past.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 40 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 19 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Montoya asks whether Prismo, Adventure Time's wish-granting stand-in for God, produced the best possible world when he restored Ooo over Farmworld. After explaining Leibniz's answer to the problem of evil—that an all-good, all-knowing God permits some evil because every possible world contains some, and ours contains the least—the chapter compares Farmworld (no Lich, but Finn becomes the Ice King, Jake mutates into the Lich, Marceline dies ancient and insane) with Ooo, where the same characters flourish as heroes. Prismo, no omnibenevolent deity, remakes Ooo out of friendship with Jake, and Farmworld's horrors vindicate the Leibnizian point that wishing one evil out of existence can unleash far worse.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 15 "6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 14 "4. Acts of God" — McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 14 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 24 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Jaime Lannister's question to Catelyn Stark - 'If the gods are real and they are just, then why is the world so full of injustice?' - launches a tour of the logical and evidential problems of evil across the religions of Westeros. Augustine's privation theory and free will defense are tested against the Faith of the Seven (with Catelyn answering 'Because of men like you'), Hume's dilemma of impotence or malevolence is applied to the old gods that Arya scolds at Harrenhal for failing to save Ned, and Leibniz's best-possible-world reply is weighed against natural evils like the storm that sank the Windproud. The chapter concludes that only the evidential problem sticks: the sheer quantity of suffering in Westeros is evidence against just gods, though nothing counts against the uncaring gods Brienne describes.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 32 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Nielsen asks whether a Green Lantern with unlimited willpower would be a god and answers no through Leibniz: God is the absolutely perfect being, where perfection excludes contradiction so that knowledge and power admit of perfection but 'the greatest of all numbers' does not, and such a being creates the best of all possible worlds. Hume's trilemma (impotent, malevolent, or whence evil?) is met with the theodicy that finite minds, like Lanterns baffled by Guardian decrees, cannot compare our world to the discarded possibilities, each perhaps as bad as Qward. Since omnipotence requires omniscience and omnibenevolence, not even Parallax, the Anti-Monitor, or Kyle as Ion counts as omnipotent: admirable and powerful, but not gods.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Blessing diagnoses Ted's 'rom-communism' as the naive optimism Voltaire satirized in Candide: Pangloss's 'best of all possible worlds' is Leibniz's greater-goods theodicy and Principle of Sufficient Reason, and its fatalism ('it will all work out exactly as it's supposed to') collapses under Ted's panic attacks and 'belief can't score goals.' Against it she sets Camus's The Plague: Dr. Rieux's absurd heroism, refusal of hope as 'philosophical suicide,' and 'strange hope' grounded in collective decency, arguing Ted's real, sustainable creed is Camus-like faith in teamwork and human goodness rather than belief that everything works out.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Freeman reads Ted as Chesterton's holy fool, in the lineage of Don Quixote and The Idiot and modeled on Innocent Smith in Manalive: his apparently foolish decisions (benching Jamie, the crooked BELIEVE sign meaning the room is 'outta whack') disclose a higher optimism that faces real evil, delights in Being as a gift, and loves the world patriotically like a relegation-threatened home team. The chapter then argues Ted's optimism diverges from Chesterton's by lacking its Christian foundation - Ted believes in belief itself, 'to which god and in what language?' - so the show can intuit but not justify the optimism it depicts.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction frames the Terminator saga as philosophy's natural territory by telling how philosophers persisted through catastrophe: Leibniz's 'best of all possible worlds' collapsed after the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, Hegel finished the Phenomenology of Spirit while Napoleon shelled Jena, and Adorno rebuilt cultural philosophy after Auschwitz. It compares that persistence to the human resistance against Skynet, and says the saga is founded on a paradox of human nature - we create our own worst nightmares. Quoting Bertrand Russell that most people would rather die than think, it urges readers to switch their CPU from read-only to learning mode and confront Judgment Day's paradoxes and the moral status of the machines.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 38 "The Odd Thought of Doctor Who" — Gregory Kalyniuk maps Leibniz's monadology onto Doctor Who. The Doctor's identity across regenerations is a thinking monad whose individual concept holds necessary predicates while appurtenant body-monads are replaced; the Time Lords play Leibniz's God overseeing pre-established harmony and permitting evil in the best world (refusing to stop the Daleks in 'Genesis'). The dimensionally transcendental TARDIS illustrates the identity of indiscernibles, the Matrix is a Leibnizian mill of confused perceptions (with the Master as Descartes's evil demon), and the incompossible Valeyard of 'Trial of a Time Lord' is read via Leibniz's Theodicy pyramid and Borges's forking paths.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 18 "9. Foundation’s Optimism" — McCrossin reads the sequels Foundation's Edge and Foundation and Earth as an Optimistic response to the problem of evil, in the lineage of Leibniz, Rousseau, and Hegel's 'All is well', set against the WWII, Holocaust, Nuremberg, and Eichmann-trial backdrop of Asimov's writing and Arendt's banality of evil. Tracking Gendibal's mantra 'all will happen well', the Gaia/Galaxia choice via Trevize's 'talent for rightness', and Daneel Olivaw's Zeroth Law and plan to merge with Fallom's brain, he uses the Book of Job to frame whether the series' recurring reassurance is earned or merely reframed.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 5 "index" — This composite chapter opens with the volume's Introduction and then runs several essays. Jeff McLaughlin's 'What If?' reads DC's Crisis on Infinite Earths and Marvel's What If? series as literal illustrations of Leibniz's possible-worlds metaphysics: the multiverse of Earth-1, Earth-2 and the 3,000 doomed universes dramatizes counterfactuals and Leibniz's Theodicy argument (via the principle of sufficient reason) that God actualizes only the best of infinitely many possible worlds, with Descartes invoked on why a perfect God permits imperfection. Amy Kiste Nyberg's essay analyzes the 1954 Senate hearings on EC horror comics (Gaines's 'The Orphan') as an applied-ethics clash between publishers' free expression and protecting children, explicitly deploying Mill's On Liberty and harm principle to argue why the child-audience framing defeats the anti-censorship case. Stanford Carpenter's piece treats the Black Captain America (Truth: Red, White, and Black) as an epistemology-of-authorship problem.

### The Knowledge Argument (Mary's Room)

The knowledge argument, framed by Frank Jackson through the thought experiment of Mary the color scientist, challenges physicalism about the mind. Mary knows every physical fact about color vision while confined to a black-and-white room; the argument contends that when she finally sees red she learns something new—what the experience is actually like. If she gains new knowledge, the reasoning goes, then not all facts are physical facts, and subjective conscious experience (qualia) escapes a purely physical description. Physicalists have replied that Mary gains a new ability or mode of acquaintance rather than a new fact.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 43 "Unknown" — Barwick argues reductive materialism fails twice. First, via the Mary story (told here from Michael Tye's retelling): a scientist raised in a black-and-white room who knows all the physical facts about color still learns something new when she sees her first rose - what it is like - which no physical theory addresses. Second, the identity claim is meaningless: 'mental state = brain state' cannot be true because the experiential report and the scientific explanation have different subject matters, against Churchland's plea that we merely lack the needed concepts - so the metaphysics underwriting The Matrix is false.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 27 "Lonesome Day" — Calef asks how fictional story-songs can teach: lyrics yield neither know-how nor know-that, since Plato's Theaetetus shows true belief is not knowledge (the 'Meeting Across the River' narrator's plan works only by luck). The answer is a third kind — knowing what something is like: 'The River' lets a comfortable listener inhabit Mary's husband's slide into a dry marriage, and 'Nebraska' lets us feel Starkweather's numb void, 'what it's like to have no soul.' Aristotle's Poetics (we delight in imitation because learning pleases; poetry is more philosophic than history because it speaks in universals) explains why sad songs satisfy us, and Sartre's universal human condition grounds the empathy that makes The Rising render 9/11 ('You're Missing,' 'Empty Sky') thinkable at a personal scale.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 18 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Andrew Terjesen asks what Death could learn from living one mortal day per century in Sandman's Death: The High Cost of Living, after a little girl's 'How would you like it?' shamed the once icy Death into the practice. Using Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Nagel's bat to probe whether knowing what mortality is like requires first-person experience, he raises the 'Soul Man Effect' objection that Didi, like the fake black student in the 1986 film, always knows she will revert to being Death, and argues that simulation, not verbal description, is the efficient way to convey life's texture (Didi's hot-dog aftertaste). The real lesson, he concludes, is the existentialist one that each of us stands alone at death and that life's meaning lies in the unnoticed 'little moments' the dying regret missing, which only immersion in the distractions of living can teach Death, which is why the one-day-a-century program must continue.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 25 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Hess asks whether the monster has a soul and makes him the test case between physicalism (Kim, Churchland, van Inwagen) and dualism: recasting Frank Jackson's Mary as a color-blind monster who learns every physical fact about color vision, receives new eyes on Walton's ship, and then learns the 'what it is like' of seeing red for the first time, he argues there are nonphysical mental facts, so physicalism is false. He then runs Plantinga's argument that we are not our bodies or brains through a machine that replaces the monster's parts and hemispheres one by one while he stays conscious, and adds near-death out-of-body evidence like Maria's window-ledge shoe to suggest we can exist disembodied. The upshot is symmetric: whatever we conclude about the monster's soul we must conclude about our own - so be careful about assuming who does and does not have a soul, even monsters.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 22 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Stoody asks whether Hammond's dinosaurs are more than bones, blood, and DNA, and answers with Nagel's bat: there is something it is like to be eaten by a velociraptor, and even a complete neuroscience of a T. rex's brain would not reveal the bloodhound-rivaling smells it experiences. He reruns Jackson's Mary as Dr. Sattler raised in a black-and-white world who learns something new upon seeing violet West Indian Lilac berries, and rebuts the physicalist two-descriptions reply using Crichton's Michael Douglas pen name. He concludes that physicalism leaves out the what-it's-like aspect of consciousness, leaving a choice between substance dualism (dinosaur souls) and property dualism.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" — Schiltz tests Janet's claim to know 'literally everything' against the philosophical definition of omniscience as believing all true propositions, finding she lacks knowledge of Michael's demonhood, of the future, and of current events on Earth. Divine-omniscience puzzles drawn from Averroes and Aquinas, and Boethius's solution that God sees all things in an eternal present, frame why Janet's ignorance of the future is what protects the characters' free will and moral responsibility. Frank Jackson's Mary thought experiment illuminates Judge Gen's failure to know what human life is like, and Janet's gradual acquisition of empathy across her reboots shows why her imperfect knowledge is a feature rather than a glitch.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 25 "What It Is Like to Be Out of the Asylum" — Ron Novy argues nobody can know what it is like to be Batman: deploying Nagel's 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and a Mary's-Room variant with a color-deprived Barbara Gordon, he shows subjective experience resists even complete physical knowledge. Simone de Beauvoir's situated freedom then explains how 'one bad day' (Bruce's parents' murder, the Joker's Red Hood plunge into chemicals) threw each man into the same terrifying glimpse of Kant's noumenal world behind appearances, yet into opposite narratives of order and chaos. Even while sharing the joke that ends The Killing Joke, Batman and the Joker remain mutually unknowable, each the only one who can 'keep up' with the other.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" — Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 14 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Phillips argues that there is something-it-is-like to be a knowledgeable coffee drinker, using Nagel's bat and Jackson's Mary thought experiments — but where the bat is 'fundamentally alien,' coffee expertise is learnable, and via David Lewis's ability hypothesis the reader can apply book-knowledge of acidity, body, finish, and flavor to abilities they already have. He then invokes Hume's 'Of the Standard of Taste' (Homer's enduring appeal, the Don Quixote wine-tasters) to claim aesthetic and moral judgments spring from the same refinable sentiments, so that examining your cup free of prejudice is, echoing Socrates' 'unexamined life,' something we almost owe ourselves: the unexamined cup is not worth drinking.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.

### The Ghost in the Machine

'The ghost in the machine' is Gilbert Ryle's mocking phrase for the Cartesian doctrine that a person consists of a physical body inhabited by a distinct, immaterial mind. In The Concept of Mind he argued that this dualism rests on a category mistake, wrongly treating mental life as a hidden inner theater causally driving bodily movements. In its place Ryle urged that talk of mind refers to patterns of behavior and dispositions rather than to a private ghostly substance, a view that helped shape philosophical behaviorism.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 37 "The Machine-Made Ghost Or, The Philosophy of Mind, Matrix Style" — Holt announces his menu: after setting aside the standard ports of entry - Descartes's malicious demon, the brain-in-a-vat remade as body-in-a-vat, and the truth-versus-happiness question - he takes up the philosophy of mind his title advertises, the 'machine-made ghost' playing on the 'ghost in the machine' picture of the mind as a spirit inhabiting the body. He previews two entrees - arguing that artificial minds are possible and that mental states are brain states - and for dessert a solution to the hard problem of consciousness.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 38 "Unknown" — Holt runs a crash course in the mind-body problem: Descartes's thinking, unextended mind - the 'ghost in the machine' he also hears in the Police album - fails to explain how essentially different substances interact; behaviorism mistakes the evidence for mental states (dispositions to say 'Ouch!') for what the evidence is evidence of; so he defends materialism, the view that mental states are brain states, against the objections that it makes mind causally inert (epiphenomenal) and that pain is multiply realizable, teasing that the Matrix machines could in principle feel silicon pain.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 9 "Wave Goodbye from the Catbus" — Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 32 "Who Wants to Be Human Anyway" — Reads Kenji Kawai's thrice-repeated minyo 'Ghost theme' as the key to Major Kusanagi's quest in Ghost in the Shell and Innocence: each richer orchestration tracks her progress from manufactured shell, through the diving-scene worry that only others' treatment makes her human, to merging with the Puppet Master. Using Koestler's holons — individuals preserved while functioning within an evolving whole — and his view of consciousness as emergent (itself a rejection of both Descartes's immaterial soul and Ryle's dismissal of the 'ghost in the machine'), the chapter argues Oshii first celebrates the Major's Atman-like self-transcendence, then subverts Koestler in Innocence by making machines human: the ghost-dubbed gynoids act as a voiceless pack while the Major, still recognizably herself, aids Batou from the net — and Kawai's music literally gives the dolls a voice.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 33 "Cyborg Goddess" — Reads Ghost in the Shell as Donna Haraway's 'Cyborg Manifesto' made flesh: Major Kusanagi is built not born, has no sexuality or romance, and relegates male partners to sidekicks, enacting Haraway's post-gender cyborg that breaks the dualisms binding women to body, nature, and reproduction. The chapter traces the 'ghost' back through Koestler to Ryle's mockery of Descartes's mind-body dualism, reads the genderless, net-born Puppet Master as the Singularity of transhumanist philosophy, and interprets the Major–Puppet Master fusion — urged to 'come out of the shadows and into the light' in an explicit Plato's-cave gesture — as a posthuman, techno-spiritual 'Cyborg Goddess' that renders both gender and humanity obsolete.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 19 "Do You Think Androids Have Souls" — The chapter sets up strong versus weak AI through Rachael's account of the Rosen Association's strategy of iterating models until one is indistinguishable, then brings in Gaita's 'non-speculative conception' of a soul via Wittgenstein's remark that 'My attitude towards him is an attitude towards a soul.' Heidegger's warning that technology tempts us to treat others as mere means is dramatized in Deckard's realization after meeting the predatory bounty hunter Phil Resch that he had been viewing androids, and hence himself, as means; his half-measure of wishing other androids did the retiring shows how far he still has to go.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 25 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Hess asks whether the monster has a soul and makes him the test case between physicalism (Kim, Churchland, van Inwagen) and dualism: recasting Frank Jackson's Mary as a color-blind monster who learns every physical fact about color vision, receives new eyes on Walton's ship, and then learns the 'what it is like' of seeing red for the first time, he argues there are nonphysical mental facts, so physicalism is false. He then runs Plantinga's argument that we are not our bodies or brains through a machine that replaces the monster's parts and hemispheres one by one while he stays conscious, and adds near-death out-of-body evidence like Maria's window-ledge shoe to suggest we can exist disembodied. The upshot is symmetric: whatever we conclude about the monster's soul we must conclude about our own - so be careful about assuming who does and does not have a soul, even monsters.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 29 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Spyros Petrounakos reads Frankenstein as a Cartesian narrative whose external events run parallel to the inner worlds of Victor and the creature, from Victor's solitary conception of 'bestowing animation upon lifeless matter' to his imprisonment in a truth nobody would believe when Justine's life is at stake. The monster's acquisition of language at the De Lacey cottage - grasping 'fire, milk, and bread' but not 'good,' 'dearest,' and 'unhappy' - becomes the test case between Descartes's private inner theater (with its evil demon) and Gilbert Ryle's reply, glossing Locke on ideas of reflection, that we learn emotion words by responding directly to behavior rather than by cracking a hidden code. On Ryle's reading the monster's deformity is horror precisely because it is put to Cartesian use, a body that seems to shield its inner life, so the creature only truly comes alive when it behaves like a human being.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 35 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud argues that when you go extinct you do not come back, dismantling our three hopes: the soul, cloning, and an essential self. Cloning a T. rex yields a new individual 'Rex' with her own perspective, not the original; the soul cannot both be beyond science's reach and record memories and move bodies; and he deploys Gilbert Ryle's view that 'soul' is a language mistake - a mind is just what a functioning brain does, the way 'Jurassic Park' is just buildings, dinosaurs, staff, and money working together, ceasing when the functioning stops. A Hammond stripped by Alzheimer's and atom-replacement of every memory, trait, and particle still gets called John Hammond, so there is no essence over time: we already die constantly and never notice, which is why a second extinction holds no fresh terror.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 28 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Marceline has lost Simon Petrikov forever now that he is the Ice King, and tests every criterion of personal identity - body, memories, beliefs, personality, soul - finding each one either something that changes over time without ending a person (Finn survives losing his arm, Jake his fear of vampires) or something shared that then explains nothing. Borrowing Ryle's deflation of the soul as just the way the brain works - like Lemongrab renaming and remaking the Candy Kingdom, killing it without touching a single building - the author concludes Simon and the Ice King are two different people sharing one piece of machinery, like two operating systems on one computer. The dark payoff: bringing Simon back permanently would delete the Ice King, and by the same reasoning our own past selves are equally gone, a 'thousand deaths' a day that the chapter offers as Marceline's consolation, with Death's line 'you're gonna be the Ice King' as the haunting exception.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 33 "20. The Intersection of Science and Philosophy, the Seediest Corner in Ankh-Morpork" — A comic sprint through Western thought anchored in the Science of Discworld books, the chapter runs from Aristotle—whose geocentric four-element physics, it notes, fits Discworld better than Roundworld, and whose condemnations of usury it digresses over—through Descartes's cogito and mind-body dualism, Ryle's 'ghost in the machine,' behaviorism, identity theory, eliminative materialism, and functionalism's brain-as-computer picture, to show how philosophy of mind advances by each theory picking on its predecessor. Newton's occult-seeming gravity, later overturned by Einstein, illustrates the chapter's real thesis drawn from Pratchett's 'Lies-to-Wizards': neither science nor philosophy erects a timeless edifice of facts, since 'every so often, you have to unlearn what you thought you already knew,' while Diogenes and the Cynics supply the model of philosophy done in the common tongue that Pratchett shares.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 10 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — White asks whether Sinestro's quip that Hal's mind is 'like a muscle unused for years' is a mere metaphor and argues willpower is a real, exercisable strength. Against the Humean desire-belief model, which cannot explain Tom Kalamaku fixing planes instead of browsing Facebook, he uses Searle's 'gaps' to locate an independent will that can choose against one's better judgment, and Kant's account of virtue as moral strength in fulfilling duty despite inclination. Holton and Baumeister's findings that self-control depletes and strengthens like a muscle fit the comics exactly: Ollie is exhausted by a single ring use in Rebirth, Hal sweats through moving a planet, and John Stewart must 'suppress my own terrors' to hold the Mosaic walls.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 12 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Gordon Hawkes uses Rick's words to Morgan over zombified Duane ('that's just his body—there's nothing of your son left in there') to set up Cartesian dualism against the materialism of Drs. Jenner and Stevens ('just tasty meat all the way down'), with Ryle's 'ghost in the machine' as the standard objection. He then explains Chalmers's zombie argument that a physically identical unconscious twin is conceivable, so consciousness is non-physical, and Dennett's 'zimbo' rebuttal that a creature endlessly reflecting on its own states would believe itself conscious. The chapter closes by asking whether there is 'something it is like' to be a walker shuffling through Atlanta, and sides with Rick's anti-materialism.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 14 "Apocalypse Within The War Epic as Crisis of Self-Identity" — Hagberg reads Coppola's Apocalypse Now as a sustained dismantling of the "privileged access" / perceptual model of self-knowledge, in which the self inspects private inner objects insulated from the outer world. Captain Willard's voyage upriver shows the opposite: he comes to know himself only relationally, by studying Kurtz's file and measuring himself against Kilgore, Chef, Lance, and Colby, and through self-defining acts like shooting the wounded woman in the sampan and finally machete-killing Kurtz. Willard's clarifying self-composition marks Socrates' examined life, whereas Kurtz—self-deceived, an "imitator of an actor" in Nietzsche's phrase, exhibiting Freudian derealization and depersonalization—is the tragedy of the unexamined life, the true Oedipus blinded by a false self-image.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 19 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — J. Neil Otte contrasts Patanjali's 'weak' dualism — in which prakriti and purusha are revealed as united in samadhi — with Descartes' 'deep' dualism of irreconcilable mind and body, whose interaction problem (Princess Elisabeth's objection, the pineal gland) it never solved. He traces La Mettrie's materialist 'Man a Machine,' Wittgenstein on public meaning, and neuroscience (Penfield, out-of-body proprioception experiments) to argue mind depends on brain, and that yoga's 'interdependence' of mind and body fits modern science better than either Cartesian dualism or eliminative materialism — so yoga's critics will come around.

### The Absurd

For Albert Camus, the absurd names the collision between the human craving for meaning, order, and clarity and a universe that offers no such answers in return. It is not a property of the world alone or of the mind alone but the confrontation between them, arising when a person who demands significance meets a silent, indifferent cosmos. Camus treats this recognition as the honest starting point for thought, and his central question becomes how to live fully once one no longer expects the world to justify existence.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 88 "Popping a Bitter Pill Existential Authenticity in The Matrix and Nausea" — The chapter frames Neo's red/blue choice as the existential choice between authenticity - honest awareness of a condition without inherent purpose or design - and inauthenticity, named as Sartre's bad faith, Camus's intellectual suicide, and Heidegger's 'levelling down of all possibilities'. It notes the irony that although existentialists praise authenticity, their literary portraits make authentic characters anxious, alienated, and near-mad while the inauthentic remain tranquil - raising the possibility that ignorance is bliss and the blue pill is wiser - before promising an argument, via The Matrix and Sartre's Nausea, for the red pill.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 12 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 16 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues the show's underlying moral vision is Nietzschean passive nihilism filtered through film noir. Tony, unlike the active nihilist who converts value-collapse into self-overcoming, sinks into resentment and life-negation: he wants to rip the throat of the 'happy wanderer', therapy never redeems him, and he quits it with 'I'm a fat fucking crook from New Jersey' in 'Calling All Cars'. The chapter traces the noir lineage (Tony watching White Heat, the Godfather references, Bogart imagery at Satriale's) and reads A.J.'s 'D-Girl' existentialism (Camus's The Stranger, 'There is no God') and Livia's 'It's all a big nothing' as the family inheritance of meaninglessness and death-dread.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 11 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Wrathall defends the film's violence by contrasting Fra Angelico's serene Descent from the Cross with Corinth's Red Christ and Gibson's Gethsemane rebuke ('You could not watch even one hour with me'), arguing the gore resists rationalizing Christ's suffering into an economy of exchange, as Camus's Father Paneloux in The Plague insists true faith must not. Drawing on Pascal's instrumental reason, Heidegger, and Merleau-Ponty, he develops a 'world-disclosive' account of faith: the tall-table scene between Mary and the young carpenter Jesus shows that new practices train new perception, and film reaches the body directly in ways written description cannot. He closes by faulting Gibson for pessimism: Christ's world looks as God-forsaken and demon-haunted as Judas's, closer to Dostoevsky's ascetic Father Ferapont than to a world made new.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 11 "The Ends of Despair From “Things Have Changed” to “Love and Theft”" — Rick Furtak traces an existential arc through Dylan's later albums, reading Blood on the Tracks ("Tangled Up in Blue," "You're a Big Girl Now") as Camus's absurd divorce between a mind that cares and a world that has gone silent, and Heideggerian care as what the narrator loses in "Simple Twist of Fate." "Brownsville Girl" and "Most of the Time" embody Kierkegaard's knight of infinite resignation - hope abandoned but the precious past never forgotten - while "Not Dark Yet" and "Things Have Changed" mark the nadir of despair. On Love and Theft ("Mississippi," "Sugar Baby") the singer turns toward an absurd, Kierkegaardian faith that keeps caring and even loves without demanding that life make sense.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 19 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Pratt reads the outlaw biker's FTW (Fuck the World) posture as pop-culture nihilism: Nietzsche's 'danger of dangers' and Camus's answer of scorn to an absurd universe ('there is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn') are embodied by Brando's Johnny in The Wild One, Sonny Barger's Hells Angels, and the wanton Born to Lose club of The Born Losers, whose smashing matches Pisarev's Russian nihilism. He then shows how Willie G. Davidson's 1977 Low Rider and events like Daytona's Bike Week sanitized and marketed the rebellion, reducing skulls and DILLIGAF patches to ubiquitous fashion worth $340 million a week. Freud supplies the psychology: the superego keeps the rest of us tame, so we voyeuristically buy a tasteful version of outlaw freedom, even though pure nihilism, denying all truth, refutes even itself.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 6 "And Where the @#$%^& is the Queen" — The editors' introduction recounts Monty Python's 1969 debut and argues the troupe's absurdism bears a deep connection to philosophy because the British Pythons absorbed the Oxford and Cambridge linguistic analysis of Russell, Wittgenstein, Moore, and Ryle while at university in the 1960s. It tours the volume's three parts, previewing each contributor's pairing: Schilbrack reading Life of Brian through Camus's absurd hero, Brighouse using the Argument Clinic for Rawls's analysis of social practices, Asma finding Buddhist mindfulness in The Meaning of Life, Huss pairing the Pythons with Hume on religion, and Spinelli reading sketches through Foucault on the social construction of madness. It concludes there is no single connection between Python and philosophy but many: sketches illuminate philosophy, philosophy illuminates sketches, and Python's empire says something about philosophy's cultural standing (with Wittgenstein's duck-rabbit figuring how the remaining chapters can be seen).
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 8 "“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism" — Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 15 "Poker and Philosophy" — Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 24 "A Political Philosophy of Vampires" — Phillip Cole takes Rousseau's remark that the eighteenth-century vampire epidemics had complete legal proof - the Arnold Paole exhumations - and argues Rousseau's real point was political: authorities manufacture imaginary monsters, as in the witch craze, to exploit fear and hold power over their own populations. Freud's account of the uncanny explains why the horror is not death itself but the returning dead (the watching eyes of Scratchy in Itchy and Scratchy, versus the serene corpses of Six Feet Under, whose absurdity the show meets with wry amusement), and Julia Kristeva's abjection explains the corpse as the ultimate boundary-breaker. The vampire then resurfaces as the demonized outsider - Stoker's Dracula coded as the unassimilated Jewish immigrant, today's terrorist - exposing political borders as arbitrary fabrications. Buffy completes the collapse of the us/them binary: Angel and Spike join the slayer, and the most shocking killings (Faith's accidental human kill, Warren's stray bullet hitting Tara) are all too human, so the real subject of border policing is the community's own members.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 11 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 15 "Would You Help Me to Carry the Stone" — Weinstein argues critics who call Waters a gloomy misanthrope misread him: he is an existentialist whose work maps point for point onto Camus's absurd, the human demand for unity endlessly frustrated. Waters's imagery tracks Camus's: the sun (Plato's cave symbol of the good, and the light Sisyphus loved on earth) against the eclipsed moon of death and madness; the stone we secrete through failed communication ('the bad blood slows and turns to stone' in 'Dogs,' 'would you help me to carry the stone' in The Wall) against Sisyphus's rock; and Pink's Trial, condemned for 'showing feelings of an almost human nature,' replaying Meursault's condemnation for failing to cry at his mother's funeral. Since the institutions of home, school, military, and the music industry's machine block every genuine encounter, Waters's persistence in making art that mostly fails to communicate is itself the absurd revolt, so with Camus one must imagine Sisyphus happy, and Weinstein imagines Waters happy too.
