- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 25 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Iuliano asks whether it even makes sense to blame Apple (not Tim Cook or the board) for the Foxconn suicides, child labor, pollution, or tax evasion, laying out the two conditions of moral agency—autonomy and the capacity to know right from wrong—via the blameless wasp. He then canvasses the corporate moral agency debate: Peter French's Corporate Internal Decision structures, which filter employees' personal reasons into corporate ones (the dividend example), and List and Pettit's functionalist group agency, whose judgment-aggregation paradox (three executives, an environmentally friendly but harmful factory) shows Apple's moral conclusions can diverge from every member's—against Quinton's 'sum of its parts' reduction—so holding the corporation itself responsible plugs the responsibility deficit left when no individual is blameworthy.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 22 "“When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”" — Lean treats Bernard's discovery in 'Trompe L'Oeil' that his son Charlie never existed as a richly detailed thought experiment about intentionality: his memories of Charlie seem to refer to nothing, so his grief looks like 'grieving about nothing.' After setting up Brentano's aboutness and Frege's sense/reference distinction (Dolores learns that 'William' and 'the Man in Black' are one referent known under two senses), he tests two consolations: a fiction theory drawing on Lamarque, on which Bernard's implanted memories are a story rather than a lie and his emotions are rationally grounded because thoughts need only be entertained, not believed, to move us; and an 'inheritance theory' on which a causal theory of reference might make Bernard's copied memories genuinely about Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that whichever theory Bernard adopts, his suffering is what makes him 'real,' echoing the Man in Black's line that suffering is when you are most real.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 29 "“King of space, right here!”" — The chapter asks whether Robert Daly wrongs the USS Callister NPCs even if they are 'merely' sentient code: his theft of co-workers' DNA violates a fundamental right to privacy, and Kant's focus on the will shows his in-game intentions aim at real people — he logs in solely to strangle James's NPC and make him confess to being pathetic, wanting to harm the actual James. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the second indictment: because hyperrealistic VR blurs game and life, Daly's daily practice of cruelty habituates vice and makes cruelty part of who he is, unlike clearly fictional violence such as Mortal Kombat. Merleau-Ponty's intentionality links avatar actions to the self, so the chapter ends by asking what our own intentions in games like The Sims or Grand Theft Auto reveal about our character.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 28 "Guilt Can be a Real Bitch" — Jason Howard argues Inception is phenomenological philosophy in Husserl's sense: the film dramatizes how dreaming, remembering, and perceiving are distinct intentional states with different 'modes of givenness' and horizons — time dilates, dreams begin mid-scene with no past, and memories carry a temporal signature that collapses when Cobb rebuilds them into dreamscapes, which is why he warns Ariadne never to build dreams from memory. Totems work because waking perception alone is governed by laws of nature and by the shared life-world (Lebenswelt): Saito's carpet with the wrong fabric, Cobb's backwards watch, and the Penrose steps that could never close real space all betray the dream. The chapter extends this to embodiment — Yusuf's dreamers register rain and balance from their bodies, and Saito's comatose body still atrophies — and closes with intersubjectivity: Cobb's guilt is 'always there reminding me of the truth' because reality is inseparable from the community of others, and the 'shades' of people in dreams and memories can never capture the real Mal or his children.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Applies Husserl's phenomenology - noesis (the act of meaning-giving), noema (the meaning arrived at), and the life-world - to Voyager's Doctor and Seven of Nine as they build selves from conscious experience. Reads "Latent Image" (the Doctor's deleted memories of choosing Harry Kim's life over another ensign's) and "Infinite Regress" (Seven's channeling of assimilated personalities) as parallel guilt experiences whose noemata teach each that past choices remain part of identity without governing it. Their forced isolation in "One", the Doctor's unrequited love in "Someone to Watch over Me", and "Body and Soul", where the Doctor savors food and sensation through Seven's body, generate a shared noema: social interaction and embodied experience are what make a life-world, even for photons and drones.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 22 "“When You’re Suffering, That’s When You’re Most Real”" — Lean treats Bernard's grief over the fabricated son Charlie as a thought experiment about intentionality, using Brentano's 'aboutness' and Frege's sense/reference (illustrated by Dolores knowing 'William' and 'the Man in Black' as one referent) to ask whether Bernard's memories refer to nothing. He offers Lamarque's fiction theory (emotion needs only entertained, not believed, thoughts, so Charlie could be a fiction rather than a lie) and an 'inheritance theory' using a causal theory of reference to ask whether Bernard's memories actually refer to Arnold's real dead son. He concludes that grieving makes Bernard 'most real' whatever the metaphysics.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Douglas McLaughlin and Cesar Torres argue that Coubertin's vague Olympism is best clarified by the phenomenological concept of intersubjectivity developed by Husserl, Merleau-Ponty, and Levinas. Treating competitive sport (via Suits's lusory attitude and the 'testing family' notion of a mutual quest for excellence) as inherently social, they use intersubjectivity to dissolve the apparent contradiction between the motto's excellence and the creed's participation, since one's victory is meaningful only through worthy opponents one is answerable to. Invoking Levinas's ethics of the face, they ground Olympic values of mutual respect, fairness, and peace in the reciprocity athletes owe one another 'running shoulder to shoulder.'
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.

### Simulacra and Simulation (the hyperreal)

In Simulacra and Simulation, Jean Baudrillard argued that in a media-saturated society signs and images increasingly detach from any underlying reality and begin to circulate on their own. A simulacrum is a copy without an original: a representation that no longer refers to a real thing but only to other representations. Baudrillard called the resulting condition the "hyperreal," a world in which models, maps, and images feel more real and more authoritative than whatever they were once supposed to depict. The concept diagnoses a culture where the distinction between the real and its simulation has effectively collapsed.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 108 "Unknown" — The chapter argues that The Matrix's ending betrays its own message: Neo is glamorous and powerful only inside the simulation, while the 'real' world aboard the ship is gray and monastic, so the film celebrates the very escapism it condemns and hypocritically sucks viewers into its illusions. eXistenZ, by contrast, ends with the game-within-game coda ('Tell me, are we still in the game?'), makes game design a metaphor for film-making, and honestly acknowledges that movies are simulations we are plugged into and enjoy because real life bores us.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 114 "The Matrix Simulation and the Postmodern Age" — Weberman dates the postmodern rupture to 1966–74—globalization, Warhol and Madonna, the abandonment of epistemological foundations, television and then computers—and presents The Matrix as the most sustained implicitly philosophical film about the blurred line between reality and simulation, winking at this with Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation in Neo's hollowed-out book. The essay then sets up four theses to test against the film: that we cannot tell the real from the unreal, that reality can be simulated and improved on, that the simulation is preferable, and that simulated reality is as metaphysically real as unsimulated reality.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 116 "Unknown" — Developing thesis two, the chapter moves from representation to simulation via Guy Debord's Society of the Spectacle—life presenting itself as an immense accumulation of spectacles mediated by images—and the film's white loading program with its two red armchairs, where any world can be piped in through the neck jack. Because the machines simulate pleasant 1999 rather than blasted 2199, and add the woman in the red dress, simulation is inherently an enhancement of reality; Walker Percy's Grand Canyon and the IMAX analogue show why 'if you've only got three hours, take a pass on the Canyon.'
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 118 "Unknown" — Developing thesis four, the chapter takes Morpheus's 'What is real?' seriously: if the real is just 'electrical signals interpreted by your brain', then virtual reality is as real as reality, and Neo's noodle-bar memories—experienced, coherent, and shared with other plugged-in minds—correspond to something that happened, by Hume's empiricism, coherence, and pragmatist standards alike. To the cyberskeptic's objection that cyberspace is not real space, the chapter answers with Plato's non-spatial Forms (and Kant on space as a form of intuition), closing that if simulations someday shape our lives more than the unsimulated world, the hyperreal Baudrillard describes will be, pragmatically, more real.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 120 "Unknown" — The chapter places The Matrix in the lineage of artificial-universe plots—The Truman Show, Philip K. Dick's Time Out of Joint, Aldiss's Starship, the POW film 36 Hours—as the American paranoid fantasy of a staged fake, arguing that in late-capitalist consumerist society 'real' social life itself acquires the features of a spectacle, irreal and dematerialized. Truman's break-out through the painted sky has a Magrittean touch, yet Žižek suggests this happy denouement is ideology at its purest if it presupposes a 'true reality' waiting outside the closure.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 33 "The Evolution of the Metaphor" — Tracy Little argues the show takes teenagers' metaphorical speech — 'high school is hell,' 'after we slept together he became a different person,' 'graduation is the end of the world' — and makes it literal: hyena-possessed bullies in 'The Pack,' invisible Marcie whom nobody noticed, Angelus replacing Angel after Buffy and Angel's first night together, and the Mayor's ascension timed to graduation. Invoking Baudrillard's simulacra and hyperreality, the copy becomes more real than the original — the monsters are real but the social horrors they literalize are worse — and the seasons-one-through-three survey traces identity, love gone wrong, and end-of-the-world metaphors as they evolve from monster-of-the-week camp to weighty questions of life and death.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 8 "U2 and Philosophy" — Wrathall's introduction argues U2 is philosophically interesting because its enormous popularity holds up a mirror to what 'we' care about (by Nietzsche's test of how a culture stands toward life) and because the band publicly wrestles with the contradictions of the technological-global economy: unprecedented freedom of choice paired with loss of rooted identity, and distant suffering ('Crumbs from Your Table') that we feel both powerless to fix and responsible for. Its showcase reading treats 'Miracle Drug' as a musical theodicy: Bono's plea 'God, I need your help tonight' is answered by the Edge's guitar and by the Matthew 25:35 refrain, so science and medicine count as works of Christian charity. The piece then frames the volume's essays: Plato's ascent of love in the early songs, Kierkegaardian despair after Achtung Baby, Bono's search for authentic identity, the simulacra of 'Even Better than the Real Thing', being-toward-death in the apocalyptic songs, and the Plato-versus-Aristotle quarrel over music's emotional power.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 14 "U2 and Philosophy" — Soper tracks Bono's public identity work across three paradigms: pre-modern Irish-Catholic inheritance, including a Du Boisian 'double consciousness' of the colonized Irish; the modernist artist-as-visionary, where Nietzsche, Freud and Marx destabilize the self and the Shalom fellowship nearly ends the band; and the postmodern masks of the Fly, Mirrorball Man and MacPhisto on the Zoo TV media collage, read via Lacan for 'Mofo' and via Baudrillard's simulacra for the 'Even Better than the Real Thing' video with its wax Beatles and cyber-sex imagery. Lyotardian skepticism toward grand ideologies explains the band's refusal of fanaticism in 'Sunday Bloody Sunday' and 'Two Hearts Beat as One'. Soper concludes that Bono fuses all three into a 'Postmodern Christian Pragmatism' that keeps Christian conviction and debt-relief activism while adopting postmodern playfulness without collapsing into ironic detachment.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 15 "U2 and Philosophy" — Thomson uses U2's self-declared postmodern phase to define postmodernity itself: a sensitivity to poetic polysemy against modernity's fantasies of total control (Heidegger's reduction of everything to optimizable resource), Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives - defended against the self-refutation charge and narrowed to the dying metanarratives of unity and emancipation - and the Marx-Nietzsche-Freud hermeneutics of suspicion that fragmented the subject, with Kierkegaard and early Heidegger as the resisters. Derrida's 9/11 analysis of autoimmunity and hauntology is read into 'Peace on Earth' and the sorrows that 'learned to swim' in 'Until the End of the World'. The payoff is a polysemic reading of 'Even Better than the Real Thing': risky as a seeming hymn to Baudrillard's simulacra, addressed to a live audience it celebrates a communal love 'even better' than personal love - Diotima's ladder generalized - making the postmodern U2 continuous with the 'Christ-ian' U2 of universal love, sealed by 'One'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Jeremy Wisnewski's mock-manifesto uses Family Guy's cutaway gags and taboo jokes (Hitler sausage vendors, Petoria at the UN, Saddam and Khadafi bonding over Seinfeld) to stage postmodernism: Lyotard's "incredulity toward meta-narratives" and Baudrillard's claim that the real is no longer real, since our families are as televisual as the Griffins, who at least know they are cartoons. The danger is that joking about everything breeds cynical passivity, "liberating us from our causes." But Foucault, the 1968 activist and prison reformer, shows through power/knowledge that one can be postmodern and still fight locally, so the Griffins, and the show's satire of religion and politics, get to live.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 10 "Freeze-Frame Ending" — Aaron Anderson reads Death Proof through Baudrillard's hyperreality: Tarantino's references to Vanishing Point and Dirty Mary, Crazy Larry become simulations that feel more real than their originals, at times collapsing into simulacra that reference nothing but other references. He analyzes Stuntman Mike with Deleuze's account of sadism and masochism—the death-proof car as an extension of his murdering body where pleasure fuses with pain—and argues the finale invites the audience to share Kim, Zoë and Abernathy's own sadism. The repeated, slow-motion car crash is where simulation, technology and the human body collide.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 19 "Youth and the Image" — Hickey argues the iPod is the 'iCon of a generation' because it is a Baudrillardian simulacrum of youth: like the Gulf War consumed as CNN fireworks or reality TV's fabricated 'real,' Apple's silhouette ads sell faceless dancers whose entire identity is the white device -- a 'symbolic cyborgism' read through Donna Haraway. The vernacular of iPodding, podcasting, and downloading forms what he calls, with Wittgenstein, a language game woven into the actions of the 'now' that authorizes this youthful, tech-savvy identity as natural, while the ads' imagery works like Platonic shadows in the caves of our desire. Still, citing Giddens's structure-agency negotiation and DeCerteau's consumer tactic of re-appropriating everyday images, he insists we are not brainwashed: we can switch off, refuse, or remake the images that 'tell us who we are.'
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 31 "The Golden Power" — Dugan reads the Triforce through Lacan's psychology of the dyad and the social symbolic: Link is the player's dyadic anchor ('Miyamoto's Framework' avatar, named because he links us to the system), while the gameworld we progressively master and explore is the social symbolic. Each Triforce piece maps onto the triangle: Courage completes the two-way player-Link bond, Power is the sword/bomb/arrow system consummated in the A Link to the Past final battle, and Wisdom is the realization that these tidy symbolic trinities (Father/Son/Holy Ghost, Brahma/Vishnu/Shiva, the three branches of US government) are simplifications. The 'golden power' is seeing that all such systems are representations posing as totality, offering pre-designed, illusory choice, and inferring who designed the games we are in.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 9 "You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World" — Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 31 "Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy" — Bradley Kaye reads Kid A as an album made under Lyotard's postmodern condition: "Everything in Its Right Place" ("what was that you tried to say?") and the murmured title track bear witness to the differend, something that must be put into phrases but cannot yet be; "The National Anthem" dramatizes incredulity toward the grand narrative of nationalism in favor of little narratives and local justice; "Treefingers" is the painful silence of the inexpressible, and "Optimistic" an ironic micro-political hope. The epigone problem (Yorke to Coldplay, Travis, and Muse: "Good luck with Kid A") and the closing Baudrillard turn — "In Limbo"'s "you're living in a fantasy world," the Marcus Welby and Perry Mason hyperreal, "it's not like the movies" — explain why even labeling the album "Best Alternative Album" Grammy presumes exactly the stable categories Kid A dissolves.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 32 "How to Reappear Completely" — Tim Footman asks whether a rock band inside the media machine can avoid becoming a simulacrum of itself, tracing Radiohead's attempts to pierce Baudrillard's hyperreality: "Fake Plastic Trees" as the chain from plastic plants to plastic people, "Fitter Happier" as a simulacrum made of training-manual words, the no-singles Kid A campaign and leaked album, and the In Rainbows pay-what-you-want release that stripped away marketing — only to congeal into a new story about the band's anti-commercial perversity, since the free download was really advance publicity for a conventional for-sale album. Even seemingly authentic moments ("How I Made My Millions" recorded at home, the fabled Glastonbury 1997 set, Yorke's Dublin dissociation that became "How to Disappear Completely") are packaged slices of reality, so the band's melancholia is less a defeat of the simulacrum than a way of manifesting within it — "the best you can is good enough."
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 33 "How Come I End Up Where I Started" — Perry Owen Wright applies Baudrillard's Seduction to In Rainbows track by track: the Enlightenment reduced sex to anatomical biology and Natural Law, pornography is its hyperreal simulacrum (the HDTV of sex, played out in "Bodysnatchers"' "pale imitation with the edges sawn off"), and what re-enchants sex is seduction — an endless game of reversible signs, appearance and disappearance, aleatory suspension, and the trompe l'oeil's hypersimulation. "Weird Fishes/Arpeggi" shows the mortal risk of entering the game (the anglerfish's dangling false eyes), "All I Need" personifies Death itself as a stalker-seducer drawn into the loop of signs, "House of Cards" reads infidelity as leaving the game for the Law, and "Jigsaw Falling into Place" reduces seduction to production ending at the orgasm. "Videotape" closes the album at the pearly gates where even death becomes a sign to be seduced — the home movie "in red, blue, green" is the immortal sign we always leave behind.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 27 "Who Watches the Watchers" — Patton and Webb unpack Colbert's coinage 'freem' — freedom without the do — from the first episode's dedication to 'the heroes' who act patriotically by watching TV, through Bush's post-9/11 call to go shopping, the Wikipedia elephant vandalism, and the WristStrong bracelet as activism indistinguishable from consuming Viacom product. Using Singer's argument that social capital (roads, satellites, infrastructure) makes the 'it's your money' cry hollow, E.O. Wilson's four-Earths arithmetic on unsustainable consumption and greenwashed market 'solutions' to global warming, and Baudrillard's Consumer Society account of news packaged for consumption beside the ads, they ask whether the Colbert Nation's ironic participation resists corporate media or completes it, concluding freem converts even critique into one more purchase.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 25 "Epilogue Girl, You’ll Be a (Whoa ) Man Soon" — Phill Alexander recounts playing the female blood elf 'Sasha' so convincingly that his guild assumed he was a woman — and that he and his girlfriend's toon were a lesbian couple — testing Lisa Nakamura's 'identity tourism' thesis that avatars are consequence-free prostheses; months of accumulated intimacy and the ethical crisis of correcting (or concealing) the misunderstanding prove there were very real consequences. Baudrillard's simulacra and the hyperreal explain how Sasha became a signifying machine as 'real' as any guildmate, and James Gee's projective identity frames the decision to recustomize Sasha into Soren — a 'WoW witness relocation' that ends the deception without destroying the community.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 5 "index" — Fairweather and Halpern defend status updates against the vanity charge using Hume's 'natural sympathy': ambient awareness of hundreds of News Feed lives exercises the fellow-feeling from which Humean moral standards grow, and Facebook's non-overlapping friend lists remove the dominance hierarchies of face-to-face groups. Butera uses Baudrillard's promiscuous 'ecstasy of communication' to read friending as gatekeeper, the status update as moderator of an avatar-self, and the News Feed as a synthesizer that lets users censor encounters, asking with Kierkegaard whether this control forecloses the openness to interruption that makes life meaningful. Doyle and Fraser stage Foucault against Habermas over the MI6 chief's wife's exposed profile, Facebook's Beacon advertising surveillance, and Iran's Twitter revolution: the same diffuse, productive power that lets citizens watch institutions back makes narcissistic self-disclosure ever more available for categorization and control. Bar-Tura's account of organizing Jewish-Muslim teen bowling nights tests Habermas's ideal speech situation and concludes that wall-to-wall interaction must become face-to-face meetings to build real solidarity.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 29 "Progress" — Gregory Gilson argues that although The Onion deliberately reports falsehoods, it embodies postmodern theories of truth better than the newspapers it parodies. Lyotard's mercantilization of knowledge and the fragmentation of dominant narratives into separate language games explain headlines like 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity' and 'Astronomer Discovers The Center Of The Universe Is His Beautiful 9-Year Old Son,' which smash incompatible discourses together, while Baudrillard's simulacrum and hyper-reality explain how The Onion — like Disneyworld — is branded fake precisely so mainstream media can seem real. Yet the chapter closes honestly: its own criticism of 'Bush Says He Still Believes Iraq War Was the Fun Thing To Do' assumed some targets were wrong, which assumes a Truth out there — the paradox of a satire whose truthfulness exceeds its own theory of truth.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 42 "Case Closed" — Burnham stages the murder of reality itself and solves it with Baudrillard: the deerstalker, Inverness cape, and calabash Holmes of The Real Ghostbusters' 'Elementary My Dear Winston' is a simulacrum built from Paget's illustrations, stage actors' pipes, and the never-spoken 'Elementary, my dear Watson' — a copy of copies referring only to earlier simulations, never to Doyle's texts. Because the media-saturated everyman Winston (Baudrillard: whoever is underexposed to the media is desocialized) recognizes the 'belief made manifest' specters while the doctorate-holding Ghostbusters cannot, and because the hyperreal Holmes, Watson, Moriarty, and Hound are immune to proton packs, the simulacrum has 'murdered' its referent and become more real than the real. The 2008 UKTV poll — 58 percent of Britons believe Holmes was real while 47 percent call Richard the Lionheart mythical — proves the murder happened in our universe too, committed by the world's greatest detective.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 23 "An Old Man, Filled with Regret . ." — Brophy argues Cobb's shared dreams are best modeled on MMORPG virtual worlds like Second Life and World of Warcraft: Ariadne is a world-building architect in the mold of Second Life's Escher Relativity House, dreamers are avatars, and the film's looping architectures mirror the toroidal grids of game worlds. Reading the film as an addict's 'long con', he claims the real inception was planting in Cobb's own head the idea that his game-world is real: Mal is a 'gamer's widow' whose in-game suicide deleted her character, and Cobb is the avatar of an unseen addicted player who has forgotten the game. Borges's map that covers the empire, Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum becomes the preferred reality, Bostrom's simulation argument, and Homer's lotus-eaters all support the warning that we already prefer simulated worlds, so the last shot means the real Cobb will one day wake as an old man filled with regret.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 24 "Architecture and the Dream Machine" — Botz-Bornstein argues Inception presents dreams neither as separate worlds nor as Freudian symbols but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense: it synchronizes kicks, safe codes and the Piaf countdown like a computer coordinating contradictory layers of time. He links inception to Dawkins's meme theory, with the planted idea growing 'like a cancer' in Mal, and to the projections of Solaris, showing how the film unusually combines cognitive and psychoanalytic models in one vertical dream structure. Democritus's atomism frames Epstein's 'grains of reality' and the film's atomized media-images of the real world, while Benjamin and Baudrillard let him read Cobb's Limbo dystopia, Mombasa and Dubai's empty skyscrapers as an allegory of a globalized world of hackable neoliberal dream machines.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 30 "How Animals Make Us Human" — The chapter contrasts the novel, where humanity is secured through empathetic relations with scarce real animals (Deckard hating his electric sheep's 'tyranny' because it does not know he exists), with the film, where photographs do the validating: Rachael's 'Look, it's me with my mother' treats the photo as a self-grounding artifact, which the chapter explains via Baudrillard's precession of simulacra, supplemented by Sontag's point that photos act as surrogate relations documenting the loved one's absence. Deckard's piano covered in old sepia photos then reads as overcompensation: abundant evidence, no current relationships, a hint that he may be an android.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 31 "Narcissism in a “More Human than Human” World" — The chapter reads Deckard's longing for a real sheep as a need for his own existence to register on another genuine subjectivity, the electric sheep having no 'there there', as fellow bounty hunter Phil Resch's devotion to his squirrel Buffy implicitly concedes. It then deploys McLuhan's 'Narcissus as Narcosis': technologies like androids, the Penfield Mood Organ and the Empathy Box are a hall of mirrors reflecting humanity back at itself, so Mercerism offers virtual others that 'generate the effects of relationship even if they lack its substance.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 32 "Empathy in a “More Human than Human” World" — The chapter shows Deckard funding empathy for animals by killing androids, then raises the stakes: since android models keep improving, even close inspection of one's ostensibly 'real' sheep might fail to disclose a clever simulation, which it names as Dick's reconfiguration of the problem of other minds and solipsism. The desert toad, seen 'through Mercer's eyes' and boxed with painstaking care, is revealed by Iran to be electric, so that 'the desert of the real offers safe habitat only for virtual creatures.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 33 "The Shock of Being Alive" — The chapter fuses McLuhan's narcosis with Heidegger's enframing: technology constrains Being to a human-centered 'world picture' in which forests become board feet and animals become production units, and like Narcissus we fall in love with an image we stamped there ourselves. It enlists the deep ecologists and David Abram ('We are human only in contact, in conviviality, with what is not human') to argue that Dick makes human identity essentially relational, and closes on Baudrillard: digital tweets have become more present for many people than birdsong.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 34 "The Lives of Electric Others" — The chapter follows Deckard past despair at universal fakery (the toad electric, Mercer a set) to his muted epiphany, 'The electric things have their lives, too', and his 'Mercer isn't fake... unless reality is fake', asking whether this extends his circle of moral concern to electric beings or merely concedes the inescapability of virtuality. It reads the film's origami unicorn and Deckard's willingness to make a life with Rachael as parallel acceptances, ending with Iran ordering 'one pound of artificial flies that really fly around and buzz' for the toad her husband is devoted to.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 63 "Chapter 09 - Matt Damon Is a Vast Sinister Conspiracy" — Argues that 'Matt Damon' is an industrially manufactured person — a simulacrum sustained by executives, marketers, and gossip media that exploits instincts once used to judge trustworthy tribemates. Reading David Norris's tie-choosing specialists in The Adjustment Bureau, Tyrell's 'More human than human,' and the novels The Simulacra and Time Out of Joint, it claims Dick's paranoid fantasy is true: manufactured fake realities keep us docile, distracted, and consuming so we never notice we would rather be lying on a rock in the warm sun.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 7 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta's introduction frames the volume with a traffic-intersection metaphor: Klosterman's campaign against the phrase 'guilty pleasure' questions whether the one-way roads of high and low culture are real at all, and the contributors deliberately violate the traffic rules (Kierkegaard meets KISS, Baudrillard meets Britney Spears). It reads Klosterman's line that 'nothing is ever in and of itself' through Kant's noumena-phenomena distinction: like Kant's knowing subject, we never reach the in-itself but only perspectives refracted through rock bands, sports teams, and TV. The introduction presents the Guns N' Roses tribute band Paradise City (identity effaced to imitate an equally constructed identity) and the rock-death road trip of Killing Yourself to Live as Klosterman's way of recovering authenticity, arguing that living with the possibility of one's own death is more authentic than fleeing it.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 15 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Rood unpacks Klosterman's 'This Is Emo' thesis that no woman will ever satisfy him: women love Lloyd Dobler rather than John Cusack, and everyone measures real relationships against Hollywood fake love (Coldplay songs, the Woody Allen Personality Type) until, as Klosterman puts it, real people actively trying to live like fake people are no less fake. He reads this through Sartre's cafe waiter and Butler's gender performativity to argue identity is learned performance, and through Plato's cave updated to a reclining-seat movie theater where we mistake projected shadows for real love. The deepest diagnosis is Baudrillard's hyperreal, glossed as a social-constructionist rerun of Kant's Copernican revolution, against which Rood's own objection lands: Klosterman covertly assumes a pure unmediated self that cannot exist, so the answer to fake love is not escape from mediation but self-control within it.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 28 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Reads Walt's descent through Lacan's distinction between constructed reality and the Real: the cancer diagnosis is the first irruption puncturing his veil of ordinary family-and-job reality, and each trauma after - dissolving Emilio, killing Krazy-8 with an 'I'm sorry', the escalating 'memory lapse' lie - re-codes his reality further into the harsh 'Desert of the Real'. The chapter stresses that choice persists at each rupture (Walt could still confess), shows illegality itself becoming his true self (car sex after the school meeting, 'because it was illegal'), and reads the nameless horse of 'Caballo sin Nombre' as an image of the unspeakable Real itself.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 23 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Kempner argues that the featherless raptors confirm Baudrillard's hyperreal: our dinosaurs are 'a real without origin or reality', like blue raspberry flavor or the never-existent brontosaurus, so the more real the clones pretend to be, the more fake they seem. He reads Wu's 'there isn't any reality here' and The Lost World's fossil-album passage as Crichton's own warnings against mistaking images for reality, while Spielberg's rejection of feathers shows the franchise teaching audiences to prefer the fake. Baudrillard himself used the film's finale, cloned dinosaurs rampaging among their fossilized ancestors in the museum, as the image of our predicament between 'our fossils and our clones'.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 36 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Jonathon O'Donnell reads DmC: Devil May Cry's Limbo City - demon-run banks, the Fox-News parody Raptor News, Virility soda - as the newest stage in the Devil's career. Tracing the shift from Dante's frozen, defeated Satan to Milton's active deceiver and the Black Mass's sacramental counterfeits, he argues the game's demons are both the hiders and the hidden: reality itself is the demonic lie, a counterfeit truth with nothing truer beneath it. When Dante and Vergil's WikiLeaks-style reveal frees humanity, what is unveiled is not God's order but just another contingent world, a secular tale of media institutions manufacturing 'truth' for a conforming public.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 36 "23. I’d Rather Stay an Orangutan Because That’s Why Discworld Exists" — In a self-fictionalizing chapter, editor Nicolas Michaud is summoned by Vetinari to prove Discworld is real, and the answer arrives in the Unseen University library: the Librarian stays an orangutan because language distances us from experience—humans never simply experience a banana, only 'holding a banana,' so for us the words create the reality. Along the way the chapter takes issue with Hume's bundle-of-perceptions view of the self, since word-using humans are never just a collection of present perceptions, and contrasts the Librarian's immediate, unmediated experience of each singular thing with our word-reduced world. It concludes that because we always experience the world as stories, narratives, and terms, 'narratives are all we have,' making the Disc no less real than the Roundworld we talk and think about.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 24 "13. The Madness of the Musician" — Lampert explains why Bowie is called the first postmodern pop star - he ironically shows that 'acting like' a rock star just is being one, refusing the genius myth by cobbling influences and confessing 'I lie an awful lot' - and grounds this in Sloterdijk's cynical reason and Diderot's Rameau's Nephew, whose honest liar Lui owns the mask-wearing vices everyone else hides. Hegel's Phenomenology supplies the title: the musician's universal deception is 'the madness of the musician,' the 'I' hollowed into pure ironic distance from all its masks (Descartes's separable self become image-manipulation), yet Hegel's hint that the cynic's vain talk can rise into 'a spiritual self of truly universal worth' points beyond Bowie's hyper-real self-referentiality to punk's DIY injunction to be your own hero - and to reading all sexuality, like Bowie's, as performance.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 18 "7. Remix in Gilead" — Walker frames Gilead as a remix: the Sons of Jacob sample scripture under restrictive rules (the Bilhah Ceremony, the doctored Beatitudes, Marx's slogan misattributed to St. Paul), like Danger Mouse's Grey Album, while Offred herself remixes the Lord's Prayer and 'Amazing Grace.' Using Pieixoto's line that Gilead's 'genius was synthesis,' he argues via Baudrillard that no original Christianity exists against which to judge Gilead—we live among simulacra, so Gilead is 'presented as unique in order to hide that it is Christianity'—and via Deleuze that Pieixoto and Wade's assembly of Offred's cassettes is a new original rather than a degraded copy. The payoff is that the question of authenticity is misguided, and gradual, unnoticed change is what lets regimes like Gilead assemble themselves.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 10 "1. Free Falling into Postmodernism" — Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 11 "1. Barb Dead, People Mad" — Holmes and Christensen read the #JusticeForBarb movement through Baudrillard's hyperreality: fans mobilized real activism for a fictional girl the show killed as a plot device (dragged by the Demogorgon while Nancy and Steve are upstairs), while real murdered women like Jamie Haggard got no hashtag, so fictional justice becomes 'more real than the real.' The show itself is a simulacrum assembled from 1980s movies (E.T., Poltergeist, Firestarter, The Goonies, Stand by Me) whose grid motif casts the series as a D&D gameboard the audience plays, and the chapter argues hyperreal power became real power when the Duffers gave Barb a Season Two funeral and apology from Hawkins Lab.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 20 "8. In Eggos We Trust" — Wigley uses Baudrillard's hyperreality and semiotics to argue that Eggos, not Eleven, are Hawkins's true savior: as Barb's Xeroxed missing-poster face drifts through generations of models away from the original photo, so Eggos accumulate new symbolic value as tokens of trust and friendship, from Mike's blanket-fort promise of 'as many Eggos as you want' to Hopper's box in the snow-covered woods that tells El she can come home. The Party's Dungeons & Dragons vocabulary (naming the Demogorgon, Dustin's 'best metaphor') is their shared code for making sense of a reality shattered by adolescence, Reagan-era image politics, and the Upside Down, and the trust the waffles symbolize extends past the screen to the viewer.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 8 "Philosophy and Reality in Blade Runner 2049" — Robin Bunce's introduction shows that the word 'real' is used in at least six different senses in 2049: Joshi's authentic, K's genuine (unimplanted) memories, Joi's natural-born 'real boy', Stelline's naturalistic 'real human responses', Mariette's physical, and Deckard's true. It argues the film makes reality an essentially contested concept, then maps how each contributor deploys a different sense of 'real', from Baudrillard's simulacra in the chapter on women and birth to socialist realism in the Wallace chapter.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 35 "22. Rachael, Weeping for Her Children" — Bonnie McLean maps Baudrillard's four-stage precession of simulacra onto the women of 2049: Joshi anchors reality, implanted memories distort it, Joi is representation masking the absence of reality, and the eye-color-wrong reconstructed Rachael is a simulacrum of a simulacrum bearing no relation to reality. Read this way, the film lionizes birth — Wallace kissing the replicant he has just disemboweled, her blood running down her legs — while stripping every woman of agency in service of K's quest, a dynamic the chapter links to pro-life politics and DACA-era savior narratives. Only by removing K from the narrative, she shows, does the women's erasure become visible.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 10 "1. RuPaul Is a Better Warhol" — Volpert maps Baudrillard's four levels of simulacra onto Drag Race's 'realness': faithful copies (Trinity the Tuck's tucking tutorial, the Season 10 Cher challenge), distorted copies (Sasha Velour and Eureka's nerve, double wig reveals), simulations masking an absent reality (Vanjie's nonsense-word meme, Valentina replacing the judges' verdict with her own fantasy), and the pure hyperreal (Bob the Drag Queen as a queen made entirely by the show, BenDeLaCrème's self-elimination as uniqueness with no referent). She then argues RuPaul is a better Warhol because Warhol merely produced superstars like Candy Darling, Holly Woodlawn and Jackie Curtis, profiting while they died unmourned, whereas Ru could compete in her own challenges and returns love to her girls. Realness, she concludes with Ru's Billboard interview and the Season 3 'Pop Art Ball', is always a wink: the facade talking about facade.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 13 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Bean reads both fake-news shows through Baudrillard's account of a media age with 'more and more information and less and less meaning': mainstream news is already simulation, and Colbert is 'a walking talking simulacrum', more O'Reilly than O'Reilly, whose five-deep receding portrait series and 'The Wørd' graphics (the abstinence-education 'Gateway Hug' bit) stage signs that refer only to themselves. Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a simulacrum, a television news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal: translating Obama's 'audacity of hope' convention speech into 'calibration of expectations' and rendering Laura Ingraham's dismissal of the party platform in Valley Girl vocal fry. Adapting Baudrillard's fake-holdup thought experiment into an 'organize a fake news broadcast' test, she argues the shows fall into the real precisely because they report on and stage simulation, anchoring audiences against media's 'communication without a response'.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 39 "Hey Goofy! Somebody Just Slipped My Culture a Mickey…" — Schuchardt argues Disney's real product is 'getting you in there' — colonizing the geography of the imagination: Pirates of the Caribbean is read as an allegory of corporate globalization, White Wilderness fabricated the lemming-suicide myth, and the parks' visual containment keeps visitors inside a world with 'more reality than nature' (Eco's hyperreality, in Baudrillard's territory). He claims Disney built this on Jung's archetypes via Joseph Campbell's Hero's Journey under the mantra 'We Create the Mythology of the Future,' so that media consolidation (the Fox merger shrinking six conglomerates to five) narrows the Overton Window and Disney's manufactured mythology displaces Christianity as the reigning worldview.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 23 "An Old Man, Filled with Regret . ." — Matthew Brophy argues the film's plot makes most sense if it is an addicted gamer's MMORPG session: Cobb is an avatar, his corporate pursuers are named COBOL after the old programming language, dream 'architects' mirror world-designers like Second Life's Furia Freeloader with her Escher Relativity House, and Mal is a 'gamer's widow' whose in-game suicide deleted her character so she could return to the real family Cobb abandoned. Using the 'egocentric predicament' that no one can access another's mind, he suggests shared dreaming can only really happen on servers, and via Borges's map that covered the empire and Baudrillard's claim that the simulacrum outlives the real he reads Second Life replicas (the virtual Texas A&M campus) as the preferred level of reality decaying the actual one. He then deploys Bostrom's simulation argument — we may already be conscious simulations — and casts Yusuf's basement dreamers, Xiao Yi's Warcraft suicide, and WoW-neglect cases as modern Lotus-Eaters, concluding that the ending is a 'long con': the real inception planted in Cobb the belief that his game is real, so he will one day wake 'an old man, filled with regret, waiting to die alone.'
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 24 "Architecture and the Dream Machine" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues that Inception presents dreams neither as divine messages nor as stylized fantasy but as hackable programs, making the film itself a 'thinking machine' in Jean Epstein's sense — a 'robot brain' whose synchronized kicks, Piaf countdown, and phone-number safes 'think' the different layers of time instead of reproducing a reality, with slow motion as cognition rather than dream-sign (against Bazin). He reads inception as Dawkins's meme theory given a psychoanalytic vertical dimension: the idea is implanted deep in the subconscious (Fischer's relation to his father), can grow autonomously 'like a cancer' as Mal's did, and subconscious projections converge 'like white blood cells' as in Solaris. The chapter then traces how the computer era — hypertext, Second Life, media-absorbed realities like Baudrillard's 9/11 — reshaped cinematic dreams and architecture, so that Ariadne's 'pure creation,' Cobb's Limbo dystopia, and Dubai's empty speculative towers all become the 'gilded dreamworlds' of an ephemeralized, hacker-ready built world — the dream machine as allegory of the globalized world, with atomized grains of reality echoing Democritus via Epstein and Benjamin's account of cinema bursting the prison of the everyday.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Lueth maps Baudrillard's four stages of the image from Simulacra and Simulation onto LEGO history. Early basic-brick town sets reflect a profound reality; the late-1980s shift to cops-and-robbers conflict play masks and denatures it — prison-striped convicts presuppose a justice system that never appears in the sets; sky-fi MOCs like the Savoia S.21 from Porco Rosso, which borrows a real WWII-era designation for a fictional plane, mask the absence of reality; and ApocaLEGO — MOCs riffing endlessly on Metro 2033, Fallout, The Walking Dead, and each other — is the pure simulacrum, images referring only to images with no real-world counterpart to check against (via Borges' 'Tlon, Uqbar, Orbis Tertius'). If Baudrillard is right that images now precede reality, ApocaLEGO is, culturally, literally building the apocalypse.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Boardman reads Miniland USA at LEGOLAND California and Florida as the nation itself rendered a 'Fan Developed Theme': an archipelago of tourist destinations — NYC, Washington DC, Las Vegas, New Orleans, 'New England' — connected not by geography but by the visitor's body performing a simulated cross-country tour that skips the flyover states entirely, with Bachelard's Poetics of Space on miniaturization and Debord's spectacle (footnoted) framing the effect. The California Freedom Tower reproduces a rejected architectural design, a literal Baudrillardian simulacrum, a copy for which no original exists, while Florida's version simply deletes Lower Manhattan and swaps Coke for Pepsi per sponsorship deals. Comparing the two parks' itineraries shows that 'America' here is constructed from circulating tourist imagery and corporate logistics — Carlsbad itself erased from its own park's map.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 23 "The Office and Philosophy" — Uses Baudrillard's three orders of simulacra to read the UK office: Neil Godwin embodies the first order where the boss's signs reflect real virtue (Aristotle's practical wisdom), Gareth's health-and-safety training of Donna - which degenerates into interrogation about her sex life - is the second order where virtuous signs mask desire, and David Brent is the third-order hyperreal, his management-speak ('team individuality', 'mutual likewise reciprocated', the 'rape' role-play outburst) signs with no referent masking that he is not a boss at all. The chapter's sting is that laughing at Brent we tacitly endorse the 'real' managerial system that produces Neil and redundancies, while Gareth - who models himself on Brent and pushes his codes to suicidal extremes ('will there ever be a boy born who can swim faster than a shark?') - instantiates Baudrillard's fatal strategy, a system carrying the seeds of its own destruction.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 36 "The Office and Philosophy" — Written as a fake email thread among University of Scranton faculty, the appendix has junior professor Joe Kraus propose reading the town through Baudrillard's simulacrum - the 'Scranton Welcomes You' sign from the credits becoming real for him only as a TV image - while senior colleagues tutor him through the history of representation theory. Stephen deploys Plato's Ion (Socrates' magnet-and-iron chain of imitation, with Ion's Brent-like obliviousness) and Aristotle on mimesis, pity, fear, and catharsis to explain the show's tragicomic discomfort, while Maria adds the Antiochene, Alexandrian, and Augustinian fourfold senses of scripture applied to Scranton; Michael Friedman contributes a Chekhovian reading of Pam's bird eulogy as subtext about Michael's fear of dying alone. The thread itself mirrors an Office plotline as the senior faculty quietly decide to cut the untenured Joe out of the project.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 31 "Live From New York" — Perez sorts SNL's realities using Plato's cave and Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation: Kate McKinnon's Bieber Calvin Klein ad is a first-phase reflection, Natalie Portman's raps a masking second phase, Ferrell's commodified Bush a second-order copy, and Maya Rudolph's Donatella Versace a third-phase simulacrum with no reality behind it that Versace herself protested. The Church Lady's 2016 Update appearance and the Palin-meets-Palin and Hillary-at-the-bar sketches show characters substituting for the real, while the May 2018 cold open where the real Stormy Daniels tells Baldwin's Trump 'a storm's a-comin',' live-tweeted by @nbcsnl, achieves Baudrillard's hyperreality where fiction and reality are abolished as distinct. Studio 8H becomes a Plato's cave viewers willingly re-enter each Saturday to glimpse the real through simulation.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Culver explains Sarah Connor's harshness through Girard's Violence and the Sacred: like any warrior she is 'stained' by contact with violence and needs purification rites before reentering society, but her society refuses to recognize her as a warrior, so her cleansing becomes psychiatric wards, nine aliases, and fugitive life - measured against the true machine Cameron, whose 'inefficient' coldness throws Sarah's residual humanity into relief. She then applies Baudrillard's hyperreal: the Connors must prove a future nobody else sees while destroying every trace of the Terminators (lowering the T-101 into the steel), a simulation where a T-1000 wears a 'To Protect and Serve' uniform and law and order themselves may be simulated. The upshot is that Sarah's failures at conventional motherhood are those of a warrior-mother raising John inside a war only she experiences, staining him too (he kills Sarkasian) to give him a future.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 20 "Living a Part Synecdoche, New York, Metaphor, and the Problem of Skepticism" — Deming argues that Caden Cotard's attempt to build a full-scale replica of New York inside a warehouse enacts a skepticism toward the givenness of life—the belief that reality can be denied and remade as art. Drawing on Cavell's claim that film is 'a moving image of skepticism' and Heidegger on world, earth, and dwelling, he shows the play traps Caden rather than freeing him: to represent the world is to be flung outside it. He invokes Wittgenstein's image of language as an ancient city one can never step outside of, and Baudrillard's simulacra (Caden even considers titling the play 'Simulacrum'), to explain why the literal doubling fails to yield the 'true self' Caden seeks.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 12 "Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple" — Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 33 "19. A Pataphysical Cherry Pie" — Pagnoni Berns, Aguilar, and Veteri argue Twin Peaks stages metaphysics—a dual reality of a physical world and an unknowable superimposed one—drawing on Descartes' dualism and Gustav Fechner's animistic day/night double aspect (souls of plants, the Log Lady's log). They then claim its real philosophy is Alfred Jarry's pataphysics, the science of imaginary solutions to real problems: Cooper solves crimes not by deduction but by absurd means—smelling trees, throwing rocks at a bottle while naming suspects, reading dreams—superimposing another plane on ours (echoing Baudrillard), so Twin Peaks is 'metaphysics with humor.'
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 23 "The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer" — Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Paulus and Adriaensens argue that Mann's 'stylized realism' is best understood not as neobaroque spectacle but as mannerism: a self-conscious, image-conscious cinema in tension between classicism and anti-classicism. Reading Mann's green-screen shooting on Heat, the hyperreal night look of Collateral and the ultra-sharp digital of Public Enemies through Deleuze's letter to Daney on cinematic mannerism, they cast Mann as a Coppola-like 'bridge-builder' who offers a pedagogy of the image and gains Nietzsche's 'powers of the false.' Baudrillard's account of Apocalypse Now as excess of means and simulation frames the immersive spectacle Mann resists in favor of realism.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Wildermuth argues that Mann dramatizes a postmodern critique of law in which justice itself becomes a commodity, drawing on Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulation, Marxist legal theory (Pashukanis's 'organized class terror'), and critical legal studies. In The Last of the Mohicans the British social contract with the colonial militia is exposed as a cover for imperial hierarchy; in Crime Story's 'Abrams for the Defense' and Miami Vice's Lao Li, and in Collateral's hit man Vincent, contracts and legalism deconstruct into simulated justice that serves the top of the economic order, so resistance is possible only locally and temporarily.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Corne unpacks Vincent Hanna's tirade in Heat against his wife's ex-husband's 'dead-tech, postmodernistic, bullshit house.' He reads the smashing of the television and the headless sculpture through Bataille's Against Architecture (buildings as latent prisons of authority) and Jameson's diagnosis of postmodern depthlessness and the silence of affect. Using Hegel, Hugo and Ruskin on architecture's obligation to tell the truth, and especially Frankfurt's On Bullshit, Corne argues the house is 'bullshit' because it is indifferent to truth; Vincent's workaholism becomes a Frankfurtian discipline, and the film reflexively treats truth, authenticity and space as a problem.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 21 "Disenchantment and Rebellion in Alphaville" — Woolfolk reads Godard's Alphaville as an imagination of spiritual disaster: the Alpha 60 computer's reduction of time to divisible units suppresses the Bergsonian durée and fundamental self, and the city's architecture of 'nonplaces' embodies Weber's disenchantment and the Frankfurt School's culture-industry critique. Following Charles Taylor, he argues disenchantment opens a new heroic framework of facing an indifferent universe with lucidity, in which Lemmy Caution—a postmodern pastiche of noir dandies—rebels through an aestheticized eroticism and Éluard's surrealist poetry, achieving a Weberian 'this-worldly salvation' of art and love that succeeds where Orwell's Julia and Huxley's Savage fail.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — The editors' introduction surveys the volume and frames Soderbergh as a maker of 'philosophical cinema' whose films engage epistemology, metaphysics, and ethics. It previews the essays' claims: that sex, lies, and videotape and Schizopolis stage epistemological questions of truth, evidence, and skepticism; that The Underneath and The Limey use Bergson's durée to explore time and self-understanding; that Traffic tests Kant's ethics against Sartrean individual decision; and that Solaris recasts memory and authenticity via Augustine and Baudrillard's simulacra. It positions Soderbergh within Indiewood filmmaking after Welles as a self-reflexive artist.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 29 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — LaRocca argues Burton's 'Ed Wood' (1994) is a metafilm that, via Baudrillard's simulacra and Plato's cave/dialectic, transforms how we watch Wood's 'bad' films. He casts Wood as a cave-dweller and naive literalist who conflates representation with reality ('film equals life,' 'that was perfect'), while Burton is the Platonic dialectician who posits two worlds and provokes thought. He distinguishes two interacting metafilm types—biographical simulacrum (a hyperreal Ed Wood with no original, per Baudrillard's 'artificial resurrection') and mimetic reenactment (loyal remakes of Wood's films)—so that Martin Landau's Lugosi and Parker-as-Fuller's non-acting reveal the emotional 'affect without illusion' latent in Wood's work.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 6 "Introduction War Films and the Ineffability of War" — LaRocca argues that a war film can never be war itself but only a mediated, post-facto fabrication, and reads the camera and the gun as twinned instruments ('point and shoot' becoming digital 'point and click' in Skyfall). He mobilizes Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' to describe war video games and CGI spectacle (Avatar, Call of Duty) as hyperreal simulacra, and Freud's 'Why War?' letter and death instinct to explain the compulsive proliferation of war representation. Foucault ('peace is a coded war'), Heraclitus ('war is father of all'), and Isaiah Berlin's plurality of incompatible values frame war's ineffability and perpetuity, while Cavell's ontology of film grounds the viewer's 'mechanically assured' helplessness before on-screen dying bodies.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 10 "Lenses into War Digital Vérité in Iraq War Films" — Peebles defends the 'digital vérité' of Iraq War films (Stop-Loss, In the Valley of Elah, The Battle for Haditha, Redacted, Standard Operating Procedure) against Garrett Stewart's charge that grainy embedded footage elides critique, arguing instead that the multiplying lenses close the distance between soldier and viewer to build empathy. She invokes Baudrillard's 'the Gulf War did not take place' to show how CNN's video-game-like distance erased the common soldier, which the up-close soldier-shot cell-phone image corrects. Reading Hank Deerfield's reconstruction of his son's fatal Humvee incident in Elah and Errol Morris's reframing of the Abu Ghraib photos in Standard Operating Procedure, she argues each frame is 'both an aperture and a restriction,' and that these tragedies are inherently antiwar.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 15 "The Violated Body Affective Experience and Somatic Intensity in Zero Dark Thirty" — Burgoyne argues that Kathryn Bigelow's Zero Dark Thirty places the violated body at the center of its rendering of the War on Terror, using somatic intensity and affective experience against Steven Shaviro's reading of the film as pure, affect-draining proceduralism. He traces Maya's arc from witness to coercive agent through the torture of Ammar, the Goya-like montage of interrogation videos, and the suicide-bomb killing of her friend Jessica, mapping the film onto Sarah Cole's poles of disenchanted violence (the raw, exposed flesh of the interrogations) and enchanted violence (the technologically choreographed, almost magical SEAL raid on Abbottabad, likened to Baudrillardian simulated combat). The closing unzipping of bin Laden's body bag deflates any triumph into embodied ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Werner Herzog**, ch. 13 "Fake News and Ecstatic Truths" — Kyle Novak uses Herzog's fabricated Pascal epigraph in Lessons of Darkness to distinguish 'ecstatic truth' from Trump-era 'alternative facts,' arguing that unlike Kellyanne Conway's deception, Herzog openly reveals his inventions to deepen an artistic experience. Rejecting Russell's correspondence theory of truth, Novak turns to Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation and The Gulf War Did Not Take Place to show how media create norms and a hyperreality independent of facts, then to Nietzsche's 'On Truth and Lies' (truth as agreed-upon metaphor) and Deleuze's affirmation of life as a non-relativist standard, concluding that Lessons of Darkness is 'sparse on facts but full of truths' that penetrate deeper than CNN footage.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 3 "01_LaRocca_Chapter_000.html" — LaRocca's introduction frames the whole volume through Plato's ancient 'quarrel between philosophy and poetry' and his critique of mimesis (Republic Book X), arguing that documentary film is just another kind of poetic imitation whose truth-claims deserve philosophical scrutiny. Drawing on Cavell's 'film was as if made for philosophy,' Kiarostami's 'cinema is nothing but fakery,' Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' and Flaherty's 'sometimes you have to lie to tell the truth,' he shows how documentary blurs fiction/nonfiction and courts fabrication. He reads the digital turn (Manovich, Rodowick) as pushing cinema toward Baudrillard's hyperreal simulacra, images that no longer index reality but simulate it.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 13 "11_LaRocca_Chapter_010.html" — Pederson and Zimmermann analyze Vincent Grenier's 'avant-doc' videos (Color Study: Slaterville New York, Watercolor: Fall Creek, Les Chaises, Armoire) as interventions in the philosophy of documentary landscape. They read his flattened tableau shots and digitally manipulated color fields against the Hudson River School and Ansel Adams's transcendentalist (Emersonian/Thoreauvian) American sublime, invoking Timothy Murray's Heideggerian poiesis of habitats and Baudrillard's simulation/simulacra to argue Grenier replaces representation of nature with simulation—e.g., the pigeon reacting to its mirror image in Armoire—dissolving the divide between the natural and the technological.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 34 "32_LaRocca_Chapter_031.html" — LaRocca argues that Casey Affleck's I'm Still Here, in which Joaquin Phoenix faked a drug-addled retirement and hip-hop career, is best understood as a 'hoax-verite' whose collapse of the boundary between real and represented turns it into a Baudrillardian simulacrum and hyperreal artifact, a documentary of images 'without an original referent.' Against Noel Carroll's account of documentary as a film of presumptive assertion and Plantinga's assertive stance, LaRocca shows how Affleck exploited audience faith (staged home movies, the David Letterman 'beat down') so that the film's metaphysical, epistemic and ethical status transformed once the fraud was confirmed. He invokes Hegel's remarks on abstract individuality and compares the case to Herzog's 'ecstatic truth,' Roth's and Kaufman's metafiction, to argue the deception paradoxically discloses deeper truths about what documentary is.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 15 "6. How the Hell Are We Supposed to Kill an Idea" — Simsek reads the 'Hell House' tulpa—a monster made real by mass belief on the HellHoundsLair website—as a philosophical challenge about the power of ideas and how one 'kills' an idea, which the brothers can only attempt by seeding a counter-belief. She invokes Socrates' call in the Republic to censor the arts that shape moral character, and the Streisand Effect, to argue that internet-amplified ideas (memes, conspiracy theories, gender and racial norms) take on autonomous, hard-to-kill life much as fandom overrides creators' intent.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 7 "Screaming for Change" — A literature review that critiques three prior scholarly frames for punk. It rejects Hebdige and the Birmingham CCCS reading of punk as mere subcultural 'resistance through style' (bricolage that only rearranges commodities and so is easily co-opted by the hegemony), then critiques postmodern 'authenticity' accounts drawing on Baudrillard and Lyotard, where the collapse of grand narratives leaves punks policing who is a 'real' punk versus a 'poseur.' Kristiansen argues all these approaches rob punk of complexity and proposes instead that punk is a philosophical/ideological system that produces the style, not the reverse.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 24 "13. Anthony Bourdain’s Antisocial Ethics" — Kitchen and Scalambrino build Bourdain's 'ethics for travelers' around his tagline 'Be a traveler, not a tourist,' arguing he preferred authentic community over abstract, Capitalist-conditioned society. Using Guy Debord's Society of the Spectacle to characterize the tourist's 'corporate commodified darkness' and Kierkegaard's dictum about contemplating death daily, they show through the Bhutan and Lebanon episodes how Bourdain's food-based humanism values lived communal reality over consuming others' experiences as banal spectacle.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate.
