Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 13 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Kellie Bean reads Colbert and Stewart through Jean Baudrillard's simulacra and the hyperreal, arguing that mainstream news has become an image unmoored from reality. Colbert is a 'walking talking simulacrum' who out-O'Reillys O'Reilly (the portrait-within-a-portrait, 'The Word' segments like 'Gateway Hug'), enacting news as pure sign; Stewart, broadcasting from a simulacrum of a news studio, instead punctures the hyperreal to expose the real, parsing Obama's convention rhetoric and Laura Ingraham's platform dodge. The 'Best F#@king News Team Ever' slogan lays bare the empty hyperbole of 'Fair and Balanced,' re-anchoring the audience to meaning.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 31 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Koppedrayer analyzes the modern North American 'traditional' and 'primitive' bowhunting movement—the Traditional Bowyer's Bible, magazines like Primitive Archer, and gatherings like ETAR—where crafting a selfbow from a single wood stave and hunting under a 'fair chase' ethic promise an authentic, unencumbered, 'really real' experience against high-tech compound bows. Drawing on Arjun Appadurai's 'synchronic warehouse of cultural scenarios,' she argues the past functions as a reproducible resource yielding a hyperreal authenticity, and that bowmakers describe the self-made bow as an embodiment of the maker's own substance and a spiritual link to earlier hunters.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 32 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy warns of a coming 'pornographic singularity' when veridical, immersive, interactive, unbounded virtual reality (extrapolated from Second Life, Rapelay, and Sony's brain-stimulation patent) makes hypersex and hyper-romance supplant real intimacy. He uses Baudrillard's hyperreal/simulacra to explain how airbrushed models and 'pornbots' render real women 'just bad porn', invokes Nozick's experience machine as literally realized, and argues that utilitarianism and Kant's humanity formula fail to condemn using pornbots, so only Aristotelian virtue theory locates the wrong—the user malfunctions and cannot flourish as escalating deviance (furries, age-play, rape games) conditions vice. His bleak prophecy is that unbounded virtual desire will corrode families and community.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Thorsten Botz-Bornstein argues contemporary female tattoos have lost their one-dimensional identifying function and instead create a new 'tattoo space.' He dismantles the paradoxical 'savage/civilized' and 'nature/purity' schemes (drawing on Baudrillard on the smooth, made-up female body-screen that reflects male desire) and Loos' 'ornament and crime' verdict on women's tattoos. He proposes that female tattoos have 'become graffiti' – a Bergsonian spatial 'center of action' and 'skinscape' that disperses meaning horizontally rather than branding an identity, recuperating the female body as a political body against commercialized post-political bodies.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 27 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Lee argues that tattooing is a performative 'practice of writing' whose meaning always exceeds its origin, comparing Holocaust survivor Tova Friedman's Auschwitz number 'A27633' with the Suicide Girl Jaylin's chosen feminist ink. Drawing on Judith Butler's account of the body as a site of inscription and counter-inscription, and Walter Benjamin's 'Critique of Violence' distinguishing law-making from law-preserving force, she claims Friedman's tattoo resists the Nazi law itself while Jaylin's only satirizes heteropatriarchy. She then invokes Baudrillard's 'ecstasy of communication' and the obscene to show tattooing can desubjectify by dissolving the embodied self into pornographic information.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 88 "83. Disco Elysium as Philosophy Solipsism, Existentialism, and Simulacra" — Khamis reads Disco Elysium's 'Pale'—a property-less substance said to be decaying human thought that consumes reality—through three idealisms. The phasmid's warning that the world might vanish if humans stop thinking it evokes Berkeley's subjective idealism (esse est percipi) but without God as guarantor, leaving Harry in existential dread. The Pale as human-produced 'second nature' laid over 'first nature' evokes Kant's and Schelling's transcendental idealism, while the Pale as decaying signs without signification—like the vacuous dockworker 'sheriffs'—matches Baudrillard's hyperreality and simulacra, where information proliferates as meaning collapses, paralleling the amnesiac Harry's own loss and remaking of self.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 90 "85. Persona 5 Royal as Philosophy Unmasking (Persona)l Identity and Reality" — Lopez and Marquez use Persona 5 Royal's Phantom Thieves to explore Schechtman's 'characterization' question of personal identity ('Who am I?') via three bases: qualia (the privately felt sense of self expressed when Ryuji names himself a 'troublemaker' and Morgana insists he is 'NOT a cat'), Wittgensteinian hinge propositions, and language-games in which identity and 'justice' get their meaning through use. Ryle and Wittgenstein's behaviorist worries about private language are set against Nagel's bat and Chalmers's qualia. The Maruki arc—offering a pain-free false utopia and Sumire living as her dead twin Kasumi—poses whether Bentham's utilitarianism, James's pragmatism, or Baudrillard's hyperreality could justify a blissful simulacrum, which the game's 'true ending' rejects for painful reality.

### The End of Grand Narratives

Jean-François Lyotard defined the postmodern condition as "incredulity toward metanarratives"—a loss of faith in the sweeping stories that once claimed to give history a single direction and legitimate knowledge. Grand narratives are overarching accounts such as the inevitable progress of reason, the emancipation of humanity through science, or the march toward a classless society, which promise to unify all lesser knowledge under one purpose. Lyotard held that these narratives had lost their credibility, leaving instead a plurality of smaller, local stories and language games with no master framework above them. The claim reframed both the status of knowledge and the character of modern culture.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 18 "Possibilities of Postmodern Education Beyond Control" — Toby Daspit reads Season Four as a drama of postmodern education: the Initiative's will to master and dissect — Walsh's Frankenstein-project Adam, who murders a boy to see how he works, fulfilling Wordsworth's 'we murder to dissect' — embodies the Cartesian split and the Hegelian drive to negate the other, while Buffy's world deconstructs fixed identity (Darla reversing the horror-movie opening, the Faith/Buffy body swap in 'Who Are You?', Jonathan's 'Superstar') and thwarts prophecy's metanarrative in 'Prophecy Girl.' Against modernist schooling's 'controlled circumstances' and Freire's banking model (Professor Riegert ejecting Buffy from class, Walsh's transmission lectures), the show models knowledge as collective work — the Scoobies' research sessions in Giles's library, Giles's fluid mentorship versus Kendra's by-the-book training, and the relational magic of 'Primeval' — offering education beyond control in an emergent, postmodern world.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 15 "Both Sides of Dylan and Politics" — Jordy Rocheleau reads Dylan's protest era ("The Lonesome Death of Hattie Carroll," "Hurricane," "Chimes of Freedom") as Enlightenment social criticism in Kant's and Mill's sense: reason can expose injustice and secure autonomy against majority tyranny. The post-protest Dylan ("My Back Pages," "Desolation Row," "It's Alright, Ma") turns postmodern - Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives, Derrida's ever-deferred meanings, and Foucault's power/knowledge, where ideals of freedom become instruments of domination. Yet Dylan keeps crying for justice ("Political World," "Dignity"), so the chapter concludes postmodern skepticism can only serve as a cautionary check within, not a replacement of, Enlightenment politics - the thief's line in "All Along the Watchtower" as commitment amid confusion.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 15 "U2 and Philosophy" — Thomson uses U2's self-declared postmodern phase to define postmodernity itself: a sensitivity to poetic polysemy against modernity's fantasies of total control (Heidegger's reduction of everything to optimizable resource), Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives - defended against the self-refutation charge and narrowed to the dying metanarratives of unity and emancipation - and the Marx-Nietzsche-Freud hermeneutics of suspicion that fragmented the subject, with Kierkegaard and early Heidegger as the resisters. Derrida's 9/11 analysis of autoimmunity and hauntology is read into 'Peace on Earth' and the sorrows that 'learned to swim' in 'Until the End of the World'. The payoff is a polysemic reading of 'Even Better than the Real Thing': risky as a seeming hymn to Baudrillard's simulacra, addressed to a live audience it celebrates a communal love 'even better' than personal love - Diotima's ladder generalized - making the postmodern U2 continuous with the 'Christ-ian' U2 of universal love, sealed by 'One'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Jeremy Wisnewski's mock-manifesto uses Family Guy's cutaway gags and taboo jokes (Hitler sausage vendors, Petoria at the UN, Saddam and Khadafi bonding over Seinfeld) to stage postmodernism: Lyotard's "incredulity toward meta-narratives" and Baudrillard's claim that the real is no longer real, since our families are as televisual as the Griffins, who at least know they are cartoons. The danger is that joking about everything breeds cynical passivity, "liberating us from our causes." But Foucault, the 1968 activist and prison reformer, shows through power/knowledge that one can be postmodern and still fight locally, so the Griffins, and the show's satire of religion and politics, get to live.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 31 "Today I Woke Up Sucking a Grammy" — Bradley Kaye reads Kid A as an album made under Lyotard's postmodern condition: "Everything in Its Right Place" ("what was that you tried to say?") and the murmured title track bear witness to the differend, something that must be put into phrases but cannot yet be; "The National Anthem" dramatizes incredulity toward the grand narrative of nationalism in favor of little narratives and local justice; "Treefingers" is the painful silence of the inexpressible, and "Optimistic" an ironic micro-political hope. The epigone problem (Yorke to Coldplay, Travis, and Muse: "Good luck with Kid A") and the closing Baudrillard turn — "In Limbo"'s "you're living in a fantasy world," the Marcus Welby and Perry Mason hyperreal, "it's not like the movies" — explain why even labeling the album "Best Alternative Album" Grammy presumes exactly the stable categories Kid A dissolves.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 36 "History and Philosophy" — Imre reads Hungary's Aranycsapat as a political-philosophical event: Sebes's socialist 4–2–4 football was meant to prove that cooperative civil society could flourish under Stalinism, and the 6–3 demolition of England at Wembley, with its self-organizing positional play, became the sporting antithesis to Rákosi's regime — culminating in the 1956 Revolution that Arendt cited as a 'true' revolution of spontaneous councils. The 1954 final loss to West Germany (contrasted with Germany's own rebirth at Berne) entrenched a fatalism that history's organic 'grand narrative' and 'final synthesis' were against Hungary, helping destroy the civil-society possibility the team embodied and pushing Hungarians into anti-politics. His lesson: talent and beauty can be quashed by the contingency of history — igazság, truth-justice, never manifested, and soccer could not overcome history.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 29 "Progress" — Gregory Gilson argues that although The Onion deliberately reports falsehoods, it embodies postmodern theories of truth better than the newspapers it parodies. Lyotard's mercantilization of knowledge and the fragmentation of dominant narratives into separate language games explain headlines like 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity' and 'Astronomer Discovers The Center Of The Universe Is His Beautiful 9-Year Old Son,' which smash incompatible discourses together, while Baudrillard's simulacrum and hyper-reality explain how The Onion — like Disneyworld — is branded fake precisely so mainstream media can seem real. Yet the chapter closes honestly: its own criticism of 'Bush Says He Still Believes Iraq War Was the Fun Thing To Do' assumed some targets were wrong, which assumes a Truth out there — the paradox of a satire whose truthfulness exceeds its own theory of truth.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 19 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Wade Newhouse reads The Graveyard Book as a fusion of the coming-of-age tale and the Gothic ghost story, from The Turn of the Screw to Stephen King's haunted narcissists, and uses Lyotard's postmodern condition to explain the hybrid: Bod's self forms not by accepting one governing metanarrative but at Lyotardian 'nodal points' among many ghosts, each a fragment of history with its own partial morality, from the Roman Caius Pompeius to the witch Liza Hempstock. The Danse Macabre, where living and dead mix under rules neither remembers choosing, dramatizes borders that feel absolute, yet Bod's development consists in violating boundaries, befriending the outcast witch and hunting the Jacks on his own terms. The ending, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' offers a postmodern self most itself by being no one, with the acceptance of death as the one metanarrative even postmoderns keep, for Bod it is the first lesson rather than the last.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 10 "1. More Golems around Than You Might Think" — Using Feet of Clay and Witches Abroad, Froehlich argues we are all like golems: our behavior is driven by the 'words in our heads,' the texts that society and the powerful put there. Lyotard's metanarratives explain how Lily Weatherwax forces Genua to live out fairy-tale plots and how Dragon King of Arms rewrites Nobby's family tree to manufacture a king, while dwarfish gender norms keep Cheery Littlebottom trapped in a culturally imposed text. Freedom comes only when, like Dorfl after Carrot buys him his own receipt, a person rejects the imposed words and chooses words of the heart - 'words in the heart cannot be taken.'
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 10 "1. Free Falling into Postmodernism" — Sewell reads Petty's 1976 debut through Jameson's postmodernism: Petty's music is a cut-and-paste amalgam of 1960s jangle, 1970s heartland rock and punk attitude whose pastiche dissolves the high/low art distinction as aesthetic production merges with commodity production, which is exactly why it feels timeless. He then applies Butler's performativity to Petty's "cool," arguing the persona was learned and performed so incessantly that Petty and his audience came to experience it as innate. Finally Baudrillard's hyperreal and simulacra frame the conclusion that there never was a "real" Petty, only copies of copies, yet if the perceived sincerity feels real and empowering, it is real enough.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 22 "11 Indiana Jones and the Quest for Agnosticism What if All Stories Are True" — Robert Grant Price observes that in Indy's world every myth — the Ark, the Sankara Stones, the Grail, and in the comics and novels Atlantis, Merlin, Noah's Ark, and the Philosopher's Stone — turns out factually true, producing a surplus of evidence for mutually exclusive religions (the personal Christian Trinity versus non-personal Brahman). Against Derrida's deconstruction and the postmodern claim that no grand narrative captures truth, in Indy's world 'the squash ball always comes back' — yet he stays agnostic, telling Spalko 'There is always another explanation.' The chapter weighs his three exits: remain agnostic, take a leap of faith as he does stepping onto the invisible bridge, or read Percival and Galahad as symbolically rather than historically true.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Milan Hosta traces a dialectical line from the individual athlete through nationalism and internationalism to the transnational Olympic movement, arguing individualism 'turns into itself again' since the whole order is reproduced by individuals like Paavo Nurmi ('I run for myself, not for Finland'). He reads Coubertin's 'sincere internationalism' as a moral epistemology of knowing others (glossed via Morgan and a Hegelian account of tolerance as recognizing but not truly accepting difference) against the hollow cosmopolitanism of tourism and 'popular ethnography.' Drawing on postmodern pluralism and the end of grand narratives, plus Hardt and Negri's Empire, he frames the IOC as a peace-preaching yet blood-bathed transnational power sustained by record-seeking individuals.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 12 "Deceit, Desire, and Dark Comedy Postmodern Dead Ends in Blood Simple" — Woolfolk argues that Blood Simple is 'resolutely postmodern': it recycles noir motifs as Jamesonian pastiche but, unlike classic noir (Double Indemnity, Detour), offers no modernist critique of capitalist civilization and no saving metanarrative, leaving only a profane comic present. He reads the three men who go 'simple'—Ray, Marty, Visser—through Girard's triangular desire, driven by unchecked, mutually imitated passions with no external mediating authority, while Visser's sidewalk individualism supplies a minimal social philosophy. Crucially the film's world is ruled by chance, not fate (the pistol's three bullets, Abby's lucky single shot), so Abby's clueless 'health' and survival affirm postmodern contingency rather than any critique of late modernity.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 21 "The Past Is Now History and The Hudsucker Proxy" — Coughlin argues The Hudsucker Proxy, far from being empty pastiche, is a postmodern meditation on history as a constructed text. Drawing on Linda Hutcheon he treats the film's parody of screwball comedy and Frank Capra as a 'value-problematizing' tool: Norville is a hollowed-out anti-Capra hero, and Moses stopping the clock and addressing the audience foregrounds the artificiality and 'telling' of all narratives. Foucault's claim that resistance uses power's own tools underwrites the reading that recycling dead styles and cultural memory (the J. Edgar Hoover quip, the array of intertexts) challenges the authority and singularity of historical representation.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 23 "The Shining and Anti-Nostalgia Postmodern Notions of History R. Barton Palmer" — Palmer reads The Shining as a postmodern anti-nostalgia film using Fredric Jameson's account of late-capitalist culture as a depthless perpetual present that can only cannibalize the past as pastiche. He argues Kubrick invokes the ghost-story and nostalgia-film conventions of 1970s Hollywood only to reject them: Jack Torrance's endlessly retyped 'All work and no play' and his entrapment between the empty present and the 1921 ballroom photo dramatize the failing artist 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness,' echoing Baudrillard's post-deconstruction art that can only play with the pieces. The Citizen Kane homage that closes the film deliberately refuses the explanation its model provided.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Conard argues that Tarantino's postmodernism makes redemption impossible in Reservoir Dogs (and Pulp Fiction, Kill Bill). Using Danto on the 'end of art', Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives', and Rorty's contingent 'vocabularies', he shows the films embrace relativism about knowledge (rearranged chronology, unreliable perspectives) and about values. Mr. Orange plays Judas and Christ; the opening tipping argument exposes moral conventions as arbitrary, so becoming a 'real person' rather than a gangster is merely being a dork rather than cool. With no metanarrative to ground it, one way of life cannot be morally superior, so redemption fails.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 20 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Palmer situates The Man Who Wasn't There within New Hollywood's self-conscious 'metagenericism', distinguishing Collins's 'eclectic irony' from the 'new sincerity' that seeks a genre's 'missing harmony'. The Coens revive James M. Cain's noir (Double Indemnity, Postman) but historicize it in 1949, layering the Heisenberg uncertainty principle voiced by the lawyer Riedenschneider ('there is no what happened', 'the more you look, the less you know') onto the plot. Ed Crane, the barber who kills Big Dave, is an absurd Camusian figure who finds preexecution peace in 'seeing it whole', making the film an existentialized meditation on unknowability and meaninglessness.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 20 "Imagining the Future, Contemplating the Past The Screen Versions of 1984" — Palmer compares the two film versions of Orwell's 1984 to argue that dystopian fiction projects present fears and desires onto an imagined future, engaging critically with the Enlightenment idea of progress (via Burnham's managerial thesis). Anderson's 1956 film 'talks to the future,' fusing science fiction and film noir to voice Cold War dread of a possible historical trajectory, while Radford's 1984 version, in the postmodern 'heritage film' mode Jameson and Higson describe, museumizes the novel: with history seemingly ended it becomes an honored, reverentially displayed relic that talks only to a dead past rather than warning of a coming one.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Tzioumakis reads sex, lies, and videotape through Lyotard's The Postmodern Condition, arguing the film is contradictory as a 'postmodern' text. Its four characters (Graham, Ann, Cynthia, John) acquire self-knowledge not from the celebrated video camera but through what Lyotard calls the flexible networks of language games: Graham's 'unexpected moves' displace Ann and Cynthia, who then master his interrogative game, while John's reactive lying dooms him. Tzioumakis contends the film's neat character transformations are legitimated by this agonistic network yet remain wedded to a strong emancipation 'master narrative' plus heterosexuality and patriarchy, undercutting its reputation as exemplary postmodern cinema and linking it back to modernity.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 16 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — de Waard argues that The Good German embodies Soderbergh's 'neo-meta' philosophy of history as polyphonic mediation, staged by Levi's line about a camera that turns the image upside-down to set it right. Shooting with 1940s-era equipment and pastiching Casablanca, The Third Man, Chinatown, and Schindler's List, the film presents not history's progression but 'history as time,' a simultaneity of broken mirrors. Reworking Benjamin's angel-of-history thesis, de Waard claims images of the present threaten to reappear ad infinitum, and contrasts Soderbergh's cold, morally relativist tale of American war-criminal whitewashing (Lena's confession that she betrayed twelve Jews) with Spielberg's emotionally manipulative Holocaust spectacle, invoking Eco on Casablanca as 'movies' itself.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Ritzer reads Kafka through Deleuze (and Guattari), Jameson, Barthes, and Lacan as a self-reflexive, schizophrenic pastiche. The film's shift from black-and-white to color as Kafka enters the castle is analyzed via Deleuze's 'colour-image' and Barthes on color as artifice, using color's sensual materiality rather than realism. Its dense allusions to Wiene, Murnau, Lang, Welles's The Trial, and German expressionism make it, in Jameson's terms, a postmodern pastiche marking the waning of historicity, while Lacanian schizophrenia (the breakdown of the signifying chain) models Kafka's paranoia about power structures controlling the individual. Ritzer finally argues the film approaches Deleuze and Guattari's 'minor cinema,' deterritorializing classical Hollywood's realism through intensity and the supremacy of sign over referent.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 29 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Moses reads Solaris through Baudrillard's Simulacra and Simulation, arguing the sentient planet is a 'dream factory' that reproduces Kelvin's dreamed Rheya as facsimiles with no original, literalizing hyperreality and the precession of simulacra. He treats Soderbergh's remake-of-a-remake status and the final scene, where Kelvin and Rheya speak directly into the camera as Solaris implodes, as pure cinema collapsing reality and representation, life and death, in Baudrillard's 'end of history' implosion. Moses extends the reading to unnatural reproduction (Baudrillard's clone/matrix, the aborted child), pervasive surveillance and monitors, and post-9/11 affects of terror, nostalgia, and melancholia, concluding the film offers no escape from postmodernity, only a way deeper in.
- **Punk Rock and Philosophy - Research and Destroy**, ch. 7 "Screaming for Change" — A literature review that critiques three prior scholarly frames for punk. It rejects Hebdige and the Birmingham CCCS reading of punk as mere subcultural 'resistance through style' (bricolage that only rearranges commodities and so is easily co-opted by the hegemony), then critiques postmodern 'authenticity' accounts drawing on Baudrillard and Lyotard, where the collapse of grand narratives leaves punks policing who is a 'real' punk versus a 'poseur.' Kristiansen argues all these approaches rob punk of complexity and proposes instead that punk is a philosophical/ideological system that produces the style, not the reverse.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — J. Jeremy Wisnewski stages a mock threat to 'kill' the Griffins to expose Family Guy as postmodernism incarnate. Its blizzard of equal-footing references (Hitler beside Scooby-Doo) illustrates Baudrillard's hyperreal where 'the real is no longer real,' and its relentless mockery of religion, war, and politics enacts Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worrying this breeds cynical conservatism, he rescues the show via Foucault's power/knowledge: like Foucault's activism, one can be incredulous toward grand stories yet still fight local battles - a little incredulity is exactly what we need.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 16 "On Beyond Modernity, or Conrad and a Postmodern Alphabet" — Jacob Held explains postmodernism as Lyotard's 'incredulity toward metanarratives' using On Beyond Zebra! Conrad's twenty-six-letter alphabet is the metanarrative that fixes what can be said and known, while the narrator's invented letters (Yuzz, Snee, Floob) show language expanding to present the unpresentable. Held casts Kant's three Critiques, phenomena/noumena, and his defining of the mind's 'alphabet' as the exemplary modern grand narrative Lyotard rejects, then turns to Foucault's Nietzschean genealogy, using You're Only Old Once! for the medicalization of life and (via a Beauvoir quotation) the claim that gender is a constructed mechanism of control that can be transgressed.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 9 "Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection" — Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 37 "Family Guy Must Die! Long Live Family Guy!" — Wisnewski casts Family Guy as pure postmodernism: its cut-away collage of Hitler, Scooby-Doo, and Tiananmen makes everything equally real, illustrating Baudrillard's hyperreal ("the real is no longer real") and Lyotard's incredulity toward meta-narratives. Worried that such cynicism breeds conservative inaction, he turns to Foucault's power/knowledge to argue that one can be incredulous toward grand narratives yet still fight local battles — so Family Guy's mockery of religion and politics can be genuine critique, and the cartoon need not be killed.

### Bundle Theory of Self

The bundle theory of the self denies that there is any persisting, unified substance underlying our mental life. Examining his own experience, David Hume found only a succession of particular perceptions—sensations, feelings, and thoughts—but no impression of a simple, continuous ego to which they belong. He therefore proposed that the self is nothing more than a bundle or collection of these fleeting perceptions, held together by relations such as resemblance and causation, a conclusion that unsettles ordinary assumptions about a stable inner subject.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 45 "Unknown" — Barwick completes his 'neo-materialism' by killing the subject: after Hume finds no self on introspection - perceptions but no perceiver - and Sartre defines consciousness as pure intentionality, a transparency through which we fall to its object, Wittgenstein's 'no such thing as the subject that thinks' leaves features like the lovable Tasty Wheat and the fearsome Agents on the side of objects. Consciousness emerges as not a thing but the revelation of things - immaterial yet no substance - forcing us to put the mind into the world rather than the world into the mind.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 21 "“Nobody’s Bob Dylan”" — Vernezze and Lulewicz take Dylan's 1964 Halloween quip "I got my Bob Dylan mask on" as an entry into personal identity, testing each theory against his life: the bodily view (Zimmerman to Dylan) survives cell turnover but stumbles on brain-transplant cases; Locke's memory theory handles them but faces Reid's brave-officer regress and Alzheimer's cases, and Dylan's reincarnation lyrics ("Shelter from the Storm," "I and I") ignore memory altogether. The Christian soul view of the gospel albums ("When He Returns," "Gotta Serve Somebody") follows Descartes and Plato but cannot justify the swirl-to-filling inference that souls exist. The chapter ends sympathetic to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist no-self: Dylan's "I is another," his name as fabrication, and the cover album Self Portrait all deny a fixed self-created essence.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks why we kill zombies with so few qualms and whether zombification releases us from obligations to the person who was, testing brain-death criteria, altered-identity and self-defense justifications against Shaun of the Dead (Shaun's mother and Ed), Day of the Dead's Bub, White Zombie, and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He borrows Hume's bundle theory - the self as a fiction, a bundle of perceptions rather than an essence - and Parfit's degrees of psychological continuity to dissolve the sharp alive/dead and same-person/other-person dichotomies that make zombie-killing easy. The payoff is that we are already partly zombie (Shaun's checkout line, Ed on the sofa, the author's all-night gaming), differing only in our capacity for brief autonomous, goal-directed choices like Shaun's three-plan montage.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 16 "I Ain’t Gonna Tell You One Thing that You Really Ought to Know . . . Ooh!" — Scott Calef reads the black 'Object' on the Presence cover—which Storm Thorgerson calls not a presence but a hole—to argue that absence permeates Zep's album art (the cut-out wheel of III, the die-cut windows of Physical Graffiti, the spindle holes of Coda) and that holes are a genuine metaphysical puzzle: immaterial yet extended, seemingly causal, and hard to see on a causal theory of perception. Descartes's immaterial soul is compared to holes (both non-physical, though holes suspiciously have size and location), Plato's Forms explain how the Object and we ourselves partake of both Being and Non-Being, and Hume's failure to find a self in introspection makes the self 'a hole'. Kierkegaard and Heidegger connect nothingness to the anxiety of death—fitting an album made after Plant's near-fatal crash—Socrates's two alternatives about death frame the end, and Wittgenstein's 'not a something but not a nothing either' caps the Object's dual nature.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 16 "Mr. Monk Is Mr. Monk" — Malloy runs the classic theories of personal identity through Monk episodes. Bodily (really brain) identity fails when 'the Monk' — the reckless medicated alter of 'Mr. Monk Takes His Medicine' — shares Monk's body and brain yet is not held responsible, and Stanley Tucci's method actor in 'Mr. Monk and the Actor' shows that copying Monk's looks and behavior does not transfer identity. Locke's memory theory breaks on the amnesia of 'Mr. Monk Bumps His Head' (Monk becomes roofer 'Jerry') and the blackout in 'Mr. Monk and the Rapper,' and Reid's brave-officer paradox yields contradiction once recovered Monk remembers being both Monk and Jerry. Hume's bundle theory — 'I never can catch myself,' the self as theatre of successive perceptions — grounds psychological continuity's graded identity, but then cult-swayed Monk in 'Mr. Monk Joins a Cult' might count as a different person, making his deprogramming a kind of murder; the chapter closes by rejecting Reid and Butler's 'simple and unassayable' escape, insisting a philosopher, like a detective, must keep theorizing how Monk stays Monk.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 9 "Zombies and Us" — Hamish Thompson asks what could justify killing zombies, canvassing self-defense, total-brain-death criteria, and release from obligations to a radically altered person, using Shaun of the Dead's mother-killing, Bub's trained shooting in Day of the Dead, White Zombie's piano-playing heroine, and the pod-people substitutions of Invasion of the Body Snatchers. He deploys Hume's bundle theory of the self as a fiction of succeeding perceptions and Parfit's graded psychological continuity (with Locke's prince/cobbler case) to argue identity comes in degrees, so zombie termination is never as clean as the genre pretends. The chapter ends by turning the lens around: Shaun's checkout-line beepers and Ed's sofa-and-video-game existence suggest ordinary lives differ from zombiehood only by intermittent acts of imaginative self-direction.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 20 "Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy" — Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 39 "You Don’t Always Get Along" — The chapter animates Hume's bundle as a 'little republic' of mental citizens without a universal citizen, staging a dialogue between Person-Hume, who cannot believe there is no self, and Philosopher-Hume, who counsels beer and billiards. It traces the view back to Plato's Republic: the tripartite soul (with Freud's id-ego-superego as a modern rerun), the example of desiring and refusing the same cold beer when you must collect your mother from the airport, and Leontius raging at his own eyes before the corpses, cross-chatter as civil strife among inner citizens, exactly what the doctors diagnose as Fred's symptom.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 51 "How Do You Know You’re Not an Android" — The chapter weaponizes the cogito for Deckard's predicament: the fact that 'the lights are on' for you seems to prove you are human, but Descartes' leap from thinking to an immaterial soul is unjustified, since introspection cannot show whether your thoughts run on a soul, a bundle of neurons, or a silicon chip. Hume's 'I never can catch myself at any time without a perception' supplies the precedent, and the conclusion is that no amount of inner experience rules out being an android, so you will have to go take the V-K test after all.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 32 "Psych and Philosophy" — Dena Hurst reads Shawn as the mythological trickster - the fool who fools fools - who brings disorder to order by overturning hierarchies (Henry's ring-in-the-box lesson in '9 Lives'), taunting Lassiter, and inventing Gus's nicknames, while using his convenient psychic act to surface clues when found and excuse blunders. She argues people buy the act because we crave patterns and motivated narratives (Alfred Mele's work on seeing what we want to see), and closes with Hume's and Dennett's view that the self is a loose narrative we star in: Shawn literally invents himself as psychic detective, an exaggeration of the identities we all construct.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 29 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Frank Scalambrino probes Carrie's 'personality paradox' through the 'You can't change your soul!' / 'Yes you can' exchange. Aristotle's Metaphysics offers one pole: only generation and corruption are substantial change, so Carrie persists essentially as human however her mania, job, and loves shift. Hume's rejoinder - sameness of kind is not given in sense experience but added by interpretation - opens the question of whether Carrie's identity is determined by intrinsic factors (love, soul, truth) or extrinsic ones (the CIA's rules, religious affiliation), with Saul representing extrinsic determination and Carrie privileging the intrinsic, while Brody's conversion shows a soul can change and re-order which factors govern a self.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 24 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Arp uses King Worm's dream-within-dreams to pose the perception-reality problem: distinguishing perceiver, perceptions, and perceived, he maps the triad onto Plato's allegory of the cave, then contrasts epistemological and metaphysical realism (the fallen tree fort still makes sound waves unheard; Pythagoras discovered rather than invented his theorem) with idealism and antirealism, whose dead end is solipsism—Lumpy Space Princess locked in a private movie theater of perceptions. Hume's picture of the mind as a theater of successive perceptions and Berkeley's Hylas-and-Philonous worry that we are trapped inside perceptual reality give the skeptical threat its force. The chapter sides with Jake—'You gotta focus on what's real, man'—while conceding that after 'King Worm' Finn and Jake can never be certain they escaped the hypnotism.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 22 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Klein and Fundora trace Jobs's Buddhism from Reed College meditation and the seven-month India pilgrimage (reading Yogananda's Autobiography of a Yogi yearly) to the Zen minimalism of Apple design, arguing his temper tantrums, harsh speech, and reality distortion field do not disqualify him from being 'on the path' since Buddhism is a practice, not a creed test. They expound the Four Noble Truths (dukkha in its three kinds, via Thich Nhat Hanh), the Eightfold Path's Middle Way, and anatta—the non-self they compare to Hume's bundle theory of the self against Descartes's thinking thing—and read Jobs's strip-away-the-essence aesthetics, the three-click intuitive iPod interface that keeps users in the moment, the non-dualist marriage of art and technology, and his Think Different self-reliance as deeply Buddhist authenticity.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 23 "12. Becoming Vetinari Personal Identity on the Discworld" — Pierce uses Moist von Lipwig's rehabilitation (Albert Spangler becomes Postmaster General), Cosmo Lavish's doomed project of literally becoming Vetinari, the Auditor Myria LeJean, Angua's transformations, the Librarian's orangutan body, Miss Level's two bodies, and duplicated Rincewind teleportation cases to test theories of personal identity. Locke's memory theory, patched by Leibniz into psychological continuity, collapses into circularity under false-memory cases like a wizard implanting Teatime's murders in Rincewind's mind, while bodily and brain-continuity views founder on Igor part-swaps, splitting hemispheres, and identical-twin-style fission. Leibniz's own soul view and Reid's treatment of identity as a primitive, unanalyzable fact get their due, and Hume's skepticism about any continuing self marks the chapter's conclusion that every available view exacts a price.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 36 "23. I’d Rather Stay an Orangutan Because That’s Why Discworld Exists" — In a self-fictionalizing chapter, editor Nicolas Michaud is summoned by Vetinari to prove Discworld is real, and the answer arrives in the Unseen University library: the Librarian stays an orangutan because language distances us from experience—humans never simply experience a banana, only 'holding a banana,' so for us the words create the reality. Along the way the chapter takes issue with Hume's bundle-of-perceptions view of the self, since word-using humans are never just a collection of present perceptions, and contrasts the Librarian's immediate, unmediated experience of each singular thing with our word-reduced world. It concludes that because we always experience the world as stories, narratives, and terms, 'narratives are all we have,' making the Disc no less real than the Roundworld we talk and think about.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 11 "3. The Flux of It All" — Ammon asks whether anything persists beneath Bowie's serial personas, staging Parmenides's denial of change (with Zeno's paradoxes) and Descartes's melting wax against the Heraclitean flux of 'ch-ch-ch-changes.' Rejecting soul-substance views, he takes the empiricist line - Hume's introspection finds only particular perceptions, never a self - warns via the intentional fallacy (Manson's 'Helter Skelter,' Bloom's hawk) against letting Bowie's own pronouncements fix his songs' meanings, and tests 'meaning is use' on Bowie's calling rock stars fascists. Recurring undercurrents (dancing, apocalypse, distrust of authority) survive, but the conclusion is that Bowie's essence just is flux, 'the river we can't step into twice.'
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — Reads the Season Two Black Lodge finale as Cooper's failed journey of self-knowledge, framed by Socrates' Delphic "know thyself" and the unexamined life. Against Hume's bundle theory — when Hume looks inward he only ever finds particular perceptions, never a self — the chapter sets the Vedanta/Tibetan Buddhist ideal of knowing the true Self beyond thought (the ocean versus its waves), with the Black Lodge as the place Hawk calls a passage "every soul must pass on its way to perfection." Cooper's screaming white-eyed Laura, the flickering Caroline/Annie corpse, and his grinning doppelgänger are Jungian shadow-projections paralleled scene-by-scene with the wrathful visions of the Tibetan Book of the Dead; entering with imperfect courage, he flees his fears instead of integrating them, splitting into trapped good Dale and the rampaging Mr. C of The Return.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley applies Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence — built from resemblance, constancy, 'force and vivacity,' and testimony — to 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' where Colonel Harrington, then Clegg Forbes, then Major Gart each cease to exist as memory and corroboration (bartender, girlfriend, general, headlines) collapse layer by layer. 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's speakeasy reunion with his dead wife Laura shows the imagination feigning the uninterrupted existence of a person whose constancy and vivacity no longer match his memories, so the senses and memory are exposed as no foundation for rational belief in continued existence.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Fetterman argues no one can do enough good to earn The Good Place because the real question is who defines good. Moving from Hobbes's state of nature and Rousseau's innate compassion to Hume's bundle theory and the Buddhist doctrine of non-self, he shows the four humans' characters were assembled by their formative communities, which is Michael's whole defense before Judge Gen. But Nietzsche's account of how communities christen their own customs 'good' exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife accountants impose their in-group preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's life of point-maximization fails, and why Michael should be asking the Frozen Yogurt Problem instead of blaming demon tampering.
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 25 "Liz Lemon and High School The More Things Change, the More They Don’t" — Shores uses Jack's cookie jar collection and his fiftieth-birthday home movies in 'Apollo, Apollo', plus Liz's catastrophic high-school reunion in 'Reunion', to examine personal identity over time. Hume's bundle theory denies any self beyond a flux of perceptions, Whitehead offers three senses of a person over time, and Augustine locates past, present, and future in the mind as memory, sight, and expectation, which explains why Jack cannot recover his tenth-birthday joy by buying the Apollo Lunar Module toy yet feels 'like a kid' after laughing until he vomits. Ryle's 'elusiveness of I' and Rousseau on happiness as a fleeting state frame the conclusion that we continually reinterpret the past from the present, so the self is a stretched-out temporal continuity.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 43 "A Dilemma" — The chapter asks 'Is your cookie you?', running theories of personal identity through Black Mirror's copies: the soul theory surfaces when Clayton signs away his 'digital self'; Locke's memory theory implies Cookie-Greta is Greta - a reductio, since one person cannot be wholly in two places at once (the same problem for Ashley Too and the thousand Hang the DJ simulations) - and the perdurantist patch recasts Greta and her cookie as time-slices of one four-dimensional person. Physical theories (Olson's animalism, Unger's brain-essentialism) rule out survival by upload, so Yorkie dies when her body dies even though digital Yorkie continues in San Junipero; Parfit's no-self bundle view and the teletransporter case then dissolve the fear, since there is no ego to lose and ordinary survival is 'about as bad' as being destroyed and replaced by a replica. The upshot: the punishment and immortality plots (Joe's million-year Christmas loop, San Junipero) require cookies to be both conscious and psychologically connected in the right way, and the episodes' horror depends on leaving that genuinely uncertain.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 14 "4. Can We Do Enough Good" — Interrogates Chidi's question 'why do we choose to be good?' through Hobbes's selfish state of nature, Rousseau's hardwired compassion (Michael's 'little voice' in Eleanor's head), and Hume's bundle theory extended Buddhist-style to a non-self, which grounds Michael's plea to Judge Gen that bad communities made the four humans bad and a better community (Team Cockroach, the Brainy Bunch) can make them good. Nietzsche's account of how communities define their own customs as 'good' then exposes the deeper flaw: the afterlife's accountants impose their in-group's preferences on all humanity, which is why even Doug Forcett's point-maximizing life cannot clear the bar. The chapter ends by asking Michael's real question: who gets to decide what's good?
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 25 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 34 "The Office and Philosophy" — Mayock runs theories of the self through the Scranton cast: Michael's burned foot in 'The Injury' enacts materialism, corrected by Aristotle's and Aquinas's distinction between accidental and substantial change; Jim's chair-and-phone role-play in 'Halloween' and his Dwight impersonation in 'Product Recall' ('Identity theft is not a joke') illustrate qualitative versus numerical identity and Descartes's cogito and dualism; Dwight's obsession with upgrading 'Assistant (to the) Regional Manager' is an ontological-status crisis met by Nietzsche's claim that the 'I' is a grammatical fiction and Hume's bundle theory. The chapter lands on Hegel's recognition - the self exists only in being acknowledged - reading Michael's office family, the Prodigal Son greetings, and his need for Pam to decode Jan's message as social constructionism in action.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 18 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Godwin reads Spider-Man 3's black-suit episode as a question about the self: with the symbiote amplifying his anger, is Peter still Peter? Against Hume's and the Buddha's bundle theories, on which the self is only an imagined aggregate of thoughts and feelings, and Reid's common-sense simple self, she advances the pragmatist 'social self' of Peirce, James, Dewey, and Mead, updated as Engel's biopsychosocial model: Peter's identity is a shifting web of biology, psyche, and relationships (Aunt May, MJ, Harry) expressed in actions and character. Eddie succumbs to the symbiote because, as Dewey says of the slave to his own blind desires, hatred constitutes who he is, while Peter's thicker web of good relations lets him shed the suit at the church bell.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley reads 'And When the Sky Was Opened' through Hume's skeptical account of belief in continued existence: Colonel Forbes's conviction that Harrington exists rests on memory's force and vivacity, and when testimony collapses (newspaper headlines, the bartender, his girlfriend, the general) the three spacemen are erased one by one, 'no longer part of the memory of man.' 'The Trouble with Templeton' gives the complementary case: Booth's belief that the woman in the speakeasy is his dead Laura is the imagination's feigned continuity, a resemblance across interrupted perceptions rather than a rational foundation. Memory alone, the chapter concludes, never grounds our beliefs that things or persons persist unperceived.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 8 "P A R T T H R E E" — James DiGiovanna uses Dr. Manhattan's origin — disintegration in the intrinsic field chamber and self-reassembly — plus his teleportations to Mars and his split into three simultaneous selves, to run the classic personal identity debates. Descartes's immaterial thinking substance, Hume's mere bundle of perceptions, and Locke's memory theory are tested against a being who remembers in both time directions and rebuilds his body from pure thought ('restructuring myself after the subtraction of my intrinsic field was the first trick I learned'); Parfit's teletransporter, physical and psychological criteria, and fission cases — mirrored in Nagel's split-brain patients — then show ordinary people cannot say whether they would survive teleporting or bisection. The chapter concludes Dr. Manhattan is the only being with fully secure identity, since his consciousness needs neither body nor an unbroken spatiotemporal path and he can encompass several points of view at once.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 12 "2. Know Thyself, Agent Cooper!" — De Carvalho reads Cooper's ordeal in the Black Lodge as a journey of self-knowledge, distinguishing 'knowing yourself' (your feelings, as Laura sought with Dr. Jacoby) from 'knowing your Self' in the deep sense of Vedanta's Brahman and Tibetan Buddhism's Mind. He sets Hume's bundle theory—the failure to catch a self behind the perceptions—against the Hindu Swami's ocean-and-waves image of an eternal Self beyond thought, and reads Cooper's confrontation with his screaming-Laura and doppelganger visions via the Tibetan Book of the Dead and Jung's shadow: facing his fears with imperfect courage, Cooper fails to integrate his shadow and is split in two.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 10 "Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall" — Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 24 "Rethinking the First Person Autobiography, Authorship, and the Contested Self in Malcolm X" — LaRocca uses Lee's Malcolm X and Haley's 'as told to' Autobiography to probe personal identity and authorship: since Haley (not X) authored the book and Lee/Washington perform Haley's literary X, he asks whether one can write another's autobiography and what becomes of the self. He surveys Locke's memory theory of identity, Descartes's thinking subject, Hume's bundle of perceptions, and Wittgenstein's denial of a thinking subject to frame X's serial renamings (Malcolm Little, Detroit Red, Malcolm X, El-Hajj Malik El-Shabazz) as a 'ceaselessly evolving,' unfinished identity. He reads Lee's techniques—nondiegetic gunshots, the spinning camera, the gliding sidewalk shot ('the eye that can finally see itself'), and the framing Rodney King and Mandela footage ending on 'by any means necessary'—as arguments that the self is a contested literary and cinematic creation.
- **The Philosophy of Tim Burton**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Tim Burton" — Ken Hada argues that Big Fish dramatizes a narrative, intersubjective account of the self against essentialist and Cartesian views. Dying storyteller Ed Bloom builds his identity through fantastic tales (the giant catfish, the Witch), while his journalist son Will—who dismisses the stories as lies—illustrates a 'circumscribed self' that refuses the social shaping every self undergoes. Drawing on Sartre's consciousness-as-nothingness and 'the Other teaches who I am,' Mead's generalized other, Aboulafia's mediating self, and Benjamin's 'The Storyteller,' Hada reads Will's climactic act of telling his father's death-scene as his becoming a mediating storyteller and granting Ed narrative immortality. Hume's 'bundle'/self-as-fiction and Descartes' cogito are invoked as the poles Ed's storied self transcends.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "7 Memory and Relationships in the Work and Music of Neil Young" — Sizer analyzes how memory shapes Young's songwriting: childhood trauma (polio, his parents' divorce, Omemee) fueling "Sugar Mountain," "Helpless" and "I Am a Child"; the "use and lose" pattern of collaborators and the ghost of Danny Whitten in Crazy Horse; and his late-life dread of memory loss watching his father's dementia. He frames this with Hobbes and Hume on memory-as-imagery, Wittgenstein's associative memory, and Locke's memory theory of personal identity (with Dennett on writing as a means to reconstruct and preserve the self).
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 20 "10. Memories Are Made of This" — Nisley reads two episodes through Hume's skepticism about the continued existence of objects and selves, which rests on memory, resemblance, and imagination rather than proof. In 'And When the Sky Was Opened,' three spacemen (Forbes, Harrington, Gart) progressively vanish as memory and corroborating testimony fail, dramatizing Hume's point that belief in continued existence needs more than force and vivacity of ideas. In 'The Trouble with Templeton,' Booth's dead wife Laura reappears but behaves unlike his memories, showing the imagination 'feigns' continuity; both episodes undermine memory as the foundation of rational belief.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 19 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "Who is Who" — On regeneration and personal identity, the chapter runs Doctor Who through Leibniz's law of identity and soul-based individuation, Locke's memory criterion of personhood, and Hume's bundle theory, testing them against multi-Doctor stories, the Ganger duplicates ('The Almost People'), 'The Girl Who Waited' (closest-continuer theory) and 'City of Death.' It then shifts to physicalism (the Morbius brain) and to a pragmatist, social theory of the self (James, Dewey, Mead's 'taking the attitude of the other,' Dennett's intentional stance), reading the reintegration of identity in 'The Doctor Dances.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.

### General mentions

- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 108 "Harry’s Near-Death Experience" — Develops the essay's boldest suggestion: reading Rowling through C. S. Lewis and the Inklings, whose associate Barfield convinced Lewis that if thought were a purely subjective event, logical and moral claims to truth would collapse, the germ of Lewis's argument from reason later refined by Plantinga and contested by Anscombe. On this view our logic participates in a cosmic Logos, which Christians identify with Christ, a point the chapter ties to Rowling's remark that it was no coincidence Harry's fateful dialogue happened at King's Cross, so what occurs in the head can genuinely put us in touch with reality.

## Martin Buber

*1878–1965 · 22 chapters in the corpus.*

Martin Buber was an Austrian-born Jewish philosopher best known for his philosophy of dialogue. In I and Thou (1923) he distinguished two basic ways of relating to the world: the "I–It" stance that treats others as objects to be used or analyzed, and the "I–Thou" encounter of genuine mutual presence, in which persons meet one another as whole beings. Drawing on Hasidic spirituality, he held that authentic human life, and even the meeting with God, unfolds in such relationships of encounter.

### I–Thou Relation

The I–Thou relation is a central idea of the Austrian-born Jewish philosopher Martin Buber, set out in his 1923 work I and Thou. Buber distinguishes two basic ways of relating to the world: the I–It attitude, in which we treat others as objects to be used, analyzed, or experienced, and the I–Thou attitude, in which we meet another as a genuine presence in a direct, mutual encounter. Authentic existence, for Buber, is dialogical, arising in these moments of meeting, which he saw as ultimately pointing toward relation with the eternal Thou, or God.

- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 15 "Bad Faith" — Lee reads the 'Breakdown' episode of Alfred Hitchcock Presents existentially: when the executive Callou coldly fires Humka and hangs up on his despair, he treats a person as a thing, Buber's 'I-It' pseudo-listening where Humka sought an 'I-Thou' dialogue with the godlike source of authority in his world. Heidegger's account of inauthenticity explains the mask of rational control behind which Callou hides, and Sartre's bad faith names the self-deception by which he pretends his godlike management of others is justifiable. Paralyzed and taken for a corpse after a car crash, Callou can be saved only when rational strategy fails and he finally weeps: the single tear reveals his caring nature, Jessie addresses him person-to-person, and, vulnerable before God and others, he becomes an authentic self, Hitchcock's pointed moral for bosses who give an employee the sack.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 182 "Chapter 34 - Beyond Lies the Wub" — Dick's first published story dramatizes the moral status of a rational nonhuman: Peterson's wub, a telepathic, philosophical Martian pig-creature, reads minds, discusses Odysseus and individuation, and pleads that it is 'a sensible being like yourselves', yet Captain Franco - obsessed with eating it - freezes it mid-sentence, shoots it looking him in the eye ('Back on the farm we had hogs'), and serves it for dinner, dismissing Peterson's grief with 'It is only organic matter, now.' The wub's personhood is established entirely through language and philosophy, but speech fails to protect it from being treated as meat, and the closing irony - Franco resuming the wub's own Odysseus meditation, as if the mind survived its meal - underscores how thin the line is between person and livestock. The story thus stages the problem of other minds and the ethics of killing sentient beings who demand to be addressed eye-to-eye rather than dined upon.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 19 "9. Are You Experienced" — Proposes an 'experientialism' — subjective conscious experience as fundamental reality, defended against eliminativists who would explain experience away as illusion — and finds its moral core in Martin Buber: the title song and 'May This Be Love' call the beloved out of an I-It world ('made out of gold and can't be sold') into reciprocal I-You relation ('take hold of my hand'), while 'The Wind Cries Mary,' 'Purple Haze,' and 'Manic Depression' lament love that is absent or unreciprocated. Experiences feel most intensely real, the chapter argues, when the Platonic order of love puts what matters most at stake — which is why kissing the sky, even without being kissed back, is worth recommending.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 27 "15. I, Thou, and the Neighborhood" — James McLachlan pairs Rogers's 'holy ground' between television set and viewer with Buber's turn from ecstatic religion to the everyday after failing the young visitor of 1914 who came to him in need: the I-You relation of full presence versus the I-It of use is what 'It's You I Like' sings. Against Sartre's 'Hell is other people' and Augustine's reading of the burning bush as the omnipotent God, Rogers and Buber (with Rosenzweig's translation of God's name as 'the One who will be present') make listening, presence, and everyday 'twinklings' the substance of neighborly love.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 18 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Edelheit, a rabbi, reads Stewart's Jewish persona as an echo of Martin Buber: both disclaim the titles (philosopher, journalist) yet 'point out the window' at what they have seen, and both practice engagement, 'You shall not withhold yourself', with genuine responsibility as real responding, epitomized for him by the face-to-face Crossfire confrontation. He walks through the 'Matzorian Candidate' segment on the Republican Jewish Coalition (the 'Yarmulkometer' ratings, Michele Bachmann's kibbutz years and mispronounced 'chutzpah'), the 'Faith/Off' Passover-versus-Easter segment pitting a chocolate egg against the Seder plate ('Jews! Camera 3'), and Earth (The Book)'s satirically rewritten Binding of Isaac and Reform-Judaism prayer jokes. All of this is read as Buberian dialogue, mocking religion from within rather than at it, and refusing silence in the lineage of Rabbi Joachim Prinz's warning that the most tragic problem is silence.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond as studies in Sartrean bad faith and authenticity: Christian Shephard's Red Sox fatalism is determinism as an excuse for moral failure, Locke swings from a Kierkegaardian leap of faith (pushing the button as his Abraham-and-Isaac trial) into nihilism when the Pearl film suggests the button is a psychological experiment, and Desmond's Humean skepticism yields to sacrificial faith in the fail-safe. He argues Jacob is the show's greatest con man, so Jack's acceptance of destiny in 'The End' remains a free choice rather than predestination. The finale's sideways world then moves Lost from secular existentialism to religious existentialism, read through Buber's I-Thou relation in Sawyer and Juliet's 'It worked' reunion and the all-religions church, where as Gandhi held every path leads to the same place.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 28 "26_LaRocca_Chapter_025.html" — Bill Nichols writes an open letter to Errol Morris explaining his bodily 'revulsion' at Standard Operating Procedure, Morris's film on the Abu Ghraib torture photographs. Nichols gives three reasons: the painfully limited, remorseless perspective of the MP guards elevated to mythic screen scale; the morally impossible reenactment tracking shots that put the viewer in the torturers' point of view (compared to Schindler's List); and the total absence of the Iraqi detainees' voices. He faults Morris for decontextualizing and fetishizing the images and forfeiting a moral center, contrasting the film with Rithy Panh's S-21, and casts the missing ethical encounter in terms of Buber's I-Thou relation of mutual honesty while wishing he had Fanon's capacity to treat the perpetrators' suffering.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 3 "Introduction" — The editors' introduction surveys Nolan's oeuvre chronologically to argue that a recurring theme of self-destruction and unstable self-identity runs through every film.
