- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 40 "Snape the Occlumens" — The section positions Snape as the third 'abandoned boy' beside Harry and Voldemort, a half-blood from an unhappy home for whom Hogwarts, as Harry observes, is where all three 'found home.' Voldemort chose power, selfishness, and a fragmented psyche while Harry opened his heart to friends and grew into integrity, and the section asks what makes this 'complicated amalgam of darkness and light,' Dumbledore's double agent and killer, tick.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 41 "Snape’s Choice" — The section reads Snape's double life through the definition of love shared by writers from Aristotle to Aquinas, willing the good of the other for the other's own sake: he protects people he dislikes because his love for Lily wills their good. As an Occlumens he empties himself of feeling to lie to Voldemort's face, concealing rather than renouncing his love for Lily, and only while dying from Nagini's bite does he freely offer Harry the memories revealing that Harry is a Horcrux.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 42 "A Work in Progress" — Tracing Snape's love from the greedy boyhood watching of Lily and the Mudblood rupture through his plea to save Lily alone, which draws Dumbledore's 'You disgust me,' the section judges it short of Aristotle's beloved as a 'second self,' since he wanted Lily's good only as it related to him. Diotima's teaching in the Symposium that 'love is wanting to possess the good forever' and Benedict XVI's love as 'an ongoing exodus out of the closed inward-looking self' frame how Snape's unrequited love gradually 'gives birth in beauty' to virtue in him.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 43 "NOTES" — The section argues that vice and virtue are habits built up over time: Snape still rages at Harry-as-James and sneers at Tonks's wolf Patronus as 'weak,' yet his own doe Patronus, matching Lily's, is the magical emblem of his transformation by love. Contrasting friends, who strengthen the soul's integrity by sharing joys and sorrows, with Voldemort, whose Horcruxes give him eight 'selves' while making him less human, it reads remorse as what knits a damaged soul back together, sealed by Harry's forgiveness and the name 'Albus Severus.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 46 "Little Hangleton" — The section collects the love-potion material of Half-Blood Prince: Fred and George's 'violently pink products' at Weasleys' Wizard Wheezes, Amortentia's mother-of-pearl sheen and the smell of freshly mown grass that Hermione dare not finish naming, Slughorn's warning that it causes 'a powerful infatuation or obsession' rather than love, and Ron's Romilda Vane episode from spiked Chocolate Cauldrons. This sets up the chapter's question of what kind of person would actually use one, answered by Voldemort's mother.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 47 "Real Love or Mere Infatuation" — Retelling Dumbledore's reconstruction for Harry, the section sets Merope Gaunt's love potion beside the Imperius Curse, one of the three unforgivable curses that robs victims of their will, as the two ways she might have won Tom Riddle Sr., noting that Harry immediately pairs them as will-robbing magic. Dumbledore's guess that Merope 'could not bear to continue enslaving him' and stopped dosing him, only to be abandoned and left to die, raises the chapter's question of what this loveless origin has to do with the prophecy.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 48 "Not His Mother’s Son" — The section argues Merope did not truly love Riddle Sr. because the potion stole his freedom: doing what you want is necessary but not sufficient for freedom, which also requires the ability to do otherwise, the 'libertarian' freedom Tom lacked. It canvasses Harry Frankfurt and the compatibilists who deny that doing-otherwise is necessary yet concedes even they would deny Tom freely loved Merope, and extends the argument to potions taken on oneself, which cheat us of becoming better persons through the hard work of real relationships.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 49 "NOTES" — Against the obvious reading of Voldemort's loveless begetting, the section argues he is 'not his mother's son': he imitates Marvolo and Salazar Slytherin, while Merope, on Aristotle's principle that we are what we consistently do, redeemed herself by stopping the potion, renouncing magic entirely, and choosing love over hate at the cost of her life. Character is destiny only if forged by genuinely free choices rather than blood or fate, so Merope shows not even the most tragic beginnings are destined for darkness, while Voldemort, who never loved and never wanted a friend, chose otherwise, leaving Harry as the true mother's son, shielded by 'a more ancient and powerful magic than any potion.'
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 54 "The Triumph of Love" — Reading the series' set pieces as the triumph of traditionally feminine values over masculine aggression, the section moves from Lily's sacrificial love burning Quirrell, through Harry sparing Pettigrew for Lupin's and Sirius's sake, to love expelling Voldemort during the Ministry possession, where 'it was your heart that saved you' and Dumbledore names a force 'more wonderful and more terrible than death.' Harry's kindness to Kreacher, Griphook, and Dobby pays off in the Horcrux hunt, his plea that Voldemort 'try for some remorse' redefines true manhood as incorporating the feminine, and the Forest sacrifice wins the war with a defensive Expelliarmus rather than a duel, showing love more important than aggression.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Southworth and Tallman defend the Underwood marriage by way of Richard Wasserstrom's three grounds for condemning adultery (promise breaking, deception, pain): Frank and Claire's openly negotiated nonmonogamy - Frank disclosing the Zoe affair over breakfast, the Meechum threesome, Claire's nights with Adam Galloway - breaks no promise and involves minimal deception, so it is morally permissible. They reject Vincent Punzo's dualist claim that sex must merge souls, arguing that view rests on unverifiable theology and sets people up for guilt. The marriage's real strength is its egalitarian mutuality - Claire's sabotage of the watershed bill works as tit-for-tat strategy that restores the partnership - and agreed nonmonogamy suits Frank's bisexuality better than monogamy, which would force him to give up part of what it means to be Frank.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Defends the Underwoods' open marriage by applying Wasserstrom's account of adultery (wrong via promise-breaking, deception, and pain): Frank and Claire's mutually negotiated nonmonogamy-frank transparency with Claire about Zoe, Claire rushing home to Frank from Adam's-apartment avoids all three wrongs, and Punzo's dualist claim that sex merges souls is rejected as unverifiable and damaging. It reads the marriage as an egalitarian partnership whose tit-for-tat renegotiation after Claire's watershed-bill sabotage and their agreed childlessness ('I promise you freedom from that') show that nonmonogamy strengthens rather than corrodes their bond.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 31 "The Office and Philosophy" — Arp and Watson sort Dunder Mifflin's relationships into five conceptions of love: Roy's erotic 'best sex of your life' Valentine's offer to Pam as blind eros; Angela and Dwight's pursuit of an idealized mate read through Plato's Forms and the Symposium's ascent to Beauty; Aristotle's three friendships, under which the office's alliances are mere utility while Jim and Pam's teapot sacrifice in 'Christmas Party' approaches virtue friendship; the Stoic-Kantian 'equal loving' of universal respect, laughed at when Michael ranks himself with Bono and Lincoln; and agape-style family loyalty that leads Dwight to supply Michael his urine in 'Drug Testing'. The chapter concludes that Michael exemplifies a selfishness Western philosophy has no name for, failing at every form of love.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 29 "Dysfunctional Family Feud The No Special Obligations View" — Southworth and Tallman use David Spade's 'falling star' joke about Eddie Murphy, and Murphy's twenty-year SNL boycott, to test three theories of familial obligation against the show's self-described 'family.' The role-based Just Because View, identified with Confucian filial piety, condemns Spade's disrespect toward an SNL elder but also forbids Murphy's divorce from the family; the contractarian Reciprocity View says Spade owes Dennis Miller but not Murphy, unless Murphy's saving the early show counts; and Jane English's No Special Obligations View, on which family should work like friendship, love rather than debt, clears Spade entirely. Sketches from the Vogelchecks' kissing family to Dysfunctional Family Feud supply the counterexamples.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 24 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Taliaferro and Little ask whether Spider-Man can champion justice and love Mary Jane at the same time, framed by Mandela's tension between obligations to family and to community. Through paired scenarios — rescuing an endangered coworker at possible mortal cost versus a lover's plea to become a surgeon rather than join a deadly crime-fighting unit — they conclude that justice trumps romance in unforeseen emergencies, while romance can rightly govern the choice of a vocation. For Spider-Man the two fuse rather than conflict, since MJ loves him partly for his commitment to justice, though Gwen Stacy's death on the bridge — where his webbing snapped her neck — shows a hero can lose both at once.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 25 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Spanakos asks why Spider-Man is called 'friendly' by testing Peter's relationships against Aristotle's three philias (pleasure, utility, virtue) and the proportionality principle that the morally inferior friend should love the superior more — a principle that breaks down for a superhero as godlike as Spider-Man. Peter's secrecy and self-sacrifice block true Aristotelian fellowship with MJ, whose crush on Spidey is mere fantasy-love, and Harry's friendship rests on pleasure and utility, failing every Aristotelian test. Yet against philia the chapter sets Christian agape (St. Basil, John 15, C.S. Lewis's Four Loves): unconditional, self-sacrificial love for the unlovable, which Peter practices toward his betrayers and which Harry finally enacts when he dies saving Peter in Spider-Man 3 — an agape that makes him Peter's equal.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Taliaferro and Beck trace a philosophy of love through Anakin: fatherless, he attaches compulsively to Shmi and then Padme, refusing the Stoic limits on control that Yoda and Epictetus teach, so that love curdles into the vow to 'stop people from dying.' Vader's fatherhood is the caricature of love - offering Luke power instead of care - until Luke's compassion and Vader's final self-sacrifice redeem it. The lesson: love must be tempered by humility about what Zeno and the Stoics placed outside our control, and broken family bonds can be partly repaired through costly self-sacrifice.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 25 "Humanoids and Droids Having Sex" — Munn and Weijers argue that Lando and L3-37 in Solo display all the hallmarks of friendship and one-sided romantic love: Lando abandons self-preservation to carry the injured L3 to the Falcon and endorses her droid-emancipation crusade, while L3 tells Qi'ra she has considered a relationship with him but finds them 'not compatible'. Testing Bennet Helm's four accounts of love (union, deep mutual caring, valuing, emotional state) against the film, they conclude humanoid-droid love is genuinely possible, and that L3's claim that sex with Lando 'works' is plausible once sex is defined broadly as any activity yielding sexual reward. They ground droid friendship in Aristotle's incomplete versus complete friendships, contrasting the rewarding partnerships of R2-D2 with Anakin and BB-8 with Poe against the merely strategic Han-Lando Sabacc rivalry.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 42 "Overcoming Death through the Force of Love" — Lawler reads the nine-film saga as a love story in three acts structured by Plato: Anakin and Padme's passionate love - which Diotima's ladder in the Symposium treats as the necessary first rung the Jedi wrongly condemn - drives his fall, in a Phaedrus-style conflict between the upward rational horse and the downward sensuous one. The original trilogy centers the detached Platonic love of Luke and Leia, while the Rey-Kylo 'dyad in the Force' fulfills Aristophanes' halfling myth of reunited other halves and brings balance, just as Alcibiades' failure to climb beyond the first rung parallels Anakin's fixation on one person. When Ren revives the dead Rey in a Romeo-and-Juliet inversion, the chapter concludes Yoda was wrong: the Force transforms into the dead rather than them into it.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 24 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Goguen reads the Winchesters through two masculine ideals: the warrior (Dean and Michael, chivalric protection culminating in Dean's 'protecting Sam... it's who I am') and the sovereign (Sam and Lucifer, whose freedom is analyzed with Isaiah Berlin's negative and positive liberty, with nods to Hobbes's absolute sovereign and Nietzsche's Übermensch). The show's stoic culture, where 'baring my soul like a freaking girl' is an insult, keeps the L-word unspoken, making Ellen's dying 'I will always love you, baby' to Jo a foil the brothers cannot match. Plato's Symposium, via Aristophanes' myth of split soulmates, and Aristotle's claim that the purest love is between virtuous male friends make sense of the 'psychotically, irrationally, erotically codependent' bond, and the chapter concludes that true masculinity requires embracing the seemingly supernatural: love.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 32 "Notes" — Baggett asks whether Rupert is beyond the grace the show extends to everyone else. She surveys theories of forgiveness - Butler's change of emotion, treatment and performative accounts, and Stump's Aquinas-based framework grounding forgiveness in the love that desires another's good and union, separable from reconciliation - then applies Aristotle's corrupted bad person whose vice 'makes moral truths invisible' as Rupert's limit case. Ted's darts-based tough love is contrasted with Sassy's vengeful certainty and Deborah's cheap grace, and the chapter leaves Rupert's turnaround possible but entirely his choice, while his choices have already been making him.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" — Klayman treats 'The Lonely' as a case study on whether Corry's love for the robot Alicia is true love. Using C.S. Lewis's four loves plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim (a concept's meaning is its practical effects), he argues Corry showed affection and appreciation but not Eros: he gave Alicia nothing, needed her merely against loneliness, and boarded the ship without sacrificing anything for her. Denying that a machine could be loved, he adds, would be a prejudice akin to Singer's speciesism, and Kendall Walton's 'Fearing Fictions' explains how Corry becomes fictional alongside a make-believe person.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 29 "Notes" — DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 30 "Notes" — Mahon debunks three myths about the original magic lasso: it is not a magic lie detector (Diana already runs a real polygraph on the spy Elva Dove), it is not an enslavement device (slavery is domination, and even the chained Amazons never submitted), and its truth-compulsion is no coincidence. Reading Marston's four-emotion psychology, he shows the lasso and the bracelets of submission are metaphors for love's asymmetric inducement/submission bond - Aphrodite captivates, the Amazons submit - and since lying is precisely an attempt to impose one's will and dominate the hearer (Rotenstreich), a perfectly lassoed person lacks all dominance emotion and so can only submit, and therefore cannot lie. The lasso's later depowering into a mere 'lasso of truth' becomes evidence of the comic industry's discomfort with feminine power.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 33 "Seventeenth Hole More Than a Playing Partner Golf and Friendship" — Andy Wible argues that although golf looks like the ultimate solitary sport, it is unusually good at fostering friendship, and analyzes friendship through Aristotle's three kinds (utility, pleasure, and the highest, based on the friend's good character), supplemented by Laurence Thomas (choice, equality, mutual trust) and Blum on care as a moral phenomenon. Golf's long unhurried rounds, self-called penalties, handicap system, shared memorable shots, and retirement communities build the intimacy, trust and equality Aristotle prizes, and Robert Simon's 'mutual quest for excellence' reconciles competition with goodwill. Wible then confronts friendship's partiality—exclusionary country clubs and the sex-segregated LPGA—using Marilyn Friedman's voluntary friendship communities to argue clubs should drop discrimination on race, sex, religion and orientation while keeping friendship's care and loyalty.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 24 "Two Ways of Enduring the Flames The Existential Dialectics of Love in Kierkegaard and Bukowski" — Andreas Seland argues that Kierkegaard and Bukowski offer opposed responses to a Romantic 'paradox of love': the beloved is a dialectical object, part inner imago (Shelley's veiled maid in 'Alastor,' Stendhal's crystallization, Lacan/Zizek) and part uncontrollable external person, and this gap breeds despair. Kierkegaard's Knight of Faith in Fear and Trembling resolves it by infinite resignation and the absurd leap, internalizing the gap and severing the tie to the real to love the princess only interiorly. Bukowski's Chinaski in Women does the opposite, deliberately choosing unstable 'Lydia-object' women who embody the gap, seeking the insecurity itself as a line of flight beyond bourgeois love and even beyond himself.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 15 "Me and You Identity, Love, and Friendship in the Films of Charlie Kaufman" — Den Uyl argues that Kaufman's films are really about friendship rather than romance, reading them through Aristotle's character friendship (the friend as 'other self' and mirror of self-knowledge) and Montaigne's ideal of a free, voluntary friendship that also engages the body. Charlie's fictional twin Donald in Adaptation externalizes the integrity Charlie lacks, and only after internalizing Donald can he say 'I love her'; Caden in Synecdoche fails because he looks only at himself. Love succeeds, on this reading, only when grounded in the self-sufficiency and self-respect that make one capable of an 'other self,' as Eternal Sunshine's Joel and Clementine haltingly discover.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 16 "I Don’t Know, Just Wait Remembering Remarriage in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" — Day reads Eternal Sunshine as Cavell's Hollywood comedy of remarriage: the kaleidoscopic middle in 'Joel's head' is the couple's remarriage conversation, a 'green world' where they invent a shared childhood and learn what it means to have memories together. Against a tape-recorder model of memory, he invokes the later Wittgenstein's private-language argument to argue there is no private memory — what Joel remembers he can return to Clementine in conversation. He rereads Mary's Nietzsche, the eternal recurrence, not as the end of regret but as affirming it (Joel's 'I wish I'd stayed. I do.'), and claims viewers themselves remember the erased past for the pair across the hallway's ten seconds of waiting.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, about whether marital fidelity can be chosen rather than accidental. Bill's confidence in his own and Alice's fidelity is a Kantian appeal - duty and rational principle over inclination - which Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, and Bill's night among the masked orgy, expose as vulnerable to uncontrollable desire and moral luck. Hoffman argues that by unmasking and honestly acknowledging these desires (and drawing on Kierkegaard on marriage existing 'in time') the Harfords consciously rechoose their marriage, so their fidelity is no longer merely accidental.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 10 "The Recovery of Childhood and the Search for the Absent Father" — Le Gall and Taliaferro read E.T., Hook, and the Indiana Jones trilogy through a Socratic-Platonic ideal in which the true 'adventure' ends not in glory (kleos) but in homecoming, beauty, and restored parent-child love. Indiana abandons the grail to grab his father's hand and hears 'Indiana' instead of 'Junior'; Elliott becomes a father to E.T. while E.T. teaches him loss; Peter Banning must recover his Pan-childhood to save his kids. They tie this to the Republic's Myth of Er, the Symposium's ladder of love, and xenia (hospitality) as the setting for wisdom.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 23 "Allons-y into the Starry Heavens" — Donna Marie Smith uses the Doctor and Rose's separation in "Doomsday" and "Journey's End" to explicate Kantian deontology. After framing the Doctor's virtues via Plato's four virtues and Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and distinguishing eros, philia, and agape (with Reinette illustrating chivalrous self-sacrifice), she argues that Kant's categorical imperative and the duty-versus-inclination conflict explain why the Doctor and Rose Kant be together: their love pulls toward partiality while duty to save humanity is what they ought to do, so acting for the greater good is precisely what forces their parting.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 11 "3. Why Do I Have to Be Some Kind of Hero" — Zanin reads the Winchesters' sense of moral responsibility through Dostoevsky's The Karamazov Brothers, mapping Dean onto the sensualist/atheist Dmitri-Ivan and Sam onto the faithful Alyosha. Via Father Zossima's dictum that we are 'responsible to all for all,' she argues Sam and Dean's brotherhood is Christian self-sacrificial 'love in action'—shown in Dean choosing Sam over a normal life in 'Bad Boys' and the djinn world—which grounds why they keep saving strangers even after rejecting God's plan.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 14 "5. True Love or Artificial Love" — Klayman analyzes whether James Corry's love for the robot Alicia in 'The Lonely' is true love, using C.S. Lewis's four loves (charity, affection, friendship, Eros) and their three qualities (gift-, need-, appreciative-love), plus Peirce's pragmatic maxim to define 'truly loving' by its practical effects. He argues true love falls within Eros and requires a reciprocating individual, invoking Peter Singer's speciesism to reject a human-only requirement; concluding Corry showed only appreciative-love (not gift- or need-love) and that his bond was really companionship—Corry became fictional (Walton) to have something to believe in.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 11 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Winkle reads Sense and Sensibility as steering a 'middle road' between cold rational calculation and sentimental self-indulgence, and casts Austen as proto-feminist. She uses Wollstonecraft's Vindication to explain why Austen's silly wives (Mrs. Bennet, Lucy Steele) are products of a deficient female education that trains women to please rather than reason. She then reads Elinor Dashwood's measured love for Edward, and Marianne's near-fatal collapse over Willoughby, through bell hooks's claim that 'falling in love' surrenders agency, arguing Elinor chooses love as an act of will while Marianne must learn sense before finding lasting love with Colonel Brandon.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 12 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Gibson argues Austen's novels are propelled by dialectical forces (signaled by titles like Pride and Prejudice and Sense and Sensibility) that are reconciled through the marriage bond, invoking the Platonic origin of dialectic and drawing on Harold Bloom's reading of Darcy and Elizabeth as sharing a common will. Love functions as the transcendent principle that resolves opposition, but Gibson stresses (citing Derrida on the gift) that in Austen love never fully escapes the economic and social 'prisons' of marriage: Charlotte Lucas's loveless match, Fanny Price's poverty, and Anne Elliot's coerced broken engagement all show love succeeding only alongside wealth and status.
- **Jane Austen and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Jane Austen and Philosophy" — Lindenmuth pairs Austen with Nietzsche on what makes a happy marriage, reading Pride and Prejudice's clashes over Lizzy's refusals of Mr. Collins and Darcy, and Lady Catherine's and Sir Thomas Bertram's aristocratic insistence that superiors should choose for inferiors. He uses Nietzsche's 'philosophizing with a hammer' to cast Austen as smashing the dead traditions of entailment and arranged marriage, and Nietzsche's aphorisms (a good marriage rests on a talent for friendship and good conversation; sensuality makes love grow too fast) to judge the couples, concluding Austen holds an Aristotelian, objective view of happiness as a reward for getting life right rather than mere desire-satisfaction.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 20 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 20 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span closes the walk-of-shame semiotics and then applies ancient ethics to college relationships. Puka defends long-distance college relationships through Aristotle's account of philia—arguing (provocatively, per Aristotle) that love is an activity, so being apart 'murders' love unless couples make Skype, sexting, and texting into the relationship's real medium rather than a substitute. Stephens brings Epicurus and Lucretius to 'friends with benefits': since sexual passion is a natural-but-unnecessary desire that breeds anxiety and love is a wound to the mind, while friendship is necessary for ataraxia, he concludes students should skip the sex and keep the friend—'friends are the real benefits,' echoing Tina Turner's 'What's Love Got to Do with It?' Levine/Mongeau and Smith/Morrison supply communication-research data on how FWB relationships form, are negotiated (usually not), and often end when one partner 'catches feelings.'
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 7 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — In this foreword Joshua Wolf Shenk recounts an intoxicating blind date with 'Rachael' to argue that dating exposes the core existential dilemma of social creatures: we crave ecstasy (ekstasis, 'standing outside oneself') yet can only connect by holding on to a discrete identity. He blames the modern isolation of the self on Descartes' claim that the self inhabits its own subjective realm and Hobbes' picture of natural man as solitary, and cites Camus that once you choose to live, the real question is how to relate to others. His unresolved paradox—needing the mantra 'I was complete before I met you' while knowing it is false—frames love as the tension between self-sufficiency and merger.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 9 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Editors Kristie Miller and Marlene Clark introduce the volume by opening with Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics claim that the human drive to couple is even stronger than the drive to live as a political being and that fulfillment rests in loving relationships. They frame dating as a rule-governed 'game' with aims and strategies and preview each contributor's essay—Jenkins on flirting, Langan on conservative men, Samp and Cohen against unconditional love, the elevator metaphor, cyberdating, evolutionary seduction, and Colyvan's game-theoretic mate search—tying age-old ethical questions about treating partners well to new work in evolutionary psychology, decision theory, and the ethics of online romance.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 11 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Carrie Jenkins does analytic conceptual analysis of flirting, rejecting the Oxford English Dictionary's claim that flirting requires having no serious intentions. She distinguishes 'flirting' from merely 'behaving flirtatiously' (Joe who over-holds eye contact, the tourist touching her earlobe in Italy are flirtatious without flirting) and argues flirting requires an intention to act in ways disposed to raise flirter-flirtee romance to salience, done in a 'knowing yet playful' way. Borrowing Kripke's 'killer yellow' to imagine 'killer-flirts' who die on contact, and citing chatbot studies, she concludes one can flirt with an imagined or non-human target only if one believes it can respond significantly.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 12 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Emily Langan uses focus-group data from 75 self-described ideologically conservative, mostly Christian young men to argue that flirting is a site of moral decision-making, opening with Hitch's 'right broom' line to show these men reject its libido-driven premise. She reports three shared themes—flirting is not about sex but about honesty of motive, timing within a relationship's stages, and reciprocity ('it has to be a two-way street')—and three tensions (healthy vs. harmful, superficial vs. serious, overt vs. covert), drawing on courtship-stage and flirting-style research to show that, contrary to the stereotype that only women agonize over relationships, conservative men wrestle with being 'risqué yet respectable.'
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 13 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Jennifer Samp and Andrew Cohen argue against the Notebook-style romantic ideal of unconditional love, casting dating as a 'calculated exchange' explained by social-exchange and interdependence theory (comparison level and comparison level of alternatives). Adopting Aristotle's distinction between friendships of utility/pleasure and 'complete friendships' in which one values the friend as 'another self' and as an end in itself, they hold the best romances are complete friendships—yet insist even these must be conditioned. Their key thought experiment: a genuinely boundless love would survive discovering one's partner is a child-molesting murderer; since it should not, 'true love knows bounds' and remains part of a good life only because it can be defeated by such reasons.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 16 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mary Beth Yount asks whether being 'crazy in love' really resembles mental illness, noting lovesickness was a diagnosis for nearly two millennia and that love's mood swings mimic bipolar or schizophrenic symptoms. She organizes the analysis around the four Greek loves—eros (with Plato's ladder from physical beauty to the Forms, i.e., 'Platonic love'), philia (Aristotle's Nicomachean friendship of good character), storge (familial affection), and agape (C.S. Lewis's unconditional charity)—arguing a full romance blends all four. She then surveys Fisher, Aron, and Brown's fMRI work showing romantic love as a dopamine-driven mammalian mate-choice drive stronger than the sex drive, and the 'protest'/'resignation' stages of rejection, to reassure daters their craziness is normal biology, not disorder.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 42 "39. Harry Potter as Philosophy Five Types of Friendship" — Okapal uses the Harry Potter films to expand Aristotle's theory of philia (friendship/love), which recognizes friendships for virtue, pleasure, and utility grounded in other-regarding concern, intimacy, choice, and a surrounding community. He argues the films show that friendships for pleasure and utility each come in beneficent and maleficent forms distinguished by whether motivations are other-regarding or purely self-regarding: the Quidditch team and the Harry-Ginny romance are beneficent pleasure-friendships (Ginny hides the Prince's book out of concern for Harry), while the Hermione-McLaggen date and Ron-Lavender fling are maleficent and short-lived. Slughorn's Slug Club is a beneficent utility-friendship of mutual advantage one may freely leave, whereas Voldemort's Death Eaters are maleficent, with all benefit flowing one way and no exit, yielding five types of friendship and locating Gryffindor's courage, inclusiveness, and loyalty as the ground of virtuous friendship.

### The Banality of Evil

The banality of evil is a phrase coined by Hannah Arendt in her report on the trial of Adolf Eichmann, a Nazi administrator of the Holocaust. She used it to describe her impression that Eichmann was driven less by fanatical hatred or monstrous depth than by thoughtlessness, careerism, and an unreflective willingness to follow orders and cliché. The provocative claim is that immense evil can be carried out by ordinary people who fail to think about what they are doing, rather than only by demonic villains. Widely debated and often misunderstood, the idea directed attention to the moral dangers of unthinking obedience within bureaucratic systems.

- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues South Park is perceived as dangerous for the very reasons Socrates was executed — corrupting the youth and impiety — and that like Socrates it is really a gadfly promoting the examined life. Cartman is read through Arendt's Eichmann: evil as thoughtlessness, the inability to think from another's standpoint or ask if one can live with oneself, while Kyle and Stan's dialogues (such as deliberating Stan's grandfather's euthanasia request in 'Death') model the perspective-taking Arendt calls thinking. A final Freudian section explains the show's vulgarity as essential: jokes work like dreams, releasing repressed drives so the culture can talk through what it forbids.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 23 "Rising Up" — Brandon Forbes uses Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (people acting in concert, rooted in plurality and natality) and violence (instruments that ape power, one against all) to read Radiohead's violent imagery. The "Just" video shows that power lies not in what the prone man says but in everyone's collective act of lying down; "Sit Down. Stand Up." and "2 + 2 = 5" dramatize command backed by weapons and the revolutionary moment when a king's violence breeds the dissent that undoes him; "Life in a Glass House" and "Where I End and You Begin" depict totalitarian terror, the stage where violence has devoured power entirely. "I Will" ("I will rise up," "little babies' eyes") closes the chapter as Arendt's natality — the capacity of new political beginnings the gun can never defeat.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 7 "4" — Four 'Phase One' essays. Dyer reads Mark Millar's Wanted through Plato's cave: Wesley Gibson escapes a pathetic life like the freed prisoner, but like Adolf Eichmann (via Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem) he murders his conscience, so the Fraternity's consequence-free world leaves him numb and unable to value anything - a descent deeper into the cave, ending in the banality of evil. Novy explains why henchmen betray using Aristotle's utility/pleasure/complete friendship distinction (Big Cheese, Henchmen Muenster and Feta): supervillain gangs are Hobbesian pirate crews with no enforcer, so a modus vivendi of self-interest collapses under interrogation and only Machiavellian fear secures loyalty. Foresman applies Goodman and Rawls's reflective equilibrium as a 'cheat' to rank Apocalypse, Magneto, Luthor, the Joker, and Bizarro, concluding the 'best of the worst' is judged on evil ends (or evil means, as with Magneto) and even on glorious failure. Arinder and Milton, in a staged descent-into-madness frame, diagnose mad science in Victor Frankenstein and Dr. Doom as science that denies value-laden theory choice - impossible because data underdetermine theory - breeding the hubris that dehumanizes the scientist.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Comparing the Doctor's hesitation at the Dalek hatchery in 'Genesis of the Daleks' with the half-human Doctor's instant genocide in 'Journey's End', the authors argue the Daleks are mirrors of us: their survival-driven wars enact Hobbes's state of nature, while their industrial 'extermination' embodies Arendt's banality of evil and Weber's iron cage of instrumental rationality. Drawing on Horkheimer and Adorno's culture industry and Foucault's disciplinary institutions — modern techniques that mold the inner life as Davros's genetic engineering molds the Kaleds — they conclude the Dalek tendency is a human possibility, so we cannot exterminate the Daleks without indicting ourselves.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 25 "Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps" — Argues that Herbert is a genuine philosopher extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra into the twentieth century, via three narrative parallels: the Preacher entering Arrakeen mirrors Zarathustra's first down-going into the town with its tightrope walker and mocking buffoon; Paul's empire of water-fat Fremen and Alia's orthodoxy realizes the 'Ultimate Man' whom the crowd begs for instead of the Superman; and prescience reworks eternal recurrence's gateway 'Moment,' where every timeline ends in Krazilec. Reading Paul's sixty-five-billion-death jihad through Arendt's banality of evil and Herbert's 'superheroes are disastrous' thesis, the chapter concludes Paul is the failed tightrope walker and Leto II the goad—'not lightning, but lightning rod'—pushing humanity beyond man toward the Superman, with Spannungsbogen naming the tension of the drawn bow between animal and Overman.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 17 "All for Love" — Jerry Piven argues Dexter's void is not genetic sociopathy but trauma: witnessing his mother's chainsaw murder and lying in her blood deadened his feelings, and each ritualized kill restages that catastrophe with the roles reversed, Dexter mastering death as the angel of it, reducing the murderer to a drop of blood he imprisons on a slide. Reading Harry's ghost as a Hamlet-father super-ego, he contends Dexter kills not only to master trauma but to please the father who channels his rage - murder 'for love' - and then generalizes: Arendt's banality of evil, Pascal on the void and faith, Kierkegaard and Heidegger on fleeing despair into conformity, Buddhist emptiness, and Becker-style terror-management findings explain how ordinary people, frightened of death and hungry for a leader's approval, can be manipulated into sanctioned slaughter, from Abu Ghraib to jihadism.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 15 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Jonas-Sebastien Beaudry reads Neverwhere's magic invisibility as a model of real social invisibility: after Richard helps the injured Door he loses his job, his fiancee Jessica, and even the ability to be perceived, joining the homeless, slaves, and Jews under Nazism as people excluded from the moral community whose needs no longer register. Using Arendt's banality of evil to explain everyday indifference and Richard Rorty on torturers who fail to see a 'real' human, he distinguishes radical from partial invisibility, shown in Jessica stepping over the bleeding Door and misreading her need as 'sleep it off.' The remedy is Iris Murdoch's 'loving gaze' of just and careful attention, which seizes Richard before he can rationalize, backed by a practical wisdom about whose needs matter, so that acknowledging the invisible, down to apologizing to a rat in London Below, is what makes both them and us better.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 11 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cogburn protests Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments and rebuilds the system philosophically: Lawful means willing universalizable law in Kant's categorical-imperative sense (the liar and murderer treating themselves as exceptions), Good means willing the greatest happiness in Mill's utilitarian sense, yielding a nine-box grid of moral psychologies. He populates it with fantasy archetypes—Haomane Firstborn as pathological Lawful Neutral, Karsa Orlong as Chaotic Neutral, Abercrombie's torturer Glotka as Neutral Neutral in Hannah Arendt's 'banality of evil' mold, hierarchic vampires and cynical politicians as Lawful Evil, Conan's raiders as Chaotic Evil. On this scheme Chaotic Good is genuinely empty, Drizzt and Robin Hood types are really Lawful or Neutral Good, and a Neutral Good versus Lawful Good dispute over killing one innocent to save thousands shows how gameplay can stage classic ethics thought experiments.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 31 "The Devil and Philosophy" — George Dunn asks whether the Joker's 'some men just want to watch the world burn' motivelessness even makes sense. Against Baumeister's 'Myth of Pure Evil' and the Socratic-Aristotelian thesis that all wrongdoing aims at some apparent good, he tests Kant's claim that no human can be a diabolical being, Claudia Card's definition of diabolical evil as engineering others' moral corruption, and the Satan of Job as prosecuting accuser - which fits the Joker's ferry 'social experiment' and his breaking of Harvey Dent. The upshot is that the Joker's evil, fed by pride and the wish for credit for the conflagration, is instrumental, pathological, and banal after all, its best answer being the convict who throws the detonator out the window.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 26 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Paweł Dobrosielski and Marcin Napiórkowski read Flowers for Hitler as Cohen's answer to Adorno's dictum that to write poetry after Auschwitz is barbaric - Cohen writes poetry that self-consciously knows it comes after the end of poetry. Using Freud's distinction between the vocabulary and grammar of dreams, they show the collection is assembled from a small repertoire of recurring images (ovens, ashes, telephones, radios, green grass, Nazi names) whose awkward normality expresses repression: life goes on as if nothing had happened. Arendt's banality of evil, born of the Eichmann trial, is directly alluded to in 'All There Is to Know about Adolf Eichmann,' and the book ends by universalizing Holocaust memory - the poet waking with a number on his forearm, feeling like victim and perpetrator alike - until the grass itself is grown on ashes and every flower is a flower for Hitler.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 17 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Bowman argues through Arendt that Dracula is not inherently evil but thoughtless: like Eichmann he cannot think from another's standpoint, treats people as cogs and means (Harker as captive, humans as prey), uses violence as a constructive tool, and protects himself with rhetorical safeguards like 'Enter freely' so he need never face his own cruelty. Measured against the Crew of Light's thoughtfulness - Harker's memos and recipes for Mina, Mina's care for Lucy, the suitors' gentlemanly bonds - the Count's evil is banal, lazy, 'Evil Lite'; but because Dracula stands outside humanity and knows humans only as livestock, Bowman concludes that Eichmann is banal yet truly evil, while Dracula, though careless, can never be evil.
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 26 "13. The Shrieking Evils" — Piven argues that evil in the story runs from the overt villains to the beloved heroes: Humperdinck's rage at Westley is analyzed as malignant envy of true love, Rugen's torture as dispassionate sadistic curiosity, and Vizzini's pompous moralizing as narcissistic hypocrisy masking childhood shame and nightmares. He applies Hannah Arendt's banality of evil to Inigo and Fezzik, who soberly assault and abduct Buttercup, and then brands Westley - a pirate who admits he liked piracy and who slaps and strangles Buttercup to test her fidelity - as possibly the evilest character, likening his love-justified slaughter to the terrorist's logic. The point is that we adore these characters only by ignoring deeds we would condemn in real life.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 32 "16. You’re Not Starving" — Argues Louis's 'my life is evil, I drive an Infiniti' bit and 'we make them die with our cars' capture Singer's drowning-child argument that famine relief is a duty of the affluent rather than charity, since the obligation to prevent bad outcomes at little cost holds across distance. It then amplifies the harm claim with Pogge's account of a rigged global institutional order (WTO protections, sweatshop-made smartphones) and frames unthinking consumer participation in that system as Arendt's banality of evil—the 'terrifyingly normal' thoughtlessness of Eichmann repeated at the checkout.
- **The Man in the High Castle and Philosophy - Subversive Reports from Another Reality**, ch. 32 "19. What if Evil Had Won" — Verena Ehrnberger reads the High Castle world through Hannah Arendt's Eichmann report: Smith's 'It was necessary work. We did it,' Kido's 'The law is the law,' and the surveillance room named Iwazaru ('speak no evil') show evil as thoughtless, self-protecting obedience rather than sadism, embodied in the disturbingly loving Smith family. The real conflict, on this reading, is not Resistance versus Reich but obedience versus the few — Tagomi, Wegener, Juliana, eventually even Smith — who dare to think and feel for themselves, and the chapter weighs the security obedience buys against the freedom and humanity it costs.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 22 "11. When Cruelty Is Not Enough" — Conway argues the real horror of 1984 is not the torture chamber but O'Brien's worldmaking: he cultivated Winston and Julia's affair from lust into a hopeful little home precisely so that destroying it, and hope itself, the Party's true enemy, would be total. Against Rorty's influential reading of O'Brien as a torturer who breaks Winston for pleasure, Conway adds two amendments: Arendt's thoughtless technocrat, with O'Brien as an Eichmann figure whose Party affirms his competence and insulates him from rebuke, and Horkheimer and Adorno's warning that technical rationality has become a secular religion whose 'priests of power' sanctify cruelty. The result is a portrait of a warm-blooded, situationally sympathetic sadist who genuinely excels at building the selves and worlds he is then charged to dismantle.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' (Lutze tried by his victims' ghosts at Dachau and sentenced to madness) and 'He's Alive' (neo-Nazi Vollmer groomed by Hitler's ghost) as Serling's twin responses to the Eichmann trial, situating them among the docufiction Operation Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman episode, and his abhorred Hogan's Heroes. Tracking Serling's maturation from the heartless, monstrous Lutze to the needy, speechmaking Vollmer — 'frustrated men, sick men, angry men' — he argues the later episode foreshadows Arendt's banality of evil, evil as the end product of a political process and a thoughtless inability to think from another's standpoint, all framed by Susan Neiman's problem of evil.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann builds 20th-century totalitarianism from three TZ episodes: 'He's Alive' shows Aristotle's account of persuasion — rhetoric aimed at an audience's anger and fear — fueling Vollmer's neo-Nazi movement under Hitler's ghostly tutelage; 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' instantiates Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference, banning even Plato and Dostoevsky; and 'Deaths-Head Revisited' gives Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' alongside Arendt's verdict on Eichmann's thoughtless, mechanical obedience. He then argues the phenomenon has mutated: Debord's society of the spectacle explains Black Mirror's 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits,' where image-politics becomes authoritarian and even Bing's suicidal act of defiance is sold back as an avatar product.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 29 "16. Who Is the Meanest of Them All" — Frunză and Grad apply Arendt's banality of evil to Gilead: the Commander is 'not Iago, not Macbeth' but an Eichmann—sheepish, Scrabble-playing, 'thinking about how not to think'—and no character holds a monopoly on evil because everyone is 'too banal' for demonic profundity. They test his 'just doing my duty' against Kant (duty requires universalizing what reason can will and never treating persons as means, so the Aunts' reeducation camps fail the test) and use The Origins of Totalitarianism to read Handmaids as rightless people whose 'two-legged wombs' status mirrors statelessness. Arendt's web of guilty complicities explains why resistance is scarce, and the chapter ends with banality eroding all criteria for judging—leaving Offred's 'the darkness within; or else the light' as the final choice.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 27 "14. Anything that’s Spiked Is Fine" — Volpert asks where rebellion lives, in the lone guitarist or the listening group, using Hardt and Negri's claim that a rebel's true opposite is not failure but co-option, i.e. selling out. Arendt's distinction between totalitarian and authoritarian systems models the music industry as authoritarian (creativity permitted so long as profit at the top goes unchallenged), and her banality-of-evil analysis of Eichmann prompts the question of whether there is a banality of rebellion. Petty's satirical puppetry of authority voices in "Century City" and the silent spiked-collar punk of "Spike," kin to Bartleby and James Dean, show that individuals can rebel against authoritarian packs while groups, even the Heartbreakers, only ever drift into authoritarianism.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 31 "19. And God Created Replicants in His Own Image" — Jerry Piven argues both films are dark mirrors of human inhumanity: we create beings who feel, then declare them soulless 'skin jobs' so we can enslave and slaughter them without guilt, disavowing and projecting our own evil onto our creations. Roy's nail-pierced hand, his saving of Deckard, and his 'tears in rain' lament make him a Christlike figure whose grace shames the humans, while 2049 replays Exodus — Rachael with the matriarch Rachel, K renamed Joe the liberator — only to reveal the true messiah is the concealed daughter Ana. Beneath it all lies the banality of evil and an existential dread of death that drives men like Wallace to play God and murder what they cannot gestate.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 12 "4. The Case of the Other Renegade Refugee" — McCrossin reads 'The Case of the Renegade Refugee' (aired December 9, 1961, days before Eichmann's verdict) alongside the film Operation Eichmann and Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem as three competing pop-culture portrayals of the Nazi criminal: monstrous, repentant, and banal. The episode's 'other' refugee, Arthur Hennings/Max Kleinerman, whose Father Paul-inspired 'religious peace' lets him recant on the stand and save Mason's client Harlan Merrill (himself a Battle of the Bulge 'deserter' living a lie created by concussion), supplies what Arendt found absent in Eichmann: empathy and genuine acceptance of guilt, complicating her banality-of-evil picture. The whole is set against the Holocaust as the century's starkest form of the problem of why the innocent suffer while the wicked thrive, and closed with Hogan's Heroes' provocative reuse of the same actors four years later.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 14 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 27 "#WithGreatPowerComesGreatResponsibility" — The chapter weighs the #dangers of trial by Twitter — Tess's suicide attempt after a mob turned on her, Clara Meades killed over a war-memorial photo, the fundamental attribution error and echo chambers convicting the innocent, and Rawls's point that unpredictable, lawless punishment destroys liberty — against the #benefits, above all #MeToo as 'the beautiful flip side of #DeathTo' that finally held powerful abusers accountable when courts would not. Arendt's banality of evil explains both Garrett Scholes's bee-drone scheme and the ordinariness of the shamers: Parke's 'He's ordinary. That is the type,' and Liza Bahar's crowdsourced 'Fucking Bitch' cake show diffused responsibility enabling cruelty. The moral drawn is that anonymous power over others' lives demands conscious, individual responsibility for every click.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 25 "Philosopher of the Dangerous Perhaps" — Claims Herbert is a philosopher whose Dune saga is a novelistic thought experiment extending Nietzsche's Zarathustra in the light of twentieth-century horrors: the Preacher's entry into Arrakeen parallels Zarathustra's first discourse on the Ubermensch at the tightrope, Paul is the failed tightrope-walker while Leto II is both devil-buffoon and goad toward the Superman, and the empire of Dune Messiah is enumerated trait by trait as Nietzsche's realm of the Ultimate Man. Eternal recurrence is paralleled with prescience as both the trap of destiny and the gateway 'Moment' that frees humanity from apparent necessity, and Arendt's banality of evil frames Paul's sixty-five billion jihad deaths as an ordinary, human result rather than demonic villainy.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 11 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Cogburn attacks Fourth Edition's contraction of the nine alignments to five: it deletes archetypes that fantasy literature needs, since Karsa Orlong (who wills the destruction of all civilization without sadism) and Jacqueline Carey's Haomane Firstborn (who loves cold mathematical order while his laws lead to genocide) fit nowhere in the new scheme. He rebuilds alignment by taking it to describe what a character wills in Kant's sense, mapping the law-chaos axis onto the categorical imperative (the liar and murderer must take themselves to be exceptions to universal laws) and the good-evil axis onto Mill's greatest happiness principle, which yields a Lawful Good of Gandhi and King, a Neutral Good modeled on Jesus breaking Sabbath law out of love, and Lawful Evil exemplified by vampire hierarchies and politicians whose policies create hell abroad. Joe Abercrombie's torturer San Dan Glotka becomes the archetypal Neutral Neutral, 'banality of evil' in Arendt's sense, and the chapter concludes Chaotic Good is empty because willing the destruction of universalizability cannot consistently will less pain.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 17 "Should Mao Be Pardoned" — R. S. Leiby stages the trial of Jules-Pierre Mao alongside Hannah Arendt's report on Adolf Eichmann to ask whether someone can commit great evil without being evil. Mao, like Eichmann, would plead 'not guilty in the sense of the indictment': he mourns Julie at her tree, momentarily defends the children on Io ('We're torturing children'), yet lacks the imagination to think from the standpoint of his victims on Eros, the Canterbury, and Ganymede — unlike the genuine fanatics Dresden and Cortázar, whom appeals to morality cannot touch. The 'anyone would do it' defense is tested through Milgram's obedience experiments and Miller's killing of Dresden ('I killed him because he was making sense'), showing how seductive moral tradeoffs are; following the Eichmann court's rule that responsibility increases with distance from the fatal instrument, the chapter concludes that Mao — a free, autonomous agent with even less excuse than Eichmann — should not be pardoned.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 19 "The Upsides of Amos" — Diana Sofronieva asks whether Amos is evil and answers no — in some ways he is better than most. Drawing on psychopathy research (Blair's moral/conventional distinction), Glover's 'moral resources', and Damasio's somatic markers to explain both his emotional absence (cauterized by a Baltimore childhood where children were sold for sex) and his difficulty making choices ('I've been trying to make choices of my own lately, and I can't seem to make the right ones'), she distinguishes him from bloodthirsty killers like Murtry and from Cortázar, who surgically chose the emotionless life Amos wants to escape. Against Arendt's banality of evil, Amos is no thoughtless 'joiner': he holds an uncompromising inner code (family first, bullying punished), deliberately selects good people — Naomi, Anna, Holden — as his moral compass after verifying their reasons, and his honesty, loyalty, trust in competence, and selflessness make him paradoxically less capable of evil than nearly anyone else on the Roci.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 21 "A Crossroads in Human History" — Trip McCrossin reads season five's asteroid strikes on Earth as a 9/11 allegory (Delgado's 'at least now they know it's an attack') and applies Michael Walzer's five conditions to define Marco Inaros' terrorism: deliberate harm to randomly selected innocents, meant to terrify a cohort into political change, as in Marco's 'crossroads in human history' broadcast. This yields the terrorist's dilemma — justice toward victims versus compassion toward beneficiaries — while Avasarala's opening gravity-torture scene and her 'dirty hands' assign the opponent blame for failing to relieve the oppression that makes terrorism seem a last resort. Lydia's 'churn' ('float to the top or sink to the bottom') and her lesson that one can 'lead a good life without being a good person' explain how Amos and Clarissa redeem each other on the road to Baltimore, whereas Marco, like Arendt's Eichmann, cannot think from anyone else's standpoint ('everything we ever dreamed of'); the chapter ends with Avasarala's proposed Inners-Belters union as her own redemption — 'this is how we win.'
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 29 "Iron Man The End" — The Housels read Iron Man through Butler's gender performativity and Arendt's 'right to have rights': the male-voiced Jarvis replacing the female AI Jocasta, Tony's womanizing, and the evolving corporeal styles of Black Widow, Bethany Cabe, Madame Masque, and Sunset Bain all enact society's gender script across the waves of feminism, with the black leather suit arriving only in 1970 amid Second Wave Feminism. Arendt's Eichmann reporting and the 'banality of evil' — coined the same year, 1963, that Lee, Lieber, Heck, and Kirby, all children of Jewish immigrants, launched Iron Man — supply the justice frame: Tony's transformation of conscience after Afghanistan and his vigilante justice against his own oppressors refuse silent conformity and insist, ignoring political boundaries, that all oppressed people have rights.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 7 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Young argues that South Park is perceived as dangerous for exactly the reasons Socrates was tried and executed in Plato's Apology: both 'corrupt the youth' by mocking religion, questioning authority, and exposing that the supposed teachers (Mr. Garrison's flip-flopping creationism, Mrs. Broflovski's moral panics, the 'Death' boycott of Terrance and Phillip) do not know what they think they know. He diagnoses Cartman as an Eichmann figure whose banal, thoughtless evil—feeding Scott Tenorman his parents, torturing Muslims with farts—consists in the inability to think from another's standpoint, while Kyle and Stan's friendship embodies Arendt's dialogic thinking and Aristotle's mean between ideological extremes, as when they see both the merit and the smugness of hybrid drivers in 'Smug Alert'. Freud's theory that jokes break through repression explains why the show's vulgarity is essential rather than gratuitous: it verbalizes what culture silences so that it can be thought through, making South Park a Socratic gadfly rather than a corrupter.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited,' where SS Captain Lutze is tried by his Dachau victims and driven mad, and 'He's Alive,' where a phantom Hitler grooms the failed neo-Nazi Peter Vollmer, as Serling's two-part response to the Eichmann trial. Setting them against the film Operation Eichmann's monster-Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman, Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, and Serling's hatred of Hogan's Heroes' comic Klink, he traces a maturation: from the Nazi as heartless monster to Arendt's banality of evil, the thoughtless, frustrated everyman. Vollmer, the chapter argues, shows what Lutze's origins were, and remembering the Dachaus is the guard against becoming his like.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann assembles a 'time capsule' of totalitarianism from Twilight Zone and Black Mirror: Vollmer's neo-Nazi rise in 'He's Alive' as Aristotle's rhetoric, persuasion by playing on an audience's anger and fear, weaponized; Marilyn's forced Transformation in 'Number 12 Looks Just Like You' as Eco's Ur-Fascist fear of difference; and Lutze's 'I functioned as I was told' at Dachau as Arendt's banality of evil, the mechanical non-thinking of the Eichmann trial. 'The Waldo Moment' and 'Fifteen Million Merits' then carry the lens to Debord's society of the spectacle, where an empty cartoon bear wins crowds and even Bing's shard-wielding rebellion is instantly commodified into a product. The totalitarianism of screens, the chapter warns, needs no tanks.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 13 "“Haven’t Thought of You Lately at All”" — George Dunn uses Dr. Kinny's mock-prison experiment at Hearst — where 'cool guy' Rafe torments Horshack, even gentle Wallace turns taunting guard, and Mercer perhaps first bonded with his future victim Moe — as a rerun of Zimbardo's Stanford prison experiment, arguing that bad situations and corrupting power, not just bad apples, produce Neptune's villains. Against pure situationism he sets Hannah Arendt's diagnosis that great evil usually requires not wicked hearts but an 'inability to think': Woody Goodman's rehearsed excuses about neglected boys and Mercer's 'I'm just taking what you would have happily given' show wrongdoers rationalizing rather than reflecting. The chapter ends by suggesting the town's gulf between 09-ers and everyone else may be the situational 'apple barrel' breeding the arrogance, entitlement, resentment, and envy behind Neptune's crime wave.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 30 "The Resistance New Humans, New Gods" — Dinello reads Westworld as a totalitarian concentration camp via Arendt's The Origins of Totalitarianism, tracing the hosts' dehumanization through the killing of the juridical person (no rights, 'live without limits'), the moral person (Bernard forced to murder Theresa), and individuality (Peter Abernathy lobotomized). He casts Ford as a mad-scientist dictator modeled on Frankenstein, Moreau, Mengele, and Hitler who plagiarizes John Ford's Westerns, then turns to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth to justify the hosts' revolutionary violence — Maeve as a self-resurrecting 'Lady Lazarus,' Dolores executing Ford and the Delos board — as the birth of a new species that must ultimately unify beyond hatred.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 19 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Hibbs argues that nihilism, a working assumption in neo-noir, turns the noir protagonist's quests pointless, absurd, and thus comic, and that the Coen brothers exemplify this comic response. Using Nietzsche on nihilism, the 'last man', the 'pathos of distance', and aristocratic self-creation, he reads films like The Silence of the Lambs and Cape Fear as celebrating the 'super-antihero'. The Big Lebowski comically levels nihilism (Walter: the German nihilists are 'cowards'; nihilism cannot be lived), while Fargo and Raising Arizona affirm family and fertility, a 'banality of goodness' answering Arendt's banality of evil, letting nature's comedy perpetuate itself.
- **The Philosophy of Spike Lee**, ch. 13 "Monsters and Moralism in Summer of Sam" — Palmer argues Lee's Summer of Sam is less ethnography than moralism about the diffuse 'evil energy' that spreads through an Italian American Bronx enclave during the 1977 Son of Sam killings. Against Dan Flory's reading of the film as a veiled lynching parable, he contends Lee dismantles any clean line between the psychopath Berkowitz and his supposed innocent victims: the vigilantes become victimizers, punk outsider Richie doubles the killer through his violent stage act, and Vinny destroys himself through compulsive infidelity. Evil is shown as symptomatic of a whole social order in decline rather than located in one monster.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 18 "9. Foundation’s Optimism" — McCrossin reads the sequels Foundation's Edge and Foundation and Earth as an Optimistic response to the problem of evil, in the lineage of Leibniz, Rousseau, and Hegel's 'All is well', set against the WWII, Holocaust, Nuremberg, and Eichmann-trial backdrop of Asimov's writing and Arendt's banality of evil. Tracking Gendibal's mantra 'all will happen well', the Gaia/Galaxia choice via Trevize's 'talent for rightness', and Daneel Olivaw's Zeroth Law and plan to merge with Fallom's brain, he uses the Book of Job to frame whether the series' recurring reassurance is earned or merely reframed.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 9 "The Talking Cure for Our Culture" — Young argues that South Park, like Socrates in Plato's Apology, is accused of corrupting youth and impiety but is really a philosophical gadfly. Kyle and Stan reach moral conclusions (e.g., refusing to kill Stan's grandfather) through Socratic questioning and dialogue, while Cartman's thoughtless, imitative cruelty mirrors Arendt's banality of evil in Eichmann. Young reads the show's vulgarity through Freud, arguing its crude jokes release repressed drives so we can examine them, making the show a Socratic 'talking cure' for a mindless culture.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 33 "20. The Totalitarian Zone" — Altmann traces totalitarianism from The Twilight Zone into Black Mirror. 'He's Alive' shows Vollmer wielding Aristotle's rhetoric to grow a Nazi movement; 'Number 12' shows Umberto Eco's fascist 'fear of difference'; 'Deaths-Head Revisited' illustrates Arendt's banality of evil in Lutze's 'just following orders.' He then argues Black Mirror episodes ('The Waldo Moment,' 'Fifteen Million Merits') realize Guy Debord's 'society of the spectacle' and hyper-capitalism, where politics becomes entertainment and even resistance is commodified—a totalitarianism that needs no tanks.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "Broadcast Dystopia" — Foy and Dale read the Bachman dystopias The Running Man and The Long Walk through Hannah Arendt's distinction between power (collective coordination) and violence (coercion by implements), arguing King's states substitute broadcast spectacle for genuine power and so hemorrhage legitimacy the more violence they apply. The gladiatorial Games Network and the Walk pacify the masses while chants of 'KILL HIM' sever the affective bonds of humanity. The chapter invokes Arendt's Eichmann-in-Jerusalem 'banality of evil' to explain the soldiers, Hunters, and cheering citizens as ordinary people uncritically 'doing their jobs,' and reads Ben Richards's suicide flight into the Games Building and Garraty's exhausted walk as futile personal revolts that change nothing.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 30 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Gray gives a psychological account of Ted Bundy and Dennis Rader (BTK), stressing that serial killers are ordinary-seeming — Arendt's banality of evil — and are psychopaths, not psychotics: rational, remorseless, genetically shaped, unable to learn conditioned fear, and guided by scripted fantasies of domination. He reads their pursuit of control as Nietzsche's will to power, citing Bundy's manipulation of preacher James Dobson and Rader's cold courtroom allocution. But he argues the psychopath is a failed, unnatural predator, not Nietzsche's ubermensch: lacking vision and moral self-discipline, he only masters deceit in service of petty, narrow fantasies.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 31 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Piven mounts an 'epistemology of murder,' invoking Hume and Nietzsche to argue that most of what we 'know' about serial killers and terrorists is projected fantasy and prejudice, amplified by fear (Terror Management Theory). Rereading Lord of the Flies and the Milgram studies, he claims violence follows from shame, humiliation, and abuse (Athens's 'violentization') rather than innate evil, and uses Freud's fort-da game and repetition compulsion to argue killers displace their own woundedness and 'soul murder' onto surrogate victims. He controversially links serial killers, who sexualize death and merge with victims, to terrorists who sanctify displaced sexual rage as God's will — a 'serial killer in sheik's clothing.'
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "Who is Who" — Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.
