Her flexible, relational problem-solving (the lighter-sprinkler trick against the Facehuggers, learning the pulse rifle) beats Gorman's mission-first command, and the trolley-style arithmetic she rejects when the one on the tracks is her little girl is not a moral failing; even nuking the Queen's eggs raises Singer-style speciesism questions.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 21 "A Professional, a Mother, and Someone Who Cares" — Asks whether Ripley is a feminist and answers 'only sometimes': her quarantine refusal ('Yes, I read you. The answer is negative') and her reasons for killing the Alien3 specimen ('a lot of innocent people will die') invoke rules, chain of command, and anonymous future victims - Kohlberg's post-conventional reasoning, not Gilligan's care voice - whereas the hot-chocolate scene with Newt and the unhesitating hive rescue exhibit the care-focused feminism of Gilligan and Noddings. Against the status-oriented reading of Vasquez's 'have you ever been mistaken for a man?' exchange, Ripley emerges as atypical of either stereotype: a professional, a mother, and someone who cares.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads ATLA through the feminist ethics of care, using Joan Tronto's phases of caring-about, taking care of, and care-giving to analyze Katara: freeing Aang from the iceberg, offering to heal Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, and her full arc as the Painted Lady feeding, healing, and freeing a polluted village. Care also misfires ('Imprisoned') and is devalued as feminine 'women's work' when Toph calls Katara motherly ('The Runaway'), a myth the chapter rejects. Care scales politically too: the Gaang's defeat of Fire Nation imperialism is care repairing the world, while Azula's indifference to Ty Lee and Mai marks her villainy.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 21 "Repairing Our Worlds" — Fice reads Katara through Joan Tronto's care ethics, tracking the phases in episodes: 'caring about' the refugees on 'The Serpent's Pass' and Zuko's scar in the Crystal Catacombs, 'taking care of' in freeing Aang from the iceberg, and 'care-giving' in 'The Painted Lady,' where she feeds, heals, and cleans up a polluted factory town. Care misfires are part of the theory, as when she pushes Haru to earthbend in 'Imprisoned' and gets him arrested, and Toph's 'motherly' jab lets the chapter reject the myth that care is essentially feminine, citing bell hooks. The larger claim is political: the Gaang's war against Fire Nation imperialism is care at world scale, repairing the world so its people can live well.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 30 "What Not to Do as a Parent" — The chapter pinpoints Marie's failure in Arkangel using Feinberg's parental-rights framework: by filtering out every fright (the neighbor's dog, her father's stroke) she violated Sara's right to an open future, misconstrued her welfare and protection rights, and stunted the empathy that makes a child a fully functioning human being. Aristotle's golden mean frames over-parenting as a vice of excess — as damaging as neglect — and Ruddick's maternal ethics of care also convicts Marie, since mothering requires fostering growth and social acceptability, not just preserving life. The Philip K. Dick comparison lands the conclusion: an android is distinguished from a human only by lacking empathy, so Marie has manufactured a partial android rather than raised a child.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 31 "Learning from Mia’s Mistakes" — The chapter grades each of Mia's escalations in Crocodile — helping Rob hide the cyclist's body, killing Rob fifteen years later, then killing Shazia, her husband, and baby Ali to keep the secret — under Kant's categorical imperative (the cover-up cannot be universalized and treats persons as means), the utilitarian calculus (which also condemns every killing once the widow's suffering and Mia's guilt are counted), and feminist care ethics, which rejects her defense that she killed to protect her family because care obligations never cancel proportionality and others' rights. Aristotle's virtue ethics supplies the diagnosis: Mia's undoing is lack of practical wisdom — every split-second choice (which she never had time to deliberate) went wrong because she lacked virtuous habits. The chapter urges practicing everyday virtue so we never take the first step down her path.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 17 "How Far I'll Go" — Maps the four waves of feminism onto Disney princess history: Snow White, Cinderella, and Aurora as chattel passed from parents to fairies to princes, betraying even first-wave rights; Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman' and Friedan's feminine mystique explaining why the original trio's happiness is measured by marriage. Third-wave princesses are read with Wolf's beauty myth (Ariel and Jasmine as iron maidens), Butler's gender performativity, and Gilligan's care ethics (Ariel's and Belle's contextual, caring moral reasoning versus their fathers' principles). The fourth-wave princesses from Tiana to Moana need no man at all while male leads (Naveen, Flynn, Kristoff, Maui) become vulnerable sidekicks, ending with #GiveElsaAGirlfriend and the thought that equality is balance rather than sameness.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 17 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Olson's first D&D Encounters session handed her a sexualized female miniature in a chainmail bikini and high-heeled boots, and the chapter audits the game as a feminist would: research on the 'token girl' and male-default storytelling, women like Dowsett pushed to play male characters to be taken seriously, and harassment ranging from 'date at least one of the party or bring food' to condescension toward women in the industry. Against this she argues the rules themselves are egalitarian — identical power pools for male and female characters, embodying Plato's Republic claim that women 'are by nature the same with respect to guarding the city', and even the evil deities are stereotyped symmetrically (scheming Lolth and Tiamat versus war-god patrons of power) — while the collaborative party structure (clerics healing strikers, shared goals) has exactly the care-ethical, anti-individualist flavor Friedman and Bolte attribute to women's moral perspectives. Sexism is thus a consequence of unreflective practices, marketing that ignores women, and industry culture rather than the game; all-female systems like Portal Worlds are a real response but, she worries, separatism risks deepening the divide.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 37 "Notes" — Opening from the author's own grief — she nearly stopped playing Fallout 4 because its murdered spouse and kidnapped son echoed the loss of her real infant son — the chapter applies the ethics of care of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto to Fallout's wasteland. Care relationships structure the games: the Fallout 3 father whose flight from Vault 101 propels the plot, Dogmeat's loyal responsiveness as relational reciprocity, and the Fallout 4 son Shaun, where caring for your child collides with caring for a Commonwealth his Institute endangers. Settlement-building, faction choice (Lyons's Brotherhood handing out clean water versus the Railroad's liberation of synths), and even the Black Widow perk path that saves Megaton all become care-laden moral acts — care as protest against the wasteland's ethos of bare survival.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 28 "15. Chidi’s Indecision" — Surveys the 'Big Three' through the show: Kantian deontology (Chidi's boots lie, Tahani's mere-means charity), Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism (Jason's alligator frame-up, the trolley simulation), and Aristotle's golden mean (courage between Jason's rashness and Chidi's paralyzed deficiency), arguing their shared rationalism cannot accommodate the real uncertainty Chidi feels. John Dewey's 'Three Independent Factors in Morals' — the Good, the Right, and the Virtuous as irreducible — explains why Chidi sees only binaries while Eleanor finds 'option C' and imagines the Medium Place. The chapter concludes the show's unstated moral theory is care ethics: relational selves, justified partiality toward friends, and moral growth through the experience of being cared for, as when Chidi models care rather than lecturing it.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 11 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Donovan and Richardson read the Maltusian split, with the male Guardians banning emotion through the Book of Oa on Oa and the female Zamarons leaving to found the violet light of love on Zamaron, as the Western association of men with reason and women with emotion. They deploy Gilligan's different-voice reply to Kohlberg, the Pythagorean table of opposites via Genevieve Lloyd, Hegel's exclusion of women from the public sphere, and Jaggar's liberal-feminist critique of 'ahistorical' reason, whose comic-book analogue is the third law banning relationships between Lanterns. The chapter ends by arguing the standoff is a false dichotomy the comics themselves begin to dissolve: Kyle's 'Lanterns with heart' speech to the Guardians, the repeal of the third law, and the Indigo Tribe's plan to recombine the seven corps into the white light of creation.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 28 "NOTES" — Reads the show's eclipse icon against Plato's sun of the good — goodness has become hard to discern — and tests four theories of evil on the characters: Socrates' claim that no one errs knowingly is half-confirmed since villains like Angela and Nathan always take themselves to be doing right; Aristotle's akrasia and vice as an excess or deficiency of disposition fit Sylar's blood-scrawled 'Forgive me' apartment and his uncontrolled hunger; and Nietzsche's Übermensch and pre-Christian master morality raise the uncomfortable question of why Sylar preying on inferiors is not heroic like Achilles. The chapter's endorsed answer is Gilligan's ethics of care: the heroes are good because they care — Matt for Molly and Daphne, Bennet for Claire — while evil is the absence of care, though Bennet's authoritarian, family-only care shows that care itself must be both widened and restrained.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 29 "NOTES" — Explains the seemingly incomprehensible things Heroes characters do for family by sorting their motives into three theories of family obligation: universal justice (framed by Socrates confronting Euthyphro for prosecuting his own father), care ethics' partiality to loved ones, and Confucian role-based duty with its asymmetrical parent–child, husband–wife, and sibling obligations. Noah Bennet turns out to be Confucian in practice ('I'm your father, Claire Bear') despite his universalist Company rhetoric, Hiro defies Kaito's Confucianism for the greater good while Kaito still teaches him the sword because that is a father's role, Niki and Janice act from care while D.L. and Micah act from roles, Mohinder's duty is Confucian sonship to his dead father, and the Haitian kills his own brother Baron precisely because stopping him is his brotherly role.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 22 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Averill argues that Katniss's morality is built on care for particular people rather than impartial principle: she volunteers for Prim, protects Rue because the girl resembles her sister, and spares a wounded District 2 soldier at the Nut because he recalls her father and the Seam. Measured against Kant's impartial justice perspective (embodied by Thresh sparing Katniss to repay a debt to Rue), she falls short — but Gilligan's care perspective and Noddings's distinction between natural and ethical caring recast this as a valid, even heroic, moral development. Using Noddings, the chapter traces Katniss's arc from natural care for Prim toward ethical care for strangers and even enemies, and reads her assassination of Coin as care for all of Panem's future children rather than revenge. Care, the chapter concludes, can even justify violence when it protects the vulnerable.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 14 "5 Feminism and Indiana Jones A Field Guide" — Kate Schmidt applies feminist media tests (Bechdel, sexy lamp, Mako Mori, Pierce, Landau) to show the films usually fail — Willie is a screaming prop and human shield in Temple, the eyelid-writing student exists only to display Indy's sex appeal, and all four films fail the Bechdel Test — while Marion, Spalko, and above all Elsa in The Last Crusade are mixed cases with partial autonomy. Drawing on Iris Marion Young's account of women as Other and Carol Gilligan's care ethics, she argues Crusade is the series' most feminist film not for its women but for its men: Indy's open hurt after Elsa's betrayal and the father-son reconciliation embody care ethics against 'boys don't cry' toxic masculinity. She concludes that one can love flawed media without endorsing its sexism.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Kolb reads the whole franchise through Carol Gilligan's ethics of care and the ecofeminism of Ariel Salleh and Mary Mellor: Max begins as a caregiver in an egalitarian marriage, Toecutter's gang and the Citadel embody toxic masculinity, and Aunty Entity shows women can administer patriarchal capitalism too. In Fury Road, 'We are not things,' the milking mothers, and water branded as Aqua Cola literalize Salleh's claim that capitalist patriarchy treats women and nature as resources. The Vuvalini, the Keeper of the Seeds, Max washing in mother's milk, and his voluntary blood transfusion to Furiosa enact the ethic of care as the film's saving alternative to domination.
- **Mad Men and Philosophy - Nothing Is as It Seems**, ch. 24 "“To a Place Where We Know We Are Loved”" — Myers grades the moral development of the Sterling Cooper cast with Kohlberg's justice stages and Gilligan's ethics of care in order to find Aristotelian friendships, which require equals in moral development who wish each other good for the other's sake. Don and Peggy emerge as moral equivalents, each hiding a dark secret (the stolen identity; the baby given away) and each having done for the other what no one else could, from the hospital visit ('Move forward') to Don's 'nobody understands that, but you do' recruitment pitch; Joan and Roger form a second pair whose mutual esteem survives his marriage to Jane and her departure, shown when he trusts her to build Sterling Cooper Draper Pryce. Closing with Aristotle's claim that friendship holds states together, the chapter gives the new agency a better-than-average chance because these friendships are 'not for sale.'
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 26 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Frames the show's tension between the masculine public sphere (the chapel table, guns, club politics) and the feminine domestic sphere that actually sustains life, using Aristotle's oikos/polis division and Arendt's The Human Condition on the public/private realms. Gemma, dismissed as 'just an old lady,' proves the private sphere's power: she brought the club to Charming, orchestrates Jax's rise to the presidency, and converts her rape by Weston's LOAN goons into family solidarity that puts Jax's VP patch back on. Gilligan's and Baier's ethics of care then reads Lyla's abortion as a caring choice about family size, Tara's 'my job as your old lady is to be strong when and where you can't be' as care turned to strength, and Gemma's care curdling into retributive justice against Clay.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 26 "Notes" — Argues Star Trek functions like the Greek myths Nussbaum describes: modern tales of transformation (Gary Mitchell in "Where No Man Has Gone Before", Charlie X, Roger Korby) that let audiences judge what makes someone human. It rejects the Cartesian reading (Richard Hanley's Is Data Human?) in which Data's humanity is just a matter of being a rational mind, and develops instead a feminist, developmental account of personhood drawn from Annette Baier: persons are "second persons" who learn the arts of personhood from caretakers. Data, Seven of Nine, and Voyager's Doctor, all lacking real childhoods and families, must learn play, touch, love, and interdependence from their crews, with Janeway modeling family for Seven and Kes socializing the Doctor. Picard's farewell to Shinzon in Nemesis and to Data's B-4 caps the claim that humanity is an achievement of self-improvement in relationship, not a fixed essence.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 35 "“So, What Happens If You Take That Thing Off ”" — Ebner charts Din Djarin's moral development from a rights-based frame - hierarchy, Guild rules, 'I can bring you in warm, or I can bring you in cold' - to Carol Gilligan's ethics of care, a shift catalyzed by Kuiil's lessons ('You can trade', 'I have spoken') and completed by the Child. He re-reads Gilligan's pharmacy dilemma through 'The Sin', where Mando hijacks a speeder droid at gunpoint, and 'The Marshal', where trading with Cobb Vanth recasts the armor dispute as responsibility toward a threatened town rather than a contest of rights. Djarin's helmet decisions - refusing Omera, unmasking for Mayfeld's facial scan, and finally removing the helmet to say goodbye to Grogu - track his metamorphosis from rules and entitlements to responsibilities and relationships.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Young uses bell hooks's patriarchal masculinity (with Kate Manne on misogyny as enforcement) to read the show: Jamie is patriarchal terror's product, Rupert's promiscuity and Rebecca's subjection are two sides of male control, and Roy Kent's 'hard man' persona inherits the hardness Nietzsche praised and philosophy's traditional suspicion of emotion. Against this, hooks's definition of love as the will to nurture spiritual growth explains Ted's coaching, the training-room exorcism's shared vulnerability, Sam's openness, and Nate's status-hunger as the struggle to invert the gender pyramid, ending with Nate refusing Rupert's poisoned patriarchal gifts.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 32 "Notes" — This multi-author epilogue collects short 'cutting-room-floor' reflections on poignant WoT quotes. Cooke reads Ingtar's confession as the existential fear of historical oblivion (historia as both history and story) driving a patriot into Darkfriendship. DeVan uses Covril's oak-and-wind metaphor to argue arguments strengthen through opposition, marshaling Confucius, Proverbs, al-Kindi, Milton, and Socrates's unexamined life. Held reads Min's arranged-marriage counsel with Nietzsche's amor fati and Epictetus's Heracles to reject resentment of unchosen fate. Pike reads Nynaeve sentencing the sul'dam through Carol Gilligan's and Annette Baier's ethics of care versus obligation (care can judge more harshly, per C.S. Lewis). Xhignesse reads the oak-and-willow line as Aesop woven into Randland's background.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Johnson-Moxley tests Perez's lasso of truth - which makes people face truths about themselves, like being dragged from Plato's cave - against four ethical touchstones: Kantian duty (truth-telling as a perfect duty, respect for autonomy), utilitarianism, virtue ethics, and care ethics. Cases drive the argument: binding Ares so he sees his apocalypse annihilates what he rules, freeing Vanessa from Dr. Psycho's false memories only with her permission, and lashing two warlords into 'twins of pain' to end bloodshed. She concludes via Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity that compelling truth is justified only to restore someone's rational self-direction, never paternalistically, with Gandhi's satyagraha ('truth-force') as the model of active, compassionate truth-telling.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Bein argues Wonder Woman uniquely fuses two supposedly incompatible moralities: bushido - Nitobe's eight samurai virtues, Sun Tzu's benevolence of ending war swiftly, worthy-opponent rituals mirrored in superhero costumes - and the feminist ethics of care Gilligan and Noddings built against a Western canon (Aristotle, Kant) that called women too emotional for morality. Wonder Woman's killing of Maxwell Lord to free Superman is re-read as the care-ethical beach case: saving your own child over a stranger's is not a failure of impartiality, and in his Gotham-versus-Themyscira invasion thought experiment she would defend Gotham because its people are vulnerable non-combatants, not because a utilitarian ledger favors it.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 31 "Notes" — Chavez, Gavaler, and Goldberg trace Marston's 'Love Leader' kink - bracelets of submission, Venus girdles, Paradise Island bondage games, Earth One's collaring of Steve Trevor - to nineteenth-century maternalist feminism, then map the care ethics of Gilligan, Noddings, and Tronto onto both the comic and real-world BDSM. Reform (later Transformation) Island embodies a care-based alternative to punishment: rather than retribution, von Gunther and Irene are transformed by loving authority into people who save their captors, and Wonder Woman rescues the drowning villain Eviless because 'Aphrodite's Law commands us to save lives always - enemies or not.' The BDSM community's 4Cs (consent, communication, caring, caution) turn out to be Tronto's four elements of care, so the good dominant just is the good care-giver.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 14 "Fifth Hole How Golf Builds and Shapes Moral Character" — Beller and Stoll ask why empirical moral-reasoning research finds that sport generally does not build character, yet golfers score highest of all athletes. Using Aristotle's account of right conduct and Lickona's triad of moral knowing, feeling, and acting, they argue character forms through role models, social environment, and cognitive dissonance, supported by neuroplasticity research on the brain's capacity for moral growth. They contrast golf's self-policing tradition (Bobby Jones, Meg Mallon, Greg Norman, the film Bagger Vance) with the gamesmanship coached in team sports, and address Gilligan's 'different voice' by reporting that female golfers reason at least as highly as males, concluding that golf's honor-bound moral community sets it apart.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 23 "11. The Mother of All Bombs" — Kolb argues Laura Palmer embodies the 'Angel in the House' ideal (Gilbert and Gubar) whose perfection is a beautiful dead girl, and reads The Return's linkage of the Trinity bomb to BOB/Judy through Arendt's On Violence—violence begets a more violent, hostile world that especially victimizes women. Using Gilligan's In a Different Voice, she shows how women's voices (Naido/Diane, the Log Lady, Laura's diary) are silenced by toxic masculinity (Mr. C, Richard, Chad), while the 'good men' embody an ethic of care; the manufactured post-war social order names its bombs after mothers and treats women as perfect-yet-fallen others.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 17 "A Spielbergian Ethics of the Family in Saving Private Ryan and The Color Purple" — Clewis defines a 'Spielbergian ethics of the family,' a care-based virtue ethics holding that we owe unique obligations to family and close friends grounded in personal identity, and contrasts it with utilitarian and Kantian approaches. In Saving Private Ryan the squad-as-family and the Ryan brotherhood explain why Miller says Ryan must 'earn this' and why living an ordinary good life suffices; in The Color Purple sisterhood (Nettie/Celie), fatherhood, and motherhood ground obligations of care, forgiveness, and reconciliation. He evaluates the view's feasibility while warning it neglects wider social influences and the is/ought gap.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Laura Geuy Akers argues the Doctor lives by a relational ethics of care rather than deontology, utilitarianism, or virtue ethics. Drawing on Noddings's care ethics and Buber's I-Thou versus I-It stance, she shows the Doctor responds to particular others (insisting the Ood is "a he, not an it," addressing each companion individually before surrender) and even ethically cares for the Master. She pairs this with Nussbaum's and Kant's accounts of wonder and the sublime, arguing the Doctor's human companions (Rose, Martha, Donna) restore his sense of wonder and give his immortal life meaning.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Renee Kyle contrasts Dr. House's detached 'doctor knows best' justice ethic with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, sees patients as embedded in social networks, and refuses to deceive or bully (as with Ezra and the newborns in 'Maternity'), whereas House treats patients as abstract puzzle-pieces. Kyle also voices the feminist worry that valorizing care can lead women to care at personal cost, as when Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 17 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nease lays out a game plan for raising ethical children, using Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics – eudaimonia as a flourishing life, virtue as the mean between extremes, and the master-skills of practical wisdom and self-control – as the core, mocking 'character counts' posters as no substitute for early habit-formation. He folds in Kant's motive of duty, Nietzsche's will-to-power (glossed via Janet Jackson's Control) as the drive to master oneself, and argues empathy (Theodor Lipps' inner imitation), self-awareness, concentration (Husserl's foreground/background), and a respect for justice must be cultivated to 'stack the deck' toward a good adult.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 18 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Terjesen defends a distinctively paternal form of caring against care ethics' maternal bias. Reviewing Kohlberg's moral-development scale, Gilligan's justice-vs-care orientations, and Noddings' 'engrossment' model of caring, he argues these frameworks make it seem fathers like his own undemonstrative Norwegian dad don't care. He reconceives 'paternalism' (via Gerald Dworkin's soft paternalism and examples like Darth Vader and Bambi's father) as tough-love caring focused on the child's future self, complementary to maternal caring and distinct from the impersonal justice orientation.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 25 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Mattern argues the heart of good fatherhood is mercy – 'faithful, compassionate love' – as an attitude of the heart, not a technique. Drawing on Aquinas's account of habitus and his ranking of mercy among the greatest virtues, plus Gabriel Marcel's 'creative fidelity,' Solovyov, Jean Vanier, and Karol Wojtyla on love as affirming another's value, he contrasts remote, justice-oriented fathers with empathic ones. He illustrates with overlapping Venn-diagram circles of father and child and with responding to his 7-year-old son's shoplifting through listening and repair rather than spanking.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "MOTHERHOOD" — Chris Mulford, a nurse and lactation consultant, analyzes infant feeding as an ethical question of rights, duties, and responsibilities, drawing on a feminist ethic of care and the claim that women learn empathy through caregiving (linked to oxytocin's role in birth and nursing). She argues that the right at stake is the mother-child dyad's 'protection from interference' with breastfeeding, that no mother is saddled with a solitary duty to breastfeed, and that the duty toward breastfeeding falls on the whole community; she frames the mother's dependency on 'the kindness of strangers' via A Streetcar Named Desire and the innate 'breast crawl.'
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 35 "You’re Basically “a Stuffed Animal Made by Grandma”" — Kyle contrasts House's detached, impartial "ethic of justice" with Dr. Cameron's feminist ethic of care, drawn from Carol Gilligan's In a Different Voice. Cameron builds trusting relationships, refuses to deceive patients, and attends to their social networks — letting parents hold their dying baby in "Maternity," defending Ezra's autonomy in "Informed Consent." But Kyle also presses the standard critique that valorizing care can cost the carer: Cameron's own grief over her dead husband derails her professional judgment in "Acceptance" and pushes her toward Houselike tactics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 16 "14. The Doctor as Philosopher The Collectivist-Realist Pacifism of the Doctor and the Quest for Social Justice" — Smithka argues the Doctor is a 'collectivist-realist pacifist': morally opposed to war yet willing, as a last resort, to use lethal force for social justice. She places the Doctor on Cady's warism-to-pacifism continuum (past absolute and collectivist pacifism), augmenting it with Martin Luther King Jr.'s realist pacifism — ethical appeals 'undergirded by constructive coercive power' — and Gandhi's ahimsa and belief that no one is beyond redemption (the Doctor sparing Davros, offering enemies a choice). She tests Kant's duty ethics and respect for persons (Rule 1: the Doctor lies), Ross's prima facie duties, Mill's utilitarianism ('The Fires of Pompeii,' 'The Beast Below'), Gilligan/Noddings care ethics, and Wolterstorff's 'life of needs,' and reads 'The Day of the Doctor' as a Rawlsian veil of ignorance brokering Zygon-human peace.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 27 "25. The Mandalorian as Philosophy “This Is the Way”" — The chapter argues that The Mandalorian defends virtue ethics with care as the primary virtue. It maps Mando's creed and 'Canons of Honor' (strength, honor, loyalty, death) onto Stoicism's discipline of desire and cardinal virtues, quoting Marcus Aurelius and Seneca, and reads his transformation after adopting Grogu as Aristotelian moral development toward eudaimonia and flourishing. Using Stocker's critique of impartialist ethics and Noddings's and Slote's ethics of care, Belluomini argues Mando's caring relation with Grogu, his engrossment and motivational displacement, and his removing his helmet at the end show that care ranks highest among the virtues and should guide our own 'Way.'
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### The Look (hell is other people)

The Look is Sartre's analysis of what happens when another person's gaze turns me into an object in their world, revealing that I exist not only for myself but also for others. Being seen can bring shame or self-consciousness, because the other apprehends me as a fixed thing over which I have no control, and I in turn objectify them. This conflict of freedoms lies behind the famous line "hell is other people," expressing how our being is perpetually contested in the presence of other subjects.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 16 "No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others" — Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 20 "The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose" — Gines reads hip hop's sexual imagery through Black feminist thought - Tupac's feud with C. Delores Tucker over "Wonder Why They Call U Bitch", Patricia Hill Collins's controlling images of the jezebel and welfare mother, bell hooks on the slave-rooted devaluation of Black womanhood, Nelly's "Tip Drill" video with a credit card swiped between a woman's buttocks, Jay-Z's "Big Pimpin'". Applying Sartre's keyhole gaze from Being and Nothingness and his Anti-Semite and Jew point about hierarchical societies, she argues the gaze under racism and sexism is non-reciprocal - women are seen without seeing - and that Lil' Kim's reversal of it reinforces rather than subverts the stereotypes; Butler's gender performativity then frames the closing Sartrean choice of authenticity or inauthenticity, Nas's "I Can" and "the life we choose."
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider use the mockumentary camera of The Office (British and American versions) as Sartre's Look: Pam caught gazing at Jim and Karen in "The Merger" stages shame at being fixed as an object by the Other, while David Brent's bragging over his Inside Paper cover is pride as bad faith, an attempt to control the Other's gaze that requires denying the employee's freedom. Dwight and Angela's furtive affair and the Michael-Jan speakerphone call in "Cocktails" illustrate Foucault's panopticon: the mere possibility of the camera makes characters police themselves. The viewer, positioned behind the lens, becomes complicit in the objectifying Look that constitutes the show's comedy of embarrassment.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 6 "What Do We Hear when We Listen to Our iPods" — Wittkower opens with his cat Wallace at the window to show hearing is selective, then applies Sartre's account of the Look -- the voyeur at the keyhole hearing a footstep, the other as a 'void within being' -- to ask when sounds announce another person, the iPod-era rustle becoming the sudden 'appearance of a face.' Drawing on Marx's early claim that our senses are socially estranged, so that we meet others only as waiters, clerks, and price tags ('we are not our khakis'), he argues the audio cocoon both limits and enables encounter: mostly we hear our own identity reflected back ('I am the kind of person who listens to Amy Winehouse'). The governing image is Odysseus lashed to the mast, hearing the Sirens without being able to act, and the chapter closes by rehabilitating Marx as the first philosopher of technology alongside Heidegger, Dewey, Lukacs, Adorno, and Habermas.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 12 "Rise and Shine It’s On Again Off Again" — Surber proposes Kristeva's 'abject aesthetics' as the new pair of shades that makes Radiohead legible: 'Creep' expresses abjection (the creep excluded even from recognition by the beautiful people), the android of 'Paranoid Android' is a borderline phenomenon neither human nor machine, and the bodily imagery of 'Bones', 'My Iron Lung', and the corpse in 'Knives Out' enacts the eruption of the pre-linguistic, formless abject, as do Donwood's dissolving Kid A letters. He contrasts the Beatles' aesthetics of psychedelic transcendence and Pink Floyd's existentialist aesthetics of alienation — built on Sartre's 'Hell is other people' gaze and the being-for-itself/being-in-itself split — with Radiohead's fluid, boundary-less world where meanings never come into focus and no existential revolt is possible because the embodied self is part of the world. Against the charge of nihilism, he reads Hail to the Thief and In Rainbows ('How come I end up where I started?') as postmodern reconstruction: if boundaries and meanings are fluid, they can also be remade.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 3 "index" — This file spans book chapters 4-11. Elizabeth Losh reads Facebook games (Zombies, Mob Wars, Scrabulous, Parking Wars, PackRat, (Lil) Green Patch) through Goffman's 'face', Brown and Levinson's politeness, and Derrida's gift-obligation, showing that aggressive games can be played politely while altruistic ones coerce; Jeremy Sarachan analyzes profile pictures through Barthes's studium, punctum and 'air' and Benjamin's mechanical reproduction (the webcam image that has no original). Mimi Marinucci pairs Glaucon's Ring of Gyges with Suler's online disinhibition effect to argue that Facebook's forced integration of audiences (students, colleagues, Mom all reading one profile) suppresses 'fronting' and so can foster authentic self-expression; Mariam Thalos answers with Sartre's analysis of the gaze and Beauvoir's woman-as-Other that the elective, endlessly plastic profile cannot anchor the bonding only face-to-face encounter provides - hence 'Why I Am Not a Friend' - while Wandel and Beavers use Groundhog Day's Phil Connors and Goffman's presentation of self to defend identity play as real self-discovery, and Vejby and Wittkower ask whether Facebook is Debord's Spectacle 2.0 or a platform for Situationist detournement. Finally, Craig Condella measures 'friending' against Aristotle's three friendships and Cicero's 'handmaid of virtue' (via the Seinfeld episode where Keith Hernandez asks Jerry to help him move), and Matthew Tedesco sets 322 Facebook friends against Godwin's burning archbishop to press the utilitarian impartiality challenge, deploying Williams's 'one thought too many' shipwreck case and criticizing Frank Jackson's sector-plan defense of partiality.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 36 "Bad or Bad Faith" — Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 41 "The Scanner-Self" — The chapter identifies Kant's deeper, non-experiencing self, the pure organizer of data behind ordinary experience, as 'a Kantian scanner', then maps the police scanners planted in Arctor's house onto Sartre's analysis of the gaze: another's look downgrades you from observing-subject to observed object, and God's all-penetrating stare would strip you of subjectivity and freedom entirely. Arctor's relentless surveillance culminates in Bruce, the identity-less pure watcher, the scanner-self incarnate, with a closing joke that Facebook profiles are how 'we see ourselves through a profile darkly.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 26 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Round argues the real horror of The Walking Dead is humanity itself, read through existentialism: walkers cannot choose, so the humans who attack, torture, and steal from each other are the true 'zombie Other.' She traces Rick's self-made, revisable moral code — from law-enforcer to 'You kill? You die' to killing Dexter — as authentic situation-based morality, paralleled with Kierkegaard's Abraham and with Abraham Ford's confession 'I did what I wanted to do' set against Eugene's bad-faith 'I did what I had to do.' Suicides like Jim, Jacqui, and Carol embody existential angst before an absurd world, the Governor's Woodbury is an Adorno-style inauthentic hierarchy that manipulates its people, and Rick's 'WE ARE THE WALKING DEAD!' speech uses facticity to insist the group admit what they have already become.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 26 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Reads Larry as a textbook existentialist: his agonizing over trivia ('Doctor?... Pharmacist?') instantiates Heideggerian anxiety and Sartrean anguish, because every choice, even yanking his 5 wood out of a casket in 'The 5 Wood,' proclaims an image of how everyone ought to live. Since existence precedes essence there is no fixed human nature for Larry to appeal to; he must author his values alone, which the chapter says also makes him an optimist ('I'm not an inventor, but I'm an improver'). Larry dispels others' bad faith when he tells Susie she obviously can share the brownie recipe in 'The Benadryl Brownie,' and his baldness crusade, firing the toupee-wearing chef Phil Dunlap in 'The Grand Opening,' is a demand for authenticity about one's facticity. The 'Larry David Stare' is analyzed through Sartre's Look: the squinter tries to inspect another consciousness empirically and necessarily fails, since the other's freedom can never be objectified.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 23 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 16 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James McLachlan splits the Satans of history into 'the Rebel' of Romanticism (Blake, Shelley's turn to Prometheus, the sexy vampires of film) and 'the Asshole' who wants to be God. Using Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the desire to be a complete being, he reads Dracula, Scarface's Tony Montana, and Bond villains as figures who cannot endure the otherness of real persons. With Bohme and especially Schelling's two wills - self-assertion and love of others - he argues evil is a positive, perverted order of pure egoism, and that not even Satan can achieve the total asshole-ness he wants, because selfhood exists only in relation to others.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 21 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Lisa Warenski reads 'Suzanne' as staging a phenomenological account of self-awareness: with Husserl and Merleau-Ponty the body is not an object but the lived first-person perspective - so 'touch a perfect body with a mind' is literal - and with Sartre's keyhole example from Being and Nothingness we become aware of ourselves through the gaze of the other. Developmental psychology's mother as 'magical mirror,' who reflects the child's emerging mind, is connected to Hegel's paradox of recognition, and to Aristotle's and Neera Badhwar's friends as mirrors of the soul. On this basis Suzanne's mind-touch has epistemic value: love reflects you truly and shows you what you might become, whether as Jesus's agape or Suzanne's appreciative philia.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 18 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 27 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Felder stages Sartre against Merleau-Ponty on the mind-body problem and other minds, opening with the shower scene where Taystee's 'you got them TV titties' makes Piper an object under a gaze, as Pornstache's look converts being caught into shame. But Piper pulling her towel back to appraise her own breasts 'sees-with' Taystee, and the audience's access to Piper's feelings shows perception is shared, not solipsistic. Merleau-Ponty's incarnated subjectivity, the flesh of the opening credits' real inmates' eyes, and actors' embodied performances dissolve the problem of other minds that Sartre's alienated subject-object model leaves open.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 25 "11. Louis C.K.’s No-Bullshit Philosophy" — Marie Snyder uses Sartre's existentialism to unpack Louis's Conan monologue about the 'forever empty': with God gone we are condemned to be free, thrown into a world with no ready-made purpose and alone with our choices - which explains both the cellphone distraction economy and the Live in Portland bit that 'even if you're with someone, you're alone.' Authenticity means ruthlessly honest self-awareness and owning every choice with no excuses - Sartre's waiter example, the claim that there is no cowardly temperament, and Louis's refusal to let 'a flaw in the human male' excuse the tits bit or porn masturbation. Since in choosing for ourselves we choose for all humanity, Snyder pairs Sartre's universalized responsibility with Louis's 'act in a way that, if everybody acted that way, things would work out,' and reads intimate others, as in the Sartre-Beauvoir open relationship, as mirrors that reflect us back to ourselves against the connectionless 'we're just cummers' porn culture. Bad faith - self-deception, distraction, blame - is the fallenness Louis keeps diagnosing in his audiences and confessing in himself.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" — Hooke frames the volume through Levinas's claim that the face presents itself from a dimension of transcendence, with Kierkegaard's Abraham, Sartre's existential look, and Beauvoir's faces of the elderly and the second sex in the background, plus Lingis on trust. He shows how TZ masks its deadliest figures with trusted faces — Robert Redford as Death in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's avuncular Pip revealing 'This is the other place!' in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' the witch of 'Jess-Belle,' the gentle Kanamits whose book turns out to be a cookbook — so that proof of trust is nearly impossible and the show has us laughing with the Devil. The Turing test is applied to Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' (clearly in love 'regardless of the organs or hardware beneath'), the slot machine of 'The Fever,' and the aged couple of 'The Trade-Ins,' whose faces silently recognize a lost shared life.
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 19 "8. Tom Petty Didn’t Really Need to Know" — Zelinski and Fallis chart Petty's epistemic arc. His early songs ("I Need to Know," "Fooled Again," "Shadow of a Doubt") crave certainty about lovers' fidelity, a Desmond-free obsession closest to Descartes' quest for certainty beyond doubt, except Petty's problem is other minds, not the external world, and his trust that eyes directly reveal feeling sides with Moore's common-sense perception; Sartre's "hell is other people" names why another free person's future love can never be certain. From Full Moon Fever onward ("Into the Great Wide Open," "Time to Move On," "Learning to Fly") Petty instead embodies Pyrrhonian suspension of judgment and the Buddha's "don't know mind" and Daoist farmer's "we'll see," finding tranquility in uncertainty, craving nothing, flying with eyes open.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 20 "9. Another Wig Underneath" — Cooper argues that the 'vulnerability' Drag Race demands is really a marketable persona, not truth. Working through Butler's Gender Trouble (built on Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but rather becomes a woman'), she concedes drag reveals gender's imitative structure, but shows it also confirms identity: Latrice Royale's padded 'Natural Woman' lip sync reads as authentic, and trans queens like Peppermint and Gia Gunn use drag to articulate womanhood, with Husserl's intersubjectivity invoked to insist that constructed gender is no less real for not being empirical. Willam's edit-spliced 'I'm not acting' breakdown and Shannel's deliberate wig-doff show honesty becoming inconsequential next to spectacle, while Untucked's Interior Illusions Lounge is framed as Sartre's No Exit hell of unending observation. Against RuPaul's 'born naked' self-help nihilism ('identity is a joke'), she ends warning that the show no longer lets Katya take off the chicken suit.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" — Berk compares the show to Sartre's No Exit, where Garcin, Inez, and Estelle are locked in a drawing room as each other's torturers, and notes that Michael's experiment 'in the spirit of Sartre' fails because the four humans befriend and improve each other instead. She then corrects the standard reading: Sartre himself insisted 'Hell is other people' is conditional on twisted, bad-faith relationships of over-dependence on others' judgment, as with Tahani's craving for her parents' approval, and the footnote in Being and Nothingness about a 'radical conversion' to authenticity leaves room for healthy relations. Read this way, the show's message that flawed people can find salvation through each other is compatible with, not a refutation of, Sartre.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 14 "The Grain Can Lead Us to Know Too Much" — The chapter argues that the Grain in The Entire History of You ruins Liam and Ffion's marriage not because the truth is bad but because total transparency destroys trust (via Luhmann), feeds a paranoid cycle where any deleted footage looks like guilt, and strips Fi of authority over her own life story. Goffman, Plessner, and Simmel ground the claim that social masks, tact, and privacy are preconditions of selfhood, while Sartre's 'look' explains Fi's shame when Liam forces her to replay her infidelity and Rousseau explains how dependence on others' gaze makes us unfree. Framed by Foucault's reading of Oedipus as a victim of his own knowledge, it concludes that Liam should have let the past lie — and ends with Byung-Chul Han's transparency society as our own already-arrived trajectory.
- **Black Mirror and Philosophy - Dark Reflections**, ch. 22 "A Black Mirror of Our Anxieties" — Nosedive's star ratings are read as a digital panopticon — Bentham's prison design generalized by Foucault's Discipline and Punish — with China's Zhima Credit and Social Credit Systems showing the 'future is already here.' Rousseau's general will and Plato's ship-of-state frame the tyranny-of-the-majority worry (Chester destroyed by an office mob, Lacie jailed for a wedding toast, post-truth tribalism), which Mill's harm principle rebuts: Lacie's rant harms no one and should not be punished. Sartre's 'look' and No Exit explain Lacie's staged cookie photo ('Heaven!') and her final liberating exchange of insults with her cellmate, while Goffman's masks ground the epistemological worry that digital profiles are performances we nonetheless trust, and Bourdieu's symbolic capital names what the scores actually measure.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 10 "A Hope for the Future" — Reads The Little Mermaid as a step forward from the man-requiring damsels of Snow White and Sleeping Beauty: Ariel reverses the rescue by saving Eric, and Aristotle's 'all men by nature desire to know' is stretched to cover her curiosity about the human world. But Ursula's bargain trading Ariel's voice for legs dramatizes the long history of silenced women (Eve, Pandora, Cassandra, the scold's bridle), and the film's sexy, silent Ariel is exactly what Mulvey's male gaze, built on Sartre's 'the look,' criticizes. Applying Beauvoir's 'one is not born but becomes a woman,' the chapter argues Ariel shows biology is not destiny yet still regresses into needing a man, concluding she is a flawed but real advance toward better heroines.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 30 "16. Is Hell Other People" — Puts the show beside Sartre's No Exit, its acknowledged inspiration: Michael's neighborhood, like Garcin, Inez, and Estelle's drawing room, locks flawed people together to torture each other, but the four humans keep helping each other instead ('we improved each other, and the four of us became a team'). Against the standard reading, it uses Sartre's 1964 preface ('if relations with someone else are twisted... that other person can only be Hell'), the Being and Nothingness footnote about a 'radical conversion' from bad faith to authenticity, and his late remark that 'Heaven is each other' to argue the two works are compatible: other people are Hell only under dependence on their judgment — Season One Tahani's condition — while authentic relationships can succeed.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Chelstrom uses the progression from guided DUPLO builds to free design to argue that autonomy develops in degrees and is relational rather than purely individualist. Kant's self-thinking agent — for whom precepts and formulas are the 'ball and chain' of immaturity — explains Emmet's dependence on Octan's instruction booklets and Lord Business's profit from deference, and Korsgaard's definition frames the individualist autonomy the Master Builders embody. Yet their lone-wolf autonomy fails, and Sartre's look plus Beauvoir's account of woman forced to assume herself as Other explain Wyldstyle/Lucy's deference to others' expectations; Catriona Mackenzie's relational autonomy recasts 'Everything is Awesome' as peers supporting each other's self-development, with Emmet's friendship letting Lucy accept herself.
- **The Office and Philosophy - Scenes from the Unexamined Life**, ch. 22 "The Office and Philosophy" — Applies Sartre's Being and Nothingness to the mockumentary: Pam's bad faith consists in pretending she has no choice between Jim and Roy (her garbled 'I'm not into Jim' conversation with Karen in 'Ben Franklin'), while the camera's Look - Sartre's keyhole peeper caught in the hallway - turns her into an object not of her making when she is caught watching Jim and Karen in 'The Merger', and her shame finally lets her own her feelings. David Brent's pride (posing with his Inside Paper magazine cover) tries to control the Other's look and fails, since the freely respected gaze he craves cannot be extracted; and the ever-possible camera functions as Foucault's panopticon (Bentham's prison design), visible and unverifiable, silencing Jan on speakerphone in 'Cocktails' and forcing Dwight and Angela's 'Don't linger. Break left' choreography, which makes the viewer a complicit co-worker.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 10 "Responsibility" — Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 12 "4. Faces from Another Dimension" — Hooke uses Levinas's account of the face (and Lingis on trust) to read the Zone's faces: the bandaged woman and pig-faced surgeons of 'The Eye of the Beholder' unseat our standards of the normal, while trusted faces are weaponized by Robert Redford's Grim Reaper in 'Nothing in the Dark,' Sebastian Cabot's Satan in 'A Nice Place to Visit,' and the gentle Kanamit of 'To Serve Man.' Alicia's tear in 'The Lonely' and John and Marie Holt's wordless recognition in 'The Trade-Ins' show trust and love exceeding proof or evidence. Sartre's existential look, with Kierkegaard's Abraham and Beauvoir's second sex, frames how a face puts our freedom and trust in question.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 9 "Acknowledgment" — William Irwin diagnoses Neptune, from the 09-ers down to the PCH-ers, with status anxiety (via Alain de Botton's Status Anxiety) and prescribes the Stoic remedy: Epictetus on the insult lying in our judgment rather than the insulter, and Marcus Aurelius, the emperor who chose serenity over vengeance, show how Keith and Veronica ground self-worth in virtue no one can take away. Sartre's 'hell is other people' and the look explain how Veronica is reduced to a dumb blonde and Duncan to a murderer until he flees to Cuba, while Schopenhauer's choice between loneliness and vulgarity frames Mac's switched-at-birth longing, Wallace's basketball-bought status, and Weevil's self-made standing as PCH leader. Irwin closes by offering the show itself as Aristotelian catharsis-through-comedy, art as therapy for the viewer's own status anxiety.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 21 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Schmetkamp reads The Ice Storm through the philosophy of love and Hegelian recognition theory, defending a dialogical model of love (Krebs, Scheler's shared feeling) against union (Plato, Nozick, Solomon) and care (Aristotle, Frankfurt) models. She shows the Hood and Carver families lack autonomy-granting mutual recognition: Ben and Janey's affair is mere egoistic gratification, Elena would surrender her 'I' for a 'we', and Mikey seeks stilled 'molecules' and the Fantastic Four's negative zone. Invoking Sartre's the-look as objectification and shame, she argues Mikey's death finally breaks the ice through empathy and sympathy (Scheler, Stein), as Jim weeps and Elena speaks Ben's name.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — McMahon argues After Hours uses dark comedy to reveal the existential truth that anyone, at any moment, is vulnerable to absurdity. She sets Sartre's account (absurdity as the contingency of existence, fled via bad faith) beside Camus' (absurdity as a feeling born of the clash between human need for order and the world's silence), then maps Paul Hackett's nightmarish SoHo night onto Sartre's Nausea (the ordinary Roquentin overwhelmed by objects and people) and No Exit ('hell is other people'), where others become the mechanism that discloses the absurd. She contends comedy, like horror, exploits our fascination with grim spectacle, and that laughing at absurdity—rather than horrific spectacle—lets audiences acknowledge and manage existential anxiety and still live well.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 12 "4. A Muscle Car and a Mythic Quest" — Huntingford reads Sam and Dean as the Cowboy incarnation of Jung's universal Mythic Hero archetype, their Impala road-trip an odyssey of Campbell's monomyth and Jungian individuation confronting the 'shadow' (Amara as the Darkness). She uses Hegel to cast the brothers' alienation as the start of self-discovery toward absolute knowledge, Kierkegaard to praise their nonconformity over the crowd, and Sartre's 'hell is other people' and freedom-as-otherness to argue the Quest requires killing the false narrative self—Chuck the Trickster—to become free.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 17 "8. Self-Hatred as Identity" — Cash argues that Jimmy and Mike become their Breaking Bad selves through a 'negative self-relation' (a term from Martin Hägglund) rather than Walt's outward resentment. Mike's 'I broke my boy' speech in 'Five-O' shows him internalizing guilt for making Matty 'debase' himself, leaving nothing to live for but stashing money for Kaylee; Jimmy internalizes Chuck's verdict that he is 'Slippin' Jimmy with a law degree, a chimp with a machine gun,' so each success as Saul only confirms the worst image of himself. Cash uses Sartre's Being and Nothingness—that one cannot truly be evil 'for myself' without judging oneself as an other—to argue Jimmy's self-hatred must become unconscious for the Saul mask to become his face.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider use The Office's mockumentary camera to dramatize Sartre's 'the Look' and bad faith. Pam pretends she cannot choose between Roy and Jim (bad faith as being-in-itself), and is shamed when the camera catches her watching Jim and Karen; David Brent's prideful self-promotion tries and fails to control the Other's gaze. They tie the ever-present camera to the Foucault/Bentham panopticon: Jan, Dwight, and Angela police themselves because they might be watched, making the viewer complicit in the workers' existential crises.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 16 "It Worked" — Sander Lee reads Jack, Locke, and Desmond through Sartre's bad faith and authenticity and the objectifying 'Look' (the keyhole example), casting Jack the man-of-science as a Humean skeptic who condemns his father's fatalist evasion of responsibility while Locke's devotion to pushing the button is a Kierkegaardian leap of faith modeled on Abraham and Isaac. Desmond David Hume embodies skepticism yet opens to omens and self-sacrifice; and Lee argues the finale's multi-faith 'church' moves Lost from Sartre's secular existentialism toward Kierkegaard and Buber's I-Thou relation, exemplified by Sawyer and Juliet's redemptive bond and Gandhi-like religious universalism.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 16 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 11 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Winters reads the Zodiac Killer's taunting letters through Sartre's account of 'the look' from Being and Nothingness. He argues Zodiac's letters function like a snapped twig or a lit window: they make Northern Californians experience themselves as seen objects, hunted 'slaves' and pawns in Zodiac's game rather than free subjects. A phenomenological (first-person) analysis of the fear Zodiac induces, and of how his letters restrict the choices available within our facticity, is offered as superior to psychological or analytic accounts for explaining our fascination with the macabre.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 11 "Who is Who" — Focused on the 'Monstrous Other' and the 'base under siege' story, the chapter uses Hegel's master-slave struggle for recognition and Sartre's 'the look' to read Cybermen, the Flood ('Waters of Mars') and the Silurians as Others through which humans define themselves, with Levinas on the face and history. Its final section frames the Doctor and the Master as Gothic doubles of love and strife, using Spinoza's monism, principle of sufficient reason and conatus to argue the power-hungry Master paradoxically fits Spinoza's system better than the order-imposing 'Dark Doctor.'
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 33 "The Viewer and the Look" — Meyer and Schneider read The Office through Sartre's "the Look" and bad faith: the mockumentary camera catches characters as objects, as when Pam is caught gazing at Jim and freezes in shame, or pretends she has no choice about Roy (bad faith). David Brent's prideful posing tries to control the Other's look and fails. They add Foucault's panopticon — Dwight, Angela, and Jan police themselves because the camera might be watching — making the viewer complicit in exposing the employees' existential crises.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 49 "46. The Shawshank Redemption as Philosophy Freedom and Panopticism" — Hooke reads The Shawshank Redemption through two lenses. From Sartre he takes 'hell is other people' and the objectifying look from No Exit and Being and Nothingness — Shawshank's warden and 'sisters' embody a worldly hell of 'never' and 'always' — but argues Andy and Red's friendship, Andy's Mozart broadcast, and the hopeful ending invert Sartre, making freedom the shared warmth of friendship rather than the devouring gaze. From Foucault's Discipline and Punish he reads the prison's shift from spectacle to disciplinary surveillance and solitary confinement as panopticism, extending Foucault's insight that prisons, schools, and hospitals mirror one another (illustrated by his COVID-era campus). He closes with Nietzschean genealogy and redemption through laughter, joy, and giving.

### Objectification

Objectification is the treatment of a person as a mere object or instrument rather than as a being with dignity, autonomy, and a subjectivity of their own. In feminist philosophy it names especially the reduction of a person, most often a woman, to a body or a set of parts valued for the use or pleasure of others, denying full agency and moral standing. Philosophers such as Martha Nussbaum have analyzed it into distinct elements—like instrumentality, denial of autonomy, and fungibility—to clarify when and why treating someone as an object is wrong.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 106 "Unknown" — The chapter catalogues the film's penetration scenes—the Agents' scorpion bug forced through Neo's navel, its bloody extraction, the fetal pod farm and 'birth' down the flush tube, the acupuncture rebuilding, the neck-plug uploads, and finally the bullets he becomes immune to—arguing that Neo's arc ends in a perfect, closed body with no vulnerability and no relation to actual flesh. It attacks the gender stereotypes: Trinity is reduced to a decorative, nurturant sidekick who never hacks and exists as love interest, the Oracle is a cookie-baking 'Mammy' figure, and there are no female Agents—the machines are sexist too.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 24 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Cynthia Freeland reads the film's women through feminist ethics of care: the two Marys function like a Greek-chorus of grieving observers, while Claudia and Veronica — and the casting of Bellucci as the repentant whore opposite Morgenstern's ageless Madonna — lock them into the virgin/whore double bind. Using Carol Gilligan's critique of Kohlberg's Kantian standard and Nel Noddings's and Sara Ruddick's point that mothering is reflective 'attentive' work, she argues Gibson's Mary is one-dimensional: flashbacks of 'I am here' show maternal instinct, never moral deliberation. She ends by suggesting the historical Jesus, like Socrates, was more radical toward women than the film, and that Irigaray's reading of Christ's bleeding wounds as a feminized maternal body sits oddly with Gibson's muscular, 'take it like a man' Savior.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 30 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — A café dialogue pits second-waver Marie against third-waver Dorothy over whether Atkins can be a feminist tool: Marie wields the feminist critique of Cartesian dualism (Descartes made the mind essential and the body animal, and women were stigmatized as body), Foucault's internalized surveillance — 'every mirror becomes a guard, every scale an alarm,' with Lifetime Maintenance as 'maniacal' hyper-vigilance — Lorde's 'master's tools,' and Young's 'Throwing Like a Girl.' Dorothy answers with Our Bodies, Ourselves self-knowledge, Title IX athletes like Venus and Serena Williams, Frye's Willful Virgin, and existentialist facticity and bad faith (we are in bad faith when we abdicate control), defending dieting as a chosen women's project. The exchange ends drawish, over Brazilian waxes, French women, and whether ugliness is a feminist virtue.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 20 "The Possibility of Authenticity The Life We Choose" — Gines reads hip hop's sexual imagery through Black feminist thought - Tupac's feud with C. Delores Tucker over "Wonder Why They Call U Bitch", Patricia Hill Collins's controlling images of the jezebel and welfare mother, bell hooks on the slave-rooted devaluation of Black womanhood, Nelly's "Tip Drill" video with a credit card swiped between a woman's buttocks, Jay-Z's "Big Pimpin'". Applying Sartre's keyhole gaze from Being and Nothingness and his Anti-Semite and Jew point about hierarchical societies, she argues the gaze under racism and sexism is non-reciprocal - women are seen without seeing - and that Lil' Kim's reversal of it reinforces rather than subverts the stereotypes; Butler's gender performativity then frames the closing Sartrean choice of authenticity or inauthenticity, Nas's "I Can" and "the life we choose."
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 28 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Kieffner applies Foucault's deployment of sexuality to show how power centers constructed biker sexual stereotypes: the psychiatric profession behind Time's 1970 'Motorcycle Syndrome', the press that sexualized the Van Buren sisters and filled Easyriders with centerfolds, police 'gauntlets' that pull over bikes but not cars (and ask Raw Thunder's Char Zack if she is a lesbian), and even Harley-Davidson's own 'mystique' video deploying eroticism to sell bikes and HOG memberships. Following Foucault's rule of the tactical polyvalence of discourse, he ends with resistance within the same power structure: riders' rights organizations videotaping police encounters, and the tactical discourses of queer, lesbian, and female riders, from Evelyn Greenway's 1921 'Do it with a motorcycle' onward, who refuse the labels of sexual outlaw and gender traitor.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 29 "The Male Vampire as Metrosexual . . . Sort Of" — Joan Grassbaugh Forry asks how conventional standards of beauty, femininity, and masculinity operate in the vampire aesthetic of Interview with the Vampire, Buffy, and Queen of the Damned.
