She extends this to Young's own "backgrounding" of the women in his life (Pegi, Carrie Snodgress) in Waging Heavy Peace, comparing him to William James's reliance on his wife Alice.
- **The Philosophy of Documentary Film**, ch. 32 "30_LaRocca_Chapter_029.html" — Linda Williams analyzes Michelle Citron's What You Take for Granted, a feminist film that inhabits the gray zone between documentary and fiction by having actors impersonate real women workers (a truck driver, a doctor, a welder) entering male-dominated trades. She argues the film exposes the price women pay to be admitted to a male world of work structured by an absent, idealized-and-vilified paternal authority, mirroring the absent-mother structure of Citron's earlier Daughter Rite. By blending polished pseudo-documentary interviews with an improvised cinema-verite fiction of Anna and Dianna's friendship, the film interrogates the process of representation itself and shows how documentary 'truth' about women's typical experience is itself a fictional shaping.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 16 "7. More Mothers, Lovers, and Other Monsters" — Brace surveys the later-season mother figures—Mary, Kelly, Jody, Rowena, Mrs. Butters, Charlie—arguing they are repeatedly used as emotional tools against the Winchesters, which she reads through Kant's warning against treating persons merely as means. She stresses loss of free will and agency: Mary's British Men of Letters 'realignment' and Mrs. Butters's coercive programming strip their autonomy and reduce them to objects/killers, while their reclaimed agency and self-sacrifice restore their Kantian standing as ends in themselves.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 25 "14. Did Bourdain Go #MeToo Far" — Finn tests Catharine MacKinnon's 'Rape Redefined' — rape as sex compelled by inequality rather than lack of consent — against Bourdain's #MeToo allyship and his payment to Asia Argento's teenage accuser Jimmy Bennett. She argues MacKinnon's power-based standard could recognize Argento's act as assault, and reframes Bourdain's hush-money payment, via the Wendat/Huron compensation practices in Graeber and Wengrow, as a compassionate vengeance-staying reparation consistent with his empathy.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 17 "From There to Here, from Here to There, Diversity Is Everywhere" — Tanya Jeffcoat builds a philosophy of diversity around 'normative hubris' and 'totalizing tendencies,' using the Sneetches, the butter-battling Yooks and Zooks, and Daisy-Head Mayzie as cases of in-group/out-group dehumanization. Encountering the Other is framed through Buber's I-It versus I-Thou (Yertle treating his subjects as a throne), Fanon on the psychic violence and alienation of the oppressed, McIntosh's invisible knapsack of privilege, and Freire's humanization. Horton and the Lorax model standing with the disenfranchised, and Jeffcoat rebuts moral relativism via universal human rights and Dewey's democracy as a personal way of life that condemns intolerance.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "MOTHERHOOD" — Maureen Sander-Staudt uses a feminist ethic of care – especially Carol Gilligan's mole-and-porcupine fable of reciprocal accommodation – to argue that pressuring women to nurse privately or covered imposes 'lactational burkas.' She runs public breastfeeding through the Miller obscenity test to show it is not obscene, opening with Gloria Steinem's 'If men could menstruate' to imagine 'milkmen,' and cites the Emily Gillette Freedom-flight ejection, Facebook's photo removal, the Janet Jackson Superbowl scandal, and PETA's human-milk proposal to expose hypocritical, biologically reductive double standards about the female breast.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 32 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 33 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Merskin takes an ecofeminist view (Karen Warren's linkage of the domination of women and nature) of women who hunt, testing Marti Kheel's 'happy/holistic/holy' hunter typology against online interviews with female hunters and finding their motivations mirror men's. She surveys how hunting became a male-coded rite of separation from the mother—drawing on Freud's 'instinctive urge'—and how hunting media (Traditional Bowhunter) juxtapose women, animals, weapons, and sexual conquest as objects of male predation. Invoking Artemis/Diana and Mary Zeiss Stange's 'woman the hunter,' she argues women who hunt expose aggression as a human, not merely male, trait.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 15 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Evolutionary psychologists Anne Gordon and Shane Kraus coin 'porngasm' and, via a survey of 264 undergraduates, argue that watching porn may make men bad lovers because porn caters to male short-term mating psychology and misrepresents female orgasm (which they estimate is 80–95% faked on screen). Men more than women infer that female porn stars genuinely enjoy the sex, and more viewing predicts stronger such belief. They explain the male bias through the correspondence bias (reading moans as real arousal despite the filming situation) and Haselton and Buss's error-management theory, whereby men systematically over-infer women's sexual interest.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 16 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Theodore Bach argues that consuming porn co-opts the mind-reading 'simulation heuristic' (the same process behind the Mr. Tees airport puzzle), so that a viewer like 'Max' watching Naughty Office simulates being the boss rather than objectively watching. This explains porn's popularity, the money shot (a prop that keeps the viewer inside the off-line simulation), and why heterosexual men watch penises — they simulate their own. Invoking Nozick's experience machine and extending MacKinnon's critique via simulation and motor-imagery research, Bach warns that simulating aggressive, degrading acts toward women may transfer those dispositions into the real world.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 20 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Fiona Woollard asks whether Zach's solo use of pornography (while partner Kelly is out) counts as cheating on their monogamous relationship. Drawing on her account of monogamy as restricting sexual intercourse to loving relationships, she argues that masturbation to porn is not sexual intercourse — there is no interaction with 'Jenna' — and that fantasizing about loveless sex is not the same as having it, so it need not undermine the significance of lovemaking; indeed masturbation aids healthy sexual self-exploration. She concedes, however, that porn which eroticizes the degradation of women (per Dworkin and MacKinnon, and Alice Walker's story 'Porn') can betray a loving relationship by revealing objectifying attitudes.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 24 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Mimi Marinucci asks 'what's wrong with porn?' and, rejecting both the Dworkin-MacKinnon censorship route and Strossen's pure free-speech reply, uses Audre Lorde's notion of the erotic as power and the personal test 'it feels right to me' as an entering wedge. She examines 'feminist porn,' resisting its easy equation with lesbian or couples porn, and contrasts it with 'fuck machine porn' (e.g., machines named Annihilator, Predator), which feels wrong to her not for size or domination but because mainstream porn fixates on decontextualized acts and the money shot. Citing Irigaray on women's diffuse, non-localized sexuality, she argues women want more richly contextualized representations than porn typically offers.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 29 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Rose takes a paradigm plotless YouPorn-style clip and tests the four standard charges against porn—obscenity, coercion/exploitation, harm to women, and harm to society—arguing each either collapses into cultural relativism or applies equally to any aesthetic object. He answers the feminist (MacKinnon/Dworkin-style) claim that porn subordinates women by noting that unjustified hierarchical power distorts the self-understanding of dominator and dominated alike (comparing it to 50 Cent's 'P.I.M.P.' and blaxploitation), so the wrong is not gender-specific. His conclusion is that porn should not be treated as different in kind from other art but judged aesthetically and morally by whether it distorts equitable social relationships, locating the real problem in capitalist cultural production rather than in porn as such.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 34 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Parkhill challenges Jenefsky and Miller's second-wave feminist reading of Penthouse 'girl–girl' pictorials (that they present lesbians as sexually available to naturalize heterosexuality) by arguing that what some straight men enjoy is their own ABSENCE from the scene. He deploys Butler's 'Imitation and Gender Insubordination' to show mock-lesbian-wedding drag can subvert rather than confirm heterosexual 'originality', Foucault's repressive hypothesis and productive power to argue the lesbian is a product of, not outside, patriarchal norms, and Lacan-derived 'projective identification' and feminine jouissance to explain the male viewer's libidinal investment in his own ego-erasure. He concludes both the 'conqueror' and the self-shattering 'jouissance-chasing' pleasures coexist, and that girl–girl porn is ethically no different from ordinary hetero porn since the consumer still assumes a right of access to women's bodies.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 36 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — In this interview, dominatrix-director Mz. Berlin answers the classic moral objections to porn from inside the industry: she rebuts objectification by insisting she chooses to be 'a commodity' and that choice makes it permissible, rejects the rape-myth/harm claim by citing declining rape rates and comparing porn to violent TV, and grounds BDSM's legitimacy entirely on INFORMED CONSENT, contrasting her voluntary waterboarding with her real torture abroad. Endorsing a strongly Millian self-ownership view ('my body is my own commodity'), she extends consent to selling kidneys, assisted suicide, and even display of her corpse, while drawing hard limits at sex with children, animals, or the dead where genuine informed consent is impossible. She also frames femdom porn as subverting male hegemony and normalizing fluid gender roles.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 10 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — The editors' introduction argues that fashion, despite philosophers' contempt for it, raises serious questions in aesthetics, ethics, identity, and political philosophy. It surveys the volume's contributors: fashionability as an expert-plus-masses property (Prinz/Farennikova), Zangwill's alienation thesis, Russell on 'cool' as aesthetic virtue, the objectification of women through Barbie play and sweatshops, and Singer's demand (via the drowning-child argument) that spare money go to poverty relief rather than trendy clothes. It uses concrete cases — Ugg boots, the National Airlines 'Fly me' campaign, Tommie Smith and John Carlos's 1968 Olympic salute, foot binding — to show fashion carries the zeitgeist and can both liberate and enslave.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 17 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Freeland analyzes perfume advertising — chiefly Chanel's mini-film campaigns for No. 5 (Kidman/Luhrmann, Tautou/Jeunet) versus the younger, jauntier Coco Mademoiselle ads with Keira Knightley — to trace how fragrance is sold 'aspirationally' by tying scent to lifestyle, romance, and couture. She examines male-fragrance ads (Bronson's Mandom, Chanel Egoiste, Old Spice's Isaiah Mustafa) and celebrity scents fronted by women of color, exposing gender anxiety, colonialism, and near-explicit racism in perfume marketing. Invoking commodity fetishism and feminist critique, she argues the ads manipulate female desire but do not make consumers passive dupes: blog parodies and critical commentary show active resistance to the fantasy.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 22 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Ashwell and Langton ask whether fashion is a 'badge of slavery' (Wollstonecraft), opening with Socrates in the *Phaedo* disdaining adornment and Rousseau's girl who becomes 'her own doll,' and using Kant's humanity formula and Nussbaum's seven-feature account of objectification. Focusing on denial of autonomy in ordinary followers, they distinguish the 'Servile Fashionista' (obeys experts) from the 'Sensible Fashionista' (follows what looks good), then argue that via Johnston's 'authority of affect' even the sensible one is under an *epistemic* bondage: fashion's extrinsic social pull is misperceived as the garment's intrinsic goodness, a projective illusion (like the Müller-Lyer) that on a Kantian view undermines agency and masks misogynist or racist norms such as straightened hair or the 'lotus feet' of stilettos.
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 23 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Collins analyzes paradigmatic Barbie play — dressing the doll and identifying with her as an idealized future self, from the 1959 TV ad to BarbieGirls.com — arguing it trains girls to define identity through fashionable bodily self-presentation for a male gaze (Brumberg's 'body project'). Using Sandra Bartky's feminist reworking of Foucault's *Discipline and Punish*, she treats beauty norms as a discipline producing 'docile bodies' whose self-surveillance internalizes a 'panoptical male connoisseur' (Bentham's Panopticon), offering cycles of pleasure and pain that bind women without any single sovereign to blame. Rather than banning Barbie (the failed 'Happy to be Me' doll), she proposes subversive play — Plump and Proud Barbie, Mursi lip-plate Barbie — as Heyes-style 'practices of freedom.'
- **Fashion – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking with Style**, ch. 25 "FASHION - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Pierlott examines sweatshops in the garment industry through the lens of ancient Cynicism (Antisthenes, the Stoics' Zeno of Citium and his thieving slave), using the Cynic critique of fashion-driven consumption to strip legitimacy from the demand that feeds sweatshops. He rebuts the 'inevitability argument' (comparing it to excusing the Holocaust as inevitable) and the free-choice defense using Aristotle's category of 'mixed' action — sweated workers' consent is coerced by desperate alternatives — and argues, via Adam Smith on the undervaluing of labor, that giant retailers like Wal-Mart distort natural labor prices. He stresses that sweatshops overwhelmingly exploit young women, tying objectification of women as fashion consumers to their oppression as producers.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 15 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Kimberly Baltzer-Jaray and Tanya Rodriguez argue, against George Carlin's 'mobile art gallery' joke, that the only thing separating tattooing from fine art is its fleshy canvas. They show how formalist, expressionist and institutional theories historically excluded both women's craft and tattoos, then use feminist aesthetics (Korsmeyer, Iris Marion Young on the gaze) to reclaim the female tattooed body as an assertion of agency against objectification. They then apply Gadamer's hermeneutics – art as play, festival and symbol – to argue tattoos make a claim on the viewer, build a 'hermeneutic collective' community, and function as inexhaustible symbols prompting self-recognition.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 18 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Nancy Kang argues tattoos can function within a liberatory feminist ideology, accentuating rather than diminishing femininity by exposing the differential treatment of tattooed women. She surveys radical, Marxist, liberal and corporeal feminism (invoking Aristotle's dismissal of women, Mill's Subjection of Women, and Gramsci's hegemony), then reads pop-culture cases – Crash's tattooed Latino worker, Black Swan's Lily, the Perry 'pricks as needles' sexualization, carnival 'Tattooed Ladies' like Irene Woodward marked 'by the father's hand,' and the McGee/Bullock/Kat Von D scandal – to show corporeal feminism treats tattooing as a risky, self-owning revolutionary act.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 19 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span (the book's front matter plus the Part I 'Hook-Up Culture' essays) argues that college hook-up culture can be examined philosophically rather than merely lived. Hole and Chen recast reckless sexual 'experimentation' as a Socratic self-experiment, having students name a change, run it, and interrogate a 'big question' (e.g. Chen's dare to abstain all freshman year) to become a 'wiser lover.' Romaya argues that gay and lesbian students' opposite-sex 'straight sex experiments' undermine fixed sexual identity, invoking Buddhist anatman and Hume's bundle theory to reject a static self. Bruce gives a phenomenological reading of how Facebook/MySpace profiles and text/level-jumping alienate courting students, and Lunceford treats the 'walk of shame' outfit via Peirce's index/symbol semiotics as a sign of feminine sexuality marked shameful.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 21 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — This span turns to the ethics and epistemology of college sex. Kania argues there is no clear line between close friendship and a sexual relationship, so condemning student-professor sex logically forces condemning student-professor friendship—rejecting Golash's split and defending carefully-conducted consensual relationships. Layne narrates Socrates/Alcibiades, Abelard/Heloise, and Heidegger/Arendt to contrast Socratic eros (Plato's Symposium, love as a friend of wisdom directed at the soul) and Heideggerian authentic love ('I want you to be what you are') against Abelard's exploitative lust. McDowell mines epistemology (justification, taking beliefs 'to heart,' reflective equilibrium) to argue better thinking yields better, more autonomous sex. Pinku weighs 'plain sex' against Nagel's interpersonal-arousal account of embodiment to ask whether sex needs love, and Brophy uses Kantian dignity (treating the body as a mere means, not an end) to argue that prostitution and webcam porn undertaken to pay tuition violate the student's autonomy.
- **College Sex – Philosophy for Everyone - Philosophers With Benefits**, ch. 22 "College Sex - Philosophy for Everyone Philosophers With Benefits" — The essay argues that soaring tuition drives college students into sexual self-commodification—egg-selling ('Pay your tuition with eggs'), craigslist/backpage escorting, and dorm-porn webcam sites like VoyeurDorm and CocoDorm—and reads these cases through Kant's second formulation, condemning them as treating oneself and others as mere means rather than ends of intrinsic dignity. It applies Marx's notion of false consciousness to Natalie Dylan's virginity auction and Ashley Dupré's 'empowerment' claims, comparing them to women choosing high heels as internalized oppression. It uses Rousseau's Social Contract and Mill's On Liberty to argue that prostitution is a form of illegitimate 'voluntary slavery' because one cannot rightly alienate one's own inalienable freedom, and contrasts coerced cases (Helena in Singapore, Rosie Reid's traumatic auctioned deflowering, John Gechter's porn suspension from a Christian college) with less-coerced ones to argue moral concern should track the degree of circumstantial coercion.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 20 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Luna Dolezal's 'Yoga for Women?' argues that Western yoga, once a male ascetic path, has been absorbed by consumer capitalism into a female beauty practice organized around 'body capital.' Reading Yoga Journal covers, Lululemon's 'Say No to Camel Toe' ad, and Toesox's nude campaigns, she shows the fashion/beauty industries cultivate shame to sell the yoga body, objectifying women. She counters that Hatha yoga should be a laboratory for compassionate self-acceptance beyond comparison and competition — 'yoga for every body' — rather than another instrument of the market's normalized ideal.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 21 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Nicole Dunas's 'The Feeling of Beauty' recounts founding the Real Beauty Yoga Project after a teacher-training 'modeling day' where consultants photographed only the five thinnest students, enacting division rather than yogic union. Framing the beauty question against Kant's claim that beauty is objective, and drawing on David Abram's participatory perception and Susan Bordo on airbrushed bodies, she argues that objectifying beauty into an image to be gazed at (the male gaze, the isolated cosmetic-surgery gaze) severs us from it, whereas Hatha yoga's tantric, present-moment embodiment lets beauty be lived rather than consumed.
- **Yoga – Philosophy for Everyone - Bending Mind and Body**, ch. 22 "YOGA - PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Debra Merskin content-analyzes 52 Yoga Journal covers (2000–2008) and finds every model white and 96% shown full-body, mostly looking away — posed as unaware of a scopophilic, hierarchical gaze that puts them in vulnerability. She uses Goffman's gender-display coding and the male-gaze framework to argue that a publication about a mind–body practice (which, contra Descartes' mind/body divide, neuroscience shows are intertwined) bears a special responsibility to present racially inclusive, non-objectifying images rather than reproducing the 'sex sells' formula of Cosmopolitan or Maxim.
- **Blues – Philosophy for Everyone - Thinking Deep About Feeling Low**, ch. 28 "BLUES" — Meghan Winsby answers George Carlin's gibe that white people have nothing to be blue about by arguing that women — black or white — legitimately sing the blues because they share an experience of oppression. She applies Iris Marion Young's 'five faces of oppression' (exploitation, marginalization, powerlessness, cultural imperialism, violence) to women's silencing, sexual objectification, and gender exploitation, showing that early blueswomen (Ma Rainey, Bessie Smith, Memphis Minnie) and later ones (Bonnie Raitt) asserted sexuality and independence against a patriarchal order. She then weighs, without fully endorsing, the moral cultural-appropriation and audience-appropriation objections (via James O. Young) to white men playing the blues.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 19 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Kyla Reid and Tinashe Dune attack the bestselling dating manual The Rules by Fein and Schneider, focusing on Rule 4 (never go Dutch—let the man pay) and Rule 12 (dump him if he gives no romantic gift like jewelry). They line up 'Rules Girls' against sex workers offering a paid 'girlfriend experience' and 'professional girlfriends'/gold diggers, arguing that all three approach relationships in a systematic, 'business-like' way that packages and markets the woman as a product, measures her worth by what the man spends, and treats gifts like performance bonuses. Because monogamy, public recognition, and belief in the relationship cannot make it authentic, they conclude The Rules obstruct genuine intimacy and that everyone should be more critical of dating conventions about who pays and what gifts mean.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 27 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 67 "63. Amy Schumer as Philosopher Fuck the Feminine Mystique" — Elsby argues Amy Schumer's honest comedy revolts against a 'feminine mystique' broader than Friedan's housewife version, running back to Beauvoir's claim that woman is constructed as the 'Other' and to Aristotle's 'rational animal' definition that cast women as irrational and thus less than human. Through bits like 'Madame President,' 'Last Fuckable Day,' the 'New Twitter Button' sketch, and gross-out honesty about pregnancy and her own body in Growing and The Leather Special, Schumer refuses to let women's physical, sexual, and social experience stay mysterious. Elsby reads this as de-'othering' and re-humanizing women by forcing our concept of 'woman' to expand to include flawed, fully human hot-mess figures.

### Humanity as an End in Itself

The humanity formula is one of Immanuel Kant's expressions of the categorical imperative, requiring that we treat humanity, whether in ourselves or in others, always as an end and never merely as a means. Because rational beings possess an intrinsic worth, or dignity, that is not exchangeable for any price, they must never be used simply as instruments for someone else's purposes. The principle grounds duties such as honesty and respect and has become a touchstone for arguments about human dignity and the wrongness of manipulation and coercion.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 17 "Conquering the Inner Demon" — James Lawler casts Buffy as a contemporary allegory of Plato's cave-escaped philosopher and reads the show through Kant: the Slayer moves between a hellish lower world of instrumental appetite and an intelligible higher world of the soul, and Kant's Copernican revolution ('objects must conform to our knowledge') explains Marcie's invisibility in 'Out of Mind, Out of Sight' and the fear-made-flesh Master of 'Nightmares.' Kant's formula that every rational being exists as an end in himself grounds Buffy's duty in 'Anne' ('I am Buffy, the Vampire Slayer'), her rejection of Spike's chip as no substitute for a soul in 'Crush,' and her 'As You Were' admission that using Spike treats him as a mere means. Season Six explores 'too much heaven': Buffy's blissful death in 'The Gift' makes earthly life hell, and only conquering the inner demon — Willow's fear-driven dark magic defeated by Xander's yellow-crayon love in 'Grave' — restores the balance between heavens and hells.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 24 "Following the Moral Law" — Applies Kant's Formula of Universal Law and Formula of Humanity on two levels. Individually, Buffy's sacrifice in Dawn's place in 'The Gift' and her post-resurrection return to duty in 'Once More, with Feeling' show her will determined by duty rather than the inclination to a normal life, while Oz's werewolf episodes show inclination swamping reason. Systemically, the Slayer's coercion of demons is justified only because their actions destroy a Kantian state of right in Sunnydale, and Kant's account of radical evil — subordinating the moral law to the maxim of self-love — explains why demons and human villains like Warren's Trio are evil; the chapter closes worrying that the Slayer, like the Initiative's Adam, answers to no one.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 32 "The Moral Sophistication of Buffy the Vampire Slayer" — Greene and Yuen reconstruct seven moral principles from Buffy's conduct — slay those who typically harm humans, never harm humans (Faith's accidental killing of the Mayor's henchman), spare the defenseless and the controllable (chip'd Spike, caged Oz) — and note that blackmailing Spike and roughing up demons would violate Kant's Formula of Humanity if the patients were rational persons, exposing the show's human/non-human moral hierarchy and its animal-rights parallel. 'The Gift' dramatizes deontology (Buffy refuses to kill Ben) against consequentialism (Giles strangles him), and the chapter ranks BtVS above after-school-special, culpable-clown, and faux-realist TV morality because it supports its stands by appeal to general moral principles while keeping Aristotelian habituation and real-life moral complexity in view.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 74 "Harry’s Cloak, the Ring of Gyges, and the Temptations of Power" — This section contrasts Voldemort and Dumbledore as two figures tempted by power. Tom Riddle's egocentrism - frightening and controlling other children at the orphanage, treating his 'friends' as mere followers, killing Lily, and splintering his soul for Horcruxes - violates Kant's dictum never to use persons merely as means and fits Plato's category of the least trustworthy rulers. Dumbledore, though tempted in youth by Grindelwald's 'for the greater good' schemes and later by Marvolo Gaunt's ring, is venerable for Socratic self-knowledge: knowing 'I was not to be trusted with power,' he repeatedly refused the Ministry and so promoted justice by teaching.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 13 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Taliaferro, writing as a personalist, worries that Gibson's relentless focus on torture eclipses the whole person of Christ: like torture victims losing peripheral vision, viewers lose sight of his teaching, healings, nonviolence, and resurrection, and the satisfaction-theology framing risks relishing redemptive suffering itself. His reconciliation thought-experiment (Patricia's betrayal of Kris and the God-man who resurrects the murdered child) argues that the resurrection, not the passion alone, completes at-one-ment, since no amount of suffering can undo past wrong. He contrasts Gandalf's laughing return in The Return of the King with a Gibson Jesus who could not plausibly laugh after rising, and invokes Scheler's St. Francis, who loves the wholeness behind sickness rather than the sickness, to urge that the film's intensity edges out a life-affirming view of persons as irreducibly valuable in themselves.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 17 "Send in the Clones!" — Hanley defends a provocative 'yes' to cloning, genetic engineering, and clone armies. He dismisses the 'yuck factor' as showing nothing inherently bad, argues via non-identity-style cases (a genetically corrected or maimed Luke is a different child who is not thereby harmed) that early genetic manipulation harms no one, and distinguishes brainwashing, coercion, and inducement (Obi-Wan's death-stick mind trick, Vader's threats to Lando, Jar Jar's exploitation) to ask when bending another's will is permissible. Turning to warfare, he applies Just War theory's conditions - judging Anakin's slaughter of the Sand People guilty on nearly every count - and concludes that troops with deliberately diminished autonomy may be the least objectionable solution to the ethics of recruitment, training, and deployment: send in the clones.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 93 "I’m a Lover, Not a Fighter!" — Turns to Kantian nonconsequentialism: persons must be treated as ends in themselves and never merely as means, from duty rather than consequences, with negative duties (not harming) stronger than positive duties (aiding) — so Reed Richards may not kill a pedestrian for organs to heal Doctor Doom's victims, though a utilitarian would require it. Since neither becoming Spider-Man nor refusing to violates any negative duty, being a superhero is supererogatory: 'with great power comes great responsibility' is at most a duty not to misuse power, and precisely because heroes don't have to do what they do — as Clark Kent's Superman II choice shows — their choosing it is what makes them praiseworthy.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 13 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Dennis uses Kant to sort eaters into the fundamentally unfree (Herbert, raised on Atkins and thieving, who merely ploughs on), the fundamentally random (Rita, whose synapses and muscles would fire in chaos), and the autonomous, arguing that only an autonomous person can genuinely decide whether to follow Atkins — by weighing friends' testimonials against the medical establishment rather than habit, whim, or advertising. The categorical imperative grounds the autonomous life: 'lie when you can gain' fails universalization, and treating humanity as an end means offering a vegetarian guest food she is comfortable with instead of pressing Atkins meat on her. His own 'Dan Dennis Diet,' built by experiment and reasoning, illustrates autonomy in practice, and the case of Kitty shows that observing someone's diet never reveals whether its holder is unfree or autonomous.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 26 "James Bond and Philosophy" — McKinney argues that '007' is a technological construction distinct from the human James Bond: drawing on Dewey's broad view of technology as technique (the shaken martini as technological artifact), Heidegger's account of naming as revealing and enframing, and Don Ihde's technological embodiment (the party-game hand axe that is art, paperweight, or tool depending on perception). Film dialogue shows the naming at work: Moneypenny calls him 'James' but announces '007 is here' to M; Goldfinger greets '007' and is corrected with 'My name is James Bond'; M threatens '008 can replace you' and, in Die Another Day, declares 'You are no use to anyone now' while rescinding his status. The chapter closes with the Kantian point that persons must be treated as ends in themselves, yet the designation '007' constitutes Bond as precisely a replaceable means to MI6's ends.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 28 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Arp and Decker examine Bond's objectification of women - using a dancing girl as a human shield in the Goldfinger pre-credits sequence, M ordering Bond to 'pump her for information' - through three moral theories. Kant's humanity formula condemns treating women as sexual tools, but Kantian autonomy generates a stalemate since consensual, reciprocal liaisons like Bond and Anya Amasova's might qualify as permissible; Millian utilitarianism condemns the male gaze by its long-term social costs yet stalls against pro-sex feminist counterarguments. They settle on Aristotelian virtue ethics - the mean between extremes, with respect as the key virtue against the power-centered virtue of Machiavelli, Hobbes, and Nietzsche - to argue objectification is vicious, and they trace Bond's moral progress from skipping the young Bibi in For Your Eyes Only to the reciprocal relationships with Kara Milovy, Pam Bouvier, Wai Lin, and Jinx.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 15 "The Virtues of Superhumans" — Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 17 "Conclusion June Love Beyond the Jordan" — Sennett builds "June Love" out of June Carter Cash's documented love, from the "Hurt" video's staircase glance to Rosanne Cash's eulogy that June saw your potential and "lifted them up" for you to see, and the love that steadied John through addictions and infidelity for thirty-five years. He stages the philosophy-of-love dilemma between appraisal theories (Velleman, grounding love in Kantian dignity that demands respect but cannot justify loving John rather than anyone) and bestowal theories (Irving Singer, on which love projects value and so cannot be justified at all), with Frankfurt's volitional account as a side note, and proposes June Love, loving the beloved's potentiality, as the hybrid that is both objective and active and can justify loving this person. He also distinguishes June Love from codependence: enabling entrenches the addict's destruction, whereas June's confronting-and-encouraging love, echoed in "Ring of Fire" and "Far Side Banks of Jordan," called Cash to transformation while leaving him himself.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 25 "Seeing Ourselves Reflected Back" — Gray asks whether Cylons deserve moral consideration, starting from Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means: the New Caprica suicide bombings and Adama's plan to weaponize a Cylon virus treat captives merely as means, while Helo's sabotage of 'A Measure of Salvation' acknowledges their intrinsic value. D'Anna's dissent before being boxed and Athena's defection for Helo show the rational autonomy Kant's personhood requires; if that is dismissed as programming, Singer's sentience criterion (Leoben tortured, Gina catatonic) and Warren's multi-criterial personhood — including Boomer's 'I have a conscience' in 'Downloaded' — still open personhood to Cylons. The chapter ends on the humans' double standard (Athena accepted, guns drawn on Caprica Six) as a mirror for our own treatment of uncertain others.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 16 "“I’ve Never Been Good at Good-byes”" — Lee treats DS9's Cardassian Occupation as a case of transitional justice like post-Holocaust and post-apartheid reckonings, asking whether Odo, security chief on Terok Nor, was a collaborator. Applying Kant's deontology — the good will, both formulations of the categorical imperative, illustrated by Kai Opaka's Kendra Valley betrayal, Quark's smuggling in 'Little Green Men', and Sisko's fraud in 'In the Pale Moonlight' — he judges Odo's letting three innocent Bajorans die in 'Things Past' as negligence, but his years-long cover-up as using the victims merely as means to protect his reputation, and hence genuine collaboration, as was his neglect of duty under the Link's pull in 'Behind the Lines.' Kant's imperfect duty of beneficence then redeems Odo's final departure from Kira: returning to cure and educate the Founders in 'What You Leave Behind' is a moral duty owed to rational beings.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 8 "There’s No Place Like Home" — Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.
- **Transformers and Philosophy - More than Meets the Mind**, ch. 23 "Transformers and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the Autobot-Decepticon war as a contest of ethical systems: Optimus's fair fighting, his refusal to ignore human casualties, and Bumblebee's friendship with the inferior Spike instantiate Kant's categorical imperative and the treatment of rational beings as ends in themselves. The Decepticons run through the egoist tradition - Hobbes's psychological egoism from Leviathan, Starscream's self-defeating normative egoism, and Megatron as Ayn Rand's rational egoist taunting 'You still fight for the weak; that is why you lose' - leaving the reader to choose between Kant's world of peaceful obligation and Rand's world of power where, like Starscream, you die alone.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 8 "8" — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 17 "Close the Door, Put Out the Lights" — Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 18 "The Legend Has Come True. The Wind Has Come Back" — Haas opposes two princesses of Nausicaa of the Valley of the Wind: Kushana of Tolmekia, whose 'whatever it takes' survivalism (invading Pejite, resurrecting a God-Warrior) is consequentialism pursued to its limit, and Nausicaa, whose attention to each act — befriending the biting fox-squirrel, staying her sword over her father's killer because vengeance would doom the Valley — restricts means, not just ends. The reductio comes from Pejite, whose torture of a baby Ohmu to bait a stampede on the Valley is exactly what strict outcome-maximization requires; against this, Kant's demand to treat beings as ends in themselves explains Nausicaa's 'mysterious power' of empathy. Because she respects the jungle and the sentient Ohmu rather than viewing nature anthropocentrically as a plague to burn, she discovers the plants are purifying the war-poisoned earth — the knowledge that saves everyone and proves Kushana's conquering approach self-defeating even on its own terms.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 40 "Lester’s Duties and Capabilities" — Maguire asks whether the Royals did wrong by trying to hit in the late innings of Jon Lester's May 2008 no-hitter, working through Kant's distinction between perfect duties (always binding—playing hard, honoring the codified rules) and imperfect duties (praiseworthy obligations that admit exceptions—respecting the unwritten convention against bunting for a hit in a blowout). Sympathy for Lester's cancer recovery must not enter the calculation, since Jim Abbott's 1993 no-hitter shows the duty must universalize; bunting would be 'bush league' rather than wrong, a lapse in imperfect duty. He extends the analysis to Francona's pitch counts and warns that wanting Ellsbury to bunt against a Yankees no-hitter would treat the pitcher as a mere means to fan pride.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 34 "Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal" — Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 15 "I’ve Got No Strings . ." — Richard Greene asks whether it was practically rational for Dexter to trust Lumen rather than kill her, to help her revenge-kill the Fowler ring, and to train her as a killer. The good outcomes do not help - Masuka's strip-club windfall shows luck is not rationality, and Socrates' Apology argument that corrupters risk harm from those they corrupt, together with Dexter's prior disaster in training Miguel, means the consequences were not foreseeably good. Kantian tests fail too - no one could will a universal law of killing, and killing violates the victim's autonomy and humanity as an end in itself - as do decision theory and instrumentality theories, so no account of practical rationality vindicates Dexter's choices, suggesting instead that the emotionless 'wooden boy' is beginning to become a real one.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 14 "Invisibility or Honesty" — Schulzke argues inception's fundamental wrongness is a violation of autonomy read through Kant: the Fischer team treats him merely as a means, and even Cobb's benevolently intended inception on Mal disrespects humanity by stripping her self-determination, leaving her - like someone acting under coercion - no longer a responsible moral agent. Extraction he judges the lesser evil, though a world of dream espionage would end private mental life, since even the most guarded secrets surface in dreams. The payoff is a new twist on the Ring of Gyges from Plato's Republic: an invisibility ring could no longer shield injustice because a dreamer's deeds remain recorded and extractable, so Kant's absolute ban on lying could make extraction an engine of honesty - as when Ariadne's extraction on Cobb exposes the danger Mal poses and ultimately saves Cobb himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 42 "The Valuable Self" — The chapter turns from metaphysics to morals: for Kant the self is the most valuable thing in the world, a subject that must never be used as a mere means, since turning a subject into an object is the ultimate immorality. The authorities' plan to hollow Arctor into an unwitting infiltrator, and Donna's lament that he 'didn't volunteer', make the point concrete: what is valuable in us is the self's fuzziness, including its mystery of free will, and to remake a person into a scanner, 'a mere thing that just watches and never chooses', is the ultimate crime.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 75 "Chapter 11 - We Can Manipulate You Wholesale" — Reads Total Recall's opening scenes — Harry's shifty eyes, then the reveal that his friendship, Lori's marriage, and even Benny's cab-driving are all sanctioned deceptions directed at Quaid — as manipulation commissioned by an outside element that sets the agenda of each relationship. Using people this way already troubles Kantian ethics, the chapter concludes, and an outside element directing individuals to do it is 'potentially enough to have Immanuel Kant spin in his grave.'
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 77 "Finding a Lever for Manipulation" — Explains the spy tradecraft acronym MISE (Money, Ideology, Sex, Ego) and walks through 'Fred's' recruitment method in A Scanner Darkly — building trust through drug purchases under false pretenses until the mark must betray another confidant for Fred's benefit. The same template covers Lori, Harry, and Hauser in Total Recall, for whom Quaid 'becomes nothing more than a means': monitoring his return to Mars, or locating the rebel leadership.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 78 "Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem" — Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 79 "Utilitarian Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Coveralls" — Lays out the utilitarian case for the spying in A Scanner Darkly: with New Path immune to inspection and Substance D addiction spreading, sacrificing Bob Arctor — secretly addicted to breakdown point and implanted with the little-flowers trigger — maximizes outcomes for the many. Against this stands the Kantian rebuttal that he should never have been made 'just another means,' likely never again to be 'an able-minded and self-determining person,' and the chapter adds the overlooked victim: the manipulator who violates the categorical imperative.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 20 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Solves the 'riddle' of Gus by showing his empire runs on corporate instrumental rationality: the careful, emotion-disciplined Los Pollos CEO launders meth through legitimate business, treats chemists as replaceable parts (the Gale plan), and exacts revenge on the cartel in 'Salud' by drinking his own poisoned tequila. The chapter defines this as the critical theorists' amoral means-end reason - Kant's hypothetical imperative without the categorical - making Gus a sociopath who violates the injunction to treat persons as ends, and reads his cartel war through Machiavelli and Hobbes's power-first picture of the state. Gus's Two-Face-like corpse reveals the split between the rage-driven avenger of Max and the respectable mask, foreshadowing what Walt becomes.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 16 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — McKendry and Da Silva build a Kantian case that walkers deserve respect as 'residual humans': Rick dwelling on organ-donor Wayne Dunlap before harvesting his corpse for camouflage shows that bodies carry the dead's chosen ends, so using Wayne is honoring, not using, him. Because walkers are corpses bound by the presumptive wishes of the deceased, and retain residual subjectivity (Jenny returning again and again to her family's door), survivors wrong them by treating them as mere objects - Merle's sport killing of walkers on the rooftop is the moral low, Rick's swift, risk-accepting headshots of Hannah and Deputy Leon the respectful execution. Jim's informed choice to be left by the road to turn, over Shane's and Rick's objections, shows the autonomy of the infected that no one else may override.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 12 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Bateman replies to Cogburn that Law and Chaos descend not from Kant but from Michael Moorcock's Eternal Champion stories, where they are liberal and conservative political tendencies held in check by the Cosmic Balance, which restores Chaotic Good, Lawful Evil, and the Druid's true Neutral as viable positions. He rejects the 'sausage machine' universalization of maxims for Kant's humanity formula and Realm of Ends, and argues act utilitarianism makes a poor model of Good: an overpopulation scenario could mandate genocide, and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure the good. Alain Badiou's ethic of truths supplies the positive case for Chaotic Good—pursuing what you take to be good without submitting to a single moral law—while Buddhist and Jain renunciation dignifies Lawful Neutral.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 24 "Psych and Philosophy" — Rocha argues Kant is not the absolutist of legend: in 'On a Supposed Right to Lie from Philanthropy' Kant denies only a right to lie - Gus could be held responsible if his lie to Shawn's pursuing murderer goes wrong - and in The Metaphysics of Morals Kant openly leaves questions like polite untruths unanswered, to be judged by agents in their concrete circumstances. The deeper ground is Kant's duty to oneself: lying shows disrespect for the honest communication through which social beings sharpen their rationality, and so 'throws away and annihilates' the liar's dignity, which is why Uncle Jack's gold-hunting lies in 'The Greatest Adventure in the History of Basic Cable' are beyond rescue. On Rocha's reading even Kant could endorse the one lie to rule them all - claiming to be psychic - because it respects rationality and human life in a society that irrationally esteems the supernatural, while Shawn's Gus-alias gags and bunny fabrications remain immoral.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 20 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Fallis sorts Atlantic City's lies to show which are wrong and why. Kant's and Augustine's absolute bans go too far and Grotius's life-saving exception does not apply - most of these lies get people killed - yet even altruistic lies (Margaret for Madame Jeunet and the ledger), lies told to those who want to be deceived, lies to liars, and Sorensen's bald-faced lies that no one believes (Jimmy's flat movie alibi, Rothstein's 'skilled player' whopper) remain wrong: they take informed choice out of the victim's hands, violating the Kantian autonomy that grounds the wrong of lying, and they corrode the trust on which even criminals' co-operation depends.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 14 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Piven argues Zapp Brannigan's 'sexlexia' - his deluded velour-and-spanking seductions of Leela and his relief at finding Lee Lemon is a woman - typifies a whole cast of clueless lovers (Fry coaching Zoidberg's courtship of Edna, Morgan Proctor's mess fetish, Bender coldly dumping the Planet Express ship in 'Love and Rocket'). Kant's condemnation of masturbation as self-abuse that throws away one's personality and violates humanity in one's own person is exposed as unsupported prejudice, and Nietzsche's claim that morality projects fear, envy, and disgust onto the despised other explains why 'perversion' is an arbitrary cultural judgment. Freud, Stoller, and McDougall then recast perversion as unconscious flight from anxiety and death, so the show's kink - up to the Monsterpus of The Beast with a Billion Backs and Amy's 'general sluttiness' - mirrors our own sexlexia and existential dread.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 22 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — James Cook grades the Third Invasion against the just war principles Ender was never taught: the war is preventive rather than genuinely preemptive (with the 2003 Iraq parallel), proper authority is compromised by deceiving the public, last resort fails since the hive-queen was trying to communicate, and non-combatant immunity condemns destroying the bugger homeworld. He stages Augustine's ban on killing in individual self-defense against Aquinas' permission of it, and uses Kant's humanity formula and Cicero's hostis/perduellis distinction to ask whether the buggers were ever treated as rational beings rather than mere threats.
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 17 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter evaluates Marshall and Lily's promise to tell each other everything through Kant: lying violates the universalizable duty of truthfulness and treats the deceived as a mere means, as with Lily's hidden credit card debt in 'Dowisetrepla', the realtor's sewage-plant omission, and Barney's fully staged seduction of Meg that blocks her informed choice. Even Marshall's kindly lie about the doppelganger fails Kant's test, alongside his infamous refusal to lie to the murderer at the door. Yet Kant's letters on reticence in friendship and his grim view of marriage as shared ends where spouses may use each other 'as if' they were things suggest that telling each other everything may itself corrode respect - the tension Lily's never-opened bathroom door dramatizes.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 25 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — King charges human exceptionality with being speciesism and asks whether dinosaurs are persons rather than humans, testing Kant's rationality criterion and Descartes' denial of animal thought against the raptor that opens the shed door and the T. rex that spins the Explorer searching for prey. He runs the dinosaurs through Mary Anne Warren's five personhood criteria, then plays his Wittgenstein trump card: animal language would be the language of a different life-form, so the raptors' calls expressing fear and summoning help count as real communication without words. He closes with Regan's rights view, arguing that the cow and goat feeding scenes, like past denials of personhood to Native Americans and women, should shame us into showing a little respect.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 32 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Nicole Pramik asks whether the demons of Brandon Mull's Fablehaven can be taught morality, using Kant's deontology as the measuring stick. Seth's kindness to Graulas looks dutiful and universalizable, and Graulas at first seems a rational agent respecting the categorical imperative - until healed, he betrays Seth, demolishes the preserve's treaty, and declares himself 'pure, deliberate evil' who used Seth as a mere means. Nagi Luna never even tries, and the Sphinx who models her is himself a serial user of persons, so the chapter concludes that rational demons remain impervious to the moral law: you can lead a demon out of Zzyzx, but you cannot make it good.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 57 "The Devil and Philosophy" — James Edwin Mahon dismantles the 'sympathy for the Devil' puzzle by testing three accounts of diabolical evil: Machiavelli's prince ('learn how not to be virtuous') shows self-interest is mere amoral Realpolitik; Schopenhauer's malice and Schadenfreude ('injure all people as far as you can') are still self-interested pleasure; and only Kant's 'diabolical will' - doing evil because it is evil, Paradise Lost's 'Evil, be thou my good' - truly captures the Devil, though Kant deemed it impossible for humans. Hence nobody actually likes the Devil; people like the intelligence, charm, and underdog status of the characters who play him in The Devil's Advocate and Angel Heart.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 13 "Homeland and Philosophy" — John Karavitis evaluates four suicide events: Afsal Hamid's suicide in CIA custody, Aileen Morgan's cutting her throat with a lens, Brody's aborted suicide bombing, and Carrie's ECT as a 'suicide' of her old self. Kant's absolute ban on suicide (it denies your humanity) clashes with Seneca's Stoic counsel that a life of miserable captivity need not be continued, and with Singer's utilitarian permission of euthanasia that reduces suffering - under both, Hamid's and Aileen's suicides are defensible while Brody's emotionally driven bombing is not. Dana's plea that her father is needed recasts Aristotle's point that suicide wrongs the community, and Sloterdijk's analysis of rage turned on oneself frames Carrie's amoral self-destruction.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 23 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Edwin Jacob contrasts the utilitarian calculus behind Walden's drone strike - Estes's eighty percent estimate, 'potential collateral damage falls within current matrix parameters', eighty-three children killed - with Kant's three formulations of the categorical imperative applied to that decision. On the universal-law formula Walden cannot will a world of strikes on one's own soil, on the humanity formula the schoolchildren are used merely as means, and the kingdom-of-ends formula condemns treating foreign lives as quantities in a matrix. The chapter adds that drones, like Brody's suicide vest, are asymmetric terror at a distance, and that blowback (Shahzad's Times Square attempt) shows the strategy fails even consequentialist test.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 32 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Dona Cayetana and Nathan Everson argue that 'enhanced interrogation techniques' is a euphemism - with Zizek and Badiou they show relabeling torture as what the West does while 'torture' is what Muslims do conceals identity between the acts, as 'Blind Spot''s safe-house interrogation of Hamid demonstrates. Utilitarianism justifies Saul's fatiguing of Hamid by its results, while the Kantian view that persons must never be mere means condemns it categorically; the chapter contends the show's framing nudges viewers to accept torture as a necessary evil. Carrie's gendered role as Zizek's 'new face of torture' - a pretty white woman whose desirability and perceived vulnerability become interrogation tools, from sex with Brody to 'You broke my heart' - feminizes and normalizes the spectacle.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 24 "Girls and Philosophy" — Wible asks whether the workplace abuse in Girls - Hannah's two unpaid intern years, the harassment at the law firm, the 30-day e-book deadline that triggers her OCD, Marnie hostessing at a gentlemen's club - is defensible by young workers' inexperience and the 'experience paradox.' Against the boot-camp defense he argues from the meaning of work (Gini's 'I work, therefore I am,' Schumacher's good work) and from Marx on alienation from the products of labor, but his core standard is Kant's: persons must be treated as ends, never merely as means, which the editor who wants the book and not the person violates. He concludes that young workers' vulnerability (no savings, no leverage, reluctance to blow the whistle) warrants paid internships, transparency, and two-way respect.
- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 21 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — Framed by Dickens's Jacob Marley, Walker asks whether Jobs deserved his posthumous accolades despite giving far less to charity than Bill Gates, and tests him under three frameworks. Aristotle's virtue ethics acquits him (character is judged holistically, and charity sits near the golden mean of open-handedness rather than being a checklisted duty); Mill's utilitarianism acquits him (his innovations maximized happiness and he violated no Harm Principle—though abandoning daughter Lisa counts as a harm); and Singer's drowning-child argument condemns him as near-morally-bankrupt for selling luxury gadgets while children starve. Kant both convicts (charity is an imperfect duty under the categorical imperative) and saves Jobs: treating the affluent individual as an end in himself, never merely a means to the destitute, blocks Singer's demand for giving to marginal utility.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 16 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Altmann stages a moral (not legal) trial of Dracula with three expert witnesses: Kant testifies that Dracula universalizes murder only for himself while fleeing Harker's kukri, and that he reduced Harker to a mere meal, violating the categorical imperative and deserving execution; Mill weighs consequences, tallying the misery done to Lucy, her mother, and the Bloofer Lady's child victims, and argues the greatest happiness lies in imprisoning the Count for medical study instead; Aristotle argues the child-brained vampire lacks the reason and self-control needed for eudaimonia and so merits imprisonment rather than death. The chapter hands the verdict to the reader, showing guilt is agreed but punishment diverges across the three frameworks.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 12 "3. What’s So Bad about Eating People" — McCraw imagines Lecter defending each class of victim with a different ethical theory: the Momund and Dortlich kills through Natural Law Theory plus lex talionis retribution (Dortlich ate Mischa, so he is eaten; Momund treated the aunt as meat, so he is treated as meat), the 'Sorbet' Rolodex dinner-party victims through a perverted Kantianism that swaps politeness for rationality so the rude forfeit humanity and corpses have no moral standing, and Krendler, Raspail, and Chilton through consequentialist accounting of worlds improved by their deaths. He concludes that only virtue ethics resists such distortion: Lecter's cold, callous, manipulative character and his isolated, paranoid, friendless life show that no possessor of good character could eat people, so cannibalism really is bad even when the murders are bracketed.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 19 "8. Consuming Homicidal Art" — McAteer uses Bullough's aesthetic distance to test whether the psychopath Hannibal can have genuine aesthetic experience, arguing against Maibom and Harold that egocentric pleasure in an artwork is compatible with aesthetic distancing - so a Lecter who loves Bach and Italian architecture (unlike Cleckley's unmoved psychopath and the Tooth Fairy's graceless 'performances') could really exist. But since psychopaths can value nothing as an end in itself - they treat persons and artworks merely as means - homicidal art like the Muralist's corpse cathedral and Hannibal's gourmet cannibalism is the logical extreme of Wildean aestheticism, proving Wittgenstein's 'Aesthetics and ethics are one' false; yet in homicidal art Hannibal's moral deficit becomes an aesthetic deficit too, because anyone who can see beauty in human bodies as mere material is over-distanced - the bodies, like any sculpture's material, matter.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 15 "Walker Bite. Let’s Just Do What’s Right" — Devlin and Cooper present Dale as the show's Kantian deontologist: he acts from duty regardless of consequences, applying the humanity formula - treat people always as ends, never merely as means - when he blocks the execution of Randall in 'Judge, Jury, Executioner' and refuses to let the group do consequentialist math about abandoning the search for Sophia. Shane, the Governor, and the Termites serve as the consequentialist foils who treat Otis, the prison residents, and their victims as mere means to survival. The chapter argues Dale dies with his humanity and dignity intact, and that the series' recurring drama is a three-sided battle between his deontology, the survivors' consequentialism, and Rick's eventual virtue ethics.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 25 "Walker Bite. If I Don’t Save the World, I Have No Value" — This Walker Bite uses Eugene Porter's exposed lie about being the scientist who can cure the outbreak (5.5 "Self Help") to ask what makes a person valuable once their usefulness collapses. Eugene himself sums up an instrumental view of his own worth - "If I don't cure the disease, if I don't save the world, I have no value" - and admits he sabotaged the bus to stall the DC mission. Against this, Tara's "We're friends. We have each other's backs... You're stuck with us. No matter what" argues that persons are valued for themselves within a community rather than as means, and the chapter lands on Abraham's "people need people" as the real ground of Eugene's place in the group.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 11 "2. Golem Morality in the Modern World" — Skene weighs Peter Singer's 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' - opened with a River Ankh drowning-child variant - against the golem morality of Going Postal and Feet of Clay. Mr. Pump's charge that Moist von Lipwig's frauds 'hastened the deaths' of 2.338 people grounds a golem standard of actuarial murder that Skene applies to the 2008 banking crisis and Mao's Great Leap Forward. With Kant, the chapter holds that free choice is the foundation of moral responsibility and respect for others' wills, but unlike Singer's unlimited demands, golem morality asks us to own the foreseeable consequences of our choices without sacrificing everything.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 11 "3. Hero or Villain" — Kevin McCain asks whether Darrow the hero and Nero au Augustus the villain can really be told apart, noting both hold noble goals (Eo's dream versus preserving humanity) and share brutal means. Consequentialism fails to separate them: Darrow's sacrifice of dockworkers and Sons of Ares to Romulus mirrors Nero's 'I do what I need to do to protect the greater good,' and Harmony's sacrificing Evey shows the same ends-justify-means reasoning. Kantian ethics condemns both, since each lies to people and sacrifices them without consent, treating them as mere means to an end.
