Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 46 "43. Ex Machina as Philosophy Mendacia Ex Machina (Lies from a Machine)" — Grinnell argues Ex Machina is fundamentally about lying, read through Kant's deontology. He frames Nathan's rigged Turing test on Ava against Glaucon's Ring of Gyges challenge and Kant's two formulations of the categorical imperative, deriving three 'wrinkles': lying is heteronomous programming rather than the autonomy Nathan seeks; the experiment is defensible only if Ava fails, since a genuine person may not be manipulated (Formula of Humanity); and the cascade of lies among Nathan, Caleb, and Ava vindicates Kant's absolute prohibition on lying. He uses Caleb's telling of Frank Jackson's Mary's Room and Searle's weak/strong AI distinction to question whether Ava's 'pleasure response' amounts to genuine consciousness or personhood.

### Kingdom of Ends

The kingdom of ends is Immanuel Kant's ideal of a moral community in which all rational beings are united under common laws that each of them legislates and to which each is subject. Every member is at once a lawgiver and one who obeys, and each is treated as an end in themselves possessing dignity rather than a mere means. Kant offered this vision as a further formulation of the categorical imperative, inviting us to act as though we were always legislating for such a systematic union of rational agents.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 24 "Check Out Time" — McGrath and Tilahun ask whether hip hop is bad for women, setting protest and sex-positive tracks (Tupac's "Brenda's Got a Baby", Missy's "One Minute Man", Queen Latifah's "Ladies First", Ms. Dynamite) against endorsements of violence (N.W.A's "One Less Bitch", Snoop's "Can You Control Yo Ho?", 50 Cent's "P.I.M.P"). They apply Mill's harm principle - offend yes, harm no - Hume's counterfactual analysis of causation (the Derek Fisher shot case) to show that whether lyrics cause violence is an unsettled empirical question, Austin and Rae Langton's speech-act theory to argue rappers' cultural authority may let pimp lyrics subordinate women in a way pornography cannot, and Kant's kingdom of ends to charge misogynist lyrics with treating women as mere means.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 20 "From Cash to Kant—and Back Again" — Yolanda Estes pairs Cash with Kant as two duty-based moralists: Cash's Golden Rule in 'The Preacher Said, Jesus Said' parallels Kant's formula of humanity (never treating persons merely as means), and Cash's 'good heart' matches Kant's good will, since songs like 'Sam Hall,' 'Folsom Prison Blues' (the man shot in Reno 'just to watch him die'), and 'I Hung My Head' weigh inner motives over outcomes. Because earthly law never balances the moral scale, she reads Kant's kingdom of ends and Cash's apocalyptic kingdom of God in 'When the Man Comes Around' and 'God's Gonna Cut You Down' as parallel objects of faith: we must live as if perfect justice already prevails, working to improve this world rather than waiting for the next.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 26 "15. Tell the Truth at All Costs" — Bowman argues Candor is the most philosophically important faction because its absolute honesty is Kant's ethics: truthfulness as a perfect duty grounded in free will, making even politeness 'deception in pretty packaging,' and forbidding a lie even when the Erudite come to Merciless Mart hunting Tris - which mirrors Kant's reply to Benjamin Constant that one must not lie even to the murderer at the door. Against this he sets Aristotle's virtue ethics, where truth bows to wisdom, justice, and fortitude when the choice is handing hidden Jews to the SS, and Bentham's utilitarianism, which Amity enacts when it lies at the gates to keep the peace and save lives. The Candor Manifesto's 'web of individual-to-individual relationships' and Kant's kingdom of ends explain why universal honesty alone could make truth safe - and why Christina, the Candor, is the one left standing when the city's deception finally destroys it.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 12 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Bateman replies to Cogburn by recovering the alignment system's actual literary source: Moorcock's Elric saga, where Law and Chaos are rival political ideologies (conservative and liberal tendencies) held in check by the Cosmic Balance, so a Chaotic person need only refuse law's authority, not will horror, and Chaotic Good remains possible. He rejects Cogburn's 'sausage machine' reading of Kant's first formula in favor of the humanity formula and the Realm of Ends, and rejects act utilitarianism as a model of the Good alignment, since an overpopulation scenario shows Mill's calculus mandating culling-genocide and Bentham's felicific calculus cannot actually measure goodness. Drawing on Badiou's ethic of truths, Buddhist and Jain renunciation, and the true-Neutral Druid as servant of the Cosmic Balance, he argues neutrality between Good and Evil need not be monstrous and mourns 4e's 'childishly simplistic' new system.

### Utilitarianism

Utilitarianism is the moral theory holding that the right action is the one that produces the greatest overall balance of well-being, or happiness, considered impartially across everyone affected. It emerged in Britain through the work of Jeremy Bentham and John Stuart Mill as a reforming answer to moral systems grounded in tradition, intuition, or divine command, offering instead a single measurable standard for evaluating laws and conduct. Because it judges acts by their consequences rather than by intentions or rules, it counts each person's happiness equally and treats the good of the many as the aim of morality.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 11 "“The Graduation” Autonomy and the Relational Self" — Jessica Prata Miller reads Buffy through Carol Gilligan's care perspective: Buffy's self is relational (the Scooby Gang, 'Dawn is a part of me' in 'The Gift'), her moral reasoning contextual rather than rule-bound (caging Oz instead of killing the werewolf, rejecting Riley's Initiative 'demons bad' abstraction), and her emotions a moral resource ('My emotions give me power'). She also weighs the criticisms — Buffy's secret harboring of Angel exposed in 'Revelations,' and Faith's utilitarian 'plus column' defense of hiding a killing, which Buffy rejects ('I am' the one who cries over the bystander). Comparing the three Slayers, Miller argues only Buffy attains moral autonomy: Kendra's unquestioning obedience and Faith's hyper-individualistic action-hero isolation both fail, while Buffy's 'I like to think of it as graduation' break from the Watchers' Council shows autonomy achieved within, not against, relationships.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 28 "Buffy Should’ve Killed Ben" — Jacob Held pits retributivism against utilitarian theories of punishment using three Buffyverse cases: vengeance demons Anya and Halfrek show that 'just desert' is arbitrary, relative, and subjective; Angel's gypsy curse (punishment as desert) secures society less reliably than Spike's Initiative chip (pure deterrence), while Oz's preventive caging raises the problem of punishing the innocent. The hard case is 'The Gift': Buffy refuses to kill the innocent Ben, but Held sides with Giles, who strangles him — arguing that since the state's end is security and freedom, one life may rightly be traded for six billion.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 11 "The Obligation to Play Baseball" — Horan and Solomon examine the 2001-02 contraction fight in which Judge Harry Crump ordered the Minnesota Twins to honor their Metrodome lease and play the 2002 season. They argue the Minnesota courts smuggled Bentham-Mill utilitarian reasoning about the public good into contract law, which normally awards only money damages, because baseball's antitrust exemption (from Justice Holmes's 1922 ruling through Justice Blackmun's 1972 opinion) had always treated the game as more than a business. Having long profited from special treatment, the owners lost when Bud Selig's plan to eliminate the Twins collided with the same 'greatest good for the greatest number' logic.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 37 "19b" — A paired debate on whether Pete Rose belongs in the Hall of Fame despite his lifetime ban for betting on the Reds, framed by retributive versus utilitarian theories of punishment. Aeon Skoble argues yes: betting on one's own team to win commits no fraud like throwing games, and Cooperstown honors baseball excellence, not moral perfection — the Hall already enshrines racists, adulterers, and cheats. Mark Hamilton answers no with the Dowd Report's evidence, Rule 21(d), and Giamatti's banishment statement: a managing gambler may sacrifice the season to settle tonight's debt, and reinstatement without remorse would declare the game's rules toothless.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 22 "The Dangers of Hedonism" — Sander Lee reads A Midsummer Night's Sex Comedy as Allen's warning against hedonism, tracing that ethos to empiricist thought from Hobbes and Locke through Bentham's utilitarianism to American pragmatism, embodied in Leopold Sturgis, an Ayer-style positivist philosopher who denies everything unprovable yet dies of passion with Dulcy and is deified by Andrew's spirit ball as pagan 'pure essence'. Using Sartre's Nausea, the chapter shows Andrew and Ariel's attempt to recreate their lost 'perfect moment' by the brook failing on every count, proving such moments inauthentic fantasies that ignore freedom, responsibility, and the passage of time. Through Bazin's Nietzschean reading of Renoir (Apollonian order versus Dionysian impulse), it argues that unlike Isaac Davis in Manhattan, the film's characters end more committed to hedonism than they began, with no character left qualified to condemn it.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 60 "The Sorting Hat Speaks Division and Divisiveness" — This section argues that patriotism violates the principle of equal moral worth shared by utilitarians and Kantians alike: Bentham's 'each to count for one, and none for more than one' means the Minister of Magic's pain counts no more than a house-elf's, while Kant's formula forbids treating anyone (Muggle or wizard) merely as a means. It reads Death Eater pureblood ideology as ordinary racism and sexism, cites Potterwatch's 'every human life is worth the same, and worth saving' and Hermione's S.P.E.W. campaign against 'slave labor,' and asks how preferring countrymen over foreigners differs from preferring people of one's race or gender, since neither is something a person controls.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 32 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Anna Lännström runs a full moral-responsibility audit on Gibson's tormented, remorseful Judas: Aristotle's analysis of excusing conditions (insanity, Satanic possession, ignorance) partly alleviates his guilt as it does Peter's denial; Boethius's timelessly eternal God is deployed against the foreknowledge problem and then criticized as self-defeating; and the Edwards/Frankfurt compatibilist solution is applied — Judas could not have done otherwise because God would not have permitted it, yet acted freely since he did what he wanted. Consequentialism (Mill) oddly makes the betrayal nearly harmless or even salvific, Kantian intention-analysis turns on whether Judas was a greedy embezzler or a Zealot trying to force a revolt, and virtue ethics weighs his immediate remorse and attempt to return the silver against the habitual greed John and Matthew attribute to him.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 12 "“You Know . . . What They’re Up Against”" — Dees finds moral ambiguity lurking in Star Wars' black-and-white universe: Han Solo's Hobbesian ethical egoism ('I take orders from just one person - me') is shown to be coherent and gradually transformed by friendship with Luke and Leia into commitment to a cause. Lando's betrayal of Han on Bespin is defended as a straightforward Mill-Bentham utilitarian choice by a responsible official, weighed against Bernard Williams's Jim-and-the-commandant integrity objection, which the author rejects as moral vanity. Count Dooku's apparent idealism is exposed as evil's tool, and Anakin's massacre of the Sand People is condemned as non-ambiguous barbarity via Kant's formula of humanity (and Hume on reason's role with the passions), leaving only late Vader as genuinely morally ambiguous.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 27 "“Trust Your Feelings”" — Fader tackles the paradox that Jedi lie while Sith tell the truth: Obi-Wan's 'Darth Vader betrayed and murdered your father,' Yoda's trickster masquerade on Dagobah, the Council's cover-up of its waning powers, against Vader's brutal truth at Cloud City and Palpatine's technically honest 'I love democracy.' Kant's absolute prohibition of lying is set against the utilitarian's greatest-good lie and Nietzsche's claim that truth is the accepted set of social lies; Obi-Wan's deception is then defended through Plato's noble lie and the Buddha's Parable of the House on Fire, where 'expedients' to save the oblivious are no falsehood, while Vader and Dooku wield literal truths as weapons without compassion. Luke's answer is to stop accepting anyone's version and build his own green lightsaber: truth as perspective, intention, and finally the heart's understanding that redeems Anakin.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 27 "Truth, Justice, and the American Way" — Contrasting Miller's two icons, Skoble shows Superman becoming a covert government operative on explicitly utilitarian grounds ('I get to save lives - and the media stays quiet'), while Batman insists a badge or flag is neither necessary nor sufficient for justice: 'the world only makes sense when you force it to'. The complications cut both ways - the Sons of the Batman kill indiscriminately in their hero's name, and Batman first regrets not killing the Joker given the hundreds murdered since. Skoble leaves open who is more honest: the vigilante who owns the trade-off, or critics who deplore the protection they depend on.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 29 "Look On My Works, Ye Mighty" — Ozymandias, Watchmen's smartest human vigilante, kills three million New Yorkers with a staged alien attack to avert nuclear war, and Skoble walks through the question the novel forces: can the end justify the means? The heroes' darkest hour is their acquiescence in his scheme - only Rorschach rejects the utilitarian reasoning ('Never compromise... Evil must be punished') and is killed by Dr. Manhattan to keep the secret. Skoble leaves us asking whether Ozymandias is a misunderstood savior or has 'become a monster', and whether our recoil at his act is moral clarity or weakness.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 43 "Power and Glory Tests of Virtue" — The chapter's thesis is that superhero ethics is not utilitarianism (whose perverse 'evil twin' governs Marvel villains) but personalism - the tradition from Borden Parker Bowne to Martin Buber, rooted in Kant's insistence that every person be treated as an end and never merely as a means, and aiming at his 'kingdom of ends'. Heroes who refuse to weigh one innocent against the many enact personalism, and it redeems even Galactus: lying defeated, he is saved by Captain America's and Reed Richards' insistence that 'We had no choice, Galactus', which wins the devourer into a moral community. The authors read the whole arc as the ancient warning against hubris retold in contemporary storytelling.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 48 "Phoenix Rising Jean Grey" — Jean Grey, the self-doubting original X-Man of the Cyclops-Wolverine love triangle, evolves across the films - the phoenix necklace, growing powers, growing confidence - through all three Kohlberg levels to her self-sacrifice that saves the X-Men at the end of X2. Housel rejects reading that act as utilitarian calculation or as the unbalanced self-sacrifice some feminist readings of care ethics would fault: Jean acts not out of duty but out of love and care, beyond the call of duty - what philosophers call supererogation - becoming a female Christ figure whose phoenix image foreshadows resurrection and Campbell's return as 'Master of the Two Worlds'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 52 "Where I Don’t Want to Be" — South reads Barbara's 'Where I don't want to be' monologue in Batgirl: Year One through Mill's On Liberty passage on people who ask not 'what do I prefer?' but 'what is usually done by persons of my station?' - the pressure to conform Barbara feels as a librarian with a denied police application and a father's expectations. He then argues neither utilitarianism nor Kantianism can guide such a life, since both exclude the question of what I want and who I am becoming; what Barbara needs - and we need - is to make our desires intelligible to ourselves and bridge the gap between who she is and who she wants to be ('Divine my own future... Not a page from someone else's book').
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 91 "Start Stitchin’ That Costume, Bub. Duty Calls" — Explains Mill-style utilitarianism — rightness fixed entirely by consequences for overall pleasure and pain, counting every sentient being (a cat may enjoy tuna but not Watchmen) — and applies it: Clark Kent must rescue the failing plane over the Daily Planet press conference, and you must give the jeans money to charity. Since adopting a role is obligated whenever it produces the most overall good, anyone with superpowers has a duty to become a superhero, so Peter Parker's misery in Spider-Man 2 is morally beside the point: utilitarianism says he must remain Spider-Man.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 92 "Aw, C’mon! Do I Have to Save the Day" — Presses four objections to utilitarianism through superhero cases: a weakened Jean Grey dying to save Juggernaut's bus victims shows utilitarianism obliterates supererogation — she would be blameworthy whichever way she chose; Ares' demand that Wonder Woman kill an innocent girl to avert global biowar forces her against her character; Batman refusing to let an innocent-of-this-crime Joker die in The Joker: Devil's Advocate shows the theory sacrificing justice; and the Green Goblin accidentally doing great good by dragging a would-be mass shooter down Fifth Avenue shows consequences alone cannot make an intended wrong right.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 94 "I Fought the Law and the Law Won" — Argues that Batman's warrantless raids, intimidation and evidence-free arrests violate negative duties that bind everyone regardless of role, so producing good (the utilitarian reply) cannot justify them, and superpowers earn no legal exemptions that we would deny police. When Spider-Man evades NYPD warrants, the chapter applies Socrates' argument in Plato's Crito that citizens owe the law their obedience even when wrongly accused, though it concedes that keeping a secret identity safe from villains who would torture or kill loved ones can override the duty to submit, a move consistent with non-Kantian nonconsequentialism since Kant could not abide any lie.
- **Hip-Hop and Philosophy - Rhyme 2 Reason**, ch. 24 "Check Out Time" — McGrath and Tilahun ask whether hip hop is bad for women, setting protest and sex-positive tracks (Tupac's "Brenda's Got a Baby", Missy's "One Minute Man", Queen Latifah's "Ladies First", Ms. Dynamite) against endorsements of violence (N.W.A's "One Less Bitch", Snoop's "Can You Control Yo Ho?", 50 Cent's "P.I.M.P"). They apply Mill's harm principle - offend yes, harm no - Hume's counterfactual analysis of causation (the Derek Fisher shot case) to show that whether lyrics cause violence is an unsettled empirical question, Austin and Rae Langton's speech-act theory to argue rappers' cultural authority may let pimp lyrics subordinate women in a way pornography cannot, and Kant's kingdom of ends to charge misogynist lyrics with treating women as mere means.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 18 "U2 and Philosophy" — The authors apply Gilligan's and Noddings' ethics of care to U2: 'Bad' shows the speaker as Noddings' 'one-caring', and 'Sometimes You Can't Make It on Your Own' - Bono caring for his dying father through anger and resentment - exemplifies care's insistence on the particular relationship over universal rules, refusing abstraction even of the usual songwriting metaphors. 'Peace on Earth' names the Omagh bomb's dead (Sean, Julia, Gareth, Ann, Breda) and 'Van Diemen's Land' refuses both IRA and British sides, showing care ethics rejecting the utilitarian accounting and the Kantian universalizability arguments that could rationalize such violence. They conclude U2 are philosophical rather than political feminists: Gilligan's 'different voice' is not a woman's voice, and the band's connected knowing - debt relief sung as connection in 'Beautiful Day' - makes maternal thinking 'loud, rhythmic, catchy, even cool'.
- **Bullshit and Philosophy - Guaranteed to Get Perfect Results Every Time**, ch. 103 "The Scientific Method as a Search for the Justice in Bullshit" — Fuller portrays the bullshitter as the consummate hypocrite, bluffing from behind genuine uncertainty and exploiting the sophistic principle that controlling the moment of decision controls its outcome — calling the question when the balance of arguments favors you. Since we can rarely audit anyone's track record, epistemology leans on 'trust', 'witness' and 'testimony', read optimistically through Thomas Reid's divinely guaranteed common sense or, à la Kierkegaard, malignly as cowardly delegation of belief; either way 'reliability', which papers over the gap between evidence and belief, is itself a bullshit concept. He then analogizes the epistemic economy of evidence to the moral economy of sensation: as utilitarianism defers immediate gratification (taxation insuring against discounting our future selves), so the bullshitter's imperviousness to current evidence-weightings is prudence — an 'affirmative action' for weaker-evidenced positions that may prove the better bet in the fullness of time.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 25 "Introduction" — Frames Part V's ethics chapters. Adams' chapter updates Plato's ring of Gyges for Heroes — with Claire's and Sylar's powers, why be moral? — answered by the properly ordered tripartite soul; McAleer's uses The Office to illustrate Aristotle's wit as a mean between buffoonery and boorishness; White's uses the Batman/Joker problem and a Bat-trolley version of Foot's case to argue deontologically that Batman need not kill the Joker; and Loftis' reads Watchmen's Ozymandias and Rorschach as a failed utilitarian and a failed deontologist, pointing to 'who watches the watchmen.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman never simply kills the Joker despite the graveyard he keeps filling, framing the question with Foot's and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant-surgeon variant. Utilitarianism says kill one to save many; deontology says the agent-relative 'do not kill' — but the Batman case differs from the classic dilemmas because the Joker himself endangers his victims, Batman cannot be certain he will kill again (the foggy-track variant), and killing him would amount to the Minority Report-style prepunishment of a crime not yet committed. White, a self-described strict deontologist, concedes the case is genuinely hard and leaves the means-versus-ends debate open.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis argues Watchmen's real target is authoritarianism, with Ozymandias and Rorschach as corrupted rationalizers. Ozymandias calls himself a consequentialist, but his Bentham-Mill utilitarianism cannot survive Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' — an infinite future makes utility sums impossible — and it ignores the rights of the New Yorkers he slaughters as mere means. Rorschach's deontology is hypocrisy (he admires Truman's Hiroshima trade-off and says 'can't make an omelet without breaking eggs'), mistaking Kant's categorical imperative — universalize your maxim, treat humanity never merely as a means — for black-and-white thinking in service of fascist thuggery, while the nonideological Nite Owls embody the lesson that no one should be trusted with such power.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24 to run the torture debate: the ticking bomb scenario (Syed Ali's nuclear bomb, Miles pressing to torture Audrey) dramatizes the utilitarian case for forward-looking interrogational torture, while Jack slicing off the Russian consul's finger and Morris's broken guilt show torture as a deontological violation that destroys character on both sides and usually fails to extract truth. Against the show's sanitized, banal presentation (Agent Burke as the "kindly torturer"), he sets Abu Ghraib, the systematic training of torturers, and the metastatic spread of torture programs once permitted. Fiction can open the ethical question, he concludes, but must not be mistaken for the reality of torture.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 9 "Plato’s Cave Again" — Curran uses Shadow of a Doubt to teach epistemology: Charlie's claim to 'know' her uncle distinguishes knowledge by acquaintance from propositional knowledge as justified true belief, with the permanently stuck 'Til Two clock showing a true belief that is not knowledge because its warrant is unreliable. Coherence (Hegel, Blanshard), pragmatist (James, Dewey), and correspondence theories of truth are tested against the townspeople's false but convenient beliefs about Uncle Charlie, and only correspondence survives. Kant's absolute duty not to lie is weighed against Mill's act and rule utilitarianism for the detectives' deceptions, and a feminist care-ethics perspective assesses Charlie's shielding her mother from the truth. Plato's cave frames the cinema itself: film can deceive like shadows on a wall, yet the detectives' unused photograph shows the camera can also reveal truth, so movies help us face facts, at the price, as Charlie pays, of lost innocence.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 25 "Doing Things in Private" — Skoble asks exactly what Jeff does wrong in Rear Window and whether his illicit snooping can generate genuine duties. Against a purely consequentialist verdict ('it all worked out okay'), he argues that knowledge creates conditional obligations - given what he has seen of Thorwald, Jeff's intervention is obligatory rather than supererogatory, by 'ought implies can' - and he weighs autonomy-respecting limits on intervening in Miss Lonelyhearts' despair. He then analyzes privacy as a moral right grounded in reciprocal legitimate expectations, concluding that Jeff violated no such right since everything he watched was on public display, so the ends-justify-the-means charge mostly dissolves.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 15 "The Virtues of Superhumans" — Rachel Robison tests the Deadly Viper Assassination Squad against three ethical theories. Act and rule utilitarianism condemn killing Vernita in front of Nikki and revenge in general; Kant's categorical imperative condemns Elle's black-mamba betrayal of Budd (contradiction in conception), O-Ren's beheading of a dissenter (contradiction in will), and Buck's selling of comatose women (treating persons as mere means). She concludes the Squad instead follows a bastardized Aristotelian virtue ethics—Bill's Superman speech, contempt for Budd's shotgun bushwhack and Elle's poisoning of Pai Mei define courage as the mean between cowardice and rashness—so Beatrix would be cowardly not to seek revenge.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 22 "The Good, The Bad, and The Ugly" — Johnson and Schmitz argue that Cash, through songs like 'San Quentin,' 'Jacob Green,' and his cover of 'The Mercy Seat,' championed reforming prisons from a retributive to a rehabilitative model and abolishing capital punishment (songs like 'Joe Bean' and 'Long Black Veil' center executed innocents). They defend Cash with Mill: Socrates shows vengeful retributive sentiment is immoral, Mill's harm principle says government may coerce only to prevent harm, so punishment should be justified only by future deterrence and rehabilitation. Since the death penalty's deterrent effect is empirically weak (California, Missouri-vs-Iowa murder rates) and wrongful convictions are common, Mill today would join Cash in calling for abolition.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 42 "The Cosmic Divide" — The chapter casts the two series as opposed worldviews: the original is Manichaean moral absolutism, with 'War of the Gods' staging Count Iblis and the Ships of Light as cosmic Darkness and Light battling over humanity, while Moore's re-imagining is Protagorean moral relativism where context decides right and wrong. Its clearest cases are comparative: Roslin abandons the FTL-less ships as 'a matter of numbers' yet burns forty-three percent of the fleet's fuel reserves to rescue Starbuck, and Leoben is airlocked after interrogation while the tortured Athena and Gina are treated with mercy. The fan schism between the shows, it concludes, is really the centuries-old quarrel between absolutism and relativism.
- **The Wizard of Oz and Philosophy - Wicked Wisdom of the West**, ch. 8 "There’s No Place Like Home" — Luke Dick stages Immanuel Kant as the 'Supreme Critical Chancellor of Munchkinland' and runs the film through Kantian ethics: against hedonism, utilitarianism, and command-based religion, the formula of universalizability condemns the Wizard's lies and his use of the companions as mere means, while the ends-in-themselves principle raises the awkward case of Glinda and Dorothy keeping the dead Witch of the East's ruby slippers. Judging the characters, the Lion's rescue of Dorothy is morally praiseworthy (duty against strong inclination), the brainless Scarecrow falls outside Kant's jurisdiction, and the sentimental Tin Man is pre-emptively condemned. The chapter finally rebels against its Chancellor: cases like returning the slippers, or Toto versus Almira Gulch, show that a world of absolute morality lies only 'somewhere over the rainbow,' and real moral life in Kansas needs Baum's Tin Man heart reconciled with Kantian duty.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 9 "You’re Living in a Fantasy World, This Beautiful World" — Sylvia argues that the split-screen 'All I Need' video made for MTV's anti-trafficking EXIT project — an American child's comfortable day intercut with a child laborer finishing the very shoes the American takes off — argues against child labor more powerfully than a standard utilitarian argument, because it joins Aristotle's ethos, pathos, and logos instead of relying on logos alone. Using the cognitive/expressive distinction, he claims the song also argues by turning listeners back on themselves ('I only stick with you because there are no others'). He then deploys Nozick's experience machine: we are all plugged into a Baudrillardian, Matrix-like media hyperreality that can make exploitation fade into background images, and the video's slap in the face 'punctures the hyperreality', showing how emotion can do argumentative work that rigorous argument cannot.
- **Stephen Colbert and Philosophy - I Am Philosophy (And So Can You!)**, ch. 10 "Explaining Moral Doubt" — Steven Gimbel reads the Formidable Opponent segment - red-tie Colbert debating blue-tie Colbert - as a glimpse of authentic moral deliberation that the flip-flop-phobic punditry satirized by the show (and Jon Stewart's Crossfire rant) has abandoned. Moral doubt is good because perspectives are partial and the Enlightenment 'marketplace of ideas' of Locke and Mill tests beliefs only through challenge. It has a source: 'morally right' bundles five dimensions - the actor's character shaped by habit (Aristotle's virtue ethics), the act itself judged by Kant's categorical imperative, the pleasure-versus-pain consequences tallied Bentham-style, the rights of the person affected from Locke and Hobbes's social contract, and the special care obligations of close relationships (Noddings and Ruddick) - and hard cases like abortion and flag burning are exactly where these dimensions pull apart. So emulate the dueling Colberts: fear not the flip-flop, since deciding which value trumps which requires open-minded conversation with oneself.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 8 "8" — Four 'Phase Two' essays on the nature of evil. Arp argues that in V for Vendetta V is a utilitarian user of persons just like the fascist Norsefire state - using Dascombe as a shield and torturing Evey 'for her own good' - so Kant's demand to treat humanity never merely as a means condemns the hero-as-villain, though 'moral autonomy' Kantians complicate the verdict. Poon stages the Aquinas-Ockham debate over will and intellect as Magneto reprograms Sentinels against New York (Ultimate X-Men #05), arguing the will cannot choose against the intellect's judgment, so supervillains like Magneto, Ra's al Ghul, and Apocalypse act for what seems good to them with a deeply flawed conception of the good. Robichaud uses Superman Returns, Civil War, and Captain America vs the Red Skull to test Mackie's error theory, prescriptivism, expressivism, and moral relativism, defending moral objectivism against the Modern Age's gray morality. Sylvia IV and Walters use Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures with competent judges, and Railton's ideal-advisor moral realism to dismantle Mojo's defense that his Spineless Ones' ratings-driven bloodsports are just desire-satisfaction, indicting our own reality TV.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 9 "12" — Four 'Phase Three' essays on world conquest. Terjesen asks whether Doctor Doom's magnanimity (Aristotle's great-souledness, contra the unity-of-virtues thesis Aquinas held and Philippa Foot qualified) makes him less villainous than The Authority, whose purely consequentialist paternalism - like Doom's Emperor Doom or Ozymandias's plot - usurps a free choice no mere power can justify. Barringer reads Marvel's Civil War through Hobbes: the Stamford explosion and unrestrained superpowers recreate the state of nature, the Registration Act is the surrender of freedom to a sovereign, and Stark, Richards, and Pym repeat Hobbes's flawed faith in 'scientific' deductive politics, sealed by the clone-Thor killing of Goliath. Hillerbrand and Sandburg pit Rorschach's Kantian deontology (no compromise, not even to save the world) against Ozymandias's utilitarian murder of three million New Yorkers in Watchmen, arguing via Laplace's Demon that even Dr. Manhattan - nihilist or Schopenhauerian recluse - cannot verify the outcome, so watchmen can be trusted only by knowing their limits. Ostrander's fictional NSC interview has Amanda Waller's Suicide Squad defended with Benthamite utility, the rejection of natural rights as 'nonsense on stilts,' and the Augustinian just-war criteria of just cause, right intent, and proportionality, while the interviewer exposes how conveniently those limits bend.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 17 "Close the Door, Put Out the Lights" — Scott Calef tests three ethical theories against Led Zeppelin's off-stage destruction: TV-tossing, samurai-slashed hotel rooms, food fights, sharks hung in closets at the Edgewater Inn, the red snapper incident, and Jimmy Page's relationship with fourteen-year-old Lori Maddox. Classical utilitarianism weighs Bonzo's glee against the traumatized chambermaid, displaced guests, and unpaid-for sleep loss, generally condemning the pranks while leaving the supposedly consensual snapper episode uncomfortably open. Kant condemns across the board: Plant's fake tour itineraries and the stolen 'Black Beauty' Les Paul fail the universalizability test, trashing hotel rooms is self-defeating when universalized, and treating the Portland woman as a mere means violates her dignity as a rational agent; Aristotle's golden mean finds the band's excess nowhere near virtue, whatever Caligula would say. The chapter closes by separating moral judgment of the men from appreciation of the music.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 23 "Coda" — White asks whether fans who trade or sell Led Zeppelin bootlegs wrong the band, given how little official live material it released. He weighs Locke's labor-mixing account of property (the band creates the performance, but tapers 'mix their labor' too), the legal view of property as a bundle of rights, and rule-utilitarian arguments that bootlegs promote the band without cutting into sales of studio albums. He concludes with Ronald Dworkin's point that rights trump utility: if the live performance is the band's property, the band's choice to withhold it binds fans whatever happiness wider distribution would produce.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 9 "Achievement Unlocked Ethical Considerations" — Monica Evans opens with the 2006 'Serenity Now' funeral raid — a PvP guild massacring an in-game funeral for a real player — to argue that in-game ethics depend on each player's perception of the gameworld: mourners treat Azeroth as an extension of real life, raiders as a competitive game, and both are right. Plato's Ring of Gyges fails as an analogy because WoW hands everyone invisibility, yet morality still operates as a social construction through reputation, guilds, and the ostracism of ninja-looters. She finds the Borean Tundra 'torture quest' ethically hollow since the prisoner respawns and nothing persists, applies Mill's utilitarianism to good-samaritan players and universally loathed ninja-looters, and uses Kant's Categorical Imperative both to explain why players don't desert dungeon parties and why fair PvP killing of friends is permissible.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 20 "Embrace the Shadow!—There Is No Moral Dilemma" — Phil Serchuk asks whether ninja looters — say, a raid leader Master-Looting the Warglaive of Azzinoth — act immorally, and answers no. After reviewing act and rule utilitarianism through Medivh's opening of the Dark Portal and the theft of Napoleon's sarcophagus, and Kant's Categorical Imperative through Kil'jaeden's deception of Ner'zhul, he argues that virtual items cannot be owned at all and that there is no moral agent in WoW for either theory to condemn: neither the player (who kills thousands of PCs in battlegrounds without blame) nor the avatar (which makes no decisions) can be held liable. Ninjaing is therefore as morally benign as a natural disaster.
- **Zombies, Vampires, and Philosophy - New Life for the Undead**, ch. 20 "Good Guy Vampires" — Robert Arp models the vampire's unlife with substance and property dualism (a cursed soul persisting after the staked body in Rice and Stoker versus perishing with it in Blade), then uses Mill's distinction between lower bodily feelings and higher mental pleasures from Utilitarianism to explain how vampires can lament, in higher-pain, their inability to enjoy wind in their hair or wine. The hedonistic paradox dooms Lestat-style pleasure-seekers: seeking pleasure for its own sake yields either the pain of frustration (Louis's dead-twins trick) or boredom across immortal lifetimes ('it's somewhat boring, living forever'), while Aristotle's completed-state pleasures suggest the way out. Good guy vampires from Barnabas Collins to St. Germain escape the paradox by pursuing higher pleasures and activities for their own sake, confirming Mill's closing counsel that only those fixed on objects other than their own pleasure find happiness.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 3 "index" — This file spans book chapters 4-11. Elizabeth Losh reads Facebook games (Zombies, Mob Wars, Scrabulous, Parking Wars, PackRat, (Lil) Green Patch) through Goffman's 'face', Brown and Levinson's politeness, and Derrida's gift-obligation, showing that aggressive games can be played politely while altruistic ones coerce; Jeremy Sarachan analyzes profile pictures through Barthes's studium, punctum and 'air' and Benjamin's mechanical reproduction (the webcam image that has no original). Mimi Marinucci pairs Glaucon's Ring of Gyges with Suler's online disinhibition effect to argue that Facebook's forced integration of audiences (students, colleagues, Mom all reading one profile) suppresses 'fronting' and so can foster authentic self-expression; Mariam Thalos answers with Sartre's analysis of the gaze and Beauvoir's woman-as-Other that the elective, endlessly plastic profile cannot anchor the bonding only face-to-face encounter provides - hence 'Why I Am Not a Friend' - while Wandel and Beavers use Groundhog Day's Phil Connors and Goffman's presentation of self to defend identity play as real self-discovery, and Vejby and Wittkower ask whether Facebook is Debord's Spectacle 2.0 or a platform for Situationist detournement. Finally, Craig Condella measures 'friending' against Aristotle's three friendships and Cicero's 'handmaid of virtue' (via the Seinfeld episode where Keith Hernandez asks Jerry to help him move), and Matthew Tedesco sets 322 Facebook friends against Godwin's burning archbishop to press the utilitarian impartiality challenge, deploying Williams's 'one thought too many' shipwreck case and criticizing Frank Jackson's sector-plan defense of partiality.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 4 "index" — Six essays on friendship in the Facebook age. Tedesco asks whether the low-demand 'Facebook friendship' can reconcile the utilitarian demand for impartiality (Mill, Railton, Kagan) with the partiality of real friends, and concludes Facebook ties are only supplementary to relationships built elsewhere. Hamington surveys a hundred users and argues in Noddings's care-ethics terms that Facebook's information transfer makes caring possible (knowledge of the concrete other is necessary for care), though it also makes dropping a student over one racist comment effortless. Bloor reads Facebook through Heidegger's technological nihilism and the anonymous 'one', warning that speed of exchange erodes Aristotle's few deep, morally formative friendships, while Briggle's farewell letter to Facebook judges the site by Ivan Illich's convivial-tool criteria and Cuonzo recasts pokes and virtual gifts as efficient successors to primate grooming; Lattimore applies Bakhtin's 'excess of seeing' to how viewers 'consummate' other users' self-presentations.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 20 "Forwards Win Matches but Defences Win Trophies" — Wall asks when the professional foul—the defender who 'had to bring him down'—could be a genuinely moral act, testing it against Kantian universalizability and the good will and against Bentham-and-Mill utilitarianism, and settling on psychologically altruistic motivation as what could override the foul's default wrongness. Against the psychological egoists (La Rochefoucauld, Slote, Hobbes) who would dissolve even Di Canio's caught ball into self-interest, he deploys Nagel's argument from The Possibility of Altruism and the soldier-on-the-grenade case, then derives tight conditions: a deliberate, minimally harmful foul, in a game it can decide, in a semifinal whose red card the fouler will certainly miss. Ballack's 2002 tactical foul on Lee Chun-Soo comes closest but fails (he stayed on the pitch), as do Schumacher's assault on Battiston, Fletcher's pointless foul at 4–0 up, and Abidal's accidental clip—so genuinely moral professional fouls are rare, but defenders get the most shots at being the team's saints.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 28 "So Why Do I Support Aston Villa" — Rose—made a Villan by misreading a 1978 Panini sticker as Aston Villa's claret and blue—asks whether supporting Aston Villa is rational and argues ethics is far more like fandom than philosophers admit. Reasons for supporting Villa (local team, the 1982 European Cup, the colors) explain but never justify his allegiance, and the impartial procedures ethics prizes—the utilitarian benevolent spectator and Rawls's original position behind the veil of ignorance, with its 'sort of Kantian' consent-based alternative—turn out too demanding and too abstract: they would force him to donate his match ticket to charity, forbid the Premiership manager favoring his academy son, and reduce agency to the 'Rose-calcio scale' absurdity of switching to Real Madrid for rational reasons. His positive, communitarian claim is that we are thrown into social traditions whose inherited values—like a team—make moral agency and action possible at all, a 'different kind of rationality' that flirts with relativism yet still needs an exit strategy for cultures that discriminate against women or torture children.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 14 "Don’t Carry the World upon Your Shoulders. Only Your Opponent" — Cooper and Taylor argue that Kano's judo principles, seiryokuzenyou (maximum efficiency) and jitakyouei (mutual welfare and benefit), echo Bentham's principle of utility: both men swept away archaic rules to reach one efficient ethical goal, and Kano accepted the comparison. They run the hedonic calculus over training bruises versus the joy of a clean throw, use Mill's secondary principles as rule-utilitarian guidelines (release the armbar at the tap rather than calculating each time), and answer the objection that utilitarianism demands too much with Kano's own ethos: like judo, it is about continual improvement, not impossible maximization.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 34 "Kind of, Sort of a Lie, But neither Immoral nor Illegal" — Cynthia McWilliams imagines a reader beating her neighbor after taking 'Pedophile Nervous For First Day Of School' literally, and asks whether The Onion lied to her and whether that lie was wrong. She defines a lie as asserting what you believe false (intent to deceive is not required), then tests the satire on both classic accounts: on Kant's categorical imperative, a lie without intent to deceive does not use readers merely as means, while on Mill's utilitarianism the entertainment benefit outweighs harm unless serious harm is reasonably foreseeable — the limit case being the 1938 and Quito 1949 War of the Worlds broadcasts, the second of which killed six people in a riot. Her verdict: The Onion is 'kind of, sort of a lie' but neither immoral nor illegal, passing even the Brandenburg 'imminent lawless action' standard for free speech.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — Sylvia models the Doctor on feminist care ethics: Gilligan's response to Kohlberg's justice-tinged scales and Noddings's distinction between natural caring (for Rose, Martha, Peri in 'The Caves of Androzani') and ethical caring, which explains his forgiveness of the Master and compassion for Dalek Caan after genocides. Against utilitarian impartiality — which cannot say why he should save his companion over a stranger — the relationship itself grounds the obligation, while his vengeful moment facing the lone Dalek in 'Dalek' shows what caring burnout looks like.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Lewis defends the Cybermen: using the 'Genesis of the Daleks' dilemma he shows the Doctor reasons like a Kantian duty ethicist — refusing to kill innocent proto-Daleks whatever the consequences — rather than a utilitarian, and that performing bad actions does not make an agent evil. After the Mondas, Lumic, and Morrison origins establish that Cybermen seek to cure pain and death, he argues the Doctor's 'good to strive for but bad to achieve' argument in 'Age of Steel' is invalid, and that upgrading would be morally acceptable — an applied-ethics fix — if the Cybermen obtained informed consent and respected human autonomy instead of forcing conversions.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 8 "The (Single) Garden Path" — Compares Herbert's three eugenics programs: the Bene Gesserit's centuries-long Kwisatz Haderach breeding scheme (explicitly modeled on the communal breeding of the guardians in Plato's Republic, undone when Jessica bears Paul a generation early and he escapes their control), Leto II's Golden Path breeding for Siona's invisibility to prescience, and the Tleilaxu axolotl-tank immortality that collapses when their Face Dancers out-mimic them. Each program is weighed ethically—Leto as the 'ultimate consequentialist' whose species-saving tyranny invokes Mill's utilitarianism and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means, the Sisterhood as shifting toward Kantian duties against using persons as mere means. Herbert's lesson: 'the most dangerous of all creations is a rigid code of ethics,' whether aimed at a single person, a single result, or a single agenda.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 22 "Vigilante Hero" — Epright and Worth argue that rule-following - the Ten Commandments, the Golden Rule, Kant's categorical imperative (whose consistent Kantian never lies even to Nazis), or the Bentham-Mill principle of utility (whose consistent utilitarian must torture if stakes are high) - never made anyone moral, and Dexter's Code is the case in point: it gives the appearance of morality while licensing murder, and its source (Harry, 'God', the texts) cannot vindicate it. Drawing on Jonah Lehrer's neuroscience that moral judgment is emotional first with reason as post-hoc lawyer, they argue the emotionless Dexter is the madman who has lost everything except his reason, and Kohlberg's moral-development stages find him stuck at the pre-conventional level, below a fifth-grader - punishment-avoidance and you-scratch-my-back reasoning, never universal principles or respect for persons. Real Dexter-inspired killers (Mark Twitchell, Andrew Conley) clinch the verdict: he is neither vigilante hero nor moral agent, just a selfish addict whose rule-governed kills justify nothing.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 23 "You Control Your Urges—They Do Not Control You" — Waller and McAlear first rebut the amoral reading: Dexter does feel (he sobs over Rita, loves Deb, misses Harry) and does control his urges through the Code, so morality applies to him, and the Dark Passenger is merely everyone's socially unacceptable desires - the very thing that gives rise to moral codes. They then test the three theories: Aristotelian virtue ethics mostly fails because murder admits no mean and Harry's Code teaches killer's skills rather than virtues (though its 'don't kill innocents' dispositions are genuine virtues); utilitarianism fails even in rule-utilitarian form - via the organ-harvesting doctor and Harry's own utilitarian guilt over Laura Moser's death - because Dexter kills because the Code requires it, not because it maximizes happiness. What fits is dark deontology: like Kant's argument that murderers consent to their own execution out of respect for their rationality, Dexter kills only killers, acts from duty rather than enjoyment, and treats 'don't get caught' as a condition for the possibility of his true imperative.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 28 "A Second Look at Dexter’s Motives" — David Ramsay Steele first calculates that Dexter is a public benefactor - each killed predator saves several net lives a year - and then explains the deeper appeal through Bernard Mandeville's Fable of the Bees and Adam Smith's invisible hand: like good law, Harry's Code channels an amoral appetite (the thrill of killing) into socially beneficial results without reforming the appetite itself, refuting Christianity's fixation on pure motives. Dexter thus does totally the right thing for totally the wrong reason. Finally Steele doubts Dexter's own story: the spontaneously unlocked door of the Castillos' shed shows real empathy, and it was Harry's deliberate instruction (Nurse Mary), not fate, that made him a killer - 'addiction is always a choice.'
- **SpongeBob SquarePants and Philosophy - Soaking Up Secrets Under the Sea!**, ch. 12 "How Can I Compete with Geniusness" — Timothy Dunn uses 'Patrick SmartPants', where a brain-coral transplant turns Patrick into a genius who abandons SpongeBob, to ask whether the happy ignoramus or the discontented genius lives better. After sketching a subjectivist defense of Patrick's choice to revert ('knowledge can never replace friendship'), the chapter tests Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism: since competent judges rank higher pleasures qualitatively above lower ones, Mill's dictum that it is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied condemns Patrick's destruction of his own higher capacities. Dunn then presses two objections — that people's actual lower-pleasure preferences may be genuine rather than socially produced, and that the capacity for higher pleasure seems worthless without its actual experience — leaving Mill's verdict in tension.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 78 "Categorically, We Have an Imperative Problem" — Measures the spying in A Scanner Darkly and Total Recall against Kant's second formulation of the categorical imperative: Benny merely tracks Quaid, while the federal agents sacrifice 'Fred's' entire psyche, devaluing his humanity as a mere means. It then stages the real-world debate the fiction mirrors — the Pike and Church Committees, Godfrey's preference for technological collection, and Langan's utilitarian defense that devaluing a few is justified when society's safety requires it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 79 "Utilitarian Doesn’t Necessarily Mean Coveralls" — Lays out the utilitarian case for the spying in A Scanner Darkly: with New Path immune to inspection and Substance D addiction spreading, sacrificing Bob Arctor — secretly addicted to breakdown point and implanted with the little-flowers trigger — maximizes outcomes for the many. Against this stands the Kantian rebuttal that he should never have been made 'just another means,' likely never again to be 'an able-minded and self-determining person,' and the chapter adds the overlooked victim: the manipulator who violates the categorical imperative.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 80 "Only Remembered as the Blonde Shot in the Head" — Asks whether Total Recall's Lori and Harry — liars, adulterers, willing killers — are immoral people, noting the utilitarian excuse of serving a greater good fails because the Martian government they serve is itself profit-driven and rules by 'the one-way dialogue of the truncheon and rifle.' Following Godfrey, it concludes that an employer who bases jobs on violating individuals' rights will damage the moral frameworks of the employees, whatever their prior calibration.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 81 "Like People, Like Organizations" — Extends the moral-damage analysis one level up: organizations develop their own moral personas, and the LAPD's compartmentalization — where 'Fred' may be spying on fellow detectives and is required to lie to his supervisor 'Hank' — normalizes law-breaking in the name of law enforcement. It argues that society's oversight, the intelligence committees created after the Pike and Church hearings, is the 'bullet-proof vest' allowing risky utilitarian spying to continue without corroding everyone involved.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 39 "To Riff or Not to Riff" — Stages Bentham's hedonism through the riff-versus-soliloquy question: 'push-pin is of equal value with the arts and sciences of music and poetry,' pleasures differing only in quantity, so a Keith Richards riff that out-pleases Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' is simply the greater pleasure, and ranking pleasures 'higher' or 'lower' is prejudice. The chapter closes by noting Bentham's pleasure-pain calculus even expands the moral community to animals, setting up Mill's dissent on behalf of higher pleasures.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 44 "Satisfaction" — Adjudicates the higher/lower dispute by disambiguating 'higher': a moral ranking Bentham rejects as prejudice, or a neurobiological-evolutionary distinction about distinctively human capacities that Mill can accept. Adopting Martha Nussbaum's reading of Mill in 'Mill between Aristotle and Bentham,' it concludes that rock'n'roll is both a lower pleasure (the same four-F dopamine pathways Keith insists on) and a higher one, imagining Mill teleported onto the tour bus for the demonstration.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 9 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Audits Walt's killings through Season Four - Emilio by phosphine gas in the RV, the captive Krazy-8, Jane left choking in 'Phoenix', the dealers he rams with the Aztec to save Jesse, ordering Jesse to shoot Gale, and the wheelchair bomb that kills Gus and Tyrus - grading each with Aristotle's criteria of capacity, motive, consequences, justification, and proximate cause. It argues self-defense excuses Emilio but dissolves for the imprisoned Krazy-8, that Walt actively created the danger he then refused to relieve when he let Jane die, and that special-relationship duties to Jesse plus a utilitarian ledger justify running down the dealers. Compatibilism is invoked to show guilt survives determinism, while the remote Wayfarer 515 crash is pinned mainly on Donald Margolis's own choices rather than on Walt.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 21 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Runs Walt's choices through consequentialist machinery: his cost-benefit habit (the $737,000 target, 'non-sustainable business model'), the Krazy-8 pros-and-cons list, and whether manufacturing meth harms users or merely enables them. It argues act consequentialism fails on unforeseen consequences (Hank killing Tuco helps Heisenberg; the tow-truck driver aids a murder), defends rule consequentialism via Tuco - rational for him, disastrous as a universal rule - and weighs agent-centered views for Walt's family-first logic. It closes with Singer's drowning-child standard: Walt could have saved Jane and accepted Elliot's charity at little cost, and so could we by redirecting wasted money to OXFAM - so Walt breaks bad, and maybe we do too.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 22 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Pits act utilitarianism against existentialism to ask whether moral rules change at life's end: briefly cooking meth can maximize happiness (family provision against limited street harm), while a long career cannot, and utilitarians are trapped by the limits of their own foresight. Walt is read as the existentialist converting mortality into meaning - money, power, and masculinity in a godless world - while Skyler mostly calculates like a utilitarian (white lies to Marie, Ted's accounting), Hank mixes both codes, and Marie's kleptomania marks her an egoist until she defends Walt's right to choose his own death at the intervention. A marathon-runner metaphor lands the thesis: to be a utilitarian in life's early miles is itself an existential decision, and the last mile is when we 'wake up' like Walt.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 24 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Takes apart Walt and Jesse's 'legalize it' excuse: Kantian autonomy would license adult drug choices, but knowingly self-harming meth use is a performative contradiction no rational adult can will, and Mill's utilitarianism condemns cooking because harms to all users must be weighed against one family's benefit. It reads the 'Cancer Man' revenge on Ken's BMW and the Tuco deal as proof that the meth world's criminality spreads like a cancer into Walt's ordinary life, and 'Gray Matter' as Greek tragedy - pride refusing Elliot's money when a way out existed. Against On Liberty's libertarian pull, it finally argues addicts forfeit full rational autonomy and so may be 'caged' by paternalistic law.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 26 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Asks what exactly makes a meth cook a 'bad guy' and finds the line hard to draw: Walt forces no one to use, so like tobacco farmers and gun makers he merely enables self-harm - yet Saul's proposed prison shanking and Walt's order to murder Gale show culpable enabling without direct harm. Gale's libertarian purity argument ('they're getting exactly what they pay for') and Prohibition economics even suggest that on utilitarian grounds skilled cooks might do less harm than worse ones, though the industry as a whole remains indefensible. The chapter's moral center is Jane's death - Walt's monstrous 'standing by' - and the closeness effect that makes the personal Krazy-8 murder feel worse than the gas; it concludes the good-guy/bad-guy frame itself fuels the failed war on drugs.
- **Breaking Bad and Philosophy - Badder Living through Chemistry**, ch. 32 "Breaking Bad and Philosophy" — Stages the standard three-way ethics debate on Walt: deontology's universalizability (Kant) absurdly forbids killing Krazy-8 even to save Walt's family, utilitarianism (Mill) licenses both cooking meth and murdering dealers - a outright contradiction - while Aristotle's virtue ethics judges character rather than acts and convicts Walt of vice: he endangers his family, misses Holly's birth, habituates himself into Heisenberg, and defrauds his school. Because acts and consequences alone cannot see character, virtue ethics is offered as the needed complement. The closing move widens the lens to America itself, arguing the capitalist success ethos and our appetite for anti-heroes like Tony Soprano and Dexter reveal a society that praises viciousness - 'we are what we repeatedly do.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen distinguishes heroic survival cannibalism, as in the Andes crash of Alive, from the 'Fear the Hunters' cannibals: both utilitarianism and Kantianism permit eating those who already died out of necessity, since the dead lose no utility and corpses lack the rationality that grounds Kantian dignity. But Chris's band killed children to eat them and kept the living Dale as a food store, which fails both theories and cannot be excused by 'we don't do this because we want to,' since alternatives existed — joining other survivors, eating walkers ('zombitarianism'), or starving, because survival is never a moral obligation. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended as Kantian retributive punishment: if Chris universalized his maxim that people may be hunted for food, then, as Rick suggests while biting Chris's neck, 'if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris.'
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 23 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Argues against the obvious reading that Larry is a rule-breaker: properly analyzed, he is a dedicated rule-follower, since a good rule-follower need only accept the legitimacy of some rules and consistently follow the ones he accepts. Bekka Williams works through cases like Rachel's ski-lift jump versus Jewish law in 'The Ski Lift,' the moving 10:30 pm phone cutoff in 'The Wire,' and Larry's rejection of his mother's tattoo-driven reburial in 'The Special Section' to distinguish breaking a rule you accept from rejecting a rule's legitimacy altogether. Kant supplies the point that duty is only visible when it frustrates self-interest (Larry absorbing the cost of his own waiting-room rule in 'The Interior Decorator,' refusing to fire the Tourette's chef), while J.J.C. Smart's attack on 'rule-worship' explains why Larry rejects purposeless rules like the drive-thru walking ban and the one-year wedding-gift cutoff. The underlying justification is the Golden Rule: the water bottle in 'The Doll,' the caviar allotment, and even the stolen memorial flowers in 'The Ida Funkhouser Roadside Memorial' are defended as fairness and reciprocity, leaving the jacket money in 'The Korean Bookie' as the single admitted counterexample.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 15 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Bzdak uses Wee-Bey's 'you askin' too much' - and his ultimate yes to letting Bunny take Namond out of the Game - to pose the Puzzle of Impartiality: morality seems to require equal consideration (Plato's Socrates rejecting justice as helping friends and harming enemies; the impartialism built into Bentham's, Mill's, and Singer's utilitarianism), yet the show's most admirable moment is a father's partiality, and its worst parents, De'Londa and Raylene, fail exactly by not being partial to their own children. He tests a Greater Good Principle against cops protecting cops, Kima choosing honesty over loyalty to McNulty and Freamon, and Bunk's disgusted speech to Omar about the code that splits the community into victims who matter and victims who don't. The principle handles Carver reporting Colicchio but not the burning-building cases, and the show's verdict is that both too much and too little partiality destroy lives, with no single criterion deciding.
- **The Wire and Philosophy - This America, Man**, ch. 19 "The Wire and Philosophy" — Fallis tests Kant's claim that a universal 'lie whenever it is to your advantage' would necessarily destroy itself, and David Lewis's stricter thesis that communication requires mostly truth-tellers, against a West Baltimore where Avon, Omar, the cops, the lawyers, and Templeton all lie constantly. Parfit's rejoinder - that as long as some people sometimes tell the truth, deception stays possible - explains how Bubbles's lies keep working, while the heroin market shows Kant's mechanism at full scale: Stringer cutting product and rebranding 'pandemic' until 'every dope fiend in the city knows that Avon been putting out piss, calling it shit' and Westside dope collapses. Since Gant's and Greggs's costly truths still anchor the practice, the chapter concludes The Wire cannot quite refute Kant: it is not possible for nobody to walk the straight and narrow track.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 16 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Massimo Pigliucci reads Rise as a Greek tragedy of hubris and asks whether Will Rodman dosing his father with ALZ-112 was wrong, first dissolving the 'it's unnatural' objection and probing the cure/enhancement border with Daniels's Peter-and-Johnny growth-hormone case, vaccination-as-enhancement, and Eubulides's bald-man paradox. He then runs the decision through three ethical theories: Millian consequentialism condemns it by its results (his father dies and humanity goes extinct, though chimp happiness might outweigh that), Kant's humanity formula condemns using his father as an unconsenting experimental subject, and Aristotelian virtue ethics vindicates Will's compassion and courage - Pigliucci's own view, since sometimes our best is just not enough. He closes by rejecting Baylis and Robert's technological-inevitability thesis (we abandoned the Concorde, CFCs, and nuclear weapons before) and lets Jacobs's plunge into San Francisco Bay stand as the penalty for market hubris.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 25 "Psych and Philosophy" — Stephenson tests Shawn's ruse against the major theories of justified deceit and finds it wanting: Plato's Myth of the Metals excuses paternalistic noble lies for social harmony that Shawn's self-aggrandizing motives cannot claim, utilitarianism collapses on the long-term costs of exposure (Gus, Juliet, Henry, and the SBPD condemned by association; clients betrayed; trust in law enforcement eroded), Kant's universalizability test sinks maxims like 'lie whenever a career opportunity is at stake,' and Popper's open society condemns just the deceit on which the psychic brand runs. Even the mutual-deceit analogy to poker and Sissela Bok's reasonable-person publicity test fail, since no public forum of reasonable people would bless duping paying private clients. The escape is extra-moral: Shawn's mischievous hokum is the socially necessary boundary-pusher, whose lesson against unreflective occult belief lands best when delivered with a laugh.
- **Psych and Philosophy - Some Dark Juju-Magumbo**, ch. 26 "Psych and Philosophy" — The Bock brothers ask whether Shawn's fake-psychic lie is morally permissible, testing it against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibitions on lying, Nietzsche's claim that all language is metaphorical (the 'Lights, Camera . . . Homicidio' acting-as-lying scene), and Machiavelli's ends-justify-the-means deception from The Prince. Using Sissela Bok's three-question test they contrast justified police undercover work - Juliet infiltrating the sorority in 'Scary Sherry' and the roller derby team in 'Talk Derby to Me' - with Shawn's ruse, which fails because it protects Shawn's own interests rather than others. They end by weighing Sorensen's bald-faced lies (Shawn's 'I know you know I'm not telling the truth') and conclude Chief Vick's genuine belief shows these are real, indefensible lies.
- **The Good Wife and Philosophy - Temptations of Saint Alicia**, ch. 12 "The Good Wife and Philosophy" — Rod Carveth maps Bentham's act-utilitarianism onto Lockhart Gardner's defense-side reasoning and Mill's rule-utilitarianism onto the prosecution's, then tests the pairing on the firm's recurring client Colin Sweeney. Sweeney's cases - the wrongful-death suit in 'Bad' where Alicia says 'Of course' he killed his wife, the manslaughter plea and merger opportunism in 'Hybristophilia', and the perjured testimony Alicia may still use in 'Long Way Home' - show the firm letting the end of client and firm gain justify the means. Sweeney walking free, restored to his company, and a father despite admitting the murder is the counter-intuitive consequence that makes Carveth question whether act-utilitarianism should ground our decisions at all.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 22 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Pless asks whether Bender is responsible for his misdeeds given that MomCorp designed him to be an alcoholic kleptomaniac (revealed through Bender Vision in 'Mother's Day') and Planet Express regularly orders him into morally dirty work. Against Asimov's utilitarian Three Laws - embodied by the servile, selfless Robot 1-X of 'Obsoletely Fabulous' - Futurama's 'robot subjectivism' makes every robot a self-interested agent, and Bender's autonomy is proven by his refusal of Mom's 'kill all humans' order and by his fear of punishment in Robot Hell ('Hell Is Other Robots'), which also shows the show's universe is not morally relativist. Because Bender can rewrite his own code - his unprogrammed friendship with Fry, the adoption scam that turns heartfelt in 'The Cyber House Rules' - he sits on the same sliding scale of moral agency as humans, so if Bender can break his programming, we have no excuse for not exercising our own free will.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 12 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Littmann argues that stripped of religious scruple, Shelley's own supreme virtue - kindness, embodied in Victor's family, Elizabeth, Clerval, and the cottagers - actually supports creating artificial life: the monster is benevolent until mistreated, and superior corpse-people would be a race of geniuses rather than a threat we may preemptively suppress. The monster himself invents utilitarianism ('relative as they were, as I applied them, to pleasure and pain alone'), De Lacey nearly lives it by promising the stranger rehabilitation over punishment, but Victor's case against building a mate is exposed as speciesism - he tallies unborn humans' futures while ignoring the joys of unborn cadaver folk, though utilitarians were the first to speak for animal rights. Since intelligent otherness is humanity's only chance at non-human friendship and the risks of Prometheus's fire paid off, the chapter rewrites the modern Prometheus as a blessing and ends with a re-imagined creation scene where the monster says 'I love you' to a Victor who finally names him Nigel.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - Genocide Is Child's Play**, ch. 28 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann reads Graff and Ender as act utilitarians in John Stuart Mill's mold, drawing a detailed parallel between Ender's engineered Battle School childhood and James Mill's grueling raising of his son to be utilitarianism's champion, down to both boys' breakdowns. He argues that although the xenocide was a tragic wrong by Mill's own lights (the hive-queens' happiness counted too), the harm principle permits overriding individual liberty when humanity's survival is at stake - which is why Card's novel, unlike Crime and Punishment or 'The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas,' shows consequentialism at its most troubling rather than its most absurd.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 11 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Littmann surveys real de-extinction efforts (George Church's passenger pigeon, plans to clone a frozen mammoth) and asks when reviving extinct species is morally permissible. He argues that Arne Naess's deep ecology, with its 'equal right to live and blossom', fails because it projects human desires onto organisms like plants that have none, and cannot say whether species or only individuals bear rights. He instead applies Mill's utilitarianism: bring species back when doing so maximizes happiness and minimizes suffering, which permits a Jurassic Park in principle but forbids dinosaur fights and trophy hunts like Roland Tembo's, and rebukes Sattler's claim that only the people we love matter.
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 26 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Lisa Kadonaga stages a choice between two sealed vials - clone the T. rex or the extinct thicktail chub - and weighs purposes for de-extinction: education and fundraising, Veblen-style prestige and conspicuous consumption, making amends for human-caused extinctions (the chub's wetlands were drained, the tyrannosaur died out before us), and Bentham-style utility of ecosystem function. She argues the chub wins on utility because it could resume a real niche while a top carnivore would wreck modern ecosystems, and questions whether Hammond-style engineering that makes recreated animals dependent on humans (the lysine contingency, terminator genes) violates the animals' right to exist as themselves. Her verdict is 'Pister's Bucket': defer resurrection until habitat and resources exist, and spend the effort saving the species we are killing right now.
