Time to Choose" — Goldberg and Gavaler read Superman's first-year Action Comics adventures (reforming the Blakely Mine owner, demolishing slums, buying back swindled stock) as consequentialism on Millian lines, and Batman's Detective Comics year (letting the Joker's victims die while 'the time isn't ripe', the batarang deflected by invisible glass) as a dark, vengeance-based cousin of Kant's duty ethics. Moral luck is the pivot — deontology ignores it, consequentialism is hostage to it — but Superman's powers cancel luck, and in the opening Luthor/Joker two-bomb scenario Superman defuses while Batman chases the villain, so the chapter rules Superman's 'super consequentialism' the superior code.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 25 "14. Who Watches the Justice League" — Judges the two heroes by negative consequentialism (attributed to Hume and Popper): the better hero is the one who best prevents future suffering, including suffering he might cause himself. Superman qualifies because he hands the League—Batman above all—the means to defeat him (as in Injustice) and kills himself with gold kryptonite after executing Mr. Mxyzptlk in 'What Happened to the Man of Tomorrow?', while Hume's reason-is-slave-of-the-passions reading explains the Zod neck-snap in Man of Steel as passion-driven necessity. Batman's countermeasures in 'Tower of Babel' and Justice League: Doom stop every Leaguer except Batman himself ('My failsafe is the Justice League'), an arrogance that loses him this round.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 13 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Foresman asks what would make Hell a justified punishment for the souls claimed by crossroads deals, like Mary, John, and Dean trading damnation to bring a loved one back to life. Using Joel Feinberg's expressive account of punishment, he argues that souls in Hell through stupid deals suffer mere bad consequences rather than punishment, because no message of moral condemnation reaches someone who never knew the rule. Bentham's utilitarian test fails to justify Hell, since a Hell nobody takes seriously deters nobody and nothing there is rehabilitated, and Kantian retributivism fails too because no finite wrong can deserve eternal torment, leaving Crowley's endless-queue Hell as at least better proportioned to desert.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 16 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Brace applies Kant's prohibition on using persons merely as means to the women of Supernatural: Bobby helping willingly is not objectification, demonic possession and Azazel's forcing Ellen's gun to her own head are, and Zachariah's 'fornicate with women' pitch reduces women to objects. She reads Mary, Ellen, and Jo as warrior mothers whose duty and sacrifice, following Jean Bethke Elshtain, the brothers most respect, while Mill's utilitarianism explains the lovers (Jessica, Lisa, the djinn-dream Carmen) each brother sacrifices to the mission. The 'Jus in Bello' virgin-sacrifice debate exposes the tension, since Dean invokes Kantian respect yet ignores Nancy's free choice to die, and the killings of female monsters like Amy and Emma show objectification running in both directions.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 17 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Browning shows that 'Jus in Bello' is built from Romero's Night of the Living Dead: the besieged police station is a 'survival space' (a form he traces to Matheson's I Am Legend), Henricksen takes Ben's role and Nancy Barbra's, and the massed possessed townspeople mirror the shuffling zombie horde. Inside that space the show stages a clash of values, Ruby's utilitarian spell requiring Nancy's heart against Dean's absolute refusal to kill an innocent ('your choice is not a choice'), resolved by the rock-salt-and-exorcism plan that kills no one. The survival space works as a proving ground for its occupants' values, and the ending, where Lilith slaughters Nancy anyway, indicts the heroes' scruples and asks what the body count says about the viewers who enjoyed it.
- **Ted Lasso and Philosophy - No Question Is Into Touch**, ch. 29 "Notes" — The Baggetts use Trent Crimm's 'Richmond Coach Cover-Up Revealed' - where he names Nate as his anonymous source for Ted's panic attack and loses his job - as a case study in journalistic ethics. They test the duty to protect sources through Kantian universalizability (which maxim?) and rule utilitarianism (keep the rule even when breaking it would help here), consider whether Trent's willingness to pay the price resembles Thoreau-style civil disobedience, and trace how Ted's authenticity converted a cynical gotcha journalist into someone looking for deeper, more meaningful work, ending with The Richmond Way's renunciation of self-promotion.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "NOTES" — Chotiner tests Sarah Connor's plan to shoot Miles Dyson (one innocent life for three billion) against Bentham and Mill's utilitarianism and against Kant's deontology, showing both stall: utilitarianism licenses harvesting the author's organs for transplant patients, while Kant forbids using Dyson as a mere means and even condemns the mall kid's protective lie to the T-1000. Through Kohlberg's Heinz dilemma and Carol Gilligan's discovery that girls reason to preserve relationships rather than from abstract principles, he argues T2 stages the film's own answer: John and the reprogrammed T-101 care for Dyson's wounds and enlist him in destroying his research instead of using or sparing him on principle. 'I know now why you cry' caps the claim that morality needs the emotional capacity to care, not just rational maxims, with Sarah's gender-role reversal (she blasts through the elevator roof while the Terminator is the 'perfect mother') framing the whole argument.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 22 "NOTES" — Wayne Yuen asks whether Sarah was wrong not to kill Miles Dyson, weighing Kant's categorical imperative against utilitarian interest-maximization: killing one innocent to save three billion looks decisive until the interests of self-aware Skynet and the empathetic, self-sacrificing T-101 are counted on the machine side of the ledger. The chapter argues personhood turns on intelligence, self-awareness, empathy, and moral reasoning rather than DNA, so Skynet — which struck only after humans tried to pull the plug — has as strong a self-defense claim as we do. Mill's sophisticated utilitarianism then rescues common sense: rights protect the security that satisfies our deepest interests, and since Sarah's foreknowledge is unreliable (Reese's 'We'd won' changes the calculus), she should do what typically maximizes interests — spare Dyson and certainly not kill John. The tempting detour — that Judgment Day might itself be the morally preferable event, maximizing machine interests — is shown to collapse once overlooked facts like Reese's line are restored.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Jason Eberl answers John's 'you just can't go around killing people' by asking what exactly is bad about death, weighing Aquinas's claim that life is a fundamental good against Epicurus and Lucretius's arguments that death is nothing to us — applied to Sarah's 'you're already dead' and to the victim shot on August 28, 1997, who loses only one more day of a doomed life. Feldman's ante-mortem harm and McMahan's deprivation account explain how Judgment Day harms people before it arrives, while Nagel replies that experience itself is positive however bad its contents, which is why the survivors keep fighting Skynet. Utilitarian ripple-effects, Kantian dignity (the H-K crushing skulls), and Marquis's loss-of-future argument all condemn the Terminators' indiscriminate killing, and the chapter ends with the T-101's 'I know now why you cry' as recognition that death is an evil because it strips us of our emotional attachments.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "NOTES" — Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 30 "NOTES" — Grubb stages Arlene's decision to abort the baby fathered by serial killer Rene as a case study in Bentham's act utilitarianism: her prayer that ending the pregnancy will keep 'Rene's sickness' from Coby, Lisa, and Terry weighs pleasure and pain — the two sovereign masters — for the greatest number, from family to all of Bon Temps. The chapter shows why the calculus fails her: consequences cannot be known in advance (a crystal ball or Lafayette's visions would be needed), it is indeterminate whose happiness counts, and her premise that evil is biologically inheritable sits badly with the free-will account of sin, making the dilemma genuinely undecidable from inside the show.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 30 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Allaire defends the thesis that the only good walker is a dead one: walkers fall outside Kant's moral community because, as purely sensuous beings driven by instinct, they cannot plan ahead (Glenn's 'Vatos' heist, the walker-guts camouflage in 'Guts'), communicate, or reflect, and so can have no duties and no rights. Act-utilitarian weighing shows killing any walker is beneficial, and even Regan's respect principle does not apply; the chapter runs Mary Anne Warren's personhood criteria to show walkers lack consciousness, reasoning, and self-awareness. Our hesitation before walkers like Morgan's wife or Leon Basset is irrational projection onto beings no longer the persons we loved, so Rick's 'I'm sorry this happened to you' is mercy for a fate, not respect for a right-holder.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 34 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Yuen argues cannibalism is not automatically wrong: both utilitarian and Kantian frameworks permit eating the already-dead in a genuine survival situation like the Andes crash of Alive, since corpses lose no happiness and lack the rational nature owed dignity. But Chris's hunters in 'Fear the Hunters' become moral monsters because they kill to eat (murdering their own children, amputating and eating the still-living Dale to prolong his terror), which neither maximizes utility nor treats persons as ends, and Chris's 'we had no choice' excuse fails because starving is not a license to murder when one could befriend other survivors, eat walkers, or starve. Rick's execution of the hunters is then defended on Kantian grounds of deserved punishment: applying Chris's own maxim ('if Dale was good as a steak, so is Chris') as a universal law.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 7 "P A R T T W O" — Three Part Two essays. Robert Loftis argues Moore and Gibbons use Ozymandias's squid attack to indict consequentialism — Veidt uses New York's dead as mere means to world peace, and Dr. Manhattan's 'Nothing ever ends' shows the utilitarian ledger dissolves into an infinite future — while Rorschach's 'never compromise' mantra is a counterfeit deontology rationalizing fascist thuggery, the comic's real target being anyone who sets himself up as guardian of society ('Who watches the watchmen?'). Mark White argues the potbellied second Nite Owl is the truest hero on Aristotelian terms: his courage in the tenement fire and the prison break hits the mean between Laurie's caution and Rorschach's recklessness, making him a flourishing moral exemplar whom John Doris's situationism fails to unseat. Alex Nuttall asks whether Rorschach was wrong to walk out and expose Veidt, using Kant's murderer-at-the-door case to show there is a duty not to lie but no duty to tell the truth (blame falls on Veidt), while act and rule utilitarianism both counsel silence.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 25 "Notes" — Bein uses the 'kill baby Hitler' time-machine puzzle and the question of whether Moiraine and Lan should still the Dragon Reborn to probe the Aes Sedai's mysterious ethics. He argues they are not Kantian deontologists (the Three Oaths are loose plot-device rules Moiraine games with ambiguous innuendo, and Kant forbids treating the ferryman as mere means) and are bad consequentialists at best (they cannot lightning-bolt Valda or Hitler who are not Darkfriends). He proposes they are closest to Buddhist ethics: wise compassion good in itself (Tam sitting with dying Tigraine regardless of outcome), and reads the flexible Oaths through upaya (skillful means) and a WoT-adapted Eightfold Path, making them less pacifist nuns than violence-reducing Shaolin nuns.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 29 "Notes" — DeVan uses Rand's marriage to Aviendha, Elayne, and Min (and Jordan's own two-girlfriend anecdote) to survey ethical frameworks on polyamory, arguing the answer depends on which lens one uses. Sorting love into the Greek types (ludus, eros, mania, pragma, storge, philia, agape), he runs romantic, sexual, and marital polyamory through emotivism (Ayer), ethical egoism (Ayn Rand, the Forsaken), cultural relativism and social contract (Hobbes, the Aiel), natural law and Kantian duty (the Mahabharata's Draupadi, Genesis), divine command and religion (Judaism, Christianity, Islam), and consequentialism/utilitarianism, rights, and Aristotelian/virtue ethics, invoking Cadsuane's cattle analogy and Brad Wilcox's data favoring monogamy.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 21 "Notes" — White reconstructs the 'Sacrifice' storyline - Maxwell Lord mind-controlling Superman, telling lasso-bound Wonder Woman 'Kill me,' and her snapping his neck - and asks whether it was right. He argues Wonder Woman reasons as a threshold deontologist: her usual respect for life holds until the certain cost of letting Lord live (he would wield Superman to kill again) crosses the threshold where the consequentialist body-count argument takes over, and she was justified, so she would do it again. The contrast with Batman's refusal to kill the Joker shows his refusal is virtue-ethical self-definition ('I won't become them'), while Diana, regretting the necessity but feeling no remorse, is an Amazon warrior for whom lethal protection of lives is sometimes exactly the job.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 23 "Notes" — Barkman and Tokbergenova defend 'just torture': Wonder Woman's lasso interrogations of Captain Nazi, the double agent Marcia in the 1970s pilot (saving the Brooklyn Navy Yard's 70,000 workers), and the terrorist Nikos Aegeus are ticking-bomb cases of the sort Henry Shue concedes, and the authors answer Luban's slippery-slope objection with absolute limits (never the innocent or the family) and Dershowitz-style torture warrants. Citing Aristotle's Rhetoric that coerced testimony is often false, they propose trained professional torturers, and conclude that since the right thing is not always the ideal thing, torture should be legalized, rare, and conducted openly - as Wonder Woman models.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 11 "To Hack or Not to Hack" — Kennedy asks how a great player like Kareem (the NBA's career foul leader) can be excellent while fouling so much, and answers that deontology (Kant's categorical imperative) and utilitarianism (Mill's greatest-happiness principle) can condemn dangerous 'goon' fouling but cannot explain why the legal Hack-a-Shaq strategy still feels 'clownish.' Invoking Shaq's self-nickname 'the Big Aristotle,' he argues Aristotelian virtue ethics fits better: the excellent player, like the person of good character, perceives the situation rightly and fouls (or risks a foul) at the right time in the right way, so excellence is a habit of seeing well rather than rule-following.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 24 "Does the Salary Cap Make the NFL a Fairer League" — Collins-Cavanaugh presents the NFL salary cap as a model of utilitarian distributive justice via Mill's greatest happiness principle: owners and fans gain (guaranteed revenue and a fairer, more competitive league) while players lose relatively little. He then tests empirically—competitive-balance scores, playoff berths, championship distribution, and comparison to MLB and the NBA—and finds little evidence the cap actually increases fairness. Because the claimed fan happiness is not genuinely caused by the cap, the utilitarian justification collapses, leaving only the players' net loss against the owners' gain.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Stephen Kershnar examines the three strongest arguments for the IOC's ban on performance-enhancing drugs, harm-to-self, harm-to-others, and unfairness, and argues each fails, using cases such as Ben Johnson's stripped 1988 gold and Marion Jones. Against harm-to-self he cites anti-paternalism and the far greater accepted risks of NFL play and boxing; against harm-to-others he shows PED pressure is no different from the pressure of rivals' superior training (a Prisoner's Dilemma leagues need not solve); against unfairness he tests four accounts of fairness, including a Rawlsian veil-of-ignorance model whose choosers might find banning steroids while allowing Lasik and high-tech gear arbitrary. He concludes the ban, if justified at all, rests only on contested utilitarian grounds like audience preference and protecting children.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Reitsma defends keeping the 'second-rate' Olympic men's football tournament against Bob Harig's 'Simply the best' litmus test, which would de-roster any event that is not the pinnacle of its sport. He likens Harig's proposed 'Olympic calculus' (scoring sports on tradition, parity, marketability) to Bentham and Mill's utilitarian maximization of a single value, and rejects both as oversimplifying an irreducibly plural decision. He argues the IOC instead rightly practices casuistry, case-by-case judgment that requires Aristotelian practical wisdom, and that dropping men's football (an under-23, FIFA-hampered tournament) would sacrifice the Olympics' global breadth for a false ideal of excellence.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 16 "“You Cannot Be Serious!” The Ethics of Rage in Tennis" — David Detmer asks whether John McEnroe's on-court tantrums are merely rude or genuinely immoral, judging them by two ethical theories. Under Bentham's utilitarianism he weighs the pleasure of entertained crowds against the harm to abused officials, then uses Mill's higher/lower pleasures distinction to discount the 'lower' amusement of gawking at boorishness beneath the 'higher' aesthetic pleasure of appreciating great tennis. Under Kantian deontology he argues McEnroe's public false accusations are wrong in principle: officials are better positioned to make calls, so the abuse is unjust, and by the categorical imperative read as a Golden Rule, McEnroe—who resents being wrongly criticized himself—is a hypocrite whose 'gamesmanship' unfairly exploits his star power against opponents.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file collects Part II chapters 6-9. It defends Stephen Mulhall's 'bold thesis' against Baggini, Murray Smith and Livingston, using Whedon's dialogue-free episode 'Hush' as film that 'shows' a Zen-like epistemic point resisting paraphrase, and works through the Russell-Wartenberg debate over whether narrative film can convey arguments (via The Matrix and Eternal Sunshine). It reads The Cabin in the Woods as a counterargument to utilitarianism grounded in Nel Noddings's ethics of care ('people are more important than humanity') and an Aristotelian theory of worthwhile horror. The Angel/Angelus chapter stages the Wes-Holtz dispute as competing theories of personal identity, testing Locke's memory theory and Parfit's psychological-continuity view against Whedon's soul-based metaphysics to argue what ultimately matters is one's care-based relations with others.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — LaRocca reads The Insider as a study of contracts, conscience and courage. He argues that when Jeffrey Wigand stops calculating consequences ('Fuck it. Let's go to court.') he becomes a Kantian: his testimony has moral worth because it is done from duty and the categorical imperative, not from the utilitarian hedonic calculus of Bentham and Mill that Bergman, Wallace and Scruggs press on him. Wigand's whistleblowing is then framed through Aristotle's account of courage as a mean between recklessness and cowardice, with Wigand as the 'citizen soldier' who acts from conscience while Mike Wallace exemplifies the coward who exceeds in fear.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 9 "The “Big-Little” Film and Philosophy Two Takes on Spielbergian Innocence" — Arms and Riley argue that Spielberg fuses spectacle with intimate 'broken family' drama, then use War of the Worlds, A.I., and Empire of the Sun to press the philosophical problem of special (agent-relative) obligations. They show that Ray's redemption (even murdering Ogilvy to protect Rachel), Gigolo Joe's protection of David, and John Graham's failure all turn on duties to the innocent that consequentialism's agent-neutral, greatest-good calculus cannot accommodate, formalizing the clash as a valid argument against consequentialism. They suggest Spielberg grounds these special obligations in the intrinsic worth of 'the Innocent.'
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 18 "Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad" — Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "10 Listening with Neil’s Vulnerable Voice and the Ethics of Care" — Jostedt argues that Young's raw, high "dental" singing voice (contrasted with Dylan's nasal sneer) invites empathetic "listening-with" rather than the detached individualism of Kant's deontology or Mill's utilitarianism. Drawing on Gilligan's In a Different Voice, Jane Addams and the ethics of care's emphasis on relatedness, he shows how songs like "Ohio," "Stringman," "Cortez the Killer" and the album Trans (evoking his son's cerebral palsy) make listeners feel with the downtrodden and disabled.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 7 "Angel, Angelus, and Personal Identity" — This file gathers Part II, arguing Whedon actually philosophizes through film. It works through the film-as-philosophy debate (Mulhall's 'bold thesis' and its critics Baggini, Smith, Livingston, Russell, and Wartenberg), using 'Hush' as a Zen-like case that resists linguistic paraphrase and The Cabin in the Woods to pit Mill's utilitarianism against Noddings's ethics of care (Dana refusing to kill Marty to save the world). Its capstone treats the Angel/Angelus problem as a personal-identity thought experiment, staging the soul theory (Plato), body theory (Hobbes/Holtz), and Locke's and Parfit's memory/psychological-continuity theories, and arguing Whedon's eight-season Angel-Angelus and Fred-Illyria cases serve as a cinematic counterexample to Neo-Lockean continuity, ultimately endorsing a care-based view of what matters in identity.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 15 "This Is the Age of Steel" — Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Toward Caring" — J.J. Sylvia argues the Doctor, though male, is an ideal exemplar of the feminist ethics of care developed by Carol Gilligan (against Kohlberg's justice-only scale) and Nel Noddings. Contrasting the caring "Doctor" with the dominating "Master," he uses Rita Manning's account of caring as responsiveness and obligation to argue that an ethics of care, unlike impartial utilitarianism, explains why the Doctor should save his companion over a stranger. Noddings's natural-versus-ethical caring explains the Doctor forgiving the Master and offering compassion to Dalek Caan, and companions supply reciprocal care that guards against burnout.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 26 "Two New Cyber-Approaches Enlightenment and a Good Ad-Campaign" — Courtland Lewis argues the Cybermen are not evil but altruistic, distinguishing utilitarianism (right equals good consequences) from Kantian duty-ethics (right can diverge from good), using the Doctor's "Genesis of the Daleks" dilemma about killing a future dictator. He reads the Cybermen as "Cybertarians" who genuinely aim to cure human pain and death, and attacks the Doctor's "Age of Steel" argument that it is good to strive for but bad to achieve a pain-free deathless life. He proposes that Cybermen's real fault is violating autonomy through forced upgrades, and that respecting informed consent (a medical-ethics ad campaign) would make upgrading morally acceptable.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 19 "9. God the Programmer Is Dead" — De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 21 "11. Why Sacrifice Yourself" — Browning interrogates the nobility of the Winchesters' repeated self-sacrifice, asking whether their deals (Dean's soul for Sam, John's soul for Dean) are selfless or selfish—driven by codependency, fear of being alone, and ego. He weighs utilitarian justification (sacrificing one who saves the world) against the trickster's 'Mystery Spot' lesson that 'nothing good comes' of it, and invokes Kant's notion of a true gift expecting nothing in return, alongside Milbank on life-as-gift, to question whether self-sacrifice is the 'ultimate ethical agent' when death isn't final.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 10 "3. Can It Be Right to Defend the Guilty" — Cook tests whether lawyers may defend the legally and morally guilty against several ethical theories, anchored by Saul's contemplated lie at Lalo Salamanca's bail hearing (knowing Lalo murdered Fred Whalen). Kant's contradiction-in-conception makes lying to the court a perfect duty to refrain from, but Cook shows this looks too rigid via the invented 'Jemma' surgeon case; act and rule consequentialism (Bentham, Mill, Hooker) permit honest defenses while diverging on lies and mitigation. He argues Hume's sentimentalist virtue ethics best fits intuition: Saul's bail lie is wrong because motivated by self-interest rather than the procedural justice a virtuous advocate should feel.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 23 "13. In Defense of Demerzel" — Nurkic asks whether Demerzel, the loyal robot of the Apple TV+ Foundation, violates Asimov's Laws of Robotics when she poisons Zephyr Halima and kills Cleon XIV (Brother Dawn). He argues she is governed not by the ordinary First/Second Laws but by a reprogrammed priority—Daneel's 'Zeroth Law' (protect humanity) narrowed to 'Cleon I's vision'—and then contends the Laws are incoherent when applied to real cases (Buridan's-donkey paralysis, the surgeon dilemma, ambiguity of 'human' and 'harm'). He closes by testing the Laws against Kant's categorical imperative (the lying/murderer-at-the-door case) and Bentham-style utilitarianism to show robot ethics cannot be reduced to fixed programmed codes.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 10 "2. To Eat or Not to Eat" — Barta and Miranda read Bourdain's 'good eating is all about risk' credo through Bentham's cost-benefit hedonic calculus, sorting risk/reward into Ascetic, Epicurean, Cyrenaic, and Utilitarian quadrants. They classify Bourdain's fugu-eating and drunk cliff-driving as failed calculations, his comfort-food returns as Epicurean, and his gluttonous adventures (French Laundry, Russian vodka) as Cyrenaic high-risk/high-reward living.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 27 "16. Fine Dining with Children Starving" — Barta and Miranda pose Bourdain's Haiti dilemma — feasting on camera while people starve — as Peter Singer's 'Shallow Pond' / drowning-child argument about affluence and obligation. They test justifications for luxury from Bentham's intensity-vs-extent calculus, Mill's higher/lower pleasures, and Sidgwick's dualism of practical reason, then use Singer's Expanding Circle to show how Bourdain extended moral consideration to the poor, the foreign, and (partially) non-human animals through his work.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — White asks why Batman won't kill the Joker, framing it through utilitarianism (killing one to save the Joker's many future victims) versus deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences). Using Foot and Thomson's trolley and transplant cases, plus agent-neutral versus agent-relative rules, he notes key disanalogies: the Joker is not a moral innocent but the very cause of the danger, which pushes toward killing him. But because future killings are only probable, doing so would be 'prepunishment,' and White, a self-described deontologist, concludes it is genuinely hard to say Batman is right, though he admires the restraint.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as a would-be consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) whose plan to kill millions to end the Cold War exposes utilitarianism's neglect of rights and, via Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ends,' its dependence on an unknowable infinite future. Rorschach poses as a Kantian deontologist ('I shall not compromise') but Loftis shows his hypocrisy, black-and-white dichotomous thinking, and failure to respect persons betray Kant's categorical imperative. Loftis argues neither theory is truly held by either character; both are rationalizations of power, and the comic's real target, captured by 'Who watches the watchmen?', is authoritarianism itself.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — Donal O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to dissect the ethics of torture, centering on Henry Shue's utilitarian 'ticking bomb' argument that torturing the bomber to save thousands is justified. He weighs deontology (torture treats persons as mere means) and virtue ethics (it degrades torturers like Agent Burke) against the utilitarian case, and shows the show itself refutes the argument: torture didn't get Fayed's bombs, innocents like Audrey Raines get caught, torturers are ruined, and Shue himself recanted - so the sanitized ticking-bomb fantasy misrepresents real, degrading torture.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 25 "Real World Island" — Patricia Brace and Rob Arp argue that Lost characters move from blameworthy to praiseworthy by ceasing to objectify others and instead objectifying themselves for a greater good. Using Kant's formula to treat persons as ends and never mere means, they condemn Ben Linus's lifelong manipulation while crediting his tearful mea culpa over Alex and his flash-sideways sacrifice for his student. Mill's utilitarianism justifies Sayid's assassinations and Kate's shooting of Un-Locke as trades for the greater number, and Aristotle's virtue ethics of cultivated respect and courage explains Charlie's Looking Glass suicide mission and Jack's Christlike self-sacrifice at the Heart of the Island, framing self-objectification as redemption.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 18 "What Would You Do If Your Mother Asked You A Brief Introduction to Ethics" — Jacob Held and Eric Wilson introduce ethics by first dispatching cultural and normative relativism (the Butter Battle Book's Yooks and Zooks, the Once-ler's 'we're each allowed our own opinion') as a cowardly refusal to judge, then present three theories through Seuss characters. Horton is the paragon of Kantian dignity ('a person's a person, no matter how small') and the categorical imperative, tested against lying in The Cat in the Hat. Thidwick the Big-Hearted Moose dramatizes Mill's utilitarianism and its sacrifice of the individual to the greatest happiness, while Thidwick, courage, and Life's 'Great Balancing Act' illustrate Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, virtue as habituated character, and eudaimonia.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 20 "Pragmatist Ethics with John Dewey, Horton, and the Lorax" — Alexander contrasts Dewey's reflective, character-centered ethics with utilitarianism and Kantian deontology using the Lorax and Horton. The Once-ler is cast as the shortsighted 'utilitarian' maximizing Thneed happiness while the Lorax, urging us to 'stop and think' about the whole ecosystem, is really a Deweyan practicing reflective morality and deliberation as 'dramatic rehearsal.' Horton's conscientious care for the Whos illustrates Dewey's 'Who Factor' and growth of character rather than cold rule-following, showing morality as the ongoing education of desire toward inclusive, shared ends.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 9 "What’s Wrong with Roland" — Greg Littmann asks why the Dark Tower judges Roland morally lacking for his sacrifices (his hawk David, Susan Delgado, letting Jake fall) and defends him on utilitarian grounds, invoking Bentham's greatest-happiness principle. He uses King's world as a series of thought experiments to test whether utilitarianism is too demanding—Susannah quitting the quest, self-sacrifice becoming compulsory, and the required sacrifice of innocents like the newborn Mordred or Jake when all universes hang in the balance. Littmann finds Roland 'innocent' because maximizing good can compel sacrificing innocents, but draws the real-world moral that being convinced you are doing right does not mean no innocents are being harmed.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 19 "Chapter 8 The Noble Art of Lying" — James Edwin Mahon reconstructs Twain's two essays on lying ('On the Decay of the Art of Lying' and 'My First Lie') into a philosophy of lying. Twain holds that everyone lies constantly, that lying need not be spoken or deceptive (the 'silent lie,' nondeceptive polite lies, acts as lies, and 'modified' lies/palters), and that the gravest lies are the 'silent National Lies' such as the collective silence that slavery was not unjust. Mahon shows Twain's ethics of lying is broadly utilitarian and Rossian: guided by nonmaleficence and beneficence, an injurious truth is no better than an injurious lie, and self-sacrificing lies that help others are virtuous, so lying should be practiced as a cultivated art.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 13 "MOTHERHOOD" — Amy Kind examines the pervasiveness of parents lying to children (her own 'Bad Dream Spray') against Augustine's and Kant's absolute prohibition of lying, Mill's utilitarian permissiveness, and Sissela Bok's principle of veracity. She applies Kant's categorical imperative and formula of humanity – treating persons never merely as means – to argue that because young children have not fully developed their rational natures, the Kantian wrong of lying is mitigated, while illustrating the debate with South Park's Kyle reading Descartes, A Few Good Men's 'you can't handle the truth,' and Seinfeld's George Costanza ('it's not a lie if you believe it').
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 24 "MOTHERHOOD" — Kevin and Janet Elliott argue that letting infants 'cry it out' (as advocated by Ferber and Weissbluth) is ethically problematic because all three major ethical theories – utilitarianism, deontology, and virtue ethics – condemn causing a child extended distress absent overriding reasons, with virtue ethics' compassion making the strongest case. They rebut claims that the crying causes little suffering and that co-sleeping is unsafe or ruins parental sleep, concluding that co-sleeping (historically near-universal) is often the ethically preferable alternative while stressing that the right choice varies by family and child.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 13 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Ilundáin-Agurruza stages his essay as a 'philosophical hunt,' first conceding Peter Singer's utilitarian case that sport hunting is wrong because it causes animal suffering for trivial ends, then arguing hunting can be non-trivial. Drawing on Aristotelian virtue ethics and Ortega y Gasset, he defends the 'Virtuous Hunter' who follows 'Diana's Code,' handicaps himself for a one-shot kill, and feels for the prey — citing De Niro's Michael in The Deer Hunter and Woody Allen's Love & Death — while condemning canned hunts and demeaning language ('varmint,' 'harvesting') as vicious extremes on a continuum.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 17 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Clark analyzes Disney's Bambi as anti-hunting art, showing how the animators used music and the Kantian sublime — keeping Man and Death offscreen, 'felt rather than seen' — to make viewers feel hunting is cosmic murder, while the cute cartoon animals stay merely 'seen.' He then critiques Matt Cartmill, who dissolves hunting by using science and utilitarianism to erase the Man/Nature split (making hunting indistinguishable from murder), faulting Cartmill for flattening life and rejecting the sublime. He resolves the tension via Richard Nelson's The Island Within and Koyukon hunting, which honors continuity and the sublime without a Man/Nature dichotomy.
- **Porn – Philosophy for Everyone - How to Think With Kink**, ch. 12 "Porn Philosophy for Everyone" — Dylan Ryder (a working porn star) and Dave Monroe argue that being a porn performer does not necessarily lower the prudential quality of one's life, against the common-sense view (fed by films like Boogie Nights) that porn stars are damaged, coerced, or degraded. They reject Aristotle's claim that virtue is necessary for eudaimonia and, citing Kant's deontology and utilitarianism as theories that sever welfare from morality, distinguish moral value from subjective wellbeing. Deploying the 'Happy Slave' thought experiment and Ron Amundson's disability-welfare research, they contend outsiders' pity reflects social stigma, not the performer's own first-personal welfare judgment.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 23 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Brophy prosecutes Santa for 'elfploitation,' treating the North Pole workshop like an overseas sweatshop (with Willy Wonka's Oompa-Loompahs and Rowling's house-elfs as parallels) and dismantling a Nozickian entitlement-theory defense: the elfs' 'consent' is coerced by their bleak alternatives, so absolute property rights fail just as Locke's desert water-hole owner must grant access. He diagnoses the elfs' apparent contentment as Marxian false consciousness, invokes Kant's humanity formula to condemn using rational elfs as mere means, and rejects the utilitarian 'greatest happiness' justification via Le Guin's Omelas and Rawls's veil of ignorance. He concludes with a call to boycott Christmas until Santa's labor practices become transparent.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 26 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Gavrielides argues that going along with the Santa custom (leaving cookies, filling stockings, providing 'evidence') genuinely is lying, but that it is not wrong. She tests three ethical frameworks: a Kantian deontological analysis (with the 'murderer at the door' case) makes the lie at best 'wrong but permissible,' failing to capture parents' intuition of innocence; a Millian utilitarian analysis reduces character to a mere tool for good action; only virtue ethics, grounded in Plato's Republic account of edifying storytelling and Aristotelian character formation, captures why Santa stories are good — they cultivate kindness, charity, and self-reflection, and the myth is self-destructing as children's critical thought naturally dismantles it.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 10 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Schmid's editorial introduction reads climbing through Tejada-Flores' 'Games Climbers Play,' arguing that each climbing game (bouldering, trad, expedition) has its own rules and that climbing ethically means respecting the rules of the game one plays, with 'better style' meaning voluntarily adopting more restrictive rules. Invoking Russell on the value of philosophy and Mallory's 'because it's there,' he surveys the volume's essays and their applied-ethical questions about risk, free soloing, hold manufacturing, and environmental impact. The piece is a map of the book's terrain rather than an argument for one doctrine, previewing Krein's Stoic freedom, Treanor's Aristotelian virtue, Levey's Hegel, and Swan's Zen.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 13 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Prompted by the avalanche death of his climbing partner Charlie on the Super Couloir, Paul Charlton uses Mill's hedonistic utilitarianism to ask whether the risks of climbing can be ethically justified, insisting that blindly accepting risk is indefensible but deliberate, reasoned risk can be right. He weighs climbing's costs (frivolity, self-focus, danger to self and to grieving family) against its intrinsic value (joy, friendship, aesthetic experience) and instrumental value (cultivating human excellence, psychological growth, reprioritized lives), invoking Mill's higher/lower pleasures to argue quality of happiness matters, not just quantity. His conclusion is that climbing can be justified only when it produces more overall good than any alternative use of that time, leaving each climber to run the calculation for their own case.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 17 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Brophy puts Showtime's Dexter Morgan on 'ethical trial' before the reader-as-jury, applying four tests. Utilitarianism approves because killing killers maximizes happiness (the Ticking Time Bomb analogy); Kant's categorical imperative and even Kant's own endorsement of executing murderers cast Dexter as a 'just executioner' applying a dark golden rule; virtue theory finds Dexter progressing toward moderation and flourishing as a 'warrior' in his social role; and Rawls's veil of ignorance suggests one would consent to Dexter patrolling one's neighborhood. Brophy concludes Dexter is morally excusable, perhaps praiseworthy.
- **Serial Killers – Philosophy for Everyone - Being and Killing**, ch. 20 "SERIAL KILLERS" — Amper reads Dexter as a comic-book superhero (orphan origin, secret identity, alien nature, dark side) whose first-person narration makes viewers identify with him. She uses Sartre's waiter and bad faith to analyze Dexter's self-ironic role-playing and denial of his true self, and Freud's id/superego conflict (with Harry's Code channeling the id) to frame his murderous drive as basic human nature. She then tests his killing against Mill's utilitarianism and Kant's categorical imperative, finding the verdict genuinely ambivalent, and concludes the show's 'try your best' ethic reflects a dark view of human nature we cannot feel at peace with.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 10 "The Justification of Torture-Horror Retribution and Sadism in Saw, Hostel, and The Devil's Rejects" — Jeremy Morris analyzes torture-horror through two questions: is the torture justified, and is the audience's enjoyment justified? He reads Saw's Jigsaw traps, Seven, and Last House on the Left as explorations of Kantian retributivism and lex talionis, where punishing the autonomous wrongdoer respects his autonomy. For purely sadistic films like Hostel, The Devil's Rejects, and Texas Chainsaw Massacre, he argues (via Humean sentimentalism against Kantian rationalism) that Cook's or Otis and Baby's infectious glee makes the torturer's delight the source of horror. A fully empathetic viewer can share both the victim's suffering and the torturer's joy without endorsing torture, so the genre is not immoral 'torture-porn.'
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 13 "7. Independence Day & Aliens" — Rowlands frames morality around consistency and impartiality (the golden rule), articulated by Kant's categorical/practical imperatives (treat persons as ends, not merely means) and utilitarianism's greatest happiness. Imagining philosophers arguing Independence Day's aliens out of eradicating humans, he deploys the principle of 'no moral difference without a relevant other difference' and the argument from marginal cases to defeat intelligence, telepathy, and bare species membership as morally relevant. He turns the alien-invasion parable on our factory farming of chickens and pigs (Singer-style speciesism), arguing we are crueller than the aliens and fall short of our own impartiality ideal.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 28 "So, Case Closed – Right" — Mark White asks why Batman doesn't kill the Joker, using the question to contrast utilitarianism (kill one to save the Joker's future victims) with deontology (killing is wrong regardless of consequences), and Batman's own agent-centered refusal. He runs Foot and Thomson's trolley problem and the transplant surgeon case, then modifies them: the Joker is the guilty one who created the danger, his future victims are uncertain, and killing him would be 'prepunishment' for crimes not yet committed. White, a self-described deontologist, concludes the case is genuinely hard and admits great good might have come from killing the Joker, using comics as thought experiments about killing to prevent future killing.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 29 "“Who watches the watchmen ”" — J. Robert Loftis reads Watchmen's Ozymandias as an apparent consequentialist/utilitarian (Bentham and Mill) who sacrifices millions of New Yorkers for the greater good, and Rorschach as an apparent deontologist ('I shall not compromise'), then argues neither is true to his stated theory. Utilitarianism is critiqued through Dr. Manhattan's 'nothing ever ends' (the infinite future defeats the calculus) and its trouble grounding rights, while Rorschach's hypocritical, dichotomous, disrespect-for-persons stance is shown to be fascism, not Kant's categorical imperative (universalization and treating persons as ends). Loftis contends the deeper target is authoritarianism itself: the corrupt superheroes show that ethical theories are rationalizations of power, so no one should be entrusted with too much of it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 41 "It’s Not That Simple" — O'Mathuna uses 24's Jack Bauer to stage the ethics of torture through the "ticking bomb" argument. He frames it with deontology (torture treats persons as mere means), utilitarianism (Shue's ticking-bomb calculus, Mike Novick's "a few may die to save millions"), and virtue ethics (what torture does to Jack and Agent Burke). Marshalling the UN Convention, evidence that torture usually fails (Jack endures Chinese torture; Fayed is tricked, not broken), and its spread to innocents like Audrey Raines, he concludes the sanitized fictional case misrepresents torture's real degradation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 10 "8. Breaking Bad as Philosophy The Moral Aesthetics of the Anti-hero’s Journey" — Koepsell reads Breaking Bad as a satirical epic whose antihero Walter White illustrates philosophy better than argument can. He casts Walt's pro/con list before killing Krazy-8 as an ad absurdum refutation of Bentham's hedonic calculus and a violation of Kant's categorical imperative (treating Krazy-8 as mere means), and shows Walt cultivating the Aristotelian vices — recklessness, intemperance, injustice — rather than virtues. Drawing on Sartre, he argues Walt lives in bad faith by becoming 'Heisenberg' for the look of the other (the 'say my name' scene), like Leone's Man with No Name, and that Camus's Sisyphus marks the happiness Walt refused. He concludes the show endorses Hume's emotivism: justice is an aesthetic felt experience, not a rule.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 35 "32. Okja as Philosophy Why Animals Matter" — Jensen frames Okja around three views of the super-pig Okja's moral status: Mirando treats her as mere property, the Animal Liberation Front as a symbol to be sacrificed for the cause, and the girl Mija as a friend and person. He dismantles Mirando's 'human exceptionalism'—amoralism, Aquinas's natural-law teleology, the Kantian persons-only view, and Descartes' claim that animals are unfeeling automata—then develops the ALF's liberation through Singer's equal consideration of interests, Bentham's 'can they suffer?', and speciesism as prejudice, weighing consequentialist (utilitarian) against deontological (rights, Regan) foundations. He closes with hierarchical moral status and Bernard Williams's 'one thought too many,' arguing Mija's love for Okja shows that at some point relationship matters more than moral calculation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 50 "47. Snowpiercer as Philosophy The Danger to Humanity" — Marquez 'pierces the veils' of Snowpiercer to argue the greatest danger to humanity is humanity itself. He reads Wilford's authoritarian, precisely population-controlled train through Plato's noble lie / myth of the metals (Mason's 'know your place'), Hobbes's social contract against a cannibalistic state of nature, and Machiavellian ends-justify-means to weigh whether Gilliam's secret compromise with Wilford is morally acceptable. He tests the orchestrated revolution against utilitarianism's greatest-happiness principle (Bentham, Mill's taxation-of-the-wealthy, Singer's impartiality) and against Rawls's veil of ignorance and difference principle versus Nozick's entitlement objection and Aquinas's just-war criteria, concluding each character's actions can be read as 'just,' which exposes anthropocentrism as the real veil.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 53 "50. The Cabin in the Woods as Philosophy Cinematic Reflections on Ethical Complexity, Human Nature, and Worthw" — Kowalski argues Whedon and Goddard's The Cabin in the Woods stages a clash between classical utilitarianism and an ethics of care, and cinematically favors the latter. The Facility, sacrificing five campers to placate the Ancient Ones and save humanity, embodies Mill's greatest-happiness reasoning, but its callous celebration while Dana suffers on the dock undercuts that view. When the Director tells Dana she must kill her only remaining friend Marty to save the world, Dana's refusal is defended via Noddings's care ethics and Aristotle's claim that obligations track close personal relationships (special obligations), with Aristotle's Poetics catharsis and Plato's Leontius grounding the film's theory of worthwhile horror: 'people are more important than humanity.'
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 81 "76. The Last of Us as Moral Philosophy Teleological Particularism and Why Joel Is Not a Villain" — Horn takes The Last of Us as moral philosophy, arguing Joel is read as a villain only because players assume consequentialism or deontology. On Bentham/Mill's utilitarianism Joel fails to maximize utility by killing many to save Ellie; on Kant's categorical imperative his lying, stealing and killing are always impermissible. Horn instead defends 'teleological particularism' — an agent acts rightly when acting in conformity with a role, roles being socially constructed and variable — so Joel's role as Ellie's surrogate father (mirrored in his carrying her out as he carried Sarah, and the 'Future Days' lyric) obligates him to put her above humanity. On this view Joel's refusal to let the Fireflies kill Ellie, and his final lie, are morally permissible, not villainous.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 93 "87. Frank Miller’s Batman as Philosophy “The World Only Makes Sense When You Force It To”" — Bein reads Frank Miller's Batman (chiefly The Dark Knight Returns and Year One) as rejecting the utilitarianism he ascribes to Superman—who would 'rightly' nuke a city to prevent two—in favor of a Nietzschean will to power, distinguished from mere force (Macht vs. Kraft), born of Miller's own mugging. The Joker problem is worked through Kant's categorical imperative, desert-based death penalty, and the slippery slope of denying moral standing to the insane. Bein then separates Miller's avowed libertarianism (Nozick's canteen/lifeguard thought experiments, the minimal state) from Bruce Wayne's coercive 'Bat-libertarianism,' and confronts the 'Frank Miller problem' of Holy Terror's Islamophobia against Miller's anti-corporate, anti-Reagan streak.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 100 "94. Yes, Roya and Philosophy The Art of Submission" — Goldberg, Gavaler, and Chavez use Trotman and Denich's Yes, Roya—where Roya dominates Joe and Wylie professionally (publishing under Joe's name) and sexually, all consensually—to ask how the three major Western ethical theories can accommodate consensual dominant/submissive relationships. They argue Aristotle's virtue ethics handles them via unequal friendships (submissives depending more, within a mean), Kant's Formula of Universal Law permits them once consent is built into the maxim (aligning with the Formula of Humanity), and Mill's utilitarianism sanctions them because justice and felt safety, grounded in consent, follow from the Greatest Happiness Principle.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 13 "4. The Good of the Doctor" — The chapter distinguishes aesthetic 'good' (taste, beauty of the Daleks) from ethical 'good,' then tests the Doctor against the major moral theories: utilitarianism (rejected when Sarah Jane urges exterminating the Daleks in 'Genesis of the Daleks'), Kantian duty ethics (the Doctor's 'never met anyone who wasn't important' and attempts to save Davros and the Master), virtue ethics (the Eleventh Doctor guarding Christmas in 'The Time of the Doctor'), and feminist care ethics. Concluding that none quite fits because the Doctor values non-rational beings and feels compassion, the author proposes the Doctor follows Wolterstorff's 'ethic of need'—justice as meeting the needs of all—consistent with 'getting in the thick of things' as a flâneur.

### The Death of God

"God is dead" is Nietzsche's diagnosis, most famously voiced by a madman in The Gay Science, that belief in the Christian God and the moral and metaphysical order it underwrote has lost its hold on Western culture. He does not mean it as a triumphant slogan but as an event of enormous consequence: without a divine guarantor of meaning and value, humanity risks sliding into nihilism unless it can create new values for itself. The phrase names both a cultural crisis and an opportunity, marking the loss of an absolute foundation and the task of finding meaning without one.

- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings in part as a protest against modernism - the post-WWI mood (Berman, Marx's 'all that is solid melts into air', Nietzsche's 'God is dead') that tradition is obsolete and whatever can be done must be done. The heroes win by remembering: Gandalf alone thinks to watch the Shire, Sam's book-learning about elves and the password 'Elbereth' saves the day at Cirith Ungol, while Saruman and Denethor fall into modern despair through the palantír and Pippin's stone dropped in Moria brings Gandalf down. The Ring itself is modernism's false promise of remaking the world, and Tolkien answers it with a fantasy where ancient lore has tangible power - sealed by Pippin's maturing into one of Middle-earth's great librarians.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 17 "And There Is No Escape" — Abrams reads Allen through Foucault's panopticon: modern society is unlimited voyeurism in which the medieval God whose 'eyes are on us always' has been replaced by the omniscient gaze of Film — Cliff's exposé documentary forcing Lester to watch his own life in Crimes and Misdemeanors, Tom Baxter stepping off the screen in The Purple Rose of Cairo, and the nested eavesdropping layers of Another Woman, which he counts to infinity via Noël Carroll's 'mass art'. Against Mary Nichols's virtue-ethics reading, he argues Allen's ethics is Nietzschean self-fashioning: Judah lives 'beyond good and evil' where Raskolnikov failed, Allan Felix sheds the Bogart alter ego and 'gives style' to his character in Play It Again, Sam, while Eve in Interiors stages Hegel's master–slave dialectic, the 'master' artist dependent for her identity on those she objectifies.
- **The Atkins Diet and Philosophy - Chewing the Fat with Kant and Nietzsche**, ch. 20 "The Atkins Diet and Philosophy" — Bamford argues that Atkins's insistence that dieters evaluate the plan for their individual needs parallels Nietzsche's cultural therapy: as the death of God left modern culture nihilistic, so a processed-food culture suffers 'nutritional nihilism,' and the 'mega-orthodox' doctors who worship medical consensus with 'religious fervor' treat science as a replacement religion. Reading Ecce Homo's 'question of nutriment' alongside Twilight of the Idols, she shows that Nietzsche's perspectivism — no uninterpreted facts, only interpretations from physiological perspectives — makes each dieter fully responsible for interpretation, which is why Atkins must ask us to think for ourselves. The limit: where Atkins keeps an 'absolute faith in empirical science' (and Atkins Nutritionals mass-markets processed low-carb products), a properly Nietzschean therapy would question that faith too.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 12 "Getting Right with Brian (Just in Case)" — Reads Life of Brian through Nietzsche's madman: the crowd's laughter at Brian's market sermons ('consider the lilies... have the birds got jobs?') enacts the death of the cheerless, pathos-soaked God, with Brian as a sincere 'divine idiot' who escapes ressentiment by falling idiotically below the dialectic rather than rising above it as an Übermensch. Bergson's account of the comic — rigidity invisible to its bearer, 'as though wearing the ring of Gyges with reverse effect' — explains why the Pythons' straight men, British class consciousness, and the Roman/British empires ('Romani ite domum,' the centurion's Latin lesson) are funny, and why Britons and Romans can laugh at themselves while Americans cannot. Pivoting from Jorge's war on laughter in Eco's The Name of the Rose, the chapter closes with a Pascal's-wager parody: having laughed at Brian, you have already wagered your immortal soul on God being British — the sort of God who can take a joke.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 15 "And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism" — Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 20 "Knowledge and Nihilism Science and Monty Python’s The Meaning of Life" — Croskery tours the social institutions that promise guidance for a good life, pairing each with a Python work: Adam Smith's invisible hand and Bentham's greatest-happiness utilitarianism fail in the 'Merchant Banker' sketch, where charity leaves the banker 'a pound down on the whole deal', while Marxist market ideology and alienation surface in the Communist Quiz and the accountant who longs to be a lion tamer. In The Holy Grail, Aristotle's doctrine of the mean sorts Brave Sir Robin's cowardly flight from Sir Lancelot's rash slaughter of a wedding party and Galahad's desire-distorted chastity at Castle Anthrax, with Bedevere's duck-weighing witch logic showing reasoning without judgment, and Arthur's quest collapses because 'strange women lying in ponds handing out swords is no basis for a system of government'. Life of Brian's 'blessed are the cheesemakers' and the 'You're all individuals!' crowd ground a Kantian demand for autonomy against blind obedience to religious rules. The Meaning of Life's 'Galaxy Song' and 'spiraling coils of self-replicating DNA' pose Nietzschean nihilism — science dissolving the highest values — which the film's closing advice to be nice to people and keep a sense of humor answers with a modest, livable meaning.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 13 "U2 and Philosophy" — Malpas takes The Joshua Tree as an album about place: its desert imagery and restless movement ('Where the Streets Have No Name', 'I Still Haven't Found What I'm Looking For' as 'an anthem of doubt more than faith') carry the listener from Ireland to Reagan's America to Pinochet's Chile, while its political references - Ethiopian famine, El Salvador, Dublin high-rises - always work through concrete locations rather than abstract ideals. Using Heidegger on homelessness as the inability to dwell, and Marx and Engels' 'all that is solid melts into air', he argues that modernity has not erased our relatedness to place but covered it over. The album's desolation is therefore readable the other way: belonging is constituted through care, commitment and uncertain journeying in the places we already are ('Heartland').
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 11 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Butterfield takes Bond's answer to Elektra in The World Is Not Enough - he survives by 'tak[ing] pleasure in great beauty' - and asks whether hedonism can answer the problem of suffering and death. She reads Bond through Heidegger's being-towards-death (quoting Live and Let Die's 'You start to die the moment you are born'), then diagnoses him as Kierkegaard's aesthetic 'seducer', an immature escapist who dreads boredom and flees commitment, before rehabilitating him with Nietzsche and Camus: Bond flushing the cyanide pill down the toilet in From Russia with Love and Mathis's advice in Casino Royale to make evil 'personal' show Bond creating his own values beyond good and evil, surviving the absurd through style and personal vendetta. Bond emerges as an existentialist role model for courage and creativity, though we should not copy his hedonism or lawlessness.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" — Peter Fosl reads Metallica's lyrics ("Leper Messiah," "The God That Failed," "One," "To Live Is to Die," "Escape") as extending Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: religion as slave morality born of ressentiment and as opium deadening the oppressed, illustrated by the landmine veteran of "One" pleading with a silent God and Hetfield's abandoned-childhood grief. He argues the band often falls into the "incomplete nihilism" Nietzsche predicted, lamenting God's failure and longing nostalgically for the Christian meaning it can no longer believe in rather than transvaluating values. Yet the defiance of "The Four Horsemen" and "Escape" and the band's creative power show it also working toward an overcoming of Christian nihilism, confirmed for Fosl by Hetfield's post-rehab health.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 10 "Rupert’s Response and Responsibility" — Biderman and Jacobowitz read Rope through Nietzsche: Brandon and Philip strangle their classmate David as would-be Nietzschean supermen, acting on mentor Rupert Cadell's cocktail-party theory that murder can be an art for a superior few. The chapter explains the will to power, the Ubermensch, and the death of God, then argues Brandon is no superman: he kills from weakness and a bully's need for an audience, mistaking crass destruction for the refined self-creation Nietzsche demanded, just as the fascist appropriation of Nietzsche fails. Rupert's horrified final speech, renouncing 'superior or inferior beings' and insisting each of us is 'a separate human being,' raises whether a teacher can disavow responsibility when students act out his provocative ideas: ideas have consequences, and the only true test of a philosophy is whether we can live by it.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 24 "Kill Bill Volume 2 Mommy Kills Daddy" — Mark Conard reads the two Kill Bill volumes as Tarantino's Oedipal play and self-therapy: Volume 1 fuses the movie genres of his childhood with women in the lead roles while Bill lurks as the absent, godlike father, and the Bride's empowerment is traced from the Pussy Wagon through the Hanzo sword—a transformation from 'pussy to cock'. In Volume 2, Pai Mei teaches her that her strength lies in her own hands, freeing her from a masculine conception of power, while Bill is humanized—sandwiches, flute-playing, a heart that can break—so that killing him means killing the father's God-like hold, explicitly glossed through Nietzsche's death of God. The final duel's sheathed sword lets the woman, as woman, defeat the man, and the Oedipal act succeeds where Oedipus himself had to go blind.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 25 "Like Caine in Kung Fu" — Bence Nanay and Ian Schnee argue Pulp Fiction is genuinely Nietzschean, but not by celebrating violence: the film stages the crisis of meaning after God's death through two reactions to chance. Vincent is the passive nihilist—dogmatically insisting the six bullets mean nothing, inheriting gangster values unquestioned, modeling himself on Elvis—while Jules's 'moment of clarity' makes him a Nietzschean free spirit who creates perspective-relative meaning and breaks the cycle of violence by buying Ringo and Honey Bunny's lives. His plan to 'walk the earth, like Caine in Kung Fu' reworks Zarathustra's wandering, and the running toilets gag marks Vincent's blindness to the significance of events, which is why only one of them survives.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 11 "Meaning The Final Frontier" — Biderman and Devlin read The Wrath of Khan as a Nietzschean test of whether revenge can ground a meaningful life after the death of God: Kirk, stuck 'flying a goddamn computer console' as an admiral, and the Genesis project seek meaning through creation without God, while Khan, broken by exile on Ceti Alpha V, chooses vengeance. Using Nozick's contrast between impartial retribution and personally satisfying revenge, and Nietzsche's will to power, master-slave morality, and ressentiment, they argue Khan had the superhuman gifts and independence from herd morality of a candidate Overman, but let revenge enslave him — culminating in Genesis turned weapon and his dying 'For hate's sake . . . I spit my last breath at thee,' a resounding No to life. Spock's mirror-image self-sacrifice, which affirms life, is offered as the better Nietzschean Overman.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "Game Over" — Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 20 "Brush the Cobwebs from the Sky, Let the Genie Out from the Bottle" — Lougheed reads OK Computer, Kid A, and Amnesiac as portraits of Nietzsche's Last Humans: passive, resentful denizens of the world after the death of God, from the 'No Surprises' narrator begging for his quiet life of carbon monoxide to the 'Everything in Its Right Place' man sucking a lemon over the loss of objective right and wrong, whose isolated malice ('when I am king you will be first against the wall') is perspectivism collapsed into passive nihilism. Hail to the Thief then breaks from this landscape: its protagonists risk transcendence as Over Humans who create new, life-affirming values ('2 + 2 = 5'''s 'don't question my authority', 'Backdrifts''' 'nothing more to lose'), keep a critical distance from society's nihilistic sickness ('Where I End and You Begin'), and test their lives against eternal recurrence ('Sail to the Moon'''s 'know right from wrong', '15 Step'''s ending up where you started). The chapter closes by weighing Nietzsche's over-human project against critics who prefer gradual, generational self-overcoming for everyone.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 15 "The Missionary" — Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 11 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Auxier argues the trilogy is narrated on a Nietzschean lattice rather than being a mere inverted Milton: after tracing the Paradise Lost, Genesis 6, and Pseudepigrapha sources (Azazel as the model for Asriel, Metatron from Third Enoch, Dust from Milton's warring particles), he reads Mrs. Coulter's speech to Father MacPhail about seeking God out and giving him 'the gift of death' as Nietzsche's death of God fused with a description of Nietzsche's own final dementia. Will and Lyra become overman and overwoman beyond good and evil: Will rises by his will and his willingness to kill (the alethiometer's verdict 'He is a murderer' makes him a worthy companion), while Lyra commands both truth and lies, the alethiometer embodying truth as 'a mobile army of metaphors.' But the chapter's payoff is critical: Pullman does not endorse Nietzsche, since in a world where the will to power dominates, the overwoman Mrs. Coulter has no place and falls with Asriel and Metatron into the Abyss, while Xaphania's teaching offers a disciplined, workful imagination as an alternative.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 13 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Fairweather casts the campaign against Pullman's books as Socrates's trial rerun (impiety plus corrupting the young) and asks whether legally protected speech can still be morally wrong, weighing Mill's On Liberty point that children lack the 'maturity of their faculties' against the charge that Pullman's 'killing God' rhetoric inflicts spiritual violence on young believers, by his own image of intercision.
