The answer comes through Nietzsche's Three Metamorphoses: Asriel, Will, and Lyra play the lion that slays the great 'thou shalt' of the Authority, but the lion's destruction is only the possibility of freedom, since full freedom is Nietzsche's child creating its own values rather than lapsing into nihilism or Sartrean bad faith. Pullman's Republic of Heaven, with its virtues of courage, compassion, love, kindness, and curiosity held in community, is a social ideal rather than a radically Nietzschean one, so the charge of corrupting young readers is deflated.
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 12 "Death Knight as Overman" — Luke Cuddy asks whether playing WoW can answer nihilism, using Schopenhauer's bleak remark on our sudden existence and Nietzsche's death of God to set up the problem — King Bangalash dies and WoW goes on, just as humans die and the universe continues. Entering Huizinga's Magic Circle gives Azeroth its meanings, but the player must then dissolve the circle, recognize that the game itself is meaningless, and keep playing anyway — creating the toon as a work of art in the Dionysian spirit. A maxed Death Knight still is not Nietzsche's Overman, because the player affirms only her in-game existence; the fifth step is carrying that self-creation back into real life.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 12 "Oh to Be a Gooner" — Kilpatrick reads Nietzsche's madman's question 'what sacred games shall we have to invent?' as answered by the stadium: after the death of God, soccer has replaced religion as the shared narrative where modern communities make and worship heroes. Using The Birth of Tragedy, he reads a goal as an Apollonian–Dionysian fusion—the scorer's individuated ecstasy merging with the collective joy of teammates and fans—and, on Nietzsche's claim that existence is justified only as an aesthetic phenomenon, argues the game is defensible only when played creatively and artistically rather than by negative, win-at-all-costs tactics. Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism (the state as 'the new idol', the 'good European', Zarathustra's 'children's land') means club over country, and Wenger's Arsenal—with its dietary and training laboratory at London Colney cultivating an Overman, its Invincibles season, and its young, passport-blind signings—emerges as the club Nietzsche would support through its very will-to-power.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 20 "Gene For Pedantry Same As Gene For Philosophy" — Loader's chapter is a spread of fake 'Existential Times' news parodies: an uncompliant student who answers every robot thought experiment with 'But you're not' drives his professor to swearing over the problem of other minds; Wisconsin scientists find the self as a half-centimeter of Silly Putty in the neck, joking that Hume 'may simply have been looking in the wrong place' when introspection found only a bundle of perceptions; a poll finds not one American philosopher has read Hegel's Phenomenology of Spirit beyond 'the bit about the master and the slave'; and a student essay on Sartre's Existentialism and Humanism wanders off into Planet of the Apes and calls Sartre 'Mr Horse.' The Philososcope prescribes page 232 of Heidegger's Being and Time, a movie loser quotes Nietzsche ('There is always some madness in love') before falling into a pond, an archaeology department's found remains of God back Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' and a Marxist begs capitalism to hold off collapsing until her book is published—philosophy satirized as pedantry, posing, and self-importance.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 30 "I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You" — Reads the Doctor as a Christ-figure and savior (the 'Voyage of the Damned' ascension that drew Christian Voice protests, Martha's year of gospel-telling in 'The Last of the Time Lords'), applying Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideals onto God. But the show under Russell T Davies also distrusts godlike power: Davros's 'you made this' accusation, the Racnoss massacre, and Joan Redfern's question in 'The Family of Blood' show the lonely god's devastation. Against this, companions like Donna embody Nietzsche's Übermensch ('There's no such thing as an ordinary human'), so the chapter concludes the Doctor and ordinary humans need each other, mutually overcoming their weaknesses.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 35 "The Ethics of Dexter’s Appeal" — James F. Pontuso reconstructs Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals - promise-keeping, the unpayable debt to ancestor-founders that becomes God, cruelty turned inward as bad conscience, and Christianity's divine self-ransom that only deepens guilt - to explain why Dexter, who feels no guilt, is not abnormal but a man before morality. Following Gibbon's picture of Roman soldiers whose civil religion justified slaughter without remorse, he imagines Dexter thriving in the legions ('Dexter SPQR') rather than hiding behind Harry's Code, and argues the show appeals because Aristotle's ethics concerned outward conduct and justice rather than inner conscience. In our levelled age we secretly crave what Nietzsche craved: the sight of 'something perfect... still capable of inspiring fear.'
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 7 "His Work Is Its Own Reward" — Timothy Sexton argues the real Overman is not Doyle's flat 'calculating machine' but Jeremy Brett's Granada Holmes: the sneer with which he frees the Blue Carbuncle thief and the 'I am not retained by the police' outburst show him stepping beyond the herd's good-and-evil after the death of God. Brett's theatrical style, from the pivot before Lady Brackenstall in 'The Abbey Grange' to 'Gentlemen, we can do better than that' in 'The Norwood Builder', enacts Nietzsche's grand art of giving style to one's character, sublimating nihilistic dread into the pleasure of proving superiority. Where Rathbone-era Sherlocks solve crimes for truth, justice and the Victorian Way, Brett's Holmes makes the work its own reward, satisfying Nietzsche's demand that the Overman 'attain satisfaction with himself'.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 23 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Brandon Kempner reads Gaiman's Batman: Whatever Happened to the Caped Crusader? as Nietzschean eternal recurrence: Batman dies and is reborn as the infant Bruce Wayne to repeat his life exactly, because Gaiman first strips away every teleological ending, Catwoman kills Batman, Alfred reveals he invented the Joker, and the Moore-style domestic bliss of the Superman farewell is denied. With God dead there is no Heaven, telos, or external reward, so, like Nietzsche's Overman who creates values above the city's conventional morality, Batman's meaning can lie only in the lived repetition itself: 'the only reward you get for being Batman? You get to be Batman,' the highest formula of life-affirmation. Kempner extends the pattern to the funeral-framed rebirth of a new Dream in Sandman: The Wake, showing Gaiman's recurring obsession with cycles that have 'no endings' across his work.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 18 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Zanelotti takes up the charge that Larry is a self-hating Jew, from whistling Wagner to 'The End,' where learning he is a gentile turns him into a churchgoing enthusiast who sings 'Go Tell It on the Mountain' and gives Richard Lewis his kidney. Sartre's bad faith diagnoses both poles: Larry denying his facticity by imagining he can simply shed his Jewish past and re-adopt it at will, and critics who demand he live up to an 'authentic' Jewish essence; Marx's false consciousness, meanwhile, explains the self-hating baldy who buys into the haired agenda. Using Ronald de Sousa's rejection of the 'Just Joking Defense'—we are accountable for laughter because we let ourselves become people who cannot restrain it—the chapter argues the show sets a comic frame that mocks bad faith rather than Judaism. Its deeper target, via Nietzsche's death of God, is the overenthusiastic meaning we manufacture when faith is 'curbed,' which is why Larry ridicules only public displays of religion, not belief itself.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 13 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Greene asks whether Nucky is Nietzsche's Ubermensch and works through each criterion. Nucky, Gyp Rosetti, and the other mobsters are passionate, active shapers of their world (Van Alden fails here), and Nucky is a genuine creator of values after the death of God - his whopper to the Temperance League, his flip-flopping sermons to black and white congregations, and his 'I. Am. Not. Seeking. Forgiveness.' over Jimmy's body reject slave morality where the other gangsters merely follow the objective moral code of omerta. He sacrifices lesser lives (Hans Schroeder, Gillian) and has the required dark side, but he fails the final test of teaching the eternal recurrence, so he remains only 'well on his way' to Superman - a status the show's women (Margaret, Lucy, Gillian) never approach, hovering closer to the last man.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 17 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Ketcham reads the monster as Zarathustra's dark double: both are exiled 'godless men' who begin their journeys at a cottager's door, but where Nietzsche's prophet preaches the Übermensch, the will to power, and living so one could will eternal recurrence, the monster traverses the three metamorphoses in reverse - born the innocent child, becoming the lion who tells Victor 'you are my creator, but I am your master,' and ending the camel carrying his maker's corpse to a self-immolating pyre in the polar dark. Shelley's abyss is science usurping God and drawing Promethean punishment; Nietzsche's abyss is the shadow of the dead God (The Gay Science) that keeps humanity from the great noontide and traps Frankenstein as a 'last man' whose will is subjugated to pleasant happiness. The monster, bastard of a godless man and bridge to neither animal nor Übermensch, shows a will that is sheer power without any foundation for overcoming man - 'whither humanity?'
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 32 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Kenn Fisher reads the franchise as the extinction of the Great Chain of Being: from Plato's humans mid-way between gods and beasts, through Genesis dominion and Descartes's non-conscious animals, to Malcolm's 'God creates man. Man destroys God. Man creates dinosaurs' - with computers (Hammond's control room, Wikipedia, Google) replacing God at the top. He then tracks animals' ascent from property: Francione on welfare versus personhood, Bentham's 'Can they suffer?', and Singer's equality-as-prescription, applied to Dieter Stark tasering a compy (punished by the compys) versus the unexamined electric fences that keep InGen's 'zoo animals' caged. He closes with Carol Adams's meat-masculinity link - Roland Tembo will hunt only a male T. rex, the dinosaurs are all female - and holds up vegetarian Lex as hope that the Chain bends into a Circle.
- **Adventure Time and Philosophy - The Handbook for Heroes**, ch. 20 "Adventure Time and Philosophy" — Namvol argues that 'Glob' is the post-apocalyptic corpse of the Christian God: combining Don Cupitt's claim that gods live only in worship and practice with Nietzsche's 'God is dead,' he traces how the Mushroom War destroyed the believers, churches, and rituals that kept God alive, leaving Ooo an empty exclamation. Pantheism fails as a rescue because evil is native to Ooo's nature (Gunter, the eternally self-existing Abadeer), so God cannot simply have become the land. Against Dostoevsky's 'without God all things are permitted,' the chapter sides with Žižek—that morality's shadow, guilt, outlives God—as when Finn's self-regulation kicks in after 'All the Little People' and 'Dungeon Train,' making Finn, not Glob, the true savior of a godless world.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 19 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Michaud reads the novel through Nietzsche: the Crew of Light are resentful sheep banding together to kill a lion, damning Dracula not for wrongdoing but for his will-to-power, his hunting, and his reproduction - things humans do daily to animals - while the tale's enduring popularity over Nietzsche's heresy proves the death of God never happened, since we still use religion to console ourselves about dying. Following Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, he argues Dracula stories are humanity's immortality project: we must narrate the destruction of physical immortality to persuade ourselves it is a curse ('it would suck to be immortal') and that heroic, spiritual salvation in heaven is the better eternity.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham asks whether primogeniture and entail make Downton Abbey a social embodiment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence - the same estate, without revision, turned over generation after generation like the eternal hourglass of existence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he tests royal continuity against death duties, the nihilism of industrial capitalism, and the Great War that killed heirs and empires, and borrows Kant's categorical imperative as an analogy for Britain's uniquely preserved 'royal categorical imperative' of continuity. The Abbey's recurrence survives only anthropomorphically - Violet, the family, the servants, and the tenants as its living organs - and the chapter wonders whether such ossified continuity, like dinosaur bones, is really eternal.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 22 "10. The Light from Friendship" — Pavelich sets Aristotle's account of friendship - recognized and reciprocated goodwill between equals, perfected in the friendship of the good who 'share our souls', a standard met only by Jack and Bella Crawford - against Nietzsche's friendship as striving between overmen, who honor 'one's best enemy' in the friend and grow through conflict. He reads Hannibal's treatment of Will (hiding the encephalitis, framing him, serving the Nietzschean trout) as Nietzschean friend-making - Lies that are supposed to spur Will's growth, consistent with an Übermensch who tells Will 'Killing must feel good to God' and says 'I don't hide from God' - while Will's masquerade of friendship is betrayal in both senses, since Will seeks an Aristotelian soulmate and finds a killer he must stop. Because each betrays the other, neither Aristotelian nor Nietzschean friendship survives, though the moments before the Mizumono bloodbath - Hannibal inviting Will to just walk away - glimpse a real friendship already made impossible.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 12 "1. Everything’s Amazing and Nobody’s Happy" — Max Elder reads Louis through Nietzsche's Gay Science claim that all philosophy is unconscious memoir, arguing Louis's confession-like comedy reveals dark truths we would rather flee - the Conan 'everything's amazing and nobody's happy' bit, the 'I know the darkness' exchange with the Christian woman, and the Subway/Pamela scene where a homeless man bathes behind a subway violinist. Using Nietzsche's line that man alone laughs because he suffers so deeply, and The Birth of Tragedy's comic as the artistic discharge of the nausea of absurdity, the chapter argues Louis's laughter performs a gestalt switch that ties the ugly to the beautiful and so redeems it. It reads the religions-supply-meaning argument - God's mockery-laughter versus Nietzsche's holy laughter - as the reason redemption now happens in comedy clubs rather than churches, and closes with Louie's 'Country Drive' scolding of Jane ('you don't get to be bored') as Nietzschean embrace of the amazing fact of being alive.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" — Holdier argues that neither hero is Nietzsche's Übermensch: Superman's servile mild-mannered Clark Kent guise would strike Nietzsche as slave morality, while Batman's self-loathing (his Hush confession that deep down he is not a good person) and breakable human body disqualify him too. Instead, reading them through The Birth of Tragedy and Grant Morrison's Supergods, Superman embodies the Apollonian force of order, sunlight, and rationality and Batman the Dionysian force of chaos and passion, so their battles (The Dark Knight Returns, Batman v Superman) are the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles. The fight's real winner is the reader, who gets both deities at once.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 14 "5. How Heroes Argue" — LaBauve opens with a staged Justice League debate over rescuing the Joker's hostages, where Batman's emotional, vengeance-tinged appeal loses to Superman's trust-based plea, and reads it through Aristotle's On Rhetoric: Batman persuades almost entirely by pathos (the relatable brokenness of Nolan's trilogy) with detective's logos, while Superman balances pathos, logos, and above all ethos, since Aristotle calls the speaker's character the strongest appeal. Against Max Landis's claim that Superman is irrelevant, he pairs the Death of Superman with Nietzsche's "God is dead" parable and the Kill Bill monologue to argue that Superman is a mythology of virtue - alongside real moral heroes like Gandhi, King, and Jesus - showing humans the ideal they ought to become, so Superman not only wins but must win.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 16 "6. The God We Need Now" — Ketcham stages the essay as a 1939 diary (a boyhood piece longing for a new god now that the biblical God has, he feels, abandoned the Depression-era world) followed by an old man's reread: America made Superman its messiah - born in a flash of light like the star of Bethlehem, canonized by DC's "publishing synod" much as the church redacted the New Testament - but he suspects the god will age as badly as the God of Abraham. Rereading after Korea, Vietnam, and Wall Street scandals, he argues we now need and worship a darker god modeled on Hades: the rich, hidden, vengeful billionaire Bruce Wayne, whose subterranean mansion, Cerberus-like Alfred, and tax-break tributes from citizens mirror the underworld god and Greek sacrifice. He ends imagining our grandchildren's next god as a cyber-god of AI, and declares Batman, not Superman, the god we need now.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 31 "18. Thus Slaughtered Deadpool" — The chapter argues Deadpool is neither hero nor anti-hero but Nietzsche's Ubermensch beyond good and evil: perceiving the writers as the 'man at the typewriter' who keeps the Marvel cast as unwitting sheep under a slave morality, he kills the Marvel Universe in Deadpool Kills the Marvel Universe to free them from their creators. In Deadpool Killustrated he murders the literary archetypes (Moby-Dick, the Little Mermaid, Tom Sawyer) so the heroes they inspired can never be written, compared to the Overman demolishing inherited values before they corrupt the next generation, and in Deadpool Kills Deadpool he slaughters every version of himself to force the creator-god into the open. Since 'good' and 'bad' are categories of the herd whose very source is corrupt, the author declines to judge the slaughter at all.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 21 "8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir" — Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 25 "11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them" — Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 11 "3. Mermen and Dismemberment" — Contends that Hendrix's discord is philosophy-as-discord: 'I Don't Live Today' (the Native American dead-in-life), the Woodstock 'Star-Spangled Banner' with its bombs and sirens against sporting-event sentimentality, 'Machine Gun,' and 'House Burning Down' lacerate listeners so they actually feel war's atrocities instead of parroting patriotic clichés. Against this the chapter sets the oceanic, womb-like escape fantasies of '1983 (A Merman I Should Turn to Be)' and 'Valleys of Neptune,' treating them through Schopenhauer as metaphysical consolation, Marx's opiate, and Nietzsche's 'hangman's metaphysics,' and concludes that Hendrix finally refuses such world-denying illusions — and Heideggerian inauthentic withdrawal — in favor of existential engagement with suffering here and now.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 23 "11. 999 Fingers" — Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.
- **1984 and Philosophy - Is Resistance Futile**, ch. 31 "19. Nineteen Eighty-Four’s Religion" — Crossley and Markou trace Orwell's ambivalence about religion — a lifelong atheist who loved the Church of England's liturgy — into the novel: Goldstein's book repeats the socialist critique of priests who 'softened by promises of compensation in an imaginary world beyond the grave' propped up hierarchy, yet the Party then occupies religion's vacant place itself, with O'Brien as 'priest of power', Goldstein as arch-heretic, and 'Thou art' replacing the old despotisms' 'Thou shalt not'. They argue Orwell thought a purer socialism needed the communal goods of religion, from the proles' fuzzy 'Christianness' to the radical Christian tradition of the Diggers and Levellers, and read Ingsoc as that utopian tradition betrayed. The novel's warning is therefore double: what fills the gap when religion dies, and how religion itself can be a blueprint for totalitarianism.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 9 "Scientifically, Introductions Are an Idiot Thing" — The introduction frames the whole book through the Rick/Jerry opposition: Rick is a Nietzschean artist-creator who insists the world is objectively meaningless and Godless yet keeps choosing his family, while Jerry is the herd-animal chasing socially approved values. It claims the show, like Nietzsche's deliberately difficult writing, sorts its audience into Jerrys who enjoy the dick jokes and Ricks who do the hard philosophical work of finding microscopic meaning in a meaningless cosmos. It closes with Socrates's 'unexamined life is not worth living' to justify submitting to philosophy's perplexity even if the Eyehole Man kicks the shit out of you.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 19 "8. Neither the Hero You Deserve Nor the Hero You Need" — Reading 'Vindicators 3' through Nietzsche, the chapter argues the superhero team are slave-morality charlatans whose duty to protect the weak is the herd's imaginary revenge, while Rick, who defeated Worldender drunk, embodies master morality and honest will to power, against Jerry's dishonest version in the Pluto-not-a-planet fight of 'Something Ricked This Way Comes'. Rick's casual destruction of Worldender becomes Nietzsche's death of God, the collapse of the value-source that gave the Vindicators' lives meaning, which Vance Maximus denies at the cost of his life. The chapter then tests Rick against the Ubermensch via the camel-lion-child metaphor and concludes he is at best Nietzsche's lion, tainted by resentment over his lost family rather than the value-creating child, leaving Morty and Simple Rick as long-shot candidates.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 25 "14. After the Blackout" — Martin Muchall treats the offscreen Blackout as an emblem of the moral catastrophe diagnosed in MacIntyre's After Virtue: our moral vocabulary has shattered into emotivist hissing and clapping, with Roy's murder of Tyrell, his 'God of biomechanics', staging the death of God and the 'everything is permitted' that follows. Utilitarian pleasure and Kantian cold reason (Spock, who must tell the truth to the murderer at the door) have both failed, leaving neoliberal hypercapitalism — corporate psychopathy, the orphanage sweatshop, the Baseline as workplace performance review — as the real villain. Against this, K's ending models the Buddha: everything is impermanent, there is no self to defend, and his selfless, empathetic death points to a morality grounded in evolved and cultivable altruism.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 15 "5. RuPaul versus Zarathustra" — The van der Wielen sisters read RuPaul against Nietzsche's Zarathustra: both are outcasts who descend from solitude bearing a spiritual teaching in a marketplace that mocks them, and both announce that inherited values are ungrounded — Zarathustra through the death of God and the call to become the over-man, Ru through 'we're all born naked and the rest is drag' and the cosmic life force that makes every identity a costume. But where Zarathustra refuses followers and shuns the people's values, Ru's creed polices female stereotypes (long hair, breasts, heels) and pulls the cart of consumerist values — money, fame, individualism — so that she comes to resemble the priests and wise men Zarathustra condemns. Her openly admitted fakeness and opportunism (the Wigstock 'gender fuck' abandoned for the glamazon brand) leave the chapter asking who flies higher: the tragic free spirit or the pragmatic, honestly dishonest superstar.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" — Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 10 "2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap" — This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe. Tony Stark embodies Sartre's existence precedes essence, defining himself through free choice up to his final 'I am Iron Man' snap that erases Thanos and his army; the merged Professor Hulk lives Camus's Sisyphus, embracing the absurd and concluding 'all is well' after watching his own past rage; Captain America lives Levinas's ethics of the Other, from refusing to abandon brainwashed Bucky in Civil War to wielding Mjolnir to save Thor; and Ronin-era Hawkeye enacts Nietzschean nihilism until Black Widow's Vormir sacrifice, read through Zarathustra's burning in one's own flame, restores his meaning. The authors conclude Marvel's answer is affirmation: courage to affirm freedom, the Other, and life itself against Thanos as personification of genocide, climate change, and war.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 24 "“You are…a beautiful, beautiful, butterfly”" — Argues the Xenomorph realizes Nietzsche's Ubermensch: it is what Ash describes - unclouded by 'conscience, remorse, or delusions of morality' - and perfects its predatory function down to its acidic blood, while paycheck-fixated crewmen like Brett and Parker are Nietzsche's complacent 'last men,' the type Zarathustra's townspeople clamor for. The alien's egg-Facehugger-Chestburster-adult metamorphosis maps onto the camel, lion, and child of the three metamorphoses of the spirit, and the chapter closes by wondering whether the creature's monstrosity might have made Nietzsche himself reconsider the vital perfection he preached.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 9 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — William Irwin reads the Ozzy-era catalog as unwitting British existentialism: "Johnny Blade", "Paranoid", and "Wheels of Confusion" voice Camus's absurd, the mismatch between our desires and a world where life has no meaning and "hell is other people" explains why Iron Man, saved yet treated as a mindless thing, plans vengeance. The chapter argues the band moves from despair toward freedom and self-creation: "Supernaut" and "Under the Sun" reject religion in the spirit of Nietzsche's death of God, "Cornucopia" depicts bad-faith conformity to plastic suburban lives, and "Children of the Grave" plus Sabbath's own music-making exemplify the claim that artistic creativity is the proper response to pain, with the fan invited to sculpt himself into an authentic individual Sisyphus-style.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 5 "A Shared Higher Thirst" — Cleary reads Strange as a would-be Nietzschean Übermensch — brilliant, striving, and flirting with nihilism via the 'tiny momentary speck' line — whose narcissism, not his ideals, blocks both self-overcoming and love. Strange's rage at Christine Palmer's wine and cheese ('don't pity me') is explained through Nietzsche's attack on pity as herd morality, and his fixation on restoring his old surgeon-self as refusing Zarathustra's call to burn oneself to ashes. The Ancient One leaving him to die on Everest, Mordo's hard training, and Wong refusing to laugh at his jokes exemplify Nietzschean friendship as challenge and 'war,' culminating in the 'shared higher thirst for an ideal above them' that lets Strange overcome himself.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 29 "17. Downton Abbey as Eternal Recurrence" — Christopher Ketcham provocatively equates primogeniture and entail - the legal machinery that returns Downton intact to each generation - with Nietzsche's 'greatest weight,' the eternal recurrence. Working through Lawrence Hatab's five interpretations of the doctrine, he asks whether the Abbey's continuity is cosmological (it is not, since estate taxes and squandering heirs keep chipping away), a Zarathustra-style life-affirming yes to the agrarian world against the 'nihilism' of capitalist fashion, or merely symbolic like a listing in Burke's Peerage beside fossilized dinosaur bones. His answer comes via Violet, the family, and the servants, who have 'become one with the property': the Abbey recurs only anthropomorphically, and even that stickiness is dissolving under industrialization, the death tax, and the war that killed off three royal cousins' empires.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 9 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Kylie Prymus asks whether Kefka is truly mad, using Foucault's Madness and Civilization to argue that madness is a label society applies to dismiss what it cannot control, so players and heroes refute Kefka with the ad hominem 'you're crazy' rather than answering him. She then reads Kefka's 'monument to non-existence' through Nietzsche: his godlike discovery that existence has no justification echoes the death of God, our horror at him reflects slave morality's relabeling of noble strength as evil, and the heroes' appeal to purposes he lacks fails because existence is only a hypothetical imperative. Kefka ends up a failed Ubermensch who overthrows the gods but cannot overcome nihilism, leaving the World of Ruin heroes the genuinely Nietzschean task of creating meaning where none is given.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 21 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — David Hahn argues that Spira's Yevon religion is exactly what Machiavelli and Nietzsche warned against: hope for the Calm and a Sin-free future makes Spirans otherworldly and passive, forbidding machina, revering self-sacrificing Summoner martyrs, and blaming themselves for Sin, just as just-war Christianity left Machiavelli's princes passive and dependent on mercenaries, paralleled by Seymour and Kinoc standing idle at Operation Mi'ihen. Nietzsche's slave revolt in morality explains Yevon's sanctification of meekness and death, while Machiavelli's account of religion as a political instrument, from Numa to Scipio's oath, explains why the lie of Yevon held Spira together, and why its collapse may bring either Nietzschean rebirth or Machiavellian chaos.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 23 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Christopher Wood reads Cloud's arc as an existentialist quest: Heidegger's thrownness in Cloud's tumble off the Midgar train and his initial 'It's not my problem' denial of being-in-the-world; Nietzsche's death of God in Mako-powered Midgar's nihilism, with AVALANCHE as a call for revaluation of values and Sephiroth as a false aspirant god; and Sartre's bad faith in Cloud 'playing at being a SOLDIER,' a persona borrowed wholesale from Zack along with his sword and mercenary dream. Through the Lifestream reunion with Tifa, Cloud faces his fabricated past, admits 'I never was in SOLDIER,' and turns to authenticity by resolving to live without pretending, which Wood presents as the player's own existential task.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" — Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 18 "8 Nietzschean Themes in Raiders of the Lost Ark God May Be Dead, But Best Not Disturb His Corpse" — Duncan Gale reads Raiders through Nietzsche's Genealogy of Morals: the Nazis' contempt for those they exploit ('They hire only strong backs and they pay pennies') enacts master morality, while their ressentiment-driven project is itself a fatal misreading — both of the Ark and of Nietzsche, whom Walter Kaufmann shows was distorted by his anti-Semitic sister rather than responsible for it. Indy emerges as an overman candidate whose improvised self-legislation ('I'm making this up as I go,' casually shooting the scimitar-wielding warrior) creates life-affirming values, unlike Belloq, who has no code at all. The finale inverts the death of God: the Nazis die because they disturb a divine power they cannot harness, while America's de facto agnosticism — warehousing the Ark with 'top men' — proves the survivable response to nihilism.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Toni Fellela gives an existentialist reading of Zelda, confessing she leaves Ocarina of Time and Twilight Princess permanently paused before the final Ganon fight because the meaning lies in the process of becoming, not the ending. Sartre's existence precedes essence structures Link's growth from a swordless Kokiri boy collecting equipment into the hero; Nietzsche's death of God ('we must become gods') fits Link restoring meaning to a godless Hyrule, while Camus's Sisyphus dignifies the repetitive drudge work of slashing grass for rupees. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy anchors the chapter's payoff: even the most mundane tasks — in a camp or a laundromat or Hyrule Field — become bearable and meaningful when connected to a future goal, which is why the author can play for four hours straight.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 10 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Kukkonen reads Peter's never-extinguished guilt over Uncle Ben as an 'infinite debt' modeled on Anselm's atonement theology: no good deed repays the primal transgression, so even the heroic serum rescue for Aunt May in 'The Final Chapter' (Amazing Spider-Man #33) leaves the debt intact. Against the Nietzschean escape into self-sufficient magnanimity (Ben's ghostly blessing in 'Doom Service!'), he argues via Levinas and Derrida that Peter's responsibility extends to every stranger, as when a rescued policeman with Uncle Ben's face calls him back in 'Spider-Man No More!' (#50). Following Kierkegaard's Works of Love, the chapter concludes that Peter's heroics do not pay off but deepen his debt of love, since every choice heeds one call while unavoidably failing others.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 15 "Notes" — Victor Grech presents Klingons as a cultural pastiche—Mongol horde stereotypes, Japanese Bushido, Viking Valhalla, Shakespeare 'restored to the original Klingon'—whose 1500-year honor code and embrace of honorable death (Klag's dishonored father, Jadzia's rebuke of Kang) make them Nietzschean Ubermenschen who slew their own gods, echoing Nietzsche's 'God is dead'. The Kahless clone of 'Rightful Heir' ('perhaps the words are more important than the man') shows a messianism surviving deicide. He then reads Worf through Roland Barthes's 'Occidentalism' and one-way acculturation—Picard praising Worf's 'humanity' after 'Reunion'—while Azetbur's 'human rights' is racist jab in The Undiscovered Country and Trekkers' Klingon cosplay raise cultural relativism and appropriation.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 41 "Notes" — Argues that despite Roddenberry's strident atheism, Star Trek develops a "humanist theology": godlike beings - Gary Mitchell, Charlie X, Trelane, Q, and Apollo in "Who Mourns for Adonais?" - are demoted to powerful aliens whose demand for worship disqualifies them as gods, echoing the 1960s death-of-God theology in which god-figures are consistently disappointing and the God of traditional theism is symbolically dead. Divinity is relocated into a possible human future requiring compassion above power - Kirk's charge to the dying Mitchell that "a god needs compassion", and Picard's "perhaps there's a residue of humanity in Q after all". The chapter also weighs Trek's anti-posthuman bias ("Dr. Korby was never here", the Borg) against the consensual Decker-V'Ger union in The Motion Picture, and reads Star Trek V's "What does God need with a starship?" as the uneasy remainder of Shatner's religiosity inside Roddenberry's secular vision.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 9 "1. Where Have All the Supermen Gone" — Holdier tests each hero against Nietzsche: Superman looks like the Übermensch but his mild-mannered Clark Kent pose is slave morality that would turn Nietzsche's stomach, while Batman's will-forged heroism (his Year One vow, 'what does not kill me makes me stronger') seems more overman-like until his self-loathing in Hush ('deep down, I'm not [a good person]') disqualifies him too. Neither qualifies; instead Superman embodies the Apollonian sun-god force of The Birth of Tragedy and Batman the Dionysian, so their Dark Knight Returns clash is the inevitable but never-final friction of art's twin poles — and the readers are the ones who win the fight.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 16 "6. The God We Need Now" — Ketcham frames a fictional 1939 memoir asking which god a god-forsaken age gets: Depression-era America needed Superman as a messiah (Siegel and Shuster as gospel-writers, DC's clerics redrawing him all-good like the church editing the New Testament), but a jaded modern America, he argues, now worships the dark billionaire as a Hades figure — Wayne Manor's hidden underworld with Alfred as Cerberus, the rich sacrificed to like Greeks propitiating Zeus. Superman is dismissed as unattainable alien fiction while Bruce Wayne is the self-made god of the American dream, with the essay ending on the prospect of a cybergod for his grandchildren.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 33 "21. Batman Is Superman" — Argues that Christian Bale's Batman, not the alien Superman, embodies Nietzsche's Übermensch: a mortal, flawed, lonely hero whose identity is forged in the unreconciled struggle between Dionysian vengeance and Apollonian reason across Nolan's trilogy. Batman Begins enacts eternal recurrence as Bruce repeatedly relives and integrates the well, the opera, and his parents' murder; The Dark Knight's Joker is Batman's Janus-faced shadow whose ferry experiment nearly proves the herd's 'gravity of madness,' and Dent's fall shows what Batman resists becoming. Superman II's temporarily mortal Superman is beaten by a truck driver and retreats to invincibility, proving the immortal alien can never overreach mortal limits as the Übermensch must.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 6 "H O N O R" — This file gathers three Part One essays. Jacob Held reads Rorschach's 'evil must be punished' credo (drowning Big Figure, executing the multiple rapist) as Kantian retributivism: wrongdoers are punished because they deserve it, out of respect for their dignity and honor, punishment restoring the moral order (with Hegel) — and Rorschach's flaw is lacking the humility and checks that keep just deserts from degenerating into the Black Freighter's vengeance. Tony Spanakos applies Max Weber's definition of the state as the monopoly of legitimate violence to argue the Keene Act rightly criminalizes vigilantes like Rorschach and Veidt, and that even state-sanctioned heroes (the Comedian gunning down his pregnant Vietnamese lover, Dr. Manhattan's amoral ending of Vietnam) show a badge cannot make superhero coercion legitimate. J. Keeping reconstructs Nietzsche's Übermensch — confronting the death of God and nihilism, creating values by 'giving style' to one's character via the camel-lion-child metamorphoses — and tests each Watchman against it, concluding only self-created Ozymandias comes close, though his mass murder is mere utilitarianism rather than genuine value creation.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 9 "The Human Comedy Perpetuates Itself Nihilism and Comedy in Coen Neo-Noir" — Hibbs argues that neo-noir turns classic noir's grim fatalism comic by making nihilism a working assumption, and that Nietzsche supplies the diagnosis: the 'death of God,' the passive 'last man,' and the aristocratic 'pathos of distance' of will-to-power super-antiheroes (Hannibal Lecter, the villains of Cape Fear/Basic Instinct). He reads The Big Lebowski as the Coens' comic leveling of nihilism, with Walter insisting the Germans are 'nihilists' and 'cowards' and the Dude 'abiding,' showing that full nihilism cannot be lived. In Fargo and Raising Arizona, Marge's 'banality of virtue' (a comic counterpoint to Arendt's banality of evil) and the resilience of familial/procreative instinct reassert a comic order over the noir trap.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 17 "“Takin’ ’er Easy for All Us Sinners” Laziness as a Virtue in The Big Lebowski" — Douglass and Walls read the Dude's 'principled laziness' as a coherent ethos and test it against the film's rival worldviews: the villains' hollow nihilism (which they distinguish from Nietzsche's will to power and death-of-God), Bunny's Aristippan hedonism versus Epicurus, the Big Lebowski's Nietzschean master-morality egoism, and Walter Sobchak's rules-worship read through Kant's categorical imperative and Locke's social contract. They argue dude-ism works as a personal path to contentment but, lacking any objective standard, cannot condemn true evil like Bunny's threatened murder, exposing its purposeless-universe premise as its real flaw.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 5 "Foreword" — Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 9 "Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir" — Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 12 "Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir" — Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 13 "From Sherlock Holmes to the Hard-Boiled Detective in Film Noir" — Jerold Abrams argues that the noir detective inherits the Holmes/Dupin detective logic but inhabits a fundamentally different maze. Using Eco's three labyrinths, he maps the classical Greek maze (with faith as Ariadne's string) and the mannerist maze (with Cartesian/Kantian pure reason) onto the escapable world of classic detection, and the Deleuzian rhizomatic maze, born after Nietzsche dissolved reason into will to power, onto noir's inescapable world (The Third Man, Kiss Me Deadly, The Maltese Falcon's fake statue). He shows both detectives use Peircean abduction (the logic of guessing) rather than pure deduction, illustrating it with knife-wound examples and Calloway's trapdoor inference in The Third Man, while the noir femme fatale becomes the anti-Ariadne whose thread of clues leads only to the hangman's rope.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 16 "The Horizon of Disenchantment Film Noir, Camus, and the Vicissitudes of Descent" — Alan Woolfolk reads noir through Weber's disenchanted world and Charles Taylor's cultural horizons, arguing the noir protagonist can neither resist the darkness like Conrad's Marlow nor fully embrace it like Coppola's Willard, remaining trapped between times in an ethically irrational universe. He contrasts Camus, who counters disenchantment with an ethic of honesty grounded in a Rousseauian benign nature (The Stranger's Meursault) and with the Baudelairean dandy as aesthetic model, against noir protagonists (Neff, Marlowe, the Swede, Scottie Ferguson) whose 'banked fires' fail and who lose self-possession. Drawing on Freud's id as 'a cauldron full of seething excitations,' he argues the femme fatale drags the protagonist downward into the timeless unconscious where anything is possible (Noah Cross's incest in Chinatown, the radioactive box in Kiss Me Deadly, Body Heat's Ned Racine), and reads noir as backward- and downward-looking through Palmer/Bakhtin's chronotope.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 17 "Symbolism, Meaning, and Nihilism in Quentin TaranTino's Pulp Fiction" — Conard reads Pulp Fiction as a study of American nihilism in Nietzsche's 'God is dead' sense: with no transcendent framework of value, Jules and Vincent orient their lives by transient pop-culture icons (Jack Rabbit Slim's, the Fonz) and by Marsellus Wallace's arbitrary power, so the mysterious briefcase has worth only because he wills it. He contrasts this void with Aristotelian ethics, where a thing's good lies in realizing its rational essence. Jules's transformation begins when he survives the misfired shots and reinterprets his Ezekiel 25:17 recitation as a call to be 'the Shepherd,' while Butch's choice of the samurai sword over the baseball bat signals a return to an objective warrior code beyond the empty pop icons.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 11 "Chaos, Order, and Morality Nietzsche’s Influence on Full Metal Jacket Mark T. Conard" — Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics: reality is ceaseless becoming with no fixed identities, so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who alone keeps his real name and uniqueness, embodies the folly of that project; his murder of Hartman and suicide unleash the chaos of the film's Vietnam half. Reading collapsed oppositions (combatant/civilian, male/female, sacred/profane) and Hartman's 'God has a hard-on for marines' line, Conard concludes that in a Nietzschean world after the death of God, absolutist morality fails and not all killings are alike—Joker's mercy killing of the sniper being humane where Pyle's is senseless.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 27 "Nietzsche’s Overman as Posthuman Star Child in 2001 A Space Odyssey Jerold J. Abrams" — Abrams reads 2001 as a cinematic staging of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, mapping the film's ape-to-human-to-Star-Child arc onto Zarathustra's evolutionary vision of the overman. He casts the discovery of the buried moon monolith as Kubrick's death of God (proving aliens, not God, seeded us) maintained by a Platonic noble lie, the astronauts as Nietzsche's higher men, and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus Poole's fall as the last man and the dying tightrope walker. He then argues the prophecy may come true not via aliens but through Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's posthuman 'mind children'.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Abrams argues Scorsese's key protagonists embody a Nietzschean 'cinema of madness' distinct from the merely destructive gangster: creative madmen who, like Nietzsche's Gay Science madman and Zarathustra, destroy old values and will new ones. He reads Cape Fear's Nietzsche-reading Cady, Taxi Driver's Travis (whose 'true force' is a will to power revaluing society), Last Temptation's Jesus (a mad revaluator of the law, glossed via Foucault's Madness and Civilization), the failed witness Frank Pierce in Bringing Out the Dead, and The Aviator's Howard Hughes as figures channeling divine madness. He ties them to Plato's Phaedrus/Ion and Nietzsche's death of God and overman, insisting the true madman stands outside the herd to remake reality.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 10 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Conard argues Full Metal Jacket dramatizes Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, rooted in Heraclitus: reality is ceaseless change with no fixed 'thing,' so Sergeant Hartman's attempt to erase the recruits' individuality (shaved heads, nicknames, identical drills) is a doomed imposition of order on chaos. Private Pyle, who keeps his real name and personality, embodies that impossibility and his murder-suicide unleashes the chaotic Vietnam half. Conard links the collapse of oppositions (combatant/civilian, sacred/profane) and Nietzsche's death of God and will to power to show that in a world in flux absolutist morality fails and 'not all killings are alike' - Joker's mercy-killing of the sniper is humane where Leonard's is senseless.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Palmer reads The Shining through Fredric Jameson's account of postmodernity as a 'perpetual present' that has lost its past and can only cannibalize it as pastiche and nostalgia film. He argues Kubrick's film enacts an 'anti-nostalgia' that invokes the nostalgic impulse—Jack Torrance's wish to escape an empty present into the Overlook's endless 1921 party—only to destroy him with it, refusing the genre's happy-ending wish-fulfillment. Drawing on Baudrillard's image of art 'adrift in a kind of weightlessness' merely 'playing with the pieces,' he casts Jack, endlessly typing 'All work and no play,' as the failed postmodern artist trapped between times, reduced to pointless Nietzschean ressentiment, with the film's Nietzschean death-of-God flux underlying its refusal of stable meaning.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Abrams argues that 2001 films the whole evolutionary arc of Nietzsche's Thus Spoke Zarathustra, from ape-men through humanity to the Star Child as the overman/posthuman. He maps the moon monolith's discovery onto the death of God (science debunking the creation myth, guarded by a Platonic 'noble lie' cover-up), the astronauts Bowman/Poole/Floyd onto the Enlightenment 'higher men,' and Bowman's decadent hotel-room decline plus his and Poole's fatal spacewalks onto the last man and the falling tightrope walker whom Zarathustra carries. He then extends the vision toward Kurzweil's Singularity and Moravec's 'mind children,' while criticizing Kubrick for replacing Nietzsche's godless self-overcoming with alien 'replacement gods' that thin out the death-of-God insight.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 19 "“Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch" — Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "I Thought It Was Just the Doctor that We Needed, but It’s Both of You" — Ruth Deller reads the Doctor as a savior/redeemer figure onto whom fans project ideals, invoking Feuerbach's claim that humanity projects its ideal self onto Christ, then pivots to Nietzsche. Rather than a flawless Messiah, the Doctor is a flawed being who must overcome himself, and his 'ordinary' companions (Donna, Harriet Jones, the Hostess in 'Midnight', Rose in 'Turn Left') exemplify Nietzsche's Ubermensch by rising above their weaknesses. She argues the Doctor and humans have a symbiotic relationship: the universe needs a savior, but that savior must be challenged, so both overcome themselves together.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 9 "1. Human, All Too Human" — Holdier reads Supernatural's finale through Nietzsche, arguing that Chuck's exposure as a cruel author-God and his defeat by the Winchesters dramatizes the 'death of God' as the freedom to invent one's own meaning. Dean and Sam's stubborn refusal to 'stay down' on the lakeshore against Chuck embodies amor fati—saying yes to circumstance—while Jack, birthed and taught by ordinary humans, becomes the Ubermensch who replaces God, showing humanity as a bridge to something greater than itself.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 19 "9. God the Programmer Is Dead" — De Vries defines a 'monster' in Supernatural as one who breaks the social contract, then argues Sam and Dean are deontologists loyal to a rigid duty—but a 'social contract of two' (family) that produces double standards toward Cas and Jack. She contrasts the angels' box-checking utilitarianism and Hobbesian collapse without God, Hell's contractual capitalist democracy, and Chuck as a controlling 'programmer God' whose perfection cannot tolerate imperfection; Jack's hands-off deity and Chuck's Nietzschean death-of-God let humanity write its own moral code.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 10 "Introduction" — Golomb and Wistrich frame the volume's guiding question—how Nietzsche came to be called the philosopher of the Third Reich—by walking through the 1934 photograph of Hitler before Nietzsche's bust, Elisabeth Förster-Nietzsche's and Alfred Bäumler's appropriations, and Mussolini's 'live dangerously' slogan. They argue the Nazi reading rests on a confusion of Nietzsche's spiritual Macht with brute Kraft, and stress his anti-nationalism, anti-anti-Semitism, and admiration for the Jews as future 'creators of values,' concluding he was a prophet of the nihilistic vacuum Nazism filled rather than its godfather.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 15 "3. Experiences with Nietzsche" — Müller-Lauter interweaves memoir—hearing 'Praised be what makes hard!' and 'What does not kill me makes me stronger' torn from context in Nazi Weimar—with a systematic account of Nietzsche's nihilism as the devaluation of the highest values following the death of God. He traces the move from 'incomplete' to 'perfect' nihilism and the revaluation of values through the free spirit and the legislating Dionysian philosopher, insisting (against Bäumler's and Lukács's systematizations of the unauthorized Will to Power) that Nietzsche's experimental, fragmentary thought resists both fascist and Marxist appropriation.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 17 "5. Nietzsche and the Jews" — Brinker surveys Duffy-Mittelman, Santaniello, and Yovel to argue that reading Nietzsche as simply pro-Jewish oversimplifies a genuine ambivalence toward the 'Jewish race' running through all periods of Jewish history. He shows that in The Antichrist Nietzsche separates ressentiment from decadence: Jesus is the 'most perfect decadent' incapable of hatred, while Paul and the priests embody ressentiment, and the Jews, being too strong to be decadent, cunningly poison their conquerors with a faith they do not share—an old anti-Semitic stereotype transplanted into new soil. Brinker concludes this ambivalence, plus Nietzsche's post-Zarathustra equation of equality, democracy, and socialism with slave-morality decadence, is exactly what let the Nazis manipulate him.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 18 "6. Nietzsche contra Wagner on the Jews" — Yovel reads Nietzsche's break with Wagner as a self-overcoming that freed him to hand Wagner's redemptive role—catalyst of a new Dionysian Europe—to the modern secular Jews Wagner despised. He maps a structured ambivalence: fierce anti-anti-Semitism (grounded philosophically in Nietzsche's rejection of nationalism, racism, the state-cult, and ressentiment) coexisting with a fierce critique of ancient 'priestly' Judaism as the genealogical root of Christian slave morality. Contrasting Nietzsche with Wagner's Judaism in Music, he shows Wagner legitimized public hate-speech (dramatized in Siegfried's gratuitous loathing of Mime) while Nietzsche prized self-mastery, so the two men's later Nazi abuse—by Elisabeth and Winifred, the two 'women-priests'—rests on opposite relations to what each actually held.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 19 "7. Between the Cross and the Swastika A Nietzschean Perspective" — Wistrich answers the charge that Nietzsche was a philosophical godfather of fascism by marshalling his biography and letters—the 'shoot all anti-Semites' twilight notes, the rupture with the anti-Semite Förster and with Wagner, the praise of Heine, Offenbach, and Spinoza. He distinguishes Nietzsche's demonization of Christianity and priestly Judaism as the 'slave revolt in morals' from his admiration for biblical and Diaspora Jews as Europe's toughest race and a possible catalyst of the Übermensch, arguing that the Nazi and Hitlerian echoes (via Table Talk and Rosenberg's forgeries) grossly distort a 'good European' who denounced nationalism, racism, and the state-cult, and would have been repelled by the swastika.
- **The Godfather and Philosophy - An Argument You Can't Refute**, ch. 27 "14. Critique as Apologetics Nolte’s Interpretation of Nietzsche" — Stackelberg critiques Ernst Nolte's essentialist reading, in which Nietzsche's Ecce Homo 'party of life' and its call for the 'ruthless destruction of all that is degenerate' furnish the counter-concept of extermination mirroring Marx, dignifying fascism as an anti-Bolshevik European civil war. He shows Nolte must explain away Nietzsche's denunciations of anti-Semitism, nationalism, the Reich and Wagner, and counters that Nazism was itself a moralistic 'slave revolt'—the ascetic, purity-seeking mentality Nietzsche attacked—so that Nietzsche's real susceptibility to Nazi use lies in his shared anti-egalitarian enemies and his refusal of concrete social analysis, not in an exterminatory program.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" — Peter Fosl reads Metallica lyrics through Nietzsche's and Marx's critiques of Christianity: 'Leper Messiah' and 'The God that Failed' cast religion as a slave morality born of ressentiment and as Marx's 'opium' that pacifies the exploited. He asks whether Metallica achieves Nietzsche's transvaluation of values or stays trapped in 'incomplete nihilism' - songs like 'One' and 'To Live is to Die' longing nostalgically for the God that failed - while 'Escape' and 'The Four Horsemen' point toward a life-affirming overcoming of Christianity.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 7 "“Gan Is Dead”" — Garret Merriam reads the ending of The Dark Tower—Roland scaling the Tower only to be flung back to the Mohaine Desert to repeat his quest—as a literal enactment of Nietzsche's eternal recurrence and its demon's test. Roland fails the test ('Please, not again!') because he treats his life as a teleological quest ('all things serve the beam') rather than embracing that 'ka is a wheel'; the Horn of Eld and Furth's hope of 'escaping the trap' miss the point. Merriam argues that once Roland accepts 'Gan is dead'—that meaning must be self-made, not bestowed from the Tower—he could achieve amor fati, and closes with Camus's Sisyphus: we must imagine Roland happy.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 27 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Hales uses Nietzsche's verdict that truth matters less than a myth's usefulness (The Gay Science, The Anti-Christ) to argue Santa Claus is a truer exemplar of Christmas than Jesus. He traces Nietzsche's account of God's degeneration from a proud tribal mascot like Yahweh into a trivialized 'domestic servant,' and the 'death of God' as belief becoming useless. Documenting Christmas's commercial, pagan origins (Sol Invictus, Saturnalia, Mithras on December 25), he casts Santa as a practical, this-worldly demigod propped up by movies and NORAD — a giver who, unlike the credit-demanding Christian God, wants no thanks, embodying anonymous selfless generosity and thus the god Nietzsche awaited.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Douglas Blount casts Sauron as a candidate for Nietzsche's Ubermensch, embodying the unabashed will to power in a world where God is dead, life is meaningless, and taste rather than reason or morality guides the self-created life. Tolkien answers this not by argument but by a rival portrait whose beauty lies in community, humility, love, and self-sacrifice: Gandalf dying on the bridge, Frodo's mercy to Gollum, and Sam refusing the Ring's vision of 'Samwise the Strong.' Blount argues that on Nietzsche's own criterion of taste, Tolkien's picture of abnegation is the more compelling vision of a life lived well.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 25 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Joe Kraus argues Tolkien wrote The Lord of the Rings as a protest against modernism, the mood that 'all that is solid melts into air' and that the past no longer matters, voiced by Marx, Freud, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead.' Tolkien's heroes survive because they remember lore and tradition (Gandalf watching the Shire, Sam's book-learning at Cirith Ungol), while Saruman and Denethor embody modern despair: they misuse the palantir, lose faith in tradition, and can only try to destroy the present. Against Berman's claim that there is no escape from modernism, Kraus reads Middle-earth as a fantasy where clinging to tradition still yields real, tangible power and certainty.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 31 "Metallica, Nihilism, and Nostalgia" — Fosl argues that Metallica's lyrics echo Nietzsche's and Marx's moral critiques of Christianity: songs like "Leper Messiah" and "The God that Failed" cast religion as slave-morality ressentiment, mind-control, and Marx's "opium of the people." He then asks whether the band achieves a Nietzschean transvaluation or lapses into the very nihilism Nietzsche said Christianity breeds — reading "To Live is to Die" and "One" as nostalgic death-wish, but "Escape" and "The Four Horsemen" as genuine defiant self-overcoming after the death of God.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 41 "38. The Big Lebowski Nihilism, Masculinity, and Abiding Virtue" — Fosl argues that The Big Lebowski critiques traditional masculine ideals (soldier, tycoon, detective, patriarch) and offers in The Dude an alternative 'abiding' virtue rooted in Epicurean contented poverty and ataraxia (his simple pleasures, White Russians, and indifference to property), Aristotelian civic friendship or philia with Walter and Donny that holds a divided polity together, and a Wittgenstein/Aristotle-informed flexibility about applying rules that positions The Dude at a mean between Walter's rigid absolutism and the nihilists' deficiency. Most centrally the film confronts Nietzschean European nihilism ('God is dead'); The Dude answers it as a halfway Ubermensch through comedy, friendship, and Kierkegaardian and Camusian existential repetition (bowling as rolling the rock, Sisyphus made meaningful), abiding and reproducing his form of life against despair, death, and disillusionment.

### Buddhism

Buddhism is a family of traditions arising from the teachings of Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, in ancient India, aimed at understanding and ending suffering. It diagnoses ordinary existence as marked by dissatisfaction rooted in craving and ignorance, and it offers a path of ethical conduct, mental discipline, and insight leading toward liberation, often described as nirvana. Rejecting reliance on a creator deity for salvation, Buddhism emphasizes practices such as meditation and the cultivation of wisdom and compassion, and it has developed into diverse schools across Asia and beyond.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 56 "Unknown" — Brannigan reads the film's mirror imagery through the Buddha's mirror instruction to his son Rahula: Neo touching the dripping mirror and becoming the mirror marks his awakening to the naked truth (aletheia as nakedness) that his world is a programmed illusion, Smith's dark sunglasses distort while Morpheus's mirrored glasses clarify, and Neo's reflection in the spoon-bending boy's spoon signals clarity. 'There is no spoon' parallels the Zen mondo where neither flag nor wind moves but only mind, and shows that reflected images are not reality - the world is maya. The deepest lesson is anatman: just as there is no spoon there is no Neo, no fixed self, and Rahula's lesson grounds the interdependence (pratityasamutpada) of all actions on others.
