- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 58 "Unknown" — Brannigan tests whether The Matrix is a Buddhist film and finds four incongruities: its Zoroastrian good-versus-evil dualism (the system and those in it as 'enemies') against karuna and metta, its glorified gun violence ('guns, lots of guns') against ahimsa, its crass language against right speech, and its human-centeredness against the Buddha-nature of all sentient beings, including 'sentient programs'. He concedes the slaughter might be read symbolically as slaying the mind's three poisons, as Manjusri's sword does, but rejects calling the result 'American Buddhism'. He concludes the film is a deliberate syncretism of Christianity, Platonism, and Buddhism that still conveys the Buddhist message of liberation from the mind.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 61 "Unknown" — The chapter argues the film is by no means a Christian movie: Neo is a violent, far-from-sinless mere human savior; the fundamental human problem is ignorance and illusion (Gnostic and Eastern) rather than sin and alienation from God; the rebels' belief that Neo is the reincarnation of the earlier liberator mirrors the Dalai Lama search the Wachowskis cite, though reincarnation is rejected by all major Christian sects; and 'there is no spoon' asserts the illusoriness of empirical reality that Christianity denies. The film's malleable, cyclical time and the Wachowskis' answer that faith is 'in oneself' complete a syncretistic tapestry the essay goes on to examine as religious pluralism.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki compare Tolkien with Zen Buddhism and Taoism on four themes while insisting on the real differences. Tolkien's talking trees (Old Man Willow, Treebeard's 'half awake' forest) invite comparison with Buddhist universal sentience and Dogen's walking mountains, but Tolkien anthropomorphizes where Buddhism grants non-human modes of sentience; the hobbits' ties to the Shire echo dependent origination, though Tolkien's stewardship and preference for the domesticated Shire over sinister wild nature remain Western. Frodo's succession of mentors (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, and the unlikely 'Master Samwise') parallels the Zen master-student relation, while Tolkien's war of light against darkness - nine Walkers against nine Riders - is decisively not the Taoist balance of yin and yang, for Taoists destroying either cosmic force would itself produce evil.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 28 "Ballparks, Dojos, and Other Places of Enlightenment" — Bassham argues that the core advice of hitting instructors like Ted Williams ('get a good ball to hit') and Charley Lau ('tension is the enemy') echoes Zen Buddhist principles, walking through patience, relaxation, self-knowledge, visualization (Reggie Jackson, Willie Stargell, Barry Bonds's on-deck imagery), practice, Bruce Lee-style kime concentration, and mushin or no-mind. Mickey Mantle going 0-for-30 after over-thinking Ted Williams's hitting tips, and Tony Gwynn's 'see the ball and react,' show how conscious analysis interferes with the muscle memory a half-second fastball demands. If kendo is practiced in a dojo — a 'place of enlightenment' — he concludes, ballparks and batting cages may be dojos too, with the caveat that Cobb, Ruth, and Mantle hardly model egoless humility.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 29 "What’s Wrong with Generalization" — Brannigan uses Japanese baseball to ask what is wrong with cultural generalization. He presents the Bushido case — samurai-style self-denial, absolute loyalty (Kawakami's Yomiuri Giants), Suisha Tobita's 'training of death,' resolve (konjo), team harmony (wa), and a relational self grounded in Buddhism's no-self and Confucian identity-through-relationships — then tests it against counter-evidence: Sadaharu Oh's flamingo swing owed as much to individual talent and Hiroshi Arakawa's unconventional kendo-and-aikido coaching as to sensei imitation, the 'new breed' (Ochiai, Egawa) flouts the old ways, and William Kelly's 'Whiting problem' warns against polarizing Japanese and American baseball. The chapter's 'three strikes' against the label 'Japanese baseball' conclude that generalizations become dangerous when treated as monolithic nets cast over an entire culture.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 8 "“A New Broom Sweeps Clean, but an Old Broom Knows Every Corner”" — Callis interweaves a memoir of the teenage boyfriend who played her Dark Side and later killed himself with an account of Easy Star Records' 2003 reggae remake, Dub Side of the Moon, arguing that the album's themes of time, money, materialism, and madness translate naturally into Rasta reasoning. Nyabinghi drumming, singjay toasting, and bong-bubble effects re-read 'Money' (the cash register replaced by a lighter firing the chalice) and 'Time' (Ranking Joe's 'Time is the master') through Rasta rejection of Babylon, anti-capitalist subsistence, and 'soon come' patience, which she glosses with the Buddhist principle that things happen in their own time. The reggae setting, she concludes, weaves all this pain and madness, from Barrett's collapse to her own ghosts, into something more optimistic than the original ever sounded.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 17 "There is No Dark Side of the Moon Really. Matter of Fact It’s All Dark" — Johnston reads The Dark Side of the Moon through Buber's I and Thou: modern life traps us in the I-It mode of experience, from 'Welcome to the Machine' to teachers who treat students as replaceable Its ('Hey, teacher, leave us kids alone!') and Horkheimer's instrumental reason that turns personnel into 'human resources,' while the album repeatedly calls us to the I-You encounter, from 'Echoes'' strangers whose glances meet ('I am you and what I see is me,' Waters's origin of empathy) to 'Breathe''s 'don't be afraid to care.' He links the opening heartbeat and the breath of 'Breathe' to Buber's eternal You, defends Buddhism against Buber's charge that enlightenment is worldless monologue (the Buddha becomes one with the world, a perfect reciprocity like the innate You of the womb), and accepts Nietzsche's point that the Enlightenment's abstract God is dead while insisting, with Buber, that encounter with the eternal You remains possible. The album itself, he concludes, resists degenerating into an It: even if 'the sun is eclipsed by the moon,' the light persists and Dark Side can be the antidote to the It-world.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 24 "Alchemic Heroism" — Reads Edward and Alphonse Elric as a single composite 'alchemic hero' who fuses Japanese heroic archetypes: the dual-hero rooted in the Izanami-Izanagi creation myth and yin-yang complementarity (brash yang Ed, calm yin Al whose armored body actually fights better), the student hero forged by Izumi Curtis's brutal island training, and the wandering redemption seeker atoning for the forbidden attempt to resurrect their mother. It argues that the sacrifice built into this fusion — Al's lost senses, puberty, and body — mirrors Japan's own cultural alchemy of absorbing Buddhism, Confucianism, and yin-yang thought while retaining a coherent national identity.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 5 "Fighting Talk" — The editors' introduction argues that philosophy and fighting have been companions since Socrates the soldier and Plato the wrestler (whose name means 'broad shouldered' from the gym), and that each can illuminate the other. It tours the volume through concrete cases: budo courtesy drawn from Shinto, Confucianism and Zen; the Shaolin monks' exercises as a route to Buddhahood; Western chivalry and Gordon Marino's boxing as educations in Aristotelian courage; fencing's egoism and value; and the Stoicism of karate and utilitarianism of Kano's judo. Philosophy clarifies fighting traditions, while fights supply puzzles for ethics, aesthetics, and the philosophy of mind.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 22 "What Monkey Should Have Known" — Mortensen opens with Monkey from Journey to the West beating six robbers to death despite Tripitaka's protest, and asks whether a practitioner of budo can be a Buddhist. He defends three principles, Take No Life, No First Strike and Stop Before Harm, qualifying them via the Upaya-kausalya Sutra's sea captain, Funakoshi's 'there is no first strike in karate', Ueshiba's purely defensive aikido, the initiator's bad karma, and the exception of multiple attackers; then he applies them to weapons, arguing that wooden weapons (the jo, Musashi's bokken, above all the humble walking stick, the 'last legal weapon') fit the precepts where the katana does not. Monkey, in short, should have carried a stick.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 17 "All for Love" — Jerry Piven argues Dexter's void is not genetic sociopathy but trauma: witnessing his mother's chainsaw murder and lying in her blood deadened his feelings, and each ritualized kill restages that catastrophe with the roles reversed, Dexter mastering death as the angel of it, reducing the murderer to a drop of blood he imprisons on a slide. Reading Harry's ghost as a Hamlet-father super-ego, he contends Dexter kills not only to master trauma but to please the father who channels his rage - murder 'for love' - and then generalizes: Arendt's banality of evil, Pascal on the void and faith, Kierkegaard and Heidegger on fleeing despair into conformity, Buddhist emptiness, and Becker-style terror-management findings explain how ordinary people, frightened of death and hungry for a leader's approval, can be manipulated into sanctioned slaughter, from Abu Ghraib to jihadism.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 18 "Halo as a Catalyst for a Buddhism Videogame" — Luke Cuddy uses Halo 3 checkpoints and emulator save states—two mutually exclusive Flood-fight outcomes both in some sense true—to make David Lewis's possible worlds and modal truth concrete, with Leibniz as the doctrine's ancestor. Halo's infinite lives make players genuinely angry, and the chapter argues this is upaya territory: like the father in the Lotus Sutra's parable of the burning house, the game promises mastery (the goat-, deer-, and ox-carts) to lure players toward something greater outside it. Master Chief becomes a Bodhisattva whose avatar slides between extension of self and other, provoking the 'who am I?' crisis that reveals the ego as empty at the ultimate level of the Two-Fold Truth, while the Dalai Lama's enemies-as-teachers turns the seven-year-old who pwns you into practice in the first two Noble Truths' suffering and anger.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 37 "The Awakened One" — Callis reads Holmes as a Buddhist practitioner despite the cocaine and the cigars in the coalscuttle: 'You see, but you do not observe' and 'The emotional qualities are antagonistic to clear reasoning' match Vipassana bare attention and the Theravada ideal of the cool, rational, emotionally distant sage, and his improvised violin scraping works like Thich Nhat Hanh's walking meditation — a witness without commentary. The picture is completed by Doyle's Buddhism of Ceylon in The Sign of Four, Holmes's two years 'spending some days with the head lama' in Tibet ('The Empty House'), and his sitting 'like some strange Buddha' in 'The Veiled Lodger.' She maps his method onto the Yoga Sutras' dharana, dhyana, and samadhi — patient attention to the blood-scratched plaster, sustained fixation on the crime scene, ego-surrendering contemplation — making Holmes an 'awakened one' who loves truth for its own sake while Watson lives on autopilot.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper reads Inception as epistemology rather than metaphysics - not what is real but how we could know - running from Plato's Theaetetus (the first dream-recognition question) through Descartes's deceptive demon and Freud's royal road to the unconscious, to Wittgenstein's point that 'I may be dreaming' is senseless because the remark itself would be dreamed, and Heraclitus's line that only the waking share a common world. The Ariadne thread is the clue: as in the Theseus myth, dream architecture gives the labyrinth a shareable narrative place, but only a hint, never a way to wake. He then goes east - Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflecting jewels, Schopenhauer's universe dreamed by a single dreamer, William James's many consciousnesses - to ask how many times we must die before waking, ending with Buddhism: 'Buddha means awakened one', and Cobb's turning from the top enacts Nirvana, where the real-versus-dream question stops pertaining.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 27 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Liane Heller pairs Cohen and Schopenhauer - born and died on September 21st, the autumnal equinox - as two explorers of the world's irrational negativity who both retreat to 'a room' to create. Schopenhauer's directionless Will, his pessimism about a life of constant suffering, his notorious misogyny in 'On Women,' and his ascetic denial of the will-to-live (with his contempt for Judaism and preference for the Upanishads and Buddhist compassion) are set against Cohen's affirmation that love is 'the only engine of survival,' his five-year Zen retreat that could not hold him, and his return to the Judaism of the 'little Jew who wrote the Bible.' A closing imagined dialogue has a humbled Schopenhauer confronted with Cohen's self-compassion and ordinary joys, admitting the limits of his own field of vision.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 11 "3. Tris Finds Enlightenment" — Rhine argues that Tris's heroism rests on Buddhist practice: her breath-counting on the Ferris wheel and inside Four's fear landscape, her emotional intelligence, and her awareness of the parental 'voices in her head' are classic meditative disciplines for calming the ego whose clinging, on the Buddhist account, is the cause of suffering (dukkha). She reads Abnegation's gray houses, plain food, and four-times-a-year mirror as ritual ego-diminishment - a middle way between indulgence and the extreme asceticism the Buddha rejected - that explains why most Divergent arise from Abnegation. Contemporary neuroscience is then recruited: the amygdala-versus-prefrontal-cortex struggle Will describes, and monks' heightened gamma waves, explain how Tris can see the simulation as a simulation, like Neo in The Matrix, and act while others are paralyzed by fear.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 15 "6. Bowie the Buddhist" — Muchall reads 'Quicksand' and 'Where Are We Now?' as suffused with Tibetan Buddhism: 'Don't believe in yourself' voices the anatta teaching Bowie absorbed studying with Chime Rinpoche and from Chogyam Trungpa, whose 'spiritual materialism' warns that ego converts even spirituality and ideologies to its own use. After retelling the Buddha's life, the Four Noble Truths' three kinds of dukkha, and the five aggregates that reveal no permanent self, the chapter maps the song's 'ragged hole' and bardos onto the Tibetan Book of the Dead's after-death journey, and reads Bowie's morphing personas as lived acknowledgment that there is no fixed self - 'there's nothing in here.'
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 25 "13. The Origins of Self-Love" — Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 7 "Preface" — Aaron Ehasz, ATLA's head writer, reflects that the show tested its characters' belief systems against their humanity: Aang's attempt to comfort himself with Buddhist detachment fails when Appa is taken, and he cannot let go of his love for Katara to unblock his final chakra and enter the Avatar State. Yet Uncle Iroh shows the opposite lesson, since by studying Water Tribe ideas he invents lightning redirection, the technique that lets Zuko survive his father and lets Team Avatar save the world. The preface concludes that philosophy both limits and unlocks human potential, capped with a joke about Hegel and hard ice cream.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — De Cruz and De Smedt argue that ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang's training is slow and non-linear, he needs dedicated teachers, and saving the world is a team effort in which Katara leads and Sokka plans. The show's central theme is oneness, voiced by Guru Pathik's 'illusion of separation' ('The Guru') and Huu's banyan-grove tree ('The Swamp'), which the editors trace to Daoist, Huayan Buddhist (Fazang's golden lion), and Indigenous traditions of interdependence. They frame the volume's engagement with genocide, imperialism, ecological destruction, and Ba Sing Se's authoritarian denial as proof that philosophy is needed for human flourishing.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 12 "The Wisdom of Combination" — Isrow maps each bending art to its real martial art and source philosophy: Katara's Taiji waterbending embodies Daoist wu-wei when she forgoes revenge on Yon Rha ('The Southern Raiders'); Toph's Hong Jia earthbending expresses the Buddhist eightfold path's Right Speech through her insistence on truth; Zuko's Northern Shaolin firebending enacts the Four Noble Truths, his desire-driven suffering ending only when he abandons chasing the Avatar; and Aang's Daoist Baguazhang airbending makes freedom openness to change, shown in his receptivity to Iroh's advice. The Avatar's true power is combining these character strengths, not merely wielding four elements.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 28 "What Can We Learn" — Argues ATLA repeatedly dissolves false alternatives rather than solving conflicts, modeling the Buddha's middle way from the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta: refuse the two extremes instead of picking one. Earth is the case study — Bumi is both crazy and wise, Toph both blind and the most powerful bender, and 'The Cave of Two Lovers' shows the first earthbenders using their art for love, with Oma ending the feud by declaring the war over rather than destroying both villages. Aang's energybending against Ozai dissolves the kill-or-be-killed framework, Bumi's 'neutral jing' rejects fight-or-flight, and Toph's life refutes the capable-vs-helpless and girl-vs-fighter dichotomies her parents impose.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Rebuts Ozai's taunt 'you are still weak' with a Buddhist reading of energybending: Aang wins not by domination but because his unbendable spirit is total vulnerability, a true heart that has abandoned the five hindrances (sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, doubt — each traced through the chakras, the Serpent's Pass, and 'Nightmares and Daydreams') and a true mind freed from the fundamental delusion of a separate self that 'The Swamp' and 'The Guru' dissolve. The spirit-merging with Ozai is read through Indra's net, and Aang's merciful halt mirrors Indra's Jataka victory where compassion for eagle hatchlings — not force — defeats the demons. Fearlessness, on Sylvia Boorstein's Zen story, is the natural corollary of compassion, so Aang's weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely his power.
- **Avatar and Philosophy - Learning to See**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's journey alongside the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's Interconnected: both bear exalted titles that isolate them from friendship (Aang forbidden to play with peers and taken from Gyatso; Dorje taken from his family at seven), and both learn that heroism is relational — the series replaces the rugged-individual hero's quest with a communal model in which Katara, Sokka, Toph, Pakku, Jeong Jeong, and Zuko co-author Aang's moral training. Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra over his attachment to Katara illustrates the Karmapa's warning that local attachment can block universal compassion, and Zuko's path from betrayal to forgiveness shows enemies as people enslaved to their own disturbing emotions. Aang ends as the Karmapa's 'interdependent individual', victorious only alongside the White Lotus and his friends.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 7 "Preface" — Head writer Aaron Ehasz asks what philosophy is for in ATLA and answers with the writers' unconscious conclusion: characters' belief systems are always tested against their humanity, and Aang's Buddhist detachment fails him twice, once when he loses Appa and once when opening the final chakra demands he let go of Katara. The counterexample is Iroh, whose study of Water Tribe techniques lets a firebender invent lightning redirection, the skill that lets Zuko survive his father and lets the saga resolve. So philosophy is not crushed by human need but is the key that unlocks humanity's potential, provided we stay open to ideas from other cultures.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — The editors argue ATLA subverts the Chosen One trope: Aang learns slowly and non-linearly, needs a teacher for each element, stays weaker than Katara or Toph in specific skills, and saving the world is a team effort in which he is neither leader nor brains. They identify the show's unifying theme as oneness, the 'illusion of separation' voiced by Guru Pathik and the swampbender Huu, and trace it to East and South Asian schools such as Huayan and Chan Buddhism and to Indigenous traditions. Philosophy is presented as the tool the show itself uses against genocide, imperialism, and ecological destruction, with Ba Sing Se's 'no war' denial as the cautionary case.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 34 "Sometimes We Can Let Go" — Sets the intuition that angry blame is how we hold people responsible (Strawson; Katara's useful fury at Pakku's sexism, Iroh's 'whatever you do to that spirit, I will unleash on you tenfold') against the Senecan and Buddhist verdict that anger is greedy for revenge, and reads ATLA as modeling ways to hold people responsible without toxic anger. In 'The Southern Raiders' Katara neither forgives Yon Rha nor kills him, showing that blame can be set down when expressing it is pointless, while she forgives Zuko in Lucy Allais's 'wiping the slate clean' sense because his past betrayal no longer speaks to his present character. Iroh's handling of the mugger in Ba Sing Se ('I was never angry; I was afraid that you had lost your way') models responding to the suffering behind wrongdoing with compassion instead of blame, and Zuko's self-anger is diagnosed as hypocritical self-blame whose antidote is self-compassion: acknowledging how he himself was hurt is what finally lets him take ownership of his wrongs.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 38 "Fearlessness and Power" — Argues that Aang's energybending victory over Ozai vindicates a Buddhist conception of power against Ozai's equation of power with domination: the Lion Turtle's 'unbendable spirit' is not resistance but thorough vulnerability, achieved through the true heart (overcoming the five hindrances mapped onto Aang's sensory desire, ill will, dullness, restlessness, and doubt across the series) and the true mind (overcoming the fundamental delusion of a self separate from others, learned from Huu in 'The Swamp' and Guru Pathik). The merging of Aang's and Ozai's spirits is pictured by the metaphor of Indra's net, and Indra's own Jataka victory, halting his assault to protect eagle hatchlings and disorienting the demons, parallels Aang's refusal to win by killing. Drawing on a Zen story of the abbot who could 'be run through by a sword without batting an eye', the chapter concludes that Aang's fearlessness flows from compassion, so that weakness by Ozai's standard is precisely the power that defeats him.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 39 "Overcoming Dilemmas" — Frames Aang's conflict between his Avataric duty to restore balance even by killing Ozai and his Air Nomad duty of ahimsa as a genuine dilemma only if both obligations are non-negotiable (Tessman's negotiable and non-negotiable duties), then argues the show resolves it because Sublime Ahimsic Practice, the Four Sublime States joined to non-harm, reshapes the very conditions the dilemma rests on. Aang's cultivation of loving-kindness and his grasp of dependent origination (Huu's banyan-grove insight that everything is interconnected) keep him open to the world, which is what leads him to the Lion Turtle; energybending then lets him stop Ozai without killing, dissolving the kill-or-be-killed framework rather than choosing a horn. The Avataric role itself is read as Daoist yin-yang balance-keeping, and the chapter links Aang's triumph to the lessons of Gandhi, Martin Luther King Jr., and nonviolent movements: becoming different people changes which options the world affords.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 40 "Journey’s End and a Vision of a New Community" — Reads Aang's quest through the Karmapa Ogyen Trinley Dorje's book Interconnected: like the seventeenth Karmapa, identified at age seven and taken from his family, Aang learns that an exalted title complicates friendship and that freedom is self-control rather than the rugged individualism of the American hero's quest. Training episodes (Katara's jealous competition in 'The Waterbending Scroll', Jeong Jeong's warnings, the Toph-versus-Katara sifu debate in 'Bitter Work') show moral training as communal, widening from Team Avatar as adoptive family toward universal compassion, with Aang's refusal to open the seventh chakra illustrating how local attachment can obstruct universal love. Zuko's counter-arc from competition, isolation, and betrayal to humility, forgiveness, and contentment shows compassion turning an enemy into a friend, and the finale's simultaneous battles (White Lotus liberating Ba Sing Se, Sokka and Toph destroying the fleet) affirm that Aang wins as an 'interdependent individual', never alone.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 15 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Lynch tests the fan claims that the Dude is 'the Duddha' or a practicing Daoist: the Dude has wu wei in his effortless arts of bowling and abiding and shares Zhuangzi's withdrawal from society (the Nixon bowling poster, learning from drunks, Donny's ashes scattered with naturalistic acceptance), but lacks Daoist metaphysics, the Dao's inexpressibility, and any articulated views. The Buddha parallels are real — nonattachment, practice over theory (the poisoned-arrow parable), compassion for Bunny — yet Gautama's radical discipline and middle path are the opposite of the Dude's laziness, so Dudeism emerges as an undisciplined American cousin, and the Dude follows 'just his way and his alone'.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 12 "a4.xhtml" — Bronson argues that walking is a philosophical practice against modern placelessness (Giddens' 'phantasmagoric' locality): Thorin survived Smaug's attack because as a youth he 'was a good adventurous lad, always on the move', and Tolkien's wise figures - slow, flower-stopping Tolkien himself, Gandalf who 'went to look ahead' and was brought back 'by looking behind', Bilbo's silent walking, Beorn's bear-travels - all practice attentive movement through place. He backs this with Montaigne's retirement to his tower and bringing thoughts back to the orchard, Thoreau's woods-walking that must be spiritual as well as physical, the Tao Te Ching's 'good travelers leave no tracks' and Zhuangzi's wandering virtues, and Buddhist walking meditation from the Buddha's wandering monks to Thich Nhat Hanh's peace steps.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 17 "Do We Give Shakespeare the Last Word" — Kapper treats Inception as a hip epistemological puzzle — unlike The Matrix, the question is not what is real but how we could know — and follows Ariadne's thread (her mythological clue-giving names the chapter) through the tradition: Plato's Theaetetus and Descartes's supremely cunning deceiver pose 'Am I dreaming now?', Wittgenstein shows the doubt is senseless since 'if I am dreaming, this remark is being dreamed as well', Freud makes dreams the royal road to the unconscious, and Heraclitus says only the waking share a common cosmos. The payoff is Eastern: Zhuangzi's butterfly, Indra's net of mutually reflected jewels, and Schopenhauer's single-dreamer universe turn waking up into an endless regress, so the Buddhist ideal of the awakened one — nirvana, where the ideas of real and dream cease to pertain — becomes the reading of Cobb turning away from the top.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Kahn argues LEGO play embodies the Buddhist teaching of impermanence that the Buddha states in the Digha Nikaya ('Impermanent are all component things...'): his childhood urge to superglue creations and Finn's father's Kragle dramatize the clinging that produces anxiety when things change, from brick formulations to discontinued sets and even funerals' wilting flowers. The LEGO Star Wars Death Star illustrates non-self — no Death Star exists apart from its 3,803 pieces, and no self apart from shifting aggregates — and the five aggregates (form, sensation, perception, formations, consciousness) are unpacked through building experiences like discovering a daughter has opened the mint Taj Mahal set. Tibetan sand mandalas, painstakingly built then ritually dissolved, model the ceremonial demolition of LEGO creations, teaching acceptance of change without sliding into a nihilistic 'why bother building at all'.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 7 "Buddha ex Machina" — Siobhan Lyons applies Mori's 'uncanny valley' to the hosts' physical and personality evolution (Ford's jerky old model versus seamless newer hosts, Maeve and Clementine), noting empathy grows as they near sentience. She argues via Aristotle's account of virtue, vice, and brutality that the guests and technicians (Logan's casual cruelty, the Man in Black's beastly sadism) fall short of human excellence while the suffering, consciousness-seeking hosts transcend it, treating humanity as a way of behaving rather than being, and casting the hosts as Derridean undecidables. Invoking Nietzsche on suffering as the cultivator of greatness and Mori's 'Buddha in the robot,' she claims the hosts earn a humanity the biological humans merely inherit.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 10 "Beat U-topos or Taking Utopia on the Road The Case of Jack Kerouac" — Adamo argues Kerouac's 'On the Road' is a new kind of utopian text: because classical collective utopias (Plato's Republic through More) were judged by Berlin, Popper, and Arendt to slide into totalitarianism and to conflict with political liberalism's individualism, Kerouac relocates utopia from place to the individual life lived 'on the road' (u-topos = no-place). He reads Sal Paradise's disillusion with Dean Moriarty—who uses people up—versus his admiration for Mississippi Gene and the hobos as dramatizing J. S. Mill's harm principle, fused with the Buddhist vow to harm no living thing, radicalizing personal liberty as perpetual movement without injury to others.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 15 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — James Whitehill treats sailing his Cape Cod catboat, named Garuda, as a Zen practice modeled on Zen archery (kyudo) and tea ceremony. He organizes it into 'outer work' (technique and ritualized performance) and 'inner work' (cultivating ki energy through breathing and belly-awareness, then 'self-forgetting'), quoting Dogen's dictum that studying the self is forgetting the self, and forgetting the self is being authenticated by all things. The goal is a boat-and-sailor unity in which the sailor 'sails without sailing' — reaching, through mundane repetitive discipline rather than a sought-after peak experience, a nirvana-like state where wind, wave, and self merge.
- **Climbing – Philosophy for Everyone - Because It's There**, ch. 21 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Eric Swan argues that climbing embodies the principles and spirit of Zen, the experience of 'ordinary mind' finding the extraordinary in the ordinary and living fully in the present. Tracing Zen from the Buddha's Flower Sermon and Bodhidharma through Suzuki's 'Beginner's Mind' and Huineng's finger-and-moon, he maps Zen's four training paths—physical work, zazen (sitting meditation), koans, and interviews with masters—onto climbing: routes are like koans solved by insight and action rather than logic, 'being in the zone' is meditative absorption, and breath-regulation at the crux is zazen in motion. He holds up free soloist Derek Hersey, grinning hundreds of feet up Eldorado Canyon, and Chris Sharma, who writes of flowing 'like water' on the rock, as modern Zen masters who dissolve the separation between self, climb, and world.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 29 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Jennifer McMahon and Steve Csaki test Buddhist and Taoist parallels in the novel and find many only apparent. Tolkien's talking trees and ents anthropomorphize nature and grant it human-like consciousness, whereas Buddhism attributes sentience to all beings without projecting human consciousness, and Tolkien privileges domesticated over wild nature and stewardship over membership in nature. His master-student chain (Bilbo, Gandalf, Aragorn, 'Master Samwise') genuinely echoes the Zen necessity of the right master, as in Dogen's mushroom-cook mentor; but his good-versus-evil war, with light privileged over a personified dark power to be defeated, contradicts Taoism's yin-yang balance in which evil is imbalance, not a force to destroy.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 45 "42. Up in the Air as Philosophy Buddhism and the Middle Path" — Duffy reads Ryan Bingham's arc in Up in the Air as a Zen Buddhist parable paralleling Hesse's Siddhartha. Ryan preaches an 'empty backpack' philosophy of nonattachment and treats the miles as their own point, but Duffy argues he only intellectually grasps the four noble truths — dukkha, its cause in attachment (tṛṣṇā), and the eightfold path — until his failed attachment to Alex and his mentorship of Natalie make him actually suffer. Like Siddhartha with his son, Ryan learns wisdom must be experienced, that the anattā (non-self) doctrine undercuts the identity he built on his job, and that the goal is not escaping the world but living the Middle Path within it, present to suffering rather than spinning silver linings.

### Judgment of Taste and the Sublime

In his account of aesthetic experience, Immanuel Kant distinguished the judgment of taste—our claim that something is beautiful—from mere personal liking by arguing that it is disinterested, universal in its demand, and grounded in a free harmony between imagination and understanding. When we call an object beautiful, we speak as if the pleasure should be shared by everyone, even though the judgment rests on feeling rather than a concept. The sublime, by contrast, arises when we confront the vast or overwhelming in nature; our sensibility is overpowered, yet reason's capacity to conceive infinity reveals a dignity within us that exceeds any sensory magnitude. Kant developed these ideas in the Critique of Judgment, linking aesthetic feeling to the wider unity of his philosophical system.

- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 14 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Irwin defends the film's violence aesthetically: beauty (Michelangelo's Pietà) distracts from moral truth rather than serving it, and Aristotle's Poetics fits the film neither as tragedy (a flawless Christ cannot fall through hamartia, and a good man's fall from prosperity is 'repulsive', so no catharsis explains why we watch) nor as the Plato-banned spectacle that inflames the passions, since it leaves viewers numb rather than belligerent. Instead he applies Cynthia Freeland's four features of the cinematic sublime, drawn from Burke and Kant: the flogging scenes, the grotesque Satan clutching his deformed child, Judas harried by demon-children to suicide, and even the Aramaic and Latin subtitles produce the pain-pleasure conflict, overwhelming vastness, and jolt from feeling to moral reflection that make the experience sublime. The violence is thus justified as Gibson's deliberate delivery of the sublime, provided viewers leave fear at the gates.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 25 "Last Thoughts" — Theodore Gracyk asks what makes Dylan an artist rather than a "song and dance man," testing three theories of art. Expression theory (Collingwood's standard, applied by Greil Marcus to Self Portrait and by Heylin to the two Blood on the Tracks versions) explains Dylan's rasp and "nasty" remakes but cannot separate genuine from conjured emotion in live performance. Formalism praises the verbal patterning Ricks and Gray admire but undervalues Dylan's improvisatory aesthetics of imperfection; Kant's theory of genius - free play of imagination constrained by taste, from "Slow Train"'s metaphor to "Knockin' on Heaven's Door" - is judged the most satisfying account of the career.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 21 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Bourne argues that bikes like the Ducati 916 and Harley V-Rod are genuine works of art: Kantian disinterested attention is both possible and actual (he bought his Ducati Monster on styling alone), and Hume's standard of taste shows that judgments like calling a Honda Gold Wing elegant are answerable to criteria and informed comparison, so taste is not mere subjectivity. Against Wollheim he deploys Currie's account of the artwork as a type of action, so mass-produced instances are no obstacle, exactly as copies of Sartre's Nausea are the same novel; against Danto's aboutness requirement he claims motorcycles are about motorcycles, and should be evaluated like architecture, where function enters the aesthetic judgment. On Bauhaus principles the Ducati 916 expresses its own construction authentically while the V-Rod's styling compromises its ground clearance, which is what makes the Ducati, at least, high art.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 19 "To Join in with the Game" — Gracyk argues Waters is wrong that Pink Floyd ended when he quit in 1985: Waters's case rests on an illicit use of the identity of indiscernibles, since if losing Waters's lyrics destroys the band's identity, then losing Barrett's or Wright's, or adding 'Lucifer Sam,' would too, which proves too much. Borrowing Locke's distinction between the same man and the same person (the oak that remains the same oak through change; the unrecognized Syd in Abbey Road's Studio Three) and Kant's contrast between free and dependent beauty to explain how intentions change aesthetic evaluation, he defends actual intentionalism over hypothetical intentionalism: Hendrix really sings 'kiss the sky,' and interviews with Waters genuinely aid interpretation of Wish You Were Here. He then argues for collective agency, that groups can have intentions through members charged to act responsibly on the group's behalf, so no single member can disband a collective: Waters had a duty to leave, Gilmour, Mason, and Wright were entitled to continue the group's longstanding intention of making and performing original music, and the Echoes compilation is therefore an accurate portrait of the real Pink Floyd.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "Paradise Found" — Brown reads The Minish Cap's Hyrule as a working utopia: its Royal Family, guards, and market traders loosely realize Plato's Republic classes from Book V onward, but with fluid social boundaries (Zelda wanders the festival unharassed), no slavery, and relaxed state control that Plato's static order lacked. The town matches Aristotle's polis design (walled, defensible, right-sized, river-powered yet self-sufficient), while the surrounding pastoral landscape embodies Kantian disinterested beauty in nature and the Schillerian idea that through beauty we arrive at freedom. Its vague, prophet-free Picori religion of benevolent Christs-in-miniature needs no Kierkegaardian leap of faith, so unlike Hitler's Germany or Stalin's Russia, Hyrule is utopia actually achieved, and explorable, through Link.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 8 "2. - Radiohead, or the Philosophy of Pop" — Greif asks how pop music could ever 'incarnate a particular historical situation' and answers with Radiohead's portrait of broadcast culture around 2000: an environing, objectless dread in which each person lives at a knot of shouted messages no one sent and complaining only marks you as a crank. The band's turn to electronica was not avant-garde innovation but the discovery of the sound of that second nature, with Yorke's sampled-and-broken voice alternately absorbed into the machine and reasserting the human, and the lyric 'we' sliding between a scared individual lying that he is not alone, a wished-for collectivity, and the ventriloquized tyrant (as with Brecht's Pirate Jenny). Radiohead's church-tinged sublimity observes the storm from inside it — an internalized, inhuman sublime rather than the tradition's safe vantage on crushing power. Pop, he concludes, neither mirrors us nor preaches: it lets us retain and reactivate knowledge social speech forbids, and its deepest effect is not revolution but defiance — the retention of a private voice, a politics of re-created privacy — epitomized by 'There There' warning 'just 'cause you feel it doesn't mean it's there' inside an art form devoted to making you feel.
- **Radiohead and Philosophy - Fitter Happier More Deductive**, ch. 10 "Are Musical Experiences Universal" — Slowik uses Radiohead's evolution — from the standard pop structures of Pablo Honey and The Bends to the layered, quasi-classical textures of Kid A and Amnesiac ('In Limbo''s independent melodic lines, the wordless climax of 'Pyramid Song') — to introduce the philosophy of music. He weighs what a musical work is, testing nominalism, idealism, and realism against 'Like Spinning Plates' and its live versions, then pits the emotion theory against formalism in explaining how songs like 'Like Spinning Plates' move us. The chapter closes on whether musical experience is universal and on Hume's 'Standard of Taste': if the test of time validates greatness, then the argument over whether OK Computer or In Rainbows is the better album might actually have an objectively right answer.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 8 "From Low to High Culture Where’s That Confounded Bridge" — John Stone-Mediatore argues that Led Zeppelin's music, especially in concert, is a quintessential experience of the sublime. He applies Burke's catalogue of sublime qualities (loudness, darkness, rudeness, the artificial infinite) to Bonham's cavernous drum sound on 'When the Levee Breaks', Page's rough overdriven tone and 'sloppy' technique, and the dissonant mandolin intro and nocturnal imagery of 'The Battle of Evermore'; Longinus's inspired, thunderbolt-like genius explains Plant's overnight writing of the 'Stairway to Heaven' lyrics at Headley Grange. Kant's account of imagination, understanding, and reason then shows why the impossible stairway to heaven, 'our shadows taller than our soul', and 'when all are one and one is all' frustrate concepts and delight us through reason's superiority. The chapter concludes that once rock attains the sublime, the high/low culture distinction is mere aesthetic snobbery.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 9 "Bring It On Home to You" — Jeanette Bicknell argues that the two classic models of creativity—Plato's Ion, where the rhapsode is a divinely possessed conduit, and Kant's solitary genius who issues new rules—cannot explain a four-piece rock band, since both are individualistic, purely mental, and end in mystery. Her positive account uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind (Page describes his guitar as 'an extension of you', instruments and notation as cognitive props) and Keith Sawyer's collaborative emergence: Zeppelin's creativity happened in rehearsal and performance, as with the stairwell-recorded drum groove of 'When the Levee Breaks' that framed every later musical decision. The transformation of Joan Baez's 'Babe, I'm Gonna Leave You' into a whisper-to-cry hard-rock template shows the band creating something no member could have produced or predicted alone.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 10 "Authentic Rock" — Theodore Gracyk asks whether Zeppelin's uncredited borrowings—Willie Dixon's 'You Need Love' into 'Whole Lotta Love', Spirit's 'Taurus' into 'Stairway to Heaven', Jake Holmes's 'I'm Confused' into 'Dazed and Confused'—undermine their status as an authentic rock band whose value supposedly rests on sincere self-expression and original songwriting. Using Hanslick's thought experiment as staged by Little Roger and the Goosebumps's 'Gilligan's Island (Stairway)' parody and Handel's recycling of his own music into the Messiah, he argues a song's expressive power comes from the interaction of words and music (guarding against the fallacies of division and composition), and that by itself music is neither angry nor spiritual. Since Zeppelin's instrumental arrangements diverge radically from their sources and the lawsuits turned on Plant's lyrics, the chapter concludes that transformation, not narrow originality, grounds their genius—so the rock-versus-pop authenticity standard must be loosened.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 24 "Is Led Zeppelin, after All, the Most Philosophical of Rock Bands" — Surber asks why we really listen to Zeppelin when the lyrics carry no philosophy. Kant's Critique of Judgment ranked music lowest among the arts — a 'mere play of sound sensations' at the zero point of philosophy — while Nietzsche reversed him by rooting philosophy in Dionysian rhythm; Deleuze's 'surface' philosophy (height, depth, surfaces; flows, intensities, blockages, repetition-with-difference) then resolves the question. Zeppelin enacts the bodily surface flow — 'Stairway''s gradual build, the flow-blockage-new-flow segues of the 25-minute 'Dazed and Confused' on How the West Was Won, Plant dropping lyrics to use his voice as an instrument — syncing us with lived experience, which makes them the most philosophical of rock bands precisely without saying anything philosophical.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 26 "Top Eleven Contributor Top Ten Lists" — Eleven contributor top-ten lists, several applying the book's philosophical tools in miniature: Stone-Mediatore ranks ten songs by how they exemplify Burke's, Kant's, and Longinus's theories of the sublime ('Stairway to Heaven' first), Flynn ranks ten by Nietzsche's Dionysian criterion of celebrating the natural forces that undo us ('When the Levee Breaks' first), and Dick pairs ten songs with Schopenhauer's misogynist essay 'On Women.' The remaining lists — resources, sideman appearances, cover versions, oral fixations, gigs attended — are fanzine fare without philosophical content.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 23 "The Loneliness of the Goalkeeper (Again)" — Winters celebrates the goalkeeper's fingertip save—Gordon Banks denying Pelé's header in 1970—as football's aesthetic summit, reading the keeper as the lonely, 'stark mad' outsider of existentialist fiction, a lineage he anchors in Camus, the goalkeeper of Algiers who said all he knew of morality he learnt from football. Kant supplies both the dove of the first Critique—needing the air's resistance, just as the tango's strict steps enable the dancer's personality—and the target of critique: against Kantian disinterested contemplation, he adopts Graham's Nietzschean, Dionysiac aesthetics of participation, so spectators proprioceptively feel the keeper twisting in mid-air, as Wittgenstein's question about the galloping horse picture suggests the movement enters our muscles and joints. Understanding a save or a back-heel means seeing it under a general type ('that' free kick, 'that' volley, from Beckham at Wembley back to Garrincha), and Bloch's ruminations in Handke's The Goalie's Anxiety at the Penalty Kick show the keeper alone at the liminal limit where concession and prevention meet.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 25 "VHS, DVD, YouTube" — Vargiu seats Kant in the Maracanã grandstand (after the Monty Python philosopher match) to test aesthetic disinterest against football: the judgment of taste is 'merely contemplative' and indifferent to the object's existence—explained through Gadamer's reading of the third Critique—so the gambler, the torcida chanting 'we won', the ultras, and the players themselves (whose attention and struggle preclude contemplation) all fail the test, and Kant stands alone except for the neutral spectator and the Panofsky-style purist. Kant's free versus accessory beauty explains why knowing the offside rule adds an intellectual liking to the aesthetic one (Denilson's inconclusive samba dribbles versus Garrincha's effective ones), and the second feature of taste, general validity—saying 'that Maradona goal is the most beautiful ever' claims everyone's agreement without objective rules—underwrites FIFA's Goal of the Century polls and connects the third Critique to public, communicative reason. Finally, the rewatched match on VHS, DVD, or YouTube, where the result is already known and no bets can be laid, is where fans most often approach genuine disinterested contemplation of the object's mere image.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 21 "A Better Way of Living Your Life" — Akers argues the Doctor follows neither rule deontology, utilitarian calculation, nor virtue ethics, but a relational ethics of care in Noddings's and Slote's sense, expressed as Buber's I-Thou stance — insisting an enslaved Ood is 'a "he," not an "it"' and addressing Donna, Jack, and Rose each as individuals in 'Journey's End'. Linking this to Nussbaum's claim that wonder widens moral concern and to Kant's dynamic and mathematical sublime, she argues the Doctor needs human companions like Rose, Martha, and Donna as a human-scale reference point that renews his wonder — and with it his ethics — while his wiping of Donna's memory shows the care tradition's dangers of power imbalance.
- **Doctor Who and Philosophy - Bigger on the Inside**, ch. 37 "A Beautiful Destiny" — Asks whether the Dalek casing can literally be beautiful, contrasting Kant's aesthetics (free beauty as the mind's fit with reality versus merely 'dependent' beauty of Davros-designed purpose) with Hegel's claim that beauty is thought embodied in matter, peaking in the human form, and Plato's view (via Nehamas's Phaedrus reading) that beauty begins the desire to care for a thing. Alexander of Hales's beauty-within-the-order and the Fourth Doctor's 'Genesis of the Daleks' echo, then Rosenkranz's aesthetic inferno where ugliness exists only as beauty's negation, show beauty and monstrosity need not be opposites. The conclusion is deliberately open: the puzzle forces us into metaphysics about mind and reality, not mere taste.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 27 "Humanism Needs Its Evangelists, Too" — Treats Snakes & Arrows ('Far Cry,' 'Armor and Sword,' 'Faithless') as secular humanism stung by resurgent fundamentalism, and reads Peart's revolutionary trilogy — 'Beneath, Between and Behind,' 'Bastille Day,' 'A Farewell to Kings' — as Enlightenment humanism already anxious about its own decline. The core argument is rhetorical: Rush deliberately clothes humanist content in sacred and mystical language ('Something for Nothing''s Lord's Prayer motif, 'Jacob's Ladder''s storm read through Spinoza's God-as-nature and the experience of the sublime) because humanism needs evangelists who inspire wonder rather than mere argument.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 13 "Genius" — Auxier traces the modern habit of calling individuals 'a genius' to Kant's Critique of Judgment, quoting the definition of genius as the innate talent through which nature gives the rule to art and noting Kant's view that geniuses cannot explain their own powers. He applies the concept to the Glimmer Twins, suggesting that the songs, shows, and videos are better called works of genius than either man taken alone. His amendment to Kant is that genius sometimes operates only when two people work together, which returns the discussion to what Mick and Keith achieve jointly.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 30 "What’s Puzzling You Is the Nature of My Game" — Goodman turns to Kant's Critique of Judgment to solve the problem of how rock'n'roll can be genuinely new yet intelligible: a work must be made according to rules that give it context — tuning-noise with a song's notes is not a song — yet a work following the rules too well, like the cover bands in Keith's 'shitty little suits', is no good. Kant's genius resolves this: nature gives the rule to art through the artist's inborn productive faculty, which is why artists say 'the thing just wrote itself' and cannot describe scientifically how their products come to be, unlike engineers or businessmen whose creativity is fully determined by an articulable plan. The section sets this machinery up to explain what could make a Stones song new.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 31 "The Beggars at the Banquet" — Goodman presses Kant's theory against the obvious objection: the Stones were decidedly unoriginal, 'beggars at the banquet table of music history' who stole songs, singing styles, lyrics, and licks. His solution is that they altered the aesthetic object itself by making their bodies — Mick's maniacal dancing, Keith's slouch, Bill's statuesque motionlessness — a constitutive part of the music, so that 'Brown Sugar' and 'Jumpin' Jack Flash' summon the band's persons in a way 'Strawberry Fields Forever' never summons Lennon. Because the Stones know sincerity is the real enemy of rock'n'roll, Mick cannot get satisfaction while singing that he can't get no satisfaction: the work now includes the singer, a philosophical necessity rather than a psychological claim.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 29 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Takes the show's title as a literal ethical command and asks which senses of enthusiasm should be curbed, tracing the concept's history: Plato's muse-inspired poet in the Ion and Apology, the early Christian Enthusiasts, Wesley and Shaftesbury's attempts to separate good from bad enthusiasm, and the Enlightenment ridicule of Locke and Hume, for whom enthusiasm meant fanaticism, a pretended insight into the supernatural that Larry is right to mock. Kant gets the most sustained treatment: enthusiasts of friendship, religion, or patriotism inflame a good principle beyond its proper degree, which explains Larry's failure as a friend, while 'aesthetic enthusiasm,' the sublime 'idea of good with affect' before the morally good, is valuable, and Larry's single moment of it comes when the Arizona preacher's sermon on moral goodness sends him flying back to Los Angeles to donate his kidney to Richard Lewis. The verdict: curb fanatic and inauthentic enthusiasm (Ted Danson's everything-is-heaven), keep ordinary resoluteness and aesthetic enthusiasm, and accept that a society needs a few Larrys, the Socratic fools who yell for society.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 26 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Pete Wolfendale and Tim Franklin argue that D&D founded a genuinely new art form because role-playing yields a distinctively Kantian aesthetic experience: not passive button-pushing like a kitten video, but the disinterested 'free play' of the cognitive faculties whose exercise is itself pleasurable. In a D&D session that free play just is the collaborative simulation of a world, where dice and DM rulings let consequences spiral beyond anyone's plan, as when a Polymorph Other turns a spider demon into a small purple platypus or a fumbled Bluff check lands the whole party in jail. They call this autonomous, unforefillable quality the 'depth' of a game world, and the pleasure of role-playing is feeling our own world-building power cope with a friction that mimics reality.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 33 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — William McGinney argues Jerry Goldsmith's modernist score, with its twelve-tone themes, ostinati, cuica, slide whistle, and ram's horn, carries no inherent meaning but acquires it through learned associations: its dissonance recalls Cold War modernist concert music promoted as the high art of Western freedom, while its Stravinsky-like rhythms and 'primitive' timbres mark the apes as other and feed the film's deconstruction of the human-ape, advanced-primitive, civilized-barbaric oppositions. Because Taylor is given no heroic music, the score undercuts identification with him as an anti-hero, and its modernist associations implicate the technocratic, militarized West he represents in Earth's self-destruction. The chapter's machinery is the semiotic view of Kant, Adorno, Cage, Peirce, and Saussure: music modifies a film's images the way adjectives modify nouns.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 18 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Edward Winters answers his sister's question - why listen to such depressing music - through Lorca's duende, the 'black sounds' of deep song that, as Nick Cave says, every true love song must contain. He argues duende resists definition yet is recognizable in Cohen, and connects it to Nietzsche's Dionysian art of participation (war dances, anthems, 'Dance Me to the End of Love') as against Kant's disinterested aesthetic distance, so music can re-enchant a disenchanted world. Via Kant's account of artistic genius and Cohen's testimony that Lorca and six flamenco chords gave him his voice, Winters concludes Cohen's dark, honest beauty has duende - which is why it lifts and tears at the heart rather than depressing.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 29 "16. Divine Hatred—Dalek Beauty" — Bowman uses 'Asylum of the Daleks' - where the Daleks preserve broken, insane Daleks as embodiments of 'divine hatred' - to test whether beauty is objective or subjective. Plato's Theory of Forms explains how hatred could be beautiful (the more a thing instantiates its Form, the more beautiful it is), while the Hume-Kant antinomy of beauty, Kant's disinterested judgment of taste (illustrated by Rory and Amy's invested judgments of each other versus the TARDIS's detached 'pretty'), and Nietzsche's account of beauty leading to divinity frame the Dalek hive mind's shared conceptual scheme. Since Kant says beauty is a symbol of morality, the Asylum-as-museum reveals Dalek values - which is why human-on-the-inside Clara is enshrined under maximum security, and why the Doctor is sickened to learn that he is himself an object of Dalek beauty.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 14 "5. Jimi, Janis, and Jim" — Traces 'genius' from the indwelling genie of an art to Goethe as the first person the public called a genius, then applies Kant's doctrine — the genius gives the rule to future art, produces what no determinate rule can govern, and cannot explain or teach what he does — to Jimi (having the Experience learn 'Sgt. Pepper' on one hearing to play it back to the Beatles three days after its release), Janis ('a victim of my own insides'), and Jim. Schopenhauer's dark side of genius — more mind than character, a will that 'affirms its own life by denying the life of others' — explains why the 27 Club burned out, and why we say 'Jimi lives' but 'Jim is still alive.'
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 25 "14. Hendrix from the Bottom Up" — A rhythm-section-first ('bottom up') listening of Electric Ladyland and the Fillmore East Band of Gypsys shows Hendrix re-grounding his music in blues, R&B, and jazz time: Steve Winwood's organ anchoring 'Voodoo Chile,' Buddy Miles's shuffle freeing the vocal-like guitar of 'Rainy Day, Dream Away,' and the communally stretched measure before 'Power to Love.' Kant supplies the vocabulary — the 'mercenary art' of studio craft versus art, and the Transcendental Aesthetic and the sublime — for the claim that the Gypsys' collectively felt rift in time approaches a rock'n'roll sublime that is 'felt as exceptionally and undeniably bad ass.'
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 17 "6. But What Does It Mean" — Argues that asking "what does it mean?" of Twin Peaks is the wrong question, because Lynch builds the show out of aesthetically incomplete material. Kant's "purposiveness without purpose" and the free play of understanding and imagination explain the opening credits' waterfalls, pines, and mill blades, while Russell's incomplete symbols ("the present king of France is bald") model the swaying traffic light and Harriet's "full blossom of the evening," and Quine's underdetermination of theory by evidence applies to Black Lodge clues like "the man in the smiling bag" and the Arm's whoops, which support many consistent but unprovable interpretations. Susanne Langer's account of film as a dream-like virtual present, capped by Part 8's atomic-bomb sequence, grounds the claim that Lynch means viewers to complete the meaning themselves.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 24 "12. It’s Not About BOB—It Never Was" — Argues that Lynch elevates madness over rationality as a route to truth: Socrates' Phaedrus account of god-sent madness ("the manic art") makes Cooper a dream-oracle in the lineage of Delphi and the Romantics' furor poeticus, with his melancholia a superior state of insight rather than illness. Cooper is read as Romantic hero and tragic hero alike — his ka, modeled on Stephen King's Gunslinger, drives him even into becoming BOB's host — while Kant's sublime recasts BOB, garmonbozia, and the atomic blast not as sublime objects themselves but as triggering the power behind them, a madness that reveals the truth that mysteries are not always meant to be solved. Rousseau's ethics of truth-seeking supplies the imperative to confront the darkness (the Dweller on the Threshold), even though not all truth makes us happy.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — The Forests ask whether Westworld is self-referential modernist art or 'meta-kitsch,' reading the park's dueling productions (Sizemore's clichéd narratives versus Ford's ambitions, with Cullen's corporate meddling mirroring HBO's pressure on Nolan and Joy) through Kant's relocation of aesthetic judgment to the subjective, Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch divide, Adorno's contrast of liberating autonomous art with standardized heteronomous commodity culture, and Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles. Guests mistaking Teddy for a fellow guest and actors' 'reverse-reveries' show that host/guest indiscernibility mirrors the show's own indiscernibility from formulaic prestige TV. Their conclusion: the series counts as art rather than entertainment only for 'autonomous viewers' alert to its self-referential critique, the viewer-side counterpart of Dolores's 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free.'
- **Tom Petty and Philosophy - We Need to Know**, ch. 23 "11. Forever the Wild One" — Anders grounds Petty's artistic freedom in Kant's Critique of Judgment: genius, the innate talent for original art freed from patron control, describes Petty's refusal to let commercial success measure his work. Singer's practical ethics supplies the frame for the $8.98 fight over Hard Promises, where Petty weighed outcomes for all affected, especially teenage fans, and threatened to withhold the masters or rename the album "Eight Ninety-Eight." Marx's worker-owner analysis maps the Shelter-to-MCA contract saga, in which Petty was sold like a piece of meat, countersued, hid the master tapes nightly, and filed for bankruptcy like a worker confronting the owners who pocket the value of the records he produced.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 13 "4. The Aesthetics of Being a Person" — S. Evan Kreider argues that aesthetic capacity evidences personhood in replicants: Kant's beautiful and the mathematically and dynamically sublime explain both K's cowed passage through Los Angeles and his storm-soaked defeat of Luv through strength of will and moral conviction. After Plato's and Aristotle's arousal and catharsis theories of art, he turns to Croce, Collingwood, and Suzanne Langer's expression theory and the 'virtual', reading Sapper's home-grown garlic, Joi's holographic dinner and rain scene, the Mariette-proxy sex as expressive symbol, and Stelline's memory-making ('we recall with our feelings') as aesthetic-emotional communication only persons can sustain. Even K's baseline judges personhood by the aesthetics of how he responds, not what he says.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 17 "7. The Sublime Sabotage of the Inner Saboteur" — Ryan reads Drag Race ontologically through Kant's two forms of the sublime from the Critique of Judgment: the spinning-prop disaster challenge in 'RuPocalypse Now', where queens like Jiggly Caliente are overwhelmed and then rise ('I couldn't let my fall be the death of me'), embodies the mathematically sublime, while Violet Chachki's sixteen-inch corset cinch and oxygen tank on the 'Death Becomes Her' runway dramatizes the dynamically sublime, the recognition of a power in us greater than what threatens us. She argues the queens' testimonies — Chi Chi on growing up poor, black and queer in the Deep South, Kim Chi's fear of her mother, Katya's confessed terror of failure — show free will and authenticity overcoming the determinism of normative structures of gender, race and class. The 'inner saboteur' is overcome through sublime self-overcoming and the solidarity of werkroom heart-to-hearts, even within a capitalist reality-TV machine she checks against the Paris Is Burning appropriation critique.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 31 "19. Beauty of The Elder" — Courtland Lewis uses KISS's reviled concept album Music from 'The Elder' as a case study in aesthetics. He contrasts objective theories of beauty (Plato and the Golden Ratio, tested against the 4/4 stomp of 'Rock and Roll All Nite') with Hume's taste and Kant's immediacy thesis that beauty is judged without inference, adds the disinterestedness of aesthetic pleasure, and applies Noel Carroll's moderate actual intentionalism (with Jerrold Levinson on what a musical work is) to argue that fans and band co-create the album's meaning. Peter French's collective memory explains why 'The Elder sucks' hardened into fan identity after Casablanca reordered the track listing and wrecked the boy-hero story, and Schopenhauer's claim that music expresses the in-itself of the world redeems the fans who find the album beautiful.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 26 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Wolfendale and Franklin argue D&D is a genuine art form with its own aesthetic. Tracing the medium's birth from Gygax's Chainmail to Arneson's invention of the persistent campaign setting, they use Kant's account of aesthetic experience from the Critique of Judgment, in which disinterested pleasure arises from the 'free play' of the cognitive faculties, and claim that in role-playing that free play just is the collaborative generation of a fictional world. The result is 'depth': consequences no one planned, like a sorcerer Polymorphing a spider demon into a purple platypus or a fumbled Bluff check turning a session into a prison break. This pleasurable because it exercises, under realistic friction and constraint from rules and dice, the mind's world-building power.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 12 "Howl at the Moon If You Want To" — Michael J. O'Neill argues that infinite space is The Expanse's most constant on-screen character, conveyed through chiaroscuro cinematography that deliberately echoes the seventeenth century (the Don Quixote references, 'Dulcinea', the Rocinante's name), when humanity first confronted infinite space. He reads Pascal's terror at man as 'a middle point between all and nothing' into Avasarala's losing debate with Nancy Gao over the Ring gold rush and into Miller's agoraphobic quest for Julie, then contrasts this with Kant's mathematically and dynamically sublime: spacewalks, the Behemoth dwarfed at the Gate, the Arboghast disassembled over Venus, and Inaros' asteroid attack as the weaponization of the infinite. Against Pascal's insignificance, Kant's sublime reveals our freedom — Holden's 'crazy notion about free will' while descending to the Ring station, Drummer's 'nothing in the void is foreign to us', and Amos' 'we're still here' — so the awe the show's visuals provoke is an intuition that we are greater than all nature's power.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 25 "a11.xhtml" — Tallon reads The Hobbit as an exercise in aesthetics: Tolkien half-accepts the Kant-era 'art for art's sake' settlement - dwarves once made 'things of beauty for pure delight', elves sing 'lovely nonsense' without shame, Gandalf blows smoke-rings and fireworks - while rejecting both Victorian moralism and Wilde's amoralism. Instead aesthetic sensitivity is a moral thermometer grounded in Augustine's ordo amoris: orcs 'make no beautiful things, but many clever ones', dragons cannot tell good work from bad nor mend a loose scale (which is how Bard's arrow finds Smaug's bare patch), and Aule creates dwarves out of love so others might enjoy the beauty of Ea while Saruman's 'mind of metal and wheels' breeds Uruk-hai for domination. Beauty also acts morally: the dwarves' song awakens Bilbo's 'love of beautiful things made by hands' and, as Scarry and Murdoch hold, that awakening of desire beyond oneself is what prepares us for justice.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 8 "Notes" — Willard poses the paradox of creativity: how can a toy that promises creativity come with rigid instructions and a purist fan culture that polices what counts as legitimate building? She reads The LEGO Movie as staging three rival models — the Master Builders' unfettered recombination (Plato's Ion on poetic madness and Kant's mysterious free-playing genius), Emmet's 'thinking outside the box' that yields the mocked double-decker couch, and Finn's father's meticulous vision. Following Aristotle against Plato that poetic skill is a teachable craft, plus psychology of jazz-improvisation studies, flow states, and Zhuangzi's butcher Cook Ding, she argues creativity is the joyful mastery of a process, so following instructions is the etude-stage that builds the database of moves from which free creation grows.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 26 "Paradise Found" — Paul Brown maps The Minish Cap's Hyrule onto utopian theory: Plato's Republic classes reappear as royal family (guardians), castle guards (auxiliaries), and market traders (producers), but Hyrule improves on Plato with no slavery, fluid social boundaries (Princess Zelda wandering the festival unrecognized), and Mayor Hagen's local democracy. Aristotle's polis supplies the town's design — small enough for community, walled for defense, river-powered — while Kant's disinterested appreciation of the beautiful fits Miyamoto's 'miniature garden' of pastoral idyll. The spiritual dimension completes the utopia: the benevolent Picori/Minish are a God walking unseen among people, a fuzzy religion without prophet or persecution, so no leap of faith is even necessary.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 24 "Indiscernibles and Autonomous Viewers “Time to Write my Own Fucking Story”" — Forest and Beckley-Forest ask whether Westworld is self-referential 'high art' or 'meta-kitsch,' tracing aesthetic modernism from Kant's subjective turn through Greenberg's avant-garde/kitsch split and Adorno's autonomous versus heteronomous art. They read Sizemore's clichéd Western narratives and the park's stock characters as commodified kitsch that mirrors the show's own corporate constraints under HBO, and use Danto's Brillo Box problem of indiscernibles to argue that host/guest and entertainment/art distinctions lie in the viewer's reflection. Dolores's line 'when I discover who I am, I'll be free' models the Adorno-style liberation available to an alert viewer.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 17 "The Beauty of the Game" — The Brands stage a broadcast-booth debate about whether a championship game was 'beautiful,' with Dickie V defending Hume's subjectivism ('beauty is in the eye of the beholder' and the expert's delicacy of taste) and Billy defending Plato's objective Form of Beauty. Jim exposes each side's flaw (Hume's circular appeal to experts, Plato's third-man regress from the Parmenides/Aristotle) and proposes a synthesis: games have 'outer beauty' (universally observable fluid motion, like improvised jazz or dance) and 'inner beauty' (the strategy and reason the knowledgeable fan grasps), reconciling the objective and subjective.
- **Football and Philosophy - Going Deep**, ch. 14 "The Beauty of Football" — Parker asks what pleases football fans and argues the answer is beauty, framed around a Michael Vick scramble against the Ravens. He applies Kant's Critique of Judgment—beauty as disinterested, an end in itself, and its judgments nonconceptual yet universal ('you should too')—to explain why fans watch games rather than read box scores, and why skilled offensive play by Barry Sanders or Joe Montana strikes us as beautiful. Using Ted Cohen's 'circles of taste' and an informal survey, he concludes beauty admits of degree and depends on the viewer's grasp of context.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 10 "Second Hole On the Beauty and Sublimity of Golf" — Fudge and Ulatowski argue that golf's aesthetic appeal has two sources: the course as a designed landscape best appreciated (via Walton's 'Categories of Art') under the category of gardens, and the sublimity of players' character. They apply Kant's 'Observations on the Feeling of the Beautiful and Sublime' to distinguish beautiful courses (Augusta) from sublime ones (Pebble Beach, St. Andrews) and to explain Bobby Jones's self-imposed penalty at the 1925 U.S. Open as the noble sublime, since 'subduing one's passions through principles is sublime.' They link the consistent rule-following golf demands to Kant's categorical imperative and read human dignity as 'beyond price' against Hobbes's price-based account, while Schopenhauer's critique of the French garden frames the environmental objection to courses.
- **Golf and Philosophy - Lessons from the Links**, ch. 30 "Fifteenth Hole The “Ideal” Swing, the “Ideal” Body Myths of Optimization" — Jason and Laurence Holt attack two 'optimization' myths in golf culture via a philosophy of kinesiology: the averaging model (that the ideal swing is the statistical mean of elite swings) and the athlete model (that more general fitness makes a better golfer). Against the first they invoke multiple realizability from philosophy of mind—there is no single perfect swing, since Bobby Jones's over-parallel backswing, Hagen's short fast swing, and the quirky swings of Trevino and Furyk all succeed on different bodies. Against the second they note golf's modest physical demands and argue Tiger Woods's heavy conditioning caused injury without improving results. They diagnose the false ideal as an aesthetic bias favoring 'beautiful' swings and athletic-looking bodies, using Suits's definition of games to defend golf as a genuine sport of gross physical skill.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 30 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Sharpe analyzes the Olympics as an aestheticized 'spectacle' (Debord, after Marx's commodity analysis) whose real product is the shareable 'Olympic moment.' Reading Kant's Critique of Judgment through Terry Eagleton, he argues the games trade on the sensus communis Kant finds in the judgment 'this is beautiful', an intimated universal harmony among humans that mirrors the ancient Olympic ekecheiria (truce). He links Beijing 2008's simulated fireworks and lip-synced girl to Baudrillard's simulacra, and uses Benjamin's 'Work of Art' essay, Riefenstahl's Olympia and Hegel's account of Greek sculpture to show how the Nazis' 1936 Games weaponized this aesthetic power, warning the spectacle serves both good and evil.
- **Tennis and Philosophy - What the Racket Is All About**, ch. 11 "Federer as Religious Experience" — David Foster Wallace argues that watching Roger Federer live at Wimbledon delivers a near-religious experience because top sport is a prime venue for 'kinetic beauty'—a beauty rooted in human beings' reconciliation with the fact of having a body.
