- **Steve Jobs and Philosophy - For Those Who Think Different**, ch. 23 "Steve Jobs and Philosophy" — White argues Apple's 'Think Different' commercial packages together two distinct character traits: genuine independence, in Rand's sense of judging from the facts of reality (thirteen-year-old Jobs confronting his pastor with the problem of evil via the Biafran children—'Does God know about this?'—rejecting dogma at Stanford, killing the iPod's screen, bending Corning to make gorilla glass on schedule), and pseudo-independence that asserts the primacy of consciousness over reality (refusing to bathe because his diet 'prevented' odor, treating cancer with fruit juice, NeXT's impossible eighteen-month promise). Using Binswanger's 'fallacy of false integration' (the surgeon-and-murderer 'cutter' example), he charges the ad with merging the traits into one folder, so Jobs should instead be praised without qualification for his independence and blamed without qualification for his pseudo-independence.
- **Divergent and Philosophy - The Factions of Life**, ch. 15 "6. Tris’s Compassion and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Tris's whole arc as a struggle with the problem of evil, both the theological version from Job and the modern secular one Susan Neiman describes, in which unreasonable suffering threatens trust in human reason. He casts Tris as cut from Rousseau's mold - her insistence on making the evils of Jeanine, Marcus, and Evelyn intelligible - against Voltaire's Candide refusal to rationalize suffering, and treats the faction system as Rousseau's social-contract strategy for containing the inclination to evil while Tris herself plays a wartime Emile. The key is Tobias's lesson that selflessness and bravery are not that different: selflessness enables the courage that compassion motivates, from pressing her forehead to Jeanine's gun in the fear landscape to taking Caleb's place at the weapons lab, so that the trilogy ends with Tobias's 'we mend each other.'
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 31 "18. Wondering What It’s All For" — Trip McCrossin reads Lord Grantham's 'we've dreamed a dream' as an echo of Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 and follows the war story line - Matthew and William missing before Amiens, William's slow death, Mr. Lang's shell shock, Mrs. Patmore's nephew Archie shot for cowardice - to show how obscure war's causes and realities remain to those who have not lived them. The Dowager Countess's 'we don't always get our just deserts' as Matthew dies under his car, and the stretcher-bearer's 'it comes down to luck,' raise the problem of evil from the Book of Job: good and bad fortune fall without premonition or meaning. Against complacency about war's inevitability, the chapter argues that since class and traffic harms can be reduced, warfare's can be too - we should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret the wars a few dream up, and not allow them to come to be.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 14 "4. Acts of God" — McCrossin reads Lecter's parable of the church collapses - 'It must feel good to God - He does it all the time, and are we not made in His image?' - as Lecter's solution to the problem of evil in both its theological (Job) and secular (Neiman) forms: a malevolent deity of the kind de Sade's Saint-Fond describes, doing God's work becomes Lecter's justification, and killing feels good because 'if one does what God does enough times, one will become as God is'. Following Neiman, he sets Rousseau's tradition (evil must be made intelligible - 'All is well leaving the hands of the author of things') against Voltaire's Candide refusal of theodicy, showing that Will and Starling live in Rousseau's camp except when facing Lecter himself, and that the Hannibal/Hannibal Rising revelation that Mischa's murder 'happened' to him radically revises his earlier claim that 'we don't invent our natures', with Starling's reason finally making 'a place for Mischa' in Lecter and Starling together.
- **Hannibal Lecter and Philosophy - The Heart of the Matter**, ch. 16 "6. The Psychiatrist as Sociopathic God" — Hassert takes Lecter's 'First principles, Clarice' at its Aristotelian word - nature is revealed through capacities and action, as an acorn's telos is not pumpkins and a kitten will never be a Great Dane - to explain Lecter's psychiatry: he reads each patient's essence and potential, prescribing Mason Verger's face-peeling so appearance finally matches essence, and force-raising Will toward equality so that Aristotelian perfect friendship between the alike-in-virtue (which Franklyn's flattery can never reach) might become possible. Reading God through Augustine's account of evil as the destruction of a preexisting good and Mischa's murder, the chapter argues that Lecter emulates a capricious deity - 'Typhoid and swans - it all comes from the same place' - and, unlike Nietzsche, does not pronounce God dead but merely misconceptualized, while his friendships fail because he must corrupt the other into his own image rather than love an equal.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud grants that Superman is godlike and turns Hume's problem of evil on him: if Superman is all-powerful, all-knowing, and good, why does suffering persist that he could prevent at super-speed - the desert animal dying painfully for no purpose, the crimes that happen while he picnics with Lois - and the free-will defense and "it's all part of the plan" excuses fail him even worse than they fail God. Superman then becomes our excuse for doing nothing, and like belief in immortality and the afterlife (holy wars where no one "really" dies, prayers instead of feeding the starving) he dulls our sense that this life is all we get. Reading Nietzsche's "God is dead" as the discovery that we keep gods only to feel special and saved, Michaud concludes we would live more meaningful, Batman-like self-reliant lives if the savior-Superman were dead to us.
- **Batman, Superman, and Philosophy - Badass or Boyscout_**, ch. 32 "20. What It Takes" — The chapter argues Batman is the more heroic superhero because his heroism is supererogatory and replicable: like Wesley Autrey the Subway Samaritan rather than the duty-bound Captain Sullenberger, he acts beyond obligation with human abilities we could imitate, while Superman's alien powers make his help barely optional and himself impossible to emulate. It frames Batman as Bruce's answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular version - Rachel Dawes's challenge that good people must 'do something' about Falcone's Gotham - siding with the Rousseau line that reason must make evil intelligible against Voltaire's refusal. Batman earns his 'super' by marshaling reason as well as wealth, like the cell-phone sonar he submits to Lucius Fox's veto in The Dark Knight, and his parting 'anyone can be a hero' to Gordon shows heroes begetting heroes, which Superman's otherworldliness never manages.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 12 "4. Raising Darrow" — Trip McCrossin reads Darrow's storyline as an engagement with the problem of evil in both its theological form (Harmony dubbing him Lazarus, the parables of John and Luke) and its secular form, which Susan Neiman traces to the Rousseau-Voltaire dispute: must evil be made intelligible or not? Darrow begins Voltairean—incredulous before the rigged Laurel and Eo's hanging ('She left me')—but his resurrection and political awakening on the surface remake him Rousseauian: evil is the misalignment of individual and general wills, and humans are corrupted by society, not born bad. The chapter reads Darrow's 'Man was born free' broadcast in Morning Star, his new social contract with Victra, and the education of Pax (with Lysander left to Cassius to 'raise him right') as Rousseau's Social Contract and Emile program—break the chains, then educate each generation so its contracts align ever closer with the general will.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 32 "18. Gods and Beetles" — Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 34 "20. Cersei, Sansa, and the Problem of Evil" — McCrossin reads Cersei and Sansa's post-imprisonment rises in season six as opposite answers to the problem of evil, framed by Susan Neiman's claim that Enlightenment thought split between making evil intelligible and refusing to. Cersei, taught by Tywin that 'the gods have no mercy - that's why they're gods,' becomes Sade's cruel god of Juliette, doing whatever feels good as the gods do; Sansa, hardened by Ramsay and Littlefinger's betrayal into 'no one can protect anyone,' embodies the Kantian response that virtue and happiness come apart, so one governs only what can be controlled - character, family, justice - as she engineers the Battle of the Bastards and has Ramsay eaten by his dogs without mercy or vengeance.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 40 "25. Deadpool Kills God" — The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 41 "26. Why We Love to Watch Deadpool . . . Play with Himself" — Using the Deadpool video game, the chapter argues Wade is a god who is all-powerful (rewriting the game world with his crayon-scrawled script and manufacturing fake credits), all-knowing (reading the player's mind through the fourth wall and literally entering Rogue's), and plainly not all-good (slapping an unconscious Wolverine, ogling dead Vertigo, ignoring Apocalypse three times for a billion dollars), so that dystheism - belief in a god with serious issues - dissolves the problem of evil. The free-will defense collapses because Deadpool wrote the script the villains obey, giving players only the illusion of choice. The voices in Wade's head are explicitly cast as Freud's structural model, with his Ego and SuperEgo talking while WadePrime, the Id, does most of the voice-work.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 25 "11. The Gods Are Dead and Elliot Has Killed Them" — Robison-Greene reads Elliot's chapel monologue - 'If I don't listen to my imaginary friend, why the fuck should I listen to yours?' - as a Problem of Evil argument: an omniscient, omnipotent, omnibenevolent God is incompatible with the unnecessary suffering of his father's death and of massive income inequality. The 'gods' Elliot kills are also Mr. Robot ('like all gods their madness takes you prisoner') and the religion of materialism, and Nietzsche supplies the blueprint for what follows: the Genealogy's slave revolt in values as the model for fsociety's uprising, and the Parable of the Madman plus the Ubermensch to cast Elliot-as-Mr. Robot as the creator of new values - though unlike Nietzsche's slaves, the oppressed here are complicit in their own subordination.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 11 "2. Just Not the Hero Type (Not!)" — McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (moral, altruistic, atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) and tests it on Wesley Autrey versus Captain Sullenberger and a Super Autrey thought experiment: Iron Man's engineering-based feats are refinements of abilities we share and so inspire imitation, while there can only ever be one Captain America, making Tony the more heroic. The Sokovia Accords debate then contrasts two humilities, with Stark's willingness to accept oversight more heroic than Rogers' safest-hands-are-our-own confidence. The chapter closes by explaining why we invent super heroes at all through Susan Neiman's account of the problem of evil after twentieth-century atrocities, from the Stamford explosion to Charlie Spencer's death in Lagos.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" — Tests three accounts of evil against the show. Augustine's privation theory — evil as nothingness, forged against Manichean dualism — fails to capture a Twin Peaks that is genuinely Manichean, with the Experiment vomiting BOB out of the Trinity blast and the Black and White Lodges in eternal conflict; Ricoeur's symbolism of defilement fits the filthy-haired BOB, the sooty Woodsmen, and the frog-moth contaminating the sleeping girl. The decisive framework is Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics triad of vice, incontinence, and bestiality: Ben Horne's and Laura's weakness of will, the town's ordinary vices, and BOB's appetite-only bestiality ("I don't need anything. I want") versus Windom Earle, whose intact but corrupted reason — the macabre chess game, murdering Catherine beside Cooper, hunting Cooper's soul — makes him, per Aristotle's claim that vice is worse than bestiality, the show's truly evil person and proof that evil is human and fightable.
- **The Twilight Zone and Philosophy - A Dangerous Dimension to Visit**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' (Lutze tried by his victims' ghosts at Dachau and sentenced to madness) and 'He's Alive' (neo-Nazi Vollmer groomed by Hitler's ghost) as Serling's twin responses to the Eichmann trial, situating them among the docufiction Operation Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman episode, and his abhorred Hogan's Heroes. Tracking Serling's maturation from the heartless, monstrous Lutze to the needy, speechmaking Vollmer — 'frustrated men, sick men, angry men' — he argues the later episode foreshadows Arendt's banality of evil, evil as the end product of a political process and a thoughtless inability to think from another's standpoint, all framed by Susan Neiman's problem of evil.
- **The Handmaid's Tale and Philosophy - A Womb of One's Own**, ch. 19 "8. From the Handmaid’s Tale to the Handmaids’ Tale" — McCrossin reads Offred's silent prayers ('I want to know what I did to deserve this') as channeling the Book of Job, using Susan Neiman's distinction between the theological and secular problem of evil: even if we stop demanding explanations from God, we must still make evil intelligible, as Janine's Testifying cruelly refuses to do. He sets Rousseau against Voltaire on whether morality requires making evil intelligible, finding June Rousseauian for piecing together Gilead's hidden prehistory at the Boston Globe and for acting from compassion, as with the bread-truck driver's secret Quran. The Salvaging refusal—Ofglen first, then Offred, then sixty-five stones dropped with 'I'm sorry, Aunt Lydia'—shows compassion becoming solidarity and solidarity becoming a general will, transforming The Handmaid's Tale into The Handmaids' Tale.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 12 "2. Can Anything Good Come from the Upside Down" — Kuzma maps Augustine's two cities onto the two Hawkinses: not two places but two mixed moral orientations in one world, since Will is literally 'right here' in the same house flipped upside down. Augustine's privation view of evil (evil as absence of good, a nougat-less Three Musketeers) explains how Dart can come from the 'evil' Upside Down yet love Dustin and let the party pass, while Brenner, from the right side up, is ruled by libido dominandi like the Mind Flayer and Dr. Owens proves Hawkins Lab is not automatically bad; it is how you act, not where you are from.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 43 "I Know What’s Real" — Trip McCrossin's afterword works out what Deckard can mean by 'I know what's real': given the green eyes in the Voight-Kampff playback versus the brown eyes in Wallace's staged memory, Deckard is claiming the overwhelming authority of his own lived experience — of Rachael's eye color, their love, her personhood — over any recording or replica. He folds this into the book's larger move from the problem of personhood to the problem of evil, why bad things happen to good people, and the secular task of justifying the ways of Wallace, Tyrell, and the other ersatz gods. With Mr. Cotton's 'raining fire' echoing the Book of Job, the afterword presents the volume as an invitation to save ourselves by saving one another.
- **Mister Rogers and Philosophy - Wondering through the Neighborhood**, ch. 36 "23. The Neighborhood Is Us" — Trip McCrossin frames the show, via Susan Neiman, as Rousseau's answer to the problem of evil: bad things (including bad television) happen to good kids, but education can mitigate evil, which is why Rogers prefers Rousseau's demand to make evil intelligible to Voltaire's Candidean refusal and Pangloss's best-of-all-possible-worlds. Rogers pursued only Emile's second prong, making us as we ought to be by loving children 'just the way they are,' and the post-9/11 PSAs before King Friday's empty castle merge Make-Believe into reality, the last 'modulation' of his thirty-four-year ministry.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 17 "8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil" — Ray Bossert reads Endgame through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, arguing that Doctor Strange and Tony Stark, who permit the Snap and five years of suffering for the sake of the one winning outcome, run 'uncannily parallel' to Thanos, who decided for Gamora that her unwilling death served the greater good. Strange's viewing of 14,000,605 futures illustrates Boethius's distinction between an infinite being riding along the timeline and an eternal one seeing all moments at once, and the refusal to tell Stark his role mirrors why God's foreknowledge sees our choices without compelling them. Boethius's providence weaving free choices into justice, the Avengers' passion-driven failures on Titan (Star-Lord and Thor avenging lost lovers), justice as the wicked's own punishment (Thanos dying wretched twice in one film), and Umberto Eco's 'Myth of Superman' all frame a universe where suffering is allowed because it is woven into a pattern that ends in justice.
- **Perry Mason and Philosophy - The Case of the Awesome Attorney**, ch. 12 "4. The Case of the Other Renegade Refugee" — McCrossin reads 'The Case of the Renegade Refugee' (aired December 9, 1961, days before Eichmann's verdict) alongside the film Operation Eichmann and Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem as three competing pop-culture portrayals of the Nazi criminal: monstrous, repentant, and banal. The episode's 'other' refugee, Arthur Hennings/Max Kleinerman, whose Father Paul-inspired 'religious peace' lets him recant on the stand and save Mason's client Harlan Merrill (himself a Battle of the Bulge 'deserter' living a lie created by concussion), supplies what Arendt found absent in Eichmann: empathy and genuine acceptance of guilt, complicating her banality-of-evil picture. The whole is set against the Holocaust as the century's starkest form of the problem of why the innocent suffer while the wicked thrive, and closed with Hogan's Heroes' provocative reuse of the same actors four years later.
- **The Avengers and Philosophy - Earth's Mightiest Thinkers**, ch. 25 "Equal Opportunity—for Deities" — Barkman argues the Marvel Universe's 'One-Above-All'—depicted as Stan Lee and Jack Kirby—is the eternal Judeo-Christian Creator, and arranges its beings in a graded hierarchy: the Living Tribunal as God's judge, cosmic beings like Eternity and Galactus, elders, sky fathers Odin and Zeus, down to mortals, with only God eternal and everything else, gods included, able to die yet enduring by His decree. Ontological rank guarantees nothing morally—Mephisto, the Goddess, and Hera are powerful and wicked, and even Hercules can be beaten by the Wrecking Crew. A free-will theodicy answers where evil came from: 'no other gods before me' never denied other gods' existence but commands loving the Good above all, which mortal Avengers like Thor, loving justice perfected by sacrificial love, manage as well as any deity.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 14 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Smith weighs Sheldon's vendetta against Wil Wheaton — the skipped 1995 Dixie Trek convention, the fake dead 'Nana' that won the Mystic Warlords tournament ('Game over, Moon Pie!'), the bowling-alley sabotage of Leonard and Penny — against theories of evil: Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds theodicy (with Voltaire's Candide objection), Buber's claim that the lie is the specific evil humanity introduced into nature, and Arendt's banality of evil at Eichmann's trial, which shows Wil's deceptions are bad moral choices rather than evil. Nietzsche's will to power would instead admire Wil, and even Khan-style revenge, as proto-Übermensch exploitation. The chapter closes by reading Sheldon's 'Comic Book World paradigm' (the Green Goblin to his Spider-Man) through Ricoeur's view that evil is grasped through myths and symbols: Star Trek and comics are the symbolic framework by which he interprets wrongdoing he cannot otherwise fathom.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 10 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — Liz Stillwaggon Swan surveys Sabbath's pictures of moral evil (nuclear annihilation in "Electric Funeral", heroin's "deadly pin" in "Hand of Doom", social oppression allegorized as the Satan of "Black Sabbath") and argues the band poses the problem of evil without solving it theologically. Against the view that invoking evil presupposes God, she aligns Sabbath with Augustine's rejection of Manichaean evil-as-a-force, reading evil as a privation traceable to free human choices, and with Bertrand Russell's "A Free Man's Worship": "Children of the Grave", "Into the Void", "Spiral Architect", and "Symptom of the Universe" urge that we defeat evil by imagining and building a better possible reality through love, vegan-pacifist Geezer Butler being the living proof behind the stage persona.
- **The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy - More Moments of Zen, More Indecision Theory**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci reads the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series (Helms's Dayton, Tennessee reenactment-town piece, Stewart's panel with ID proponent Dembski and the scrotum question) as one of the best media treatments of the creation-evolution controversy. Popper's falsificationism marks intelligent design as non-science, since Dembski's designer works outside testable law and miracles are, as Larson says, unrepeatable and unfalsifiable, while Stewart's bad-design jokes about the scrotum and Mayr's 99.99% extinction figure replay the problem of evil. A compressed tour of rationalism (Plato to Descartes's radical doubt) versus Hume's empiricism explains why science yields tentative conclusions, and the chapter ends that resolving the controversy, like Aristotle's eudaimonia, is a lifelong personal project.
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 27 "The Dread Conclusion!" — The chapter asks whether Dormammu is truly evil and tests him against Augustine's three types of evil: metaphysical evil as privation fails because Dormammu is a positive being with a face and a voice, natural evil fails because he is a sentient agent with intentions, so he lands squarely in moral evil—freely intending to deprive intelligent beings of the good of existence. It entertains the Galactus-style alternative that Dormammu, like a lion taking a gazelle, is an amoral force consuming worlds for survival, but his rage in the time loop ('your world is mine, like all worlds') reveals a drive for domination rather than sustenance, while conceding we know him only through the Ancient One's possibly biased testimony.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - The Truth Is Neither Here Nor There**, ch. 31 "18. Wondering What It’s All For" — Trip McCrossin follows Lord Grantham's 'We've dreamed a dream' - an allusion to Nebuchadnezzar in Daniel 2 - through the warfare story line of seasons 2 and 3, from Matthew and William missing in action to Matthew's death under a truck. Mr. Lang's shell-shocked confrontations with the eager volunteer William and with Mrs. Patmore over her executed nephew Archie dramatize the gulf between those who know what war is like and those who can only imagine it, while the meaningless deaths of Matthew and the stretcher-bearer who is shot mid-sentence raise the Job-like problem of evil in the Dowager's words, 'we don't always get our just deserts.' The chapter argues against complacency about warfare's inevitability: because total war is dreamed up by the few, the rest of us should 'band together as Daniel,' interpret those dreams in advance, and refuse to let them come to be.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 18 "The Emergence of Good from Evil" — Reads David Lynch's Dune as staging the problem of evil on an interplanetary scale: Baron Harkonnen as Satan-like evil personified against the Fremen, Paul's prophetic dreams as biblical-style revelation, and 'the sleeper must awaken' as spiritual awakening. Against the free will defense it deploys J.L. Mackie's argument that an omnipotent God could have created beings who always freely choose good, and uses the sandworm destroying the spice crawler as natural evil the defense cannot easily cover. It then proposes the film's own implicit theodicy, that goodness is defined against and emerges from evil (the Fremen's goodness awakened by liberation from Harkonnen tyranny, Paul good against the background of the Baron), closes with John Hick's point that moral growth requires challenges, and concedes the evidential problem posed by the sheer quantity of evil.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 8 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Jeremy Proulx reads Ender's refrain 'I didn't want to hurt him!' through Schelling's account of evil as a real 'contraction into the self' rather than Augustine's mere privation of good: the beatings of Stilson, the boy on the shuttle, Bonzo, and the Giant reveal a Peter-like monstrosity in Ender that he can neither understand nor control. Graff's engineered isolation forces Ender to confront this dark ground, and his moral development culminates in Valentine's 'Welcome to the human race' — the recognition that freedom is tainted by a necessity we do not choose, so Ender stays responsible for xenocide even though he was tricked.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 24 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Jaime Lannister's question to Catelyn Stark - 'If the gods are real and they are just, then why is the world so full of injustice?' - launches a tour of the logical and evidential problems of evil across the religions of Westeros. Augustine's privation theory and free will defense are tested against the Faith of the Seven (with Catelyn answering 'Because of men like you'), Hume's dilemma of impotence or malevolence is applied to the old gods that Arya scolds at Harrenhal for failing to save Ned, and Leibniz's best-possible-world reply is weighed against natural evils like the storm that sank the Windproud. The chapter concludes that only the evidential problem sticks: the sheer quantity of suffering in Westeros is evidence against just gods, though nothing counts against the uncaring gods Brienne describes.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 32 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Nielsen asks whether a Green Lantern with unlimited willpower would be a god and answers no through Leibniz: God is the absolutely perfect being, where perfection excludes contradiction so that knowledge and power admit of perfection but 'the greatest of all numbers' does not, and such a being creates the best of all possible worlds. Hume's trilemma (impotent, malevolent, or whence evil?) is met with the theodicy that finite minds, like Lanterns baffled by Guardian decrees, cannot compare our world to the discarded possibilities, each perhaps as bad as Qward. Since omnipotence requires omniscience and omnibenevolence, not even Parallax, the Anti-Monitor, or Kyle as Ion counts as omnipotent: admirable and powerful, but not gods.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 34 "Notes" — Treats Frank's soliloquies-strangling the dog's 'useless pain', the Peachoid eulogy that goads a grieving congregation toward hating God, urinating on his father's grave 'to seem more human'-as a Heideggerian tour of concealment and disclosure, where truth is disclosure rather than correspondence and Frank alienates himself from responsibility and even from being human. Quoting Iris Murdoch on how fiction makes goodness seem dull and invoking Roth's 'theodicy of protest', the chapter warns that Frank's shuffling of morality into maneuver relaxes our moral guard about blame, God, and evil.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 34 "Rescuing Princess Zelda" — Dwayne Collins runs the problem of evil against Hyrule: Mackie's logical problem sets the all-good, all-powerful Goddesses against the existence of Ganondorf, and Plantinga's free-will defense transposes neatly because the wish-granting Triforce must permit evil wishes or its power would be limited. The evidential problem and John Hick's soul-making theodicy get recast as a 'game-making theodicy': if Hyrule's evil were neither excessive nor randomly distributed, its people (like players of a too-easy game) would stop striving to overcome it. Hyrule's distinctive solution, unavailable on Earth, is Link — a divinely chosen hero who counteracts excessive evil and returns the world to a 'normal' amount of it.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 20 "Fighting the Real Enemy" — Johnson asks why Sinead O'Connor tearing the Pope's photo ended her career while SNL's own religion sketches drew little fire: 'DJesus Uncrossed' targets Tarantino's gratuitous violence rather than Jesus, the Tebow sketch ridicules prayers for football wins that Nietzsche said cheapen God into a servant of chance, and 'God's a Boob Man' satirizes the God's Not Dead films' strawmanning of atheists. Louis C.K.'s God monologue, he argues, raises the burden of proof and the problem of natural evil, best answered by Carlin's joke of a God subject to physical laws. The Church Lady embodies Warmke and Tosi's moral grandstanding, whereas O'Connor's protest does not, and the chapter ends on Plato's Republic: better to be a virtuous person scorned as a villain, like O'Connor, than a celebrated villain, though her tragic life strains Plato's promise that virtue pays.
- **Spider-Man and Philosophy - The Web of Inquiry**, ch. 13 "Spider-Man and Philosophy" — Barkman argues that Spider-Man's ethics, while universal enough for Jews, Platonists, and Confucians, are specifically Christian in emphasis: God creates for friendship, which requires free choice, so 'with great power comes great responsibility' restates Luke 12:48 — the more one is given, the more justice is required, as Peter's refusal of MJ and Octavius's wasted intelligence in Spider-Man 2 show. The free-will solution to the problem of evil (chosen evil, fallen angels, Adam's curse, a law-governed physical world) is read through Peter's questioning God in 'The Big Question' (Peter Parker: Spider-Man #48). The chapter culminates with Spider-Man 3, where the symbiote inflames Peter's grief into revenge against Sandman — a perversion of justice — until Peter forgives Flint Marko, enacting mercy as the perfection rather than the absence of justice.
- **The Ultimate South Park and Philosophy - Respect My Philosophah!**, ch. 14 "THE ULTIMATE SOUTH PARK AND PHILOSOPHY" — Johnson formalizes Kyle's crisis in 'Cartmanland'—evil Cartman inherits a million dollars and buys the amusement park while good Kyle suffers hemorrhoids and loses faith—as a valid argument from the logical problem of evil, then evaluates the town's theodicies against the philosophical ones. The Job story Kyle's parents read him fails like skeptical theism (it proves too much and ends in moral agnosticism), Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' mirrors Calvin's and Edwards's God-glorifying account, Stan's restored faith via Cartman's perfect misery is a greater-goods response, Augustine's free will defense purchases goodness at the price of God's control of prayers and elections and cannot explain natural evils, and Hick's soul-making theodicy founders on fawns, tsunamis, and Kenny's deaths. Pascal's Wager and Plantinga's divine sense are dismissed in turn: evil does not disprove God, but proportioning belief to evidence makes non-belief the rational stance.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Asks how an all-encompassing, good Force can have a dark side: after framing the Force as panentheistic, it tests Augustine's privation theory (Alderaan's destruction as an absence of 'measure, order, and form') and a Daoist reading of Yoda's equanimity modeled on Zhuangzi drumming and singing after his wife's death, rejecting both because Vader's evil is active, disciplined, and full of the Force rather than a lack. The answer endorsed is Schelling's: the will needs a dark 'ground' - Yoda's 'anger, fear, aggression' - which is benign when ordered by the will of love and becomes evil when it separatisitically defies it, which is what 'bringing balance to the Force' means.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 20 "10. Gods Are Overrated" — Michaud runs Hume's problem of evil against a Superman who is nearly all-powerful, all-knowing, and good yet takes dates with Lois while animals and children suffer pointlessly — and unlike God he cannot hide behind mystery, only laziness. God-like protectors breed excuses ('Superman is our great excuse' for doing nothing about homelessness or starving children), and belief in afterlife and divine rescue cheapens this life; following Nietzsche's death of God, the chapter argues we should stop believing in saviors, face the infinite night, make our own meaning, and be more like Batman — self-reliant people who try to save others themselves.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 32 "20. What It Takes" — Argues Batman is more heroic than Superman because heroism requires supererogation and replicability: Wesley Autrey's subway rescue, done without obligation, outranks Sullenberger's 'just what we're trained for,' and unlike otherworldly Superman, Batman's human abilities let the rest of us imagine imitating him—heroism begets heroism, as Gordon's coat around young Bruce's shoulders helped make Batman. Batman is framed as the answer to the problem of evil in Susan Neiman's secular form: Rachel Dawes' challenge that good people do something, on the Rousseau side of the Enlightenment debate that morality must make evil intelligible (against Voltaire's refusal). Superman's overwhelming power makes relying on reason superfluous, so he becomes a symbol of what we can't be, while the Dark Knight models what we can.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 19 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Haas uses Dean's stubborn refusal to believe in God, even after meeting Castiel, escaping Hell, and visiting Heaven, to run through the problem of evil. Casey's challenge in 'Sin City' states the logical problem; the free-will theodicy answers it but falters before Supernatural's designed horrors like the rugaru, a creature God built to suffer an irresistible hunger that ends with it eating its spouse. Dean's real objection is the evidential problem, that the amount and severity of apparently pointless evil makes the omni-God unlikely, and neither a 'natural order' defense (Dick Roman humanely farming humans for food) nor John Hick's soul-making theodicy explains suffering far beyond what character formation requires.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 20 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Curry argues that angels like Anna and Castiel can reasonably be atheists, because a higher perspective confers no epistemic advantage about God: Anna admits only four angels have seen him and the rest 'take it on faith.' Aquinas's cosmological argument, illustrated by the endless causal chain behind the Impala, yields at most an uncaused first cause rather than an omnipotent, omnibenevolent one, and Paley's design argument, an Impala in the desert implies a designer, is undermined by Darwinian natural selection, which Castiel himself witnessed ('Don't step on that fish'). The free-will theodicy fails against natural evils like famine and childhood cancer, and the principle of parsimony tells angels to expect a natural explanation for their own existence, so Uriel's 'There is no will. No wrath. No God.' turns out to be rational.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 25 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Evolutionary biologist Graves applies naturalist method to the Supernatural universe: assume natural explanations first, as the Catholic Church does before granting an exorcism, and only posit the supernatural where naturalism fails. He builds a naturalistic phylogeny in which souls behave like genetic codes (50,000 new souls when Balthazar unsinks the Titanic), and demons, ghosts, and most monsters derive from human souls, which explains why mundane salt, iron, fire, and burned bones work on them, while pagan gods killable by wooden stakes and dog's blood are 'more akin to monsters' than gods. The framework yields rules and predictions about the Colt, holy water, and the Croatoan virus, and even suggests God and Death may be natural beings obeying laws lesser beings do not share.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 23 "NOTES" — Barkman answers 'God hates fangs' with Aquinas: evil is no-thing, so God creates nothing inherently evil — fangs, sex, and free will are good gifts whose misuse explains fallen angels, witches (via the Malleus Maleficarum and Allatius's demon-animated vampires), and human sinners like Rene and the Rattrays. Since True Blood's vampires stand unmoved before crosses, hold church meetings, and can choose as Bill does, they are not soulless minions of the devil but created beings who, like humans, go wrong only by misusing free will — which is why Harris's inclusive Episcopalianism lets Gran say there is a purpose for everything God makes, even a vampire.
- **Twilight and Philosophy - Vampires, Vegetarians, and the Pursuit of Immortality**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited,' where SS Captain Lutze is tried by his Dachau victims and driven mad, and 'He's Alive,' where a phantom Hitler grooms the failed neo-Nazi Peter Vollmer, as Serling's two-part response to the Eichmann trial. Setting them against the film Operation Eichmann's monster-Eichmann, Perry Mason's repentant Kleinerman, Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, and Serling's hatred of Hogan's Heroes' comic Klink, he traces a maturation: from the Nazi as heartless monster to Arendt's banality of evil, the thoughtless, frustrated everyman. Vollmer, the chapter argues, shows what Lutze's origins were, and remembering the Dachaus is the guard against becoming his like.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 16 "Notes" — Silver argues WoT gives a new spin on the free-will defense to the problem of evil: when Rand weaves a world without Shai'tan in A Memory of Light, Elayne appears as if turned, robbed of the ability to be an individual, showing that freedom's value lies in authentic individuality and that abolishing evil equals a world run entirely from the Dark One's single perspective. On fate, he reads ta'veren as freedom-affirming rather than controlling and defends Rand's Dragonmount epiphany via 'deep self' compatibilist views (Frankfurt, Watson) while calling it partly bad faith. On the Wheel's eternal recurrence he sets Nietzsche's amor fati against Adorno's charge that it is a failure of hope, arguing Rand's 'do better next time' is hope, not acceptance.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "Notes" — Held reads Rand's final confrontation with the Dark One in A Memory of Light as a recapitulation of the free-will defense to the problem of evil, opening with Hume's statement of Epicurus's questions and Camus's refusal to love a world that tortures children. Drawing on Augustine (evil as privation, our limited perspective, the corruptible will) and Alvin Plantinga's claim that a world with significantly free creatures is more valuable, he argues Rand's competing visions teach that a world without Shai'tan removes choice: Elayne 'simpering,' Aviendha vapid, people reduced to complacent automatons who cannot choose to be good. He concludes with Camus that the struggle itself justifies existence and that heroism is impossible without the possibility of cowardice.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 14 "Notes" — McCrossin builds a six-part definition of heroism (systematic, moral, altruistic, radically atypical, supererogatory, replicable safeguarding) using Wesley Autrey's Harlem subway save against Captain Sullenberger's Hudson landing, and argues Wonder Woman is genuinely heroic because her mission is voluntary and supererogatory - she wins the contest to leave Paradise Island and can retire to it at will, unlike a compulsory Superman. He then uses the demoted, powerless Diana Prince era with I Ching to show her deeds stay in principle replicable, like Batman's rather than Superman's. The payoff: Wonder Woman works only as a 'super hero' who inspires imitation, which is how 'we' answer the problem of evil - why innocent people suffer destructive, ruthless evil.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Clayton distinguishes the philosophical problem of evil (Aquinas's deductive argument, its inductive/evidential successors, and Plantinga's free-will defense) from what Plantinga calls the pastoral problem — the personal crisis suffering brings. He argues Eastwood, as 'practical philosopher,' registers the philosophical problem visually in Mystic River (camera panning heavenward at Katie's murder, the intercut Communion) but pointedly refuses to resolve it. In Hereafter the tsunami, deaths, and the twins' loss are met not with theodicy but with a recurring pastoral pattern of listening, being present, and acting compassionately (Dr. Rousseau with Marie, George's reading of Marcus), religion offering no answers.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 28 "15. The Evil in These Woods" — Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 9 "‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life" — The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 32 "Escape to Doctor Who" — Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 23 "12. Finally Free" — McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 24 "13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe" — Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 18 "9. Foundation’s Optimism" — McCrossin reads the sequels Foundation's Edge and Foundation and Earth as an Optimistic response to the problem of evil, in the lineage of Leibniz, Rousseau, and Hegel's 'All is well', set against the WWII, Holocaust, Nuremberg, and Eichmann-trial backdrop of Asimov's writing and Arendt's banality of evil. Tracking Gendibal's mantra 'all will happen well', the Gaia/Galaxia choice via Trevize's 'talent for rightness', and Daneel Olivaw's Zeroth Law and plan to merge with Fallom's brain, he uses the Book of Job to frame whether the series' recurring reassurance is earned or merely reframed.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci uses the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series and the Dover trial to argue that intelligent design is not science because it is unfalsifiable and invokes supernatural causation. He cites Popper's falsificationism (and Popper's recantation about Darwinism), contrasts Descartes's rationalism with Hume's empiricism to characterize science as a tentative blend of the two, flags Feyerabend's 'anything goes' as an irrational view of knowledge, invokes Aristotle's eudaimonia to argue meaning in life is a personal work in progress, and turns Dembski's theistic-evolution concession into a Pyrrhic victory via the problem of evil ('argument from bad design').
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil" — James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 30 "MOTHERHOOD" — George Dunn asks whether classical theism can call God 'Mother,' beginning with the Book of Job (taught in his Problem of Evil course) and the divine name Shadday's link to womb-love and 'blessings of breasts and womb.' He works through Anselm's 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' the attributes of impassibility and incorporeality, and Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, arguing Aquinas wrongly rejected maternal God-language because he swallowed Aristotle's biology of woman as 'defective and misbegotten'; drawing on Nel Noddings's caring 'receptivity' and Julian of Norwich, Dunn contends divine impassibility should yield to a maternal, receptive God, with a nod to Homer Simpson's burrito paradox.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 9 "Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection" — Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "Who is Who" — Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 38 "35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force" — Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 78 "74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates" — Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

### Will to Power

The will to power is Friedrich Nietzsche's proposed principle for understanding the deepest drive in living beings—not merely a wish to survive or to feel pleasure, but a striving to grow, overcome resistance, expand, and impose form on the world. Nietzsche developed the idea partly against Schopenhauer's blind will to life and against theories that reduced life to self-preservation, suggesting instead that organisms and individuals seek to discharge and enhance their strength. He extended the notion, in his notebooks especially, toward a broader interpretation of nature, knowledge, and value, though he never systematized it into a finished doctrine. It became central to his critiques of morality and to his vision of self-overcoming and the creation of new values.

- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 10 "Persuasion As Drama" — Karl Schudt contends that Nietzsche's genealogy of slave morality cannot be refuted by reason (Nietzsche denies reason itself), so drama must persuade where dialectic cannot: a believable story of a Nietzschean life acts as an empathic experiment. Faith is constructed as the Nietzschean ideal — strong, healthy, ruthless ('Find a couple of studs, use them, and discard them'), dismissive of reflection ('You think too much') — serving Mayor Wilkins, whom Schudt reads as a genuine Übermensch sacrificing mankind's mass for his ascension. Watching her world collapse (the accidental killing in 'Bad Girls', her mirror scene in 'Who Are You?', the torture of Wesley and confession on Angel) gives viewers an Aristotelian pity-and-fear warning that the unjust life ends badly, completing her 'leap from Nietzsche to Socrates.'
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Eric Bronson places Tolkien among the 'sometimes merry' existentialists: Nietzsche's artist who says Yes amid catastrophe and needs 'the power to forget', Jaspers on machines estranging us from our past, and Arendt on Eichmann's obedient inhumanity and the few who create joy in dark times. The elves' songs in Rivendell and Lórien are joy born of sorrow and dispossession - Galadriel suffers because she remembers too much, trying to 'embalm time', while Arwen forgoes immortality for Aragorn. Her refusal of the Ring ('I will diminish, and go into the West, and remain Galadriel') embodies the existentialist affirmation: trust your own light, know what to remember and what to forget.
- **The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy - One Book to Rule Them All**, ch. 20 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Douglas Blount tests Nietzsche against Sauron, whose forging and grasp of the One Ring - even striving to supplant Ilúvatar - enacts the will to power, exploitation, the death of God, and the ideal of the Übermensch. He argues that in Middle-earth the naked will to power appears not as a brave new humanity but as plain evil, and that Tolkien answers Nietzsche not with argument but with a rival portrait: Gandalf's self-sacrifice on the Bridge of Khazad-dûm, Frodo's mercy to Gollum that becomes Middle-earth's salvation, and Sam's humble refusal of 'Samwise the Strong'. Judged by Nietzsche's own aesthetic criterion of taste, Tolkien's vision of community, humility, and abnegation is the more beautiful - and therefore the more compelling - portrait of reality.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 24 "An Empire of Fear and Trembling" — Cameron reads the Emperor's dominion through Hegel's master-slave dialectic and struggle for recognition: fear is the Empire's currency, from Alderaan's destruction as visible demonstration ('fear will keep the local systems in line') to Vader's deliberately undefined threats ('The Emperor is not as forgiving as I am'), while hatred binds the Sith Master to Maul, Dooku, and Vader. Because the master can never win recognition from an unequal slave, Palpatine's will-to-power rule is a historical dead end, whereas the slave - Anakin laboring in Watto's shop, Luke overcoming his fear in the cave and under Yoda - can transform himself through work and courage. Vader's final turn is thus his achievement of a new self-consciousness, recognizing himself as 'something other than a slave' at the moment Luke's unshakeable faith forces the truth on him.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 20 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Tim Mosteller identifies Lewis's Tao from The Abolition of Man with Aquinas's Natural Law, an objective moral order knowable by all rational beings, and maps three responses onto Narnian characters: wholehearted acceptance (Peter, Lucy, Tirian, Reepicheep), selective 'Innovators' who pick and choose (Shift and Miraz, with Nietzsche's invented master-values as the philosophical extreme), and total rejection by 'Conditioners' (Ginger the Cat, who reverts to dumb beast, and Uncle Andrew, who loses the animals' speech). Individual laws are illustrated by Mr. Tumnus freeing Lucy, Aslan scratching Aravis for her gladness at the slave girl's beating, Nikabrik's treacherous Realpolitik, Lucy's eavesdropping spell in the Magician's book, and Jill's showing-off at the cliff.
- **The Undead and Philosophy - Chicken Soup for the Soulless**, ch. 31 "A Meditation on the Word" — Randall Auxier and Eileen Townsend fictionalize the history of philosophy as vampire predation in letters, emails, and IMs (1983-2009) between the 800-year-old Etienne Lavec - a student of Siger de Brabant who drained Thomas Aquinas over the Summa's Treatise on Angels, which wrote vampires out of existence - and Paulie, a freshman turned at Memphis State. Lavec recounts tasting Pico, Spinoza, Hegel, and the willing Kierkegaard, sparing Nietzsche who 'stole some of my ideas about free death', and contrasts vampire self-knowledge (embracing desire) with the Socratic beginning in affirmed ignorance. The centerpiece is Foucault: Lavec summarizes his genealogies of how institutions create the sick, the mad, the prisoner, and the pervert, fails to drain him, and is then haunted for decades by posthumous publications, taunting 'nietzsche26' emails, and finally a catacombs trap - power/knowledge that refuses to die. Lavec's embedded 'Meditation on the Word' recasts the Logos of John's Gospel so that vampires are the uncreated darkness at the boundary of the divine Word, pure self-grounding desire 'beyond good and evil', while the closing Twilight-era chats satirize Stephenie Meyer's sparkling, abstinent Edward as Foucauldian 'sin by words'.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 16 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Matheson examines the 'master animal' imagery saturating Fleming's novels - Donovan Grant's reptilian physique in From Russia with Love, Blofeld's animal magnetism, villains feeding victims to sharks and crocodiles - as an exercise in Social Darwinism where, as Mr. Big puts it, wolves live by wolf's laws and sheep call them criminals. Using Nietzsche's Übermensch, the blond beast of the Genealogy, and Zarathustra's self-overcoming, she distinguishes Apollonian eaters like M (who curb appetite) from doomed Dionysian gluttons like Giuseppe Petacchi, arguing that Fleming makes dining and will power the test of who counts as an Overman. Bond differs from his megalomaniac foes only in keeping his own will to power and stomach under control, and the chapter closes by warning that Hollywood's romanticizing of the master animal keeps us valuing a brutally primitive masculinity Fleming himself mocked as a 'cardboard booby'.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 17 "James Bond and Philosophy" — Landa argues that Bond's apparent defense of democracy against Übermensch villains is itself profoundly Nietzschean: Bond's exquisite, disciplined hedonism (the Minton-china breakfast, disgust at Mr. Du Pont's 'eating like a pig'), his obsessive competitiveness at baccarat and golf, and his contempt for mass democracy mark him as an aristocratic bourgeois hero in Nietzsche's mold. The gambling scenes enact a Calvinist logic of predestination in which losing at Casino Royale devastates Bond because his very worth depends on winning, and the 'human muck' he defends at Blades turns out to be the exclusive elite. Dr. No, Mr. Big, Drax, and Blofeld are cast as evil, explicit Nietzscheans while Bond serves a good, unspoken Western Nietzscheanism - so the Cold War showdown with Blofeld, who invokes Nietzsche by name, is elitism fighting counterfeit elitism, making Bond 'a secret agent in the service of Nietzscheanism'.
- **The Beatles and Philosophy - Nothing You Can Think that Can't Be Thunk**, ch. 6 "PROLOGUE “WHAT’S THAT SUPPOSED TO MEAN ”" — The prologue closely re-watches Bob Dylan's 1965 Newport 'going electric' set and argues that the famous booing began for mundane musical reasons — the bassist missing the change to the five chord in 'Maggie's Farm' and an under-rehearsed band — not ideological betrayal by folk purists. It contends that the audience collectively transmuted a flawed performance into an epochal myth of folk-vs-rock rupture, and that this shared fiction, not how the music actually sounded, is what mattered culturally. Framed by the Nietzsche epigraph on self-overcoming, it reads Dylan as a catalytic, quasi-messianic figure who performed the 'necessary murder of the old order' (culminating in the 1966 'Judas!' shout), enjoyed even the booing as part of the cultural drama, and refused every label by calling his new style 'vision music.'
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 10 "Rupert’s Response and Responsibility" — Biderman and Jacobowitz read Rope through Nietzsche: Brandon and Philip strangle their classmate David as would-be Nietzschean supermen, acting on mentor Rupert Cadell's cocktail-party theory that murder can be an art for a superior few. The chapter explains the will to power, the Ubermensch, and the death of God, then argues Brandon is no superman: he kills from weakness and a bully's need for an audience, mistaking crass destruction for the refined self-creation Nietzsche demanded, just as the fascist appropriation of Nietzsche fails. Rupert's horrified final speech, renouncing 'superior or inferior beings' and insisting each of us is 'a separate human being,' raises whether a teacher can disavow responsibility when students act out his provocative ideas: ideas have consequences, and the only true test of a philosophy is whether we can live by it.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 29 "Will You Say Yes" — Bruce finds Nietzsche's eternal return in the NES Zelda's clockless, endlessly restartable structure: the same game recurs every time you press start, yet since the player changes, each playthrough manifests the forces anew, and the demon's question 'do you desire this once more?' becomes 'do you will to play once more?'. Link's growth through eight dungeons to face Ganon is read as will-to-power, personal strength and self-overcoming rather than mere domination, and saying yes to the struggle is amor fati. Against Plato's two-worlds doctrine of Forms and the Christian after-worldly (both Nietzsche's targets), the original Zelda offers no guide, no Bible, and no linear time to a final judgment: this looped world is the only one, so it must be affirmed.
