Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 8 "Who is Who" — The introduction argues that Doctor Who and philosophy share a common origin in wonder (quoting Plato's Socrates and Aristotle) and traces the show's shifting worldview across the eleven Doctors. It claims early Who embodied Enlightenment 'positivism' (the pro-science Hartnell/Pertwee eras) but that the post-1996 and post-2005 series turned toward Romanticism and Sartrean/de Beauvoirian existentialism, framing the surviving Doctor's post-Time War 'angst,' homelessness and burden of freedom through existentialist themes.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "index" — This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 17 "15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey" — The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 55 "52. Fight Club as Philosophy I Am Jack’s Existential Struggle" — Oya reads Fincher's Fight Club in existentialist, nonethical terms as the story of the unnamed narrator 'Jack' and his struggle for an authentic, self-governed life. Consumerism (the 'Ikea nesting instinct'), the masculinity of underwear ads, religion, and finally Tyler Durden's hunter-gatherer creed are all rejected as externally imposed answers that deny authenticity; Fight Club and Project Mayhem merely swap one alienation for another. Jack's shooting himself to purge Tyler dramatizes self-affirmation. The chapter grounds this in Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity ('the genuine man will not agree to recognize any foreign absolute'), contrasts Nietzsche and Unamuno on self-affirmation, cites Hobbes on the brutish state of nature to condemn Tyler's utopia, and invokes Plato's cave to argue a comfortable but externally governed life is still not authentic.

### Existence Precedes Essence

"Existence precedes essence" is Jean-Paul Sartre's slogan for the core of atheistic existentialism: there is no fixed human nature given in advance, so a person first exists and only afterward defines what they are through their choices. Unlike a manufactured object whose purpose is set before it is made, the human being arrives without a predetermined role and must create meaning and value through action. This places the full weight of self-definition, and hence responsibility, on the individual.

- **Seinfeld and Philosophy - A Book about Everything and Nothing**, ch. 16 "No Exit and The Vault Sartre and Seinfeld on the Inescapability of Others" — Jennifer McMahon defends the heretical reading of Sartre as a relational theorist of the self: in Being and Nothingness consciousness is a nothingness, not an essential ego, and only the Other - 'the Other accomplishes... to see ourselves as we are' - lets us grasp ourselves as objects. Seinfeld illustrates this better than Sartre's own suspicion of others: Jerry's identity exists only through his entanglement with George, Kramer, and Elaine (change them and you get a 'bizarro-Jerry'), and the finale's prison cell ('The Vault') replays No Exit's locked room with the trial's parade of wounded minor characters - except that Seinfeld's chattering foursome shows friendship as a positive, not hellish, dependency.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 90 "Unknown" — The chapter walks through Nausea as the ordinary-world twin of the red pill: Roquentin, an unremarkable 1930s historian, is unravelled by a beach pebble, a handshake like 'a fat white worm', a door-knob that seems to grab him back, and finally the chestnut tree's 'naked World' - discovering that existence is a gelatinous, unjustifiable 'messy suffering' and that the order, names, and values we take for reality are only a veneer consciousness projects onto an indeterminate whole. His nausea is the horror of authenticity before it becomes anything else, the price Neo pays for swallowing the pill.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Bob Dylan and Philosophy - It's Alright Ma (I'm Only Thinking)**, ch. 14 "Sick of Love" — Krein and Levin read Dylan's portraits of fallen socialites in "Like a Rolling Stone," "Just Like a Woman," and "To Ramona" as critiques of bad faith - characters who hide from freedom and responsibility in consumerist status games, in Sartre's sense that existence precedes essence. But Beauvoir's Second Sex exposes the cost: the women Dylan praises ("Girl from the North Country," "One More Cup of Coffee") are praised precisely for staying in immanent, pastoral passivity, denied the transcendence that for Beauvoir constitutes full humanity. Borrowing Benjamin's and Buck-Morss's notion of modern "dreamworlds," they finally read Dylan's pastoral utopias as a counter-dreamworld spun after the collapse of the mass-utopian promise of consumer happiness.
- **Harley-Davidson and Philosophy - Full-Throttle Aristotle**, ch. 14 "Harley-Davidson and Philosophy" — Auxier uses the question 'Would Bruce Springsteen ride a Honda?' as an ontological probe: Honda embodies defensible middle-class values while a Harley is not primarily a machine but 'a decision about life and what makes it valuable', a suicide machine Jesus could have ridden into Jerusalem and whose absence would render Easy Rider meaningless even if Fonda rode some other Harley. His own boyhood purchase of a Honda XL 70 over the Harley Z90 becomes a lesson in Heideggerian honesty, since he knew he belonged on a Honda, while buyers who choose for appearances are consumed by das Man, the they-self that lives inauthentically through images and slogans. Using Husserl's method of imaginative variation on the question, he concludes that the Harley as cultural icon represents an existential decision and the life that follows from it.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 21 "A Nietzschean Conclusion" — Slowik argues the Pythons have a positive existentialist message: Kafka's bureaucratic insanity, where ordinary people beat helplessly against irrational rules, recurs in the 'Cheese Shop' and 'Dead Parrot' sketches, and Camus's Sisyphus lives on in the monotonous lives of Palin's city stockbroker and the accountant who dreams of lion taming — repetition without Sisyphus's defiance. The core claim is that Python endorses individual-centered existentialism: Brian's 'You've got to think for yourselves. You're all individuals!' is the troupe's rare direct statement of Sartre's 'existence precedes essence', confirmed by Cleese's and Palin's interviews about resisting those who tell you how to behave, a theme the chapter extends through Nietzsche's critique of moral tradition and organized Christianity. Sartrean bad faith explains Python's stereotyped characters — the aggressive policeman, the pepperpots, and Mr. Praline insisting 'I am not a loony!' while demanding a fish license for his halibut — while Arthur Pewtey's meek 'Right. Right.' and Ron Obvious's physical limits raise nature/nurture objections to Sartrean freedom. The 'Nietzschean Conclusion' is that Monty Python itself exemplifies will to power as 'giving style' to one's character, constantly overcoming its own formulas rather than repeating what succeeded.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 14 "Poker and Philosophy" — Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 15 "Poker and Philosophy" — Vernezze uses Dostoevsky to make gambling existential: Notes from Underground's insistence that will trumps reason ('what do I care for the laws of nature and arithmetic?') and The Gambler's portrait of the calculating gambler — who loses like everyone else and worships money with a 'German' soul — prefigure existentialism's three traits: lost confidence in reason, despair as part of the human condition, and the willed overcoming of absurdity (Camus' Sisyphus happy, Sartre's condemned freedom). Dostoevsky's own roulette addiction fuels the reading, with Amarillo Slim and Brunson's side bets as heirs. The Cincinnati Kid's climax clinches it: Lancey Howard 'making the wrong move at the right time' by chasing a straight flush proves poker's essence lies beyond reason — a truly Dostoevskean activity.
- **Hitchcock and Philosophy - Dial M for Metaphysics**, ch. 19 "Identities, Selves, and Others" — Patterson uses Thornhill's being mistaken for the fictitious George Kaplan to test theories of personal identity: the body theory fails a CIA thought experiment in which a Kaplan double is slowly rebuilt from Thornhill's own replaced cells; Locke's memory theory fails on amnesia scenarios and circularity, since one cannot have memories of a self unless one already has a self; and Parfit's psychological continuity survives, with Thornhill drifting along a 'Psychological Spectrum' toward 'one hundred percent Kaplan' as he plays the spy. The chapter then turns existentialist: with Sartre, no essential nature fixes who Thornhill is, so he is totally responsible for the self his choices create, from 'Expedient Exaggerations' to risking death on Mount Rushmore. Charles Taylor's claim that a self exists only in dialogue with a community explains why Eve and others literally help make Thornhill into the person he becomes.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 27 "Lonesome Day" — Calef asks how fictional story-songs can teach: lyrics yield neither know-how nor know-that, since Plato's Theaetetus shows true belief is not knowledge (the 'Meeting Across the River' narrator's plan works only by luck). The answer is a third kind — knowing what something is like: 'The River' lets a comfortable listener inhabit Mary's husband's slide into a dry marriage, and 'Nebraska' lets us feel Starkweather's numb void, 'what it's like to have no soul.' Aristotle's Poetics (we delight in imitation because learning pleases; poetry is more philosophic than history because it speaks in universals) explains why sad songs satisfy us, and Sartre's universal human condition grounds the empathy that makes The Rising render 9/11 ('You're Missing,' 'Empty Sky') thinkable at a personal scale.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 11 "The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities" — Cuddy asks how gamers relate to BSG videogame avatars — as an extension of the ego or a disposable other — using Freud's id/ego/superego to cast the avatar as a socially safe venue for reconciling forbidden desires (piloting a Cylon Raider) with the superego's demands. Against Rehak's claim that gamers simply drop the avatar when losing, he enlists Sartre: blaming the game or 'cheating' opponents is bad faith, a denial of the freedom to create one's own essence, with Lee's '33' debate about responsibility for the Olympic Carrier and Baltar's vacillation as in-show parallels. Sartre's facticity bounds the freedom — hard missions are fixed facts to deal with — so the gamer, like Adama's fleet, must take responsibility within limits.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Fellela reads Link's endless drudgery (slashing grass for rupees, collecting bottles, leaving the final Ganon fight at a 'permanent pause') through existentialism: Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' is dramatized in Ocarina of Time's opening, where Link must acquire sword, fairy, and skills to make himself the hero, and Nietzsche's 'God is dead' call to become gods is answered by Link restoring meaning to a hostile Hyrule. Camus' Sisyphus figures the repetitive world-saving quest as an absurd hero's owned task, and Frankl's logotherapy (meaning as the tension between what one is and what one should become) explains why humiliating menial tasks, in camp or in laundromats or in Zelda, become bearable and even meaningful. Link's fixed options even illustrate Frankl's point that freedom is the stance we take toward conditions, not freedom from them.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 15 "The Missionary" — Christopher Hoyt reads Buffett's escape from Catholicism as a case study in secular meaning-making after Nietzsche's death of God, taking the Mardi Gras ritual of Folly swatting Death out of town as Buffett's core spiritual attitude — interpreted the way Wittgenstein criticized Frazer, as an expression of our stance toward death rather than mere magic. Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' frames the post-1960s task of self-definition without God, while Marx's alienation explains what the persona of *Jimmy* refuses: the impersonal work and borrowed values that leave moderns living an alien narrative, like McGuane's character Skelton in Ninety-Two in the Shade. The twist is that *Jimmy*'s pop-culture vocabulary — Tully Mars built from Donovan's Reef and Slim Pickens, Bogart, the Brylcreem jingle — is itself authentic, and the 'semi-true story' of the myth tells deeper truths than a literal biography could, making Buffett something like a pop prophet for late modernity.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 10 "15" — Three 'Phase Four' essays. Moseley reads the Joker across Batman #1, The Killing Joke, The Dark Knight, A Death in the Family, and Dark Knight Returns as a 'moral monster' who knowingly does evil - and, following Anscombe and Scanlon's guise-of-the-good analysis, pursues aesthetic 'higher values' in a Camus-like affirmation of the absurd, embracing the irrationality Batman's rational moral order cannot fathom. Levin uses X-gene biology (Beast's explanation in Astonishing X-Men, genotype vs phenotype, M-Day) to strip Magneto's Homo sapiens superior claim of any genetic or phenotypic basis, then argues via the moral community of rational persons (Kant's criterion) that mutants and humans share one moral community, condemning both the Registration Act and mutant separatism. O'Neil's prose piece traces Harvey Dent from Calvinist certainty through the acid that scars him to cosmic doubt - quantum randomness, many worlds, Sartre's condemnation to freedom - until Nietzsche's amor fati lets him embrace duality and let the scarred two-headed coin decide good and evil.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 14 "True Selves Found or Made" — Theodore Schick reconstructs Aleister Crowley's philosophy of Thelema to explain Jimmy Page's devotion—Boleskine Manor, The Equinox bookstore, the Zoso sigil, 'Do what thou wilt shall be the whole of the law' etched in Led Zeppelin III's run-out groove—and reads 'Stairway to Heaven' stanza by stanza as an allegory of awakening to the True Will. He then dismantles the framework: no spell has ever worked under controlled conditions (post hoc fallacy), Sartre's existence precedes essence denies any divinely written True Will or human nature, and Schopenhauer (via Einstein) argues we can do what we want but cannot want what we want. Using second-order desires and autonomy, the chapter concludes that selves are made, not found—so even if a True Will existed, following a program we did not write would make us 'loyal plastic robots', not free.
- **Mr. Monk and Philosophy - The Curious Case of the Defective Detective**, ch. 14 "Mr. Monk’s Greatness" — Lewis argues Monk is Nietzsche's Übermensch. Sketching Sartre's existence-precedes-essence through the contrast between the designed wipe and self-defining humans, the chapter claims Monk creates his own essence through choices — keeping the coffee table askew in memory of Trudy, 'dirtying' his house in 'Mr. Monk Makes a Friend,' drinking stream water in 'Mr. Monk Gets Cabin Fever' — and lives by self-prescribed values (hourly flossing, bagged tissues, relentless truth-seeking) that separate him from the herd of the Court of Public Opinion. The comparison with Stottlemeyer — Nietzsche's lookalike with the mustache, 'the quintessential man' of the herd — inverts the expected hierarchy: 'He was a yardstick for me, of both detection and character' ('Mr. Monk Goes to Mexico') shows the badge-carrying everyman is the inferior one. Monk therefore challenges the macho sci-fi stereotype of the superman: the Übermensch can be gentle and kind, fight for truth and a cleaner world, and still have room to improve ('What does not kill me makes me stronger').
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 39 "Manny" — Santaniello reads five nonconformist Red Sox through ethical theory. Ruth's sale to New York becomes a Kantian case: he tore up his signed three-year contract and demanded a trade while expecting others to keep promises, violating the categorical imperative on promise-keeping. Ted Williams's lifelong war with the 'Knights of the Keyboard' exemplifies existentialist authenticity ('It just wouldn't have been me' tipping his cap), Spaceman Bill Lee embodies Sartre's condemned freedom and existence precedes essence, Jim Rice's Hall of Fame delay is Aristotle's failure to hit the mean between silent deficiency on Boston's racism and excess toward reporters, and Manny's 'Gas is up and so am I' money grab shows Aristotle's point that wealth is an incomplete end pursued for the sake of something else.
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 2 "index" — This file holds the book's front matter, Wittkower's introduction 'A Reply to facebook Critics', and the 'facebook Itself' essays. Wittkower answers critics of trivial status updates with Sartre's claim that lives have no given meaning (so their value is ours to create, from the inside), Hegel's argument that real freedom means choosing alongside others (against both Sunstein's 'Daily Me' echo chamber and the forced community of family and hometown), and Schopenhauer's microscope image from 'On the Vanity of Existence', concluding that we care about a friend's dinner update for the same reason we care about our own. James Grimmelmann's 'The Privacy Virus' rebuts the claim that Facebook users don't care about privacy by arguing they practice a contextual, Nissenbaum-style privacy (untagging keg-stand photos, the News Feed revolt, the Miss New Jersey blackmail), while Facebook's architecture breaks the 'know your audience' rule and recruits users into spreading violations like a virus. Graham Meikle reads wall posts and status updates as a convergence of personal messaging and broadcast media (citing the MI6 chief's wife's holiday photos and the Sunday Express's Dunblane survivors story), and Ian Bogost applies McLuhan's media ecology to Facebook as an 'extension of man': it enhances the directory and the yearbook, obsolesces the reunion and the secret, retrieves the small town and the soda shop, and reverses into campus life and high school.
- **Martial Arts and Philosophy - Beating and Nothingness**, ch. 15 "Living the Absurd Life" — Krein asks why he has spent fifteen years on karate when pepper spray and avoidance would serve self-defense better, and answers with existentialism rather than Buddhism. Nietzsche's death of God and Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence leave life objectively meaningless, but the dojo supplies a self-contained standard for Sartrean transcendence (kata quality is judged within the art), trains the courage and clarity authenticity requires, and enforces excuse-free responsibility: in sparring you either score or you don't. Studying a traditional martial art is thus a heroic, 'act without hope' defiance of the absurd.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 15 "Let Your Heart Be the Anchor and the Beat of Your Own Song" — Berti reads Neil Peart's 1997-98 catastrophes (his daughter's car accident, his wife's cancer death) and the 55,000-mile Ghost Rider motorcycle exile through Sartrean existentialism: existence precedes essence, so with no God-given script Peart must author his own reactions, exactly as Sartre's student had to choose between mother and Resistance. The chapter tracks alienation ('I do not know who I am'), the duty to choose rather than lean on outside voices, and 'The Pass' as the voice telling a suicidal teenager to walk back from the razor's edge. Thoreau's Walden retreat supplies the model for the healing road, and Peart's own directives ('keep moving; kick your own ass, gently') enact 'Freewill' and 'Something for Nothing': we are the ones who choose, and the choice to live made all that followed (re-marriage, Vapor Trails, five more tours) possible.
- **Dexter and Philosophy - Mind over Spatter**, ch. 36 "Bad or Bad Faith" — Rebecca Steiner Goldner reads the show through Sartre's Being and Nothingness: Dexter's watching is the Look that crystallizes his victims into a fixed essence - Matt Chambers can never again reinvent himself in a new town - and the kill room stages the demanded shame and confession ('Look at what you did!'), echoing Sartre's caught peeping-Tom. She then argues Dexter's belief that he was born a killer, that his Dark Passenger leaves him no choice, is itself bad faith: existence precedes essence, and by Sartre's account even the reformed thief remains responsible for his past, as with Jeremy Downs and Dr. Meridian. We viewers root for Dexter because we see the freedom he denies - and love him because he never makes the authentic choice to abandon his murderous project.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 53 "What Does A Scanner See" — The chapter answers Arctor's question with Sartre: the gambler cannot observe his way out of deciding again, because consciousness is a nothingness with no determinate essence to be observed, so a scanner used to find yourself 'sees nothing', and Fred watching his own footage is bad faith, hiding from freedom behind presumed facts about himself. Butler then flips the bleakness into Sartre's optimism, reading Dick's 'I myself, I am not a character in this novel: I am the novel' as the author freely remaking his life through the book, his first written without amphetamines, after the break-in he suspected he had staged himself.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 147 "Chapter 23 - Lonely Wolves" — Travis Paterson's introduction reads A Scanner Darkly as Dick's most autobiographical novel and explains Arctor's disgust at the over-happy Brown Bear Lodge audience through Sartre's Nausea: Roquentin's discovery that existence is sheer contingency, that we are superfluous, vaguely alarmed beings who cannot define existence as necessity. Arctor never finds Roquentin's slender chance of acceptance, so the nausea curdles into addiction and the wolf parable, the magnificent lone wolf shot to protect the meager, over-fed animals, poses the chapter's question of why the sensitive outsider is the one sacrificed.
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 116 "A Footloose Man" — Dick expounds Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism' through the essentialist picture — a God-given blueprint, like Keith's Bentley designed before manufacture — against Sartre's claim that we exist first and invent essences afterward, marriage and family included. Monogamy thus emerges as a human choice mandated by Western authority and imposed on conquered peoples, not an absolute ethic handed down from heaven, a freedom humans exercise even in dropping Deuteronomy's stoning rule. Keith, Mick and Simone discarded the inherited tradition of monogamy, while Charlie Watts chose to stick with it.
- **Neil Gaiman and Philosophy - Gods Gone Wild!**, ch. 25 "Neil Gaiman and Philosophy" — Robert Tally Jr. reads The Graveyard Book as 'spectral existentialism': Bod's climax, 'I'm Nobody Owens. That's who I am,' is Sartre's existence precedes essence made literal, a self made rather than found, and the climactic claiming of the name enacts the self-ownership of the nursery-rhyme pauper 'who nobody owns.' Heidegger supplies the uncanny not-at-home-ness (unheimlich) of the graveyard, which Tally, citing Foucault's 'Of Other Spaces,' calls a heterotopia, while Silas the vampire embodies Lukacs's transcendental homelessness and Kierkegaardian anxiety is transmuted by Bod into the spectral gift of Fear he wields on his bullies. The identity-leeching ghouls named after the Duke of Westminster and the 33rd President are the avatars of bad faith, and the Jacks' attempt to dodge the prophecy fulfills it like Oedipus's, showing that Bod's fate, too, is self-made.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 25 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Kempner reads The Walking Dead through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old value-system gone, survivors who cling to pre-made essence die — Hershel keeps his zombified son locked in the barn awaiting restoration, and Shane tries to steal Rick's old cop-and-husband identity rather than live his own existence. Rick's waking in the hospital is a rebirth: he first exists in the new world, then creates a way of being human, and his relapses into the sheriff uniform nearly get him killed. Carl shooting Shane to save his father completes the family's existential freedom (children are no longer 'innocent'), walkers — without will or choice — are the ultimate inauthentic beings, and the volume's tagline, 'forced to finally start living,' makes the zombie world a sternly optimistic humanist story.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 26 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Reads Larry as a textbook existentialist: his agonizing over trivia ('Doctor?... Pharmacist?') instantiates Heideggerian anxiety and Sartrean anguish, because every choice, even yanking his 5 wood out of a casket in 'The 5 Wood,' proclaims an image of how everyone ought to live. Since existence precedes essence there is no fixed human nature for Larry to appeal to; he must author his values alone, which the chapter says also makes him an optimist ('I'm not an inventor, but I'm an improver'). Larry dispels others' bad faith when he tells Susie she obviously can share the brownie recipe in 'The Benadryl Brownie,' and his baldness crusade, firing the toupee-wearing chef Phil Dunlap in 'The Grand Opening,' is a demand for authenticity about one's facticity. The 'Larry David Stare' is analyzed through Sartre's Look: the squinter tries to inspect another consciousness empirically and necessarily fails, since the other's freedom can never be objectified.
- **Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy - Bootleg This Book**, ch. 23 "Boardwalk Empire and Philosophy" — Robison-Greene reads the returning soldiers through Camus and Sartre. War reveals the absurd - Jimmy's Argonne story of the German soldier who would not die even in a hopeless situation strips life of inherent value - and Van Alden's fervent Christianity is the escapist response to absurdity, bad faith that denies his own desires. Jimmy and Richard are trapped in bad faith over facticity and transcendence, Richard pinned by 'the look' of a community that only sees his ruined face ('Hell is other people'); neither fully becomes an absurd hero like Meursault, since Richard still craves meaningful ties, but Jimmy finally embraces the absurd at the War Memorial, arranging his own death with the calm of a man who 'died in the trenches, years back.'
- **How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy - Being and Awesomeness**, ch. 12 "How I Met Your Mother and Philosophy" — The chapter uses Sartre to diagnose Barney's fixed persona of suits, womanizing, and Bro Code worship as bad faith: having freely chosen to become the suited businessman who stole Shannon, Barney now acts as if those are his only options, denying his radical freedom. Hardy maps Sartre's own examples onto the show - Wendy the Waitress play-acting a stereotypical waitress, the woman who ignores the knee-touch, Barney tuning out criticism with 'I'm awesome' - and reads emotions, via Sartre's Sketch for a Theory of the Emotions, as magical transformations of the world like Marshall's 'best burger' quest and the Bob Barker paternity story. Barney's love for Robin and his secret reunion of Marshall and Lily are the moments he breaks out of bad faith and chooses freely against his persona.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 19 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Elizabeth Butterfield reads The Devil's Advocate through Sartre: Kevin Lomax's 'You set me up!' excuse - after defending the guilty Gettys and Cullen and abandoning MaryAnn - is textbook bad faith, a lie to himself about his own free choices. Milton the Devil plays existentialist, insisting 'I'm no puppeteer... I only set the stage. You pull your own strings,' until Kevin admits his vanity, his drive to win, motivated every choice. Radical freedom entails radical responsibility, and Kevin's final suicide is his last free act, chosen to keep coming out on top, while free will remains the one limit the Devil cannot breach.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 10 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Talia Morag reads Brody's colliding roles - Marine, congressman, father, Muslim, follower of Abu Nazir - and Carrie's unstable ones (CIA agent, bipolar patient, lover) through Korsgaard's notion of practical identities, whose contradictory obligations (kill and not kill) demand reconciliation. Following Kierkegaard's advice to rethink labels like 'Christian', Brody reinterprets his suicide tape as acting 'as a Marine' against domestic enemies - a rationalizing move the chapter treats as bordering on bad faith - while Dana's phone call in 'Marine One' reasserts the father identity and stops the bombing. Carrie's 'Q&A' re-description of Brody as a good man and future hero shows identities are constructed through choices, Sartre's point that we are not summaries of our past.
- **Girls and Philosophy - This Book Isn't a Metaphor for Anything**, ch. 17 "Girls and Philosophy" — Archibald reads Jessa as Girls' quintessential existentialist: her unbothered abortion ('I'm offended by all the supposed to's'), her 'I am a junkie' honesty, and her refusal to blame her rough past (Sartrean facticity) enact existence precedes essence and Camus's embrace of the absurd. Kierkegaard's 'the crowd is untruth' and 'leveling' explain her contempt for rehab group conformity, while her panic marriage to Thomas-John after Katherine's motherly intervention is diagnosed as bad faith and angst. Her assisting the dying Beadie's suicide attempt - and calling 911 when Beadie recants - becomes the chapter's closing confrontation with Camus's one serious philosophical question, answered by living 'without appeal.'
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 24 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Walker contrasts Pennsatucky's Christian fundamentalism with Piper's secular humanism (Kurtz's six features) in their 'Fool Me Once' confrontation. With no God, Sartre's existence precedes essence makes Piper condemned to create her own meaning: owning her crime to her mother and confessing the Pennsatucky prank, while Red and Vee play Sartre's cafe waiter, reducing themselves to chef and dealer, and Pennsatucky's 'defender of the unborn' persona is de Beauvoir's sub-man sheltering behind ready-made values. Marx's opium-of-the-people analogy explains why comforting, unverifiable belief can block the authentic, responsible pursuit of a meaningful life.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 14 "3. I Want You to Survive" — Seth Walker asks what makes a life worth saving, testing the show's survival choices against instrumental value (usefulness to the group) and Tom Regan's subject-of-a-life criterion of inherent value. Shane's sacrifice of Otis for Carl, Lori's fatal pregnancy and Judith's birth, the Governor's obsession with Meghan, and the hunts for Sophia all show that neither usefulness nor Regan's equal, non gradated inherent value explains why children are selectively elevated - and perceived 'innocence' fails with the colder Carl and with Lizzie. He concludes with Bob Stookey's line in 4.10 'Inmates' ('Not everything has to mean something... but it can'): following Sartre's claim that man is nothing but what he makes of himself, the survivors are condemned to be free and must make their survival mean something, as Daryl and Carol's search for Sophia did.
- **David Bowie and Philosophy - Rebel Rebel**, ch. 9 "1. The Actor Tells the Truth" — Reisch argues Bowie's parade of characters (Ziggy, Aladdin Sane, the Diamond Dogs persona) was never metaphysical chameleonry but a postwar, cold-war project: by crediting himself only as 'the actor' and calling Dylan out as Robert Zimmerman's artifice, Bowie exposed the 'denim and hippies' authenticity cult as itself a construction. Diamond Dogs' '1984' and 'Big Brother' tie this to the era's totalitarian nightmares of manipulable humanity, and Sartre's 'Man is nothing else but that which he makes of himself' becomes 'the first principle of Bowie' - only constant reinvention keeps us from being fooled by ourselves or others, even at the anguished cost of 'Who Can I Be Now?'
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 16 "7. Being for Red" — Courtland Lewis asks who Darrow is—Red, Gold, hybrid, savior—and surveys theories of the self: Plato's immortal soul ruling the body, Descartes's cogito as thinking thing, and Hume's denial that introspection ever reveals more than a stream of perceptions (we never experience a soul, only thinking). Freud's id-ego-superego offers a secular soul, but Sartre carries the chapter: Darrow is being-for-itself, perpetually projecting what he is not, tortured by the Look of others—Eo seeing a savior, Mustang holding him at gunpoint, Roque's betrayed friendship—and prone to bad faith through 'guardrails' like the Vale, excuses about Eo and Uncle Narol, and pining for Mustang instead of owning his choice. Since existence precedes essence, Darrow is nothing but the sum of his free choices, and to live otherwise is to choose slavery.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 16 "5. Guilty of Being a Dwarf" — Engels runs Tyrion's arc through Sartre's existentialism: his facticity as a dwarf makes everyone from Catelyn to Tywin presume his guilt, while 'Never forget what you are, wear it like armor' states the Sartrean authenticity of owning facticity while freely choosing one's essence. Catelyn's dagger accusation, the comic confession at the Eyrie, the wildfire ship at Blackwater, and the trial outburst ('I am guilty of a far more monstrous crime: the crime of being a dwarf') show him choosing rather than being defined; the murders of Shae and Tywin dramatize the slide into bad faith - embracing the 'monster' essence others assigned - before his choice to join Daenerys resumes the burden of self-creation.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 13 "2. 3eanuts and the Existential Schulz" — The chapter introduces existentialism and reads Peanuts through it: Charlie Brown's defeats expose the 'groundlessness' of value, and the 3eanuts web project (deleting each strip's final gag panel) restores the despair that punchlines normally defuse. It explains Sartre's 'existence precedes essence' and the ideal of authenticity versus passively inhabiting roles, Heidegger's care and Dasein (even in despair there is an inner place where it happens), and Camus's absurd and Sisyphus revolting against a fate he cannot change. Lucy's hillside sermon ('WELL, LIVE IN IT, THEN!') and the final image of Charlie running at the football figure his revolt: he keeps kicking because in that moment a world without boxes exists in him.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 18 "8. Facing Up to the Realities" — Argues that 'Machine Gun' and its Berkeley introduction ('people... fighting wars... within themselves, not facing up to the realities') make Hendrix an existentialist: since existence precedes essence, each of us lives multiple realities we must author responsibly. The lyric variants diagnose Sartrean bad faith twice over — 'evil man make me kill ya' is the helplessness that denies freedom, 'fight like a farmer' the blame that locates failure out there — before the reprise's acceptance ('let your bullets fly like rain') and free judgment ('I know all the time you're wrong') achieve authenticity amid the solo's sonic battlefield.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 17 "Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities" — Engels reads William's transformation through Sartre's existential project: the white-hatted William and the black-hatted Man in Black are not a hidden true self finally revealed but two successive free choices of oneself, and the Man in Black's claim that the park showed him 'who he really is' is bad faith — a denial of his freedom that lets him absolve himself of cruelty, just as Ford's deathbed pivot cannot erase the facticity of his role in the hosts' suffering. Maeve's choice to leave the train is analyzed as her first self-chosen end and value judgment, suggesting a programmed android can begin constructing her own project despite Sartre's humanism. The open-ended finale — hosts free to fight back, the Man in Black smiling as he is shot — embodies Sartre's 'I am an infinity of possibilities' and the burden of being condemned to be free.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 21 "10. On Being and Meeseeks" — The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.
- **Blade Runner 2049 and Philosophy - This Breaks the World**, ch. 32 "20. Sympathy for the Existential Devils" — James McLachlan reads the films through Sartre: replicants are made like penknives, with an essence before existence, and their drama is going 'off baseline' — the freedom of nothingness by which Batty murders his maker-gods (Tyrell the Father, Chew and Sebastian the trinity) and K disobeys everyone. Sartre's Satan from his Baudelaire biography, Blake's Orc and the Marriage of Heaven and Hell's contraries, and the Great Chain of Being's contradiction between filling one's place and moral freedom frame Luv as a perfect penknife, a 'good angel' who fulfills her vocation, while Batty and K are redeemed by the love that breaks their programming. 'More human than human' turns out to mean: existence precedes essence.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 25 "13. The Origins of Self-Love" — Anna Marie Fennell reads RuPaul's 'If you can't love yourself, how in the hell you gonna love somebody else?' through theories of self-love. Erich Fromm's four elements of love and Buddhist non-attachment (Jinkx Monsoon's 'water off a duck's back,' the Season Ten Inner Saboteur characters like Eureka's Eufilthior) ground the claim that self-love precedes healthy love for others. Against Aristophanes' myth in Plato's Symposium - the round beings split by Zeus, forever seeking their other half, retold in Hedwig and the Angry Inch - she sides with Ru: completion comes from within, not from a soulmate. Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity (the sub-man and nihilist archetypes seen in self-sabotaging queens like Nina Bo'Nina Brown) and bell hooks's All About Love with Branden's six pillars of self-esteem map onto winners like Jinkx, Sharon Needles, Violet Chachki, and Bianca Del Rio, whose drag personas show existence preceding essence.
- **RuPaul's Drag Race and Philosophy - Sissy That Thought**, ch. 28 "16. Death Becomes Her" — Hendrik Kempt reads Drag Race's pervasive death imagery - death-drops, the 'lip sync for your life,' mirror messages, the 'Death Becomes Her' runway - through the philosophy of death. Epicurus's 'death is nothing to us' and Stoic self-possession (Ru's 'pay them bitches no mind,' Violet Chachki enduring a tiny corset) explain why elimination, like death, gives no ground for worry once it arrives, while Socrates' 'philosophy is training for death' makes the show a workout video for dying - Socrates even dying fussing over a rooster like a drag mother to Miss Fame. Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death set up Sartre's radically free, future-oriented self - so voluntary exits like BenDeLaCreme's self-elimination and Charlie Hides's listless lip-sync betray one's own plans - and Camus's Sisyphus makes Chi Chi DeVayne and Roxxxy Andrews's doomed All Stars returns models of 'acceptance without resignation.' The closing weighs transhumanism's promise of conquered death against a DragCon-forever thought experiment, concluding with Ru's roast eulogy for Lady Bunny that love and irreverence, not immortal life, are the point.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" — Montoya reads Chidi's breakdown upon learning he has been tortured for three hundred years as Nietzsche's death of God, quoting the Parable of the Madman from 'Jeremy Bearimy' to show how the guaranteed meaning of Chidi's worldview collapses into nihilism. Michael's midlife-crisis makeover and partying embody Camus's embrace of the absurd, while Sartre's existence precedes essence, abandonment, and anguish explain why Eleanor's confession to Michael and her sacrifice in the Judge's test count as authentic choices. With the Judge's verdict stripping away any hope of reward, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake, which the chapter presents as the show's answer to nihilism.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 10 "2. What Does Life Mean after the Snap" — This chapter reads four post-Snap Avengers as existentialist answers to how life keeps meaning after catastrophe. Tony Stark embodies Sartre's existence precedes essence, defining himself through free choice up to his final 'I am Iron Man' snap that erases Thanos and his army; the merged Professor Hulk lives Camus's Sisyphus, embracing the absurd and concluding 'all is well' after watching his own past rage; Captain America lives Levinas's ethics of the Other, from refusing to abandon brainwashed Bucky in Civil War to wielding Mjolnir to save Thor; and Ronin-era Hawkeye enacts Nietzschean nihilism until Black Widow's Vormir sacrifice, read through Zarathustra's burning in one's own flame, restores his meaning. The authors conclude Marvel's answer is affirmation: courage to affirm freedom, the Other, and life itself against Thanos as personification of genocide, climate change, and war.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 27 "16. KISS Goes Disco and Boogies on Simmons’s Bad Faith" — Christopher Innes defends 'I Was Made for Lovin' You' and KISS's disco turn on Dynasty against Gene Simmons's own scorn. Insisting that KISS is essentially and only hard rock treats the band's facticity as an in-itself, like Sartre's waiter who becomes nothing but his role — the bad faith of Simmons and rockist fans alike — whereas human transcendence and nothingness mean the band can authentically choose disco, grunge, or anything new, as Donna Summer's 'I Feel Love,' Pink Floyd, and Queen exemplify. The twist: bad faith is also a comfort, and the chapter ends by conceding that Simmons's hard-rock constancy may itself be an authentic filling of his own nothingness — so who is to say he is wrong?
- **30 Rock and Philosophy - We Want to Go to There**, ch. 17 "Liz Meets the Elephant in the Room" — Barkman reads 'Rosemary's Baby' as staging second-wave feminism in Rose Howard's comfort-sacrificing activism against third-wave feminism in Liz, who sells her dignity for the $10,000 Followship Award and likes comfort and the status quo. Sartre's existence precedes essence supplies third-wave feminism's non-essentialist claim that anyone can be a feminist in any manner, while an Aristotelian essentialist standard of human flourishing shows Liz's 'have it all' optimism, from the wedding dress bought in 'SeinfeldVision' to the adoption schemes of 'Do-Over', is a delusion because career and family each demand everything. Jack's confession that 'you have to choose' lands the chapter's verdict that the third-wave promise leaves women in Liz's predicament.
- **Alien and Philosophy - I Infest Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "Its Structural Perfection is Only Matched by its Autonomy" — Defends the Xenomorphs: if the Queen's tactical intelligence (incubating her eggs under the reactor, ordering drones to hold fire, cutting the power) and the species' hive organization satisfy Sartre's criteria of self-creating persons, then their 'attacks' are legitimate self-defense on the model of Sartre's preface to Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, where the colonized's violence restores a denied personhood. Read without anthropocentrism, Alien is the story of a newborn extraterrestrial hunted to death by humans, and Weyland-Yutani, the Marines, and the colonists of LV-426 - not the aliens - are the series' true villains.
- **Arrested Development and Philosophy - They've Made a Huge Mistake**, ch. 12 "Arrested Development and Philosophy" — Uses Sartre's cafe waiter, directly mirrored when Gob play-acts a waiter in 'S.O.B.s', to define bad faith as denying one's freedom by disappearing into roles: illusionist, Bluth Company president in George Sr.'s suit, 'any man' winning back Marta, Ward Cleaver father to Steve Holt (!). Distinguishing bad faith from impossible self-deception (beings-for-themselves have no pre-given essence), the chapter argues that even sincerity ('be yourself, Gob') is bad faith, and provocatively concludes Gob is happier and kinder to others in bad faith, reversing Socrates' 'know thyself'.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 27 "Paradox and Peace" — Christopher Drohan reads Batman and Alfred through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: Batman, like Abraham, believes 'by virtue of the absurd,' resigning himself to an infinite, never-realizable justice as a knight of infinite resignation, while Alfred embodies the higher knight of faith whose justice is concrete love expressed in mending the suit, making sandwiches, and guarding the manor. Heidegger's thrownness and Sartre's condemned freedom frame both men's absurd existential condition, including Batman sparing Joe Chill and even allying with him against the Reaper. The chapter's verdict is that Alfred's faithful devotion to one person is the superior ethic, and that peace begins with him.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 11 "The Avatar Unparalleled Opportunities" — Cuddy argues the gamer's bond with the avatar is an extension of the ego: Freud's id/ego/superego model explains why playing a Cylon Raider or flying the 'Bastille Day' mission lets gamers reconcile unconscious desires with the superego's demands in ways reality forbids. But when we lose we disconnect from the avatar and blame the game or 'cheating' opponents, which Sartre diagnoses as bad faith, a denial of freedom, contrasted with Adama's 'a man takes responsibility for his actions' in '33' and Baltar's vacillation over the vice-presidency. Through facticity (the unforgiving no-save 2003 game) and existence preceding essence, the chapter concludes that videogames offer unparalleled opportunities to practice Sartrean responsibility and achieve Freudian reconciliation through the right avatar.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 29 "Living with Our Choices" — Peters reads 'The Resistance' webisodes through Sartre's occupied-France dilemma from Existentialism Is a Humanism (resist, collaborate, or do nothing, modeled on his student's choice between joining the Free French and caring for his mother): Tyrol joins the resistance for his family's future, Jammer joins the New Caprica Police to save lives and pays with execution by his former friends in 'Collaborators,' and Duck's choice to do nothing ends with wife Nora's death in the Temple massacre and his revenge suicide bombing. Since 'man is nothing other than what he makes of himself,' the chapter argues morality lies in the freedom to choose and in living with the consequences: Duck's refusal to accept his choice, not the choice itself, is the failure, and the Final Five revelation cannot retroactively alter choices made in good faith by Tigh, Tyrol, Anders and Foster. Which side holds the ethical high ground may simply be whichever side won and gets to write history.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 21 "“I Am Moana!”" — Stages Moana's dilemma between her father's Aristotelian essentialism — everything on Motunui has a fixed function, so Moana's essence as chief precedes her birth — and Sartre's existence precedes essence, with Heihei the unchanging chicken as a being whose essence really does precede existence. Tui embodies bad faith and the crowd (his own aborted voyage left him enforcing 'no one goes beyond the reef'), while Tala and then Moana live authentically through anguish, forlornness, and despair, until 'I am Moana!' marks her self-defined identity. Nietzsche's 'become who you are' and 'what does not destroy me makes me stronger' frame her resilience, which lets her free Maui ('Hook. No hook. I'm Maui.') and unmask Te Ka as Te Fiti whose stolen heart 'does not define you.'
- **Doctor Strange and Philosophy - The Other Book of Forbidden Knowledge**, ch. 6 "The Existential Redefinition of Doctor Strange" — DiGeorgio traces Strange's 'existential conversion' from scientific nihilism ('matter and nothing more') through Sartrean bad faith — playing the brilliant surgeon while not really believing life meaningless, refusing the Ancient One's widened keyhole — to authenticity. His hesitation to stay and fight after killing a zealot, and the Ancient One's 'it's not about you,' set up his choice to defend humanity as Sartre's universal decree, choosing for all humankind in anguish and freedom. The endless time loop imposed on Dormammu is read as Nietzsche's eternal recurrence demanding total commitment to one's choices, so that by the end Strange lives existence-precedes-essence: what he does, not his 'brilliant surgeon' essence, defines him.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 23 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Christopher Wood reads Cloud's arc as an existentialist quest: Heidegger's thrownness in Cloud's tumble off the Midgar train and his initial 'It's not my problem' denial of being-in-the-world; Nietzsche's death of God in Mako-powered Midgar's nihilism, with AVALANCHE as a call for revaluation of values and Sephiroth as a false aspirant god; and Sartre's bad faith in Cloud 'playing at being a SOLDIER,' a persona borrowed wholesale from Zack along with his sword and mercenary dream. Through the Lifestream reunion with Tifa, Cloud faces his fabricated past, admits 'I never was in SOLDIER,' and turns to authenticity by resolving to live without pretending, which Wood presents as the player's own existential task.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 31 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Daenerys's fatalism - she feels truly free only once she believes fate is in control - can coexist with freedom in a Westeros where class and gender fix everyone's essence. Aristotle's sea-battle argument from bivalence and Cicero's Idle Argument (Dany will rule whether or not she leaves Meereen) are dismantled as having no practical consequences for deliberation, while Sartre's anguish and bad faith explain Cersei's 'necessity' excuse for arresting Ned and Sansa's refusal to own her lie about Joffrey and Mycah. Heidegger's authenticity then resolves the paradox: like Ned choosing between family and honor and Jon choosing his Night's Watch vows over kinship, freedom is not escape from one's past but owning it - Heraclitus's 'character is destiny,' becoming who you are.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 19 "8. The Death of God and the Death of Meaning" — Reads Chidi's 'Jeremy Bearimy' breakdown — quoting Nietzsche's Parable of the Madman ('God is dead. God remains dead. And we have killed him') after learning he has been tortured for three hundred years — as the nihilism that follows the death of God, where the Judge's verdict that the humans seek only 'moral deserts' strips their moral project of purpose. Michael's post-crisis makeover party is Camus's embrace of the absurd (Sisyphus pushing the boulder), and Sartre's Existentialism Is a Humanism supplies the way out: abandonment, anguish, and the French Soldier dilemma clarify Eleanor's confession in Season One and her lie that she failed the Judge's test as authentic choices. Once there is no hope of the Good Place, the humans finally choose goodness for its own sake.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 13 "Why I Can Play Zelda for Four Hours Straight" — Toni Fellela gives an existentialist reading of Zelda, confessing she leaves Ocarina of Time and Twilight Princess permanently paused before the final Ganon fight because the meaning lies in the process of becoming, not the ending. Sartre's existence precedes essence structures Link's growth from a swordless Kokiri boy collecting equipment into the hero; Nietzsche's death of God ('we must become gods') fits Link restoring meaning to a godless Hyrule, while Camus's Sisyphus dignifies the repetitive drudge work of slashing grass for rupees. Viktor Frankl's logotherapy anchors the chapter's payoff: even the most mundane tasks — in a camp or a laundromat or Hyrule Field — become bearable and meaningful when connected to a future goal, which is why the author can play for four hours straight.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 10 "Responsibility" — Christiansen reads SNL's first head writer Michael O'Donoghue ('Mr. Mike') through Sartre: the Least-Loved Bedtime Tales (Brer Rabbit skinned alive, 'there's no moral... just random acts of meaningless violence') dramatize a world where existence precedes essence and narratives lie; 'Sartresky and Hutch' stages the absurd via a Vietnam veteran with PTSD; and the needles-in-the-eyes impressions embody Sartre's vulnerability to the Other, which Mr. Mike's dark glasses shut out. The chapter ends with Sartre's Marxist turn in the Critique of Dialectical Reason, arguing O'Donoghue's angry 'Police State' sketch shows that scarcity, alienation, and organized state violence are contingent and can be fought, which is where his nihilism leaves room for hope.
- **Saturday Night Live and Philosophy - Deep Thoughts Through the Decades**, ch. 32 "Getting the Joke" — Gray reads Jack Handey's Deep Thoughts and Fuzzy Memories as packaged existentialism: Sartre's existence precedes essence grounds Handey's responsibility for self-made meaning ('if you're robbing a bank and your pants fall down... life is funny'), Camus's absurd and Sisyphus's happy perseverance match 'sometimes I think the world has gone completely mad. And then I think, Aw, who cares?', and Beauvoir's ruts of inferiority warn against the ease of 'just sitting there' wanting money. Heidegger's authenticity and mortality appear in the parachute-swimming gag, dying laughing rather than in dread. The chapter also explains why the deadpan delivery over serene stream imagery makes morbidity funny, and worries that Handey's 'truth is... unreal' anticipated post-truth politics.
- **Superman and Philosophy - What Would the Man of Steel Do_**, ch. 35 "22. Unmasking the World and Its Heroes" — Claims the Superman-vs-Batman debate misses the point: both heroes are cave-escapers who must first see beyond appearances—Bruce renouncing vengeance on Joe Chill and then shaking Gotham from apathy (the ferries refusing the Joker's detonators), Clark learning from Jonathan and Jor-El that his powers are not for touchdowns but to lead humanity out by example. Masks serve the Socratic warning of the Apology that the just man must act privately to survive—Jonathan Kent dies keeping Clark's secret—yet risk becoming their own trap, from Smallville's Red Kryptonite ring to Batman's sonar surveillance that Lucius Fox calls too much power for one person. The chapter closes on Socratic ignorance and Man of Steel's genesis chambers: a hero, like Socrates, knows his wisdom is worth nothing, and anyone who chooses can be one.
- **True Blood and Philosophy - We Wanna Think Bad Things with You**, ch. 25 "NOTES" — Peppers-Bates and Rust stage Weber's disenchantment of the world in Sookie's relationship with Bill: her scientific-naturalist demand to know what animates him meets his 'magic', and although Searle and Nagel show consciousness resists scientific reduction (so 'miracle' is not absurd for the mind), Bill's vitalist, quasi-Cartesian dodge is a bait-and-switch about digestion. Sookie's real question is Sartrean — whether vampires, seemingly driven by blood bonds, hierarchy, and appetite, can freely choose their projects — and the chapter answers yes: Malcolm's cruelty presupposes he could do otherwise, Sookie's 'blood tie thing' excuse is bad faith in Eric's eyes, and Eric's wooing of her after regaining his memory is a freely chosen project that re-enchants her world.
- **True Detective and Philosophy - A Deeper Kind of Darkness**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Reads Cohle's arc as an existentialist passage toward authenticity, using Sartre's being-for-itself to explain why Hart's 'family man' identity is bad faith — a clinging to social roles that denies the freedom of a consciousness that is an activity, not a thing. Beauvoir's analysis of women as the passive, objectified Other illuminates why Rust, despite his nihilism, persistently protects vulnerable women and children such as Sophia, Dora Lange, and Marie Fontenot: threats to others' freedom threaten our own. Nietzsche's Silenus wisdom, the spirit of gravity on the tightrope, and the shepherd who bites the head off the snake frame Ledoux's and Childress' warped eternal return as the poison Cohle must overcome before he can will life eternally and declare 'the light is winning.'
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 25 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Kempner reads the comic through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old world gone, survivors like Rick, Michonne, and Dale must create their own values, while characters who cling to pre-apocalypse essences (Hershel keeping his zombified son in the barn, Shane waiting for the government) bring death on themselves. Rick's hospital awakening is treated as an existential rebirth in which his cop uniform is an 'essence precedes existence' trap, and Carl shooting Shane (and later Ben in 'Fear the Hunters') shows children making free choices outside conventional morality. The chapter concludes the series is 'sternly optimistic' because total freedom, not zombification, is what defines the humans: 'in a world ruled by the dead, we are forced to finally start living.'
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 17 "Conclusion An Infinity of Possibilities" — Kimberly Engels reads William's transformation into the Man in Black through Sartre's existential 'project': rather than discovering a pre-existing true self 'among the dead,' William's new situation in the park (loving and losing Dolores, killing the Confederados, Logan's betrayal) produces an existential rupture in which he chooses new ends, symbolized by trading the white hat for the black. She argues the Man in Black's claim to have 'found himself' is Sartrean bad faith, denying his freedom and facticity to evade responsibility for the harm he causes. Extending existentialism to androids, she reads Maeve's choice to leave the train and seek her daughter as her first freely formulated project, the start of her own 'infinity of possibilities.'
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Donovan uses the New 52 Azzarello run's gods as a catalogue of gender stereotypes - jealous Hera hunting Zola, woman-incinerating Apollo, hyper-masculine First Born, self-sacrificing Demeter - then tracks Hera's transformation after Apollo makes her mortal as a Beauvoirian passage from immanence (being Zeus's Other, defined by his desire) to transcendence (charting an independent identity, aiding baby Zeke). Foucault's Panopticon explains how gender norms are internalized without an enforcer, and Butler's drag example grounds the claim that Wonder Woman accepting the god of war mantle - leading a female Amazon army 'not as your princess but as the god of war' - is a subversive performance of gender.
- **X-Men and Philosophy - Astonishing Insight and Uncanny Argument in the Mutant X-Verse**, ch. 7 "X-Men and Philosophy" — This block finishes Davis's essay (Xavier's 'good nonsense' rules vs. Magneto/Dennett/Hobbes evolutionary morality) then runs several more. Robichaud's 'Professor X Wants You' weighs whether Storm should join the X-Men or Brotherhood using Nozick's experience machine (Rogue vs. 'Eugor') for well-being and Dworkin's civil-disobedience tiers for when violent resistance is permissible. Housel's 'X-Women' reads Jean Grey, Rachel Summers, Scarlet Witch, Storm, Mystique, Rogue, and Kitty through Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' bad faith, Ortega's project, and Baudrillard. McWilliams uses Singer's speciesism and human-rights declarations to ask if mutants deserve moral consideration and whether torture/experimentation on them can be justified. Darowski reads Deadpool's fourth-wall breaks as postmodern metafiction raising Plato's-cave ontological questions.
- **The Philosophy of Ang Lee**, ch. 22 "The Philosophy of Ang Lee" — Koepsell reads The Ice Storm as an existentialist masterpiece dramatizing Sartre's Being and Nothingness in Nixon's America. He maps Paul's Fantastic Four 'negative space/void' monologue onto Sartrean no-thing-ness and the tension between being-in-itself, being-for-itself and being-for-others, arguing the alienated, bourgeois Hoods and Carvers live inauthentically in bad faith, objectifying one another. Mikey's joyous reveling in the ice storm before his electrocution is a fleeting authentic immersion in existence (like Roquentin in Nausea), and the closing embraces—Wendy hugging Sandy, a weeping Ben meeting Paul—show characters momentarily overcoming alienation and freely remaking their essence.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 14 "“I am not an I” Performative (Self)Identity in the Poetry of Bob Kaufman" — Pynn reads Bob Kaufman's poems ('Forget To Not,' 'Would You Wear My Eyes?,' 'Benediction,' 'Jail Poems') as enacting a performative, intersubjective selfhood: against Beauvoir's 'flavor of death' in American conformity and Sartre's dictum that existence precedes essence, Kaufman replaces the drive to invincibility with 'nakedness' and vulnerability. Merleau-Ponty's embodied intercorporeity and Buddhist ontology—impermanence, non-self, compassion, and ahimsa—let the poet's 'I am not an I' burn the isolated ego into a communal 'thousand me's,' with slavery's trauma inscribed on the body and Kaufman's 1963 Buddhist vow of silence as liberating practice.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 18 "John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism" — Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 27 "William Burroughs as Philosopher From Beat Morality to Third Worldism to Continental Theory" — Jones Irwin makes the case for 'Burroughs as philosopher,' tracing an 'impassioned moralism' and antihumanism (human as adjective, not noun) that separates him from other Beats and postmodernists. He links Burroughs's critique of alienation to Marcuse's One-Dimensional Man and to Sartrean existentialism and bad faith ('there are no victims, just accomplices'), and reads the Beats' 'third force' Third Worldism via Freire, Fanon's Wretched of the Earth, and Paz. Close readings of Naked Lunch's 'Bradley the Buyer' and the sex-and-death delirium of 'AJ's Annual Party' connect Burroughs to Artaud's body without organs, Bataille's Sadean tradition, and Derrida's deconstruction of embodiment and 'distance touching.'
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 22 "Human Nature and Freedom in Adaptation" — Ganssle uses Adaptation's four main characters to test Sartre's claim that existence precedes essence against Walker Percy's account of immanence and transcendence. Laroche, endlessly adaptable ('Done with fish'), embodies Sartrean radical freedom and pure immanence; Donald owns his love ('You are what you love, not what loves you') and lives without bad faith; Orlean and Charlie are paralyzed in bad faith, unable to choose. Ganssle contrasts Sartre's rejection of a fixed human nature (grounded in atheism, against Plato's and Augustine's Forms) with Percy's view that persons are unlike infinitely mutable orchids, arguing the film sides with Percy: the antiessentialist self is 'lost in the cosmos.'
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 24 "“What Kind of Man Are You ” The Coen Brothers and Existentialist Role Playing" — Gaughran argues the Coens presuppose an absurd, valueless world (announced by Blood Simple's 'you're on your own' voice-over) in which characters must, per Sartre's 'existence precedes essence,' invent a self by adopting a style. He surveys the hats of Miller's Crossing, Everett's Dapper Dan dandyism in O Brother read through Camus's The Rebel, and Ed Crane of The Man Who Wasn't There as a Meursault-like figure who forges an identity through violence. Against Camus, murder and suicide are illegitimate revolts, and Sisyphus—not the nihilistic killers—stands as the true absurd hero who never resolves the tension between mind and indifferent world.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 26 "Thinking beyond the Failed Community Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn’t There" — Palmer reads Blood Simple and The Man Who Wasn't There as a diptych re-composing James M. Cain's The Postman Always Rings Twice and Double Indemnity, whose core theme is a failed community where self-interest poisons human bonds. Blood Simple dramatizes the Cainian problem—Visser and the others destroyed by instrumentalization and fatal miscommunication—while The Man Who Wasn't There, framed by Camus's The Stranger and Sartre's Nausea, stages its utopian solution. Ed's Sartrean disgust at hair and physicality drives his dry-cleaning scheme; like Meursault he kills and is condemned for the wrong crime, but unlike Cain's solipsistic heroes he ends yearning for communion with Doris beyond the grave, imagining the restoration of the lost community.
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 6 "The Peculiarities of Free Will" — This file collects Part I chapters 1-5. It argues Whedon's heroes (Angel, Buffy, Spike, Simon, Echo, Captain America) achieve authentic selfhood by resisting depersonalizing forces, reading their 'angst' through Heidegger and Sartre while insisting Whedon is more Socratic than existentialist because he affirms objective goods, synthesized via a Rawlsian just society. It then adds Aristotle on friendship and community (Toy Story, Jayne, Angel's team) and defends an atheistic ethics grounding natural rights in Locke and Kant plus Aristotelian virtue (Spike's re-ensoulment), using the Euthyphro to reject divine-command theory. The title chapter argues Whedon's paradoxical portrayal of free will in The Shepherd's Tale, Dollhouse and Cabin fits neither hard determinism nor compatibilism but Robert Kane's libertarian self-forming actions.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Barad uses Blade Runner to test what distinguishes humans from machines. Against Turing's claim that indistinguishable input-output makes a computer a mind, she deploys Sartre's dictum that in humans existence precedes essence while manufactured replicants (like a designed android) have essence first, so they can blame their maker. She reads the Voigt-Kampff empathy test through Sartrean forlornness and despair, and argues Roy Batty achieves authentic humanity when he kills Tyrell and freely chooses to save Deckard, becoming a life-giver rather than his programmed combat model.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 10 "Recalling the Self Personal Identity in Total Recall" — Biderman uses Quaid/Hauser in Total Recall to test criteria of personal identity: the body criterion fails on Kuato and George sharing a body, the brain and Lockean memory criteria fail on implanted false memories and memory gaps, and psychological continuity fails on how radically Quaid differs from the malicious Hauser. Facing Hume's conclusion that the self is a fiction (echoed by Wittgenstein and Derrida's deconstruction), he argues Quaid escapes it through the Sartrean existential route: thrown into existence, he takes a stance toward his facticity and, following Kuato's 'you are what you do,' authentically creates himself by rejecting Hauser and saving Mars.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 19 "“Back Off to What ” The Search for Meaning in The Wild Bunch" — Richard Gaughran reads Peckinpah's The Wild Bunch as an existentialist western set in 1913, a world 'unhinged' by Nietzsche's death of God where no a priori values remain. Pike Bishop's code of loyalty ('when you side with a man you stay with him') keeps failing—he abandons Crazy Lee, Sykes, and Angel—showing, in Sartrean terms, that only action, not talk or intention, creates meaning. Dutch's question 'Back off to what?' opens onto the abyss; the Bunch's final suicidal march to rescue Angel is read as a Camusian act of revolt that fashions authentic meaning where none was given, saying 'Let's go!' rather than surrendering to the deathward drift.
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 15 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Barnwell argues that fatherhood can constitute the ultimate meaning of a man's life, answering the paradox that a meaningful life 'all about the kids' seems not to be about the father by noting fatherly acts are still the father's own freely chosen activities. He confronts Camus's Myth of Sisyphus – the worry that childrearing is endless pointless rock-pushing across generations – by insisting children, unlike rocks, have intrinsic value, and invokes the Sartrean existentialist idea that choosing an activity confers value on it (illustrated by his buying oatmeal for 'Sally').
- **Fatherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Dao of Daddy**, ch. 22 "FATHERHOOD PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Collins-Cavanaugh asks what makes a 'real' father, framing it as authenticity. He pairs Sartre's existentialist authenticity – free choice, anxiety, and the bad faith of adopting others' ready-made plans, with 'real cookie' and Derek Jeter examples – against Charles Taylor's dialogical authenticity, in which choices are made within a 'horizon of meaning' set by others. He argues authentic fatherhood combines both: a father must freely own his choices (provider dad vs nurturer dad) while grounding them in his child's needs, concluding he'll go bake cookies with his son Connor.
- **Dating – Philosophy for Everyone - Flirting With Big Ideas**, ch. 27 "DATING PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE" — Silber uses his own Match.com romance with Karin to argue that virtual 'meeting' differs phenomenologically from face-to-face meeting, which Buber's I-Thou (vs I-It) makes into a whole-being encounter that online traces and aspects cannot supply, invoking 'all real living is meeting.' He treats the dating market as a site of Kantian danger, contrasting price with the dignity of persons in the kingdom of ends, and warns that the market's efficiency threatens objectification and commodification. He then deploys Sartre's bad faith, facticity and transcendence, and 'existence precedes essence' to diagnose online self-misrepresentation (lying about height, age, photos) as inauthenticity, while briefly setting Derrida's 'nothing outside the text' against Plato's Phaedrus preference for speech over writing.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 77 "73. Hasan Minhaj as Philosopher Navigating the Struggles of Identity" — Singh reads Minhaj's comedy of identity through existentialism, arguing his call for 'authenticity' over the first generation's 'assimilation' (the 'American dream tax' and 'biryani' arguments about choosing one's life) enacts Sartre's existence-precedes-essence and rejection of bad faith. He frames Minhaj's Indian-American-Muslim conflict via Heidegger's thrownness and facticity and the move from the they-self (das Man) to authentic self, contrasting it with Sartre's facticity as a limit on freedom.
