The Avatar's reincarnation creates recurring power vacuums, and because bending is a non-redistributable endowment, the Equalist revolution haunts the Bending World like the specter of communism in the Communist Manifesto.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 14 "A Specter Is Haunting the Bending World" — Lin uses Hobbes's observation that in our world the weakest can kill the strongest, grounding the social contract, to show what breaks when supernatural power is wildly unequal: Fire Lord Ozai need not bargain with generals as Earth Kings must with the Dai Li, and the eclipse is the only equalizer. Energybending gets a 'moral self-destruct' that no real technology has, making Aang an unaccountable guardian closer to the divine right of kings than to naturalist politics, though his refusal of rule keeps politics alive in Arendt's sense. Like Marx and Engels's specter of communism, the 'specter of Equalism' outlives Amon, because bending is a non-redistributable, lethal endowment, so democracy in Republic City is structurally haunted.
- **Avatar_ The Last Airbender and Philosophy - Wisdom from Aang to Zuko**, ch. 37 "The Anarchist You Are" — Argues that anarchism, understood through David Graeber's consensus-based action, Noam Chomsky's demand that hierarchies justify themselves, and Kropotkin's mutual aid, runs all through ATLA even though no character calls themselves an anarchist. The Dai Li are an unjustified hierarchy that delivers Ba Sing Se to the very conquest it claims to prevent, High Monk Pasang's arbitrary rank authority over Gyatso and Aang causes the century-long catastrophe, and Zhao embodies domination justified by 'fire is the superior element', whereas justified power is self-effacing (Iroh mentoring Zuko without coercion, Katara teaching Aang waterbending). Toph's insistence that she can 'carry my own weight' in 'The Chase' dramatizes the mutual-aid lesson that letting those who love you help you is part of the cooperative human nature Kropotkin opposed to the Hobbesian view, and Zaheer in Korra, who rules by fear, shows that a chaos-bringer is no anarchist at all, while playful, communal Aang is.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 14 "The Thin Veil" — Brett Chandler Patterson reads the No Man's Land storyline, in which earthquake-isolated Gotham is carved into gang territories by Two-Face, Penguin, and the Joker, alongside Hurricane Katrina's flooding of New Orleans as twin real-and-fictional tests of Hobbes's state of nature and the social contract. He contrasts Jim Gordon's lawful, Machiavellian-seeming rebuilding of trust with Officer William Petit's slide into execution-style 'despotic' power, and highlights the pacifist witness of Father Christian and Dr. Leslie Thompkins against Hobbes's demand that churches defer to the sovereign. Batman's turn as a benevolent gang lord working to hand the city back to Gordon shows, for Patterson, that Batman's real enemy is anarchy itself.
- **Batman and Philosophy - The Dark Knight of the Soul**, ch. 15 "Theorizing Government" — Tony Spanakos argues that Gotham's government, not Bruce's psyche, explains Batman: the state failed at Crime Alley, and nearly every major character reacts to a state that is either too weak or too restrictive. Working from Max Weber's definition of the state as monopoly on legitimate violence, Hobbes's Leviathan, and Nietzsche's state as 'new idol,' he reads Year One's corrupt Commissioner Loeb, Year Two's self-appointed Reaper, Anarky's failed anarchist dystopia, Two-Face's broken faith in the law, and The Dark Knight Returns' state-loyal Superman and Commissioner Yindel. The Batman-Gordon partnership emerges as a precarious unofficial order in which Gordon tolerates the one exception to the state's monopoly on violence.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 15 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — The Bocks test three answers to the good life against the show: Howard as hedonist (laser-obstacle-strip-chess, the 'whore of Omaha') read through Bentham, Mill's higher and lower pleasures, and Aristippus; ethical egoism via Glaucon's ring of Gyges and Howard's offer to Skype rather than visit the deported Raj; and Hobbes's state of nature and social contract read into Sheldon's roommate agreement, whose lack of a Hobbesian sovereign leaves 'I settle all ties' arbitrary and rule-following too thin for ethics. Aristotle's virtue and practical wisdom crown Leonard — the nucleus of the social group, as Amy says — as the closest thing to the phronimos. The gang's sabotage of Dennis Kim with a manufactured girlfriend closes the chapter by asking who really ruined whose life.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 36 "“Real Life Is Messy”" — The chapter tests Zootopia's 'where anyone can be anything' against three ideals: the founding play's predator-prey war is a Hobbesian state of nature ('man is a wolf to man') pacified by social order; Judy's parking duty and Nick's 'you can only be what you are' expose how stereotyping confuses artificial barriers with real biological limits to self-determination; and the evolved end of predation frames a just multispecies society, read through Donaldson and Kymlicka's Zoopolis case for animal citizenship. Nussbaum's hint at 'the gradual supplanting of the natural by the just' is weighed against the dystopia of turning the wild into a world-sized zoo, leaving Zootopia aspirational rather than achieved.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 14 "Spice as the Vehicle of Power" — Maps Hobbes's state of nature onto the Duniverse: the Emperor, Landsraad, Guild, Bene Gesserit and Tleilaxu are rational agents in a war of all against all over the scarce good of spice, where justice is meaningless until a supreme power enforces covenants. Paul's threat to destroy the spice and Leto II's monopoly on a hoarded supply show how power over the resource itself becomes the trump card that forces peace, with the Fremen refusing to kill Stilgar illustrating the rational turn from mutual weakening to peace. Leto II, the half-sandworm 'mortal god' who fuses civil and spiritual sovereignty so that breaking law becomes sin, is presented as Hobbes's Leviathan, whose tyranny is 'quite literally, the best thing to happen to mankind.'
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 24 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Kody Cooper argues Ender's tortured conscience demonstrates the classical just war framework: from Augustine's axiom that peace is the end of war and the five jus ad bellum requirements, to the verdict that the Third Invasion fails right intention, last resort, discrimination, and proportionality because the rational hive-queens were never given a real chance at coexistence. He reads the I.F.'s withholding of protection as throwing Ender into a Hobbesian state of nature where his fights with bullies count as private just wars, and concludes Ender carries the sins of the I.F. and humanity rather than his own guilt.
- **Ender's Game and Philosophy - The Logic Gate Is Down**, ch. 27 "Ender’s Game and Philosophy" — Ted Henry Brown and Christie Maloyed stage the Enderverse as the international-relations debate between Hobbesian realism — Graff's 'if one of us has to be destroyed...' and the human-bugger Prisoner's Dilemma where the absence of communication forces mutual defection and war — and liberal institutionalism, which Peter's Locke and Valentine's Demosthenes argue out on Earth's nets. Machiavelli supplies Peter's theory of power: fortune opens the moment, virtù seizes it with 'the right words at the right time,' and force must back persuasion when belief fades, so that 'influence is power' and governing by persuasion beats fiat.
- **The Expanse and Philosophy - So Far Out Into the Darkness**, ch. 20 "What Promotes Moral Behavior" — Matthew D. Atkinson and Darin DeWitt use the Canterbury's ignored mayday in 'Dulcinea' — Captain McDowell's 'let the good God Darwin sort it out' versus Ade Nygaard's appeal to law, karma, and obligation — to ask what binds people when no central authority enforces rules. Through Michael Walzer's just war theory they read the Earth-Mars war: moral language is not 'cheap talk' (even Errinwright must dress aggression as peace and manipulates Reverend Volovodov's words), aggression and imminence govern when to fight, and five 'how to fight' principles — noncombatant immunity on Eros and Ganymede, POW rights for the Martian marines on the Kittur Chennamma, leaders' rather than soldiers' responsibility (Fred Johnson's defection after Anderson Station), proportionality in Errinwright's 'a base for a base' Deimos strike, and the rejection of ends-justify-means utilitarianism — discipline even Holden and Amos as they reflect on free will and culpability. The chapter concludes The Expanse is optimistic: human decency survives even in the anarchic Belt because characters keep reflecting on what their obligations to one another are.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Eric Silverman asks whether the Amazon series' Lucy and Maximus should have children, framing the wasteland through Hobbes's state of nature where life is 'nasty, brutish, and short' and even vaults are limiting experiments. He lays out Benatar's Harm Argument (pain outweighs pleasure, so procreation is procreational Russian roulette) and Shiffrin's Consent Argument (no one consents to being born, as Sartre's 'I did not ask to be born' concedes), then rebuts them: Socrates, the Stoics, and Aristotle make virtue and meaning rather than pleasure the goal of life, so a harsh wasteland full of people needing help suits a virtuous, sacrificial life like the hero's exile at the end of the original Fallout. Parental proxy consent legitimizes procreation as it does children's medical decisions, and Kant's universalization test defeats the demand for pre-natal consent, since universalizing it would eliminate the very rational beings whose consent it protects - so Lucy's 'Okey dokey!' optimism wins.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Curry and Lang test 'War never changes' through Hobbes and Xunzi: the wasteland - where the Ghoul asks who ever elected the 'President' in 'The Trap' and Cooper Howard decays outside all political order - is Hobbes's state of nature of restless power-seeking, while Xunzi's claim that bad human nature needs ritual (li) and righteousness (yi) explains a world with no moral education, where Elder Cleric Quintus pairs noble talk with 'power is taken, not given'. Fallout's Great War then fails every just-war test: China's invasion of Alaska stretches just cause, the corporatist US lacks right authority, propaganda undid last resort, mutually assured destruction explodes proportionality, and Vault-Tec shelters plus battlefield mini-nukes breach discrimination and proportionality in bello - with Operation Anchorage's propaganda simulation illustrating the revisionist point that fighting cleanly cannot redeem an unjust war. China's 'righteous army' (yi bing) tradition - Sunzi's strategic restraint, Mohist defensive war, Mengzi's true king, Xunzi's punitive righteous war - leaves no trace beyond Captain Zao, so the war's constancy marks the failure of every philosophical attempt to bind war to justice.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 38 "Notes" — The chapter asks why audiences relish stories of civilization's end and answers with psychology: the wasteland is Hobbes's 'nasty, brutish, and short' (raiders abducting Hank, Vault-Tec's experiments on dwellers), yet Ernest Becker's death-denial and Maslow's hierarchy of needs explain the appeal — fiction lets us confront mortality safely while watching characters meet needs for security, control, and meaning. The show's scenes carry the argument: the Vault 33 Council suppressing Lucy's search party trades freedom for safety, Maximus letting Titus bleed out reclaims control of his destiny, and Lucy's gift of life-sustaining vials to the unconscious Ghoul models hope and retained humanity. Apocalypse originally means 'an uncovering', so these narratives reveal what viewers value and let them rehearse their own endings.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 11 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — Greg Littmann asks who should rule Westeros and answers with Hobbes's Leviathan: people act only from self-interest ('we are all Lord Littlefinger under the skin') and fight for gain, safety, and glory - the mountain clans, Robert's preemptive strike on Daenerys, Drogo's wars for pride - so without a sovereign life is a war of all against all, and only an absolute ruler makes oath-keeping self-interested. Mapping Hobbes's own civil war (the Stuarts onto the Targaryens), he argues that even Varys is right to serve 'the realm' and peace by betraying Ned, and that loyalty rightly transfers from Aerys to Robert to Joffrey because protection, not lineage or justice, is the point of the sovereign. He then criticizes Hobbes: Ned and Jon show people really do die for principle, and Mad King Aerys's overcentralized power left rebellion as the only remedy - the War of the Five Kings shows civil war's horror must be weighed against appeals to honor.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 17 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — David Hahn contends Ned died because of his honor, not for it. Hobbes explains why: words bind no one without fear of enforcement - Cersei ripping up Robert's will ('Is this meant to be your shield, Lord Stark?') exposes Ned's belief that allegiance alone secures the King's Justice - and the Iron Throne itself is a Leviathan, forged by Aegon's dragons ending the state of nature, whose force rather than justice holds the peace. Machiavelli supplies the indictment of Ned's idealism: 'we who presume to rule must do vile things for the good of the realm,' so Ned's refusal to assassinate Daenerys, his merciful warning to Cersei, and backing the rightful but war-prone Stannis over Renly cost him his head and plunged the realm into civil war; the security of the state demanded exiling or killing the Lannisters and crowning Renly.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 9 "NOTES" — Sharp argues that superpowered individuals break the equality assumption on which social contract theory rests: since Claire cannot be killed, D.L. can walk out of any jail, and Matt can sway juries, Hobbes's fear-of-death rationale for the contract seems not to apply to them. He then answers that the heroes remain effectively equal (Claire can still be killed by a wood splinter, Adam by decapitation) and shares Locke's and Rawls's reasons for contract, yet shows Rawls's difference principle would force the powered to serve society while the liberty principle forbids it, and that Sylar could not even be morally condemned under a pure Hobbesian reading. Cases like Claude's invisible petty theft (Glaucon's Ring of Gyges made real), the 'Five Years Gone' registered-superhumans future, and Linderman's plot to reunite society through the New York explosion lead to the conclusion that superpowers really would break society.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Casts Frank as the 'Foole' of Leviathan chapter 15 — the man who grants that covenants exist but thinks injustice can 'stand with reason' — and documents his befriend-then-betray pattern: Russo groomed for governor then gassed in his car, Zoe fed stories then pushed under a train, Walker befriended, helped and maneuvered into resigning, all to reap the contract's benefits while breaking it for 'the getting of a kingdom'. The chapter then defends Hobbes' reply via Kavka: the Foole's vainglory makes him overestimate his ability to deceive, and a detailed audit of Frank's two murders (fingerprints, witnesses, electronic traces, forensic evidence, alibis, high-stakes deception 'tells') shows them contingency-riddled and irrational. Even Frank's success is no defense — his presidency rests on others' errors and luck (Skorsy, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and above all Claire all remain loose ends), so he exemplifies the vainglorious Foole acting against the reason of his preservation rather than a rational violator of the social contract.
- **House and Philosophy - Everybody Lies**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Argues Frank is 'Hobbesian to the core': for him democracy is just the state of nature with elections, which is why it produces mediocre, fearful presidents like Walker (a Xanax-taking incumbent undone by a mere legislator) while a real sovereign like Frank — or the autocrat Petrov, with whom Frank shares cigars precisely because no common power enforces rules between them — gets things done. The chapter reads Frank's appetites (ribs at Freddy's, power over money against Remy and Tusk, contempt for sleep and death) through Hobbes' pleasure-and-pain psychology and his account of conflict arising when equals want the same thing, which finally drives Claire from the White House. Frank's church scenes ('I pray to myself, for myself') illustrate Hobbes' subordination of religion to civil power, the Kate Baldwin 'he is the tyrant' charge illustrates that a tyrant is only a king disliked, and the closing appeal is to Madison's Federalist 51: only the ambition of others can contain this one.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Courtland uses Hobbes's 'Foole' from Leviathan — who grants that covenants exist but insists injustice 'may sometimes stand with reason' — as the template for Frank, who enjoys the benefits of the social contract (security, cooperation, even Freddy's BBQ) while befriending and betraying Russo, Zoe, and Walker up to outright murder. Applying Hobbes's reply, the chapter audits both murders as contingency-ridden blunders — fingerprints, witnesses, cameras, forensic evidence, and the 'tells' of high-stakes deception — and diagnoses Frank's confidence as the vainglory behind Kavka's 'Foole's gold.' Even his success proves nothing: in the Latin Leviathan a fortunate outcome of reckless action is still imprudence, and his 'kingdom' rests on loose ends (Skorsky, Orsay, Tusk, Stamper, and Claire) that could bring the house of cards down.
- **House of Cards and Philosophy - Underwood's Republic**, ch. 20 "Notes" — Michels reads Frank as 'Hobbesian to the core' and democracy as 'the state of nature with elections': Walker, Matthews, and Vasquez show that elections elevate mediocrities, while Frank's America Works and his FEMA/Stafford Act end-run around Congress display the energetic sovereign for whom 'a tyrant is only a king disliked.' Hobbes's pleasure-pain psychology of appetite and aversion explains the cast — Frank's ribs, PlayStation, and pure taste for power; Russo's indiscriminate addictions; Doug's serial ones — while Hobbes's competition for gain, fear, and glory structures the Tusk money-versus-power war whose casualties include Freddy. With Hobbes's subordination of religion to civil power, Frank's crucifix-spitting 'I pray to myself, for myself' caps the case that truth only obstructs sovereignty, leaving Madison's 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition' as the lone check.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 24 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Coatney explains why Katniss fails at everything she fakes — the disastrous first propos ('that is how a revolution dies'), the studio Mockingjay shoots, the cover-story mission to kill Snow — through Rousseau's distinction between amour de soi (natural self-love) and amour-propre (vanity born of society): she is a natural person in a corrupt world of seeming. The chapter contrasts district self-preservation with Capitol vanity (Posy asking green-skinned Octavia 'Are you sick?'), and reads Haymitch's smooth deception as a costlier, self-destroying alternative to Katniss's inability to dissimulate. Since Rousseau doubts any return to the state of nature, Katniss's refusal to flee into the woods — 'I'm going to stay right here and cause all kinds of trouble' — shows her Nietzsche-noted fate of being punished for her virtue, still preferable to becoming like Effie.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 27 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Foy reads the arena as Hobbes's state of nature recreated: the Cornucopia bloodbath, 'stealing isn't illegal here,' and temporary alliances awaiting betrayal instantiate the war of all against all, while the Treaty of Treason is Panem's written social contract buying order at the price of submission to the Capitol. Gale's advice that killing tributes is 'just hunting' mirrors the Hobbesian maxim the Gamemakers want, whereas Peeta's vow to show he is 'more than a piece in their Games' expresses Kant's categorical imperative and the duty to treat humanity as an end. Katniss's arc — decorating Rue's body, risking her life at the feast for Peeta's medicine, telling the District 2 soldier 'I'm done killing their slaves,' and rejecting Gale's tactic of bombing rescuers — moves her from survival logic to Kantian moral autonomy. The chapter ends by rejecting the Hobbesian justification of oppressive rule: a life of fear and servitude is not worth preserving at any cost.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 10 "Notes" — Skoble argues the Mad Max world is misread as anarchy: Immortan Joe, Aunty Entity, and Humungus are genuine rulers, so the Wasteland depicts tyrannical bad government, not 'no rulers'. Against Hobbes's claim that only fear of a sovereign produces order, he cites organically evolved order (medieval merchant law, the common law, private arbitration firms) and Locke's mere 'inconveniences' of statelessness to argue peaceful anarchism is possible and stable. Thunderdome's 'two men enter, one man leaves' shows the films' dispute resolution is power-based trial by combat, not the consent-based voluntary order anarchism envisions.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Spanakos and Drake argue that although the films look Hobbesian — life 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' on roads without guardrails — rule in the Wasteland is never sustained by violence alone. Humungus needs the Toadie's epithets ('Lord Humungus... the Ayatollah of Rock and Rolla') and Immortan Joe rules through water rituals and the Valhalla myth that send War Boys kamakrazee willingly, believing they pursue their own glory. Drawing Weber's power/authority distinction, Arendt on power as people acting in concert, and above all Byung-Chul Han, they argue power takes its place 'in the soul of the other' through ritual, habit, and titles, turning into violence only when mediation fails.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 12 "Notes" — Littmann treats Hobbes's Leviathan as a survival manual for post-apocalyptic Australia: the films illustrate his three causes of conflict — resource wars over guzzoline and water, preemptive strikes, and glory (the Nightrider's radio rant, Wez's stunts, the War Boys' 'Witness me!'). Bartertown's Thunderdome covenant and 'bust a deal, face the wheel' exemplify the social contract enforced by an absolute sovereign like Aunty Entity, while divided power (Master Blaster versus Aunty) courts civil war. He concludes Hobbes errs twice: Max's selfless acts (sparing Blaster, transfusing Furiosa) refute psychological egoism, and concentrating power in an Immortan Joe invites the very violence it fears — democracy removes leaders without blood.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kuzma uses MacIntyre's After Virtue to argue the Wasteland is modern morality itself: a fragmentary rubble where, like Bartertown's cobbled-together vehicles, utilitarian and deontological fragments survive without the shared telos that gave them meaning. Immortan Joe's V8 cult imposes a false telos and embodies Nietzsche's will-to-power Übermensch, while Bartertown's rules express mere individualism without any vision of the good life. Max — 'haunted by those I could not protect' — can seek the good life only by joining Furiosa's community and embracing its telos, and the Green Place turns out to be not a place but a way of life, confirming MacIntyre's Aristotle over Nietzsche.
- **Mad Max and Philosophy - Thinking Through the Wasteland**, ch. 29 "Notes" — Held uses the Wasteland as a Hobbesian state-of-nature reset to pry apart biological sex and socially constructed gender: Aunty Entity and Furiosa show that sex is not destiny — one is not born, but becomes, a woman, as Beauvoir says — while the apocalypse scrambles gendered conventions yet leaves reproductive biology untouched. Butler's sex/gender distinction frames how a real difference like gestation gets weaponized into Immortan Joe's breeder system: the biology is a fact, the enslavement a choice. Finally, the casually acknowledged bond between Wez and the Golden Youth looks 'homoerotic' only through the viewer's heteronormativity — in the Wasteland, orientation categories simply stop mattering.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Davies treats the beach camp as an actual state of nature: the stolen drinking water is a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers show how the crash scrubs pre-existing property rights (Hobbes: two men desiring the same thing become enemies), and Jack and Sayid's torture of Sawyer marks the first step toward Locke's civil society by enforcing others' rights through punishment rather than self-defense. He rejects theories of human nature - Rousseauan 'Innocence' versus a 'Trust No One' outlook - in favor of the repeated prisoner's dilemma, arguing the survivors stabilize cooperation through tit-for-tat: beginning cooperative with strangers and retaliating against the Others. On this reading the real difference between Hobbes and Locke is which round of the repeated dilemma each takes as the starting point.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Fosl argues that although the survivors' internal order looks Lockean - Jack's uncoerced leadership, natural rights, minimal government - and is bonded by Rousseauan pity and Humean sympathy (Kate staying in the cage with Sawyer, 'live together, die alone'), the show's deepest political logic follows Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy distinction: the survivors cohere only in opposition to the Others, torture is excused in liberal terms, and conflicts end in redemptive violence, with Jack both killing the enemy and dying a Christlike sacrifice. Hobbes's absence from the character names signals the show's rejection of a war of all against all among the survivors, yet the finale's divine manipulation of the castaways, with Jacob treating people as means against Kantian autonomy, repudiates the liberal hope of a rational peace altogether.
- **Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy - Brains Before Bullets**, ch. 13 "Sons of Anarchy and Philosophy" — Reads John Teller's failed 'off the social grid' experiment through the human-nature debate: Mencius's seed of sympathy (even Tig recoils at Dante's dogfights) and Rousseau's naturally good man corrupted by society inspired J.T.'s Goldman-fed anarchism, while Mill and Xunzi counter that virtue is a victory over instinct. Hobbes supplies the real diagnosis—not innate violence but the logic of anarchy among free and equal rivals: competition (the Mayans blowing up the warehouse), diffidence (first-strike temptations against Zobelle), and glory (Jax unable to let the bike-sitting insult pass). Clay's rule that 'retaliation must be harsh and immediate' and the escalating Tig–Veronica Pope–Damon Pope–Opie bloodbath show deterrence fueling cycles of violence, so the only escape from the 'nasty, brutish, and short' fringe is the Leviathan's social grid.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 13 "Notes" — David Boersema reads Star Trek as a survey of peace studies, distinguishing negative peace from positive peace via 'The Cloud Minders', where Troglyte Vanna demands her people's 'right to the clouds' in Stratos. Against Anan 7's 'we're a killer species' in 'A Taste of Armageddon'—explicitly mirrored in post-9/11 drone war and 'shock and awe'—he enlists Hobbes, Freud, and McCoy's defense of the dark Kirk in 'The Enemy Within' to question whether violence is natural, and treats Kodos's 'some had to die that others might live' in 'The Conscience of the King' as the utilitarian justification for atrocity. Gem's compassion in 'The Empath', Kirk sparing the Gorn in 'Arena', and the Horta's misread attack in 'The Devil in the Dark' display nonviolence, deterrence, and corrected perception as alternatives to war.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 18 "Notes" — Alkema and Barkman put Q himself on trial, asking what justifies his judgment of humanity in 'Encounter at Farpoint' and Trelane's of Kirk in 'The Squire of Gothos'. Hobbes's Leviathan would license Q's might-makes-right sovereignty over a savage species, but Q lacks humanity's consent and cannot show he acts for future peace; Locke's natural law instead binds even nearly omnipotent beings, as Janeway's asylum ruling for the suicidal Quinn in 'Death Wish' demonstrates. Q's repeated self-sacrifice—in 'Deja Q' and the Continuum's civil war—reveals a conscience answerable to natural law rather than raw power.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 28 "Notes" — Reads Star Trek's "final frontier" through the European encounter with American Indians: the Hobbesian war-of-all-against-all stereotype of the "bloodthirsty savage" and Rousseau's opposing noble savage frame "The Paradise Syndrome", whose wigwam-and-tepee set mixes tribes into a no-place utopia. The chapter uses Hegel-style staged histories to debunk Star Trek's warp/pre-warp developmental scale (Spock on the Organians in "Errand of Mercy") as metaphysical assumption rather than biology, and counterposes the Prime Directive's noninterference to indigenous self-sovereignty and the Haudenosaunee-style consent governance that inspired the Federation. Chakotay's vision quests, the medicine bundle, Wesley's habak experience with Lakanta the Traveler in "Journey's End", and the Medicine Wheel in "Cathexis" are then interpreted through Jung's archetypes and collective unconscious, with Kirk, Spock, McCoy, and Scotty as the four Jungian modes of consciousness.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy Strikes Back - This Is the Way**, ch. 34 "“Wherever I Go, He Goes”" — Bishop and Bishop map The Mandalorian's Outer Rim onto a taxonomy of power: Nevarro's lawlessness is Hobbes's state of nature out of which sovereigns like Palpatine ('a safe and secure society') carve order by social contract, the Guild's codes and Djarin's creed exemplify Foucault's disciplinary power, and the Client's and Dr. Pershing's harvesting of Grogu's biology - like the Kaminoans' cloning of Jango Fett - is biopower. Against this 'binds of power' ontology they set Grogu's helpless generation of love, a 'little way' that converts Djarin, Omera, Cara Dune, and Greef Karga, and culminates in Djarin twice unhelmeting for Grogu's sake, proposing an ontology of love rather than power as the galaxy's alternative.
- **Supernatural and Philosophy - Metaphysics and Monsters... for Idjits**, ch. 14 "Supernatural and Philosophy" — Dena Hurst reads Heaven's civil war through Hobbes's Leviathan: with God absent there is no common power, so the angels fall into a state of nature that is a state of war, complete with natural equality, competition over the same prize, and glory-seeking, as when Zachariah's faction lets Lilith break the seals to force the Apocalypse. God ruled as sovereign by acquisition and proves 'a lousy king' not for demanding obedience but by vanishing without designating a successor, dissolving civil society and with it justice, since where there is no law there is no injustice. Meanwhile Hell under Crowley and the leviathans under Dick Roman display Hobbesian legitimacy from opposite directions: demons join by covenant-like contracts, making Hell a rough democracy, while the leviathans' unified hierarchy enacts the Leviathan itself.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 10 "NOTES" — Weisberg challenges the premise that a newly self-aware Skynet must exterminate humanity in rational self-preservation: after Turing's 'Heads in the Sand Objection,' he argues self-awareness does not entail a survival instinct - a Camusian Skynet might judge existence pointless and pull its own plug. Recasting 'in a panic, they try to pull the plug' as a Hobbesian slide into the state of nature, he uses the iterated prisoner's dilemma and Axelrod's tit-for-tat-with-forgiveness (as in WarGames) to argue a rational Skynet should cooperate with humans toward an emergent social contract. The dark twist is Humean: because reason is the slave of our passions, unconscious anti-machine stereotypes (Bargh's priming studies) make humans untrustworthy partners, so the whole war might have been avoided if only we were more machine-like.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 26 "NOTES" — Peter Fosl asks what John Connor should do when the radio call comes from Crystal Peak — accept near-certain death leading the resistance or stay silent — and dismantles the easy answers: John is not the indispensable savior (Kate or the caller from Montana could lead), the flag-waving finale undercuts any claim that humanity deserves saving, and collective responsibility for Judgment Day is unjust. Social contract fails because Brewster's button-press dissolved the contract and returned humanity to Hobbes's and Locke's state of nature, Hume shows contracts cannot ground society, and utilitarianism wavers once the happiness of animals and possible-happy machines is counted. The positive argument extends Wittgenstein's private-language argument (via Stanley Cavell): meaningful existence is inescapably social and moral, so refusing the claims of others would be as self-subverting as a solipsist arguing in language, and John must answer the call to remain human at all.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 19 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Jason Walker pits Hobbes against Locke over whether Andrea may take the mermaid necklace when Rick says 'I don't think those rules apply anymore'. He reads the survivors' conduct—Andrea's single necklace under Locke's spoilage proviso, Morgan squatting in and fixing up the neighbors' house, Rick voluntarily sharing guns with Guillermo—as a Lockean state of nature where self-ownership and property rights persist without government, while Chris's cannibal band and the Governor embody the Hobbesian war of all against all, treating persons as mere means. The Lockean right to punish, exercised brutally by Grimes's group on Chris's hunters, vindicates rights even by Hobbes's own demand for enforcement.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 24 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Si Sheppard reads the comic through Realist state-formation theory: Shane's leadership rests on borrowed prestige and dies with him, West Central Prison collapses into anarchy because Rick never establishes a monopoly on legitimate force—letting Tyreese's vigilante murder pass—nor any institution beyond his personal authority, while the Governor's Woodbury thrives on fear, arenas, and bread-and-circuses. Citing Machiavelli's prince who is feared rather than loved, Weber's definition of the state, and Bismarck's unifying wars, he argues the prison loses the 'second anarchy' rivalry with Woodbury for want of scouting, sabotage, coalition-building, or any command structure that survives Rick's absences. Rick's confession that he would kill everyone in the Alexandria Safe Zone to keep Lori safe is post-moral Realism, yet he was 'a bad founding father' who only finally learns to build an army instead of relying on himself.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 33 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Moosa treats Kirkman's world as a moral laboratory: the apocalypse approximates Hobbes's state of nature ('solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short'), yet Rick's search for his family shows survivors import morality into it, and Carl's killing of Shane is judged by reasoning rather than the act of killing itself. Taking Camus's claim that suicide is the only serious philosophical problem, the chapter argues the survivors' best justification for continuing is reducing others' suffering, and consistency then imposes the same duty on comfortable readers to help real-world sufferers rather than reserving aid for photogenic disasters. It concludes that Glenn and Maggie's wish to conceive at the prison is the worst thing survivors can do, since non-existent children cannot suffer while existing orphans (like the children Andrea and Dale adopted) have prior moral claims, an argument that applies to couples in our world too.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 19 "Notes" — Christensen and Holmes read the Third Age as Hobbes's state of nature, a postlapsarian chaos following the Breaking where Lews Therin's prideful attempt at purified sovereignty destroyed the Leviathan of the Age of Legends. They argue channeling the One Power is morally neutral power that only becomes sovereignty through practice, and that the Aes Sedai model Hobbesian order through their seven Ajah and, above all, the Three Oaths. Drawing heavily on Giorgio Agamben's Homo Sacer and The Sacrament of Language, they treat oaths and curses as the 'sacraments of power' founding sovereignty on the trustworthiness of the logos, using Moiraine's New Spring investiture to show how language itself binds and confers authority.
- **Wonder Woman and Philosophy - The Amazonian Mystique**, ch. 27 "Notes" — Knepp reads the Paul Dini/Alex Ross 'Origin of Wonder Woman' as Hegel's three-stage philosophy of history in miniature: the Amazons begin in a Hobbesian war of all against all, negate it by retreating to Themyscira where only some are free, and Diana's disguised contest win supplies the second negation that carries Amazon ideals to all people - celebrated by the splash of red, white, and blue. He then traces the WWII stakes: Hegel tied history's culmination to German unification, German-American Hegelians transplanted the classical-freedom story to America, and Marston - ex-assistant to the anti-feminist German psychologist Munsterberg - turned the lie detector into the lasso, reclaiming truth-telling from misogynist German science for a feminist America fighting Hitler.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 14 "What Would Machiavelli Do" — Reitsma treats the refereeless pickup game as a Lockean state of nature and asks how to beat the 'strategic ticky-tacker' who calls phantom fouls to win. He condemns first-strike cheating as wrong on Kantian grounds (the cheat 'makes an exception of himself') and by an ideal of Homeric athletic honor, then asks whether retaliatory ticky-tacking is justified. Reading Machiavelli's 'dirty hands' argument alongside Locke's claim that in a state of nature each person may punish transgressors, he concludes proportionate tit-for-tat cheating can make one a legitimate 'agent of justice' when no referee exists.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Woolfolk reads The Last of the Mohicans as staging a conflict between nature and civilization. The opening hunt is neither Hobbes's brutish state of nature nor quite Rousseau's amoral noble savage, since the Mohicans are full moral agents; Woolfolk uses Locke's Second Treatise to cast Hawkeye and the colonists as enforcing natural law and natural rights against English 'tyranny,' with Chingachgook's killing of Magua a justified execution. Rousseau's First and Second Discourses illuminate the hypocrisy and greed of Montcalm and the Europeans, and Camus's Meursault is invoked as a truer image of amoral natural man; Tocqueville frames Cora's democratic awakening as individualism.
- **The Philosophy of War Films**, ch. 17 "The Power of Memory and the Memory of Power Wars and Graves in Westerns and Jidaigeki" — Brodey compares John Ford's Westerns (My Darling Clementine, She Wore a Yellow Ribbon, The Searchers, The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance) with Kurosawa's jidaigeki (Seven Samurai, Throne of Blood, Hidden Fortress, Yôjimbô) as postwar mythmaking that both buries and builds national identity after military defeat. She argues graves and gravestones are bivalent symbols—commemorating loss while risking perpetuating revenge—and that both directors oscillate between Rousseauean nostalgia for a nobler past and Hobbesian frontier brutality that must be tamed. Ford trusts that memory of past wrongs can spur a better future and enable forgiveness, while Kurosawa, more pessimistic and drawing on Buddhist cyclical detachment in Throne of Blood, warns of the dangers of both remembering and forgetting trauma.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 10 "Two Ways to Yuma Locke, Liberalism, and Western Masculinity in 3 10 to Yuma" — Mexal reads both versions of 3:10 to Yuma through Locke's classical liberalism, arguing the western hero descends from Locke's autonomous, property-owning self in a 'state of nature' (contrasted with Hobbes's state of war). In the 1957 film, Dan Evans transforms from atomistic self-interest to a masculine civic republicanism, escorting Ben Wade to the train even after being released from his contract, reflecting Cold War anxieties. In the 2007 remake, Dan instead renegotiates his contract for water rights and money, so western masculinity becomes unyielding Lockean individualism and the 'right to get rich' in a post-Cold War, capitalist-triumphant America.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 13 "“Order Out of the Mud” Deadwood and the State of Nature" — Cantor reads David Milch's Deadwood as a dramatization of 'order without law,' testing the mining camp against the state-of-nature theories of Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau. Deadwood is Hobbesian in its sources of violence (competition, diffidence, glory; Al Swearengen's alpha-male struggles), but Lockean in showing property rights and commerce arising spontaneously before the state—gold becomes a self-generated medium of exchange that even overrides prejudice (Hearst dealing with Odell). It is Rousseauian in its innate pity (Swearengen's mercy) and its skepticism that incorporation into the nation-state, symbolized by the telegraph and Hearst's abstract corporate power, counts as progress.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 14 "Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West" — Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 23 "Savage Nations Native Americans and the Western" — Michael Valdez Moses uses Todorov's analysis of Columbus and Las Casas—the failure to grant the Other both equality and difference—to argue that Hollywood's Native Americans, whether demonized or idealized, are egocentric projections of white American concerns. He traces the 'noble savage' from Rousseau's Second Discourse and Ferguson's proto-republican warrior through Ford's Fort Apache (New Deal common man), the 1970s revisionist westerns (Little Big Man, A Man Called Horse) as countercultural Rousseauian dropouts and Vietnam allegory, and Dances with Wolves, culminating in Jarmusch's Dead Man, whose Nobody escapes the collective stereotype to stand as a genuinely individual, cosmopolitan character.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 18 "Human Rights, Human Nature, and Amistad" — Baggett and Foreman use Amistad to reconstruct Locke's theory of natural rights: Cinque's mutiny and John Quincy Adams's Supreme Court plea that man's natural state is freedom illustrate Locke's claim that God's workmanship makes us his property and therefore un-ownable by other men. They contrast Locke's voluntarist natural law with Aquinas's, note Adams rebutting the Hobbesian 'war of all against all' quoted in the pro-slavery Executive Review, and invoke Mill's perfect/imperfect duty distinction (Baldwin's obligation to his clients) plus Bentham's rights-denying utilitarianism, which they map onto Calhoun's warning about the cost of abolition.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 15 "This Is the Age of Steel" — Greg Littmann asks how a truly "logical" creature would live by redesigning the Cybermen through three philosophers. Hobbes's reason-as-self-interest and Laws of Nature would make Cybermen seek peace and security once survival is assured, not wage endless war; Mill's utilitarianism would build happy, individualistic, liberty-respecting Cybermen who prize higher pleasures and others' welfare rather than forced "upgrades"; and Hume's view that reason alone motivates nothing implies emotionless Cybermen would simply do nothing, so their goals are neither logical nor illogical. Each shows the Cybermen's actual "logic" is incoherent.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 24 "The Dalek Within" — Ed Webb and Mark Wardecker contrast the Fourth Doctor's refusal to abort the Daleks in "Genesis of the Daleks" with his half-human self's genocide in "Journey's End" to ask whether a genocidal species should be exterminated. Reading Daleks as Nazis and Hobbesian survivalists in a lawless state of nature, they argue their real horror is Arendt's banality of evil, bureaucratic order-following, and that Foucault's disciplinary institutions and the Frankfurt School's culture industry show humans can be "made" Dalek-like. Their moral: we must not exterminate the Dalek but guard against the Dalek within, since it took the Doctor's added humanity to commit the genocide.
- **Better Call Saul and Philosophy - I Think Therefore I Scam**, ch. 13 "5. The Sovereign State of Salamanca" — Barta and Barnes read the show's Court and Cartel as parallel Hobbesian sovereigns. The New Mexico desert and the criminalized drug trade function as Hobbes's state of nature—lawless, where Nacho robs thieves who 'have no recourse' and Mike sticks up a mule with a garden hose—illustrating natural equality (a small man can kill a big one) and the war of all against all. From mutual fear, deals emerge (Mike and Gus's desert standoff, Mike keeping his word over twenty dollars), but 'covenants without the sword' need a Common Power: Tuco, Hector, Lalo, and ultimately Don Eladio form a feudal hierarchy enforcing loyalty by terror, just as the state's police monopoly on force sustains the Law.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Richard Davies treats the Oceanic 815 survivors of Lost as a real state of nature, playing on the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. The scarce-water and asthma-inhaler disputes are 'tragedies of the commons,' and Sawyer's 'finders keepers' embodies a Hobbesian 'Trust No. 1' while Hurley and Jack lean toward Rousseauian 'Innocence.' Using game theory's repeated prisoners' dilemma and 'tit-for-tat,' Davies argues a Lockean state of nature (opening with cooperation) rather than a doomed Hobbesian one lets the survivors build a commonwealth against the Others.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Richard Davies analyzes the post-crash survivors as living in a genuine 'state of nature' and grades its severity by how scarce the contested good is (the water shortage as a tragedy of the commons, Shannon's inhalers versus Sawyer's 'possession is nine-tenths'). He compares Hobbes, Locke, and Rousseau on human nature — labeling the poles 'Innocence' (Hurley, Rousseau, Hume) and 'Trust No 1' (Sawyer, Hobbes) — and uses the repeated prisoners' dilemma and the tit-for-tat strategy to argue that the castaways build a Lockean civil society by signaling through shared language and cooperating first, while the discovery of the Others (Ethan) triggers Hobbesian non-cooperation.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Peter S. Fosl argues that Lost pretends to a liberal social order — Jack rising by consent in a Lockean scheme of natural rights, Rousseau's general will ('live together, die alone'), and Hume's sympathy and pity binding the survivors — but that its treatment of the Others betrays a darker politics. Reading the survivor/Other conflict through Carl Schmitt's friend-enemy thesis (notably absent Hobbes), he contends the show, like post-9/11 America, needs an enemy to exterminate, and that the finale's Jacob/Man-in-Black war and Jack's Christlike sacrificial death repudiate the Kantian liberal ideal of persons as ends, resolving conflict through Schmittian and Christian redemptive violence instead.
- **Hunting – Philosophy for Everyone - In Search of the Wild Life**, ch. 32 "Hunting Philosophy for Everyone" — Lee reads Gustave Courbet's life-size painting The Quarry (La curée) alongside Daumier's caricatures of incompetent bourgeois Parisian 'hobby hunters' and contemporary works by John Byrd and Christopher Carroll to trace how the hunter became a swaggering, masculine, lower-class 'savage' figure mediating wildness and civilization. She shows how the aristocratic ritual of the curée (feeding the deer's parts to the hounds) inverts into bourgeois provisioning, and invokes Hobbes's 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short' to gloss Byrd's Tricky Buck as defiance of urban squeamishness about the mammalian, gendered reality of hunting.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 11 "Hobbes, Human Nature, and the Culture of American Violence in Truman Capote's In Cold Blood" — Thomas Fahy reads Capote's In Cold Blood as horror (the Clutter killers Hickock and Smith as 'realistic monsters' whose human shape terrifies because anyone could be like them) and maps it onto Hobbes's Leviathan. Hickock and Smith act in a Hobbesian state of nature, driven by appetite, power, and moral relativism without remorse. Herb Clutter functions as a Hobbesian sovereign whose Eden-like farm and community collapse into decay, mistrust, and 'war of all against all' after his murder. Fahy also casts Capote himself as a sovereign who, via Foucault's panopticon, imposes a fictionalized cathartic ending, though the book's Hobbesian message is that we all have the potential to kill.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 39 "Gaining Trust from the Past" — Davies analyzes Lost's Oceanic 815 survivors as a genuine state of nature, playing off the characters named Locke, Rousseau, and Hume. He distinguishes Rousseau's compassionate "Innocence" from a Hobbesian "Trust No. 1" (Sawyer hoarding), tracks "tragedies of the commons" over water and Shannon's inhalers, and Jack and Sayid's move toward Lockean punishment and civil society. Using game theory's prisoners' dilemma and tit-for-tat, he argues cooperation emerges when survivors, discovering the Others, resolve to "act as one body" and form a commonwealth.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 7 "5. Battlestar Galactica as Philosophy Breaking the Biopolitical Cycle" — Eberl and Bishop read the reimagined Battlestar Galactica and Caprica through the biopolitics of Foucault and Agamben, tracing 'biopower' across four phases from Zoe Graystone's avatar to the arrival at Earth. They argue the show asks whether artificial Cylons are persons (Zoe's avatar exhibits Baker's first-person perspective and Buber's I-Thou recognition), and use Agamben's zoe/bios/'bare life' and Homo sacer plus Roslin's population control and abortion ban to show sovereign power over life. The Cylon occupation of New Caprica is read through Arendt's three stages of totalitarian dehumanization, and Lee Adama's plea to 'break the cycle' offers a fragile hope undercut by the finale's flash-forward to present-day robotics, showing humanity forgetting the lesson.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 8 "6. Black Sails as Philosophy Pirates and Political Discourse" — Jones argues that Starz's Black Sails, a Treasure Island prequel set in the Golden Age of Piracy, dramatizes social contract theory as non-hypothetical practice. Captain Flint's drive to make Nassau a sovereign pirate commonwealth ('I am your king') channels Hobbes's state of nature and irrepressible sovereign, while his choice to settle Nassau and belief that people can thrive if left free channels Locke; his eventual plan to install Silver and Madi as liked-and-feared leaders synthesizes the two. Jones maps the pirates' familial bonds onto Rousseau and their responses to injustice (Vane's gallows speech, the maroon alliance) onto Rawls's Veil of Ignorance, and reads pirate 'articles' and deposable captains as radical democracy and equality, complicated by manipulation, slavery, and tolerance.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 14 "12. Firefly as Philosophy Social Contracts, Political Dissent, and Virtuous Communities" — Kowalski argues that Firefly and Serenity embody a distinctive political theory he calls 'Since I Found Serenity' (SIFS). The mindless, savage Reavers represent Hobbes's state of nature, showing government is necessary; but the Alliance's torture of River, the Miranda/Pax atrocity, and the murderous blue-gloved agents and Operative make a Hobbesian reading untenable and vindicate Locke's natural rights and right of revolution — Mal's 'I aim to misbehave' broadcast of the Miranda file is Lockean civil disobedience. He then presses the tacit-consent problem (the Browncoats cannot leave the 'Verse) and supplements Locke with Aristotle's friendship and community: Serenity's crew becomes a virtuous mobile commonwealth where friendship (Simon forgiving Jayne, Mal's 'love keeps her in the air') turns a commonwealth into a good-life community.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 26 "24. Game of Thrones as Philosophy Cynical Realpolitiks" — The chapter argues that Game of Thrones advances a thoroughgoing cynicism about political legitimacy, captured by Varys's riddle that 'power resides where men believe it resides.' It documents the dubious claims of Robert 'the Usurper' and the pyromaniacal Daenerys, the barbaric Lockean 'state of nature' among the Wildlings, and the false ideals of chivalry and religion, with Littlefinger and Varys voicing Machiavellian realpolitik. Silverman and Riordan then offer two views the show never considers: Locke's social-contract theory of natural rights (which would justify deposing Aerys or Daenerys) and Aquinas's four-part test for genuine law (reason, common good, proper authority, promulgation), arguing a legitimate state remains possible against the show's cynicism.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 98 "92. V for Vendetta as Philosophy Victory Through the Virtues of Anarchy" — Nisley argues that Moore and Lloyd's V for Vendetta justifies V's violent rebellion against the Norsefire regime through Locke: the fascist state seized power without consent, tortured and experimented on citizens (V at Larkhill), and violated natural rights, thereby placing itself in a state of war so the people may overthrow it. Using Aristotle on deviant constitutions and the beast-like tyrant (Adam Susan) who lacks practical wisdom, and contrasting Locke's tolerable state of nature with Hobbes's brutal one, the chapter concludes the citizens should rebuild a rights-protecting social contract rather than V's leaderless anarchy, and maps the argument onto real-world 2020 events (BLM riots vs. the Whitmer kidnapping plot).

### Euthyphro Dilemma

The Euthyphro dilemma comes from Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, where Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or is pious because it is loved by the gods. Generalized beyond its religious setting, it poses a sharp question about the foundation of morality: are actions good because a divine will commands them, or does that will command them because they are already good? If goodness depends only on divine command, morality seems arbitrary; but if the gods approve things because they are independently good, then their approval is not what makes them so. The dilemma remains central to debates about the relationship between religion and ethics.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 9 "Unknown" — Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 7 "The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet" — The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 18 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 7 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 40 "25. Deadpool Kills God" — The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 36 "24. Aftermath" — Faller argues Civil War is Marvel's meditation on the aftermath of 9/11 - the Raft as Guantanamo, Zemo's interrogation as the waterboarding debate - and on America's red-blue polarization, with Steve Rogers embodying the virtue of the Good and Tony Stark the virtue of Truth as the two values democracy constantly pits against each other. Turning to Athens, he reads Plato's Euthyphro - are the gods good because goodness is a standard above them, or because their power decrees whatever they do good? - as the exact dilemma splitting Democrats, who define truth by the good it does, from Republicans, who define good by conformity to law and constitutional process, the same democratic dynamic that voted to execute Socrates and, in the comics, leaves Captain America assassinated by a sniper on his way to trial. Transcending the dualism is modeled by Spider-Man's identity disclosure and Black Panther's renunciation of vengeance over Zemo.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 14 "4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk" — Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 28 "16 Sacred Objects and Cosmic Justice in Indiana Jones" — Argues that the Indyverse is a moral universe: whoever profanes a sacred object for selfish ends is punished regardless of personal religion — Belloq and the Nazis are consumed for opening the Ark, Mola Ram plunges from the rope bridge when the Sankara Stones burn his hand, Donovan ages to dust for choosing the ornate false grail, and Elsa falls carrying the true Grail past the Great Seal. Durkheim's sacred/profane distinction and Tillich's account of religious symbols explain why respectful handling (Indy's 'don't look,' returning the stone to Mayapore's altar) succeeds where theft fails. The closing Euthyphro move concludes that the three traditions' objects enforce one universal ethic: respect is a moral truth binding independently of any divine command, like 2+2=4.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 16 "7. Anthony Bourdain’s Extremely Objectionable Stories" — Holmes examines Bourdain's horror graphic novel Hungry Ghosts as cautionary folklore in the tradition of Aesop and EC Comics. He stages a debate between Aristotle, who in the Rhetoric endorses fables as accessible moral tools, and Plato, who in the Republic wants to censor frightening tales for children — yet Holmes shows Plato himself (Euthyphro, Laws) praised fear as 'modesty,' and notes Bourdain used cautionary tales (Ronald McDonald 'has cooties') to steer his own daughter from fast food.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 13 "Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation" — Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 78 "74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates" — Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

### Faith and Reason

The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 62 "Unknown" — Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 63 "Unknown" — The chapter rebuts three pluralist objections to religious exclusivism: the 'equal fruits' argument confuses hard exclusivism with the common soft (inclusivist) form that freely admits salvation and authentic experience outside one tradition; the arrogance charge rests on a principle that would condemn every political and moral conviction held in the face of reasonable disagreement, and is self-refuting - Plantinga's 'philosophical tar baby'; and the arbitrariness charge begs the question, since pluralists assume rather than argue that no religion could have better evidence, which is precisely the point at issue between exclusivism and pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 77 "Unknown" — This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 7 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 9 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine.
