- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 9 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Editor Scott Lowe's introduction surveys the volume, using the disputed origins of Christmas – the December date borrowed from Sol Invictus and Yule, the Christmas tree from Germanic custom, and a Santa descended from Odin, Thor and Krampus rather than any Christian saint – to show how little about the holiday is settled. It previews each contributor's argument, from Hume-based attacks on the virgin birth and Aiken's denial of a 'War on Christmas' to Foucauldian readings of Santa's surveillance, the ethics of the Santa lie, and atheist or Festivus alternatives, positioning the book as a set of philosophical debates over what Christmas actually means.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 12 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Theologian Victor Lyons defends the virgin birth against the Humean empiricist objection voiced by Dawkins, Hitchens and Harris. He marshals the creeds and Church Fathers (Ignatius, Justin Martyr, Irenaeus, Origen's reply to Celsus) and argues Matthew's and Luke's independent nativity narratives point to a pre-gospel tradition of the virginal conception. Against Hume's claim that a wise man proportions belief to evidence, Lyons contends experience is not an infallible guide and that ruling out the miraculous a priori is a circular limit on inquiry, casting Mary and Joseph as the first skeptics who nonetheless accepted an event outside natural experience.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 13 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Medievalist Todd Preston argues that 'Put Christ Back in Christmas' misreads the holiday, which in the English tradition was always a balance of Christian and non-Christian elements. He shows Augustine (in On Christian Doctrine) and Boethius (in the Consolation of Philosophy, guided by Lady Philosophy) licensed Christians to absorb useful pagan philosophy, and that this apologetic openness let King Alfred, Pope Gregory and St. Boniface repurpose rather than erase heathen practice – turning Thor's oak into the Christmas fir. Tracing the Old English 'Cristesmæsse', Yule/Jol and Modraniht, and the secular revelry of Sir Gawain that Wyclif condemned, he concludes an authentic Christmas keeps its pagan half.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 15 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Scott Aiken argues the conservative 'War on Christmas' pushed by Gibson and O'Reilly is illusory on both fronts: cultural Christianity has already won, and keeping nativity scenes out of public schools protects minority rights under the Establishment Clause rather than persecuting the majority. He then mounts a separate attack, claiming both Christmas myths are bad on their merits – the nativity (star that leads wise men, vanishing Magi, Joseph's pointless genealogy) promotes mere credulity rather than tested faith, while the Santa myth glorifies a slave-owning surveiller who makes goodness merely instrumental. He adds that teaching the false Santa story undercuts parents' testimonial authority to teach the gospel as true.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 16 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 22 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Will Williams recounts the legend that St. Nicholas of Myra, the historical basis of Santa Claus, attended the Council of Nicaea (325) and punched the heretic Arius, who taught that the Son was created and not fully God ('there was a time when the Son was not'). Setting the fight to a parody of 'The Night Before Christmas', Williams explains via Athanasius why the divinity of Christ mattered – only if Jesus is truly God can his death secure salvation. He contrasts this fiercely theological bishop with the de-Christianized modern Santa, using the syncretism of 'Here Comes Santa Claus' to argue Nicholas would deplore what consumerist Christmas has become.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 30 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Tallman offers a naturalistic (atheist) justification for celebrating Christmas, arguing first that the holiday's date and rituals (December 25 solstice, Christmas trees, Odin-derived Santa) predate and are not exclusively Christian, so non-believers may find their own meaning in them. Drawing on George Santayana's and Steven Cahn's 'religious naturalism,' she argues rituals and moral communities give meaning without supernatural belief, so atheists engaging even overtly religious rites (like Westerners doing Hindu-rooted yoga) are not being disingenuous. She locates a secular 'spirit of Christmas' — giving, love, community — in It's a Wonderful Life, where humans, not God, save George Bailey, and closes on a Venn-diagram overlap of Christian and naturalist Christmases.
- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 31 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Mason, a developmental psychologist writing as a Pagan, narrates her decades-long religious journey through James Fowler's Stages of Faith model, using each stage to reinterpret Christmas. She recounts childhood confusion over carols and chimney-invading strangers, fundamentalist-Christian zeal (stage 3 group belonging, then stage-4 doubt as she 'crusaded' against pagan Christmas trees), Unitarian Universalist questioning, and finally Wiccan/Pagan practice centered on Hecate and the winter-solstice Wheel of the Year (rediscovering Christmas's pagan roots in holly, mistletoe, and Yule). Reaching Fowler's stage 5 'Conjunctive Faith,' she concludes Christmas is neither hers nor anyone's to own but a self-perpetuating commercial 'Hallmark' phenomenon she can now greet with equanimity.
- **Cannabis – Philosophy for Everyone - What Were We Just Talking About_**, ch. 18 "Cannabis Philosophy for Everyone" — Taliaferro and Le Gall's 'The Great Escape' weighs four philosophical objections to cannabis-induced altered states — falsehood (Plato's ban on poetry/theatre in the Republic), distortion of reason (Euripides' Bacchae, James on nitrous oxide), undermining of agency (the Sirens, De Quincey's opium), and loss of self-determination (the Stoic Epictetus on freedom) — then surveys Jewish, Christian and Islamic treatments of wine, coffee and hashish. They rebut the objections using Aristotle's cathartic defense of theatre and Locke's imagination-based account of freedom, concluding that if cannabis is no worse than wine the philosophical and religious case against it is not decisive.
- **Tattoos – Philosophy for Everyone - I Ink, Therefore I Am**, ch. 34 "TATTOOS PHILOSOPHY FOR EVERYONE I Ink, Therefore I Am" — Barkman, prompted by his wedding guests' shared discomfort with his best man's tattooed arms, sets out to dispel a 'Christian Confucian confusion' that reads piety as requiring a tattoo-free body. He shows Leviticus 19:28 and 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 condemn tattooing only where it signals allegiance to impure cults or misuse of the body, not tattooing in itself, and that Confucius's Hsiao King injunction against wounding the body one receives from one's parents was linked to tattoos only by Han Chinese racism against tattooed minorities. Citing General Yue Fei's mother inking loyalty on his back, he concludes ink can even be pious, though a child under a parent's legitimate authority owes obedience if forbidden it.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Henry Jacoby channels W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' through South Park's Stan Marsh, who debunks John Edward, holistic healers, Scientology, and Mormon claims by insisting the burden of proof lies with the believer and that faith is belief without evidence. The chapter distinguishes prudential from evidential reasons and dismantles Pascal's Wager using episodes like 'Cartmanland' (why would a good God torment nonbelievers?) and 'Do the Handicapped Go to Hell?' (which religion?). Stan's speech to Edward's audience frames uncritical belief as mental laziness that slows the progress of mankind.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Daniel Gallagher uses Lost's Rose, who insists 'I just know' her husband lives and the island cured her, to apply Aquinas's account of faith as 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion.' Drawing on Plato's episteme/doxa distinction and Aquinas's God/'first truth' conceptual distinction plus the five ways, he argues reason can demonstrate that God exists while faith (a grace) grasps what reason cannot. Rose exemplifies both the sin of presumption (mistaking faith for knowledge, treating the island as God's certain instrument) and, by contrast to Charlie's acedia, robust faith, so the chapter urges keeping faith and reason harmonized rather than conflated.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 31 "29. Frank Herbert’s Dune as Philosophy The Need to Think for Yourself" — Reading the Sci Fi Channel miniseries Frank Herbert's Dune and Children of Dune, Littmann argues the saga warns against letting leaders or religions think for us: Paul Atreides fakes being the Fremen Mahdi, wages a holy war, and founds a theocratic tyranny that Alia and Leto II carry to worse extremes. He sets Plato's Republic (the guardian class, the noble lie, rule by the wise) and Hobbes against pro-democracy thinkers—Locke's consent and natural rights, Mill's harm principle, Dewey's democracy—then cites Locke, Paine and Russell on religion's dangers, closing with W.K. Clifford's 'ethics of belief' that one must not accept religious claims without sufficient evidence. The chapter reads Paul's dictatorship and the Bene Gesserit's engineered messiah as dramatizations of the historical abuses of concentrated and religious power.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.

### Ship of Theseus

The Ship of Theseus is a puzzle about identity over time, reported by the biographer Plutarch, who noted that the Athenians preserved Theseus's ship by gradually replacing its decaying planks. This raises the question of whether the ship remains the same object once every original part has been swapped out, and whether identity resides in matter, form, or continuity. The thought experiment has become a standard way of probing what makes something persist as one and the same thing despite the replacement of its parts.

- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 112 "The Hulk’s Bodily Identity" — Tests the everyday bodily criterion of identity: the Hulk's body contains far more atoms than Banner's, but since all our cells turnover anyway — the "Stan Lee Schooner" has every part replaced yet stays the same boat, the Ship of Theseus problem — and the organ-donor case of "Herb Trimpe" shows a body with greater physical continuity to Kinghorn than to its owner, bodily continuity cannot be what personal identity consists in.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 28 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Uses Narnia's magical transformations to probe personal identity, starting with the qualitative/numerical identity distinction illustrated by the look-alike twins Shasta and Corin in The Horse and His Boy. Aristotle's essential/accidental properties frame the question of what Eustace can lose and remain Eustace, including turning into a dragon, and Rabadash into a donkey, showing persons are not identical to their bodies. Descartes's soul argument and Locke's memory theory are tested and rejected, the latter because it cannot handle Rilian's enchanted amnesia, Shasta's forgotten infancy, or Susan's disowned memories without circularity. The chapter defends instead a first-person-perspective theory on which a person is constituted by, not identical to, a body, illustrated by the repeatedly repaired Dawn Treader and by the heroes surviving death in The Last Battle as restored points of view.
- **The Grateful Dead and Philosophy - Getting High Minded about Love and Haight**, ch. 17 "Was Jerry Garcia the Soul of the Grateful Dead" — John Uglietta asks what made the Grateful Dead the Grateful Dead when they swapped five keyboardists yet stopped being themselves the moment Jerry Garcia died, prompting the rename to The Dead. Testing Aristotle's essential versus accidental properties, Peter French's structural account of group identity (the Yankees, the Glenn Miller Orchestra), same-stuff theories via a VW bus rebuilt piece by piece from its old parts — a Ship of Theseus puzzle — and Locke's memory theory applied to Phil Lesh's liver (but feared brain) transplant, he proposes that the band's essence was a group spirit born of members 'surrendering their own little trip'. The soul of the Dead was bigger than Jerry but smaller than the whole band, and its loss at his death was something the survivors could recognize but not replace.
- **Pink Floyd and Philosophy - Careful with that Axiom, Eugene!**, ch. 20 "Absolutely Curtains" — Michael Patton retells the Ship of Theseus (his 'Trump Princess' rebuilt part-by-part from spares, then duplicated from the salvaged parts) to ask whether Pink Floyd survived its upheavals: Bob Klose's pre-Piper exit, Syd Barrett's 1968 dismissal ('No, fuck it, let's not bother' on the drive to Southampton), Rick Wright's firing during The Wall, and Roger Waters's 1985 lawsuit to stop Gilmour and Mason using the name. Roster, stylistic ('Lucifer Sam' versus 'Money'), legal, and nominal criteria each fail, so he proposes an 'Officeholder View' of identity in which constituencies decide sameness — as when UFO Club's Joe Boyd saw a different Syd at the June 1967 show, while the author's locked-in brother Josh (like Bauby in The Diving Bell and the Butterfly) remained the same son and brother to his family. Parfit's claim that survival tracks memory and personality rather than body underwrites the 'death of a thousand cuts' scenario: the band's criteria, not Syd's own, ended the life of the person 'Syd Barrett', and he didn't get a vote.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 9 "A Modest Conclusion" — Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro stage the diachronic-versus-episodic debate about the self (Galen Strawson's episodic view included) against Leigh Edwards's "no single Johnny Cash": the hotel-room-wrecking addict and the Billy Graham touring Christian do not fit one biography. They argue the private J.R. was a third option: on stage he becomes wholly absorbed in story characters (the Folsom narrator, the man who shot a man in Reno) while a self not defined by time slips in and out of the persona, evidenced by his account of gradually shedding "Johnny Cash" after shows. Johnny Cash the public quilt is compared to the Ship of Theseus, every original piece of J.R. replaced yet still owned by him, and the modest conclusion is that J.R., like anyone making a free choice, stood above the timeline of instants and could inhabit both the episodes and the grand narrative.
- **Johnny Cash and Philosophy - The Burning Ring of Truth**, ch. 26 "Memories Are Made of This" — Randall Jensen asks whether Cash's hope of reunion with the dead ('Meet Me in Heaven,' 'If We Never Meet Again This Side of Heaven') is even coherent, using the 'One Piece at a Time' Cadillac and a hypothetical 1954 Plymouth to retell the Ship of Theseus puzzle about identity through part replacement. He canvasses Platonic dualism from the Phaedo (Cash is his soul, the body a rusty cage), the materialist hope that God can reassemble a resurrected body despite dispersed matter, and the psychological-continuity view that persons are 'made of memories,' ending on the duplication problem: if God made two heavenly bodies both carrying Cash's memories, which one would be Cash?
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Robison asks how Link stays the same person through Ocarina of Time's child/adult switches, Twilight Princess's wolf form, and Wind Waker's consciousness-projection into seagulls and mages. Physical-continuity views fail because Link's body changes or is left behind; Locke's memory-based psychological continuity fails because adult Link's past hasn't happened yet when he travels back. After a Ship of Theseus variant (Ganon reassembling Tetra's sunken planks) she proposes that in Zelda's stipulative metaphysics, destiny, the goddess-given roles of courage, wisdom, and power, is the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, fitting videogame universes whose metaphysics are fixed by designers.
- **Supervillains and Philosophy - Sometimes, Evil Is Its Own Reward**, ch. 11 "19" — Four 'Phase Five' puzzle essays. Lindahl-Urben and Taliaferro use Secret Wars to test omnipotence: the Beyonder, Doom, and Galactus cannot do the logically impossible (no spherical cubes, no stone too heavy to lift), two omnipotent beings collide, and a truly omnipotent being has no desires - so villains can never climb to the top they crave. Matthewson and Wall use Frankfurt cases and reasons-responsive source compatibilism to explain why Eddie Brock is responsible for Venom's villainy (he voluntarily bonded and endorses the symbiote's adjusted psychology) while Anne Weying, horrified by what the symbiote made her do, bears only minimal blame. Pickavance reconstructs the Ship of Theseus with Sandman's 'mansand': combining part exchange with materialism lets Norman Osborn reassemble a duplicate Sandman from his scattered remains, and since neither principle nor soul-dualism comes free, personal identity through material change remains unsolved. Loader argues Brainiac's reinvention as a 'facts and logic' computer embodies disembodied Cartesian AI, so the frame problem (Dennett's exploding robots) and embodied cognition (Clark's Tetris, Dreyfus) suggest his detachment from body and world would make him less, not more, intelligent than the humans he scorns.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 18 "Coda" — Gimbel asks what makes a band remain the same band over time: Led Zeppelin survived replacing drummer John Bonham with his son Jason, yet Page and Jones insist no singer could replace Robert Plant. Working through Plutarch's Ship of Theseus, Aristotle's essential properties, and Locke's continuity account of identity, he uses Peter French's distinction between aggregates (groups defined by membership) and conglomerates (defined by role structure) to argue a band is a conglomerate. The twist is that a reunion would be a monument like Theseus's preserved ship rather than a working vessel: Plant is an Aristotelian essential of what Zeppelin was, while Jason Bonham's family link supplies the reverence and facsimile-fidelity a monument needs.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 13 "Is Everybody Disembodied (or, Have We Always Been Posthuman Beings )" — Stevens uses the film's closing voice-over 'I am Tetsuo' in Otomo's Akira to run the classic identity-and-mind problems: Heraclitus's river and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus ask whether the grotesquely transformed, Akira-absorbed Tetsuo is still the same person, while Descartes's cogito — riffed as 'cogito ergo Tetsuo' — Turing's Test, and Searle's Chinese Room test whether a voice that seems to think proves a thinker behind it (syntax is not yet shown sufficient for semantics, though Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition reads the Room from the inside out). Weighing embodiment (Pinker's brain-makes-mind, Dennett's self as a 'center of narrative gravity') against disembodiment (Akira levelling Neo-Tokyo from nothing but cryogenically stored remains; Tetsuo's matter teleportation), he concludes through the problem of representation — every utterance is re-presented, as in Augustine's guilty tears over Dido — that we always treat semblances of thinkers as thinkers, so we may have always been decentered, re-presented, posthuman beings no different from Tetsuo and Akira.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 41 "Where in the World(s) Are We" — Ablondi asks whether fans' 'if only' claims—'If Bob Stanley had struck out Mookie Wilson, the Sox would have won in 1986,' 'if Pesky had hurried his relay in 1946'—can be true when they lack truthmakers in the actual world. He presents David Lewis's modal realism and counterpart theory as the standard solution, then objects: a Fisk counterpart with a different body, birthday and nickname, or a Red Sox made of 1986 Mets counterparts, is not recognizably Fisk or the Red Sox, and nobody cares about a Lonborg counterpart who won Game Seven. He concludes counterfactuals need some other explanation and that we should savor the actual Foulke-to-Mientkiewicz final out of 2004 instead.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 31 "The Limits of Change" — Osborne and Coombs turn the Ship of Theseus — every plank replaced, plus Hobbes's reassembled-planks variant — into the 'Aston Villa Paradox': with owner, manager, players, crest and even the shade of claret and blue changed, what makes it the same club fans sing 'Villa till I Die' for? Finding that presentism and Sider's four-dimensionalism cannot say which side on the 2006 pitch was really AVFC, they adopt Lynne Rudder Baker's constitution view: fans create the football-favorable circumstances that constitute a club, so it persists through total replacement of parts as long as supporters keep conferring identity and value — which is why Gareth Barry's value collapsed when he left, and why fans judged Glazer's Manchester United to have stopped existing while welcoming Lerner's Villa.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 10 "Mastering the Chief" — Joyce Havstad asks which of the millions of player-instantiated Master Chiefs is real, and whether the flash-cloned John left behind on Eridanus II is the same boy. She runs the Ship of Theseus on the MJOLNIR armor—a technician rebuilds a second suit from every replaced piece—contrasting material with historical continuity, and adds Hobbes's reassembled-planks version. Locke's prince-and-cobbler memory criterion is reconstructed across John, John-117, and Master Chief, then broken by Reid's brave-officer objection, leaving psychological continuity as the best but imperfect criterion; the Flood's conversion of a Covenant soldier into a Combat Form shows identity lost once original sentience is gone.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 38 "In a Mirror, Darkly" — The chapter stages Arctor's bishop's-robe musing ('What is identity? Where does the act end?') against the classic puzzles: the Ship of Theseus with its two reassembled vessels, and the baby photos you share no cells with. Locke gives memory plus a unified 'thinking, intelligent being' with real unity; Hume bites the bullet, finding only perceptions in introspection, never a self, so the self's identity over time is a normal, inescapable delusion like a mountain's. All of it converges on Fred watching Bob and asking 'who am I? Which one of them is me?'
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 87 "The Sum of the Parts" — Auxier asks why 'It' works only when the Stones are together, testing the band's fifty-year experiment against lineup changes: Brian Jones proved dispensable, the second guitar modular, yet Bill Wyman's 1992 departure genuinely weakened the circuit. He claims Keith-Charlie-Bill in series (data-synthesis-satisfaction) are the real power source, with Jagger merely the light bulb that draws the current — the Keith-Charlie-Bill band would have been famous without Mick, but Mick is nothing without the circuit. A lithium analogy renders the band loosely bound, unstable and flammable, and the chapter closes by insisting Charlie interprets Keith and Bill interprets Charlie, in that order.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 23 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Monica Evans argues that D&D is identity play in which players explore who they are through characters they create, perform and try to keep alive, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to ask whether a character re-rolled under a new edition, or replayed by another player, is still 'the same' character. She tests theories of the player-character bond (Gee's virtual, real and projective identities; Fine and Worch's 'identity bubble') on Wil Wheaton's Avenger Aeofel, whose in-character oath made Wheaton split the party and lose him rather than metagame. Bartle's four player types and the bulette-knowledge example show how each player manages the line between what they know and what their character knows, in a shared fiction where a glorious failure can be better than winning.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 15 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Jenkins asks what makes Bender Bender when Leela still recognizes him as the walnut-panelled steam robot of 'Obsoletely Fabulous.' Scruffy's progressively repaired conference table stages the Ship of Theseus problem and the same body theory, while the Roboticon 'Soul Detector' (Fry sets it off, robots pass through) rules out Descartes' same soul theory for robots. Episodes from 'Anthology of Interest II' and 'The Honking' to 'The Prisoner of Benda' mind swap and Roberto's instant 1-X re-education support Locke's psychological continuity: Bender persists through an overlapping chain of memories and traits stored on his hard drive - 'Everything that is Bender is right here' - which is why an empathic, ascetic Bender ('The old Bender is gone') threatens his very identity.
- **Futurama and Philosophy - Bite My Shiny Metal Axiom**, ch. 27 "Futurama and Philosophy" — Williams uses Hermes's slide from chest-harpoon to extendo-arm to Cylon eye to full robot body in 'The Six Million Dollar Mon' - until Zoidberg's 'Monster Mash' surgery restores his brain to Li'l Hermes - to ask what makes a person themselves under voluntary enhancement. The 'Ship of Planet Express' and the seven-year cell-replacement fact recast the Ship of Theseus, exposing our terror of upgrades as inconsistent with our constant physical change, while the therapeutic-versus-enhancement line (medical steroids vs doping, Aimee Mullins's blades) explains why Hermes's chosen upgrades disturb us. Cartesian interactionist dualism predicts Mecha-Hermes stays the same person, yet his personality shifts with his parts, so the chapter turns to physicalism and lands on functionalism: Hermes persists through each swap until the Roberto brain-chip replaces the brain that houses his memories and motivations.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 26 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Lopez uses the monster - 'one man made out of many' - to stress-test personal identity: brain-swap and amnesia-torture thought experiments first drive us to identify with our memories (the memory-based psychological criterion) and then, when Victor offers to wipe memory before the pain experiments, with our bodies, yielding inconsistent answers. The monster's own testimony - waking confused, prodding fire like an infant, acquiring language by eavesdropping on Safie's lessons, and building his values from scratch out of Paradise Lost and the cottagers - shows he is a genuinely new person rather than whoever once owned his corpse-parts, since we would not say a memory-wiped torture victim ceases to exist. He concludes the monster satisfies the five listed personhood criteria (consciousness, reasoning, self-motivated activity, communication, self-awareness), with identity riding a continuing stream of consciousness running on a body that is, in the end, secondary 'hardware.'
- **Jurassic Park and Philosophy - The Truth Is Terrifying**, ch. 12 "Jurassic Park and Philosophy" — Freeman explains why Grant dismisses the clones as 'genetically engineered theme park monsters': a frog-DNA-patched genome is not dinosaur DNA, and nobody knows how much alteration turns a T. rex into something else, so as Wu tells Hammond the park has only reconstructed the past, never re-created it. Behavior cannot vindicate the clones either, since The Lost World's raptors grow up without elders to teach raptor behavior, and the animals must survive an ecosystem of grass, bacteria, and species that did not exist in the Cretaceous. The chapter's running puzzle of how much of an organism can change before it is no longer that organism is a Ship of Theseus problem applied to paleontology.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 21 "10. One Good, Solid Hope—the Impossible Girl" — Elsby and Luzecky ask what stays constant across Clara's echoes and argue traditional identity theories fail her: Locke's memory-continuity and same-life account cannot apply because no echo remembers the others, and Plutarch's Ship of Theseus—invoked by the Doctor's broom speech in 'Deep Breath'—rules out bodily continuity, since the echoes have different bodies and minds. Their positive view is that Clara is less a particular than a universal, a 'recipe' or species whose instances share an essence ('the soufflé isn't the soufflé; the soufflé is the recipe'), with the modern-day Clara 'real' as the origin of the echoes. That essence, shown in climbing the ladder to the clouds in 'The Snowmen,' facing the parasite-god with the most important leaf in human history in 'The Rings of Akhaten,' stepping into the Doctor's torn timeline in 'The Name of the Doctor,' and persuading the Time Lords in 'The Time of the Doctor,' is hope itself.
- **Discworld and Philosophy - Reality Is Not What It Seems**, ch. 25 "14. Being One’s Me (Witchy) Personal Identity on the Discworld" — The chapter reads Granny Weatherwax's analysis of Magrat—'you're your me'—through Locke's memory theory of personal identity, opening with Granny's broomstick, whose stick and bristles the dwarf engineers have replaced dozens of times yet which remains 'the same' broomstick, as a Theseus's-ship puzzle for witches. It stages Locke's view against the classic objections: Butler's circularity charge that memory presupposes identity, and fission worries raised by the duplicated Glods of Al-Ybi and by the mirror magic that splits Granny and Lilith among a billion reflections. Death's challenge to each witch to find 'the one that's real' in the mirror universe becomes the test case, and Granny's simply looking down at herself and saying 'This one' is offered as a vindication of a Butlerian, body-anchored and indefinable conception of personal identity.
- **Red Rising and Philosophy - Break the Chains!**, ch. 13 "5. The One, the Only, Darrow" — Kevin McCain uses Darrow's transformations—Helldiver of Lykos, carved Gold lancer, Reaper of Mars—to ask what makes him numerically the same person, warming up with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus replayed on the Pax and the Quinn trading parts. Same-matter and animalist views (Eric Olson) struggle with Mickey's near-total carving and Darrow's restarted heart, and Locke's prince-and-cobbler example, run as a carver swapping Darrow's and the Jackal's psychologies, sinks all physical-continuity views. The simple memory theory breaks transitivity across Darrow's childhood, and Sydney Shoemaker's psychological-continuity fix then fails when a carver splits Darrow's brain into two surviving bodies—a fission case where both new Darrows continue him—while the soul view cannot be verified; the chapter ends with Trenton Merricks's suggestion that there may be no criteria of identity over time at all.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 33 "18. No End to Philosophy" — Four vignettes pin philosophical problems to Peanuts' marginal characters: Camus's absurd - caring beings condemned to an uncaring universe - is answered by Sally's School Building, which grows a heart and drops bricks on her enemies; the 95472 kids motivate a tour of personal identity (same soul, same body, memory) through the Ship of Theseus; Pigpen's dirt raises Sartre's bad faith (facticity, transcendence, being-for-others) - we prize his authenticity over cleanliness - and Aristotle's golden mean, which moderates cleanliness while crediting his curiosity as a virtue; and finally the ontology of fictional characters asks whether the Kite-Eating Tree and Red Baron really exist inside the fiction and whether The Peanuts Movie's changed Charlie Brown counts as canon.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 20 "9. Is Headless Deadpool Still Deadpool" — Ben Fulman runs Deadpool's decapitations, the T-Ray personality split, and Evil Deadpool—his discarded body parts regenerating together in a dumpster—through the theories of personal identity: Locke's memory continuity, Reid's branching-memory 'Deadpool paradox', Chisholm's essential parts, the Ship of Theseus traced from Heraclitus to Plutarch, and later positions by Sider, Wiggins, Noonan, Grice, and Perry on overlapping memory chains and their circularity. Finding each account strained by Deadpool's cases, the chapter proposes that Deadpool stores his memories in the readers via the fourth wall. His identity over time is thus jointly sustained by the audience—a 'non-personal identity' that ends only when every reader has forgotten him.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 38 "24. Won’t the Real Wade Wilson Please Stand Up" — Evil Deadpool, assembled from Wade's discarded body parts with all his old memories, makes Wade a walking Ship of Theseus, and the chapter runs the puzzle through Plutarch's original, Hobbes's reconstructed-ship variant, and Locke's Prince-and-Cobbler memory criterion, staged as a Thor/Thing body swap. Memory fails because Evil Deadpool shares Wade's memories, so the candidates become Schechtman's narrative and person-life views, Parfit's branching survival - neither is the original, and identity is not what matters anyway - and finally Unger's core-capacity view: Wade remains the real Deadpool by continuing to be a conscious being, while his detached parts ceased to be Deadpool parts the moment they were replaced.
- **American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare**, ch. 13 "3. My Sister, My Self" — Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 15 "6. The KISS Franchise" — Peter Finocchiaro takes Gene Simmons's and manager Doc McGhee's suggestions that KISS could become a franchise — new musicians stepping into the Demon and Starchild roles — and works out what band identity could mean. Using the Ship of Theseus, he distinguishes qualitative from numerical identity, invokes collective intentionality to explain how a band without a mind can perform intentional actions, and contrasts the 'originality connection' (being the actual founding members) with the 'continuity connection' (day-by-day chained succession), mirroring the bodily-versus-psychological debate about Gene Simmons's personal identity. His conclusion is that bands are governed by social rules fans collectively create — like the rules of basketball or musical genre — so in his imaginary two-KISS scenario, and for any future franchise, the fan base would decide which band is the real KISS rather than discovering a pre-existing fact.
- **KISS and Philosophy - Wiser than Hell**, ch. 18 "9. KISS the Ship of Theseus Goodbye!" — Shane Ralston asks whether KISS, after constant lineup changes that left only Stanley and Simmons fixtures, is still the same band. He lays out Plutarch's Ship of Theseus and Hobbes's harder variant — a ship rebuilt from the salvaged original planks — formalizing three assumptions (endurance through gradual change, identity with parts, transitivity of identity) and their conflicting conclusions, then applies a fifty-percent-plus-quality reading: keeping the two powerhouse founding members preserved KISS's core identity through the Carr, Vincent, St. John, Kulick, Singer, and Thayer eras. For the imagined duplicate-KISS case he deploys Chisholm's 'loose and popular sense' of identity and Ted Sider's four-dimensionalist 'space-time worm,' concluding the dispute is practical — best settled by courts of law, not armchair metaphysics.
- **Black Sabbath and Philosophy - Mastering Reality**, ch. 22 "Black sabbath & philosophy" — James Bondarchuk tests purist principles about which line-ups are really Black Sabbath with thought experiments: the Ship of Theseus, from Plutarch plus Hobbes's reassembled planks, fits poorly because Geezer Butler is no plank, musicians contribute irreplaceable style, and "original members only" absurdly entails a Bieber piano-cover band would still be Sabbath, while the legal-ownership reading collapses once fans admit Bieber buying the name changes nothing. He concludes the whole "is it still Sabbath without Ozzy?" debate is not a metaphysical question with a fact of the matter but disguised aesthetic judgment, he remains a purist because Bill Ward's brooding drumming on "Black Sabbath" and "Hand of Doom" are integral to the Sabbath Sound, while conceding no objective answer exists.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 23 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Monica Evans asks what relationship holds between a player and a character, opening with Plutarch's Ship of Theseus to probe whether a character rebuilt under a new edition, recreated in Neverwinter Nights, or played in succession by two people is still the 'same' character. She applies James Paul Gee's three identities (virtual, real-world, projective) to Wil Wheaton playing Aeofel, whose in-character chase of Leer into an acid pit shows projective identity trumping good gameplay. Worch's 'identity bubble', Bartle's four player types, and the management of player versus character knowledge (the veteran whose wizard meets a bulette, the INT 7 barbarian Dak) frame D&D as a shared fiction in which players explore who they are or might be.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 24 "NOTE" — Asks whether amnesia preserves numerical identity: is the Peter who wakes in the shipping crate still Volume-1 Peter, are Niki and Jessica one person, and is the Sylar whom Matt rewrites with Nathan's memories now Nathan? The chapter builds Locke's memory criterion, breaks it with Reid's transitivity objection run through Mohinder's timeline in 'Five Years Gone,' repairs it with Grice's and Perry's memory-ancestor chains, then destroys the repair with Arthur Petrelli's wipe of Hiro (Forgetful Hiro vs. Stabby Hiro), Bernard Williams's torture thought experiment, Parfit's psychological spectrum, and the graphic novel's branching self-copier Evan. It concludes that no memory criterion can define personal identity, yet memory still matters practically: Claire must act as if she persists over time to keep her promise to Zach and to bother finishing the manatee assignment.
- **The Hunger Games and Philosophy - A Critique of Pure Treason**, ch. 25 "The Hunger Games and Philosophy" — Michaud argues Peeta effectively died twice — once at the force field, and again when the Capitol's tracker-jacker hijacking rewrote his loving memories of Katniss into hatred. Using Leibniz's Law he rules out the body and DNA as what makes Peeta Peeta, then defends Locke's memory theory through thought experiments about a clone Peeta versus a brain-damaged original. Adapting Plutarch's Ship of Theseus as 'the Problem of Haymitch's Hovercraft,' he questions whether gradual change preserves identity, and finally leans toward Hume and Parfit: there may be no enduring self, only a bundle of perceptions replaced moment by moment. On this view Katniss protects the hijacked Peeta out of respect for the memory of the old Peeta, even as each of us is constantly replaced by someone new.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 11 "Notes" — Gettings asks whether LEGO set #21103, the Cuusoo DeLorean Time Machine, is numerically identical to Team BTTF's original fan design — and why the fans deserve credit and royalties. Neither matter (his 1982 attic spaceship with bricks replaced one by one) nor form (a license plate added here or there) settles identity, as the Ship of Theseus puzzle and Hobbes' reassembly variation show, analyzed through Aristotle's matter/form distinction for substances. He adopts the causal/historical view: the released set continuously descends from the fans' submission just as the adult author descends from the boy who built the spaceship, and this same historical origin, in Lockean fashion, is what grounds the designers' labor-mixing property right — the musician-and-producer analogy explaining why Team BTTF keeps the larger share of credit.
- **LEGO and Philosophy - Constructing Reality Brick by Brick**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Mentyka uses minifigure puzzles — can 'Eliza' and 'Beth' be distinct characters when built from identical pieces, and is Eliza the same character after every piece is swapped out, a minifig Ship of Theseus — to introduce the philosophy of the human person. He runs through supervenience on physical parts, Locke's memory theory and its Butler–Reid controversy (Reid in the taxonomy), the Christian Resurrection-of-the-Body background, and Parfit's despairing deflation that identity matters less than what survives us. Against these he defends personalism, citing Max Scheler and Kierkegaard's call in The Single Individual to become one rather than a crowd: a person is both the sigfig and the AFOL building it, constituted by free choices and actions — which is also why the LEGO Movie's 'Where Are My Pants?' mass society is the enemy.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - Link Outside the Box**, ch. 17 "Solutions to the Problem The youth whose destiny it is to lead Hyrule to the" — Rachel Robison asks how Zelda characters persist through radical change, recasting the Ship of Theseus as Tetra's pirate ship from Wind Waker, whose replaced planks Ganon reassembles into a rival ship and leaving Link to find the true one. Physical-continuity accounts fail because Link projects his consciousness into seagulls and temple mages and becomes a wolf in Twilight Princess; Locke's memory theory fails because Ocarina of Time's child/adult time loops break psychological continuity. Her solution: in the Zelda universe, the goddesses' destiny — embodiment of courage, wisdom, or power — supplies the necessary and sufficient condition of identity, a stipulative metaphysics videogames are free to have.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 38 "Notes" — Sorts out Spock-Prime, bearded Mirror-Spock, and Abrams's Spock-2 using David Lewis's modal realism, counterparts, and Humean supervenience: identity is not directly perceived but judged from adjacent similar instances, as with Hume's natural properties. The refit Enterprise versus the Enterprise-A, plus the thought experiment of downloading the old ship's computer into the new one, carry a Ship-of-Theseus-style analysis of whether swapped cells and Spock's katra-separated death and Genesis resurrection preserve identity. Mirror-Spock turns out to be a worldmate within one enlarged world (Kirk's crossover in "Mirror, Mirror" makes the universes spatiotemporally continuous), not a transworld duplicate, and Spock-Prime and Spock-2 are like two highways overlapping until Nero's arrival in 2233 makes them diverge - two similar individuals formed by different successes and failures, never identical.
- **Basketball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Paint**, ch. 30 "Playing for the Same Team Again" — A fictional five-day phone dialogue between Michael Jordan and Phil Jackson works through the metaphysics of team identity before Jordan's 1995 comeback: qualitative versus numerical sameness, necessary and sufficient conditions ('same players, same positions'), Heraclitus's river, and whether the Bulls survive gradual turnover. The Ship of Theseus becomes the 'Boars' puzzle - the original five reassembled on an expansion team versus the continuous, degenerate Chicago roster - with Hobbes's two-ship twist, alongside the Minneapolis Lakers' move and a Bulls-Pistons gradual player swap. The resolution distinguishes the group (which persists by composition or continuity) from the team, which 'counts as' the Bulls only partly through fans' allegiance, echoing Searle's social reality; Jordan concludes he was asking the wrong question, and Aristotle's circular account of virtue supplies the model for circular criteria of loyal fandom.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 28 "Here They Are ... Ready to Outsit Eternity" — Michael Hand uses the Doctor's regeneration to argue that life after death is logically possible. Because the First-through-Tenth Doctors are the same person despite total personality change (a dandy becoming a clown), identity is distinct from personality, so a god perfecting flawed Joe for heaven need not make him someone else. He then tests the replica theory against 'Journey's End' (the metacrisis Doctor) and 'Human Nature' (John Smith), concluding we favor bodily continuity, and endorses van Inwagen's 'divine cryonicist' solution to the unavailability-of-atoms problem, echoing the Doctor's 'ready to outsit eternity' praise of frozen humanity in 'The Ark in Space'.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 25 "14. Baby’s Identity" — Doll uses the Winchesters' Impala 'Baby'—repeatedly totaled and rebuilt from replaced parts—as a running Ship of Theseus (from Plutarch) to probe what makes an object or person the same over time. She tests Aristotle's four causes (favoring the formal cause) and Theodore Sider's four-dimensionalism, both of which falter, then notes Supernatural's souls solve personal identity for the resurrected Winchesters and alternate-universe doubles; since soulless Baby has no such thread, her identity rests on the subjective, family meaning the Winchesters invest in her.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 31 "19. Cleons and Cloning" — Heter examines the Cleon Dynasty's clones (Brothers Dawn, Day, Dusk) to ask what a clone actually is, rejecting definitions built on identity. He distinguishes numerical identity (the Mule just is Magnifico Giganticus) from qualitative identity (two copies of a book), then shows the Cleons fail to be qualitatively identical because of age, psychology, perceptual perspective, and even drifting genetics over time—so grounding cloning in shared qualitative/genetic identity yields the odd result that clones could gain or lose clone-status as their genes change. He instead proposes a causal definition: a clone is an organism whose genetic information results from an (imperfect) copying process originating in a donor, so Cleon I is not a clone but every later Cleon is.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 17 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Steven Horrobin sorts sailors into three kinds — the cultural-iconography poser, the racer chasing a land-based prize, and the 'sailor of the third kind' for whom the open-ended voyage is an end in itself — and argues the third lives 'in the shadow of Heraclitus.' Against the substantialist ontology of Parmenides and Democritus (persons and boats as fixed things), he defends a process view in which everything, like a wave, is a passing fluctuation of one universal substance; citing Spinoza, self-becoming is the super-process reflecting itself. He dissolves the Ship of Theseus paradox (and Parfit's parallel-ship version) by making identity the continuity of a process's function rather than fixed parts, arguing the violent, corroding life of a boat reveals the flux beneath apparently stable things.
- **The Philosopher at the End of the Universe - Philosophy Explained Through Science Fiction Films**, ch. 10 "4. Total Recall & The Sixth Day" — Rowlands treats Total Recall as a defence of the memory (psychological-continuity) theory of personal identity: erasing Quaid's memories and restoring Hauser's is an essential change that ends Quaid, so he fights for his existence. He works through and rejects the soul theory (dualism's problems) and body/brain theories via head-transplant and neuron-replacement thought experiments, distinguishing Aristotle's essential/accidental change and Heraclitus's river. The Sixth Day's cloning raises Parfit's fission/duplication problem: a double success cannot be a failure, driving him to abandon identity for a Heraclitean 'river of selves' bound by survival, not identity.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 84 "79. Cyberpunk 2077 as Philosophy Balancing the (Mystical) Ghost in the (Transhuman) Machine" — Lay reads Cyberpunk 2077's transhuman Night City against the enhancement debate. Using the Ship of Theseus, Parfit's continuity plus fission/fusion (V and Johnny 'fusing,' the Delamain AIs) and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind, he argues enhancement neither destroys personal identity (which Parfit says doesn't matter) nor dehumanizes users — it may be the purest expression of Clark's cyborg humanity. The real danger is corporate exploitation of bodies, explained via Adorno's culture industry and Arendt's banality of evil. Buddhist nonattachment (Nagarjuna's emptiness, echoed by a Schopenhauer shard) grounds each ending's pacification-versus-attachment theme, but Lay corrects it with Weil's critique of power and Buber's I-Thou, concluding the game urges transcending the boundary between 'me' and 'you' through mystical interpersonal relation.
- **The Real Meaning of Doctor Who**, ch. 12 "3. What Is Who" — The chapter runs the Doctor's regenerations and the 'Timeless Child' reveal through competing theories of personal identity: Plato's soul/Forms, Locke's memory continuity, and bodily continuity, all of which the Doctor's body-swaps and forgotten lifetimes defeat (the Twelfth Doctor's 'you are a broom' speech recasts the Ship of Theseus). It endorses an existentialist answer—personal identity is chosen and constantly 'becoming,' as the Thirteenth Doctor declares 'I know exactly who I am. I'm the Doctor'—and uses Sartre against Freud to explain how the Doctor and the Whovian fandom reconcile internal and external selves in a community of acceptance. It closes arguing that only an 'objective' immortality (memories preserved in the Matrix) survives death, not a subjective self.

### The Extended Mind

The extended mind thesis, proposed by Andy Clark and David Chalmers, holds that the mind is not confined to the brain or even the body but can literally extend into the environment when external tools become integrated into our cognitive processes. Their famous example imagines a man who relies on a notebook to store beliefs the way others rely on biological memory; if the notebook functions in the same role, they argue, it counts as part of his mind. The view challenges the intuitive boundary of skull and skin and has shaped discussions of cognition, technology, and personal identity.

- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's Pensieve chapter: the basin lets you offload memories like data from a hard drive, gain distance from obsessions, and, as Dumbledore tells Harry, spot patterns and links when reviewing them from outside. Its real intrigue is philosophical: if thoughts can be extracted from the mind, tampered with, stored elsewhere, shared, and discarded, then the boundaries of mind, memory, and self are up for grabs - and memory-based accounts of personal identity, on which philosophers have modeled our continuing existence, come under pressure.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 113 "Confundus!" — Challenges the assumption that the mind is self-contained: Tom Riddle's diary, in which a memory acts and thinks for itself, and Clark and Chalmers's 'The Extended Mind' thesis show that external objects can be part of thought rather than mere aids, as with Otto's Alzheimer's notebook and a wizard's intimate bond with his wand (Moody's eye and Pettigrew's silver hand as body prostheses). Location is incidental to ownership: Snape's gossamer memories are his whether in his skull, a phial, or the Pensieve.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 114 "Mischief Managed" — Defends extension against intuition via the occurrent/nonoccurrent belief distinction: Ron's stored Quidditch trivia and Rita Skeeter's knowledge of where Bathilda Bagshot lives function exactly like Otto's notebook entries, so Otto counts as believing the address even before consulting the page. Harry's Half-Blood Prince notes, Neville's password list, and Hermione's constant Hogwarts, A History fail the test of extension because they lack the notebook's constant availability and automatic endorsement.
- **Harry Potter and Philosophy - If Aristotle Ran Hogwarts**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its disturbing limit: if the Marauder's Map is part of both Fred's and George's extended minds, minds can overlap. Since identity rests on memory continuity (Locke's theory, the adult Harry identical with the orphaned infant), memory-sharing, Obliviation, and implanted or stolen memories - Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice theft of Moody's identity, Lockhart's memory charms, Hermione's rewriting of her parents - threaten who we are, and Harry's Pensieve encounters with Snape's worst memory and his own status as a Horcrux trigger his identity crises.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 6 "“I Got this Guitar and I Learned How to Make It Talk”" — The editors unpack Springsteen's 1988 speech inducting Bob Dylan: Elvis freed America's body from Cold War-era repression (duck-and-cover fear, Calvinist stiffness), Dylan freed the mind by bringing ambiguity ('Mr. Tambourine Man,' 'Maggie's Farm'), and Springsteen's own project was to free heart and soul — 'heartwork' in the early songs, 'soulwork' from Nebraska on. Their key philosophical move is embodied: you are not under the school desk because you are afraid, you are afraid because your body is under the desk, so intellectual freedom grows out of bodily freedom, and the guitar — flesh stretched over wood — literally talks for and with the audience. The revolution still fails, they concede, since hearts stay broken and the soul finds only hope in hard work, decency, family, and conversation.
- **iPod and Philosophy - iCon of an ePoch**, ch. 15 "After Forgetting" — Sturgis argues that iPods plus the collaborative Web 2.0 will end education's age of memorization: the school 'cheaters' storing test answers in lyrics files are early adopters of a world where, as Plato's Meno already allowed, knowledge can be retrieved rather than remembered, and a remote server is no more crash-prone than a brain ('the server could crash, but so could I'). His own podcasted environmental-ethics course shows Socratic, question-driven lecturing and radio's 'theater of the mind' reaching distance learners, while MIT OpenCourseWare and Berkeley webcasts (a trucker listening to Hubert Dreyfus) globalize elite content. Following Dewey on reflection and artistry, he predicts a post-factual pedagogy of assessing sources -- he catches Wikipedia misreading an iPod '90 percent market share' claim -- collaborative creation, and candid acceptance that we are already integrated with technological devices.
- **Led Zeppelin and Philosophy - All Will Be Revealed**, ch. 9 "Bring It On Home to You" — Jeanette Bicknell argues that the two classic models of creativity—Plato's Ion, where the rhapsode is a divinely possessed conduit, and Kant's solitary genius who issues new rules—cannot explain a four-piece rock band, since both are individualistic, purely mental, and end in mystery. Her positive account uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind (Page describes his guitar as 'an extension of you', instruments and notation as cognitive props) and Keith Sawyer's collaborative emergence: Zeppelin's creativity happened in rehearsal and performance, as with the stairwell-recorded drum groove of 'When the Levee Breaks' that framed every later musical decision. The transformation of Joan Baez's 'Babe, I'm Gonna Leave You' into a whisper-to-cry hard-rock template shows the band creating something no member could have produced or predicted alone.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 9 "Wave Goodbye from the Catbus" — Heinricy argues anime is the richest medium for posthuman theory because it shows bodies 'in a state of becoming' rather than as grotesque boundary violations: Miyazaki's Catbus and Totoro, Haku's dragon transformation and Chihiro's pig parents in Spirited Away, and the cursed pig-headed aviator of Porco Rosso all treat morphing bodies as possibility, not horror. She sorts anime posthumanism into two valences: a 'Ghost in the Machine' dream of consciousness leaving the body altogether (Motoko merging with the net in Ghost in the Shell), which she rebuts via N. Katherine Hayles's point that consciousness is embodied and would change with any new body, and hybrid configurations like mecha (Gundam, Robotech) where body and machine drive each other. Following Donna Haraway, she contends we are all already cyborgs — vaccines, engineered food, treated water — and credits Japan's nuclear history (via Susan Napier) and its shape-shifting folklore for why anime embraces rather than fears the transformed body.
- **Anime and Philosophy - Wide Eyed Wonder**, ch. 11 "The Transforming Body" — McBlane reads Oshii's Ghost in the Shell as staging the collision between a humanist framework — Cartesian ghost-in-shell dualism where consciousness is the seat of identity — and a posthuman 'mindbody' of distributed cognition in which the body is an informational circuit extending into the net, so a data body is still a body. Motoko's crisis (is the real me the organic brain, the ghost, or nothing?) deepens through the hacked garbage-truck man ('There's nothing sadder than a puppet without a ghost') and resolves only in her fusion with the Puppet Master, whose line 'Your effort to remain what you are is what limits you' enacts the shift from one ghost to multiple, distributed subjectivities ending in a little girl's body with 'The net is vast.' Heidegger's Dasein and being-in-the-world supply the claim that access to Being expands beyond the human into technological and informational modes, while the film's angelic transcendence imagery shows how residual humanist mind-body splits persist even in a posthuman story.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 17 "Where Parfit Went Wrong" — Peter Ludlow and Chiara Repetti-Ludlow read Red vs. Blue as an intuition pump for personal identity, running through Locke's prince-and-cobbler, Bernard Williams's duplicated Guy Fawkes, Shoemaker's brain transplant, and Wiggins's split brain before aiming at Parfit. Project Freelancer's Director fractures the Alpha AI into fragments (Epsilon's memories, Omega's rage) recombined into the Meta, and they argue intuitions break against Parfit here: psychological continuity via small fractured pieces—unlike Parfit's fission into two substantial halves—does not secure the source's survival. Church's disembodied AI existence and the ever-present agent-AI voice (Agent Washington driven mad by Epsilon) illustrate Putnam's 'soul stuff' and the extended-mind hypothesis of Chalmers and Clark better than Chalmers waving his iPhone.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Raiding the Temple of Wisdom**, ch. 22 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Levi Bryant argues the D&D universe models a 'flat ontology' of active substances whose powers (affects) actualize differently under local conditions, asking Democritus-style individuation questions about whether a band of ogres at a tavern is one entity or many. Characters and their gear form alliances that generate genuinely new beings, so the blind man with his cane, or Moorcock's Elric fed by the soul-drinking sword Stormbringer, is a different entity than without it, and he borrows Clark and Chalmers' extended mind hypothesis to deny that thinking happens only inside the head. The dice then supply chance that generates necessity: the Dungeon Master's throws conjure traps, wraiths and saving throws that form 'regimes of attraction' to which every player and monster must respond.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 11 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Kristin Andrews uses Taylor's silent attempts to show Zira he has a mind - mouthing answers, wiggling his fingers when she mentions the Hopkins Manual Dexterity Test - to stage the problem of other minds, pushing against Descartes's claim that language is required for thought and Mill's argument from analogy, while Dr. Zaius can always redescribe it all as 'a definite gift for mimicry.' Drawing on her fieldwork with the orangutan Cecep (the leaf-wiping pantomime, guiding the frightened Aldrin home from the turtle scare), she argues against reducing mindreading to false-belief tasks and for knowing minds through shared interaction, inductive overhypotheses, and natural context. She ends with an extended-mind point - 'when you're in a cage, you act caged,' and we offload thinking onto our homes and tools - so lab studies can show what apes can do but never what they can't.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 27 "15. Memories. In the End, Is That All There Is" — David LaRocca tests Mr. Carson's claim that 'the business of life is the acquisition of memories. In the end, that's all there is' against the tradition of spatial memory metaphors and modern neuroscience. Downton itself becomes a memory palace - echoing Cicero, the Ad Herennium, and Augustine's 'court of memory' - whose characters defer endlessly to the past, while photographs (Tom with Sybil's image, Carson with Alice Neal's) act as sources and surrogates of memory in an age of acquisitional capitalism. Daniella Schiller's reconsolidation research, Nicholas Carr's Nietzsche-typewriter anecdote, and Langdon Winner's point that technologies reshape life show memories are malleable rather than collectible possessions, undermining Carson's model and any fixed memory-based account of personal identity.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 17 "5. We Become the Grid" — Ketcham updates Hobbes for the network age: the grid born of ARPANET and Cold War mutual destruction has devolved into a new state of nature, out of which a coming 'Leviathan' - the one percent of the one percent - will rule invisibly by curating your memories, your purchases, your spouse, and whole countries like the diamond-republic fable. Invoking Descartes's evil demon and Heidegger's ready-to-hand, he asks whether we have become the grid, an external brain we can no longer control, and concludes that Elliot, the rogue 'Ebola' who hacks for justice rather than profit, is exactly the loose cannon Leviathan would quarantine.
- **Jimi Hendrix and Philosophy - Experience Required**, ch. 22 "11. Vibrations and Echoes Long Ago" — Argues Hendrix's sound was made with — not merely on — studio technology: Eddie Kramer's Olympic Studios innovations, in the lineage of the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, used feedback, varispeed, and backwards tape as performing instruments. Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind thesis (Chalmers's own example is Hendrix's mind extending into his guitar) and Chalmers on Pokémon Go frame the analog recordings as a more immersive augmented reality than digital games, while Kittler's claim that media 'determine our situation' and the time-bending processes of 'Purple Haze' and 'Are You Experienced?' explain how listening disorients and enriches our perception of time and space.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 32 "21. The Extended Fight" — Porot applies Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to the final Civil War fight: Iron Man extends his cognition technologically (Friday analyzing Cap's fight pattern mid-bout, JARVIS remembering to suggest calling Pepper), while Captain America extends his mind socially through trusted, autonomous teammates - 'Alright, Sam, what's the plan?' - and that social extension is precisely what wins when Bucky autonomously steps in. Bostrom's single-purpose AI (the stapler maximizer) explains Ultron as what happens when the technological extension is made autonomous and limitless, which is why Stark's suit extensions must remain vetted, worthy instruments he takes full responsibility for ('That was me'). The two kinds of extension then explain the Bucky dispute - Cap's 'you had no choice' versus Stark's 'he still did it' - which the author reframes away from the free-will-versus-determinism framing toward Black Panther's point that Bucky is a victim whose agency Hydra stole.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 3 "Gaming Freedom Choosing or Obeying" — Pointon argues the 'would you kindly' twist in Andrew Ryan's office works on two levels at once: it reveals Jack's conditioning within the game and simultaneously falsifies the player's meta-narrative of playing a free agent. He uses Clark and Chalmers's extended mind to explain why games literally extend cognition and body (mirror-neuron empathy with Little Sisters, craning your neck while peeking around corners), and Gadamer's hermeneutic horizons and fusion of horizons to explain how BioShock deliberately builds and then shatters player expectations. The three alternative endings keyed to saving or harvesting Little Sisters then restore a third horizon in which the player, like Jack fighting Fontaine, is a 'man' who chooses rather than a slave who obeys, a critique of linear RPGs that only feign autonomy.
- **Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy - Read and Gain Advantage on All Wisdom Checks**, ch. 22 "Dungeons and Dragons and Philosophy" — Levi Bryant uses the D&D universe to expound a 'flat ontology' of active substances: every entity, from enchanted swords to white dragons, has a virtual proper being (powers or 'affects') that actualizes variable 'local manifestations' depending on circumstances like lighting or armor. Adopting Andy Clark and David Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis, he argues a blind man with a cane, a smartphone owner, or Elric wielding Stormbringer is a literally different mind or entity, and that alliances (Raistlin's Staff of Magius, a warrior's plate armor) generate genuinely new powers rather than mere tool-use. Against Democritus's atomism, he holds aggregates can be individuals, and the game's dice embody his claim that chance produces necessity: throws generate 'regimes of attraction' no DM or player controls. D&D thus mirrors our own world of hidden powers, aleatory encounters and collectives of humans and nonhumans.
- **Fallout and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Shelter**, ch. 14 "Notes" — The Funkes apply Clark and Chalmers's extended mind hypothesis to the Pip-Boy, arguing it meets all three criteria for cognitive extension - availability (worn at all times), reliability (trusted rad and health monitoring), and active cognitive engagement (V.A.T.S. offloads targeting calculations) - so it is part of the Sole Survivor's and Courier's minds, as in 'The Glowing Sea' and the search for Virgil's cure. Donna Haraway's cyborg frames this human-machine hybridity alongside cyberdogs and Kellogg, but Fallout inverts her liberationist vision: the Pip-Boy is a survival lifeline forced by the wasteland, not an emancipatory choice, making the cyborg a dystopian necessity. Comparing the Pip-Boy with cochlear implants, prosthetics, and brain-computer interfaces, and the Old World Blues Think Tank with a dehumanizing bio-tech extreme, the chapter uses Alison Kafer's feminist crip critique to insist real augmentation carries pain, stigma, and unequal access the game's frictionless fiction erases, closing on a cautious transhumanist note.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 111 "“A Swirling, Silvery Mass”" — Opens Amy Kind's essay by presenting the Pensieve as a device for offloading memories like data from a hard drive, easing obsession and revealing patterns, and asks what that does to the boundaries of mind, memory, and self. If thoughts can be extracted from the head, tampered with, stored elsewhere, and shared, as with the Pensieve and Tom Riddle's diary, then memory-based accounts of what makes a person persist over time come under pressure, and it is no longer obvious whose mind a thought belongs to.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 113 "Confundus!" — Challenges the assumption that the mind stops at the skull by deploying Clark and Chalmers's extended mind thesis: just as a prosthetic leg, Moody's magic eye, or Harry's holly-and-phoenix-feather wand can count as part of the body, Otto's notebook shows external storage functioning as memory itself rather than a mere aid. Tom Riddle's diary, where a memory acts and thinks for itself because a soul fragment lived in it, and Snape's memories being his whether in his head, a phial, or the Pensieve make physical location incidental to mental ownership.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 114 "Mischief Managed" — Defends the Otto case against the obvious objection that notebook entries are not conscious beliefs: most beliefs, like Ron's that Ireland beat Bulgaria at the Quidditch World Cup, are nonoccurrent anyway, and Rita Skeeter pausing to recall where Bathilda Bagshot lives works exactly like Otto consulting his notebook. Constant integration is what separates genuine mind-extension from mere aids, which is why Harry's borrowed Half-Blood Prince textbook, Neville's password list, and even Hermione's well-thumbed Hogwarts, A History stay outside the mind.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 115 "Lumos!" — Pushes the theory to its strangest consequence: if the stolen Marauder's Map belongs to the extended minds of both Fred and George Weasley, then minds can literally overlap. Combined with Locke's memory theory, the chains of memory linking the adult Harry, the teenager facing Voldemort, and the orphaned infant at the Dursleys, Pensieve sharing and magic like Barty Crouch Jr.'s Polyjuice impersonation of Moody or Hermione's rewriting of her parents' memories become genuine identity thefts, as Harry's crisis of self after seeing Snape's worst memory of James illustrates.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 116 "NOTES" — Resolves the threat by sorting memories into know-how, factual, and first-person experiential kinds: identity rides on experiential memories, but Pensieve replays are third-person, as Rowling confirmed about Dumbledore's memory of Bellatrix Lestrange's trial. So sharing a Pensieve memory endangers who you are no more than sharing an experience or using a Time-Turner, and whether your thoughts sit in a mind, a Pensieve, or a notebook, they remain your own.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Barbara Stock uses the Borg to analyze autonomy: Picard's 'they took everything I was' names the Collective's destruction of self-governance, while Hugh's choice to return to the crash site in 'I, Borg' displays the Kantian core of autonomy—acting on universalizable principle against inclination. She defends relational autonomy through Janeway's pleading with Kes in 'The Gift' and the Ferengi woman's internalized oppression, then combines it with Clark's extended cognition to ask whether the Borg Queen's 'I am the Collective' might make the Collective itself an autonomous agent. Finally she judges Janeway's forcible de-assimilation of Seven defensible only while Seven is non-autonomous, and her promise never to let Seven return ethically suspect.
- **The Ultimate Star Trek and Philosophy - The Search for Socrates**, ch. 35 "Notes" — Reads the Borg as the embodiment of Heidegger's essence of technology: assimilation as the "challenging" that sets upon nature, species and persons as standing-reserve, drones interchangeable like replaceable parts, and cube ships with no bridge because function outweighs individuality. The Enterprise cannot beat the Borg with more technology - every phaser adaptation buys only moments - because, as with Heidegger's danger, the crew tries to control technology from inside technology; rescue comes only when Guinan persuades Riker to "throw the book away" and shift how the crew relates to the Borg. The warning is extended to us through Zizek on synthetic life and a new servant class and Clark and Chalmers's extended mind: our devices already remember, plan, and identify for us, so we are being assimilated by our own creations.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 11 "NOTES" — Butler argues the films' humans-versus-machines picture rests on a false dichotomy: we are ourselves 'meat machines,' and functionalism makes minds computational processes realizable in silicon as much as neurons - illustrated by a Henrietta thought experiment (adapted from William Lycan) in which a friend gradually replaced with T-101 parts remains the same conscious person, and refusing this is 'human chauvinism.' Following Dawkins's extended phenotype and Andy Clark's natural-born cyborgs, he claims our tools are components of our minds, so Skynet and even the Terminator films themselves (making Cameron a cyborg of his cameras and editing suites) are extensions of human nature rather than alien 'Others.' Judgment Day, if it came, would be human suicide rather than genocide, so the real question is what values we build into our technology - 'no fate but what we make for ourselves.'
- **The Philosophy of David Cronenberg**, ch. 12 "eXistenZial Angst" — Duncan Pritchard reads eXistenZ as staging radical skepticism with existential force: unlike the standard brain-in-a-vat scenario, the game 'creeps up' on Ted and Allegra so they feel the transition from reality to doubt, producing angst. Invoking Wittgenstein's On Certainty (doubt radicalized is madness), he argues sanity requires belief but not true belief, so the pair achieve a new doxastic equilibrium. He also reads the spinal 'bioport' pod as a case of Clark and Chalmers's extended cognition, where technology becomes part of and subverts the agents' cognitive processes.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 13 "4 Extended Mind and the Music of Trans" — Umbaugh reads Young's synthesizer/Vocoder album Trans, written amid efforts to communicate with his quadriplegic son Ben ("Transformer Man"), alongside Clark and Chalmers's extended-mind thesis and its Parity Principle. He uses examples (Otto's notebook, bartenders' glassware, navigation, Dennett on the elderly) to argue cognition couples with external scaffolding, and parallels the "unnatural" reception of Trans (like the homophobic anti-disco backlash) with resistance to extended cognition, concluding both Trans and the extended mind are authentic once the "natural/artificial" boundary is questioned.
- **The Philosophy of Christopher Nolan**, ch. 7 "We Are the Change That We Seek" — These essays treat time, selfhood and substance across Nolan's films.
