She then reads 'No Time Like the Past' as enacting the impossibility of changing the past: Paul Driscoll's attempt to shoot Hitler is thwarted by a maid and SS officers exactly as Lewis's 'bananas peel' account predicts, and his retreat to 1881 Homeville makes him the unwitting cause of the very schoolhouse fire he tried to prevent — his foreknowledge, not fate, was always the cause.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" — Schiltz tests Janet's claim to know 'literally everything' against the philosophical definition of omniscience as believing all true propositions, finding she lacks knowledge of Michael's demonhood, of the future, and of current events on Earth. Divine-omniscience puzzles drawn from Averroes and Aquinas, and Boethius's solution that God sees all things in an eternal present, frame why Janet's ignorance of the future is what protects the characters' free will and moral responsibility. Frank Jackson's Mary thought experiment illuminates Judge Gen's failure to know what human life is like, and Janet's gradual acquisition of empathy across her reboots shows why her imperfect knowledge is a feature rather than a glitch.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 17 "8. Time Travel and the Problem of Evil" — Ray Bossert reads Endgame through Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy, arguing that Doctor Strange and Tony Stark, who permit the Snap and five years of suffering for the sake of the one winning outcome, run 'uncannily parallel' to Thanos, who decided for Gamora that her unwilling death served the greater good. Strange's viewing of 14,000,605 futures illustrates Boethius's distinction between an infinite being riding along the timeline and an eternal one seeing all moments at once, and the refusal to tell Stark his role mirrors why God's foreknowledge sees our choices without compelling them. Boethius's providence weaving free choices into justice, the Avengers' passion-driven failures on Titan (Star-Lord and Thor avenging lost lovers), justice as the wicked's own punishment (Thanos dying wretched twice in one film), and Umberto Eco's 'Myth of Superman' all frame a universe where suffering is allowed because it is woven into a pattern that ends in justice.
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 33 "21. I Plucked My Soul Out of Its Secret Place" — Traces the Soul Stone across comics and film — Thanos courting Death, the Vormir 'a soul for a soul' trade of Gamora, and Natasha's parallel sacrifice for Clint in Endgame — reading it through sacrifice and resurrection motifs from the Binding of Isaac and asking why the film's Thanos must complete the offering Abraham was spared. It contrasts Thanos, who styles himself a god but is a 'false god,' an idol beside the sentient being that existed before all realities and became the six Infinity Gems, with Adam Warlock, who dwells in the Soul World and 'knows his soul' (the chapter's title borrows Claude McKay's poem), while Thanos is driven by destiny — 'I ignored my destiny once. I cannot do that again.'
- **Avengers Infinity Saga and Philosophy - Go for the Head**, ch. 36 "24. The Left Hand of Thanos" — Reads the Endgame 'I am' exchange through Martin Luther's two hands of God: Thanos's left-handed gauntlet enacts God's 'alien work' of law, judgment and destruction (his 'inevitability,' seen in all 14,000,605 of Strange's futures), while Tony's right-handed snap enacts the 'proper work' of grace, where freedom means relying on a promise — Strange's gift of the Time Stone, the Ancient One resting reality on Banner's promise. It applies the law/grace contrast to Thor's reconciliation with Frigga ('you're going to be the man you're meant to be'), Tony's with Howard, and Steve's gift of the shield to Sam, arguing the heroes' failures at who they were 'supposed to be' are the law's condemnation, while the promise delivers a freedom that turns Thanos's inevitability into impossibility.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 40 "To the Third Power . ." — Wolfe argues the original series is 'deeply Mormon' in ontology though not in epistemology: Kobol anagrams Kolob, the Quorum of Twelve and 'sealing' marriages mirror LDS structure, and the Beings of Light's 'as you are now, we once were; as we are now, you may become' restates Lorenzo Snow's deification couplet, while Count Iblis, like the Mormon Satan, can only rule those who freely yield - agency is supreme. Because none of this is required to follow the show, later licensees could rebuild the metaphysics: the Maximum Press comics incoherently (free will violated when inconvenient), Richard Hatch's novels with a new pure-blood-of-Kobol cosmology, and Ronald Moore with a circular 'all this has happened before' replacing eternal progression.
- **Bioshock and Philosophy - Irrational Game, Rational Book**, ch. 12 "Final Thoughts" — Squires and McBain argue the ending wrongly necessitates that Booker's baptism must produce Comstock in every possible world, cashing out the necessity in possible-world terms and quoting William James on determinism's closed future. Against this 'God of necessity' they defend a traditional omniscient, omnipresent (panentheist) God whose foreknowledge does not determine choices, citing the justice requirement for free will and the biblical case of Hezekiah's prayer adding twenty years as proof the future stays open. Read this way, Booker never had to become a racist zealot, and the game's shockingly limited ending unfairly reinforces the stereotype that deep religious devotion necessarily leads to extremism.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 28 "Changing Fate or Being Changed by Fate" — Colombo and Jones read Brave through Aristotle's virtue ethics and Heraclitus's 'character is fate': the dispute between Merida and Elinor over 'what is a queen' is whether royalty is a mere position or a character requiring cultivated excellence and habituated 'second nature,' which Elinor's poise displays and Merida's hot temper lacks. Merida's witch's bargain to 'change my fate' only scrambles fortune (turning Elinor into a bear) until she follows the riddle 'mend the bond torn by pride,' replacing pride with empathy — and only then, at the Mor'du confrontation where fate, fortune, and character converge, can it be said her fate was changed rather than she by it.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 10 "Intending the Way Out" — Works through the paradox of foreknowledge: because Paul's Caladan dream of first meeting Chani is knowledge in Plato's justified-true-belief sense, the foreseen future is factive, so his struggle against the jihad he visions (even hoping to die on Feyd-Rautha's blade rather than become a martyr) is futile. It tests the classical escape routes, Boethius's God who views all times as an ever-present eternity and Aquinas's God seeing the whole road 'under the aspect of eternity', and Laplace's Demon's causal determinism, but finds the Atreides oracles unlike God since they are creatures in time who see many possible futures rather than one. The resolution comes through Anscombe's Intention: practical knowledge lets Paul and Leto, whose present choices shift the balance of probability among foreseen timelines, intend their way out as creative authors of events.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Minds, Monads, and Muad'Dib**, ch. 26 "In The Land of the Blind, the One-Eyed Man . ." — Sequel to 'Intending the Way Out': since oracles fix the set of possible futures they see, the single meeting of two Atreides oracles in the Tanzerouft, the vision-battle where Paul's whispered 'Don't' cedes the Golden Path to Leto, shows they are free precisely where each is blind to the other. It reads Paul as a tragic hero in the ancient Greek sense whose defining flaw is his humanity, and argues that by breeding Siona's prescience-invisibility 'Leto frees himself by blinding himself', so freedom rests on a mixture of knowledge and ignorance, with ordinary intentional actors, not God, as the proper analogue of the oracles.
- **Final Fantasy and Philosophy - The Ultimate Walkthrough**, ch. 17 "Final Fantasy and Philosophy" — Nicolas Michaud asks whether the prophesied Four Warriors of Light of Final Fantasy I deserve thanks if the Sage Lukahn's foreknowledge meant they could not do otherwise, framing their plight with the problem of divine foreknowledge and Aquinas's answer that God stands outside time. He then deploys Frankfurt's preemption cases, Garland ready to mind-control you either way, to show moral responsibility can survive without alternative possibilities, but concludes the Warriors may still be unworthy of praise because they know they are predestined, a worry that spreads to us through Phineas Gage-style biological determinism: if our characters are hardwired, neither we nor Garland deserve praise or blame.
- **Game of Thrones and Philosophy - Logic Cuts Deeper Than Swords**, ch. 31 "Game of Thrones and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Daenerys's fatalism - she feels truly free only once she believes fate is in control - can coexist with freedom in a Westeros where class and gender fix everyone's essence. Aristotle's sea-battle argument from bivalence and Cicero's Idle Argument (Dany will rule whether or not she leaves Meereen) are dismantled as having no practical consequences for deliberation, while Sartre's anguish and bad faith explain Cersei's 'necessity' excuse for arresting Ned and Sansa's refusal to own her lie about Joffrey and Mycah. Heidegger's authenticity then resolves the paradox: like Ned choosing between family and honor and Jon choosing his Night's Watch vows over kinship, freedom is not escape from one's past but owning it - Heraclitus's 'character is destiny,' becoming who you are.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 26 "13. The Vessel of Knowledge Who Stole Our Hearts" — Uses the philosophy of divine omniscience (Aquinas's perfect knowledge, Averroes's self-knowing cause) to assess Janet's claim to know 'literally everything': on the all-true-propositions model she falls short — she misses Michael's deception, the future, and current events on Earth — which is a feature, since no foreknowledge means no threat to free will and no need for Boethius's eternal-present solution. Frank Jackson's Mary's room and Linda Zagzebski's omnisubjectivity frame Judge Gen's failure: 'You can't judge humans 'cause you don't know what we go through,' as Jason says, and her trip to Earth is her stepping out of the black-and-white room. Janet's gradual acquisition of experienced emotion — love for Jason, empathy for the Soul Squad — is likewise a kind of knowing no database contains.
- **Green Lantern and Philosophy - No Evil Shall Escape This Book**, ch. 29 "Green Lantern and Philosophy" — Kind uses John Stewart's Justice League arc, thrown into the future by Chronos, meeting his son Warhawk, and hiding it from Hawkgirl while dating Vixen, to stage fatalism: Pike and Taylor's arguments that a foreknown future, whether God's or a time traveler's, cannot be otherwise. Time travel itself forces a choice between presentism and eternalism, since Warhawk must 'exist now, already, in the future' for GL and Batman to visit him, and Smart's tenseless four-dimensionalism, with GL a series of timeslices and 'now' as subjective as 'here,' dissolves the fatalist worry by banishing tensed facts. The chapter lands on GL's battlefield advice to his son: 'Plant your feet,' owning a fate you cannot escape.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 29 "Varieties of Prophecy" — The section sets up Jeremy Pierce's chapter by contrasting Trelawney the 'old fraud,' whose tea leaves, tarot, and crystal balls yield elastic generalities and false death forecasts, with the two predictions Dumbledore calls her only 'real predictions,' which McGonagall and the centaur Firenze also treat as different in kind. It asks what distinguishes genuine prophecy from fortune-telling in a world where magic might connect tea leaves or dreams to actual future events.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 30 "Fallible Prophecies" — Crediting Aristotle with first raising whether the future is fixed, the section distinguishes fallible from infallible prophecies and builds a seven-fold menu of how a Seer could access the future, from fallible sense-based guessing like Muggle weather reports and Trelawney's usual act, through probabilities over possible futures, to infallible access to a deterministic outcome or to the actual fixed future. The question becomes which of these Trelawney's two genuine prophecies are.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 31 "Self-Fulfilling Prophecies" — The section argues that Dumbledore treats even the real prophecy as fallible, telling Harry he is 'quite free to turn your back on the prophecy,' which suggests likelihood rather than guarantee. Yet the involuntary trance source, Trelawney's spade readings that fit the hidden Harry she cannot see, and the lightning-struck tower card point to occasional access to possible or fixed futures beyond mere category-1 guessing.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 32 "Destiny" — Testing whether Trelawney's first prophecy was self-fulfilling, the section deploys Alexander of Aphrodisias's discussion of the Oedipus story, where a prediction that causes its own fulfillment would be the prophet's deed rather than a revelation of what was going to happen. It concludes the prophecy did not make Voldemort attack: he chose Harry as the half-blood he saw himself in, acting on incomplete information from Snape's interrupted eavesdropping, so self-fulfillment cannot distinguish real predictions from Trelawney's usual fare.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 33 "A Rodent’s Destiny" — The section spells out what Rowling's reported denial of destiny could mean, laying out compatibilism versus libertarian freedom and fixed versus open futures on which statements about future free choices lack truth values. Dumbledore's insistence that Harry could have turned his back on the prophecy fits either a genuinely open future or a fixed one that prophecies do not compel, so the books themselves must decide.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 34 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — The section argues the second real prophecy, about the servant rejoining the Dark Lord that night, cannot be merely 'likely but fallible': Wormtail's escape depended on a chain of improbable contingencies such as Lupin forgetting his Wolfsbane potion and the last-minute switch of Secret-Keeper. The first prophecy likewise required Voldemort to mark Harry through events, from Snape's plea to Lily's sacrifice, that flow from the prophecy itself, so genuine prophecy needs a stronger tie to the actual future than probability.
- **The Ultimate Harry Potter and Philosophy - Hogwarts for Muggles**, ch. 35 "NOTES" — The section defends fixed time from the Prisoner of Azkaban episode, where later-Harry casts the stag Patronus that saved earlier-Harry and nothing about the past changes, against Hermione's warnings that wizards have killed their past selves, which the author recasts as travel between possible timelines. A special-relativity argument that there is no absolute present supports fixed time, and the cascade of lucky coincidences from brewing Polyjuice in Moaning Myrtle's bathroom through Felix Felicis, Malfoy Manor, and the Shrieking Shack finally suggests that some providential guide, rather than dumb luck, steered events toward the prophecy's fulfillment.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Shores reads Volume 1 through Nietzsche's eternal recurrence as a self-test of life-affirmation: Adam sealed in a coffin embodies recurrence in its 'most terrible form,' Future Hiro's string map dramatizes Nietzsche's claim that every action is indissolubly tied to all others, and Linderman's speech divorcing happiness from meaning is answered by Nietzsche's demand to crave nothing more fervently than the eternal return. The chapter stresses where the show diverges: Claire insists 'the future is not written in stone' and the heroes rewrite destiny, while Arthur Petrelli ironically holds a copy of Thus Spoke Zarathustra while contradicting it. Hiro's failed attempts to save Charlie and his father (Kaito's 'we cannot play God') frame the amor fati question of whether free will means changing events or willing them eternally.
- **Heroes and Philosophy - Buy the Book, Save the World**, ch. 18 "NOTES" — Johnson asks whether Isaac's paintings and Hiro's visions make the future fated, running Aristotle's sea-battle argument: if propositions about the future are already true (by bivalence and the correspondence theory of a 'written timeline'), then Sylar's exploding New York is inevitable and no one is free. He extends the problem to infallible foreknowledge via Future Hiro as a stand-in for God, considers and rejects Boethius's timeless-knowledge solution, and uses open theism plus a probability calculation about Ando's waffles order to show probabilistic foreknowledge is useless. He concludes most of Isaac's 'prophecies' are really self-fulfilling, as when Noah's efforts to dodge the eighth painting cause his shooting, and that the Heroes universe leaves room to deny fate.
- **The Hobbit and Philosophy - For When You've Lost Your Dwarves, Your Wizard, and Your Way**, ch. 39 "a19.xhtml" — Sterling takes Gandalf's 'Bilbo was meant to find the Ring, and not by its maker' as a claim of providence by Eru Iluvatar, which generates the problem of divine foreknowledge: if Eru arranged for the Ring to slip from Gollum's grasp, he must have foreknown countless free choices (Bilbo choosing to follow, Dori carrying him, Gollum strangling the goblin whimper-pip). Open theism's open future fails because Tolkien's Music of the Ainur prefigures all things except the free will of Elves and Men, and compatibilist escapes (Hobbes, Hume, Frankfurt, Dennett) are dismissed as inadequate. The solution is Boethius' Consolation of Philosophy: Eru is outside time, beholding all events in an eternal present - like holding the whole film reel at once - so his 'foreknowledge' is timeless vision, and Tolkien's 'Osanwe-kenta' confirms that minds in Time cannot see the future except through Eru.
- **Ultimate Lost and Philosophy - Think Together, Die Alone**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Addey analyzes the show's web of coincidences - Sawyer and Boone crossing paths in the Australian police station, Jack meeting Desmond in the hatch - and distinguishes genuine coincidence from divine providence, fatalism, and determinism. She applies Jung's theory of synchronicity to Locke's walkabout conviction that he was 'meant' to reach the island, then uses the birthday paradox, the law of truly large numbers, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability to show why viewers and conspiracy theorists overestimate the improbability of such connections. Finally she evaluates Jacob's candidacy experiment as flawed social science: the candidates' circumstantial ignorance, maintained by the Others' deceptions, undermines the free and morally responsible choices Jacob claims to be testing, which is why the curious Hurley deserved to become protector.
- **The Ultimate Star Wars and Philosophy - You Must Unlearn What You Have Learned**, ch. 17 "Notes" — Eberl applies Augustine's theodicy to the Force: since evil is privation rather than a thing, the dark side is not a real half of the Force but its willful misuse by free beings, answering why a Force with a will permits Alderaan. Anakin's fall is Augustine's inordinate desire (cupiditas) for the temporal good of Padme's life against Yoda's counsel to let go, while Jacen Solo's willingness to kill for peace shows love destroyed rather than merely disordered, placing him beyond the redemption Anakin's rightly ordered love for his children still permits. Free will remains a divine gift whose misuse, not its giver, explains moral evil, and Anakin could still freely fulfill the Chosen One prophecy.
- **Terminator and Philosophy - I'll Be Back, Therefore I Am**, ch. 19 "NOTES" — Miller reconciles Kyle's 'no fate but what we make' with Sarah's 'you're dead already': eternalism (defended by the special-relativity argument Hilary Putnam made famous) makes 2029 as real as 1994, so Judgment Day cannot be changed, and the grandfather paradox - using Caesar's unalterable assassination as the model - blocks the T-101 from preventing its own existence. She then tests growing-block, presentist, meta-time, and branching-timeline (McCall-style) models against T2 and T3, asking whether any lets Sarah's attack on Cyberdyne legitimately delay Judgment Day. The conclusion works under every model: even on a fixed four-dimensional block, Judgment Day happens because of what humans do, not independently of them, so fixed fate and making our own future turn out to be compatible.
- **Veronica Mars and Philosophy - Investigating the Mysteries of Life (Which Is a Bitch Until You Die)**, ch. 14 "“I Know All of This Because I Have Done Everything I Can to Get to the Truth”" — Daniel Wack reads Veronica Mars as film noir refashioned for teen television: the class-riven town without a middle class supplies the corrupt noir milieu, but the genre's gender roles are reversed, so Logan becomes the homme fatal whose drunken promise of an 'epic' love offers the redemption-through-romance the femme fatale always dangles and never delivers. Following Cavell and Pippin, he argues the characters are trapped by a fatalism they did not choose — inherited zip codes, Aaron Echolls's abuse, Jake Kane's affair with Lianne — and Logan's dream of a private, redeemed world fails because accepting it would cost Veronica the active, truth-generating detective self she built after her rape. Investigating Lilly's murder, her mother's disappearance, and her own assault, she learns the truth restores nothing, but that detective work gives her a new way to order and survive her world.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 9 "H E N R I B E R G S O N" — Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.
- **The Wheel of Time and Philosophy - A Portion of Wisdom**, ch. 21 "Notes" — Kowalski uses Min Farshaw's visions in the Amazon series to explore whether foreknowledge is compatible with free action, tracing the problem from Aristotle and Cicero through Augustine. He lays out the argument that if Min truly foreknows Tam raising Rand, it must come true and thus seems unfree, then surveys reconciliation projects: Boethius and Aquinas make God timeless so he does not literally foreknow, while Augustine (in the dialogue with Evodius) argues foreknowledge does not cause what is foreknown, so choices explain foreknowledge rather than vice versa. He notes Min is not timeless and her visions are fallible (Mat spears rather than stabs Rand), concluding WoT keeps its characters both free and fated for dramatic tension while offering only 'a semblance of choice.'
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 11 "No Country for Old Men The Coens’ Tragic Western" — Gilmore reads No Country for Old Men as the Coens' tragic Western, casting Llewelyn Moss as an Oedipus-like hero whose competence-plus-hubris (wounding the antelope, going back to the dying man) triggers his ruin, per Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics and the Delphic 'know thyself.' Anton Chigurh is a Nietzschean force beyond good and evil whose coin-toss rule preserves invulnerability by subordinating desire to chance, an amoral Dionysian wildness the essay ties to Thoreau's 'in Wildness is the preservation of the world' and Nietzsche's Apollonian/Dionysian balance from The Birth of Tragedy. Heraclitus's 'geometrical mean' models the hunter-to-prey structure (Chigurh:humans::Moss:antelope), and Bell's fatalism and closing dream of carrying fire voice a Greek-tragic 'you reap what you sow.'
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 19 "The Big Score Fate, Morality, and Meaningful Life in The Killing Steven M. Sanders" — Sanders reads Kubrick's heist film The Killing through Stoic and Aristotelian ethics, casting Johnny Clay (Sterling Hayden) as a 'stoical cool' figure whose surrender line 'What's the difference?' embodies apatheia, acceptance of fate. He argues Clay's doom (the burst suitcase, Nikki's fatal horseshoe) works as Kubrick's fate-driven moral verdict but strains Aristotle's principle that a truly prudent agent would not suddenly go to pieces. Weighing Aristotelian character-evaluation against Mill's outcome-based ethics, Sanders questions why Clay 'must' fail and treats his lack of self-critical rationality as the real obstacle to a meaningful life.
- **Steven Spielberg and Philosophy - We're Gonna Need a Bigger Book**, ch. 23 "Minority Report, Molinism, and the Viability of Precrime" — Kowalski defends the conceptual coherence of Minority Report's Precrime by dissolving the freedom-vs-foreknowledge worry: the precogs' prevision of Howard Marks knifing his wife shows only that 'necessarily, if it is foreknown, it happens,' not that the act happens necessarily, so contingency and free choice survive (Anderton's rolling-ball demo and Agatha's 'You can choose!'). He recasts the precogs' power as Luis de Molina's knowledge of the conditional future (middle knowledge)—Agatha narrating the life Sean never lived—invoking Aristotle, Augustine, Boethius, Aquinas, and Ockham on the problem, and finally rejects Spielberg's shut-it-down stance as a fallacious slippery-slope argument.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Pierce uses Harry Potter's prophecies to analyze destiny, fixed time, and freedom. Distinguishing Trelawney's fraudulent fortune-telling from her two genuine prophecies, he classifies kinds of prophecy (fallible, infallible, self-fulfilling) and, drawing on Aristotle's sea-battle problem and Alexander of Aphrodisias, argues Voldemort's choice of Harry rather than the prophecy itself made it true. He then sorts compatibilist and libertarian readings of Rowling's denial of destiny, argues her time travel (saving Buckbeak) implies a fixed view of time consistent with relativity, and suggests the improbable luck fulfilling prophecies hints at providential guidance.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 6 "Part Five D Is for Destiny" — This editor's introduction (Sharon Kaye) frames the whole volume by recounting a childhood memory of being lost at a carnival and using it to argue that the show taps a philosophical fear of being cut off from everything we know, forcing the viewer to confront questions like 'Why am I here?' and 'Does my life matter?' It organizes the nineteen essays under the acronym F.O.U.N.D. (Fortune/metaphysics, Origin/epistemology, Unity/social-political, Necessity/ethics, Destiny/religion), presenting Lost's plane-crash premise as an occasion for asking the meaning-of-life and fate-versus-free-will questions the survivors face.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 14 "NOTES" — Briony Addey defines coincidence and distinguishes three theories the castaways might invoke to say events are 'meant to be' — divine providence, fatalism, and determinism — using Locke's belief in his walkabout destiny and Eloise Hawking's 'the universe course corrects' as fatalist cases. She introduces Jung's synchronicity and collective unconscious as an acausal explanation of meaningful coincidence, then debunks our intuitions with the birthday paradox, confirmation bias, and Popper's falsifiability, before criticizing Jacob's deception 'experiment' on the candidates for failing standards of informed consent and culpable versus non-culpable ignorance.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Notes on Foreknowledge, Truthmaking, and Counterfactuals from The Dead Zone" — Manninen uses Johnny Smith's clairvoyance in The Dead Zone to probe how knowledge of the future is possible without fatalism, focusing on the truth condition of knowledge and truthmaker theory rather than the Gettier-vexed justification condition. Reviving Aristotle's sea-battle problem from De Interpretatione, he argues that if Johnny's statement 'Stillson will start a nuclear war' has a truthmaker the future seems fixed, foreclosing deliberation. He resolves this via Luis de Molina's middle (counterfactual) knowledge: Johnny knows only that IF Chuck attends the party or IF Stillson becomes president, THEN disaster follows, so by blocking the antecedent (keeping Stillson from office) he can avert the linked future while the general problem of divine foreknowledge and free will remains.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil" — James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.
- **Sailing – Philosophy for Everyone - Catching the Drift of Why We Sail**, ch. 26 "SAILING Philosophy for Everyone" — Tamar Rudavsky and Nathaniel Rudavsky-Brody trace how the dangerous sea drove philosophers to grapple with fate, foreknowledge, and freedom. Aristotle's sea-battle example in On Interpretation defends an indeterminate future to salvage human freedom against fortune-telling (Diagoras the atheist mocking the votive paintings). Maimonides, mourning his brother David who drowned on the India passage, asks in the Guide why a just man drowns, and answers with Aristotle that the shipwreck is chance while divine providence attaches only to the human intellect's choice to board. Finally Nietzsche makes the open sea and Columbus his image for abandoning Christian morality — 'the sea, our sea, lies open again,' the death of God, Zarathustra's summons to daring venturers to sail uncharted waters and forge a trans-valuation of values.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 19 "Time Travel and Fixed Time" — Jeremy Pierce analyzes prophecy and destiny in Harry Potter, distinguishing fallible from infallible prophecies and cataloguing how a Seer might access a fixed or open future (raising Aristotle's sea-battle problem about future truths). He argues Trelawney's two 'real predictions' are not merely likely guesses and considers self-fulfilling readings (via Alexander of Aphrodisias and Oedipus), which he rejects since the prophecy did not force Voldemort's choice. Reading Rowling's denial of 'destiny' against her fixed-time treatment of time travel and the improbable luck that fulfills the prophecy, he suggests the story fits a fixed future guided by providence better than libertarian openness or sheer coincidence.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 60 "57. Tenet as Philosophy Fatalism Isn’t an Excuse to Do Nothing" — The chapter reads Nolan's Tenet as an argument for metaphysical fatalism set in a block-universe (eternalism), using the Sator Square, the palindromic 'ten,' and Neil's refrain 'what's happened, happened' as evidence that every event, including the Protagonist's and Kat's, was fated and unchangeable. It deploys David Lewis's solution to the grandfather paradox and reverse causation (Feynman/Wheeler positrons) to show the future cannot kill its ancestors, then argues fatalism entails no libertarian free will, rejecting Frankfurt's compatibilist second-order-desires account and citing van Inwagen that indeterministic acts are no freer. Via a back-tracking counterfactual it concludes fatalism is still no excuse to do nothing, because different action would have yielded a different (annihilated) world.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 91 "86. God of War as Philosophy Prophecy, Fate, and Freedom" — Horn argues that the God of War series dramatizes theological fatalism—the apparent conflict between foreknowledge (the Oracle, Fates, Norns, Giants) and libertarian freedom—as Kratos, Zeus, and Kronos bring about the very fates they flee. He tests Boethius/Aquinas's timeless-eternity solution (rejected because the games' seers act in time), Molina's middle knowledge (rejected because none of the beings are provident), and Ockham's counterfactual power over the past (the only one workable across both arcs). He concludes the Greek Trilogy depicts a deterministic universe with fixed fate, while the Norse Duology, via the fallible Open-Theism-style Norns and Faye's 'possible path' mural, shows fate is malleable when Kratos changes himself and 'opens his heart.'

### Matter and Memory

In Matter and Memory (1896), Henri Bergson set out to clarify the relation between mind and body by rethinking perception and recollection. He distinguished habit-memory, the bodily repetition of learned actions, from pure or spontaneous memory, which conserves the past in its entirety and is not stored in the brain like a thing. On his account the brain is an organ of action that filters and channels memory toward present needs rather than a warehouse of images, so mind and matter differ in degree and rhythm rather than being wholly separate substances. The book advanced Bergson's larger claim that consciousness is fundamentally temporal, gathering the past into the living present.

- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne argues Cobb's 'most resilient parasite' works only as an idea embedded in a coherent story - 'my father doesn't want me to be him' - and that since ideas define who we are, each person is less a host than a collection of well-planted narratives. Using Bergson on embodied, memory-and-desire-mediated perception (Cobb's fear of the bridge triggering Mal's projection) and Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil on perspectival appearance as the price of life, she claims dreams differ from reality in degree, not kind: we are beings-in-the-world who stabilize contingency through story-making and 'strive for positive logic'. Hence knowledge always demands the leap of faith that Saito and Mal demand of Cobb, the film becomes a meta-narrative with Fischer as its audience, and the wobbling top offers only an interpretation of a fact, never the fact itself.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 31 "Does the Totem Tumble" — Auxier brings Bergson's memory theory, the past gnawing into the present, all dreaming as remembering, and Whitehead's process philosophy to Nolan's 'pathologies of temporal experience', defending the film's supposedly selective physics: with each deeper level the same five minutes disperses across a larger dream space, diluting the carry-over of effects while time expands geometrically, because 'space is frozen time'. He then re-reads the ending through the narrative gaps the audience was lured across: the top was Mal's totem, which Cobb spin as an act of mourning after handling it and betraying her, and Cobb's real totem is his gun, which Saito uses to shoot them both out of Limbo. The top's tumbling in the finale matters only as a sign that Cobb, the coward who once needed total control over Mal, has finally learned the leap of faith of trusting another person.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 155 "Pay Now, Live Later" — This section reads Precrime through Bergson's duree: in Dick's story the precogs are 'monkeys' and 'idiots' emitting snippets that investigators must analyze, while the film shows a precog immersed in and living through the future visually. It explains Bergson's claim that clocks and timelines falsify time, which is really lived duration in which the past endures as memory and actively directs us toward an open future, and rehearses his reunion thought experiment: imagined futures are mere sketches, while the actual future arrives with the unique specificity of the Mona Lisa. No one, on this view, can know the future as if living it.
- **Philip K. Dick and Philosophy - Do Androids Have Kindred Spirits**, ch. 159 "Summarizing the Future" — Applying Bergson's Time and Free Will claim that recalling the past shortens it into a 'thing', the section uses the curriculum-vitae metaphor: like a CV or Facebook page, we imagine the future as a summary compiled from the past. In 'Paycheck', Jennings's sack becomes a plan only when he reflects - the wire at the police station, the token on the bus - until past, present and future fuse and he feels 'a strange elation' at fulfilling his past self's design, raising again whether awareness of the future changes what we do. The film diverges by having Jennings sabotage the atomic-bomb future he foresees, echoing Minority Report's contest between an inevitable future and present action.
- **Jeopardy! and Philosophy - What Is Knowledge in the Form of a Question**, ch. 22 "Jeopardy! and Philosophy" — Randall Auxier explains Jeopardy!'s appeal through Bergson's Matter and Memory: memory is a relation - the past acting in the present - along a continuum of matter (repetition of what was) and memory (variation), and the show strips contestants of bodily action so that what we watch is pure 'recollection', the instantaneous summoning of subtle structures from the flux. Providing the question instead of the answer forces a tiny temporal reversal, a six-step durational epoch he calls (after Edgar Sheffield Brightman) a 'shining present', which is why Jeopardy! outshines College Bowl, why champions like Ken Jennings fascinate as savants of immediate recollection, and why the slow clock music of Final Jeopardy! is the show's most exquisite torture and catharsis.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - Mind Equals Blown**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera reads Westworld as the culmination of Jonathan Nolan's Memento and Person of Interest projects, mapping seven nested 'observing systems' (Nolan, Sizemore, Stubbs and Elsie, Ford, the creators' personal stories, Maeve, and William as beta-tester) onto second-wave cybernetics (Foerster, Maturana, Varela, Hayles), where the observer participates in and constructs the observed world through feedback loops. She argues the show's hosts pass through Turing's imitation game (fake memories and personalities from textual repetition, as with Peter Abernathy's reveries), and that Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns convert prosthetic memory into experienced, autopoietic memory reconstructed in a 'Bergsonian' backward movement that gives them agency and purpose. William's two-timeline transformation into the Man in Black figures the 'semiosis of virtuality' - the hyperreal where original and copy are indistinguishable - ending in a collective bicameral mind in which everyone, audience included, inhabits the god-creator Ford's dream.
- **Alice in Wonderland and Philosophy - Curiouser and Curiouser**, ch. 25 "From Backwards -Working Memory, or Working Backwards from Memory" — Treats the Caterpillar's 'Who are YOU?' and Alice's 'Who in the world am I? Ah, that's the great puzzle!' as the classic memory-and-identity problem, rallying Plato's wax tablet and Meno doctrine that learning is recollection, Locke's memory criterion of the same person, and Diderot's dialogue on how without memory there would be no connected self. Tyler Shores reads Alice's botched recitations as Bergson's impersonal habit-memory swamping personal memory, her name-forgetting in the wood through Nietzsche's Untimely Meditations on the necessity of forgetting, the Red King's dream as Freud's alienated memory, and the White Queen's memory that 'works both ways' as a thought experiment tying memory, time, and self together.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 19 "Leap of Faith" — Dionne reads Cobb's 'idea is the most resilient parasite' as a claim about narrative: what gets incepted in Fischer is a story ('my father doesn't want me to follow in his footsteps'), and by the same token each of us is a collection of incepted stories rather than a stable self. Drawing on Bergson's account of perception mediated by memory and desire (Cobb's bridge triggering Mal's projection), Nietzsche's perspectivism — truth is a 'moral prejudice' and 'we must mistake ourselves' — and the embodiment of the being-in-the-world, she argues dreams differ from reality only in degree, since both are interested story-making under time pressure. The payoff is meta-filmic: Fischer is the spectator and Cobb the director, and the final spinning top becomes the audience's own totem — there is no fact of the matter, only interpretation, so watching the ending is itself the leap of faith.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 31 "Does the Totem Tumble" — Randall Auxier claims to settle whether the totem tumbles: it does, but it does not matter, because the top was Mal's totem rather than Cobb's — Cobb spins it as mourning for the wife whose trust he destroyed by handling her totem, while Cobb's real totem is the gun, which Saito must use (shooting them both in Limbo) once Cobb finally takes the leap of faith and entrusts his life to another person. Building on Bergson's memory theory — the past 'gnaws into the future,' all dreaming is remembering, and shared dreaming is possible because embodied species-memory can be tapped with the right chemist — the chapter recasts Cobb's rule against building from memory as the need to introduce gaps between dream and world, and his inability to keep architecting as personal memory increasingly overrunning perception with age. Through Whitehead's process philosophy — narrative as algebraic order, space as 'frozen time,' generic contrasts like 'and then I ate it' — he also defends the film's 'selective physics': at each level the same five minutes disperses across a larger dreamspace, diluting the gravitational carryover while geometrically expanding dream time.
- **Watchmen and Philosophy - A Rorschach Test**, ch. 9 "H E N R I B E R G S O N" — Three Part Three essays on Dr. Manhattan's strange relation to time and fate. Christopher Drohan reads Manhattan's simultaneous 'intricately structured jewel' of time through Bergson's Matter and Memory — perception interlaced with memory, the pure past persisting in every act, time as lived duration — so that 'Nothing ever ends, Adrian' becomes a Bergsonian insight and the thermodynamic-miracle speech an intuition of life's creative improbability. Arthur Ward argues theological fatalism (Boethius and Aquinas placing a timeless God outside time, Paley's watchmaker behind Jon the watchmaker's son with his clock-shaped Martian palace) does not doom Laurie's free will, because Jon's own claims are inconsistent — he is surprised by the cancer rumors, misses Veidt's tachyon-shielded plan, and acts drugged — so either his foresight or his fatalism must be false. Andrew Terjesen reads Manhattan as a Stoic sage: Seneca and Epictetus on emotions as false judgments explain his 'a live body and a dead body contain the same number of particles,' his Mars epiphany is the sage's 'good emotion' of joy at the thermodynamic miracle, and his impersonal 'clock without a craftsman' completes a Neo-Stoic line running through Descartes to Spinoza's God-who-is-Nature.
- **Westworld and Philosophy - If You Go Looking for the Truth, Get the Whole Thing**, ch. 21 "Memory, Imagination, and the Access for the Self Dolores and Maeve" — Trapero-Llobera situates Westworld within Jonathan Nolan's body of work (Memento, Person of Interest), arguing the show's apparent complexity hides a classic hero's-journey structure organized around observing systems and a 'semiosis of virtuality.' She reads William/the Man in Black as a 'schizoid android' and catalyst-observer, and Ford/Bernard as creator-and-prosthetic-memory pairs echoing Finch and the Machine. Turing's imitation game frames the hosts' fabricated memories, while Dolores's and Maeve's breakdowns mark a shift from prosthetic to autopoietic, Bergsonian memory-recollection that turns them into observers building their own selves.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 14 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Palmer argues that The Underneath and The Limey fuse film noir's obsession with the untranscendable past with Alain Resnais's Bergsonism, mediated by Deleuze's account of the time-image. In The Limey, career criminal Wilson's consciousness accumulates recollection-images (including Poor Cow footage of a young Stamp) and prospective imaginings (the two visualized shootings), building toward a Bergsonian intuition: confronting Terry Valentine, Wilson recognizes himself as the same kind of selfish betrayer and spares him, achieving a redemption denied noir predecessors like Get Carter's Carter and Point Blank's Walker. The Underneath, by contrast, uses achronic color-coded structure only to define Michael from the outside, which Palmer counts a partial failure of the same interior ambition.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 15 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — King analyzes The Limey as 'Get Carter as made by Alain Resnais,' using Bordwell's fabula/syuzhet distinction to show how its nonlinear editing renders what Soderbergh calls the nonlinear nature of thought. Dialogue continuity is stretched across discontinuous spaces (the Wilson-Elaine 'embarrassed/ashamed/disappointed' exchange), flash-forwards precede events, and the party shooting is replayed three times as Wilson's fantasy. King argues the whole film reads as Wilson's subjective reconstruction on the plane home, grounded in Bergson (via Deleuze's time-image) yet, unlike Resnais's Marienbad, never producing real ontological or epistemological doubt because the revenge-thriller backbone and color-coding keep it legible. The film's dominant note is nostalgia for a past that, because of Wilson's imprisonments, never really was.

### The Meaning of Life

The question of the meaning of life asks whether human existence has a point, purpose, or significance, and if so, what makes a life meaningful. Answers divide between those who locate meaning in something beyond us, such as God or an objective moral order, and those who hold that meaning is created by human beings through their projects, relationships, and values. The question gained special urgency in modern thought as traditional religious frameworks were questioned, prompting responses ranging from nihilism to existentialist affirmations of self-created purpose.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 65 "Happiness and Cypher’s Choice Is Ignorance Bliss" — Opening Griswold's essay (with Locke's line on happiness disturbed by new uneasiness as epigraph), the chapter asks why happiness - the question of existential urgency that Aristotle treated as the ultimate end of our activities - has received so little philosophical treatment (no Platonic dialogue is devoted to it) while non-philosophers assume there is an answer to be found. It presents The Matrix as a rare clever movie that genuinely presses the question of what happiness is, whether the film's answer is tenable, and how we would construct a better one of our own, with Cypher's choice as the test case.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 67 "Unknown" — Through Cypher's steak deal the chapter separates contentment - the subjective tranquility of satisfied desire, as in the contented slave, the happy tyrant, or a dog - from happiness, which must be answerable to an objective arrangement of one's life. Four thought experiments (a painless Ataraxy drug, an impostor posing as Keanu Reeves, the heating-vent fantasist imagining he is Mr. Onassis, the drunk's morning-after mirror) and Othello show self-deluded 'happiness' is unstable, truncated, and not the real thing. Happiness therefore requires reflective second-order endorsement of one's desires - wanting the desires one has - as when Neo takes the hard path of saving Morpheus, and this links happiness to a conception of the life worth living.
- **Buffy the Vampire Slayer and Philosophy - Fear and Trembling in Sunnydale**, ch. 29 "No Big Win" — Reads sacrifice, salvation, and redemption in the Buffyverse as secular myth: vampires manifest the shadow-side of the human (Liam's resentment becomes Angelus, William's repressed romanticism becomes Spike's rebellion), and the contrast between soulless Spike's genuine moral growth through love of Buffy and human Xander's arrested development shows redemption is measured by 'what have you done with what you've been given.' The Purpose of Evil section argues good and evil must stay in balance because without evil there is no free choice and hence no redemption, and Angel's 'no big win' epiphany — no grand plan, only lessening suffering one kindness at a time — locates life's meaning in the journey of becoming rather than final victory.
- **The Sopranos and Philosophy - I Kill Therefore I Am**, ch. 12 "The Sopranos and Philosophy" — Argues The Sopranos is a morality play and existential drama, an X-rated Waiting for Godot about despair and man's search for meaning. Tony's crew are Gabbard's 'band of lost boys' fleeing Christopher's 'regularness of life' through violence: on Sartre's account they assert Being over Nothingness by acting, and on Ernest Becker's they deny death and insignificance through heroic crime. The chapter contrasts Tony's professed code of honor and family with his actual motive (the thrill of the hunt, unlike Vito Corleone's necessity) and frames the series' tension as his Janus-faced attempt to be a Machiavellian boss by day and a loving family man by night, a dichotomy he cannot sustain.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 10 "The Failure of Our Attempts at Meaning" — Conard argues that Allen's films converge on one position: life is inherently meaningless because nothing in the universe is permanent, so only something eternal (God) could ground value — and God is a self-deception ('tradition is the illusion of permanence' in Deconstructing Harry; Rabbi Ben's 'blind faith' in Crimes and Misdemeanors). He traces the impermanence argument from Mickey Sachs's mortality panic in Hannah and Her Sisters and young Alvy's dread of the expanding universe in Annie Hall, to Lloyd's 'temporary convulsion' speech in September, Sandy Bates's 'Ozymandias Melancholia' in Stardust Memories, and Louis Levy's suicide. Since real value would require permanence, Conard concludes, Allen's characters' attempts at meaning through romance (Peter's 'I have to sleep alone tonight' in September) and art (Renata's failed faith in posterity in Interiors) are merely distractions and self-deceptions we need 'like we need the air'.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 13 "Hope and Despair" — Jarvie argues Allen is a 'pragmatic optimist': since dramatizing is not arguing, no character's philosophy (not Sol's 'choose God over truth', not Levy's) can be imputed to Allen, but the ongoing act of filmmaking itself affirms that life is worth continuing. He maps optimism and despair across four films — Mickey's gun and Duck Soup epiphany in Hannah and Her Sisters, the reconstituted couples' self-deceiving rationalizations in Husbands and Wives, Harry's writer's block, and Crimes and Misdemeanors, where Judah literally gets away with murder and Ben's moral-structure faith is shown as naive. Against Sander Lee's hopeful reading of the ending, he develops criteria for interpretation: avoid the biographical fallacy and 'eisegesis', respect authorial statements unless there is overwhelming argument against them.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 28 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bruce Reichenbach reads the film's choreographed pas de deux as three distinct theories of atonement: the conquest dance with Satan in Gethsemane (crushing the serpent of Genesis 3:15, Satan's final scream) enacts the Christus victor view of the Church Fathers; Simon of Cyrene's reluctant co-bearing of the cross illustrates Abelard's moral-influence view, though Gibson shows resilient fortitude rather than the love Abelard's theory requires to transform Simon; and Mary's mirrored 'parallel dance' makes her a co-redemptrix sharing her son's agony. Against this he sets Heidegger — Jesus grasps his death with anticipatory resolve, thrownness, and the 'moment of vision' with Mary, but dies for the Other rather than to authenticate his own life — and faults the film for omitting Anselm's (and Swinburne's) substitutionary atonement entirely: no sin, repentance, reparation, or penance appears, unlike Maximilian Kolbe's real substitution at Auschwitz.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 105 "Hope, Obligation, and the Big Picture" — Argues whether Wonder Woman's "must" really binds Superman — whether he is obliged to leave the Fortress and fight again — depends on one's eschatology or big-picture worldview. It contrasts Christian theism's purposeful culmination with naturalism, whose outlook is fixed by Bertrand Russell's "unyielding despair" passage: accidental collocations of atoms, no preservation beyond the grave, and all human achievement buried beneath the debris of a ruined universe, heroism included.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 130 "Superman’s Interesting Motivation" — Argues Superman inverts the usual identity rule: Kal-El's powers precede any civilian persona, so Superman is the real identity and Clark Kent the ruse. Drawing on Pascal's point that celebrity otherness is a function of imagination — a movie star at your cafeteria table changes everything — and on Krishna's disguise as Arjuna's chariot driver in the Bhagavad-Gita and Christ's messianic secret, Morris reads Clark Kent not as operational cover but as Superman's quest to live the human condition from within, loved into humanity by the Kents and refusing to be an isolated "Aristotelian God."
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 15 "And Now for . . . Comedic Eliminativism" — Argues The Meaning of Life dismantles the 'axial' picture of life as a journey toward a salvific destination (Jaspers's Axial Age thinking), instanced in the headmaster who announces Jenkins's mother's death between Empire Day announcements, the tank fish who never connect Howard's being eaten to their own fate, and the restaurant couple ordering 'philosophy for two' with no appetite for wisdom. The classical answers all fail as delivered: Socrates's philosophy as learning how to die, Heidegger's claim that facing death reveals one's own unique possibilities, and Kant's three questions (What can I know? What should I do? For what may I hope?) collapse into the question of life's meaning, but religion has gone stale and philosophy has become detached trivia. The Pythons instead accomplish the user-friendly domestication of the death of God — the hearty laughter Nietzsche and Derrida counsel — and the chapter coins 'comedic eliminativism' on the model of eliminative materialism's dissolution of Descartes's mind-body problem: replace the yearning for the meaning of life with altered reactions, laughter itself as the solution to the riddle.
- **Poker and Philosophy - Pocket Rockets and Philosopher Kings**, ch. 14 "Poker and Philosophy" — Sanders splits poker into two philosophical styles. The Rationalist — Leibniz's principle of sufficient reason, Pascal's domestication of chance into probability — plays like Sklansky, Chris Ferguson, and Howard Lederer, whose temptation is the paralysis of analysis; the Existentialist — Sartre's existence precedes essence, Camus' scorn for the absurd, Kierkegaard's leap of faith taken without decisive evidence — plays like Gus Hansen calling Antonio Esfandiari's $334,000 all-in re-raise with ten-high. A Russell-and-Popper-style regress of predictions (knowing a prediction changes its outcome) becomes the tournament 'hall of mirrors' of intentions read in Phil Ivey and Johnny Chan, and the chapter lands on Richard Taylor's existentialist point that meaning comes from committed doing, at the table as in life.
- **James Bond and Philosophy - Questions Are Forever**, ch. 13 "James Bond and Philosophy" — South reads the famous opening of Thunderball - life as 'a heap of six to four against' - as Fleming's challenge to Western philosophy's promise of a harmonious fit between reason, personal good, and social good. Bond's shame at his hangover and bad bridge (analyzed through Bernard Williams's account of shame as grounding identity) drives him to the Shrublands spa and a new healthy, patient self, but SPECTRE's atomic blackmail and an assassination attempt push him back to scrambled eggs, bacon, and bourbon: 'life's too short.' With Adorno's bleak view that modern societies are implicated in evil (SPECTRE's bureaucratically worded ransom memo, gas chambers built by the same ingenuity as medicine) and Williams's thick ethical concepts, South argues Fleming's Bond shows there is no universal pattern making life meaningful; the spy's work lies outside conventional morality, and the odds of a happy, philosophically vindicated life are six to four against.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica to weigh theism against atheism: Baltar's scientific rationalism meets Aquinas' five ways (the universe's ordered structure demands an unmoved, uncaused cause), Six's faith faces the problem of evil answered through Augustine on the perverse will and John Hick's soul-making (Starbuck's mother, 'your life is a testament to pain'), while Hume's faulty-architect analogy presses the atheist case. The chapter concludes with Russell's 'A Free Man's Worship': even in a Godless universe the Colonials find meaning in comradeship and humanity's survival — 'the gods shall lift those who lift each other.'
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.
- **Bruce Springsteen and Philosophy - Darkness on the Edge of Truth**, ch. 21 "Back from the Edge" — McKenna and Pratt use McDermott's 'Promethean self' and meliorism to answer the riddle of Nebraska's closer 'Reason to Believe': among the dead dog, the deserted bride and the groom left at the altar, 'still at the end of every hard earned day people find some reason to believe.' They trace Springsteen's shift from escape songs ('Born to Run,' 'Thunder Road') to life at the edge ('Badlands,' 'Darkness on the Edge of Town,' and the two midnight drivers of 'State Trooper' and 'Open All Night'), arguing meaning is made by cutting and connecting relations at the margins. Belief without evidence of salvation is legitimate hope but illegitimate certainty; the reason to believe is Jamesian meliorism — making things 'not perfect, simply better.'
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 6 "“I Dare You to Watch This Show!”" — Editor Josef Steiff's introduction traces Galactica from Glen Larson's 1978 series and Galactica 1980 through the Moore/Eick re-imagining, and frames the show through Edward James Olmos's campus talks, where he 'dares' audiences to watch a series he calls truth about identity, race, culture, and purpose. It endorses Orson Scott Card's claim that true science fiction, like religious literature, asks who we are, what our place in the universe is, and how we find or make meaning. It closes by explaining the book's Cylon naming conventions (Sixes, Eights, Boomers, Athenas) and its gimmick of five unattributed 'Final Five' chapters.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 38 "Embracing Death" — David Vessey argues the humanoid Cylons' resurrection denies them the 'successful death' that makes a life meaningful: like Greek heroes governed by moira or Socrates drinking the hemlock, mortals must be able to see life as a completed whole that death can crown, with how one lived shaping what death means. Cylon deaths (dying out of range of a resurrection ship, D'Anna being boxed) are always failures or shames, and their religion carries no after-death stakes, unlike Socrates' philosophical preparation for death. Camus's Sisyphus shows agency and the option of suicide remain necessary for meaning, while Plato's Symposium model of immortality through children is the only one left to the Cylons, via mortal human-Cylon babies like Hera.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 9 "“Logic Without Need Is Sterile”" — Writing as a Vulcan philosophy professor and student of Spock, the chapter reconstructs Vulcan civilization from Surak's Awakening as three interlocking modes of logic — formal logic (whose first law, Kiri-kin-tha's 'nothing unreal exists', parallels Parmenides), ethical logic (the axiom 'the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few'), and meditative discipline — and maps them onto Patanjali's Yoga: the yamas, meditation, and samadhi's cosmic oneness, with ahimsa linking Surak to Gandhi and King. It then rereads Star Trek: The Motion Picture, where V'Ger's pure logic leaves both it and Spock asking 'Is this all that I am?', and Spock's mind meld with V'Ger becomes a tantric union that integrates feeling with logic after the failure of Kolinahr. The chapter's thesis is that 'logic without need is sterile': logic is 'the beginning of wisdom . . . not the end', and Spock's rebirth culminates in choosing the human thing precisely when it is not the logical thing.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 12 "“Condemned to Be a Member of This Lowest of Species”" — Arp uses Glaucon's Ring of Gyges from the Republic to ask whether unlimited power must corrupt the just: Q's career of meddling ('Encounter at Farpoint', 'Q Who?', 'The Q and the Grey') shows the corrupted case, while Riker given Q-powers in 'Hide and Q' helps his friends instead, a counterexample Glaucon can resist by pleading insufficient time. He then explains the Q's misery — Quinn's bored suicidal plea in 'Death Wish' — through the hedonistic paradox, refining it with Mill's distinction between bodily lower pleasures and mental higher ones and Aristotle's account of the lasting pleasure of completed states like beating the ship's computer at chess. The conclusion is that Q's 'condemnation' to mortality in 'Déjà Q' reveals the human condition as enviable: it is precisely our lacking unlimited power, pleasure, and immortality that drives the striving for truth, justice, goodness, and love.
- **Star Trek and Philosophy - The Wrath of Kant**, ch. 21 "Death on Veridian III" — Uses the holodeck to re-run the problem of evil: if a safe, painless simulated world like Barclay's fantasy life in 'Hollow Pursuits' is available, why is the painful real one better? Against Hume's Dialogues complaint that a benevolent God should have cut the pain, and Leibniz's best-of-all-possible-worlds optimism, the authors stack Whitehead's 'major beauty' of intensity, Aristotle's tragic magnitude, Swinburne's good of serious responsibility, and Hick's soul-making, reading Moriarty's imprisonment in 'Ship in a Bottle,' Q's humbling in 'Déjà Q,' and Kirk leaving the Nexus because 'nothing here matters' as evidence that intensity, responsibility, and character growth exist only in the real world. Kirk's death on Veridian III in Generations supplies the cautionary counterweight: the real world's goods cost real suffering.
- **The Legend of Zelda and Philosophy - I Link Therefore I Am**, ch. 14 "Game Over" — Janssen argues Zelda is quietly obsessed with death: turning the console off models death as pure absence of experience, which we cannot otherwise comprehend, and gives the gamer a comforting structured formula in place of a chaotic universe. Link, resurrected endlessly to serve the player, is condemned to Hegelian purgatory and what Bernard Williams called the tedium of immortality, while dungeon bosses, who die once and stay dead, are the only genuinely mortal, hence most human, beings in Hyrule. The Wind Waker prologue's eternally returning Hero does suggest Plato-style dualism with an immortal soul, but the chapter notes that Nietzsche's assault on faith destroyed dualism's credibility, leaving the series as a vessel for both materialist nothingness and romantic reincarnation.
- **Jimmy Buffett and Philosophy - The Porpoise Driven Life**, ch. 5 "Jimmy Buffett, Cultural Infidel" — The editors argue Buffett is a philosopher despite his own denials, in the sense of Royce and Dewey: philosophy is critical reflection on living that returns to ordinary experience, and Buffett's songs, books, and concerts pass Dewey's test of rendering everyday predicaments 'more significant, more luminous, more fruitful.' They compare 'Margaritaville' to Plato's Republic — not equal in pedigree but equal in kind as occasions for philosophical practice — to defend meaning-making as a democratic practice open to Parrotheads, not just professors. Reading the album 'Changes in Latitudes, Changes in Attitudes' as a guide, they set Buffett's 'Porpoise Driven Life,' where purpose is found by sailing your own waters in the company of friends, against Rick Warren's revelation-based 'Purpose Driven Life.'
- **World of Warcraft and Philosophy - Wrath of the Philosopher King**, ch. 15 "Forward! Into the Breach" — Silcox and Cogburn test Nozick's three reasons for refusing the experience machine against Azeroth. Respawning kobolds and endlessly repeated quests threaten Nozick's 'we want to do things' objection — yet play genuinely changes other players and their characters, which is what the massive multiplayer element adds over a solo machine. Attribute scores let a dullard play a genius, but as with the wheelchair-bound woman who played Doom to 'get my legs back,' piloting a warrior is still something you do, like a pilot flying a plane. Against Nozick's 'man-made reality' complaint they argue that WoW, like great art, stays open to unbounded interpretation and even surprises its own designers, so the human appetite for fun is more robust and complicated than Nozick allowed.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 11 "A New Path" — Marcus Giamatti narrates his upbringing as an 'Old School' fan under 'Dame Mutability,' his father's personification of the certainty that the Red Sox would always break New England's heart through Bucky Dent, Mookie Wilson, Calvin Schiraldi and Aaron Boone. He argues that being born a Sox fan is an inescapable duty and lifelong quest whose real payoff is not a pennant but the character, faith and perseverance built by enduring, so that when he lay curled up ready to quit during Game Four of the 2004 ALCS, Millar's walk, Roberts's steal and Mueller's single vindicated the whole method. He ends by vowing to pass this philosophy of survival to his unborn daughter Ophelia in Southern California, applying the one-pitch-at-a-time discipline to acting, music and life.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 14 "April 6th, 2009" — David Roochnik interlaces a loss diary (his daughter's soccer defeat and the Sox's 1998 playoff elimination on the same Saturday, the 2003 Grady Little collapse that gave him chest pain, the 2004 comeback) to argue that losing is an art that teaches what winning cannot. The loser's 'if only' imagination transforms the past, the 'it was only a game' rationalization forces honest reflection about what matters, and shared doom forges Red Sox Nation into a community in a way no Yankees nation could exist, since victors never need to think. He applies Plato's Symposium doctrine of Eros, that to love X is to lack X as Socrates lacks wisdom, to explain why eighty-six years of championship-lack made fandom meaningful, and closes fearing that winning in 2004 and 2007 made the Sox 'normal,' eroding the art of losing that glued the Nation together.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 25 "Red Sox Future" — Peter Kreeft argues that the classic pre-2004 Red Sox fan's philosophy is 'Primitive Mysticism' across all eight divisions of philosophy: certainty comes by mystical intuition (fans 'just know' Murphy's Law will strike, as with Dent in 1978 and Buckner in 1986), Parmenides's identity puzzles frame the post-championship identity crisis, free will only chooses among fated tortures, and the greatest good is humiliating the Yankees in Manichean fashion. He opposes Hegel's rational philosophy of history ('the real is the rational') with a history written by 'an insane, drunken, demon-possessed leprechaun,' and inverts the problem of evil: eighty-six years of systematically improbable suffering is probable evidence for a God whose design is a test of faith rather than a refutation of Him. The 2004 title's new rational-optimist 'Enlightenment' identity now threatens to erase the lovable old mysticism, leaving the fan unsure whether to mourn or rejoice.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 28 "A (Bronx) Cheer to the Red Sox “Without Whom, Not as Much”" — Writing as a Yankees fan, Konig asks what makes a championship worth wanting: after Schopenhauer's picture of endless striving as suffering, he brings in Richard Taylor (meaning lies in the activity itself, never its completion) and then Nietzsche's will to power, which seeks worthy resistance to overcome. Thought experiments—a childhood 'big game' that turns out to be tee-ball, and the 2004 Sox trouncing the minor-league Atlantic League—show a title without worthy opposition is hollow. Hence the Yankees' twentieth-century dominance would mean nothing without the Red Sox as the sustained, worthy enemy (Bucky Dent, the Pedro-Zimmer melee, the 2004 ALCS collapse included).
- **Facebook and Philosophy - What's on Your Mind_**, ch. 2 "index" — This file holds the book's front matter, Wittkower's introduction 'A Reply to facebook Critics', and the 'facebook Itself' essays. Wittkower answers critics of trivial status updates with Sartre's claim that lives have no given meaning (so their value is ours to create, from the inside), Hegel's argument that real freedom means choosing alongside others (against both Sunstein's 'Daily Me' echo chamber and the forced community of family and hometown), and Schopenhauer's microscope image from 'On the Vanity of Existence', concluding that we care about a friend's dinner update for the same reason we care about our own. James Grimmelmann's 'The Privacy Virus' rebuts the claim that Facebook users don't care about privacy by arguing they practice a contextual, Nissenbaum-style privacy (untagging keg-stand photos, the News Feed revolt, the Miss New Jersey blackmail), while Facebook's architecture breaks the 'know your audience' rule and recruits users into spreading violations like a virus. Graham Meikle reads wall posts and status updates as a convergence of personal messaging and broadcast media (citing the MI6 chief's wife's holiday photos and the Sunday Express's Dunblane survivors story), and Ian Bogost applies McLuhan's media ecology to Facebook as an 'extension of man': it enhances the directory and the yearbook, obsolesces the reunion and the secret, retrieves the small town and the soda shop, and reverses into campus life and high school.
- **Dune and Philosophy - Weirding Way of the Mentat**, ch. 16 "The Spice of Meaning" — Mines Dune for an account of the meaningful life by contrasting the Harkonnens, who amass power for its own sake and grind Yueh's very identity to dust, with the Fremen, whose rigid rituals give meaning but suffocate anyone who lives entirely inside them—with Duke Leto's abolition of the beggars' water-towel custom as the failure case in between. Following Aristotle's method of starting from 'the views of the wise,' the chapter argues virtue is an open-ended, formulaless skill: rising above inherited identities while repairing the social bonds they sustain, as Paul and Jessica do by breaking selected Fremen rules and leaving the sietch stronger. The worm-rider, feet shifting on sand above a creature that can never be fully controlled, is the closing image of a struggle that never finally resolves.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 20 "Videogame Apocalypses and Secularism" — Rachel Wagner, Tyler DeHaven, and Chris Hendrickson argue Halo satisfies the Society of Biblical Literature definition of apocalypse: revelatory narrative, otherworldly mediators (Cortana, 343 Guilty Spark), predetermined eschatology, with Master Chief as a Davidic messiah whose name John-117 echoes the Gospel of John. The Covenant's Tower-of-Babel hubris versus human secularism, and the Flood read through the Book of Enoch's Watchers, turn the story into a critique of rampant consumption and blind religion. Where traditional apocalypses are quietist—God the programmer's deterministic script, salvation not depending on human action—Halo's procedural rhetoric hands agency to the player as messiah, and the chapter closes asking whether videogame apocalypse offers only temporary, magic-circle comfort for secular angst in a morally relativist age.
- **Sherlock Holmes and Philosophy - The Footprints of a Gigantic Mind**, ch. 29 "The New Man or the Old" — Marks reads Holmes as the paragon Victorian whose faith in reason mirrors his era's confidence and, underneath it, its anxiety: Holmes's outburst in 'The Cardboard Box' ('What is the object of this circle of misery and violence and fear?... That is humanity's great problem to which Reason, so far, has no answer') appears the same year Nietzsche published 'Gott ist tot' in The Gay Science, amid Marx's 'opium of the people' and Darwin's displacement of religion. Reinterpreting the 2009 Ritchie film, he rejects the obvious religion-versus-reason reading of Lord Blackwood: Blackwood's 'magic' is really chemistry and machinery (technocracy), Holmes's science serves the military (dictatorship), and Moriarty (terrorism) defeats both, dramatizing post-9/11 fears about the militarized fruits of Reason. He concludes that Holmes straddles the Victorian and postmodern divide and that replacing religion with science is Rationalism's 'siren song.'
- **The Rolling Stones and Philosophy - It's Just a Thought Away**, ch. 5 "It’s Only Philosophy but We Like It" — George A. Reisch's introduction argues that Keith Richards' autobiography Life is more philosophical than Keith's own slogan that rock and roll 'starts from the neck down' allows: its optimistic framing of addiction, arrests, and band feuds displays a distinctive perspective and mental discipline rather than a tale of greed and jealousy. He reads the band's 1990 Prague concert, where Czech fans outlasted Soviet occupation, as evidence that the Stones' music carried a liberating outlook that helped defeat communism or at least outlasted it. The piece sets up the volume's premise that a band proud of its anti-intellectual image nonetheless repays philosophical reading.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 31 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vosen answers Klosterman's hyperthetical about cats that suddenly read at a twelfth-grade level against his implied expectation: they would love Garfield rather than find it an insulting caricature. Reading the strip through Dan Walsh's Garfield-minus-Garfield project, she argues the comics reveal that Garfield is the glue keeping Jon Arbuckle from a full existential breakdown, so literate cats would find hope, renewed purpose, and the comfort that life could always be worse — they could be Jon. The exercise turns a throwaway joke into a small meditation on meaninglessness, comparison, and what keeps a life from collapsing.
