Maslow's hierarchy of needs explains the monster's fixation on a mate as a starved 'love need' created by Victor's abandonment, and Piaget's cognitive stages test whether the monster had matured enough to 'could have done otherwise' - while Nietzsche's Beyond Good and Evil attack on morality as tyrannical herd-style slave morality threatens to dissolve blame entirely, and Sartre's existentialism leaves each agent choosing without objective moral foundations. Refusing both the absolutist's unconditional verdict and dogmatic relativism, the chapter applies the criminal law's mens rea ('guilty mind') test to monster, android, and creator alike, and leaves the final verdict of guilt deliberately open.
- **Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy - Last Exit from Litchfield**, ch. 18 "Orange Is the New Black and Philosophy" — Neal reads Litchfield through Sartre's No Exit: Alex, the ex who both agonizes and galvanizes Piper, makes the other inmates, not the walls, the hell of prison, just as Piper shouts 'I love you and I fucking hate you.' The 'Scared Straight' episode ('Bora Bora Bora') drives the deeper point when Piper tells Dina that the real punishment is coming face to face with who you are: 'I'm scared that I'm not myself in here and I'm scared that I am.' Stripped of distractions, Piper undergoes an existential crisis that forces the self-awareness authenticity requires, though prison's limits keep a fully authentic life out of reach.
- **More Doctor Who and Philosophy - Regeneration Time**, ch. 40 "25. Meeting Up with Your Self" — Sylvia and Stevens use Doctor Who's crossover episodes to complicate the Self-Other distinction: existentially (via Yalom and Maslow), the Doctor's name-promise - 'never cruel or cowardly... never give up, never give in' - supplies meaning, while Ten and Eleven must stop treating the War Doctor as Other. Deleuze's account of learning through the shock of encountering the Other structures the reading of 'The Girl Who Waited,' where young Amy and her thirty-six-years-older self form an assemblage in which the older Amy relearns her love for Rory and chooses annihilation for his sake. Locke's memory theory of personal identity frames the puzzle that a version of you with different memories may be an Other, which the authors extend to confronting our recorded past selves on social media and learning empathy from the shock.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 26 "12. Confronting the “Forever Empty”" — Argues that Louis's 2013 Conan 'forever empty' confession—welcoming the sadness of listening to Bruce Springsteen alone in his car instead of texting—is an exemplary case of existentialist authenticity: Heideggerian anxiety discloses the nothingness beneath our projects, and Sartre's radical freedom, facticity, and bad faith explain why texting while driving and other distractions are escapes from self-creation. It then contrasts Eddie in Louie's 'Eddie' episode, whose suicide plan is a bad-faith loss of care and passion, with the 'Late Show' trilogy, where Janet exposes Louie's bad faith over the Letterman audition and he ends by shouting 'I did it!' at the Ed Sullivan Theater after Tardigan's scam.
- **Mr. Robot and Philosophy - Beyond Good and Evil Corp**, ch. 21 "8. Mr. Robot, Mad Son of Noir" — Hoyt places Mr. Robot in the film noir tradition born when world war proved Nietzsche's point that God is dead: as with Bogart's Spade turning in Brigid in The Maltese Falcon, the noir hero's task is existential self-definition - guarding integrity in a world without truth, justice, or absolute meaning. But where classic noir blamed gangsters, neo-noir from Chinatown through Fight Club to Mr. Robot points at capitalism and unbeatable conspiracies (Price apparently able to bend the federal government itself), and the show's cold blue offices and 'shortsighting' framings show characters breaking under the pressure of choices no space protects.
- **Twin Peaks and Philosophy - That's Damn Fine Philosophy!**, ch. 26 "13. Reason and Catharsis" — Argues that Twin Peaks frees viewers from the "tyranny of rationality" by refusing to make sense: Plato's sensible-versus-intelligible finger example explains our habit of abstracting concepts to resolve contradiction (the pale horse in the living room, Diane's texts, Dougie-as-tulpa), but Lynch keeps adding facts — the frog-moth crawling into the girl in Part 8 — that no framework absorbs. Drawing on Nietzsche's Twilight of the Idols claim that Socrates made rationality a treatment for weakness, and on the existentialist pairing of despair and freedom in a meaningless universe, the chapter says viewers can either demand the irrational fit their rationality like inauthentic existentialists or let go. Trela's alternative reading of Aristotle's catharsis — emotions purged of their connection to reality and felt for once in themselves — explains why we can savor the show's absurdity without despair, precisely because that world is not ours.
- **Amy Schumer and Philosophy - Brainwreck!**, ch. 17 "8. Sexistentialism" — Reads Schumer through Camus's absurd: Trainwreck's gender-reversed commitment-phobe and the sketch where friends kill themselves rather than accept a compliment expose the futility of finding meaning in patriarchal gender scripts. Browning argues that advocating change against so systemic a sexism is a Sisyphean task, and that the film's romantic-comedy ending is 'existential' because Amy freely chooses commitment and owns the absurdity rather than escaping it. The chapter ends by asking whether Schumer's jokes are a battle cry whose very pointlessness might be the point.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 21 "10. On Being and Meeseeks" — The chapter asks what kind of being Mr. Meeseeks is and answers with Sartre: despite being 'created to serve a singular purpose', Meeseeks exhibit subjectivity, from the self-assertion of 'I'm Mr. Meeseeks!' to transcendence in envisioning Jerry's fixed golf swing and the anguish, forlornness, and despair of 'Meeseeks and Destroy' ('Your failures are your own, old man!'), so they must be beings-for-itself whose existence precedes essence, freely choosing accomplishment as their meaning. Along the way it glosses Sartre's facticity with Morty's hopeless crush on Jessica, essence-precedes-existence with the butter-passing robot, and bad faith with Jerry's assumed mediocrity and Beth's shrinking of herself into horse surgeon, wife, and mother until Mr. Meeseeks reminds her she is still an individual.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Get an Afterlife**, ch. 31 "17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place" — Hubbard-Mattix frames the show's central paradox, each person is responsible for her choices yet those choices are formed by her relationships, as a collision between the existentialism of Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and the feminist idea of relational autonomy. Each character embodies a failure mode: Eleanor's futile rejection of social dependence, Chidi's evasion of accountability in bad faith, Tahani's destruction by living for others' approval, and Jason's unexamined loyalty to Pillboi, Donkey Doug, and the Jaguars. Their failures before Judge Gen teach the audience to choose relationships that enable growth while still owning one's choices.
- **The Big Lebowski and Philosophy - Keeping Your Mind Limber with Abiding Wisdom**, ch. 21 "The Big Lebowski and Philosophy" — Baird contrasts Camus's absurdity — the divorce between man and world demanding 'lucid indifference' and an absurd art that refuses counterfeit meaning — with Sartre's, where the world's meanings are contingent human projections and freedom entails absolute responsibility (Being and Nothingness sits by the Dude's bed). He argues the film is Sartrean rather than Camusian: the Dude weaves random events (the peed-on rug, the ransom) into the interpretation 'Bunny kidnapped herself', holding it provisionally as one story among possible ones, while Walter never takes responsibility for his Corvette-swinging choices. The viewers, knowing all interpretations are groundless, watch the absurd from the front row.
- **Disney and Philosophy - Truth, Trust, and a Little Bit of Pixie Dust**, ch. 26 "Rafiki Holds the Mirror Up to Nature" — The chapter reads The Lion King as a Disney retelling of Hamlet: Scar's murder of Mufasa parallels Claudius, and Simba's guilt-ridden exile acts out Hamlet's 'to be or not to be.' Timon and Pumbaa's 'hakuna matata' is Kierkegaard's aesthetic stage of pleasure without commitment, which Simba must leave for the ethical stage when Nala, Rafiki ('Whooo are you?'), and Mufasa's ghost demand he 'remember who you are.' Sartre's 'optimistic toughness' and Nietzsche's 'Become who you are' frame Simba's defiant 'I am' before the assembled Pride Lands as existential self-creation.
- **The Good Place and Philosophy - Everything Is Forking Fine!**, ch. 31 "17. The Forking Bullshirt of Being Alone Together in the Good Place" — Frames the show's paradox — each person is responsible for her choices, yet her identity and choices are formed by her relationships — as Sartre's 'condemned to be free' colliding with relational autonomy, then reads each character through it. Eleanor's lifelong rejection of dependence (emancipation, bringing her own birthday cake) kills her and only unwinds through Team Cockroach; Chidi's indecision is named as bad faith that ends under an air conditioner; Tahani, defined by others' approval, is crushed pulling down Kamilah's statue yet confronts her parents in the Judge's test; Jason's blind loyalty to Pillboi and Donkey Doug shows dependence unexamined. The lesson: embrace both accountability and dependence by choosing whom you let close.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Because It's Never Just a Dream**, ch. 22 "The Kick—Back to ‘Reality’" — Richardson and McWilliams read Inception as an 'existential heist film' by diving through four layers of meaning. At the layer of reality they use Descartes's dream skepticism and wax argument, Hume on belief as custom and cause-effect, and Goffman on being shocked between frames to argue the film makes touch — the fall that wakes, pain ('pain is in the mind'), Saito's wrong-textured polyester carpet, the broken totems (Cobb's top, Arthur's loaded die, Ariadne's holed chess piece) — the only semi-trustworthy sense, while Mal, who locks her totem in the dollhouse safe and picks the dream, replays the cave prisoner who chooses the shadows. The car-chase layer ('downwards is the only way forwards'), Saito's 'old man filled with regrets' limbo, and the pharmacy dreamers who 'come to be woken up' are read through existentialism (Beckett's Waiting for Godot, Jaspers on loneliness and nothingness) and Peirce on the continuity of consciousness, with Cobb cast as the ideological existentialist who chooses action and reality where Cypher in The Matrix and Vanilla Sky's David face the same choice. The chapter then treats the film's reflexivity — the team as screenwriter/producer/director, the Escher-esque Penrose stairs, cross-cut dream time à la Peckinpah — as a lesson in film theory, and finally reaches phenomenology: Cobb's angry projection of Mal shows the dream world displaying his subjective meanings, against Arthur's calm, orderly hotel mindscape.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 17 "7 Indiana Jones and Existential Self-Affirmation" — Daniel Tilsley reads The Last Crusade as an excavation of identity: the fedora Fedora bestows after young Indy's defeat, the twenty-six-year quest for the Cross of Coronado ('All my life'), and the chosen name 'Indiana' (taken from the family dog) are acts of Nietzschean self-affirmation — amor fati and the willingness to will the Eternal Recurrence of one's life. The villains fail because they seek external artifacts to patch deficient lives, whereas the Grail Knight, like Camus's Sisyphus, authentically affirms his endless task of guarding the cup. The arc completes when Henry Sr. finally calls his son 'Indiana' while hanging from the abyss, recognizing the man he chose to become, and Crystal Skull repeats the pattern with Mutt and the fedora's eventual inheritance.
- **Iron Man and Philosophy - Facing the Stark Reality**, ch. 28 "Franken-Stark" — Curtis argues Iron Man dramatizes the problem of progress: Schopenhauer's insatiable will explains why every technological fix — the chest plate, the armor, the artificial nervous system — spawns new suffering and dependency, and his pessimism, with Kierkegaard's freedom within insecurity, Nietzsche's flawed Übermensch going out 'in a blaze of glory,' and Sartre's 'cautiously optimistic' existentialism, recasts Iron Man as a tragic antihero rather than a perfected Superman or Batman. Stark's wounded heart, alcoholism as self-medication ('the demon is not in the bottle but in the addict'), and doomed romances with Bethany Cabe and Rumiko Fujikawa make him the flawed hero who has simply learned to live with imperfection. Like Mary Shelley's monster, his extensions have become him — we are all 'Franken-Starks' facing the consequences of our own inventions.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Shotgun. Machete. Reason**, ch. 25 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Kempner reads the comic through Sartre's 'Existentialism Is a Humanism': with God and the old world gone, survivors like Rick, Michonne, and Dale must create their own values, while characters who cling to pre-apocalypse essences (Hershel keeping his zombified son in the barn, Shane waiting for the government) bring death on themselves. Rick's hospital awakening is treated as an existential rebirth in which his cop uniform is an 'essence precedes existence' trap, and Carl shooting Shane (and later Ben in 'Fear the Hunters') shows children making free choices outside conventional morality. The chapter concludes the series is 'sternly optimistic' because total freedom, not zombification, is what defines the humans: 'in a world ruled by the dead, we are forced to finally start living.'
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 6 "Introduction" — Elkholy's editorial introduction defines 'Beat' (the New York/West Coast writers) versus 'beat' (a lifestyle of weariness and disaffiliation), tracing the term through Kerouac, Ginsberg's 'Howl,' and Snyder. She frames the Beats' turning-inward and self-marginalization philosophically, noting that Brustein's charge that beats pursue aimless 'kicks' echoes Kierkegaard's critique of the Romantics as engaged in purposeless, rootless striving that evades responsibility. Against this she sets Holmes's reading of beat detachment as a search for meaning and belief, and casts the Beats' global travels as anticipating an emerging cosmopolitanism.
- **The Philosophy of the Beats**, ch. 18 "John Clellon Holmes and Existentialism" — Charters recounts how John Clellon Holmes—who coined the framing question 'How are we to live?' and prompted Kerouac's 'beat generation' label—was steeped in existentialism, reading Sartre, Camus, and Kierkegaard in the postwar New York scene. She argues his novel 'Go' is an existentialist text: its beat characters (modeled on Kerouac, Ginsberg, Cassady) enact freedom, self-transcendence, and the refusal of nihilism, saying 'no' in order to say 'yes' as in Camus's 'The Rebel.' Holmes ultimately rejected Sartre's atheist existentialism for a Kierkegaardian, faith-based one, valuing 'the evidence of soul' and reading Kerouac's characters as fleeing the absurd toward spiritual conviction.
- **The Philosophy of Charlie Kaufman**, ch. 21 "“There’s No More Watching” Artifice and Meaning in Synecdoche, New York and Adaptation" — Hill argues that Adaptation and Synecdoche, New York both dramatize artists (the character Charlie Kaufman and Caden Cotard) struggling to portray 'real life' through artifice, and that Kaufman achieves authenticity not through neorealist naturalism but through surrealism and fantasy. He distinguishes the existentialist sense of authenticity—living self-awarely and choosing outside a community's rules (via Macquarrie)—from cinematic realism, tracing Kaufman's fusion of inner and outer life to Fellini's 8½. The chapter reads Synecdoche as an unflinching, near-horror examination of what it costs to make honest art, concluding its buried message is that creation is meaningless unless shared.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Calhoun argues Eastwood's films move from solitary violent individualism (the Man with No Name, Dirty Harry) to what he calls 'post-Christian Stoic existentialism.' Using Epictetus's actor-in-a-play image and Marcus Aurelius on doing one's duty, he reads Butch Haynes in A Perfect World and William Munny in Unforgiven as figures 'dragged by the cart' of fate who nonetheless play their assigned role with dignity, while God is absent — Nietzsche's 'death of God.' Francesca's Stoic governance of impulse in Bridges of Madison County, Frankie's Kierkegaardian choice in Million Dollar Baby, and Walt's sacrificial community-building in Gran Torino show autonomous moral agency amid cultural collapse, with faint intimations of transcendence.
- **The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Clint Eastwood" — Jennifer McMahon reads Walt Kowalski of Gran Torino as Camus's rebel by pairing the film with The Plague. Against the absurd—the feeling that arises when reason's demand for order meets a world that disappoints—Camus rejects plain and 'philosophical' suicide (including religious faith) in favor of revolt, embodied by Dr. Rieux fighting the plague and echoing Nietzsche's life-affirming 'yes.' Walt, like Rieux, acts lucidly and courageously against a threat (Spider's gang) that authorities and the priest Janovich cannot remedy. McMahon defends Walt's engineered death as revolt not suicide via the doctrine of double effect: he intends the community's deliverance and Thao's future, not escape, dying in cruciform sacrifice as an ordinary man who becomes an existential hero.
- **The Philosophy of the Coen Brothers**, ch. 25 "Being the Barber Kierkegaardian Despair in The Man Who Wasn’t There" — Hoffman maps Ed Crane's arc onto Kierkegaard's typology of despair from The Sickness unto Death. Early Ed, the passive barber who defines himself by profession and possessions, embodies despair as a lack of infinitude and possibility—the finitized 'mass man.' Through blackmail, killing Big Dave, and his failed attempt to manage Birdy, he becomes a man of immediacy with reflection, then shifts to 'despair over the eternal,' sensing finite things cannot satisfy. Hoffman concludes Ed ends not free of despair but as Kierkegaard's self of 'inclosing reserve'—withdrawn, watching himself, craving a confidant—having never made the leap of faith that alone escapes despair.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 26 "13. Reason and Catharsis" — Elsby and Luzecky argue that we compulsively rationalize Twin Peaks (tulpas, pale-horse omens, Diane-as-tulpa) the way we abstract concepts to tame the contradictory sensible world (Plato's long-and-short finger), but Lynch—especially in Part 8—deliberately thwarts this, exposing what Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols calls the post-Socratic tyranny of rationality. They offer an alternative reading of Aristotelian catharsis (via Trela): because the fictional world is not ours, we can experience its irrationality and absurdity, emotions purged of their tie to reality, as freedom rather than the existential despair the absurd would cause in our own world.
- **The Philosophy of David Lynch**, ch. 29 "16. Doppelgängers, Doubles, and Tulpas" — Bunce reads Twin Peaks' pervasive doubling as dramatizing self-loss versus self-mastery. Cooper is good because he integrates his rational and mystical sides into an authentic whole, while BOB is a parasitic, one-dimensional inhabiting spirit and Laura chooses death over becoming BOB. He explains self-loss through La Rochefoucauld and Rousseau on amour-propre and the modern craving for esteem (Josie's masks versus Norma's refusal to become a brand), and traces the doppelganger motif from Jean Paul's satire of Fichte's clear I/not-I distinction to Dostoyevsky's The Double—arguing that, unlike Jean Paul, Twin Peaks affirms an authentic, whole self one is responsible for.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 5 "Foreword" — Robert Porfirio's foreword traces film noir's dark sensibility to a native strain in American culture rather than only to imported existentialism, running from Puritan gloom through Poe, Melville, and Hawthorne to the hard-boiled pulp of Hammett, Chandler, and Woolrich. He argues that William James's pragmatism sounded the death knell of the Emersonian/Thoreauvian transcendentalist faith in self-reliance and nature, leaving the way open for Darwinism, Freudianism, and Nietzschean pessimism to reduce the individual to a 'waif amidst forces.' He connects this to the Germanic emigres who brought expressionist style, suggesting they were drawn to an American darkness already present, and closes wondering what post-9/11 neo-noir will make of the same fear and paranoia.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 7 "Introduction" — Mark Conard's introduction opens with thumbnail plots of Double Indemnity, The Maltese Falcon, and Out of the Past to ask what noir has to do with philosophy, then frames the definitional problem (genre, style, cycle, or mood) as itself a philosophical question about essence. It surveys the volume's thirteen essays, noting that French existentialism was contemporaneous with classic noir (1941-58, Maltese Falcon to Touch of Evil) and shares its themes of moral ambiguity, reason versus passion, and pessimism even without direct influence. It previews the arguments to come, including Nietzsche's death of God as a lens on noir, neo-noir realism, Aristotelian tragedy and catharsis, and Schopenhauer's parallels in Ride the Pink Horse.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 9 "Nietzsche and the Meaning and Definition of Noir" — Mark Conard uses The Postman Always Rings Twice and Goodis's Night Squad to survey the failed attempts to define noir (genre, style, cycle, mood) and contrasts two theories of definition: Socrates/Plato's search for the essential form versus Nietzsche's flux metaphysics, in which no stable 'being' exists behind becoming and language falsifies a world in motion, making essences and definitions fictions ('I am afraid we are not rid of God because we still have faith in grammar'). He proposes that noir is best understood as an American artistic response to Nietzsche's death of God, the loss of transcendent meaning and value that produces noir's pessimism, alienation, and moral disorientation, citing Sam Spade shrugging off his partner's murder and Ole Andersen passively awaiting his killers. Ironically, the same flux that makes noir what it is (the death of God) is what makes noir impossible to define.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 12 "Cherchez la Femme Fatale The Mother of Film Noir" — Read Mercer Schuchardt argues that The Jazz Singer (1927) should be considered the first film noir because it is the first mass-medium announcement of Nietzsche's death of God, staged as the death of Papa Rabinowitz and the old prescriptive Judaism. He reads the film through a three-stage deicide (God as God, then one god among many, then a stage prop for Jakie's voice) and through a Jungian/Neumann anima-animus opposition of the word-based patriarchal religion versus the image-based maternal love that wins out, mirroring film displacing scripture. He ties this to Porfirio's existential pessimism that undercuts happy endings, casting Jakie's blackface Broadway triumph as a bittersweet, angst-ridden creation of meaning after the loss of transcendent value, and traces later 'existential detective' descendants like I Heart Huckabees and Fight Club.
- **The Philosophy of Film Noir**, ch. 15 "Film Noir and the Meaning of Life" — Steven Sanders uses film noir to motivate philosophical reflection on the meaning of life, reading its pessimistic sensibility (Touch of Evil, Detour, Out of the Past, D.O.A., Vertigo) as the presupposition that life is meaningless per se. He runs through Schopenhauer's pessimistic arguments from the vanity and transience of existence, Nagel's rebuttal that our not mattering in a million years does not stop things mattering now, and the tension between Sartrean existentialist freedom and noir's Freudian fatalism of the inescapable past. He then lays out three models of meaninglessness (Baier's worthlessness and purposelessness, Camus/Nagel's absurdity met with irony), reading noir protagonists as ironists, before rejecting the noir view that life must be meaningless and arguing that meaning is a matter of degree, requiring realizable projects of positive value.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Editor Jerold Abrams argues Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent 'cinematic existentialism' in which a free subject stands against a cold, uncaring world, synthesized with strands of Stoicism and pragmatism. He surveys the volume's essays as variations on this theme: Camus' absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzschean flux in Full Metal Jacket, Heideggerian being-toward-death and authenticity in Paths of Glory, and Nietzsche's overman as the Star Child in 2001. The essay ties specific films (the ape's femur, HAL, Humbert, the Overlook) to the claim that each Kubrick subject must invent its own meaning in a meaningless universe.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 10 "Understanding the Enemy The Dialogue of Fear in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove Elizabeth F. Cooke" — Cooke reads Kubrick's Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove through Camus' absurdism, arguing that facing fear and meaninglessness is a task each person must do alone. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus' lucid 'stranger,' while mad Sidney and death-seeking Mac fail by fleeing into fantasy or false hope; the interchangeable soldiers and doubled enemy general dramatize the sheer contingency of which side one is on. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions (Ripper, Strangelove, the Doomsday Machine, the War Room round table), so that Sartrean bad faith becomes systemic and no one can face the absurd honestly.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 12 "Existential Ethics Where the Paths of Glory Lead Jason Holt" — Holt uses Paths of Glory to illustrate existential ethics, framing the doomed 701st Regiment as 'thrown' beings-toward-death who retain full freedom in how they meet their fate. He resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' (denying objective values while commanding authenticity) by treating authenticity as a formal, second-order virtue like integrity: Colonel Dax is sincere and consistent, General Mireau an inauthentic hypocrite acting in bad faith. Addressing weakness of will (Roget's cowardice) and the condemned Paris 'dying well' before the firing squad, Holt argues that courage—an Aristotelian character virtue—is the smuggled-in content that grounds any formalist existential ethics.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 14 "Where the Rainbow Ends Eyes Wide Shut Karen D. Hoffman" — Hoffman reads Eyes Wide Shut as Kubrick's most optimistic film, tracing how Bill and Alice Harford are 'awakened' to the uncontrollable power of sexual desire and thereby strengthen their marriage. Bill's Kantian confidence—that principled duty guarantees fidelity—is shattered by Alice's confession of overwhelming desire for the naval officer, which exposes their fidelity as mere moral luck. Through the models, Marion, Domino, and the anonymous masked orgy at Somerton (where sex is impersonal 'bodies touching bodies'), Bill seeks but fails to feel Eros; the couple finally choose a consciously chosen fidelity, and Alice's closing 'fuck' insists raw desire belongs inside marriage, which Hoffman links to Kierkegaard's view of marital love living and winning in time.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 15 "Knockout! Killer’s Kiss, the Somatic, and Kubrick Kevin S. Decker" — Decker reads Killer's Kiss (and later 2001, A Clockwork Orange, Eyes Wide Shut) through Merleau-Ponty's phenomenology of the lived body ('I am my body'), recovering the somatic that Socrates and Plato's Phaedo denigrated. In Killer's Kiss the boxing match, the mannequin-warehouse fight where bodies become weapons, spatial camera work, and the theme of contingency foreground embodiment; 2001 makes viewers feel their own bodies in space, and A Clockwork Orange's Ludovico 'cure' rewires the body-mind. Drawing on pragmatists Shusterman and Sullivan and on Foucault's biopower, he argues the anonymous masked bodies of Eyes Wide Shut turn Merleau-Ponty's projective intentionality into domination rather than communication.
- **The Philosophy of J.J. Abrams**, ch. 18 "Rebel without a Cause Stanley Kubrick and the Banality of the Good Patrick Murray and Jeanne Schuler" — Murray and Schuler argue Kubrick's unifying sensibility is a dogmatic Hellenistic-style skepticism (via Hume's 'The Sceptic' and Seneca) that yields 'the banality of the good': in a world of cosmic futility and near-state-of-nature human nature, decent characters like Dax are helpless while the wicked (Barry Lyndon, Alex, Quilty) have vitality. They read Kubrick's Playboy remarks on human insignificance as Humean size/duration tropes, and diagnose his Sartrean 'create your own meaning' answer as a self-refuting false philosophy. Using Marx's critique of Hegel's accommodation to capitalism, they contend Kubrick's skepticism and irony merely reflect the 'bourgeois horizon' rather than comprehending it, ending in present-pleasure hedonism ('fuck' as the last word of Eyes Wide Shut).
- **The Philosophy of Joss Whedon**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' on television, not merely illustrates it, by ranking degrees of filmic philosophizing (via Wartenberg, Shaw, Mulhall) and showing the Whedenverse meets them. It reads Angel/Angelus and Fred/Illyria as cinematic thought experiments that generate 'metaphysical complexity' about personal identity, playing memory- and continuity-of-consciousness theories (Locke, Parfit) against a soul theory, and reads Connor's origin as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will. It contends Whedon endorses a Noddings-style ethics of care and an existentialist yet God-independent morality, epitomized by Angel's 'Epiphany' speech ('the smallest act of kindness is the greatest thing') and 'Deep Down,' plus the 'Man on the Street' Academic monologue, staging a negative project against the claim that ethics is incoherent without God through the self-sacrifices of Simon, Cordelia, and Buffy.
- **The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Martin Scorsese" — Karen D. Hoffman reads The Last Temptation of Christ and Bringing Out the Dead through Sartre's distinction between the for-itself (transcendence) and the in-itself (immanence), arguing both reluctant saviors are tempted into bad faith. Scorsese's Jesus, tempted on the cross to abandon his mission and live as an ordinary husband and father, passively drifts toward a life of pure immanence that denies his human transcendence, until (following Kazantzakis's 'sprouting of wings' image via Judas) he reclaims his choice to be crucified. Frank Pierce inversely faces a false transcendence—the temptation to think of himself as God, or to escape via drugs, violence, or suicide—and resists it, allowing the vegetative Mr. Burke to die. Hoffman frames avoiding either exaggeration as the path to authentic Sartrean humanity and grace.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 5 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Sanders's introductory survey frames Mann's cinema as suffused with existentialist themes—alienation, freedom, authenticity, and existential choice—citing Sartre's 'condemned to be free' as the key to protagonists like Thief's Frank and Heat's Neil McCauley, who choose personal truth over surrender. It maps the volume's essays: Nietzschean will to power in the crime films, Levinas's ethics of the Other in Thief and Collateral, and Lockean/Rousseauian visions of nature in The Last of the Mohicans. Mann's outsiders repeatedly face the fateful, doom-laden choices (McCauley abandoning Eady to kill Waingro) that define existential man.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Palmer casts the protagonists of The Jericho Mile and Thief as 'outsiders' in Colin Wilson's sense—men 'awakened to chaos'—read through Camus's Myth of Sisyphus. Rain Murphy, running endless meaningless laps and hurling away the timer, is Mann's Sisyphus: his fate belongs to him, the struggle itself filling his heart. Thief's Frank, who 'gets to where nothin' means nothin',' shreds his dream-collage and destroys everything rather than be owned by Leo, enacting the absurd hero's scorn for a Hobbesian 'war of all against all' where law lacks connection to justice.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 8 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Sanders argues Mann's action serves existentialist ideas: identity, freedom, authenticity, and death. In Thief, Frank's insistence on 'the yield of my labor' and his self-immolating exit dramatize the individualist maximizer whose choice of principle—echoing Sartre's young man and Kierkegaard's 'purity of heart is to will one thing'—cannot be given from outside. The Miami Vice episode 'Heart of Darkness' is read as a morality play on authenticity: undercover agent Artie Lawson's flight into the fantasy persona is a bad-faith masquerade that ends in suicide, mirroring Crockett's own anxiety about his Sonny Burnett alter ego.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 12 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Rybin links Mann's style-versus-substance debate to the existential self-definition of his characters, focusing on Public Enemies. Dillinger, who tells Billie 'the only thing that's important is where somebody's going,' is not yet an icon but is 'becoming Dillinger' as the film unfolds. In the penultimate scene, watching Clark Gable in Manhattan Melodrama—'die the way you lived, all of a sudden'—Dillinger achieves authentic self-definition by claiming the gangster myth as his own identity, a Warshovian 'experience of art'; Mann's editing collapses the space between Dillinger and the screen just before Dillinger is gunned down, the cost of authentic selfhood.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 13 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Pomerance argues Public Enemies inverts the gangster genre's convention of the 'ecstatic' criminal viewed from law's judgmental exterior: Mann's handheld camera penetrates Dillinger's private, breathing, interior world (contrasting the mechanized, plan-driven Purvis), likening the film to Fantastic Voyage's journey inside a body. Drawing repeatedly on Walter Benjamin's Arcades Project—the flâneur who is 'utterly undiscoverable,' the bourgeois transformation of nature into interior—he reads the FBI's cataloging of Dillinger as modernity reducing an integrated person to a collectible 'public enemy,' culminating in the head shot that is both execution and publicity image.
- **The Philosophy of Michael Mann**, ch. 17 "The Philosophy of Michael Mann" — Skrodzka reads Thief and Collateral as exercises in deontology grounded in Levinas's ethics of responsibility to the Other. Frank's violent courtship of Jessie and his final destruction of his possessions, and Max's crashing of the cab after Vincent's interpellation, are staged as the self's annihilating opening to the face of the Other (glimpsed in the rearview mirror as Max's doppelganger). Using Bauman's account of liquid-modern disconnection and a leftist critique of late capitalism, she argues Mann grounds Levinasian ethics in physical labor, and defines Vincent's evil as that which is 'knowing but unknowable,' deaf to the Other's call.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Spicer argues that the noir antihero embodies existentialism's darker side (alienation, contingency, dread), and that neo-noir intensifies this via European neo-modernism. In Point Blank, Boorman renders Walker's revenge as possibly a dying hallucination, using repetition, doubling, and drained color so that the story becomes an existentialist meditation on desire, faulty memory, and fragile identity. In Memento, Nolan's reverse-chronology 'Mobius strip' structure and Teddy's claim that memories are subjective interpretations leave Leonard's identity in tatters, ending both films on profound existential ambiguity.
- **The Philosophy of Neo-Noir**, ch. 18 "The Philosophy of Neo-Noir" — Gilmore reads Chinatown as neo-noir that is itself a kind of philosophy, engaging the hermeneutics of suspicion (Nietzsche, Freud, Marx) and existentialist alienation. Curly eating the venetian blinds signals a desire to recover a less painful blindness; Jake Gittes's 'conceptual scotomas' (Dennett) and hubris make him miss counternarratives, paralleling Oedipus as detective. Using Freud on the uncanny and doppelgangers (Jake doubled with Hollis Mulwray and Noah Cross) and Aristotle's Poetics on catharsis and the sublime, Gilmore argues 'Chinatown' names the abyss where every narrative is undone, and that facing this dark sublimity is the way of wisdom.
- **The Philosophy of Science Fiction Film**, ch. 12 "The Existential Frankenstein" — McMahon gives an existential reading of Whale's Frankenstein and Shelley's novel through Heidegger's being-toward-death and Ernest Becker's denial of death. Victor Frankenstein exemplifies Becker's 'defiant Promethianism,' the offensive denial that seeks to conquer death, and the monster personifies death itself. She argues his obsession erodes his humanity, estranges him from others, and generates moral dilemmas, illustrating Heidegger's claim that only authentic acceptance of mortality restores individuality and genuine community, so that mastering death would make us monsters.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 7 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Abrams's editorial introduction argues that Kubrick's whole filmography forms a coherent cinematic existentialism in which the isolated self stands against a cold, uncaring world. It threads the individual Kubrick films through named philosophers - Camus's absurd in Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove, Nietzsche's flux and Overman in Full Metal Jacket and 2001, Heidegger's thrownness and being-toward-death in Paths of Glory, Kant's marriage-morality in Eyes Wide Shut - and notes Kubrick blends this existentialism with Stoicism (The Killing) and pragmatism. It frames each contributor's essay as reading one film through that lens.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 9 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Cooke reads Fear and Desire and Dr. Strangelove as studies of how we face Camus's absurd. In Fear and Desire the detached Lieutenant is Camus's lucid 'stranger,' while Sidney goes mad and Mac chooses a suicidal assassination as false meaning; each faces death alone, so it is not tragedy. In Dr. Strangelove the individual is dissolved into insane institutions - Ripper, Bat Guano, the War Room round table - so no one can face the absurd lucidly; Cooke uses Sartre's bad faith to name how men become mere representatives of their institutions, and contrasts both films with Descartes's and Plato's method of certainty.
- **The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick**, ch. 11 "The Philosophy of Stanley Kubrick" — Holt reads Paths of Glory as an illustration of existential ethics. The doomed men of the 701st are 'thrown' (Heidegger) into a suicidal attack on the Ant Hill, and the film contrasts the authentic Colonel Dax - sincere, consistent, refusing Mireau's command out of integrity - with the inauthentic, bad-faith General Mireau. Holt resolves the 'paradox of existentialism' by treating 'be authentic' as a formal meta-value, and argues that authenticity ultimately rests on the Aristotelian virtue of courage, shown when Paris 'dies well' before the firing squad despite an earlier failure of nerve.
- **The Philosophy of Steven Soderbergh**, ch. 26 "The Philosophy of Popular Culture" — Biderman and Devlin use Traffic's four intertwined characters to test Kantian moral absolutism, applying the three formulations of the categorical imperative: Helena's decision to have witness Eduardo Ruiz murdered fails universalization, while Javier's whistleblowing on General Salazar (motivated only by duty, refusing reward) passes the autonomy formula. They argue Kant handles these cleanly but strains on DEA agent Montel's revenge (treating Carlos as a means) and outright fails on drug-czar Robert Wakefield's conflict between two absolute duties, to nation and to his addicted daughter. Following Sartre's critique that the categorical imperative is too abstract for concrete dilemmas, they show Soderbergh siding with existentialist choice as Robert invents his own law and quits to save his daughter.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 7 "“Do Not Forsake Me, Oh, My Darling” Loneliness and Solitude in Westerns" — Biderman argues that the western hero's solitude carries philosophical benefits, distinguishing being alone from feeling lonely (McCauley in Heat: 'I'm alone, I'm not lonely'). Epistemically he likens the silent, self-reliant hero (Kane in High Noon, Shane, Munny in Unforgiven, Blondie) to Descartes retreating into methodological doubt and solipsistic solitude to secure knowledge. Ethically he sets Aristotle's claim that man is a social animal (so the friendless hero cannot flourish) against Stoic detachment and Sartrean/existentialist authenticity, concluding the hero must be 'lone' because his heroism is inseparable from his chosen solitude.
- **The Philosophy of the Western**, ch. 14 "Order without Law The Magnificent Seven, East and West" — Skoble compares The Magnificent Seven with Kurosawa's Seven Samurai, arguing the farming villages are not Hobbesian anarchies needing a sovereign but Lockean communities with a 'grown' social order that merely lack reliable enforcement against bandits. Using Hayek's distinction between spontaneous order (kosmos) and planned order (taxis), he shows the farmers legitimately hire gunslingers/ronin for self-protection rather than surrendering to private-justice worries. The warriors' willingness to honor an unenforceable contract ('That's just the kind you've got to keep') is grounded in a self-created ethics linking the Bushido/Zen and existentialist idea that one's honor and selfhood consist in one's actions.
- **Neil Young and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "9 Neil Young’s Search for the Simple Life" — Watson and Riches reinterpret "A Man Needs a Maid" not as simple misogyny but as Young's ambivalent inner conflict between craving companionship and fearing the pain of intimacy. They read his pursuit of the "simple life" ("Heart of Gold," avoidance of reading) through Epicurean simplicity, Aristotle's eudaimonia, Bowlby/Freudian avoidant attachment and cognitive dissonance, and Sartre's "bad faith" as self-deception, set against Thoreau's chosen solitude and Aristotle's claim that the non-social being is "beast or god."
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 5 "Introduction" — The introduction sets the book's guiding question of whether a fictional-narrative filmmaker (specifically Joss Whedon) can 'do philosophy' the way traditional philosophers do, using Whedon's television and film corpus as its test case. It frames philosophy as an activity of removing contradictions through argument and pursuing the examined life, invoking Socrates on the unexamined life and Sartrean/Heideggerian existentialism to argue that Whedon's Buffy, Angel, Firefly, and Dollhouse dramatize authenticity and choice. It previews reading Whedon's characters (Angel, Mal, Buffy) against Rawls, Plato, Aristotle, Kant, and Parfit to establish that the Whedonverse is genuinely philosophical.
- **Joss Whedon as Philosopher**, ch. 8 "Conclusion" — The concluding chapter argues that Joss Whedon 'does philosophy' through the Whedonverse, building on Mulhall, Wartenberg and Shaw's hierarchy of filmic philosophizing. It reads Angel's 'Deep Down' and 'Epiphany' speeches as endorsing that kindness is a self-standing good regardless of God, framing sacrifices by Simon (for River), Cordy (for Angel) and Buffy (for Dawn) as a cinematic thought experiment refuting the claim that ethics is incoherent without God. It reads Connor as exemplifying Kane's libertarian free will (Darla and faux-Cordelia 'stir up' quantum indeterminacy), Angel/Angelus as a years-long test of memory-continuity personal identity against Parfit's Neo-Lockean view, and 'The Cabin in the Woods' plus Dollhouse's 'Man on the Street' as endorsing a Noddings-style ethics of care and Whedon's religious non-realism, with Angel offered as a Socrates-like moral exemplar.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 20 "“Howzat!” Prometheus Is a Fast Bowler" — Kevin S. Decker argues the Doctor's morality is an "ethics of ambiguity" poised between Romanticism and existentialism, not any formula. Rejecting positivism, deontology, and utilitarianism as fits for the Doctor, he reads the Doctor's freedom, wandering, and rejection of Time Lord values through Sartre's radical freedom and bad faith (the student torn between mother and Free French) and Beauvoir's "adventurer" who confers value by choosing. The Romantic search for the infinite in small things and the Prometheus myth frame the Doctor as a liberating, self-defining moral exemplar.
- **Lost and Philosophy - The Island Has Its Reasons**, ch. 15 "NOTES" — Jeremy Barris argues that Lost dramatizes the structure of life itself, using Heidegger's claim that the inquirer's own being is the clue to all questions and his notion of 'thrownness' to read the castaways' accidental arrival as a mirror of our own bewildering birth into circumstances we did not make. He reframes the show's central puzzle as 'the question of life after birth,' contends against Sartre and Camus that life is neither fully sensible nor fully absurd but a half-understood riddle, and invokes Wittgenstein's On Certainty to show that total doubt is impossible because understanding senselessness presupposes understanding something.
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 24 "13. No Place like a Non-Place" — Pagnoni Berns, Juvé, and Aguilar apply Marc Augé's concept of the 'non-place'—transit spaces (roads, airports, ships, hotels, malls) of anonymity and 'supermodernity' that confer no identity—to the show's empty landscapes. Postwar gender and identity crises play out in 'Passage on the Lady Anne' (slowness versus speed), 'The Hitch-Hiker' and 'The Passersby' (the road as a non-place where dead women refuse their fate), 'Will the Real Martian Please Step Up?', 'Nightmare at 20,000 Feet,' 'The Parallel,' 'The After Hours,' and 'The Four of Us Are Dying,' where identification briefly pierces anonymity, often fatally.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 17 "MOTHERHOOD" — Elizabeth Butterfield reads her exhausting early motherhood through Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity and The Second Sex, arguing that 'the ideal mother,' like 'true womanhood,' is a social construction and that a mother is 'freedom in situation,' never a mother 'the way a stone is a stone.' She recasts Beauvoir's 'serious man' as the 'serious mother' who flees her freedom into the Motherhood Religion, and invokes Sartre's 'condemned to be free' and 'Hell is other people' (No Exit) to advocate the honest, self-aware 'genuine mother' over inauthentic self-sacrifice.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 16 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Hernandez contrasts 'dark' existentialism — Sartre's café-bound claim that hell is other people and that the self is imprisoned in others' looks (illustrated by Starbucks' Pike Place backlash reshaping its identity), and Camus's absurd alienation — with an 'optimistic existentialism' that finds meaning in community. Drawing on Kierkegaard's Christian love, Jaspers's 'encounter,' Marcel's turn toward the other (her Sweet Eugene's pregnancy story), and above all Buber's I–Thou versus I–It, she argues the coffee community (neighborhood boards, fair-trade activism, the neighborly cup) is an existential ground where isolated bodies-toward-death create shared hope by treating each patron as a Thou rather than a discarded It.
- **Coffee – Philosophy for Everyone - Grounds for Debate**, ch. 20 "Coffee - Philosophy for Everyone" — Sadler argues black coffee, unlike ceremonial tea, is the realist emblem of our anxious, isolated postmodern condition, and that the chain coffeehouse is a 'non-place' of public anonymity that only simulates the sociality we crave. Against Aristotle's confident view of humans as social animals whose eudaimonia presupposes a settled social order, she sets Nietzsche's alienated individual free to create values — then argues Nietzsche errs: using the trivial cappuccino-vs-latte choice, she shows (via Wittgenstein's private-language argument and Korsgaard) that even solitary choices need reasons intelligible to others, so individual choice cannot be self-justifying and our search for meaningful, non-arbitrary lives is irreducibly social.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 18 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Eric Bronson reads the elves of Rivendell and especially Lothlorien through the 'merrier' existentialists, arguing that lasting joy requires facing the abyss and still affirming life, and knowing, as Nietzsche urged, what to remember and what to forget. Galadriel sings in dark times yet is burdened by remembering too much, unable to let go of her cursed past, so her regret shows the danger Jaspers and Arendt also diagnosed of losing oneself. When she refuses Frodo's Ring and chooses to 'diminish and remain Galadriel,' she embodies the existentialist's affirmation and trust in one's own inner light.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 30 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — J. Lenore Wright reads the Quest through the Western journey-narrative, both outward (Plato's climb out of the cave, Augustine's conversion) and inward (Descartes's methodological doubt turning toward the cogito). Frodo's leaving the Shire and freely accepting the Ring dramatizes the outward journey and the limits of freedom, while the wounding-and-healing of Sam, Merry, and Pippin marks an existential journey toward the Nietzschean charge to 'become who you are.' Wright contrasts the Yea-saying hobbits, transformed into resilient masters, with Nay-sayers Smeagol and Saruman locked in inauthentic self-pity, and argues Tolkien's ordinary pilgrims show that binding oneself to the good makes ordinary life extraordinary.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 8 "Who is Who" — The introduction argues that Doctor Who and philosophy share a common origin in wonder (quoting Plato's Socrates and Aristotle) and traces the show's shifting worldview across the eleven Doctors. It claims early Who embodied Enlightenment 'positivism' (the pro-science Hartnell/Pertwee eras) but that the post-1996 and post-2005 series turned toward Romanticism and Sartrean/de Beauvoirian existentialism, framing the surviving Doctor's post-Time War 'angst,' homelessness and burden of freedom through existentialist themes.
- **Comics as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "index" — This composite chapter argues philosophy through several comics. Jeremy Barris pairs Plato's dialogues with Amazing Spider-Man, using the allegory of the cave, the Forms, and Platonic love/eros to show that Spider-Man's bodily beauty, awkwardness, and self-trivializing irony draw readers toward goodness the way Plato says lust for beautiful bodies leads the soul upward to truth. Iain Thomson reads Moore and Gibbons's Watchmen as a 'deconstruction of the hero,' running Rorschach, Ozymandias and Dr. Manhattan through Nietzsche's Ubermensch and 'do not throw away the hero in your soul,' Heidegger's authentic 'choosing one's hero' and the uncanny, Kierkegaard's knight of faith, and Baudrillard's idea that an extreme realization destroys its own idea. Laura and Paul Canis read Daniel Clowes's Ghost World through Sartre's existentialism: Enid's post-high-school 'three o'clock' limbo enacts thrownness, abandonment, radical freedom and the flight from it into bad faith, contrasting Enid's authentic self-creation with Rebecca's settled conformity. Aldo Regalado's essay treats Tarzan, Superman, Captain America and the Black Panther as responses to modernity and race.
- **Philosophy and the Interpretation of Pop Culture**, ch. 8 "NOTES" — Carolyn Korsmeyer uses Aristotle's Poetics dictum that the 'probable impossible' beats the possible improbable to argue popular narrative can actually conduct philosophy, not merely illustrate it. Her central case is that the TV series Angel—the ensouled, guilt-cursed vampire who concludes 'if nothing we do matters, then all that matters is what we do'—independently arrives at the same existentialist position as Simone de Beauvoir's The Ethics of Ambiguity, with no textual borrowing. She contrasts The Matrix's dramatically sustained Cartesian dream-doubt against the 'improbable impossible' Dallas dream-season, showing why one is a philosophical vehicle and the other bankrupt.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 17 "15. Grey’s Anatomy as Philosophy Ethical Ambiguity in Shades of Grey" — The chapter argues that Meredith Grey embodies Simone de Beauvoir's existentialist ethics from The Ethics of Ambiguity, rejecting the childlike 'spirit of seriousness' that treats moral rules as absolute. Through episodes where Meredith stabilizes a bomb inside a patient's chest, coaches a death-row inmate to induce his own brain death, switches an Alzheimer's-trial placebo for Adele, and commits insurance fraud to treat an immigrant child, it shows her breaking institutional protocol to positively will the freedom of others while owning her choices. It contrasts her authentic embrace of moral ambiguity and risk against Shepherd's, Bailey's, and Webber's rule-bound seriousness or self-interest, framing medical dilemmas as an ambiguous moral realm where no single correct answer exists.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 55 "52. Fight Club as Philosophy I Am Jack’s Existential Struggle" — Oya reads Fincher's Fight Club in existentialist, nonethical terms as the story of the unnamed narrator 'Jack' and his struggle for an authentic, self-governed life. Consumerism (the 'Ikea nesting instinct'), the masculinity of underwear ads, religion, and finally Tyler Durden's hunter-gatherer creed are all rejected as externally imposed answers that deny authenticity; Fight Club and Project Mayhem merely swap one alienation for another. Jack's shooting himself to purge Tyler dramatizes self-affirmation. The chapter grounds this in Beauvoir's Ethics of Ambiguity ('the genuine man will not agree to recognize any foreign absolute'), contrasts Nietzsche and Unamuno on self-affirmation, cites Hobbes on the brutish state of nature to condemn Tyler's utopia, and invokes Plato's cave to argue a comfortable but externally governed life is still not authentic.

### Euthyphro Dilemma

The Euthyphro dilemma comes from Plato's dialogue Euthyphro, where Socrates asks whether the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or is pious because it is loved by the gods. Generalized beyond its religious setting, it poses a sharp question about the foundation of morality: are actions good because a divine will commands them, or does that will command them because they are already good? If goodness depends only on divine command, morality seems arbitrary; but if the gods approve things because they are independently good, then their approval is not what makes them so. The dilemma remains central to debates about the relationship between religion and ethics.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 9 "Unknown" — Irwin parallels Neo's mission with Socrates' divine commission from the Oracle at Delphi to 'wake up' Athens: both are driven by a single question ('What is the Matrix?' versus 'What is the good life?'), both are charged by the authorities, and both sting a complacent public. He explains the Socratic method through the Euthyphro exchange on holiness, where a follow-up question ('Is the holy holy because the gods approve it, or do they approve it because it is holy?') exposes Euthyphro's ignorance, and introduces Socrates' mantra 'I know nothing' as the humility that launches his quest just as Neo's lack of self-knowledge launches his.
- **Star Wars and Philosophy - More Powerful than You Can Possibly Imagine**, ch. 7 "The Force Is with You . . . but You’re Not a Jedi Yet" — The editors' introduction argues that beneath its action scenes Star Wars stages ageless philosophical questions through the Skywalkers' struggles with identity, truth, freedom, and tragedy, opening with 'I've got a bad feeling about this' as basic philosophical wonder and doubt. It playfully transposes classic problems onto the saga: an Euthyphro-style question of whether Jedi virtues are good because the Jedi appreciate them, Anselm's question whether Yoda is a master greater than which cannot be conceived, Augustine on whether Anakin can be chaste 'but just not yet,' Machiavelli on Palpatine's Empire, Descartes' mind-body question asked of C-3PO, Hume's problem of induction applied to whether the sun will rise on Alderaan, Nietzsche's abyss for Vader, and Sartre's hell for the Sith. It previews each contributor's chapter rather than settling any question, framing the volume as a Kessel Run for the brain.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Henry Jacoby takes seriously House's nihilist sound bites ("selfish, base animals," his baiting of Sister Augustine and Foreman's chapel prayer, his clinically dead experiment in "97 Seconds") but argues House actually lives the Socratic examined life and Aristotle's life of reason: his puzzle-solving saves lives, exercises humanity's distinctive function, and issues in eudaimonia. The Euthyphro dilemma shows meaning cannot be grounded in God's plan, and House's refusal of afterlife comfort leaves "our actions here" as all that matters. Against the unexamined life, House's "What's the point in living without curiosity?" makes him a Socratic figure who chooses meaning through reason rather than faith.
- **Planet of the Apes and Philosophy - Great Apes Think Alike**, ch. 18 "Planet of the Apes and Philosophy" — Travis Timmerman argues the series dramatizes Singer's equal consideration of interests: Zira frees Taylor once he writes 'My name is Taylor' because like interests must count equally regardless of species, while Dr. Zaius's erasing the writing, lobotomizing Landon, and destroying the cave artifacts is pure speciesism in Bentham's 'Can they suffer?' sense. He rejects the crude 'humans are smarter' argument (it would strip severely cognitively disabled humans of standing) and Nussbaum's species-normal version (it would permit caging Zira and Cornelius since normal apes are mute), then deploys Plato's Euthyphro dilemma against Locke-style God-given rights: a deity bellowing that human interests outrank ape interests is arbitrary unless grounded in independent reasons. Since farming severely cognitively disabled humans is obviously wrong and species membership is morally irrelevant, it is equally wrong to factory-farm and experiment on animals - so, like Caesar in Battle for the Planet of the Apes, become vegetarian.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 7 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 40 "25. Deadpool Kills God" — The chapter declares Deadpool genuinely evil - shooting the defeated for fun, killing for money, then wiping out an entire universe - yet shifts the blame to the writers, the 'progenitors' who author every evil he commits and will not even let him think of escaping, making them the gods of the Marvel universe. By parity of reasoning it argues that if God created a world knowing every evil in it (Hitler, factory farms, tsunamis, SIDS), then all that evil is part of the plan and appealing to free will is blowing smoke. The author's real question is why anyone should obey a being who permits such suffering, dismissing do-as-he-says morality as cowardice before the lightning bolt: 'Go get him, Deadpool. Kick his bearded ass.'
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 36 "24. Aftermath" — Faller argues Civil War is Marvel's meditation on the aftermath of 9/11 - the Raft as Guantanamo, Zemo's interrogation as the waterboarding debate - and on America's red-blue polarization, with Steve Rogers embodying the virtue of the Good and Tony Stark the virtue of Truth as the two values democracy constantly pits against each other. Turning to Athens, he reads Plato's Euthyphro - are the gods good because goodness is a standard above them, or because their power decrees whatever they do good? - as the exact dilemma splitting Democrats, who define truth by the good it does, from Republicans, who define good by conformity to law and constitutional process, the same democratic dynamic that voted to execute Socrates and, in the comics, leaves Captain America assassinated by a sniper on his way to trial. Transcending the dualism is modeled by Spider-Man's identity disclosure and Black Panther's renunciation of vengeance over Zemo.
- **Rick and Morty and Philosophy - In the Beginning Was the Squanch**, ch. 14 "4. Could a Divine Creator Turn Out to Be a Selfish Jerk" — Using 'The Ricks Must Be Crazy', where Morty discovers Rick's car battery is a microverse of gooble-box workers ('slavery with extra steps'), the chapter asks whether a universe's designer must be a perfect God or could be a clever jerk like Rick. It lays out Paley's watchmaker teleological argument, Hume's point that even a real designer need not be morally perfect, the Euthyphro dilemma against Divine Command Theory (would Rick's commands for middle-finger greetings become morally good?), and Plantinga's modal ontological argument recast across the show's multiverse of possible worlds like the one where Hitler cured cancer. It concludes that Rick's advice to just not think about it is exactly what Socrates refused to do.
- **Indiana Jones and Philosophy - Why Did It Have to Be Socrates_**, ch. 28 "16 Sacred Objects and Cosmic Justice in Indiana Jones" — Argues that the Indyverse is a moral universe: whoever profanes a sacred object for selfish ends is punished regardless of personal religion — Belloq and the Nazis are consumed for opening the Ark, Mola Ram plunges from the rope bridge when the Sankara Stones burn his hand, Donovan ages to dust for choosing the ornate false grail, and Elsa falls carrying the true Grail past the Great Seal. Durkheim's sacred/profane distinction and Tillich's account of religious symbols explain why respectful handling (Indy's 'don't look,' returning the stone to Mayapore's altar) succeeds where theft fails. The closing Euthyphro move concludes that the three traditions' objects enforce one universal ethic: respect is a moral truth binding independently of any divine command, like 2+2=4.
- **The Olympics and Philosophy**, ch. 18 "The Olympics and Philosophy" — Jeffrey Fry imagines adding 'Virtuous' to the Olympic motto and awarding medals for moral excellence, then argues the reform faces near-insuperable hurdles. Drawing on Kant, he objects that rewarding virtue corrupts motive, since a morally worthy act must be done from duty, not for a prize (illustrated by a hypothetical rule giving basketball teams a point for helping up fallen opponents), and notes Kant reserves the just apportioning of happiness to God's omniscience, which human judges lack. He adds epistemological problems (cross-cultural disagreement about virtues, echoing Plato's Euthyphro; the opacity of motives and courage) and political ones (biased judges, nations losing face), proposing instead rare, formal recognition of extraordinary acts like Dorando Pietri's and coach Haakensmoen's.
- **Anthony Bourdain and Philosophy - An Appetite for Life**, ch. 16 "7. Anthony Bourdain’s Extremely Objectionable Stories" — Holmes examines Bourdain's horror graphic novel Hungry Ghosts as cautionary folklore in the tradition of Aesop and EC Comics. He stages a debate between Aristotle, who in the Rhetoric endorses fables as accessible moral tools, and Plato, who in the Republic wants to censor frightening tales for children — yet Holmes shows Plato himself (Euthyphro, Laws) praised fear as 'modesty,' and notes Bourdain used cautionary tales (Ronald McDonald 'has cooties') to steer his own daughter from fast food.
- **Dr. Seuss and Philosophy - Oh, the Thinks You Can Think!**, ch. 13 "Socratic Seuss Intellectual Integrity and Truth-Orientation" — Matthew Pierlott casts Seuss as a Socratic gadfly for intellectual integrity, built on Frankfurt's distinction between the liar (who respects truth) and the bullshitter (who is indifferent to it). Sam-I-Am's reluctant friend in Green Eggs and Ham is 'bullshitting' to be left alone; the boasting rabbit and bear of 'The Big Brag' are humbled by a worm who plays Socrates as in Plato's Euthyphro; Horton Hatches the Egg and Mulberry Street show self-delusion (believing what we wish were true); and 'What Was I Scared Of?' shows fear distorting the interpretation of evidence, all mapped against Pierlott's five aspects of intellectual integrity.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 49 "House and the Life of Reason" — Jacoby argues that despite House calling us "selfish, base animals," House lives Socrates' examined life and Aristotle's life of reason. He dismisses God-given meaning using the Euthyphro dilemma and rejects the soul and afterlife (the "97 Seconds" self-experiment), insisting "our actions here are all that matters." Meaning must be both subjective and objective; House's puzzle-solving realizes humanity's rational function, tied to action and virtue, and — per Aristotle — yields eudaimonia, so his life is meaningful even when it doesn't feel that way to him.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 21 "19. The Orville as Philosophy The Dangers of Religion" — The chapter argues that Seth MacFarlane's The Orville is a pointed critique of religion, especially when merged with political and military power. Through the warrior-god Avis worshipped by the Krill (read as stand-ins for militant evangelicals and Islamist jihadists) and the Moclans' patriarchal bigotry, it contends religion is portrayed as archaic and dangerous. It deploys Socrates's Euthyphro argument to reject divine command theory, contrasts the Krill's dogmatic certainty with the secular Union's self-correcting ethics, and invokes Buber's I–Thou to explain the 'de-souling' of outsiders, while defending Lockean separation of church and state against theocracy and theonomistic ethics.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 78 "74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates" — Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

### Russell's Teapot

Russell's teapot is an analogy devised by Bertrand Russell to argue that the burden of proof lies with the person making an unfalsifiable claim, not with those who doubt it. Russell imagined asserting that a china teapot orbits the Sun somewhere between Earth and Mars, too small to be detected by any telescope; the claim cannot be disproved, yet no one is thereby obliged to believe it. He used the image to challenge the idea that skeptics must refute religious or other extraordinary assertions rather than the claimants having to support them.

- **Christmas – Philosophy for Everyone - Better Than a Lump of Coal**, ch. 16 "Christmas Philosophy for Everyone" — Guy Bennett-Hunter treats both the Santa story and the virginal conception as mythologies whose value lies in meaning, not literal fact, drawing on Barthes and Gadamer's dictum that a myth needs no verification outside itself. He deploys Hume on miracles and Russell's Teapot to argue it is no more rational to believe the sacred myth literally than the Santa one, then turns to Tillich's religious case: taking the virgin birth literally is idolatry that drags the ultimate God into the chain of cause and effect. He urges 'breaking' the myth – keeping its significance while dropping its literal truth – a ladder to be kicked away like Edmund Gosse's childhood test of idolatry.

### On Miracles

In his essay on miracles David Hume argued that no testimony can rationally establish that a miracle has occurred. Since a miracle is by definition a violation of a law of nature supported by uniform and extensive experience, the evidence against it is as strong as evidence can be, whereas human testimony is often mistaken or deceptive. Hume concluded that a wise person should believe a miracle report only if its falsehood would be even more improbable than the event it describes, a standard he thought testimony could rarely if ever meet.

- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 8 "“Life’s a Piece of Shit” The Question of Heroism" — Argues Life of Brian is heretical rather than blasphemous: it never mocks Jesus or belief in God but ridicules gullible, smug believing — the Sermon on the Mount crowd mishearing 'blessed are the cheesemakers,' the sandal schism — a critique the chapter aligns with Hume on the appetite for the marvelous and on anthropomorphism. It reads Brian's window sermon ('You're all individuals... think for yourselves') as Kant's Sapere aude and as an existentialist, possibly Christian, humanism. Against the charge of nihilism, it places Brian squarely in Camus's absurd universe (the pointless crucifixion finale and 'Always Look on the Bright Side of Life') and asks whether Brian is an absurd hero like Sisyphus, Meursault, or Dr. Rieux; he is not — he never scorns his fate — so the chapter proposes 'absurd decent guy': Brian lives sincerely, without waiting for miracles, and humor rather than revolt is the counterweight to absurdity.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 18 "The Epilogue A Question of Belief" — Systematically pairs Hume's philosophy of religion with Python parodies: Anselm's ontological argument fails because existence cannot be defined into a concept (the Yeti-spotter who never spotted one), with Arthur 'Two Sheds' Jackson, Ron Obvious, and Confuse-A-Cat illustrating the gap between conceivability and possibility; the Galaxy Song's cosmic order and the mock hymn 'All Things Dull and Ugly' stage the design argument and Hume's reply that creation shows moral indifference as readily as benevolence; and Brian's 'miracles' — being 'taken up' then spotted sprinting, curing Simon the hermit by landing on his foot — illustrate Hume's 'Of Miracles' on the unreliability of testimony. Hume's Natural History claim that the cause of religion is fear surfaces in the 'O Father, please don't boil us' hymn and in Arthur's groveling before a God who hates it. Both Hume and the Pythons end in suspended judgment about God — settled, if at all, only by the wrestling match in which 'God exists by two falls to a submission.'
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 9 "What of Philosophical Relevance Is there in Tarantino’s Films" — Bruce Russell argues that Tarantino's films share a pattern—a cruel man's life goes awry, violence erupts, and glimpses of compassion appear, like Mr. White comforting the shot Mr. Orange—but that fiction can raise philosophical questions without justifying general philosophical theses. He uses the Pulp Fiction exchange over the bullets that missed Jules and Vincent to raise Hume's problem of miracles (divine intervention versus a 'freak occurrence'), and applies the accounts of Mill, Gibbard, Hare and Hume to show that even Vincent's twisted code—balcony drops for foot massages, execution for keying a car—counts as having a morality. His conclusion: the films raise, but never answer in depth, the questions of what a miracle is and what it is to have a morality.
- **Quentin Tarantino and Philosophy - How to Philosophize with a Pair of Pliers and a Blowtorch**, ch. 21 "Zed Is Dead" — Keith Korcz applies Hume's 'Of Miracles' to Jules's survival of the hand cannon: a genuine miracle would suspend a law of nature, but as Vincent says, 'It's a freak, it happens'—and the testimony establishing laws of nature always outweighs miracle reports, while lucky coincidences (cats surviving four-story falls) are selectively reported. He answers objections from revised laws of nature (the 1919 eclipse confirming general relativity) and from prior belief in a miracle-working god, concluding with Hume that a wise man proportions his belief to the evidence. Jules's transformation is real, but would occur regardless of whether his belief in the miracle is true.
- **Soccer and Philosophy - Beautiful Thoughts on the Beautiful Game**, ch. 16 "Added Time" — McDermid takes Maradona's cheeky 'a little with the head of Maradona and a little with the hand of God' claim literally and asks what would make either 1986 goal against England—the obvious handball or the Goal of the Century—a miracle, using Aquinas's definition of miracles as intentional divine acts beyond the order commonly observed in nature. He explores how God could intervene without breaking natural law, analogizing God to a goalkeeper exempt from the handball rule or a spectator outside the game: in a deterministic world He could only arrange initial conditions (a domino setup requiring fine-tuning at the Big Bang), while in an indeterministic quantum world He could load the chancy micro-events along Maradona's mazy, sensitively balanced run.
