The Evil in These Woods" — Rose-Barry surveys how Twin Peaks conceives evil—as Augustine's privation of good, as the Manichean clash of White and Black Lodges, and as Ricoeur's defilement (the sooty Woodsmen, BOB entering hosts)—then uses Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics distinction of vice, incontinence, and bestiality to argue Windom Earle is a better example of an evil person than BOB. Because BOB is all appetite ('I don't need—I want'), a beast lacking reason, he is like Aristotle's bestial man whose best part is merely absent; the vicious, rational Earle, who relishes wickedness and invents ever-crueler torments, has the worse condition of character—and evil, being human, can be fought.
- **The Philosophy of Horror**, ch. 9 "‘Pro-life’ and Pro-Life" — The chapter argues that horror films about pregnancy (Rosemary's Baby, Demon Seed, The Reaping, Prophecy, Inside) pit a foetal 'subject' against the pregnant woman, eroding her selfhood by conflating her body with an invadable house or environment. Drawing on Young's, Battersby's and Tyler's phenomenologies of pregnant embodiment and Irigaray's 'woman as place', it shows how foetal-imaging technology and abortion politics (The Life Zone versus Carpenter's Pro-Life) reduce the woman to a vessel while the foetus is granted autonomous personhood.
- **The Who and Philosophy**, ch. 32 "Escape to Doctor Who" — Ken Curry reads the Master as Schopenhauer's Will personified. After sketching Kant's phenomena/noumena and Schopenhauer's identification of the noumenal thing-in-itself as a blind, pointless (and thus evil) Will known indirectly through the body, he argues the Master ('in many ways we have the same mind,' 'Logopolis') is the dark Will present in everyone. Through 'Terror of the Autons' and 'The Sea Devils' he shows the Master exploiting the fatal vanity of Farrel and Colonel Trenchard as their own evil counterpart, with good (the Doctor) narrowly triumphing so the Will's cruelty entertains rather than oppresses us.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 23 "12. Finally Free" — McCrossin argues Supernatural is a rare popular treatment of the theological (not merely secular) problem of evil, with Dean's rant echoing Job and the Book of John's Lazarus (why does God let good people suffer, and why withhold guidance?). Tracing the four showrunner 'eras' as a theodicy incubator, he reads Cas's consolation—life is an obstacle course whose obstacles Chuck may have designed but whose race 'we' ran—through Kant on freedom under determinism, concluding the show's novel theodicy is that meaning comes from being the storytellers of our own lives once Chuck stops writing them.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 24 "13. Does God Have the Right to Destroy the Universe" — Foresman asks whether Chuck has a negative right to destroy the multiverse, rejecting the question-begging 'God can do whatever God wants' and the bare creation/ownership argument (using the scrambled-eggs example) as insufficient. Drawing on Locke's Two Treatises—property arises from mixing labor, but even in the state of nature one may not destroy a creature except for a 'nobler use,' and hoarding beyond use is illegitimate—he concludes Chuck is a Lockean tyrant destroying universes he could simply recreate, so Sam and Dean's rebellion is justified.
- **The Ultimate Supernatural and Philosophy - Saving People, Killing Things, the Family Business**, ch. 26 "15. God Is Good (Chuck Not So Much)" — Graves contrasts the Judeo-Christian God of scripture with Chuck, arguing Chuck fails theodicy: he neither shares human suffering (as Jesus does) nor pursues justice for the oppressed (as Yahweh does in Psalm 82), and using evolution to create sapient life guarantees disease, war, and injustice that Paley's Natural Theology design argument cannot excuse. He reads Amara's wish to unwind creation as arguably 'good,' rejects the Winchesters' fallacy that Nephilim Jack must inherit Lucifer's evil (nature versus nurture), and diagnoses Chuck as a pathological narcissist paralleling despotic real-world leaders.
- **Asimov's Foundation and Philosophy - Psychohistory and Its Discontents**, ch. 18 "9. Foundation’s Optimism" — McCrossin reads the sequels Foundation's Edge and Foundation and Earth as an Optimistic response to the problem of evil, in the lineage of Leibniz, Rousseau, and Hegel's 'All is well', set against the WWII, Holocaust, Nuremberg, and Eichmann-trial backdrop of Asimov's writing and Arendt's banality of evil. Tracking Gendibal's mantra 'all will happen well', the Gaia/Galaxia choice via Trevize's 'talent for rightness', and Daneel Olivaw's Zeroth Law and plan to merge with Fallom's brain, he uses the Book of Job to frame whether the series' recurring reassurance is earned or merely reframed.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — Johnson uses 'Cartmanland' to lay out the problem of evil: Kyle loses his faith when the wicked Cartman gains perfect happiness, giving a logical problem-of-moral-evil argument against God. Johnson shows why the story of Job and Chef's 'sweet milk of our tears' fail, then explains the greater-good and free-will defenses (invoking Augustine that only free acts are good) and the residual problem of natural evils like Kyle's hemorrhoid. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by South Park's Jesus, that God permits both moral and natural evil so we develop character, while noting the surviving evidential problem of evil's sheer amount.
- **South Park and Philosophy - You Know, I Learned Something Today**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Eberl and Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar, Six, Adama and Roslin to debate God's existence and meaning. Against Baltar's scientific naturalism they present Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, first cause, and the argument from design applied to the universe's ordered laws) and dismiss Pascal's Wager as insincere, like Baltar's. They then raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will defense and Hick's soul-making theodicy against Hume's faulty-architect analogy. Finally, contrasting Russell's meaning-amid-a-godless-cosmos with religious faith, they argue atheism need not entail nihilism and that survival and human solidarity give the Colonials common ground.
- **The Daily Show and Philosophy - Moments of Zen in the Art of Fake News**, ch. 28 "The Ultimate Daily Show and Philosophy" — Pigliucci uses the 'Evolution, Schmevolution' series and the Dover trial to argue that intelligent design is not science because it is unfalsifiable and invokes supernatural causation. He cites Popper's falsificationism (and Popper's recantation about Darwinism), contrasts Descartes's rationalism with Hume's empiricism to characterize science as a tentative blend of the two, flags Feyerabend's 'anything goes' as an irrational view of knowledge, invokes Aristotle's eudaimonia to argue meaning in life is a personal work in progress, and turns Dembski's theistic-evolution concession into a Pyrrhic victory via the problem of evil ('argument from bad design').
- **Philosophy in The Twilight Zone**, ch. 30 "17. A Shadowland Called the Twilight Zone" — McCrossin reads 'Deaths-Head Revisited' and 'He's Alive' against the Eichmann trial and Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem, framing Serling's concern as Susan Neiman's 'problem of evil.' The earlier episode's SS captain Lutze (driven insane by his victims' ghosts at Dachau) matches the grotesque-monster Eichmann of the film Operation Eichmann, while 'He's Alive' (Vollmer as a frightened man seduced by Hitler's ghost) foreshadows Arendt's 'banality of evil'—the thoughtless, empathy-less doer. He contrasts both with Hogan's Heroes, which Serling condemned for trivializing Nazi atrocity.
- **Stephen King and Philosophy**, ch. 4 "There Is No God in Desperation" — Sutton and Held use King's Desperation and its God-speaking boy David Carver to stage the problem of evil, opening with Hume's Epicurean dilemma and Rowe's and Draper's evidential arguments from superfluous suffering (Brian's coma, Pie's murder). They survey theistic replies as defenses (Augustine's evil-as-privation, skeptical-theism humility) and theodicies (Hick's soul-making 'God is refining,' the free-will theodicy, Aquinas on natural law preserving the whole), concluding with van Inwagen that we lack epistemic warrant to judge God. Held reframes evil as a human problem of suffering, and reads Marinville's arc through Kierkegaard's despair and Anselm's 'faith seeking understanding,' arguing the antidote to 'desperation' (unbelief) is a non-cognitive, affective faith that keeps investigating.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 8 "Introduction" — Alan Goldman's editorial introduction previews the volume's essays, framing Twain as a serious philosopher hidden behind humor and irony. It lays out the Huckleberry Finn debate over whether Huck's refusal to turn in Jim is weak-willed conscience versus reason-bearing sympathy (Bennett, Goldman, Fudge, Lyons, Gehrman), then Twain's late attacks on religion via Letters from the Earth and the problem of evil, plus essays on lying, animal rights, humor, and comparisons to Diogenes, the Epicureans, Nietzsche, and Hume. It treats these as genuine philosophical stakes drawn from Twain's fiction and late writings.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 16 "Chapter 6 The Gospel According to Mark (Twain)" — Craig Vasey reads Twain's Letters from the Earth, narrated by a skeptical Satan, as a defense of critical thinking rather than the ranting of a bitter old man. He unpacks Satan's mockery of a self-understanding in which God obsesses over and demands worship from humans, a sexless harp-playing Heaven, and the punishment of curious, ignorant Adam and Eve, echoing Hume's catalogue of suffering (the fly as 'divine ambassador'). Invoking Nietzsche on life-after-death as vengeance dressed as love, and Socrates' 'unexamined life,' Vasey argues Twain's real target is human gullibility and willful childishness, calling humanity to grow up, think, and take responsibility instead of scapegoating a celestial fantasy.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 17 "Chapter 7 Mark Twain and the Problem of Evil" — James McLachlan casts Twain (via The Mysterious Stranger, Letters from the Earth, and the Adam and Eve diaries) as Camus's 'metaphysical rebel': not simply an atheist but a blasphemer who indicts a Calvinist God who predestines, creates disease, and damns most of humanity, then is called 'Our Father.' He lays out the Epicurus/Hume statement of the problem of evil and Griffin's notion of 'genuine evil' (dysteleological surds), then the aesthetic defense from Plotinus and Augustine that all suffering serves the beauty of the whole. Twain rejects that defense with empirical facts of suffering (Eve's 'Fact' beats Adam's logic), and locates real love not in God but in Adam and Eve's earthly bond after the Fall.
- **Mark Twain and Philosophy**, ch. 22 "Chapter 10 Mark Twain’s Serious Humor and That Peculiar Institution" — Kramer argues, against Davenport, that Twain can be simultaneously serious and funny, using humor to attack the 'spirit of seriousness'—the dogmatic certitude and epistemic closure Sartre and Beauvoir describe—rather than sincerity itself. Drawing on Schopenhauer's account of seriousness and Beauvoir's remark that the mystified slave takes his condition as natural, Kramer shows Twain's satire of Christianity ('Little Bessie,' 'Letters from the Earth,' the anti-adultery commandment, the Philippines massacre) exposing the incongruity between professed omnibenevolence and real suffering. Like Democritus the 'laughing philosopher' and a Socratic ironist, Twain undermines complacent certainty without offering dogmatic Truth in its place.
- **Motherhood – Philosophy for Everyone - The Birth of Wisdom**, ch. 30 "MOTHERHOOD" — George Dunn asks whether classical theism can call God 'Mother,' beginning with the Book of Job (taught in his Problem of Evil course) and the divine name Shadday's link to womb-love and 'blessings of breasts and womb.' He works through Anselm's 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived,' the attributes of impassibility and incorporeality, and Aquinas's doctrine of analogy, arguing Aquinas wrongly rejected maternal God-language because he swallowed Aristotle's biology of woman as 'defective and misbegotten'; drawing on Nel Noddings's caring 'receptivity' and Julian of Norwich, Dunn contends divine impassibility should yield to a maternal, receptive God, with a nod to Homer Simpson's burrito paradox.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 9 "Through a Mirror, Darkly Art-Horror as a Medium for Moral Reflection" — Philip Tallon extends Aristotle's Poetics from tragedy to horror, arguing that where tragedy elicits pity and fear, horror mirrors the characters' visceral revulsion in the audience. Frankenstein serves as an internal critique of Enlightenment hubris, Victor's overreach making the abandoned monster more sympathetic than his creator. Against Lyotard's postmodern 'incredulity toward meta-narratives' and moral relativism, Tallon claims horror (e.g., King's 'Salem's Lot, where a priest craves a real EVIL to fight) works by violating an intuited moral, natural, and social order, thereby revealing a commonly-denied but underlying objective sense of morality and evil.
- **Horror and Philosophy - Essays on Their Intersection in Film, Television and Literature**, ch. 12 "Making Their Presence Known TV's Ghost-Hunter Phenomenon in a “Post-” World" — Jessica O'Hara argues TV ghost-hunter shows (Ghost Hunters, Paranormal State, A Haunting) stage classic philosophical problems in a postmodern key. Their reliance on technology to escape 'fallible senses' echoes Descartes's Meditations, while Husserl's intentionality raises whether clients' dysfunction makes them perceive the normal as paranormal (or invites the demonic). Baudrillard's simulation/hyperreal troubles whether a 'simulated' haunting differs from a real one; Plantinga's free-will defense frames their treatment of the problem of evil. Following Lyotard she reads the shows' micro-narratives and bricolage as postmodern, and via Derrida's Spectres of Marx casts ghost-hunting as post-9/11 mourning and the pursuit of justice, offering a Burkean/Kantian sublime.
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 21 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Scott Davison argues that The Lord of the Rings rejects the Manichean view of evil as an independent force equal to good and instead dramatizes Augustine's view that evil is a privation, parasitic on goodness. The Ring is not evil metal but Sauron's power working through it, the Ringwraiths wear robes to give shape to their nothingness, and Sauron himself is a corrupted will, not the source of all evil. Following Augustine's 'inordinate desire,' Davison locates the root of evil in the free choice to want more than one's fair share, illustrated by Boromir, Saruman, and Sauron's wish to usurp Iluvatar, and contrasted with Sam's contented 'plain hobbit-sense.'
- **The Philosophy of Tolkien - The Worldview Behind The Lord of the Rings**, ch. 28 "The Lord of the Rings and Philosophy" — Thomas Hibbs argues that Tolkien dramatizes providence as chance that brings good out of evil, chiefly through Gollum, whose theft and fall at the Cracks of Doom completes the Quest that Frodo, having claimed the Ring, could not. Providence presupposes real freedom and duty: Hibbs compares Gandalf's counsel to do what is in us for the years we are set with Kant on freely accepting duty, while distinguishing Tolkien's enchanted, morally saturated cosmos from Kant's opposition of autonomy and nature. Following Augustine's privation view of evil (echoing the volume's earlier essay), he reads Saruman's self-destruction and Sauron's blind self-projection as evil marring itself, met fittingly by wonder, joy, and gratitude at events like Gandalf's return.
- **Who Is Who_ The Philosophy of Doctor Who**, ch. 10 "Who is Who" — Titled 'Exterminate!', the chapter analyzes evil in Doctor Who through Augustine's privation theory and Kant's 'radical evil,' distinguishing irrational evil (Light in 'Ghost Light,' the Daleks) from rational 'lesser evil' calculations (the Rani, mad scientists). It reads the Daleks as Nazi-analogue Others bred for racial purity, invokes Arendt's banality of evil and capacity to think for oneself (Rose challenging the ninth Doctor over the lone Dalek and the Delta wave), and cites Kierkegaard on losing oneself when one does evil alone.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 22 "Jesus Christ and John Hick The Soul Making Theodicy" — David Kyle Johnson frames Kyle's loss of faith in 'Cartmanland' (Cartman's undeserved happiness plus Kyle's hemorrhoid) as the logical and evidential problem of evil, then tests South Park's answers against real theodicies. He rejects the Book of Job answer and Chef/Edwards/Calvin's 'God benefits from our suffering,' examines greater-good and Augustine's free-will defense (only free acts are good), and notes the free-will defense fails for natural evil. He presents John Hick's soul-making theodicy, echoed by the show's Jesus ('life is about overcoming problems'), as covering both moral and natural evil, while conceding the sheer amount of evil still fuels the evidential problem.
- **Introducing Philosophy Through Pop Culture - From Socrates to South Park, Hume to House**, ch. 24 "“You Have to Believe in Something”" — Jason Eberl and Jennifer Vines use Battlestar Galactica's Baltar (skeptic) and Caprica Six/Roslin (believers) to debate God's existence, presenting Aquinas's five ways (unmoved mover, uncaused cause, governance) against a self-explaining big bang, and noting Baltar's self-serving faith resembles Pascal's Wager. They raise the problem of evil, answering with Augustine's free-will account of moral evil and Hick's soul-making theodicy (via Hume's faulty-architect analogy) for natural evil. Writing as a theist and an atheist, they argue meaning survives without God in human solidarity ('the gods shall lift those who lift each other'), and that faith and reason can share common ground.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 6 "4. Star Trek The Next Generation as Philosophy Gene Roddenberry’s Argument for Humanism" — Decker reads Star Trek: The Next Generation as Roddenberry's argument for secular humanism, using Corliss Lamont's ten propositions to frame a naturalistic, this-worldly ethic embodied by a militantly secular Enterprise crew. The recurring antagonist Q dramatizes tests of virtue and the Ring-of-Gyges question of power without consequences, while 'Who Watches the Watchers' and 'Devil's Due' stage humanist critiques of religion: Picard refuses to become a god to the Mintakans and dismantles Ardra's 'god of the gaps' con by showing the Ventaxians saved themselves. Decker invokes Hume's proportioning belief to evidence, Bacon's idols of the mind, and the Euthyphro to argue morality needs no divine command, framing Roddenberry's 'agonism' and the professional social ethics behind the Federation.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 28 "26. Midnight Mass as Philosophy The Problems with Religion" — The chapter argues that Mike Flanagan's Midnight Mass, through its atheist surrogate Riley, mounts a cumulative case for atheism. Riley's 'campfire' theory naturalistically explains religion's origins; Riley and Dr. Gunning's refusal to call Leeza's healing a miracle enacts Hume's argument against testimony for miracles; Dr. Gunning's EPP explanation of the 'vampires' rebuts methodological naturalism. Sheriff Hassan's grief over his wife voices the problem of evil (Mackie) against the free-will defense (Plantinga), while Erin's dying monologue endorses a Humean/Buddhist no-self bundle theory over the soul. Johnson argues the series treats faith as an epistemic and moral vice and holy books as dangerously interpretable.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 38 "35. Star Wars as Philosophy A Genealogy of the Force" — Eberl builds a genealogy of the Force across the Skywalker saga, using Augustine to reject the Manichaean light/dark dualism Yoda voices ('Luminous beings are we') in favor of evil as a privation of good and as 'inordinate desire' for temporal goods, which explains Anakin's fall through his refusal to let Padme die. He casts Palpatine as a Nietzschean who declares 'good is a point of view' and pursues will to power and the ubermensch, contrasting this with the Stoicism of Seneca and Yoda ('train yourself to let go of everything you fear to lose'). The sequel trilogy's disenchanted galaxy is read through Charles Taylor, and Rey and Ben's redemption shows evil defeated not by hatred but by rightly-ordered love ('Saving what we love').
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 64 "61. God’s Not Dead as Philosophy Trying to Prove God Exists" — The chapter evaluates the arguments college freshman Josh delivers in God's Not Dead and finds them to fail while the film demonizes atheists via caricature and the Christian persecution complex. It rebuts the Kalam cosmological argument (traced to al-Ghazali) with vacuum fluctuations and a quantum-foam explanation, shows the Big Bang refutes rather than confirms Genesis, and uses Russell's teapot and Hume's evidence proportioning on the burden of proof. Against Josh's 'without God everything is permissible' it applies Plato's Euthyphro to sink divine command theory, answers the free-will defense to the problem of evil, and closes that the film's fideism makes knowledge impossible.
- **The Palgrave Handbook of Popular Culture as Philosophy**, ch. 78 "74. Stephen Fry as Philosopher The Manic Socrates" — Innes casts Fry as a 'manic Socrates,' a satirical gadfly whose Horatian, Juvenalian and Menippean satire (Bit of Fry and Laurie sketches, the Gay Byrne 'bone cancer in children' God interview, the Intelligence Squared debate) mocks the military, social class and the Church to provoke the Socratic examined life. Fry's attack on theodicy is read through Plato's Euthyphro dilemma and the problem of evil, and his flight to Belgium and relationship with the 'luvvies' through Sartre's No Exit, the Look, and bad faith. Using Bourdieu's habitus, Innes concludes Fry 'praises the institutions with faint mockery,' seeking only moderate reform he can afford as a guest of the upper class rather than Socratic radical change.

### Faith and Reason

The relationship between faith and reason concerns how religious belief stands in relation to rational argument and evidence. Positions range from rationalism, which holds that belief must be justified by reason, to fideism, which maintains that faith is independent of or even opposed to rational proof, with many thinkers seeking a middle path in which faith and reason are complementary. The debate runs throughout the history of philosophy and theology, from medieval attempts to demonstrate God's existence to modern discussions of whether religious commitment can be reasonable without conclusive proof.

- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 62 "Unknown" — Taking the film's cafeteria religion seriously as 'Neo-pluralism', the chapter distinguishes four varieties of religious pluralism and finds each wanting: extreme pluralism dies by simple logic since of 100,000 religions many contradict one another; fundamental-teachings pluralism fails because the great religions differ on genuinely fundamental doctrines (Islam's personal God versus Theravada's non-theism versus the Trinity); cafeteria pluralism produces incoherent transplantings (reincarnation fits Hinduism but not Buddhism or Christianity) and lacks any rational justification short of wishful thinking; and Hick's Kantian transcendental pluralism posits an unintelligible, wholly unknowable Real while demanding the doublethink - highlighted by Alvin Plantinga - of continuing to hold beliefs one recognizes as literally false.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 63 "Unknown" — The chapter rebuts three pluralist objections to religious exclusivism: the 'equal fruits' argument confuses hard exclusivism with the common soft (inclusivist) form that freely admits salvation and authentic experience outside one tradition; the arrogance charge rests on a principle that would condemn every political and moral conviction held in the face of reasonable disagreement, and is self-refuting - Plantinga's 'philosophical tar baby'; and the arbitrariness charge begs the question, since pluralists assume rather than argue that no religion could have better evidence, which is precisely the point at issue between exclusivism and pluralism.
- **The Matrix and Philosophy - Welcome to the Desert of the Real**, ch. 77 "Unknown" — This section explains why the moral quest needs faith: because the ideal Matrix of morality seems powerless against the hard world built on separation and egotism, Kant postulates freedom, God, and immortality as what we must believe to remain faithful to our basic moral choice. It develops the first postulate - freedom: the essence of moral experience is anti-deterministic, scientific knowledge consists in deterministic explanation and so cannot know free will without reducing it to its opposite, therefore we must have faith in our power to choose - the creed of liberators on the way to 'the promised land of Zion, the kingdom of heaven on earth'.
- **Baseball and Philosophy - Thinking Outside the Batter's Box**, ch. 13 "Who Should Be Committed" — Thomas Senor argues that rooting for the perennially losing Cubs is rationally and morally on a par with religious commitment: genuine fandom, like faith, is loyalty that survives repeated disappointment (distinguished from the zealot's 'my team right or wrong' via the Portland Trailblazers' 'Jailblazers' era). Since beliefs and fan loyalties are not under direct voluntary control, he rereads Pascal's wager not as choosing to believe but as cultivating belief indirectly: attending Mass the way moving to Chicago and following the Cubs daily can make you a fan. The believer's epistemic optimism toward religious experience and the devout's second-order hope in dark times mirror the Cubs fan's springtime optimism, so neither Cubs fans nor the religious should be committed.
- **Woody Allen and Philosophy - You Mean My Whole Fallacy Is Wrong_**, ch. 12 "From Knowledge to Faith" — Lawler reads Crimes and Misdemeanors through Kant's problem of the Highest Good: Judah's unpunished murder of Dolores shows a world where the wicked prosper and the good (Cliff, the blind Ben) suffer, the scandal Job complains of, while Levy's suicide shows that a bare existentialist 'yes' to life fails without love. Kant's 'I had to deny knowledge to make room for faith' is applied to the film's two visions: the deterministic, dog-eat-dog world of science and Adam Smith's economic egoism (with Hobbes's war of all against all) is only appearance, not reality. Kant's gallows example shows Judah could have discovered authentic freedom by respecting Dolores's dignity rather than seeing 'the black eyes of an insect', and the postulates of freedom, God, and immortality ground Ben's not-really-blind faith — so it is Judah who is truly blind.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 7 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Editor Jorge Gracia's preface frames The Passion as a phenomenon that stirs people too deeply for indifference (a minister's fatal heart attack in a Brazilian cinema, reviews ranging from zero to five stars) and argues its religious stakes give its questions more bite than those of The Matrix or The Lord of the Rings. It lays out the book's five controversies: whether Christ had to suffer violently and what atonement means, whether the film is anti-Semitic, how faith relates to truth and to reading the Gospels as God's word, why Christ was killed, and whether Judas can be morally responsible for a betrayal God foreknew and redemption required. Gracia insists the collection takes no side and offers only a point of departure.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 9 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — McInerny argues Gibson's film works like Kierkegaard's indirect communication: its shocking graphic realism, against the tamed stations of the cross and serene crucifixes of Catholic churches, targets nominal Christians and forces each viewer to hear Jesus's 'I want you' and confront the scandal of the Incarnation rather than domesticate it. He reads the film alongside Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions as embroidery with no meaning apart from the Gospels, and invokes Aquinas on the Eucharist as the continuing memorial of the passion in which Christ is hidden under bread and wine. The film is 'a sign of contradiction' that, like Nietzsche's self-declared Antichrist, divides humanity into acceptance or rejection, so that efforts to keep religion within the bounds of reason alone must distort it.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 12 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Walls argues the controversy lies not in the gore but in who died on the cross and why, and shows Gibson weaving the three classic atonement theories: Christ crushing the serpent in Gethsemane as the Christus-Victor ransom (with Augustine's mousetrap image), the Isaiah 53 scourging and Gibson's own hand driving the nail as Anselm-style penal substitution in which the innocent dies so the guilty Barabbas in each of us goes free, and the transformed characters (Mary Magdalene, Simon of Cyrene, the good thief, the kneeling soldier) as Abelard's moral influence. Against Kant's charge that atonement is a superstitious substitute for moral transformation, he cites Swinburne and Quinn: pleading the atonement requires repentance, and the tens of thousands of reported conversions and confessions show it transforms lives. He concludes that any adequate account needs all three theories, objective payment and subjective transformation alike, and that atonement aims at mercy and reconciliation rather than retribution.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 18 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Kurtz, the secular humanist, argues the film is a political weapon of the Religious Right (O'Reilly, Dobson, Gingrich) that presents fantasy as fact: Gibson claims fidelity to the Gospels while borrowing torture scenes such as the bridge plunge and the savage flogging from Anne Catherine Emmerich's visions, whitewashing the historical Pilate, and erasing that Jesus, Mary, and the disciples were themselves Jews. Applying historical criticism, he contends the Gospels are anonymous, second- and third-hand missionary propaganda written forty to seventy years after Jesus, shaped by the rivalry between rabbinic Judaism and Gentile-seeking Jewish Christianity and canonized politically at Nicaea under Constantine. He concludes by defending the freedom of inquiry, skeptical scrutiny of all sacred texts, and the First Amendment's separation of church and state against the film's power to inflame anti-Semitism and the American culture war.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 20 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bronson argues Gibson's fixation on Jesus's suffering is not a Christian oddity but a deeply Jewish mystical one: using William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity), he reads the Gethsemane opening, where Jesus crushes Satan's serpent and receives a vision of the Father, as a classic mystical trial in the line of Moses at Sinai, Daniel's chariot-throne vision, Elijah's fiery ascent, John the Baptist, Paul's blinding light, and later the Kabbalah and Hasidic masters whose path to God runs through anguish. The Platonic Socrates of the Symposium and Phaedrus (wisdom arriving through the madness of love) and the medieval agreement of al-Ghazali, Maimonides, and Aquinas that reason cannot reach God frame his philosophy-versus-mysticism contrast, including the film's mother-son floorboard scene as love but not full mystical contact. The added scene where Pilate's wife tells him 'If you will not hear the truth, no one can tell you' shows Gibson siding with the mystical path to truth over Pilate's pragmatic one.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 23 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Jorge Gracia reframes the fidelity controversy as a problem in the theory of interpretation: Gibson had to make countless choices the Gospels leave silent (Christ's worn clothing, the Italian landscape, Jesus staring into the camera at the Last Supper, added scenes like Satan raging and demon children haunting Judas), so the film is unavoidably an interpretation. He surveys five criteria interpreters of Scripture have used — personal intuition (illustrated by Augustine's 'take and read' in the Confessions), ecclesial authority and the visions of nuns Emmerich and Agreda, sola scriptura, historical scholarship, and tradition (Aquinas's camp; Veronica's veil, the Shroud, the virgin Mary's prominence) — and argues each is inadequate alone because every one rests on prior theology. Hence disputes about the film are really disputes between theologies, and the film makes sense only within Gibson's Catholic view of Jesus as the Messiah announced by Isaiah 53.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 26 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Dallas Willard defends the film's excess of violence as its whole point: it visualizes human evil as beyond the remedies of education, law, or counseling (the route Plato and Aristotle tried), with Satan — the androgynous figure carrying the smug dwarf through the scourging crowd — explaining why only Christ's non-resistant embrace of the cross can break evil's grip. Against the passive reading of 'the Passion,' he argues Jesus 'played' his judges, deliberately laying down his life to inaugurate the kingdom of God. The argument leans on the hidden God (deus absconditus): God stays hidden, contra Sartre's 'no nature' self-creation and closer to Pico della Mirandola, so that we can freely make ourselves, which is also why demanding 'more evidence' misses what belief in God requires.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 29 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Paul Moser answers the objection that an all-loving God could not plan His Son's torture by arguing the cross is God's scandalous self-giving love: Jesus is no mere moral guru but the unique atoning sacrifice (the mad/Satanic/Son-of-God trilemma, 'he who delivered me to you has the greater sin'), and the crucifixion is God's grand reversal where self-giving love defeats death. He attacks the 'nice god' of natural theology as domesticating idolatry — God hides His plans from 'the wise and the intelligent' — and holds that we know God not by philosophical evidence but through Gethsemane-style filial obedience ('not my will but yours'), noting that Gibson himself appears in the film driving a nail, casting all of us as the crucifiers whom God forgives.
- **Mel Gibson's Passion and Philosophy - The Cross, the Questions, the Controversy**, ch. 33 "Mel Gibson’s Passion and Philosophy" — Bassham and Bagget observe that amid the film's unscriptural brutality Jesus never resists — he stops Peter's sword, heals Malchus's ear, and climbs back up for a second scourging — and ask whether this nonviolence can be rationally grounded without theological premises. They reject four classic readings of 'resist not evil' (Catholic counels-of-perfection, Schweitzer's interim ethics, Luther's penitential ethic, Tolstoy's absolute pacifism, noting Jesus himself used force against the money-changers) in favor of a hyperbole-plus-implicit-qualifier reading; then they show act utilitarianism licenses atrocities, rule utilitarianism at best yields an unpalatable absolute pacifism, and Kantian single-principle deontology preserves a right of self-defense Jesus's ethic calls us to lay aside — closing with a 'character model' of the Passion (duty vs freedom vs character) on which nonviolence is becoming the kind of person for whom violence is no longer an option, justified ultimately only by the cross.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 34 "The Man and His Faith" — Morris argues Daredevil is the rare mainstream hero with a religious interior life: raised nominally Catholic in Hell's Kitchen, his absent mother a nun who calls him 'a servant of God', he prays, thinks in religious categories, and complains to God like King David in the Psalms ('Why do the wicked prosper?'). Distinguishing mere outward religiosity from authentic faith, he proposes his 'Double Power Principle' - whatever has power for ill has equal power for good, religion included - and asks whether faith is blind like Matt Murdock or perceptive like his radar sense: a source of strength or of weakness for a costumed vigilante.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 35 "Faith and Fear" — Against Quentin Beck's claim that 'a man without fear is a man without faith', Morris argues the fear-based account of religion (Freud's) mistakes superstition for faith: authentic faith is a commitment of the heart rather than intellectual certitude, so the truly fearless are likely people of strong faith, as the martyrs show. He then distinguishes paralyzing self-referential 'fear of' from motivating 'fear that' (better called concern), concluding Daredevil genuinely is the Man Without Fear precisely because his deep-down faithfulness sustains him - he lives 'by faith and not by sight'.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 106 "Gloom, Doom, and Morality" — Works out naturalism's moral cost: no purpose behind our existence, no blueprint for life, Russell's hope that sensitive souls can love the tragic beauty of it anyway, and the Wilson-Ruse claim that ethics is "an illusion fobbed off on us by our genes," which loses its grip once seen through — like Macbeth's dagger. Against this it sets Kant's moral faith: morality makes rational sense only if we postulate God and immortality so virtue is finally rewarded, and the chapter concludes naturalism offers no deep basis for the life-risking duties a hero like Superman faces.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 108 "A Theological Basis for Super-Heroics" — Proposes that Christian theism's doctrines of heaven, hell and Christ's return resolve the truth/justice tension by grounding moral obligation in God's perfectly moral nature and guaranteeing that justice prevails. It rebuts Maggin's claim that faith in a power greater than ours breeds inaction: God works through human co-creators, so Superman still has a duty to do what he can, and the objective hope of ultimate justice is exactly the corrective that despairing Superman and tyrannical, fear-ruling Batman in Kingdom Come both lack.
- **Superheroes and Philosophy - Truth, Justice, and the Socratic Way**, ch. 109 "Hope and the Human Challenge" — Reads Superman's return — "Up in the sky!", the crowd hailing "the second coming of Superman" at the UN — as the enacted theology of Kingdom Come: hope in a greater power revives a world "hungry for hope" and draws the other heroes back to the fray. The Spectre's charge to the preacher Norman McCay, "you exist to give hope," voices the chapter's conclusion that a supernatural eschatology holds hope, truth, and individual responsibility together in a way naturalism's unyielding despair cannot.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 15 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Steven Lovell reads the Green Witch's enchantment in The Silver Chair (the sun is only a copy of the lamp, Aslan only a bigger cat, Narnia a children's tale) as Lewis's staging of the Freudian critique of religion, and answers that similarity cannot tell copy from original, that the genetic fallacy vitiates arguing from a belief's origin, and that Aslan is 'not safe,' so Christianity is hardly wish-fulfillment (Augustine's restless heart and Pascal's God-shaped hole point the other way). Puddleglum's stamping out the fire and vow to live 'as like a Narnian as I can even if there isn't any Narnia' is defended through Pascal's Wager and James's 'The Will to Believe': the reality of Narnia is a live, forced, and momentous option that may legitimately be decided on passional grounds.
- **The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy - The Lion, the Witch, and the Worldview**, ch. 35 "The Chronicles of Narnia and Philosophy" — Debunks the 'Anscombe legend' that Lewis abandoned rational apologetics for children's stories after his 1948 Socratic Club defeat by Elizabeth Anscombe over the argument that naturalism is self-refuting. It shows Lewis revised and expanded the argument in the 1960 Miracles, incorporating Anscombe's reasons/causes distinction, and kept writing apologetic essays, while the Professor's trilemma about Lucy (liar, lunatic, or truthful) mirrors the Trilemma of Mere Christianity and shows Narnia using logic, not fleeing it. It rejects A.N. Wilson's identification of the Green Witch with Anscombe and argues the Chronicles teach that prudence and faith are compatible virtues: Edmund's rationalizing, Trumpkin's honest skepticism, and Puzzle's blind trust in Shift all show that fideistic faith is a vice, not what Lewis asks of children.
- **Monty Python and Philosophy - Nudge Nudge, Think Think!**, ch. 17 "Prayer (A Euphemism for Butt-Kissing and Begging)" — Argues the Pythons' religious gags perform philosophy's preliminary job of challenging doctrine: the 'every sperm is sacred' family makes God a voyeur of contraception, the Life of Brian stoning (rocks flying each time anyone utters 'Jehovah') shows blasphemy law run absurd, and 'Christmas in Heaven' exposes heavenly reward as material compensation. Deploying Socrates and Plato — the Republic's ban on portraying pettiful gods, the Apology on why the virtuous need not fear death, and above all the Euthyphro — the chapter reads the witch-weighing and the Holy Hand Grenade as the ancient problem whether acts are just because God sanctions them, and the chaplain's toadying prayer against God's own 'don't grovel' as proof that sacrifice and prayer are bargaining a perfect being has no need of. The upshot is not atheism but the Socratic verdict that the mobs punishing blasphemy, not the mocked, are the real blasphemers.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 17 "U2 and Philosophy" — Merrick sets XTC's 'Dear God' - being 'just struck' that no loving, all-powerful God rules this world - against U2's laments ('Wake Up Dead Man', 'Peace on Earth', '40') and Bono's reading of the Psalms as the blues shouted at God: both share outrage, but U2 adds yearning for the redemption promised in 'the story about eternity' plus Jubilee 2000-style action against debt and AIDS. He then argues the atheistic reaction to evil cannot be reason-producing, since neither divine design nor unguided evolution would give us a faculty that 'just sees' atheism from evil, any more than one that just sees there is no plant life on Mars. If God instead made us so that outrage at evil can trigger conviction that he will make all right, U2's reaction - 'Grace makes beauty out of ugly things' - can be as reasonable as visual perception.
- **U2 and Philosophy - How to Decipher an Atomic Band**, ch. 24 "U2 and Philosophy" — Cleveland sorts the knowing and feeling of U2's lyrics ('Vertigo', 'Beautiful Day', 'Staring at the Sun', 'Daddy's Gonna Pay for Your Crash Car') into Russell's varieties of knowledge - propositional, acquaintance, know-how - and argues that the feeling U2 champions against thought is knowledge by acquaintance: direct, concept-free awareness that, in religious cases, just is Jamesian mystical revelation as against revelation as a set of propositional truths, which is why Bono tells his father he 'hears something back from the silence' rather than holding doctrines. James supplies both the view that feeling is the deeper source of religion and the pragmatist answer to the problem of origins - 'by their fruits ye shall know them', so religious feeling is vindicated by moral transformation. Hume's slave-of-the-passions thesis explains why such feeling, not inert moral knowledge, moves Bono's social justice work: 'God is love, and as much as I respond... in acting in that love, that's my religion'.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 13 "Inquiry, Hard Work, and Progress" — Jacoby reads Stan Marsh as W.K. Clifford's ethics of belief in action: from 'All About the Mormons' ('you better have something to back it up') to 'The Biggest Douche in the Universe,' Stan insists the burden of proof lies with claimants and that faith used as a fallback is no evidence at all. 'Cartmanland' and the story of Job serve to criticize Pascal's Wager — a good God would not eternally torment the virtuous nonbeliever, and the Wager simply assumes its afterlife payoff — while the harms of Miss Information's holistic healers, David Blaine's cult suicide, and Scientology show Clifford was right that comforting unsupported beliefs weaken minds and, as Stan tells John Edward, slow down the progress of all mankind.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 21 "Introduction" — Frames Part IV's philosophy of religion chapters. Johnson's chapter sets Cartman's million-dollar theme park against God's goodness, with South Park characters giving answers echoing Calvin, Hick, and Job; Gallagher's uses Rose's 'I just know' on Lost and Aquinas' distinctions between knowledge, opinion, and faith to argue that faith is not knowledge; and Eberl and Vines' uses Battlestar Galactica's Cylon monotheism versus Colonial religion and atheism to ask whether God can be proven, whether evil disproves him, and whether life is meaningful without God.
- **South Park and Philosophy - Bigger, Longer, and More Penetrating**, ch. 23 "To Know … and Believe" — Gallagher reads Lost's Rose through Aquinas: faith is 'mid-way between knowledge and opinion,' sharing the certainty of episteme and the imperfection of doxa, so Rose's 'I just know' about Bernard's survival and her island cure confuses what she believes with what she knows. Aquinas' five ways ground natural knowledge that God exists, and the castaways' failures are diagnosed as sins against faith — Charlie's despair is acedia while Rose's certainty is the presumption (praesumptio) of elevating faith to demonstrated knowledge; the lesson is that faith perfects reason without replacing it.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — Bryan McHenry asks whether manipulating religious belief for political ends is ever moral, using Adama's motivational lie about Earth, Roslin's Pythia-driven 'dying leader' campaign (compared with George W. Bush's faith-based politics), and the Cylons' evangelical monotheism aimed at scaring Baltar into conversion. Machiavelli's Prince licenses rulers who use a religion they do not share, and the chapter judges Adama's hope-based use of the Earth myth and Roslin's uniting religiosity as essentially moral while the Cylons wield faith as a coercive weapon. Madison's Enlightenment demand that religion be directed by reason and conviction rather than force supplies the standard the fear-based Cylon conversion of Baltar fails.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Mission Accomplished or Mission Frakked Up_**, ch. 41 "So Say We All" — Richard Berger reads the 're-imagined' series through Bakhtin's dialogism: Moore's show is not a GINO remake but a polyphonic dialogue with the 1978 series and its own sources, including the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greek myth and fan fiction. That polyphony appears on screen as a spectrum of belief, from Baltar's militant atheism argued over with Number Six's fundamentalism, a staging of the Dawkins-Hitchens debate in which the two extremes prove close enough for conversion, to Roslin's prophetic politics. The chapter argues the reboot is 'more Battlestar Galactica' because it makes the original's latent religious debates explicit.
- **The Golden Compass and Philosophy - God Bites the Dust**, ch. 14 "The Golden Compass and Philosophy" — Yuen reads the silver guillotine of intercision against infant circumcision: both cut unconsenting children as acts of faith, Mrs. Coulter's belief that severing dæmons prevents original sin mirroring the Abrahamic covenant of Genesis 17. Deploying W.K. Clifford's shipowner ('It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone to believe anything upon insufficient evidence') and Hume's claim that belief is an involuntary feeling no will can command, he argues that the real moral fault lies in acting on uninvestigated beliefs in ways that harm others, while Mrs. Coulter's non-consensual experiments on kidnapped children are wrong independently of what she believes. He concludes that if cutting Pantalaimon from Lyra is wrong, circumcision is wrong for the same reasons though less severely, at worst as irresponsible as exposing a child to chicken pox.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 21 "Do You Believe It" — Patrick Tiernan argues that Fenway fandom is a genuine religion: William James's four marks of mystical experience (ineffability, noetic quality, transiency, passivity) map onto memories of Buckner's error and Dave Roberts's steal, and Peter Berger's 'signals of transcendence' structure the rituals of Truck Day, the hopes of spring training, the damnation of Bucky Dent and Johnny Damon, and the humor of 'Cowboy Up.' He roots the Curse of the Bambino in New England's Puritan-Calvinist legacy of persecution and original sin (Frazee's sale of Ruth), then deploys Hume's account of superstition from 'Of Superstition and Enthusiasm' to deflate the exorcism rituals fans actually performed, from a Sox hat on Everest to dredging for Ruth's piano, as post hoc fallacies. Even so, the rituals reveal the human need for religious practice, and Maslow's peak experience renders the 2004 comeback a brush with the sacred, so the Faithful believe because they have to.
- **The Red Sox and Philosophy - Green Monster Meditations**, ch. 24 "Breaking the Eighth Commandment" — Joel Cade maps baseball's traditionalist-versus-sabermetric war onto the faith-and-reason debate: Joe Morgan's refusal to even read Moneyball repeats Tertullian's fideism, Ted Williams's Science of Hitting exemplifies Augustine's 'faith seeking understanding,' and Wade Boggs's game-day chicken ritual completes his rational hitting exactly as Aquinas says faith completes reason. Theo Epstein's 2004 front office fused the models under the motto 'understanding justifies faith,' using statistics to discover when supposedly obsolete traditional weapons like the stolen base actually work, which is why the seemingly anti-Moneyball Dave Roberts trade paid off in The Steal against Mariano Rivera in Game Four of the ALCS. The chapter closes with the joke that Augustine, who stole pears, would bless stealing second: reconciling faith and reason is how the Sox reversed the Curse, and maybe how faith- and reason-guided people might reconcile.
- **The Onion and Philosophy - Fake News Story True, Alleges Indignant Area Professor**, ch. 28 "Get Serious" — David Kyle Johnson takes Nietzsche's suggestion that God is slowly dying and reads The Onion's religion stories — the faith healer who loses a patient during a routine miracle, Kansas fundamentalists lobbying to overturn the Second Law of Thermodynamics, and 'Evangelical Scientists Refute Gravity With New Intelligent Falling Theory' — as evidence of secularization. He splits blind faith (irrational belief despite evidence, as with Bush's 'Blind-Faith-Based Initiatives') from genuine faith as belief without sufficient evidence, arguing religion does science badly whenever it shields creationism from falsification. But science rests on unproven assumptions too, he shows via Hume's problem of induction, Descartes' skeptical problem, and Wittgenstein's charge that naming a 'strong nuclear force' explains no more than God pushing things down. Ockham's razor then decides for atheism — an unexplained universe is simpler than God plus a universe — though William James's will to believe leaves a door open for faith where evidence is impossible, qualified by Clifford's warning that beliefs likely to harm others are never permissible.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 16 "Hope" — Beck reads Snakes & Arrows as popular Epicureanism delivered by Lucretius' method: just as De Rerum Natura puts honey on the rim of the cup so Romans swallow philosophical medicine disguised as poetry, Rush's melodies smuggle reflection on pain, luck, and religion past listeners who think they are just rocking, with repeated choruses doing the work of Epicurean prolepsis. The random swerve of atoms explains 'The Larger Bowl''s unequal fortunes ('Some are blessed and some are cursed'), while the shore-watcher's relief at another's shipwreck and the concertgoer's pleasure exemplify Epicurean ataraxia. 'Faithless' and 'Armor and Sword' ('Pray and pass the ammunition') echo Lucretius' trampling of superstitious religio, and the chapter closes with Philodemus' Herculaneum scroll: don't fear god, don't worry about death.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 18 "Sweet Miracles of (Secular) Faith, Hope, and Love" — Florek reconstructs Peart's ethics as Aristotelian virtue ethics: aiming at eudaimonia rather than feeling good, 'Freewill' chooses autonomy and responsibility as virtues, and 'Vital Signs' adds persistence and courage ('courageous convictions will drag the dream into existence'), with a compassionate expansion toward ordinary sufferers in 'Distant Early Warning', 'Red Sector A' ('I must help my mother stand up straight'), and 'Everyday Glory'. Peart's existential consciousness then confronts finitude ('Time Stand Still', the fading memory of 'Vapor Trail'), contingency ('Roll the Bones' — 'Why does it happen? Because it happens'), and the absurd of Sartre and Camus ('The Stars Look Down' — an indifferent universe that answers nothing). The 1997-98 tragedies turn this existential consciousness tragic, and the post-tragic resolution of Vapor Trails and 'Faithless' is a secular faith in hope and love — Peart's answer to 1 Corinthians 13 without God — grounded in being loved by Carrie Nuttall.
- **Rush and Philosophy - Heart and Mind United**, ch. 27 "Humanism Needs Its Evangelists, Too" — Treats Snakes & Arrows ('Far Cry,' 'Armor and Sword,' 'Faithless') as secular humanism stung by resurgent fundamentalism, and reads Peart's revolutionary trilogy — 'Beneath, Between and Behind,' 'Bastille Day,' 'A Farewell to Kings' — as Enlightenment humanism already anxious about its own decline. The core argument is rhetorical: Rush deliberately clothes humanist content in sacred and mystical language ('Something for Nothing''s Lord's Prayer motif, 'Jacob's Ladder''s storm read through Spinoza's God-as-nature and the experience of the sublime) because humanism needs evangelists who inspire wonder rather than mere argument.
- **Halo and Philosophy - Intellect Evolved**, ch. 20 "Videogame Apocalypses and Secularism" — Rachel Wagner, Tyler DeHaven, and Chris Hendrickson argue Halo satisfies the Society of Biblical Literature definition of apocalypse: revelatory narrative, otherworldly mediators (Cortana, 343 Guilty Spark), predetermined eschatology, with Master Chief as a Davidic messiah whose name John-117 echoes the Gospel of John. The Covenant's Tower-of-Babel hubris versus human secularism, and the Flood read through the Book of Enoch's Watchers, turn the story into a critique of rampant consumption and blind religion. Where traditional apocalypses are quietist—God the programmer's deterministic script, salvation not depending on human action—Halo's procedural rhetoric hands agency to the player as messiah, and the chapter closes asking whether videogame apocalypse offers only temporary, magic-circle comfort for secular angst in a morally relativist age.
- **Inception and Philosophy - Ideas to Die For**, ch. 29 "Risks of Faith" — Ringer argues inception is philosophically impossible because dream consciousness lacks genuine apperception, the filling-in of an external world that structures waking experience, so Cobb's team must instead manufacture 'because of' motives, like the planted 528-491 safe combination, that let Fischer mistake his own dream for waking life. Working with the phenomenology of everyday consciousness, perception versus apperception and the coffee-cup example, he reads the totem as a sacred, untouchable object through which private revelation of reality is mediated. Tillich's distinction between faith as ultimate concern and mere evidential belief then diagnoses Mal: by locking the totem in the safe and choosing the dream world as her reality she commits idolatry, a misplaced faith whose price is her suicide.
- **Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy - The Real and the Cereal**, ch. 33 "Chuck Klosterman and Philosophy" — Vannatta reads Klosterman's born-again pop culture — the Left Behind novels, Victory TV's Steven, Kurt Warner's Super Bowl, Jesus Camp — as living Puritan Calvinism: original sin (Klosterman's cruel third-graders), justification by faith alone, unmediated access to God ('every man was his own priest'), and predestination that leaves uncertain whether our actions matter in the divine equation. The chapter's pivot is truth versus peace: Puritan-born-again certainty sacrifices peace for antecedent truth, from the 1675 Massachusetts settlements to Robertson and Falwell on 9/11. Against this Vannatta sets the pragmatist alternative — truth as the outcome of communal inquiry in service of peaceful living — recasting God as the web of relationships and dissolving his own childhood camp's contradiction between 'I'm Third' and its cult of competition.
- **The Walking Dead and Philosophy - Zombie Apocalypse Now**, ch. 27 "The Walking Dead and Philosophy" — Greeley argues the zombie crystallizes specifically modern fears: with Aristotle and Aquinas he reads walkers as humans stripped of their essential nature and potential, which Rick's uncustomary eulogies ('I'm sorry this happened to you') acknowledge. Following Philippe Aries, he ties modern death anxiety to urbanization, hidden cemeteries, and the loss of religious consolation, citing the CDC arc where Jenner's science offers only a self-destruct and Jacqui falls back on 'the wrath of God.' Rousseau's thesis that society corrupts explains why the survivors in the woods seem more alive — warlord Guillermo turns out to be protecting nursing-home patients and pizza-deliverer Glenn becomes a hero — while the 'Bradbury's Storewide Sale' sign, the Walmart trampling, and Fromm's shift from utopias to dystopias suggest the shuffling horde is an image of our own consumerist, distracted, dehumanized modernity.
- **Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy - Awaken the Social Assassin Within**, ch. 29 "Curb Your Enthusiasm and Philosophy" — Takes the show's title as a literal ethical command and asks which senses of enthusiasm should be curbed, tracing the concept's history: Plato's muse-inspired poet in the Ion and Apology, the early Christian Enthusiasts, Wesley and Shaftesbury's attempts to separate good from bad enthusiasm, and the Enlightenment ridicule of Locke and Hume, for whom enthusiasm meant fanaticism, a pretended insight into the supernatural that Larry is right to mock. Kant gets the most sustained treatment: enthusiasts of friendship, religion, or patriotism inflame a good principle beyond its proper degree, which explains Larry's failure as a friend, while 'aesthetic enthusiasm,' the sublime 'idea of good with affect' before the morally good, is valuable, and Larry's single moment of it comes when the Arizona preacher's sermon on moral goodness sends him flying back to Los Angeles to donate his kidney to Richard Lewis. The verdict: curb fanatic and inauthentic enthusiasm (Ted Danson's everything-is-heaven), keep ordinary resoluteness and aesthetic enthusiasm, and accept that a society needs a few Larrys, the Socratic fools who yell for society.
- **Frankenstein and Philosophy - The Shocking Truth**, ch. 40 "Frankenstein and Philosophy" — Trip McCrossin casts the creature as a modern Job: repeatedly and unreasonably mistreated by the De Laceys, the rustic whose child he saved, and Victor despite his benevolence, he cries 'This was then the reward of my benevolence!' - but unlike Job he loses faith, because his problem of evil is secular, justifying not 'the Ways of God to Man' but 'the Ways of Man to monsters.' The chapter traces the problem from Job and Paradise Lost through Bayle's defense of faith over reason and the Optimists' 'best of all possible worlds,' whose credibility drowned with the 1755 Lisbon earthquake, setting Rousseau against Voltaire: Rousseau's Emile ('All is good leaving the hands of the author of things') demands that we make evil intelligible through self-knowledge, while Candide counsels tending our garden. The creature embodies Rousseau's line - 'I was benevolent and good; misery made me a fiend' - yet ends in self-abhorring remorse over Victor's death, leaving open whether self-knowledge can ever answer unreasonable suffering.
- **The Devil and Philosophy - The Nature of His Game**, ch. 40 "The Devil and Philosophy" — Michael Versteeg and Adam Barkman explain C.S. Lewis's Screwtape doctrine that the Devil conquers minds not by argument but by unreason, since human reason fights on God's side. They unpack Screwtape's tactics as textbook fallacies: jargon like 'religious phase' working as a red herring, dismissing Christianity out of boredom as a non sequitur, the 'Historical Point of View' as the chronological snobbery that cuts generations off from the past, and the endless loop of pride about one's humility as an infinite regress that paralyzes thought. Because reason is, for Lewis, the road toward Heaven, the Devil's highway to Hell is built entirely of bad logic.
- **Leonard Cohen and Philosophy - Various Positions**, ch. 33 "Leonard Cohen and Philosophy" — Timothy P. Jackson argues Cohen is the closest thing today to a Biblical prophet - a 'strong poet' in Harold Bloom's sense, wearing a coat of many colors drawn from Judaism, Christianity, Buddhism, Taoism, and Sufism, sustained by an 'epistemic humility' that lives between dogmatism and doubt. Cohen leads Christian texts back to their Hebraic origins, critiques every arrogant nationalism including Israel (Book of Mercy, psalm 27), and gave his Tel Aviv concert profits to Israeli-Palestinian reconciliation. Jackson reads Cohen's equanimity at his business manager's embezzlement trial as forgiveness overcoming resentment, weighs his hesed/agape-style unconditional love against his failures in erotic love, and ends with Cohen's reticence about personal immortality - a prophet for the living.
- **Homeland and Philosophy - For Your Minds Only**, ch. 7 "Homeland and Philosophy" — Robert Arp's introduction explains that Homeland's jihadist material (Nazir, Hamid, Brody, 9/11) drew him in and previews the book's philosophizing with a sample argument: whether morality needs God. He argues jihadists ground ethics in Allah's commands, but since faith defies rational proof, competing conceptions of God conflict, and scripture (Abraham and Isaac, the Flood, the Egyptian firstborn, the genocide commands in 1 Samuel and Hosea) has God commanding atrocities, either the terrorists' God is evil or morality is better grounded in reason without God. The dilemma he poses - a good God would not command 9/11, so the command conception or God's goodness must go - is the Euthyphro structure applied to terrorism.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 15 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter asks whether Boyd's survival of Raylan's bullet in the premiere was a genuine sign from God: the atheist invokes Ockham's Razor and the promise of a naturalistic explanation, while the theist replies that a world-creating God would act through the laws of nature, making such explanations neutral rather than negative evidence. It then applies William James's pragmatist standard from his study of mystical experience - judge the sign by the fruits of the Spirit (Galatians' love, joy, peace, self-control) it bears - to Boyd's prison ministry, his urging Raylan to forgive Arlo, and his meth-lab crusade. Despite Boyd's eventual apostasy after Bo murders his congregation, the author concludes he passes James's test, since faith is a maintained journey that can be lost, and the born-again Boyd still struggles - like Jacob becoming Israel - rather than scheming coldly.
- **Justified and Philosophy - Shoot First, Think Later**, ch. 16 "Justified and Philosophy" — The chapter reads preacher Billy St. Cyr's snake-handling through Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: like Abraham, Billy performs the absurd double movement - fully resigning himself to dying by rattlesnake while believing he will be spared - which is why Boyd Crowder, who abandoned faith for Hegel's objective rational certainty, can neither buy him out nor understand him. Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical explains why Billy and Abraham may set obedience to God above self-preservation and social morality, while Boyd's showdown in 'Truth and Consequences', where he hands Billy an un-milked rattlesnake, exposes that Billy's certainty has curdled into the hubris de Silentio warns against, so Billy is no Abraham. De Silentio's three marks - love, humility, no desire to instruct others - separate genuine faith from cult leaders and violent extremists.
- **Dracula and Philosophy - Dying to Know**, ch. 35 "Dracula and Philosophy" — Ketcham's invented chronicle sends Dracula and a village rabbi to 1194 Cairo to interrogate Maimonides: can resurrection - one of the thirteen principles of faith - apply to a soulless undead being, and is his blood-drinking a divinely imposed penance? Maimonides answers from the Guide for the Perplexed and the Letter on Resurrection, offering that intelligence is the essence of the soul yet judging the Count a likely trickster, while Dracula presses that no scientific evidence of dust becoming flesh exists. The diarist closes with the heretical worry that Maimonidean resurrection - no food, drink, or sex - might itself be a kind of undeath.
- **Downton Abbey and Philosophy - Thinking in That Manor**, ch. 35 "21. God-Talk at the Abbey" — Samuel Lumpenhouwer takes the Abbey's religious silences - Anna's 'we'll only fall out,' Alfred's baffled 'What?' at transubstantiation, and the Catholic baptism fight over baby Sybbie - and brings in Aquinas to make God-talk possible. Reason alone can know that God exists (the argument from design through final causes like the candle flame, carefully distinguished from Paley's watchmaker), revelation grasped by faith tells us God is personal, and human words reach God only analogically, as when Matthew calls God 'Father' at Lavinia's grave, or by way of negation. Against Carson's 'it is not our place to reason why' about Sybil's death, the chapter insists that mystery limits rather than excuses reason, ending with Aquinas's 'straw' and the Abbey's three attitudes: confident belief, searching doubt, and keep-it-private spirituality.
- **The Ultimate Walking Dead and Philosophy - Hungry for More**, ch. 12 "1. Reading the Signs" — Di Bernardo reads the religious language of The Walking Dead as sustained irony - a 'doubleness of sense' - arguing that the walkers, churches, and signs comment critically on faith rather than endorse it. He tracks the church scenes (the Southern Baptist church of 2.1 'What Lies Ahead' with its timed bells and sitting-dead congregation, Gabriel's Saint Sarah's where Maggie answers that it is 'just four walls and a roof'), the ambiguous 'sanctuary' and Terminus signs, and the comic-book Jesus (Paul Monroe) as a machine-gun savior, concluding that the scriptural promise of eternal life through consuming flesh and blood yields only undead life. Against Epicurus's consolation that death is nothing to us, and in the shadow of Nietzsche's madman announcing the death of God, the chapter warns against investing absolute trust in any signs - religious or secular - a warning capped by Rick biting out Joe's throat as his own 'day of reckoning.'
- **The Princess Bride and Philosophy - Inconceivable!**, ch. 28 "15. It Would Take a Miracle!" — Barkman and Käärid ask whether Miracle Max's revival of 'mostly dead' Westley is a miracle, staging David Hume - for whom a violation of natural law is never more credible than mistaken or lying testimony, so Hume in Florin would call Max a deceiver and Inigo and Fezzik barbarous dupes - against C.S. Lewis, for whom a miracle is a new, unpredictable element introduced into nature rather than a violation of it. They add puzzles neither philosopher addresses: whether Westley was truly dead, whether a 'rotten miracle' would still count, and why Max's miracles seem to require 'unshattered' confidence, concluding that Florin's miracles are person-dependent in a way Hume's skepticism and Lewis's supernaturalism both miss.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 29 "14. Louis C.K.’s God" — Argues Louis's God material is a negativistic, immanent critique of religion in Adorno's sense of 'damaged human life': the 'God' episode's crucifixion doctor who makes young Louie hammer a nail shows faith wrecking children with guilt until his mother's skeptical 'malarkey' speech and donuts rescue him. His SNL 'did you look in the downstairs bathroom?' bit becomes an evidentialist ethics of belief aimed at over-certain atheists, his 'shitty girlfriend' Abraham bit and body/food/shopping jokes illustrate Tillich's functionalist test of what we treat with ultimate concern (echoing David Foster Wallace's 'everybody worships'), and the chapter closes that comedy here works like Ignatian Catholic reflection, keeping faith and doubt together.
- **Louis C.K. and Philosophy - You Don't Get to Be Bored**, ch. 30 "15. God Started in 1983" — Uses the SNL bit of a God who has been standing in a room since 1983 to argue Louis is an 'apathetic agnostic': he cannot know whether God exists, lambastes atheists who claim certainty, and thinks the question barely matters for our lives. The chapter weighs Pascal's Wager against Epicurus's four-part cure ('Don't fear god, don't worry about death'), faults Louis's 'downstairs bathroom' bit for putting the burden of proof on atheists, reads the 'Heaven' glory-hole sketch through Clifford's ethics of belief as a rejection of faith without evidence, and ends with Louie's mother's line that you have to be good to people whether or not God is watching.
- **The Ultimate Game of Thrones and Philosophy - You Think or Die**, ch. 32 "18. Gods and Beetles" — Cooper takes Jaime's challenge to Catelyn - 'if your gods are real and just, why is the world so full of injustice?' - as the problem of evil and tests three Westerosi theologies. Melisandre's Manichean divine patronage fails by Augustine's argument that evil is no rival substance but a corruption in the creature; Ockham's voluntarism, symbolized by cousin Orson smashing beetles while Tyrion watches in dread, is rebuffed by Suarez and by Tyrion's own 'why are all the gods such vicious c--ts?'; and the humanist free-will defense in Catelyn's reply ('evil exists because of men like you'), rooted in Augustine and developed by Plantinga, answers Jaime but leaves Ivan Karamazov's problem of suffering children - met only by existential responses like Dorne's 'we don't hurt little girls.'
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 16 "4. Is it God or the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown" — Using It's the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown (1966), the chapter asks whether belief without evidence can be rational, contrasting the classic evidentialist view (rational beliefs must be basic or derived from basics, in the tradition of Locke and Hume) with Alvin Plantinga's properly basic beliefs and a virtue theory of rational belief built on Aristotle-style intellectual virtues like humility, courage, and charity. Linus fails on every account - he insulates himself from counterevidence ('If you really are a fake, don't tell me'), lets the belief cost him friends and trick-or-treating, and never updates after the Pumpkin's no-show - while Sally's pumpkin-patch vigil shows rationality as a balance of evidence, value, and risk. The upshot: God-belief formed responsibly within a trusting community can be rational in a way Linus's solitary, evidence-dodging Pumpkin faith cannot.
- **Peanuts and Philosophy - You're a Wise Man, Charlie Brown!**, ch. 25 "11. The Sincerity of St. Linus" — The chapter argues Linus confuses sincere faith with indubitable certainty: on the Thomistic model (faith as chosen propositional belief held with knowledge-like certainty, between opinion and knowledge), his fateful slip into 'if the Great Pumpkin comes' wrecks his faith, turning doubt into hypocrisy. Against this it deploys doxastic involuntarism - we cannot simply choose to believe, as his failed attempts to psych himself up ('I believed with every fiber of my being') show - and philosophers like Daniel Howard-Snyder who allow faith without belief: what Linus does, staying in the patch and risking hypothermia and ridicule while doubting, is faith as action in the face of doubt. Hence the closing paradox: where there is certainty there is no room for faith, and Linus's patch only became sincere once doubt crept in.
- **Deadpool and Philosophy - My Common Sense Is Tingling**, ch. 11 "2. Deadpool the Dark Angel" — Christopher Ketcham playfully argues that Deadpool's fourth-wall escapes show he exists partly in dimensions we cannot experience, read through string theory's ten curled dimensions and Maimonides's ten realms of angels—beings of form without matter—in the Mishneh Torah. Since only God and angels traverse those hidden dimensions, Deadpool must be an angel, likely a dark one, whose shuttling between realms explains his vacillation between mercenary violence and saving souls. Ezekiel's chariot vision, the vengeful Hebrew Bible God, and massless dark matter are recruited as supporting evidence for this deadpan-earnest science-and-scripture argument.
- **Iron Man vs. Captain America and Philosophy - Give Me Liberty or Keep Me Safe**, ch. 31 "20. There’s Only One God, Ma’am" — Holt takes Captain America's line 'There's only one God, ma'am' and asks how Christian monotheism survives in a universe where Thor, Odin and the One-above-all really exist, answering with henotheism - Moses's 'I am', Jacob's household idols, and the Living Tribunal as the merely representative 'biggest kid in the playground' of a supreme Creator whose 'only weapon is love'. He then deploys Hume's Natural History of Religion, where the ignorant multitude progress from polytheism to monotheism, to explain why Cap dismisses Asgardians as superstition Thor says is 'no stranger' than his Sunday churchgoing, while Hume's own trajectory - all religion as vulgar superstition - lands instead in the post-religious rationalism of Tony Stark's 'I prefer fact to fantasy' futurism, which the Goddess calls a soul imprisoned in the ice of rationalism.
- **Stranger Things and Philosophy - Thus Spake the Demogorgon**, ch. 30 "16. Gotta Have Faith" — Winters asks what faith is when the Party risks burning and becoming demodog chow so Eleven can close the gate: after arguing via George Michael and the talisman-free tunnels that faith need not be religious, he tests Bishop's models of faith against 'The Gate' (the affective and secular hope models fit; the belief and trust models fail because everyone has seen the Mind Flayer's work on Will). Hume's account that causation is never observed, only habituated, explains the Party's hope that heat will drive the Mind Flayer from Will and that Christmas lights will reach him, and Kierkegaard's teleological suspension of the ethical and knight of faith frame Eleven's willingness to die against the absurd, since aligning her life with friendship's higher purpose is what makes it meaningful.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 31 "Damned If You Do, and Damned If You Don’t" — McHenry reads the re-imagined series as a holy-war allegory in which both sides weaponize religion, then asks whether that manipulation is ever moral. Adama's lie about Earth is Machiavellian statecraft (with Foucault's point that privileged knowledge holds power), yet defended as serving the greater good, while Roslin's Pythia-based campaign contrasts with Bush's faith-based fear politics. The Cylons emerge as evangelical fundamentalists whose conversion of Baltar through inner Number Six runs on fear, exactly what Madison's case for religious liberty forbids. The chapter concludes the show's own gods have sided with the Colonials.
- **Battlestar Galactica and Philosophy - Knowledge Here Begins Out There**, ch. 41 "So Say We All" — Berger deploys Bakhtin's dialogism to answer the 'GINO' charge: the re-imagined series is not a betrayal of Larson's show but a heteroglossic utterance in an ongoing conversation that already included the Book of Mormon, von Daniken's Chariots of the Gods, Greco-Roman myth, and later fanfic and blogs, with each version sourcing its sources' sources. The 2003 series is read as polyphonic about belief: skeptic Adama, devout Number Six, the messianic convert Baltar, and Dawkins/Hitchens-style atheist critiques of fundamentalism are all given equal voice. The show's value lies in inviting debate across the whole continuum of belief rather than preaching a position.
- **The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy - Rock, Paper, Scissors, Aristotle, Locke**, ch. 20 "The Big Bang Theory and Philosophy" — Barkman and Kowalski mine the Cooper household for science-and-religion lessons: Mary's 'Third-World demon' diagnosis of Raj raises religious diversity (exclusivism, inclusivism, pluralism), her 'But intelligently designed by a creator, right?' prompts an assessment of Behe's irreducible complexity against Darwinian counterexamples like the flagellum-turned-syringe and a warning against god-of-the-gaps reasoning.
